title: I built db-studio, a free, open-source database studio you can run with npx
description:
I'm Hüsam, a software engineer in Istanbul and the solo developer behind db-studio. It's a free, open-source database studio you can run locally with one command.

npx db-studio

Every database. One studio.

Browse tables, edit records, run queries, and explore schema diagrams in the same app. There's also a desktop app if you prefer a dedicated window.

Start with your existing database

Run the command from your project directory. db-studio looks for a DATABASE_URL in your project's .env file or environment. If it doesn't find one, you can paste a connection URL on the Connect page.

Open the local address printed in the terminal. You don't need to create a hosted account.

Connections are saved locally, and the CLI and desktop app share the same list. Each browser tab keeps its own connection, so you can work with different databases side by side.

Edit data like a spreadsheet

The latest update adds these editing workflows:

  • Select a range of cells, copy it with headers, and paste cells from a spreadsheet.
  • Review unsaved edits, revert a single cell, or undo with Cmd/Ctrl+Z.
  • Choose explicitly between NULL, empty text, and a column's default value.
  • Copy a row as JSON or a SQL INSERT statement.
  • Duplicate a row from its menu.

Editing and schema capabilities depend on the engine. For example, ClickHouse tables are read-only in the grid, while explicit mutations remain available in the query editor. A saved connection can also open read-only when its engine supports it.

Work across nine database engines

db-studio supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, MongoDB, SQLite, Redis, DuckDB, Oracle, and ClickHouse.

You can also connect to MariaDB, CockroachDB, TiDB, Turso/libSQL, and Cloudflare D1 through their supported engines.

The interface follows the database's data model. MongoDB has collections, and Redis has key types. Available operations vary with the database.

Queries, schemas, and optional AI

The query editor has syntax highlighting and autocomplete. You can save queries and inspect results as a table or JSON. Import and export support CSV, Excel, and JSON.

For relational databases, schema diagrams help you see how tables connect. You can also browse related records through foreign keys.

AI assistance is optional and uses your own provider key. It can help write, explain, optimize, or fix queries.

Both screenshots show the real app running against a local demo database.

Try it and tell me what needs work

db-studio is free under Apache 2.0. I build and maintain the database adapters, API, interface, CLI, and desktop app. Contributions and bug reports are welcome.

Website and documentation · Source code

Which database would you try first, and what's one task you'd want db-studio to make easier?

title: From Variables to Loops: First Deep Dive into Python Fundamentals
description:
**Introduction: The Building Blocks of Code

Every massive data engineering pipeline , whether ingesting thousands of e-commerce records or a distributed Spark job—starts with the exact same primitive building blocks: variables, data types, and control flow.

The Goal: A quick breakdown of how mastering variables, operators, typecasting, conditionals, and loops forms the foundation of every backend script you will ever write.

Section 1: Variables & Typecasting (Storing State)

The Concept: Variables are containers for data, but in Python, type awareness is everything.

The DE Context: Talk about how casting strings to integers or handling floats correctly matters when parsing raw JSON payloads from an API. A simple type mismatch can crash a 10,00-row ingestion job!

Section 2: Control Flow (Making Decisions)

The Concept: if, elif, and else statements.

The DE Context: How conditional logic is used in data cleaning—for example: If a transaction amount is negative, flag it as corrupt; else, pass it to the transformation stage.

Section 3: Loops (Automating Repetition)

The Concept: for loops and while loops iterating over collections.

The DE Context: Why loops are the heartbeat of batch data processing. Iterating through lists of API response pages or processing rows of a dataset before loading them into PostgreSQL.

Conclusion: The Journey Ahead

You don't need to know advanced machine learning on day one. You just need to master how to loop through data cleanly.

**

title: How to Build an AI Agent That Doesn't Go Off the Rails — The Agent Loop, Planning, Tool Use, Memory & Guardrails
description:
A demo agent takes ten lines and a weekend. A production agent is a different animal: it loops forever on an ambiguous task, calls a tool that doesn't exist, spends $40 in tokens on one question, silently returns a confidently wrong answer, and — the first time you let it near a write action — deletes something it shouldn't.

The gap between "I wired up the OpenAI API with tools" and "this agent runs unattended in production" is exactly where senior AI engineering lives. This is the whole ladder: what an agent actually is, the loop that drives it, planning, tool use done right, memory, reflection, and the guardrails that turn a toy into a system you can trust.

Every example is from Mattrx — a real multi-tenant analytics platform whose Insights agent answers questions like "why did tenant X's conversions drop last week?" by reasoning over tools, orchestrated with LangGraph and traced with Langfuse on a FastAPI service. We hardened it from a demo that looped and overspent into an agent with p95 4.2s → 1.8s and bounded cost.

The demo-to-production gap

The first agent everyone builds works in the demo and fails in production, because a demo hides five things:

  1. It loops forever — on a vague task, the model keeps "thinking" with no exit.
  2. It hallucinates tools — calls send_email when you only gave it read_kpis.
  3. It has no budget — one hard question fans out into 30 LLM calls and a surprise bill.
  4. It fails silently — a tool throws, the model shrugs, you get a confident wrong answer.
  5. It has no brakes — the moment a tool can write, an unbounded agent is a liability.

What is an agent, really?

Strip the hype: an agent is an LLM in a loop with tools and memory, deciding its own next step until a goal is met. Separate three things people conflate:

  • A single LLM call — one prompt, one answer. Control flow you write.
  • A workflow / chain — a fixed sequence of steps. You decide the path; predictable, cheaper, testable.
  • An agent — the LLM decides the path at runtime. Flexible but non-deterministic and harder to bound.

The senior instinct: don't reach for an agent when a workflow will do. Agents earn their non-determinism only when the path genuinely can't be known in advance.

The naive agent, and why it fails 

# DO NOT ship this. No exit, no tool validation, no budget, no error handling.
def naive_agent(task, tools):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}]
    while True:                                   # (1) infinite loop risk
        resp = llm(messages, tools=tools)
        if resp.tool_calls:
            for call in resp.tool_calls:
                result = tools[call.name](**call.args)   # (2) KeyError on hallucinated tool
                messages.append(tool_result(call, result))  # (4) crashes if the tool throws
        else:
            return resp.content                  # (3) no token/step budget

Four bugs in ten lines. The fix isn't a bigger model — it's structure: a bounded loop, validated tools, budgets, error handling, and guardrails.

The agent loop (ReAct): reason, act, observe

The core pattern is ReAct — Reason, Act, Observe, repeat. The single most important addition over the naive version: a hard step cap so it can never loop forever.

def run_agent(task: str, tools: dict, max_steps: int = 8) -> str:
    messages = [system_prompt(tools), {"role": "user", "content": task}]
    for step in range(max_steps):                      # HARD cap -> no infinite loop
        resp = llm(messages, tools=tool_schemas(tools))
        if not resp.tool_calls:
            return resp.content                        # the model decided it's done
        for call in resp.tool_calls:
            if call.name not in tools:                 # reject hallucinated tools
                result = f"error: unknown tool '{call.name}'"
            else:
                result = safe_invoke(tools[call.name], call.args)  # try/except inside
            messages.append(tool_result(call, result)) # observe -> feeds the next reason
    return "stopped: step budget exhausted"            # fail SAFE, never forever

That for step in range(max_steps) line is the difference between an agent that gives up gracefully and one that racks up a bill at 3am. Bound everything.

Planning: ReAct vs plan-and-execute

ReAct decides one step at a time — great for exploratory tasks, but it can wander. For multi-step tasks with a knowable shape, plan-and-execute is often better: the model first writes a plan, then executes, re-planning if reality diverges.

When to use which: ReAct for open-ended "figure it out" tasks; plan-and-execute for multi-step tasks where up-front structure cuts cost and wandering.

Tools done right

An agent is only as good as its tools, and most agent failures are tool failures. A production tool is a typed function + a clear schema + strict validation + error handling that teaches the model what went wrong.

@tool
def get_campaign_kpis(campaign_id: str, date_from: str, date_to: str) -> dict:
    """Return KPIs (impressions, clicks, conversions, spend) for one campaign in a date
    range. Dates are ISO-8601 (YYYY-MM-DD). Use this to answer performance questions."""
    validate_iso_date(date_from); validate_iso_date(date_to)   # never trust model args
    require_tenant_scope(campaign_id)                          # AUTHZ: agent can't cross tenants
    return kpi_service.query(campaign_id, date_from, date_to)

Five rules:

  • The description IS the prompt. The model chooses tools by their docstrings — write them like instructions.
  • Constrain the schema — enums, formats, required fields.
  • Validate every argument. Tool code is a trust boundary, exactly like an API endpoint.
  • Errors that teach. Return "error: date_from is after date_to", not a stack trace — the model can recover.
  • Fewer, task-shaped tools. ~10 intent-level tools beat 40 CRUD endpoints.

Security note: a tool result is untrusted input. A retrieved document can contain injected instructions. Treat tool outputs as data, not commands.

Memory: scratchpad and long-term

  • Short-term (working memory) — the running message list / scratchpad for this task. Watch the context window; summarize or trim old steps on long runs.
  • Long-term — facts that persist across sessions (preferences, prior conclusions, a vector store), retrieved when relevant. 
# LangGraph gives durable working memory + resume via a checkpointer.
agent = graph.compile(checkpointer=PostgresSaver(conn))   # state persists per thread_id
context = memory_store.search(query=task, tenant_id=tenant, k=5)  # long-term = retrieval

Reflection and self-correction

Let the agent check its own work before returning — a reflection step asks "is this correct/complete?" and can trigger another loop. It catches hallucinations at the cost of extra calls, so gate it to high-stakes outputs.

answer = run_agent(task, tools)
critique = llm(f"Critique this answer for correctness and completeness:
{answer}")
if critique.has_issues:
    answer = run_agent(f"{task}
Fix these issues: {critique.issues}", tools, max_steps=4)

Guardrails: the part that makes it production

Everything above makes the agent capable; guardrails make it safe to run unattended.

def guarded_step(state, call, tool):
    if state.steps > MAX_STEPS:      raise StopAgent("step budget")     # bound the loop
    if state.tokens > TOKEN_BUDGET:  raise StopAgent("token budget")    # bound the cost
    if tool.name not in ALLOWLIST:   return "error: tool not permitted" # least privilege
    if tool.is_destructive and not human_approved(call):               # confirm write actions
        return "paused: awaiting human approval"
    result = safe_invoke(tool, call.args)                              # never crash the loop
    return validate_output(result)                                     # schema/PII/guard checks

The production checklist:

  • Step & token budgets — hard caps on loop length and spend, per run. Non-negotiable.
  • Tool allowlist / least privilege — the agent gets exactly the tools this task needs (an analytics agent has no delete tool).
  • Human-in-the-loop for destructive/irreversible actions — the agent proposes; a human commits.
  • Input & output validation — validate args going in; validate/scan the final answer going out (schema, PII, moderation).
  • Tool-result-as-untrusted — fence returned content, defending against indirect prompt injection.
  • Timeouts & fallbacks — every tool call has a timeout; a failed run degrades to a helpful message.
  • Full tracing — every run is observable.

Senior signal: you treat "the agent can take an irreversible action unattended" as a design red flag requiring a human gate.

Orchestration frameworks: which and when

  • LangGraph — models the agent as an explicit graph. Best for control, inspectability, durable state, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints.
  • CrewAI — high-level, role-based multi-agent with minimal code.
  • AutoGen — conversation-driven multi-agent.
  • Semantic Kernel / Microsoft.Extensions.AI — the .NET path for teams on the Microsoft stack. 
# LangGraph: the agent IS a graph. Explicit, inspectable, resumable.
graph = StateGraph(AgentState)
graph.add_node("reason", call_model)
graph.add_node("act", run_tools)
graph.add_conditional_edges("reason", lambda s: "act" if s.tool_calls else END)
graph.add_edge("act", "reason")                    # observe -> reason again (the loop)
agent = graph.compile(checkpointer=memory)         # durable state + resume + HITL pauses

In production: naive vs hardened

Metric Naive (v1) Hardened (v2)
Agentic p95 latency 4.2s 1.8s
Cost per question ~$0.90 (unbounded) ~$0.12 (budgeted + cached)
Runaway loops frequent zero (hard caps)
Debuggability none full trace per run

The wins came entirely from structure — bounded loop, typed read-only tools, budgets, output validation, and full tracing — not a smarter model.

What's next

Building the agent is step one. The three skills that make it trustworthy in production: evals (test something non-deterministic), observability (trace runs: cost, latency, why it did that), and cost engineering (prompt/semantic caching, model routing). Build it, measure it, watch it, make it cheap.

This post was originally published on PrepStack. The full original has all the code and diagrams.

title: Claude Opus 4.8 Fast Mode Is Retiring: A Safe Migration Playbook
description:
A production migration guide for moving Claude Opus 4.8 fast-mode workloads to Opus 5.5 without hiding compatibility, latency, capacity, or cost regressions.

Originally published on NoorYasser.com. This DEV edition is adapted for engineers planning the migration.

Anthropic is removing fast mode from Claude Opus 4.8 on November 30, 2026. After that date, requests that combine the model ID claude-opus-4-8 with speed: "fast" will return an error.

That is a feature retirement, not a November retirement of the Opus 4.8 model. Anthropic's lifecycle page still lists the model as active, with retirement no sooner than May 28, 2027.

The practical response is not a one-line model rename. If a production route depends on Opus 4.8 fast mode, move it to Claude Opus 5.5 behind a compatibility test, an offline evaluation, and a measured canary. Track the inference mode that actually served each request, not only the mode your configuration requested.

The deadline in one table

Question Documented answer Engineering consequence
What ends on November 30? Fast mode on Claude Opus 4.8 Remove speed: "fast" from every 4.8 path or migrate it
Is Opus 4.8 itself retiring then? No; it remains listed as active Do not misclassify standard 4.8 traffic as a November outage
Recommended fast target Claude Opus 5.5 Test request and response contracts before shifting traffic
Does Opus 5.5 need the old beta header? No Remove header injection after the route moves
How do you prove the serving mode? Read usage.speed Monitor actual mode, not requested intent alone
What happens at fast-mode capacity limits? 429 or 529; a 429 can include retry-after Use bounded retries or a deliberate standard-speed fallback

The dates, supported models, request fields, pricing, rate-limit behavior, and Opus 5.5 compatibility changes below come from Anthropic's official documentation, checked on November 1, 2026. The inventory, evaluation, rollout, and fallback design are engineering recommendations.

1. Find every affected request path

Searching application code for one model ID is not enough. Fast mode may be injected by an SDK wrapper, gateway policy, environment variable, managed-agent model object, feature flag, or request template.

Inventory at least these surfaces:

  • Direct Messages API payloads containing model: "claude-opus-4-8" and speed: "fast"
  • Managed Agent definitions with the same model and speed
  • Shared clients that append the fast-mode-2026-02-01 beta header
  • Internal aliases such as opus-fast or premium-low-latency
  • Fallback branches that activate only after a timeout or capacity error
  • Scheduled jobs and rarely used admin workflows
  • Dashboards, alerts, and budgets grouped by the old model or beta feature
  • Tests that validate only HTTP success instead of the response contract

A useful internal inventory record can be as simple as:

{
  "route": "support-escalation-agent",
  "model": "claude-opus-4-8",
  "requested_speed": "fast",
  "beta_header": "fast-mode-2026-02-01",
  "effort": "high",
  "tool_choice": "required",
  "fallback": "opus-4-8-standard",
  "owner": "support-platform"
}

This is not an Anthropic API schema. It is an ownership and risk record that should expose hidden compatibility work before traffic changes.

2. Treat Opus 5.5 as a contract migration

Anthropic's migration guide documents several differences that can affect an application even when prompts stay unchanged.

Thinking and effort

On Opus 4.8, thinking is off when a request omits the thinking field. On Opus 5.5, thinking runs even when that field is omitted. Anthropic also documents a default effort change: Opus 4.8 defaults to high, while Opus 5.5 defaults to medium.

Do not let defaults decide the migration implicitly. Set effort intentionally for each evaluated workload, parse thinking-aware responses, and compare both quality and token usage.

Tool contracts

The Opus 5.5 documentation lists breaking changes around forced tool use, model-linked thinking blocks, and an earlier computer-use tool version. If an agent forces a tool, replays conversations containing thinking blocks, or uses computer_20251124, include those paths in compatibility tests. A successful text-only prompt is not evidence that an agent workflow is compatible.

Prompt caching and Priority Tier

The minimum cacheable prompt on Opus 5.5 is 512 tokens, compared with 1,024 tokens for Opus 4.8. That can change cache creation and cost patterns without an obvious application change.

Anthropic also says Priority Tier is not supported on Opus 5.5. Fast mode and Priority Tier are separate capacity products; do not assume one replaces the other.

3. Measure latency correctly

Anthropic describes fast mode as the same model running with a faster inference configuration and says it can deliver up to 2.5 times higher output tokens per second. That is a provider claim about output throughput, not time to first token.

Separate the latency components:

end_to_end = queue_wait + request_setup + TTFT + generation + tool_time + post_processing
generation = output_tokens / observed_OTPS

If queueing or tool calls dominate, higher output throughput may barely change the user journey. Long streaming responses can benefit even when time to first token stays flat.

Report p50 and p95 for:

  • Time to first token
  • Output tokens per second
  • End-to-end latency
  • Tool execution time
  • Retry and fallback latency

Anthropic's current pricing page lists Opus 5.5 fast mode at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Opus 4.8 fast mode is listed at $10 and $50. These are provider prices, not a prediction of your bill. Prompt caching and data-residency multipliers can stack with fast-mode pricing, so calculate cost from real usage records.

4. Freeze an evaluation contract before the canary

Build a privacy-reviewed evaluation set that represents every affected route. Include short answers, long streaming generation, tool sequences, refusals, cacheable prompts, and peak-context requests.

Score at least:

  • Task correctness and instruction adherence
  • Tool selection, argument validity, and completion rate
  • Response parser compatibility
  • Thinking-block and stop-reason handling
  • TTFT, output throughput, and end-to-end p50/p95
  • Input, cached-input, and output tokens
  • usage.speed distribution
  • 429, 529, and other error rates
  • Retry amplification and standard-speed fallback rate
  • Cost per successful task, not cost per raw request

Use the same prompts, tools, seed data, and scoring rules for both routes. Comparing a busy Opus 4.8 production trace with a lightly loaded Opus 5.5 development request does not isolate a model or serving-mode difference.

5. Make fallback behavior explicit

A safe router distinguishes four things:

  1. The model requested by product policy
  2. The speed requested by the route
  3. The speed reported in usage.speed
  4. The fallback that actually served the response

A simplified policy might read:

if route_flag == "opus-5-5-fast":
    call Opus 5.5 with speed="fast"
    verify usage.speed
elif route_flag == "opus-5-5-standard":
    call Opus 5.5 without fast mode
else:
    keep the approved legacy route during the canary

On a 429, honor retry-after and retry within a bounded latency budget. On a 529 or exhausted budget, fall back to standard speed only when the product contract allows it. Record the fallback reason and final serving mode.

Do not silently fall back to another model merely to turn an error into a 200 response. A different model may change quality, safety, tool behavior, and cost.

6. Roll out in controlled stages

A practical sequence is:

  1. Inventory all routes, owners, headers, aliases, and fallbacks.
  2. Compatibility test request and response contracts, tool flows, and parsers.
  3. Offline evaluate quality, latency components, tokens, and cost.
  4. Shadow or replay privacy-safe traffic without affecting users.
  5. Canary a small, representative share behind a feature flag.
  6. Expand by route only after error, quality, latency, and cost gates pass.
  7. Remove the legacy path and old beta header before November 30.

Keep rollback narrow: change one route flag, preserve request evidence, and return to the last validated configuration. A rollback that also changes prompts, tools, cache boundaries, and retry rules is a second migration, not a control.

Best practices

  • Pin the model and set effort deliberately.
  • Log requested speed and usage.speed separately.
  • Treat 429 and 529 as capacity signals, not proof of model failure.
  • Alert on any remaining Opus 4.8 fast request before the deadline.
  • Measure cost per successful task.
  • Give every fallback a product-approved latency and quality contract.
  • Remove obsolete headers, aliases, dashboards, and runbook steps after cutover.

Anti-patterns

  • Changing only the model string
  • Assuming fast mode improves time to first token
  • Treating Opus 4.8 model retirement and fast-mode retirement as the same event
  • Comparing average latency while ignoring tail behavior
  • Inferring the serving mode from configuration instead of usage.speed
  • Keeping an untested standard-speed fallback indefinitely
  • Declaring success because HTTP status is 200 while tool completion or output quality regresses

Executive checklist

Before November 30, confirm that:

  • No production request combines claude-opus-4-8 with speed: "fast"
  • Opus 5.5 request, response, thinking, and tool contracts pass
  • Quality, latency, token usage, and cost gates pass on a representative set
  • usage.speed is visible in telemetry
  • 429 and 529 handling is bounded and observable
  • The standard-speed fallback is intentional and tested
  • The old beta header and internal aliases are removed
  • Rollback and route ownership are documented

title: Temporal API in TypeScript: deadlines and time zones
description:
Being able to use the Temporal API in TypeScript was one of my favorite pieces of news around Node.js 26. Over the years I have seen plenty of code where a deadline was off by an hour because somebody wrote “plus 48 hours” instead of “plus two days” and a daylight saving change happened in between. Bugs like that don’t show up in tests. They show up in production, twice a year.

In my article on Node.js 26 LTS on Lambda I only touched on Temporal briefly. This time we go deeper: step by step, you build the deadline logic for a fictional city library, store the values cleanly in DynamoDB, deploy everything to Lambda with the Serverless Framework and deliberately test across the DST change. Afterwards you will know which Temporal type is meant for what and how to move away from Date or date-fns.

In short

Temporal replaces Date with dedicated types for instants, calendar dates and times in a time zone. Node.js 26 ships the API without a flag, TypeScript has included the types since version 6.0, and older Lambda runtimes only need a small polyfill. The biggest pitfall is choosing the wrong type: if you store a deadline as a plain date without a time zone, you only move the problem somewhere else.

What you will learn in this article

  • Which Temporal type is right for instants, calendar days and deadlines
  • How to set up Temporal in TypeScript, Node.js 26 and on Lambda with nodejs24.x
  • How to calculate and test deadlines correctly across DST changes
  • How to store Temporal values in DynamoDB, including TTL
  • How to migrate step by step from Date or date-fns

Why Date so often gets deadlines wrong

Date has been part of JavaScript since 1995 and was closely modeled on an early Java class at the time. You can still tell. Months start at 0, so new Date(2026, 9, 25) is October 25. A Date object is mutable, and if you pass it to a function you may get it back changed. On top of that, Date knows exactly two time zones: UTC and the local time zone of the machine running the code.

That last point is especially tricky in a Serverless setup. A Lambda function runs in UTC by default. Your customers, however, live in Berlin, Vienna or Zurich. Ask Lambda for “today” at 0:30 am German time and you still get yesterday. Lambda is doing everything right here. The real question is: whose “today” do you mean?

The classic example is the DST change. On October 25, 2026, clocks in Germany go back from 3:00 am to 2:00 am, so that day has 25 hours. If you create a deadline of “two days” on October 24 at 10:00 am and calculate it as 48 hours, you end up at 9:00 am on October 26. What you meant was 10:00 am. That is why Temporal clearly separates exact durations in hours from calendar arithmetic in days.

const pickup = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2026-10-24T10:00[Europe/Berlin]");

console.log(pickup.add({ hours: 48 }).toString());
// 2026-10-26T09:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]  (exactly 48 hours later)

console.log(pickup.add({ days: 2 }).toString());
// 2026-10-26T10:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]  (two calendar days later)

Both results are correct. They simply answer different questions. With Date you have to keep that difference in your head, while Temporal makes you write it down.

Which Temporal type for which purpose?

Temporal is a namespace like Math, not a constructor. It contains several classes, and all objects are immutable: every operation returns a new object. For everyday work you mainly need these types:

Type What it describes Typical example
Temporal.Instant Exact point on the timeline, without calendar or time zone Event timestamp, log entry
Temporal.ZonedDateTime Instant plus time zone, handles summer and winter time Return deadline “Nov 19 at 6:00 pm in Berlin”
Temporal.PlainDate Calendar date without time and without time zone Birthday, day of borrowing, holiday
Temporal.PlainTime Wall-clock time without a date Closing time “18:00”
Temporal.PlainDateTime Date and time without a time zone Form input before the time zone is known
Temporal.Duration Length of time in years, months, days, hours … Loan period, gap between two appointments

There are also PlainYearMonth (for a billing month, say), PlainMonthDay (recurring anniversaries) and Temporal.Now for the current time in various forms.

Rule of thumb for choosing a Temporal type

The rule of thumb for choosing a type

For every value I ask myself one single question: do I need to know exactly when this happens in the world? If yes, I need an Instant or a ZonedDateTime. A return deadline belongs in this group, because at 6:01 pm in Berlin it has expired, no matter where the server is. If the answer is no, a plain type is enough. A birthday is on May 3, whatever time zone you happen to be in.

A mistake I see often: deadlines get stored as PlainDateTime because it looks so simple. Then exactly the information you later need for comparisons is missing. PlainDateTime is meant for intermediate steps, for example a form before it is clear which time zone the appointment takes place in.

Setting up the Temporal API in TypeScript

Before you start, a quick look at support. Temporal has reached stage 4 in the TC39 process, the standards committee for JavaScript, which means it is fully specified. Firefox has shipped the API since version 139, Chrome since version 144 and Node.js since version 26. According to the proposal repository, Safari is still missing. TypeScript has included the matching types since version 6.0.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 26 locally (for native Temporal support) or Node.js 22/24 with a polyfill
  • TypeScript 6.0 or later; the example was tested with TypeScript 7.0.2
  • For deployment: an AWS account and the Serverless Framework v4 (npm i -g serverless)
  • Basic knowledge of Lambda and DynamoDB helps but isn’t required

Lambda runtime and polyfill

On Lambda, nodejs26.x is still a public preview, and AWS plans the regular launch for November 2026. Preview runtimes come without the Lambda SLA and are not intended for production use. Until then, use nodejs24.x and load the temporal-polyfill package (MIT license). Its entry point temporal-polyfill/global installs Temporal globally only if the runtime doesn’t already provide it. I checked this in the package’s source code: on Node.js 26 the import simply does nothing. So later you can switch the runtime without touching a single line of code.

Configuring TypeScript

You enable the types via the lib option. Either take all of esnext or only the esnext.temporal part. I prefer the more granular option because it makes clear which new features the project actually uses.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2024",
    "lib": ["es2024", "esnext.temporal"],
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "types": ["node"],
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["src", "test"]
}

allowImportingTsExtensions and erasableSyntaxOnly let Node.js run the TypeScript files directly. We will use that for the tests in a moment, without any build step.

Step by step: loan deadlines for a library

Our example is a fictional city library with clear rules. A book may be borrowed for 21 days. If the last day falls on a Sunday or a holiday, the return moves to the next opening day. You can return books until 6:00 pm Berlin time. Two days before the deadline a reminder goes out at 9:00 am, and every overdue day costs 50 cents, up to a maximum of 10 euros.

Step 1: Create the project 

mkdir temporal-library-loans && cd temporal-library-loans
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm i temporal-polyfill @aws-sdk/client-dynamodb @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb
npm i -D typescript @types/node @types/aws-lambda
mkdir src test

Then create the tsconfig.json shown above. Next comes a tiny file that loads the polyfill when needed:

// src/temporal.ts
// Loads the polyfill only if the runtime has no native Temporal
// (e.g. nodejs24.x on Lambda). On Node.js 26 this does nothing.
import "temporal-polyfill/global";

Step 2: The deadline logic as pure functions

The rules go into a file without any AWS dependencies. That makes them easy to test and independent of where the code runs later.

// src/loan-rules.ts
import "./temporal.ts";

export const LIBRARY_ZONE = "Europe/Berlin";
export const LOAN_DAYS = 21;
export const CLOSING_TIME = Temporal.PlainTime.from("18:00");
export const FEE_PER_DAY_CENTS = 50;
export const MAX_FEE_CENTS = 1000;

// Holidays when the library is closed (fictional selection)
export const HOLIDAYS = new Set(["2026-12-25", "2026-12-26", "2027-01-01"]);

function isClosed(date: Temporal.PlainDate): boolean {
  return date.dayOfWeek === 7 || HOLIDAYS.has(date.toString());
}

// Due date: day of borrowing + 21 days; on a Sunday or holiday, the next opening day
export function dueDate(borrowedOn: Temporal.PlainDate): Temporal.PlainDate {
  let due = borrowedOn.add({ days: LOAN_DAYS });
  while (isClosed(due)) {
    due = due.add({ days: 1 });
  }
  return due;
}

// Exact deadline: due date at 6:00 pm Berlin time
export function returnDeadline(due: Temporal.PlainDate): Temporal.ZonedDateTime {
  return due.toZonedDateTime({ timeZone: LIBRARY_ZONE, plainTime: CLOSING_TIME });
}

// Reminder two calendar days earlier at 9:00 am – wall-clock time, even across DST changes
export function reminderAt(deadline: Temporal.ZonedDateTime): Temporal.ZonedDateTime {
  return deadline.subtract({ days: 2 }).with({ hour: 9, minute: 0 });
}

// Overdue days: calendar days between due date and today (never negative)
export function overdueDays(due: Temporal.PlainDate, today: Temporal.PlainDate): number {
  const days = due.until(today, { largestUnit: "days" }).days;
  return Math.max(0, days);
}

export function lateFeeCents(due: Temporal.PlainDate, today: Temporal.PlainDate): number {
  return Math.min(overdueDays(due, today) * FEE_PER_DAY_CENTS, MAX_FEE_CENTS);
}

// "Today" from the library's point of view – not from the Lambda server's (UTC)
export function libraryToday(now: Temporal.Instant): Temporal.PlainDate {
  return now.toZonedDateTimeISO(LIBRARY_ZONE).toPlainDate();
}

A few spots deserve a second look. The due date is a PlainDate, because “21 days later” is purely a calendar question. dayOfWeek follows the ISO standard from 1 (Monday) to 7 (Sunday), so the Sunday-is-zero confusion of Date is finally gone. Only in returnDeadline do time and time zone come in, turning the calendar day into an actual instant.

For the reminder, we deliberately calculate in calendar days and then set the time with with(). If the DST change falls between reminder and deadline, it still stays at 9:00 am wall-clock time. That is exactly what people expect when a reminder is supposed to arrive “at nine in the morning”.

The libraryToday function looks harmless but matters a lot. It receives an Instant and converts it into the library’s time zone. As a result, “today” is always Berlin’s today, even though Lambda runs in UTC. And because the instant comes from outside, you can simulate any time you like in tests.

Step 3: Storing Temporal values in DynamoDB

DynamoDB has no date type. So you have to decide in which form to store the values, and that decision matters more than it seems. My suggestion:

  • Plain calendar dates as ISO strings like 2026-11-19. They are readable and sort lexicographically.
  • Instants as UTC strings like 2026-11-19T17:00:00Z. That way comparisons and range queries on a sort key work.
  • The time zone separately as an IANA name like Europe/Berlin, so you can restore local time for display.
  • For DynamoDB TTL, an additional number with epoch seconds, because TTL ignores anything that isn’t a Number attribute. 
// src/storage.ts
import "./temporal.ts";

export interface Loan {
  loanId: string;
  bookId: string;
  memberId: string;
  borrowedOn: Temporal.PlainDate;
  due: Temporal.PlainDate;
  deadline: Temporal.ZonedDateTime;
}

export interface LoanItem {
  pk: string;
  bookId: string;
  memberId: string;
  borrowedOn: string;     // "2026-10-29" – plain date, no time
  dueDate: string;        // "2026-11-19"
  deadlineAt: string;     // "2026-11-19T17:00:00Z" – UTC, sortable
  timeZone: string;       // "Europe/Berlin" – for display
  expiresAt: number;      // epoch seconds for DynamoDB TTL
}

const KEEP_AFTER_DEADLINE = { days: 180 };

export function toItem(loan: Loan): LoanItem {
  return {
    pk: `LOAN#${loan.loanId}`,
    bookId: loan.bookId,
    memberId: loan.memberId,
    borrowedOn: loan.borrowedOn.toString(),
    dueDate: loan.due.toString(),
    deadlineAt: loan.deadline.toInstant().toString(),
    timeZone: loan.deadline.timeZoneId,
    expiresAt: Math.floor(loan.deadline.add(KEEP_AFTER_DEADLINE).epochMilliseconds / 1000),
  };
}

export function fromItem(item: LoanItem): Loan {
  return {
    loanId: item.pk.replace("LOAN#", ""),
    bookId: item.bookId,
    memberId: item.memberId,
    borrowedOn: Temporal.PlainDate.from(item.borrowedOn),
    due: Temporal.PlainDate.from(item.dueDate),
    deadline: Temporal.Instant.from(item.deadlineAt).toZonedDateTimeISO(item.timeZone),
  };
}

Why not just store the string of a ZonedDateTime, i.e. 2026-11-19T18:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]? It does contain everything, but it doesn’t sort reliably once values with different offsets end up in the same column. The UTC instant doesn’t have that problem. You can read more about TTL and expiry dates in my post DynamoDB TTL: build seat holds that expire.

Step 4: Lambda handler and serverless.yml

The handler is intentionally lean. It reads the book and member from the request, calculates date, deadline and reminder and writes the record to DynamoDB.

// src/handler.ts
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb";
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, PutCommand } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb";
import type { APIGatewayProxyEventV2, APIGatewayProxyResultV2 } from "aws-lambda";
import { dueDate, libraryToday, reminderAt, returnDeadline } from "./loan-rules.ts";
import { toItem, type Loan } from "./storage.ts";

const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({}));
const TABLE = process.env.LOANS_TABLE ?? "";

export async function createLoan(event: APIGatewayProxyEventV2): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResultV2> {
  const body = JSON.parse(event.body ?? "{}") as { bookId?: string; memberId?: string };
  if (!body.bookId || !body.memberId) {
    return { statusCode: 400, body: JSON.stringify({ message: "bookId and memberId are required" }) };
  }

  const borrowedOn = libraryToday(Temporal.Now.instant());
  const due = dueDate(borrowedOn);
  const deadline = returnDeadline(due);
  const loan: Loan = {
    loanId: randomUUID(),
    bookId: body.bookId,
    memberId: body.memberId,
    borrowedOn,
    due,
    deadline,
  };

  await db.send(new PutCommand({ TableName: TABLE, Item: toItem(loan) }));

  return {
    statusCode: 201,
    body: JSON.stringify({
      loanId: loan.loanId,
      dueDate: due.toString(),
      deadline: deadline.toString(),
      reminder: reminderAt(deadline).toString(),
    }),
  };
}

🎬 Flow of a book loan with Temporal – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

For the infrastructure I am using the Serverless Framework here. Since version 4 it builds TypeScript itself with esbuild, so no extra build configuration is needed.

# serverless.yml
service: library-loans
frameworkVersion: "4"

provider:
  name: aws
  runtime: nodejs24.x        # switch to nodejs26.x once it is GA
  region: eu-central-1
  architecture: arm64
  memorySize: 256
  environment:
    LOANS_TABLE: ${self:service}-${sls:stage}-loans
    TZ: UTC                  # Lambda default; library time comes from the code
  iam:
    role:
      statements:
        - Effect: Allow
          Action:
            - dynamodb:PutItem
          Resource:
            - !GetAtt LoansTable.Arn

functions:
  createLoan:
    handler: src/handler.createLoan
    events:
      - httpApi:
          path: /loans
          method: post

resources:
  Resources:
    LoansTable:
      Type: AWS::DynamoDB::Table
      Properties:
        TableName: ${self:service}-${sls:stage}-loans
        BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST
        AttributeDefinitions:
          - AttributeName: pk
            AttributeType: S
        KeySchema:
          - AttributeName: pk
            KeyType: HASH
        TimeToLiveSpecification:
          AttributeName: expiresAt
          Enabled: true

The IAM role may only call PutItem on exactly this table. The handler needs nothing more. Deploy and try it out:

serverless deploy
curl -X POST "https://<your-api-id>.execute-api.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/loans" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"bookId":"book-42","memberId":"reader-7"}'

If you borrow on October 29, 2026, the response looks roughly like this (the loanId will of course differ):

{
  "loanId": "3f2c9a4e-8b1d-4c57-9e0a-5d6f7a8b9c01",
  "dueDate": "2026-11-19",
  "deadline": "2026-11-19T18:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]",
  "reminder": "2026-11-17T09:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]"
}

Step 5: Testing across the DST change

Now comes the part I consider most important for date logic. Tests with “today plus three days” are almost always green and prove little. They only become meaningful with fixed dates around the DST change, holidays and the day boundary between UTC and Berlin.

// test/loan-rules.test.ts
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { dueDate, lateFeeCents, libraryToday, overdueDays, reminderAt, returnDeadline } from "../src/loan-rules.ts";

const day = (s: string) => Temporal.PlainDate.from(s);

test("due date is 21 days after borrowing", () => {
  assert.equal(dueDate(day("2026-10-29")).toString(), "2026-11-19");
});

test("holidays and Sundays move to the next opening day", () => {
  // Dec 25 holiday, Dec 26 holiday, Dec 27 Sunday
  assert.equal(dueDate(day("2026-12-04")).toString(), "2026-12-28");
});

test("deadline stays at 6:00 pm Berlin time, even after the DST change", () => {
  const deadline = returnDeadline(day("2026-10-26"));
  assert.equal(deadline.toString(), "2026-10-26T18:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]");
  assert.equal(deadline.toInstant().toString(), "2026-10-26T17:00:00Z");
});

test("reminder at 9:00 am wall-clock time across the DST change", () => {
  const reminder = reminderAt(returnDeadline(day("2026-10-26")));
  assert.equal(reminder.toString(), "2026-10-24T09:00:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]");
});

test("overdue days and capped fee", () => {
  assert.equal(overdueDays(day("2026-11-19"), day("2026-11-23")), 4);
  assert.equal(overdueDays(day("2026-11-19"), day("2026-11-10")), 0);
  assert.equal(lateFeeCents(day("2026-11-19"), day("2026-11-23")), 200);
  assert.equal(lateFeeCents(day("2026-11-19"), day("2026-12-31")), 1000);
});

test("“today” is based on Berlin, not UTC", () => {
  // 23:30 UTC is already the next day in Berlin
  assert.equal(libraryToday(Temporal.Instant.from("2026-10-29T23:30:00Z")).toString(), "2026-10-30");
});

You can run the tests directly with Node.js, without a compile step:

npx tsc --noEmit
node --test test/*.test.ts

Expected result: all tests pass. I ran them on Node.js 26.13 with native Temporal and on Node.js 22 with the polyfill, both times with identical results. The repository also contains a second test for the round trip through DynamoDB and the conversion from Date, which I leave out here to save space.

Summer and winter time: what Temporal decides behind the scenes

Twice a year there are times in Berlin that are ambiguous. In spring an hour is missing: on March 28, 2027 the clock jumps from 2:00 am to 3:00 am, so “2:30 am” doesn’t exist that day. In autumn an hour happens twice: on October 25, 2026, 2:30 am occurs once in summer time and once in winter time.

Temporal solves this with the disambiguation option. The default value compatible behaves like Date: inside the gap the time is pushed forward, and in the repeated hour the earlier one wins. With earlier or later you pick a variant on purpose, and with reject Temporal throws a RangeError.

// Spring gap: 2:30 am does not exist
Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2027-03-28T02:30[Europe/Berlin]").toString();
// 2027-03-28T03:30:00+02:00[Europe/Berlin]

// Repeated hour in autumn: deliberately pick the second 2:30 am
Temporal.PlainDateTime.from("2026-10-25T02:30")
  .toZonedDateTime("Europe/Berlin", { disambiguation: "later" })
  .toString();
// 2026-10-25T02:30:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]

// Often the best choice for booking systems: an error beats a silent shift
Temporal.PlainDateTime.from("2027-03-28T02:30")
  .toZonedDateTime("Europe/Berlin", { disambiguation: "reject" }); // RangeError

Something similar applies to month arithmetic. January 31 plus one month gives February 28 with the default overflow: "constrain". If you prefer an error, pass { overflow: "reject" }. For subscriptions and contract terms this is a business decision that you should clarify with the domain experts instead of leaving it to chance.

Migrating from Date and date-fns

Hardly any project can switch everything overnight. It doesn’t have to. I would use Temporal first in new business logic and convert at the edges, wherever older libraries, ORMs or SDKs still expect or return Date.

// src/legacy.ts
import "./temporal.ts";

// Existing code still returns Date objects? This converts them without loss.
export function fromLegacyDate(value: Date): Temporal.Instant {
  return Temporal.Instant.fromEpochMilliseconds(value.getTime());
}

// For libraries that still expect Date (e.g. older SDKs)
export function toLegacyDate(value: Temporal.Instant): Date {
  return new Date(value.epochMilliseconds);
}

Going through epoch milliseconds is lossless, because Date only knows milliseconds anyway. Native runtimes and the polyfill also offer Date.prototype.toTemporalInstant(). I still prefer the explicit function, because it shows in the code where the old world ends.

With date-fns, Day.js or Luxon it pays to look at what the library is actually used for. Often it is a handful of functions like addDays, differenceInDays or format. Temporal replaces the first two directly with add() and until(). For formatting there is toLocaleString(), which uses Intl.DateTimeFormat internally. Temporal.PlainDate.from("2026-11-19").toLocaleString("en-US", { dateStyle: "full" }), for example, returns “Thursday, November 19, 2026”. Running both side by side is fine for a transition period. The only important thing is that a function works either with Temporal or with Date, not with both.

Common mistakes with the Temporal API in TypeScript

A few pitfalls kept coming up while I was trying things out.

  • Comparing with === or <: Two Temporal objects with the same value are still different objects. Use equals() or the static compare() method. Comparing with < deliberately throws a TypeError.
  • Temporal.Now deep inside business logic: Then you can’t control time in tests. Get the current time at the edge, for example in the handler, and pass it on as a parameter.
  • JSON there, but not back: JSON.stringify turns Temporal objects into strings. When reading them back, you have to convert them with from() yourself, or you keep calculating with strings.
  • structuredClone and workers: Temporal objects can’t be structured-cloned, and Node.js throws a DataCloneError. Pass strings and rebuild the objects on the other side.
  • Storing an offset instead of a time zone: +01:00 is not a time zone. In summer, Berlin uses +02:00. If you only know the offset, you can’t calculate correctly into the future.

Cost, performance and security

The polyfill has a price, but it is modest. In my example, the minified handler including the polyfill weighs about 60 KB, not counting the AWS SDK, which is part of the runtime. For a Lambda cold start that hardly matters. Once nodejs26.x is generally available, you can remove the polyfill and save those bytes entirely.

DynamoDB TTL costs nothing extra. Expired items are deleted without consuming write capacity, though not immediately: according to AWS, typically within a few days. Queries should therefore filter out expired items themselves. With global tables, however, the replicated deletes in other regions do consume write capacity.

Two notes on security. Always validate date values from requests with from() inside a try block, because invalid input throws a RangeError. And don’t accept time zones from requests unchecked; compare them against a list of allowed zones. For scheduled reminders, EventBridge Scheduler is a good fit, since it understands cron expressions with a time zone. My EventBridge cron explainer shows how such expressions are built.

My take

I consider Temporal one of the most useful additions JavaScript has received in recent years. You could build correct code with Date, too. What makes Temporal valuable is that it forces the right questions. If you have to choose between PlainDate and ZonedDateTime, you automatically think about what a value means in business terms.

At the same time, I wouldn’t rebuild everything at once. Existing code with date-fns that has been running reliably for years is not an emergency. New business logic, though, I would write with Temporal starting now, on Lambda with the polyfill for the time being. For frontends that also serve Safari, the polyfill remains mandatory for a while anyway. One point where I stay skeptical: the API is large. Teams should agree on a few types and clear storage formats, otherwise you quickly end up with a new kind of sprawl, just with more modern names.

FAQ

Can I use the Temporal API in production already?

Yes. Temporal is fully standardized and available without a flag in Node.js 26, Chrome and Firefox. For Safari and older Node versions such as nodejs24.x on Lambda, use a polyfill like temporal-polyfill.

Which TypeScript version do I need for Temporal?

The types are built in from TypeScript 6.0. You enable them with "lib": ["esnext"], with "target": "esnext" or specifically with esnext.temporal.

What is the difference between Instant and ZonedDateTime?

Both describe an exact point in time. An Instant, however, has no time zone and therefore no calendar. ZonedDateTime also knows the time zone in which the instant is viewed, so it can calculate correctly with days, months and DST changes.

Does Temporal replace date-fns, Luxon or Day.js?

For arithmetic, comparisons and time zones, in many cases yes. For formatting, Temporal uses Intl.DateTimeFormat. Special features like relative times (“3 days ago”) are covered by Intl.RelativeTimeFormat or still by a library.

Your next step

Find a place in your project where a deadline or appointment is calculated with Date today, and write a test for October 25 or March 28. If it passes, great. If not, you have found your first candidate for Temporal.

How do you handle time zones in your Lambda functions so far: everything in UTC with conversion in the frontend, or do you already calculate with local time in the backend? Let me know in the comments.

Time zones matter not only for deadlines but also for triggering jobs. I show how to start cron jobs reliably at German local time in EventBridge Scheduler time zone: cron at local time.

title: How to compute the real APR on a loan (derivation + 20 lines of Python)
description:
Two loan offers land in your inbox. Both say 6.5%. One has a $1,200 origination fee and the other has none. The monthly payment on the first is not a cent higher than on the second, because the fee is taken out of the money before it reaches you. Compare the quoted rates and the two offers look identical. On a $20,000 five-year loan, the fee turns 6.5% into a 9.12% APR.

The APR is the number that makes them comparable, and it is just the internal rate of return on the loan's cash flows. This post derives it, implements it, and shows the two places where a quoted rate misleads: front-loaded fees and flat-rate interest.

What the quoted rate actually is

A loan quote gives you a nominal annual rate r and a term of n months. The payment follows the annuity formula:

payment = P * (r/12) / (1 - (1 + r/12)^(-n))

For $20,000 at 6.5% over 60 months that is $391.32 a month, or $23,479.38 in total, of which $3,479.38 is interest. So far so ordinary. The quoted rate prices the principal on the assumption that you receive all of it.

APR is the rate where the cash flows net to zero

Now add a $1,200 origination fee, deducted at closing. You still owe payments on $20,000, but only $18,800 ever hits your account. Economically you borrowed $18,800 and are paying $391.32 a month for 60 months.

The APR is the annualised discount rate that makes the present value of those payments equal the money you actually received:

18,800 = sum(payment / (1 + i)^k)    for k = 1..60
APR = 12 * i

There is no closed-form solution for i, since the equation is a polynomial of degree 60, but there is exactly one positive root: the present value falls monotonically as i rises, and that is all a bisection search needs.

Using 12 * i rather than compounding to (1+i)^12 - 1 is deliberate. US Regulation Z defines APR as a nominal annual rate, so a monthly IRR is multiplied by twelve. Comparing it to an APY from a savings account is apples to oranges: APY compounds and APR does not.

The implementation 

def payment(principal: float, annual_rate: float, months: int) -> float:
    """Fixed monthly payment on an amortising loan."""
    r = annual_rate / 12
    if r == 0:
        return principal / months
    return principal * r / (1 - (1 + r) ** -months)


def apr(net_advanced: float, monthly_payment: float, months: int) -> float:
    """Annualised IRR of the loan's cash flows, as a decimal (0.0912 = 9.12%)."""
    lo, hi = 0.0, 3.0                      # 0% .. 300% monthly, plenty of room
    for _ in range(200):                   # 200 halvings is far past float precision
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        pv = sum(monthly_payment / (1 + mid) ** k for k in range(1, months + 1))
        if pv > net_advanced:              # rate too low: payments are worth too much
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return ((lo + hi) / 2) * 12

Two details matter in that function. Bisection rather than Newton, because pv(i) is smooth and strictly decreasing, so the search cannot diverge; a hundred iterations is already overkill and two hundred costs microseconds. And net_advanced is the money you can spend, not the face value. Fees deducted at closing shrink it, and that is the whole mechanism by which APR exceeds the quoted rate.

The worked example 

payment(20_000, 0.065, 60)                  -> 391.32
apr(20_000, 391.32, 60)                     -> 0.0650   (6.50%)
apr(18_800, 391.32, 60)                     -> 0.0912   (9.12%)

The same $1,200 fee, at the same rate, priced against different terms:

Term Payment APR, no fee APR, $1,200 fee APR, $2,400 fee
36 mo $612.98 6.50% 10.72% 15.33%
48 mo $474.30 6.50% 9.72% 13.24%
60 mo $391.32 6.50% 9.12% 11.98%
72 mo $336.20 6.50% 8.71% 11.13%

Two things show up in that table. A fee hurts more on a short loan, because it is spread over fewer dollars of interest, so the effective price per borrowed dollar rises. At 36 months the same $1,200 fee is worth 4.2 percentage points of APR; at 72 months it is worth 2.2. That is why "no fee, slightly higher rate" is usually the better trade on a short term and often the worse one on a long term.

The other is that APR measures price, not the bill. The 72-month loan has the lowest APR of the fee-paying rows and the highest total interest ($4,206 versus $3,479 at 60 months). APR answers how expensive each dollar-year of borrowing is, not how much you will pay in total. You need both numbers: APR to compare offers, total cost to decide whether to borrow at all.

Trap two: the flat rate

Some lenders, car finance and personal loans especially, quote a flat rate: interest is charged on the original principal for the whole term, and the monthly payment is (principal + principal * rate * years) / months.

6.5% flat on $20,000 over 60 months
interest = 20,000 * 0.065 * 5      = $6,500
payment  = 26,500 / 60             = $441.67
apr(20_000, 441.67, 60)            = 11.68%

The same "6.5%" is nearly twice as expensive as a 6.5% reducing-balance loan, because flat-rate interest ignores that the balance falls every month. Add the $1,200 fee and the APR reaches 14.43%. Any quote expressed as a flat rate has to be converted before it can be compared with anything, and the conversion is the same twenty lines above.

What APR leaves out

APR is a good comparator with a narrow definition. It does not include:

  • Late fees and penalty rates, which are contingent and therefore outside the finance charge.
  • Optional products such as payment protection, gap insurance and extended warranties, unless they are required to get the loan.
  • Rate resets on variable loans. The APR of an adjustable-rate mortgage is computed from the initial rate and an assumed schedule; it is not a prediction.
  • Prepayment. The calculation assumes you hold the loan to maturity. Pay it off early and the fee is spread over a shorter period, which raises the effective cost above the quoted APR.

It also varies by jurisdiction. Reg Z in the US, the APRC under the EU Consumer Credit Directive and the UK's APR all use slightly different fee baskets and rounding rules. The core identity, net proceeds equal the present value of payments, is the same everywhere.

Checking a real quote

To run a quote through this without writing code, the APR calculator on Finance Calc Kit takes the loan amount, rate, term and fees and prints the APR together with the formula and each step of the cash-flow table; the EMI calculator gives the payment and amortisation schedule. Both run client-side, so the numbers stay in the browser, and neither asks for an account. I build Finance Calc Kit, and the code above is the same maths the calculator runs, so you can check it against your own numbers.

The rule I use on any loan offer: compare APR first, because it is the only figure that prices fees; compare total payments second, because a lower APR over a longer term can still cost more; then go back to the fee list and ask which fees you can negotiate away. Every dollar removed from the fee moves the APR down more than a dollar of rate does.

If you want to check the implementation against your own loan, the function is short enough to paste into a REPL. If the APR a lender quotes you disagrees with the one it returns, ask which fees they left out of the finance charge.

title: كيف تبني متجر واتساب إلكتروني ونظام عروض أسعار وفواتير متكامل بلغة بايثون بدون اشتراكات شهرية
description:
في بيئة الأعمال الرقمية والتجارة الإلكترونية المعاصرة، يجد أصحاب المشاريع الصغيرة والمستقلون في العالم العربي أنفسهم محاصرين باشتراكات شهرية متراكمة (منصات المتاجر، أدوات الفواتير الإلكترونية، بوابات التوقيع الرقمي، ومزودو خدمة واتساب)، مما يبتلع جزءاً كبيراً من هوامش الربح قبل حتى تحقيق أول عملية بيع حقيقية.

والأخطر من ذلك هو ارتهان بيانات العملاء وقوائم الطلبات والتقارير المالية لخوادم ومنصات وسيطة تفرض شروطها وتزيد أسعارها دورياً.

في هذا الدليل الهندسي والعملي من استوديو أنتيجرافيتي (Antigravity Dev Studio)، سنستعرض بالتفصيل كيف تبني منصة تجارة إلكترونية كاملة تعتمد على واتساب، بالإضافة إلى نظام عروض أسعار وفواتير رسمية قابلة للطباعة PDF، باستخدام مكتبة بايثون القياسية (Python Standard Library) وقواعد بيانات SQLite المدمجة، بدون الحاجة لتثبيت أي حزمة خارجية من pip، وبدون دفع دولار واحد كاشتراك شهري متكرر.

1. نموذج العمل: لماذا واتساب + بايثون النقي؟

في الأسواق العربية (السعودية، الإمارات، مصر، الخليج العربي وشمال إفريقيا)، يعتبر تطبيق واتساب الأداة الأكثر موثوقية والأعلى في معدلات التحويل (Conversion Rate). الزبائن يفضلون دائماً التأكيد المباشر والمحادثة الإنسانية على نماذج الدفع الإلكتروني الطويلة والمعقدة.

بدلاً من الاشتراك في منصات SaaS باهظة، قمنا في تطبيقنا OrderFlow Pro ببناء معمارية برمجية ترتكز على:

  1. واجهة متجر سريعة للغاية (Single Page Application) بدون أطر عمل ثقيلة.
  2. محرك سلة تسوق محلي يدعم الكوبونات وحساب رسوم التوصيل والضرائب.
  3. مولد روابط واتساب ذكي يحول محتويات السلة وعنوان العميل وكود الطلب فوراً إلى رسالة منسقة وجاهزة للإرسال بضغطة زر واحدة.

إليك الكود المصدري الكامل والمجرب بلغة بايثون لتوليد رابط الطلب المباشر عبر واتساب:

import urllib.parse
from typing import Any, Dict, List

def generate_arabic_whatsapp_order_link(
    store_phone: str,
    order_code: str,
    customer_name: str,
    customer_phone: str,
    city: str,
    address: str,
    items: List[Dict[str, Any]],
    subtotal: float,
    discount: float,
    delivery_fee: float,
    total: float,
    currency: str = "SAR"
) -> str:
    """
    يقوم بإنشاء رابط ويب رسمي لتطبيق واتساب يحتوي على تفاصيل الطلب كاملة باللغة العربية.
    يعمل تلقائياً على أجهزة أندرويد، آيفون، وأجهزة الكمبيوتر.
    """
    # تنظيف رقم هاتف المتجر
    clean_phone = "".join(filter(str.isdigit, store_phone))

    # صياغة أسطر المنتجات
    lines = []
    for item in items:
        qty = item.get("qty", 1)
        name = item.get("name", "منتج")
        price = item.get("price", 0.0)
        lines.append(f"▫️ {qty}x {name} — {price * qty:,.2f} {currency}")

    items_text = "\n".join(lines)

    # الرسالة العربية المنسقة
    message = (
        f"🛍️ *طلب شراء جديد: #{order_code}*\n"
        f"━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━\n"
        f"👤 *العميل:* {customer_name.strip()}\n"
        f"📱 *الجوال:* {customer_phone.strip()}\n"
        f"📍 *المدينة:* {city.strip()} - {address.strip()}\n\n"
        f"📦 *تفاصيل المنتجات:*\n"
        f"{items_text}\n\n"
        f"━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━\n"
        f"💵 *المجموع الفرعي:* {subtotal:,.2f} {currency}\n"
    )

    if discount > 0:
        message += f"🏷️ *الخصم:* -{discount:,.2f} {currency}\n"

    message += (
        f"🚚 *التوصيل:* {delivery_fee:,.2f} {currency}\n"
        f"✅ *الإجمالي المستحق:* {total:,.2f} {currency}\n"
        f"━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━\n"
        f"أرجو تأكيد الطلب وتحديد موعد الاستلام، شكراً لكم!"
    )

    # تشفير النص ليتوافق مع بروتوكول الروابط
    encoded_query = urllib.parse.quote(message)
    return f"https://wa.me/{clean_phone}?text={encoded_query}"

2. إدارة الفواتير وعروض الأسعار في بايثون: نمط SQLite WAL

أكبر مشكلة تواجه المطورين عند بناء أنظمة فواتير محلية هي تضارب المعاملات (Database Locked) وتكرار أرقام الفواتير المتسلسلة أثناء الضغط العالي.

الحل الهندسي الأفضل هو تفعيل نمط Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) في SQLite. هذا الوضع يفصل عمليات القراءة تماماً عن الكتابة، مما يسمح لمئات المستخدمين بتصفح المتجر وعروض الأسعار بالتوازي دون إبطاء عمليات حفظ الفواتير:

import contextlib
import datetime as dt
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

class ArabicInvoiceEngine:
    def __init__(self, db_path: str = "business.db"):
        self.db_path = Path(db_path)
        self._init_db()

    def _connect(self) -> sqlite3.Connection:
        conn = sqlite3.connect(str(self.db_path), timeout=15.0)
        conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        # تفعيل نمط WAL وتطبيق القيود الخارجية
        conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;")
        conn.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;")
        conn.execute("PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;")
        return conn

    @contextlib.contextmanager
    def transaction(self):
        conn = self._connect()
        try:
            with conn: # يبدأ معاملة ذرية متسلسلة (Atomic Transaction)
                yield conn
        finally:
            conn.close()

    def _init_db(self):
        with self.transaction() as conn:
            conn.executescript("""
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS invoices (
                    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
                    invoice_code TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
                    client_name TEXT NOT NULL,
                    client_phone TEXT NOT NULL,
                    total_amount REAL NOT NULL,
                    status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'UNPAID',
                    created_at TEXT NOT NULL
                );
            """)

    def create_invoice(self, client_name: str, client_phone: str, total_amount: float) -> str:
        year = dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc).year
        now_str = dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc).isoformat()
        prefix = f"INV-{year}-"

        with self.transaction() as conn:
            # استخراج أعلى رقم فاتورة مسجل خلال العام الحالي
            row = conn.execute(
                "SELECT invoice_code FROM invoices WHERE invoice_code LIKE ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1",
                (f"{prefix}%",)
            ).fetchone()

            next_id = 1
            if row:
                try:
                    next_id = int(row["invoice_code"].split("-")[-1]) + 1
                except ValueError:
                    pass

            code = f"{prefix}{next_id:04d}"
            conn.execute(
                """
                INSERT INTO invoices (invoice_code, client_name, client_phone, total_amount, created_at)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
                """,
                (code, client_name.strip(), client_phone.strip(), round(total_amount, 2), now_str)
            )
            return code

3. طباعة الفواتير باللغة العربية (RTL) إلى PDF بجودة متجهة فائقة
