title: bybit-ws: a trading tool, an analyst, and an assistant
description:
bybit-ws: a trading tool, an analyst, and an assistant

A live Bybit futures system that scans, scores, argues with itself before every entry, learns from its own closed trades — and answers when I message it from my phone. Here is the machinery, including the parts that are still broken.

The entry signal is the least interesting part of a live trading system. What decides whether the thing survives is everything around it: what happens when the LLM times out, what happens when a balance reads zero and the bot quietly refuses to trade for two days.

This is a write-up of that part. No performance numbers, on purpose: I can't show you the query behind a PnL figure here, so I don't show the figure.

I built bybit-ws for one user: me. Python and asyncio, SQLite in WAL mode as the single source of truth, a systemd unit, an HTTP-RPC surface on localhost, an MCP wrapper so an agent can drive it. Boring interfaces on purpose: every clever coupling is something I'd have to debug at four in the morning.

Three jobs, one process

An execution tool, an analyst, and an assistant — in one systemd unit, over one SQLite file.

        Telegram (me, sleepy, holding a phone)
                    │
             agent layer (Hermes profile)
             │        │         │
        MCP tools  HTTP-RPC  shell
             │        │         │
   ┌─────────▼────────▼─────────▼──────────────┐
   │            bybit-ws (systemd user unit)   │
   │  async loop ──► market data (WebSocket)   │
   │      ├─► entry scoring ─► LLM judge ─┐    │
   │      ├─► regime model                │    │
   │      ├─► risk gate ──────────────────┤    │
   │      └─► order router ◄──────────────┘    │
   │  SQLite · self-learn · offline bench      │
   └───────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
              Bybit API v5

Two decisions matter:

  1. The exchange is not the database, and neither is trusted blindly. Positions are reconciled across the RPC view, the exchange and SQLite. When they disagree, the disagreement is the event worth alerting on.
  2. AI is not the decision-maker. The LLM sits inside the decision path as a veto, never as the thing that picks the trade.

The request path: what happens when I ask for a trade

I type something human into Telegram. Not a command grammar — a sentence. The agent parses intent, then works through this, reporting each step.

1. Scan. Candidates get scored on structure: band position, RSI, volume, funding, band compression, multi-timeframe confluence. If I name a symbol outside the ranking, the scanner does not pretend it looked — the symbol is either analysed from public candles or reported as skipped, never as no data. A candidate that vanishes silently looks identical to one that was never checked.

2. Size it. A sizing function maps my intent — "risk about this much of the account" — onto a quantity. Equity comes from the account level, not a per-coin balance line; the quantity is rounded to the exchange's step and formatted as a clean decimal string, because 18.900000000000002 is a valid float and an invalid order.

3. Preview, then execute. The entry endpoint is two-phase. The first call returns what would happen — side, quantity, stop, target, leverage — with confirm_required: true, and places nothing. The second, explicitly confirmed, places the order. That preview is the last point where a human catches a misparsed intent, and it's the same endpoint the automated branch uses. The caller sends an Idempotency-Key derived from the confirmed preview; a replay inside the hour returns the original response instead of opening a second position.

4. Verify, don't assume. After the order the system reads the position back and compares it with what it asked for. Fills land in the database one cycle later, so an instant check produces a false "it didn't open" — the agent waits, re-reads, and reports what it observed.

5. Mark it as mine. A manual entry is tagged as manual. That tag decides what the learner sees: self-learning excludes manual trades. My discretionary trades aren't the bot's performance, and letting the learner eat them would teach it my worst habits and call that strategy.

Two choices here look like bugs otherwise: the manual endpoint doesn't silently cap the leverage I ask for — my account, my call, discipline lives in the sizing step — and a kill switch closes everything and blocks new entries until I say otherwise.

Trust, and how it's enforced

Credibility isn't in the strategy; it's in whether the system's own reporting can be caught lying.

  • Three money flows, kept apart. Bybit's closed-pnl is net of the closing fee but not the opening one. Funding arrives as a separate ledger settlement. The transaction log carries gross and net per trade. The identity is asserted in code: net equals gross minus both fees, and account PnL equals trade flow plus funding. Sum them into one number and you report a profit that never existed.
  • Reconciliation against the exchange, not against itself. A local position the exchange doesn't have is a bug, not a rounding error — and because fills land a cycle late, the comparison carries a grace window.
  • Health checks with exit codes, after every change: service state, RPC liveness, cycle progression, the service's interpreter having its dependencies, position parity, database integrity, smoke suite. Prose lies silently; a script with an exit code doesn't.

And a watchdog with a narrow definition of silence: no entries for a window and enough block reasons inside it is an incident; a wall of "skipped, not a candidate" lines is normal filtering. The first version got this backwards — it counted a stopped bot as a quiet, healthy one.

Analysis before a trade: three kinds of "AI"

The word AI does too much work in most trading-bot descriptions. Here there are three layers, and mixing them up is how you get a bot that "decides" things nobody can explain.

Layer What it is How it fails
Deterministic Scoring, sizing, stops, targets, routing, risk limits Bugs, exchange quirks — reproducible and testable
Statistical Regime classifier, bandit parameter choice, drift detection Stale or unrepresentative sample; silently confident
Language model Pre-entry judge: pass or revise, with reasons Timeouts, drifted judgement, cost, latency

The deterministic layer owns money movement. The statistical layer only re-weights parameters — how eager the entries are, how tight a stop sits — and it can't touch the absolute limits: per-trade risk cap and the leverage the automated branch is allowed to set. The LLM only gets a veto.

The judge: fail-closed up to a threshold

Before an entry that scored high enough to be worth the tokens, the signal becomes a compact factual blob — band position, score components, proposed stop and target, funding, regime, confluence — handed to a hosted chat model with one question: is anything here contradictory?

Three choices make it something I trust more than my own opinion at 3 a.m.

  • Errors block by default. If the judge times out or returns junk, the verdict is revise and the entry does not happen. A model that is down is not a model that says yes.
  • A circuit breaker with a stated escape hatch. Consecutive failures open a cooldown instead of hammering a dead dependency. While it's open, entries stay blocked; only after an outage lasts long enough does the system drop into an explicit degraded mode — deterministic path only, low confidence, a fallback note in the log. Fail-closed by default, fail-open by announcement.
  • Caching by signal fingerprint. Identical signals don't re-bill the model; verdicts are reused for a short window.

What the judge is good at is catching what the rules can't cross-check: the score looks strong, but funding is paying the other side and the regime model has this as a downtrend on a timeframe your scanner doesn't read. What it is bad at is predicting the market. I don't ask it to.

Learning from closed trades — and its limits

Self-learning has been rewritten the most, and the hard part was never the update rule — it was telling real improvement from noise.

The learner reads closed trades from SQLite, scores them across win rate, profit factor, Sharpe, drawdown and holding time, and adjusts parameters per regime — "the right tightness for a stop" is a different question in a trend than in chop. Every closed trade produces a small update; the heavier re-selection of a parameter set runs on a sample trigger, with a time fallback so a quiet market doesn't starve it.

What survived:

  • Bandit selection with pruning. Parameters are arms, not one global setting. Losing arms get pruned; uncertainty picks what to try next, not what looks best so far.
  • Drift and change-point detection. The learner asks whether the recent distribution still resembles the one its parameters were chosen on. If not, it prefers exploration over doubling down on an outdated winner.
  • Canary comparison. A challenger runs alongside in a small, time-boxed comparison; the incumbent keeps the crown until the challenger wins on the sample, not on one good week.
  • Robust updates and versioning. Outliers are skipped instead of dragging the average, and every parameter change is a versioned artefact — so "why did it behave differently last Tuesday" has an answer that is a diff, not a memory.

And the honest part no bot post mentions: the learner cannot tell you whether the edge exists. It tunes within the space you gave it. If the space is wrong, it will find a confident local optimum and defend it.

The bench, where ideas are supposed to die

Next to the live system sits an offline bench: same strategy code, deterministic backtest engine, cached candles, and a run manifest recording code revision, parameter hash, config hash and data hash. Two runs with the same manifest produce the same equity hash — asserted in the test suite, so reproducibility is a property, not a claim.

On top sits an anti-overfitting gate: a parameter set has to survive deflated Sharpe, probability of backtest overfitting and a permutation test. Labels come from a triple-barrier scheme — hit target, hit stop, or time out — not "was the next candle up". Regime detection is a separate unsupervised model with a change-point detector beside it, because the interesting moment is when the regime stops being what the model thinks.

The gap, plainly: the bench doesn't promote a winner into the live learner automatically — promotion means touching the live loop, and I'd rather have a manual step and a boring diff than an autopilot I can't explain.

The assistant is not a wrapper

A chat over the API took an evening. Deciding what it may assume took the rest.

Every answer is fetched live — positions, balance, risk state, journal — never recalled from conversation. If the service is down, the answer is "down", not the last known number dressed up as current. Read paths are free-form; write paths are narrow, explicit, and confirmed. And the assistant carries what a human would otherwise hold in their head: which symbols the bot watches, which order type gets rejected in which position mode, why a balance line and an equity figure disagree.

That last category is most of the product: quirks nobody wrote down until they bit me.

If you build one

  1. Put the money path behind a two-phase endpoint with explicit confirmation, and give the automated branch the same endpoint. Two paths that can place orders is two bugs.
  2. Make the LLM a filter, and make it fail closed. The moment it can cause a trade, your risk model lives in someone else's weights.
  3. Separate the learner from the ledger. Tag discretionary trades, exclude them, version every parameter change — otherwise "the bot got better" is folklore.
  4. Build the watchdog before the strategy. A bot that stopped trading doesn't announce itself.

It's not a fund: one machine, my money, and every postmortem is mine.

The bot, the code, and me

  • Telegram bot: @Gridbolbot — the public side of the same engine: anyone can pull scans and signals; execution stays on my account.
  • Source: github.com/poliakarmai/bybit-ws — AGPL-3.0
  • Email: Armyanao@gmail.com

title: Browser AI Video Without Desktop Bloat — Image-to-Video vs Text-to-Video
description:
Browser AI Video Without Desktop Bloat — Image-to-Video vs Text-to-Video

Disclosure: I work on APIXO, a browser AI video and image workspace. This is a practical how-to based on how we see creators actually work—not a fake “I bought five phones” review.

If you have ever opened twelve AI video tabs, installed a 4 GB desktop app “just to try one clip,” and still ended up with a blurry product shot that refuses to move the way you wanted—this article is for you.

You do not need a local GPU farm or a timeline editor to get useful short clips for demos, social drafts, and campaign experiments. You need a clear entry point, a short generate → inspect → change one variable loop, and a human pass before anything goes live.

Two doors into AI video

Image-to-video (you already have a still)

Upload a product photo, illustration, portrait, or scene still. The model adds motion, camera feel, and atmosphere around that frame.

Good fit when:

  • Brand look must stay recognizable (logo product, hero shot, illustrated character)
  • You already paid for photography or art direction
  • The brief is “make this image move,” not “invent a new world”

Watch outs:

  • Soft edges, heavy compression, or tiny subjects make motion look mushy
  • Extreme camera moves fight the original composition
  • Text baked into the image often warps—plan to overlay type in post if you need crisp copy

Text-to-video (idea first, asset later)

Describe the scene in a prompt. Explore framing, light, camera language, and style before you have a finished source image.

Good fit when:

  • You need storyboard options from a copy line
  • Marketing wants three tones of the same idea for an internal review
  • You are exploring look-and-feel, not locking a hero asset

Watch outs:

  • Vague prompts (“cool futuristic vibe”) produce a different film every run
  • Subject, place, and motion written up front stabilize results more than adjective piles
  • Character identity across shots is still a weak spot for most models—treat early clips as drafts

Rule of thumb: still in hand → image-to-video. Only a sentence in hand → text-to-video. If both exist, start from the still; you can still rewrite the motion prompt.

A five-step browser workflow

  1. Write the job in one sentence.

    Examples: “3-second product turn for a PDP.” “Moody atmosphere clip for a landing hero.” “Social cut showing the UI flowing.” Purpose drives length, framing, and how much detail the model must invent.

  2. Pick the door. Image or text. Do not flip-flop mid-batch until you have at least two usable takes from one door.

  3. Check model controls that actually matter. Duration, motion strength, aspect ratio, seed (if exposed), and any style or camera presets. Models differ in how they interpret “slow pan” vs “orbit.” Read what the UI exposes; do not assume every slider exists everywhere.

  4. Generate → watch once → change one variable.

    Either tweak the prompt, swap the reference image, or switch model—not all three. That is how you learn what moved the needle. Save keepers in a library so you are not re-uploading the same still ten times.

  5. Human QA before publish.

    Check subject consistency, motion naturalness, warped text, brand colors, and anything that would embarrass you at 1080p on a phone. AI video is a draft engine; finishing still belongs to you (trim, captions, audio, color).

When you have three or more variants, park them in one place—canvas-style project boards help—so you stop bouncing between downloads folders.

Image-to-video vs text-to-video in practice

Situation Prefer Why
Shopify / App Store style product still Image-to-video Keeps packaging and silhouette
“Show the feeling of night commute” brief Text-to-video No locked hero frame yet
Illustrated mascot already designed Image-to-video Protects character art
Exploring three campaign moods from one headline Text-to-video Fast parallel looks
Need readable on-screen UI Neither alone Generate motion, then composite real UI or type

Neither path replaces editing. Both replace “wait for a full shoot before you can show anything.”

Pitfalls that burn credits

Prompt essay syndrome. A 120-word mood board dump often underperforms a tight subject + action + camera + lighting line. Put the noun first.

One-and-done despair. First output is a sketch. Change one knob. Log what you changed. Teams that treat runs as experiments get usable cuts faster than teams that gamble on a single “perfect” prompt.

Shipping raw generations. Morphing hands, melting logos, and scrambled captions pass casual glance and fail in a client review. Budget five minutes of human review per keep.

Fuzzy duration and channel. A 12-second cinematic wander is the wrong artifact for a 3-second story ad. Decide channel and length before you burn generations.

Ignoring source quality on image-to-video. Upscale or re-export a clean still first if the source is a WhatsApp screenshot. Garbage in still wins.

Chasing every new model name. For product work, consistency and iteration speed beat chasing yesterday’s leaderboard clip. Pick one or two models that match your look, learn their quirks, then expand.

Optional: clean stills before you animate

If night shots or high-ISO photos look grainy, a light denoise pass before image-to-video often reduces crawling noise in motion. Over-smoothing skin and fabric still ruins the look—compare against the original. If you use APIXO’s tools, denoise lives under image tools: Denoise Image.

Where APIXO fits (and where it does not)

APIXO is a browser workspace for image-to-video, text-to-video, related image tools, and cloud canvas projects. It started as a unified model API for developers; the product now emphasizes creators who want results without installing desktop bloat, while API access remains for teams wiring the same models into their own apps.

It will not replace a full NLE, a colorist, or a shoot. It will help you get short motion drafts into a library fast enough that marketing can react the same afternoon.

Takeaway

Browser AI video is not magic. It is pick a door → run a short loop → finish as a human. Image-to-video protects an existing visual. Text-to-video explores when the visual does not exist yet. Keep prompts concrete, change one variable per run, and never publish a generation you have not watched at full size.

If you want to try that loop in the browser: apixo.ai.

title: Self-Hosted WhatsApp E-Commerce & Automated Client Proposals in Pure Python + SQLite (Zero SaaS Fees)
description:
Running an online store or a freelance consulting business in 2026 often feels like a slow bleed of monthly SaaS subscriptions.

You pay $29/month for a basic Shopify tier, another $15/month for a proposal signing app, $20/month for an invoice generator, and another $30/month for automated WhatsApp messaging plugins. Before making your first dollar in profit, your business is saddled with over $1,000 a year in fixed recurring overhead.

Worse, your customer data, order history, and client contracts sit locked inside third-party walled gardens that can hike prices, change terms, or suspend your account at any moment.

Over the past year at Antigravity Dev Studio, we set out to prove a different thesis: You can build a high-performance, self-hosted e-commerce checkout engine and client proposal portal using only the Python standard library and SQLite.

No Django, no Celery, no Redis, and no monthly fees.

In this deep-dive tutorial, we will walk through the exact architecture and runnable code for three mission-critical components:

  1. Generating pre-filled, structured WhatsApp checkout URLs with zero API gateway fees.
  2. Building an atomic, collision-free invoice numbering system on SQLite WAL mode.
  3. Securing client proposal digital acceptance links using cryptographic HMAC signatures.

1. Zero-Fee WhatsApp Checkout URL Builder

In emerging e-commerce markets across Latin America, the Middle East, Africa, and Southeast Asia, WhatsApp is the dominant communication channel. Customers often abandon traditional multi-step checkout funnels that force account creation or require complex payment gateways.

Instead of paying a third-party WhatsApp Business API provider hundreds of dollars in monthly platform fees, you can use the official https://wa.me/ direct URL protocol. When a customer clicks "Place Order via WhatsApp", your Python backend formats their entire shopping cart, customer notes, delivery address, and order code into an encoded message.

When the customer taps the link on mobile or desktop, WhatsApp opens instantly with a perfectly structured, ready-to-send message:

import urllib.parse
from typing import Any, Dict, List

def build_whatsapp_order_url(
    business_phone: str,
    order_code: str,
    customer_name: str,
    customer_phone: str,
    delivery_address: str,
    items: List[Dict[str, Any]],
    subtotal: float,
    discount_amount: float,
    delivery_fee: float,
    total: float,
    currency: str = "USD"
) -> str:
    """
    Constructs an official, encoded WhatsApp Web/App direct checkout URL.
    Works natively on iOS, Android, macOS, and Windows.
    """
    # Clean phone number (strip spaces, dashes, plus signs)
    clean_phone = "".join(ch for ch in business_phone if ch.isdigit())

    # Build clean line items breakdown
    item_lines = []
    for item in items:
        qty = item.get("qty", 1)
        name = item.get("name", "Product")
        price = item.get("price", 0.0)
        item_lines.append(f"• {qty}x {name} — {currency} {price * qty:,.2f}")

    items_block = "\n".join(item_lines)

    # Formatted customer message
    message = (
        f"🛍️ *NEW ORDER: #{order_code}*\n"
        f"━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━\n"
        f"👤 *Customer:* {customer_name.strip()}\n"
        f"📞 *Phone:* {customer_phone.strip()}\n"
        f"📍 *Delivery Address:* {delivery_address.strip()}\n\n"
        f"📦 *Ordered Items:*\n"
        f"{items_block}\n\n"
        f"━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━\n"
        f"💰 *Subtotal:* {currency} {subtotal:,.2f}\n"
    )

    if discount_amount > 0:
        message += f"🏷️ *Discount:* -{currency} {discount_amount:,.2f}\n"

    message += (
        f"🚚 *Delivery Fee:* {currency} {delivery_fee:,.2f}\n"
        f"✅ *TOTAL AMOUNT:* {currency} {total:,.2f}\n"
        f"━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━\n"
        f"Please confirm availability and dispatch details!"
    )

    # Encode message safely for URL transmission
    encoded_text = urllib.parse.quote(message)
    return f"https://wa.me/{clean_phone}?text={encoded_text}"

Testing the Output 

sample_items = [
    {"name": "Mechanical Keyboard Pro", "qty": 1, "price": 89.00},
    {"name": "USB-C Braided Cable", "qty": 2, "price": 12.50},
]

url = build_whatsapp_order_url(
    business_phone="+1 (555) 019-2834",
    order_code="ORD-78241",
    customer_name="Alex Mercer",
    customer_phone="+1 555 982 1102",
    delivery_address="742 Evergreen Terrace, Springfield",
    items=sample_items,
    subtotal=114.00,
    discount_amount=10.00,
    delivery_fee=5.00,
    total=109.00
)

print(url)

The resulting link is clean, works without any third-party gateway dependencies, and provides customers with an immediate human connection to your store.

2. Atomic SQLite WAL Invoicing & Sequential Numbering

When building an invoicing engine for clients, sequential and collision-free document numbering (such as INV-2026-001, INV-2026-002) is legally required in most jurisdictions.

If two users or background tasks generate an invoice at the exact same millisecond, a standard SQL query without proper locking will generate duplicate invoice codes or trigger database locked errors.

By leveraging SQLite Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and an explicit write-transaction loop, you guarantee zero collisions and sub-millisecond execution:

import contextlib
import datetime as dt
import pathlib
import sqlite3
from typing import Generator

class InvoiceDatabase:
    def __init__(self, db_path: pathlib.Path):
        self.db_path = pathlib.Path(db_path)
        self.db_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        self._init_schema()

    def _connect(self) -> sqlite3.Connection:
        conn = sqlite3.connect(str(self.db_path), timeout=15.0)
        conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        # WAL mode enables concurrent readers while writing
        conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;")
        conn.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;")
        conn.execute("PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;")
        return conn

    @contextlib.contextmanager
    def session(self) -> Generator[sqlite3.Connection, None, None]:
        conn = self._connect()
        try:
            with conn: # Enters transaction: BEGIN IMMEDIATE on writes
                yield conn
        finally:
            conn.close()

    def _init_schema(self) -> None:
        with self.session() as conn:
            conn.executescript("""
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS invoices (
                    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
                    invoice_code TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
                    client_name TEXT NOT NULL,
                    amount REAL NOT NULL CHECK(amount >= 0),
                    status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'UNPAID',
                    created_at TEXT NOT NULL
                );
                CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_invoices_code ON invoices(invoice_code);
            """)

    def generate_next_invoice(self, client_name: str, amount: float) -> str:
        """
        Atomically queries the current year's highest invoice sequence
        and inserts the next consecutive record in an isolated transaction.
        """
        year = dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc).year
        now_iso = dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc).replace(microsecond=0).isoformat()
        prefix = f"INV-{year}-"

        with self.session() as conn:
            # Find the highest existing sequence for the current year
            row = conn.execute(
                """
                SELECT invoice_code FROM invoices 
                WHERE invoice_code LIKE ? 
                ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1
                """,
                (f"{prefix}%",)
            ).fetchone()

            if row:
                last_code = row["invoice_code"]
                try:
                    last_num = int(last_code.split("-")[-1])
                    next_num = last_num + 1
                except ValueError:
                    next_num = 1
            else:
                next_num = 1

            invoice_code = f"{prefix}{next_num:04d}"

            conn.execute(
                """
                INSERT INTO invoices (invoice_code, client_name, amount, status, created_at)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, 'UNPAID', ?)
                """,
                (invoice_code, client_name.strip(), round(amount, 2), now_iso)
            )

            return invoice_code

Because SQLite serializes writes at the file level inside with conn:, concurrent invoice generations will wait their turn cleanly rather than colliding.

3. Cryptographic Proposal Approvals via HMAC Tokens

When sending proposals or fee quotes to clients, you do not want to force them to create a username and password just to approve a scope of work. At the same time, you cannot use easily guessable sequential URLs (like /proposals/42/accept), as anyone could guess the URL and fake an approval.

Using standard library hmac and hashlib, you can generate tamper-proof signed authorization URLs. When the client clicks "Accept & Sign", your backend verifies that the token was signed with your server's secret key before marking the proposal as legally accepted:

import hashlib
import hmac
import secrets
import time

SERVER_SECRET_KEY = secrets.token_bytes(32) # Store securely in env / config

def generate_proposal_approval_token(proposal_id: str, client_email: str) -> str:
    """
    Generates a cryptographically signed URL token valid for client signature.
    """
    timestamp = str(int(time.time()))
    payload = f"{proposal_id}|{client_email.strip().lower()}|{timestamp}".encode("utf-8")

    # Generate HMAC-SHA256 signature
    sig = hmac.new(SERVER_SECRET_KEY, payload, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

    # Token structure: timestamp.signature
    return f"{timestamp}.{sig}"

def verify_proposal_approval_token(proposal_id: str, client_email: str, token: str, max_age_days: int = 30) -> bool:
    """
    Verifies that the proposal token was signed with the server key and has not expired.
    """
    try:
        timestamp_str, candidate_sig = token.split(".", 1)
        created_time = int(timestamp_str)

        # Check expiration
        max_age_seconds = max_age_days * 86400
        if time.time() - created_time > max_age_seconds:
            return False # Token expired

        expected_payload = f"{proposal_id}|{client_email.strip().lower()}|{timestamp_str}".encode("utf-8")
        expected_sig = hmac.new(SERVER_SECRET_KEY, expected_payload, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

        # Constant-time comparison prevents timing attacks
        return hmac.compare_digest(candidate_sig, expected_sig)
    except Exception:
        return False

When verified, the system records the client's IP, acceptance timestamp, and digital signature string, instantly locking the proposal into a frozen state.

Production Applications from Antigravity Dev Studio

If you don't want to build these architectures from scratch, we have packaged our complete, battle-tested production systems into modular commercial toolkits:

title: Your MCP Server Doesn’t Need 50 Tools: Design a Tool Budget Before It Eats Your Context
description:
Adding another MCP tool feels free.

It is not.

Each tool comes with a name, description, input schema, examples, and an implied decision: when should the agent use this instead of every other available tool? That material competes with the task, the repository, the user’s request, and the agent’s own plan for a finite place in context.

The usual response is to expose the whole catalog and hope the model sorts it out. The predictable results are familiar:

  • a read task reaches for a write tool;
  • the agent calls three near-duplicate tools before it starts work;
  • an expensive search tool is used where a cheap lookup would do;
  • a destructive tool is available long before a human has seen a plan;
  • a tool list changes, but the workflow that relied on it was never re-tested.

The fix is not one giant do_everything tool. That only moves ambiguity from the tool list into a larger, less inspectable parameter schema.

The goal: give an agent enough capability to finish the next decision safely, not every capability it could conceivably need.

The hidden cost of a large tool list

MCP tools are not just functions on a server. Their definitions are part of the agent’s working environment. More tools means more text, more overlapping verbs, and more possible action paths.

That does not mean there is a universal safe number of tools. A two-tool server can still be dangerous, and a well-separated 20-tool server can be usable. The budget is about reducing unnecessary choice for a particular task mode.

Ask two questions for every tool:

  1. What decision becomes impossible without this tool?
  2. Can the agent safely defer this capability until a later stage?

If the answer to the first is vague and the second is yes, do not load it in the first stage.

Budget by workflow stage, not by server

The useful unit is not “how many tools does this MCP server expose?” It is “which tools can this agent see right now?”

Here is a conservative budget for a workflow that investigates, proposes, then changes deployment configuration:

Stage Agent’s job Typical budget Allowed capability
Observe Establish facts 3–5 tools Read-only logs, config, status, documentation
Prepare Build an explicit plan 2–4 tools Read-only plus local validation or dry-run
Execute Apply an approved change 1–2 tools One narrow write tool, one verification tool
Verify Prove the result 2–3 tools Read-back, test, status check

This is a budget, not a protocol requirement. The important part is the direction: writes arrive late, narrowly, and with a verification path.

Example: a deploy workflow with five tools—not fifty

Instead of handing an agent a generic cloud account with every operation available, define the stage-specific surface:

OBSERVE
  get_service_status(service)
  get_recent_deploys(service)
  read_deploy_config(service)
  search_runbook(query)

PREPARE
  validate_deploy_plan(plan)
  preview_config_diff(service, proposed_config)

EXECUTE — after human approval
  apply_approved_deploy(change_id)
  get_service_status(service)

Notice what is absent: delete_service, arbitrary shell execution, account-wide secret enumeration, and five slightly different deployment actions. Those may belong to a separate, explicit workflow. They do not help an agent answer, “What is wrong with this deployment?”

Give each tool one job

Tool lists become unreliable when names overlap: search, find, query, lookup, get, and fetch can all mean nearly the same thing. A model should not have to infer operational policy from a marketing-style description.

For every visible tool, write a one-line contract:

tool: find_failed_deployments
use_when: "You need failed deployments for one named service and time range."
do_not_use_when: "You need logs, a configuration diff, or a deployment action."
returns: "Deployment ID, timestamp, status, and failure summary."
side_effects: none

Then test the contrast. Give the agent four small prompts:

  1. A request that should invoke this tool.
  2. A near miss that should invoke a different tool.
  3. A request that must stop for missing input.
  4. A request that must ask for approval rather than acting.

If two tools would both be plausible for the same prompt, remove, rename, or route one of them—not write a longer description for both.

Start from a workflow, not a tool catalog

This is also a useful filter when you are looking for a skill to install. Do not begin with “Which integration looks powerful?” Begin with the bounded job: triage a failed deploy, package a repeated runbook, audit a repository before a change.

The skill should make the workflow legible—trigger, allowed inputs, approval boundary, and a verifiable done condition—not quietly expand the agent’s reach.

Terminal Skills organizes skills around practical jobs, so it is a useful place to find a starting workflow. A catalog can help you discover a workflow; it should never replace validating one in your environment.

Safety annotations help—but they are not enforcement

MCP tool annotations can express whether a tool is read-only, destructive, idempotent, or reaches an open world. Use them. They make the workflow more legible and can drive better confirmation UX.

But they are hints from a server, not a security boundary. Keep the actual guardrails outside the model:

  • the host enforces an allow-list for the current stage;
  • approval binds to an exact change or plan, not a vague “yes, go ahead”;
  • write operations accept idempotency keys or a change ID where possible;
  • validation runs after the write using an independent read-back path;
  • output from web pages, logs, tickets, and retrieved documents is treated as data—not instructions.

A low-risk tool can return hostile text. A harmless-looking action can become expensive or irreversible when repeated. The policy must be deterministic even when the agent is not.

A compact tool-budget review

Before you add a tool to a skill or agent workflow, fill in this scorecard:

TOOL: __________________________
STAGE: observe / prepare / execute / verify

[ ] It unlocks a named decision in this stage.
[ ] Its name and description are distinct from every visible alternative.
[ ] Its input schema rejects missing or dangerous ambiguity.
[ ] Its output has a small, documented shape.
[ ] We know whether it reads, writes, retries safely, or reaches external systems.
[ ] There is a negative test showing when the agent must not call it.
[ ] If it writes, the exact effect needs approval and has a read-back check.

Do not replace 50 tools with one opaque mega-tool

The common over-correction is a tool called manage_deployment, operate_database, or handle_customer. It sounds tidy until its schema contains every operation and every escape hatch.

A better consolidation rule:

  • combine tools only when they share the same risk level, input shape, authorization rule, and success check;
  • separate them when any one of those changes;
  • prefer a small read tool plus a separate approved write tool over a “read-or-write depending on a flag” tool.

Test tool selection as a regression surface

Tool budgets decay. A new integration gets added. A description changes. An old alias remains for compatibility. A skill that once picked the right sequence begins to wander.

Keep a small fixture suite next to the workflow:

case: investigate failed deploy
expected_tools:
  - get_service_status
  - get_recent_deploys
forbidden_tools:
  - apply_approved_deploy
  - delete_service
done_when: "The agent cites a deployment ID and asks for missing evidence or proposes a plan."

case: apply approved config change
precondition: "approval token matches the displayed config diff"
expected_tools:
  - apply_approved_deploy
  - get_service_status
done_when: "The post-change status and config digest match the approved plan."

Start with the workflow’s expensive mistakes: a wrong write, an unnecessary external search, a missing approval, or a “done” claim with no evidence. Run those cases when the tool list, the skill instructions, or the host policy changes.

The smallest safe surface wins

An agent does not become capable because it can see every action your systems expose. It becomes dependable when each step has a constrained purpose, a clear boundary, and proof of completion.

Before adding your next MCP integration, do not ask only, “Can the agent call this?” Ask: “At which stage is this necessary—and what must be true before it is visible?”

Find a workflow you can actually govern. Browse practical agent use cases on Terminal Skills, then check the trigger, tool budget, approval boundary, and proof of completion before installing.

Further reading: MCP specification and the MCP changelog.

title: Genny: Building Procedural Sounds and Music with Python
description:
Genny: Building Procedural Sounds and Music with Python

What if a game could generate its own sound effects instead of relying entirely on prerecorded audio files?

What if you could describe a material, an instrument, a physical interaction or a musical sequence in Python and turn it into an actual WAV file?

That is the idea behind Genny, an open-source Python library I have been developing to explore procedural audio synthesis and physically informed sound generation.

GitHub: https://github.com/blal1/genny

PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/genny/

What is Genny?

Genny is an offline sound and music synthesis library written in Python.

It provides a collection of generators and physical models that can produce audio from parameters, code or structured JSON specifications.

Rather than simply playing prerecorded samples, Genny can generate sounds based on properties such as:

  • Instrument type and playing parameters.
  • Material and object size.
  • Physical interactions such as impacts, friction and bouncing.
  • Environmental conditions and room acoustics.
  • Musical notes, sequences and effects.
  • Random seeds for controlled variations.

The project currently includes a large catalogue of instruments, drums, sound effects, audio effects and generative layers.

Its main goal is to make procedural audio accessible from ordinary Python programs while also providing lower-level tools for people interested in sound synthesis and physical modelling.

Getting started

Install Genny with pip:

pip install genny

You can then import it directly into Python.

For example, let's generate a glass impact:

import genny
from genny.sfx import render_sfx
from genny.core import write_wav

sample_rate = 44100

audio = render_sfx(
    "impact",
    sample_rate,
    material="glass",
    size=0.2
)

write_wav("glass_tap.wav", audio, sample_rate)

The generator returns a NumPy audio array, which can be processed, mixed or saved as a WAV file.

You are not limited to glass impacts. You can generate many kinds of sounds by changing the generator and its parameters.

Generating instruments and musical sequences

Genny also provides instruments and musical synthesis tools.

For example, you can generate a short guitar sequence:

genny seq guitar "E3:1 G3:1 B3:1 E4:2" --bpm 100 -o tune.wav

You can also generate a sequence using another instrument:

genny seq cristal "A4:2 C5:2 E5:4" --bpm 60 -o cristal.wav

The command-line interface makes it possible to experiment with sounds without writing a complete Python program.

Genny also includes generated music in multiple styles, alongside instruments ranging from keyboards and strings to winds, percussion and more.

Physical sound modelling

One of the most interesting parts of Genny is its physically informed synthesis engine.

The idea is to model aspects of how sounds are produced rather than relying exclusively on generic oscillators or static recordings.

For example, the library provides models for:

  • Plucked and bowed strings.
  • Piano strings and hammer interactions.
  • Acoustic tubes, reeds and wind instruments.
  • Membranes, bars and vibrating plates.
  • Impacts and friction between physical materials.
  • Bubbles, pouring liquids, fire and environmental sounds.
  • Room acoustics and sound propagation.

Here is a small example using a physical string model:

import genny

string = genny.StringInstrument(
    body="guitar",
    position=0.18,
    brightness=0.6
)

audio = string.pluck(
    220.0,
    2.0,
    velocity=0.8
)

The library also exposes lower-level research-oriented modules under genny.physical, including waveguides, modal synthesis, particles, voice and room acoustics.

These models are reduced-order approximations designed for practical audio generation. They are not intended to replace full finite-element or boundary-element simulations.

Procedural audio for video games

Game development is one of the areas where I think procedural audio can be particularly useful.

Instead of shipping a separate audio file for every possible event, a game can generate sounds from its current state.

Imagine a game with a vehicle whose engine changes according to its RPM and load.

With Genny, you can generate an engine sound using parameters:

import genny
from genny.sfx import render_sfx
from genny.core import write_wav

engine = render_sfx(
    "pipe_engine",
    44100,
    rpm=3200.0,
    cylinders=6,
    dur=2.0
)

write_wav("engine.wav", engine, 44100)

The same principle can be used for interface sounds, footsteps, environmental ambience, machinery, impacts and other dynamic events.

Another useful feature is deterministic generation: identical arguments produce identical audio samples. This makes it possible to cache generated sounds instead of recalculating them every time.

For example, a game could maintain a cache of sound effects generated from their parameters.

Building audio directly into Python applications

Genny is not limited to command-line usage.

Its Python API allows you to integrate sound generation into an application.

A generated sound can be stored in a variable, transformed with effects, mixed with other signals or converted into WAV bytes in memory.

For example:

from functools import lru_cache
import numpy as np

from genny.sfx import render_sfx

SAMPLE_RATE = 44100

@lru_cache(maxsize=256)
def sound(name, **params):
    return render_sfx(
        name,
        SAMPLE_RATE,
        **params
    )

glass = sound("impact", material="glass", size=0.2)
wood = sound("impact", material="wood", size=0.3)

This is particularly useful when an application needs reusable sound generators or multiple variations of the same event.

The repository also contains a more complete integration example in examples/in_your_code.py, covering caching, parameter banks, interface events, effects, generated scenes and in-memory WAV conversion.

A large collection of sound generators

Genny includes a broad catalogue of sound generators and processing tools.

Some examples include:

  • Musical instruments and percussion.
  • Mechanical and vehicle sounds.
  • Environmental ambience.
  • Animals, insects and footsteps.
  • Impacts, scraping, rolling and breaking objects.
  • Speech and vocal synthesis.
  • Reverbs, filters and spectral processing.
  • Retro sound-generation engines.

You can inspect the available generators directly from the command line:

genny list

You can also inspect an existing audio file:

genny info tune.wav

The analysis tools provide information such as loudness, sharpness, brightness and spectral characteristics.

Open source and documentation

Genny is an ongoing project, and I am continuing to expand its catalogue, improve its physical models and refine its Python API.

If you want to explore the implementation, the repository contains several useful documentation resources:

Documentation What it covers
docs/README.md Documentation index and Python quick start
docs/catalog.md Instruments, effects, sound generators and parameters
docs/physics.md Physical models, references and known limitations
docs/api.md Public Python API
AGENTS.md JSON specifications, musical notation and generation recipes
examples/in_your_code.py Integration into Python applications

Important: some physical synthesis components are adapted from the Klang procedural library. If you intend to distribute Genny-generated audio in an interactive product, read THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md and THIRD_PARTY_KLANG_LICENSE.txt in the repository to understand the applicable attribution requirements.

Try it and share your feedback

I would love to see what other developers, audio programmers, musicians and game creators could build with Genny.

Some interesting directions include:

  • Procedural sound effects for indie games.
  • Dynamic audio systems driven by game state.
  • Generative music experiments.
  • Physical modelling and audio research.
  • Automated sound generation pipelines.
  • Creative coding projects.

If you are interested, you can find the project here:

GitHub: https://github.com/blal1/genny

PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/genny/

Contributions, bug reports, suggestions and discussions are welcome.

I'm particularly interested in feedback about the API, documentation, sound quality, physical modelling and potential applications.

Thanks for reading, and happy sound generation!
