title: Browser Email Tests Need a Privacy Boundary
description:
Email verification tests are usually designed around correctness: trigger the message, open it, click the link, and assert that the account is active. Privacy is often added later, after somebody finds an address in a screenshot or a token in a CI log.

That order are backwards. A test mailbox is part of the application's data boundary, even when it contains only synthetic users. A disposable address can still identify a run, expose product behavior, or be reused by the wrong test. The useful question is not whether the data is real. It is whether each system in the test path needs to see it.

The browser is part of the data boundary

Modern browser tests cross several boundaries: the page, the test runner, a mailbox API, the application logs, and CI artifact storage. Each boundary can copy more data than the test author intended.

For example, a signup test might put the email address in a URL query string, save the verification response in local storage, print the message body during a failure, and attach a screenshot showing the inbox. The test passes, but its evidence now contains a complete identity and possibly a credential-like token.

This is true whether the address is a normal test account, a disposable address, or a phrase such as facebook temp email used to find a fixture in an old test. Search terms do not make good secrets, but they can still create noisy logs and reveal how a team tests account flows.

I prefer to model the fixture as a capability with a short lease. The browser recieve only what it needs to complete the scenario. The mailbox adapter owns retrieval, filtering, and cleanup. The test report get a stable fixture id and a redacted outcome, not the entire message.

What a privacy-safe fixture should contain

A fixture need enough metadata to make a failure explainable. It does not need to preserve every field returned by the mailbox service.

Keep these values in the test-side record:

  • a random fixture id that is unrelated to a real person's identity
  • the test name, worker id, and attempt number
  • a mailbox lease or ownership id
  • the trigger time and the message id selected by the test
  • a redacted sender, recipient class, and subject match result
  • a final state such as received, expired, rejected, or cleaned

Keep verification URLs, raw message bodies, and access credentials out of normal logs. If a diagnosis genuinely needs one of them, write it to a restricted, short-lived artifact with an explicit owner. A screenshot is not automatically safe because it was created by a test.

The mailbox name should also be deterministic enough to debug but unpredictable enough to avoid collisions. A generated alias based only on the test name is not sufficient when parallel workers run the same scenario. Naming test inboxes in Playwright is a useful companion pattern for making ownership visible.

Keep test mail out of browser and CI leaks

The page should interact with the product, not with the mailbox provider. Put inbox polling in a Node-side task or service boundary. This keeps provider credentials away from browser JavaScript and makes it easier to apply a consistent redaction policy.

The boundary can return a small result:

{
  "fixtureId": "fx_7d91",
  "messageId": "msg_42",
  "received": true,
  "verificationLinkFound": true
}

Notice what is missing: the address, the token, and the message body. The browser can continue the flow with a one-time link supplied through a controlled test helper, while the report retains evidence that the correct message was selected.

CI configuration deserve the same care. Mask environment variables, disable verbose provider responses by default, and make failure attachments opt-in for sensitive tests. A debug flag that prints every API response is usefull during local diagnosis, but it should'nt become the default pipeline behavior.

Also check browser persistence. Clear local storage, cookies, IndexedDB, and service-worker state between identities. A previous run can leave an address or verification response behind, causing both a false pass and an unintended data leak. This cleanup is boring, but its effect on trust is large.

A practical fixture lifecycle

Treat the mailbox as a resource with explicit states:

  1. Allocate: create or reserve a mailbox and record its fixture id.
  2. Bind: associate it with one test attempt and one expected workflow.
  3. Observe: poll through the mailbox adapter using sender, subject, age, and ownership filters.
  4. Consume: return only the minimum verification capability to the test.
  5. Quarantine: keep failed evidence separate from normal artifacts, with a short retention period.
  6. Release: delete or invalidate the mailbox and clear browser state.

If cleanup fails, mark the fixture as quarantined instead of silently returning it to a pool. Reusing a mailbox with unknown contents can make a passing test prove nothing. A compact record like a small schema for reliable email fixtures can make these transitions visible without storing message contents.

The same lifecycle help when a provider is slow. The test can distinguish “no message arrived before the deadline” from “a message arrived but did not belong to this run.” That distinction is valuable for reliability, and it prevents teams from solving privacy and delivery problems with an unlimited retry.

Questions teams usually ask

Can we log the full email in local development?

Only when the mailbox and logs are clearly isolated and the data expires. A safer default is to log a message id and a reason for rejection. Developers can add a temporary, explicit inspection step when the failure requires it.

Is a disposable address automatically private?

No. It may still be visible to a provider, a shared mailbox dashboard, browser history, screenshots, or CI retention. Privacy comes from limiting access and lifetime, not from the label attached to the address.

Should the test store the verification token?

Store it only at the narrowest boundary that needs it, and never in general-purpose test output. Prefer a helper that consumes the capability immediately and returns a boolean or a sanitized result.

A browser email test is more maintainable when its privacy boundary is designed alongside its assertion. The goal is not to hide every detail from engineers. It is to make the important evidence durable while making accidental copies of identities and tokens difficult.

title: gRPC in the browser without grpc-web: the wire protocol over a WebRTC DataChannel
description:
grpc-web exists because browsers can't speak HTTP/2 trailers.
The usual answer is a translation proxy in front of your service.
We took a different one: run the actual gRPC wire protocol —
length-prefixed frames, HPACK-free, all four call shapes — over a
single WebRTC RTCDataChannel, and generate the runtime for it
from your .proto.

grpc-over-datachannels is that experiment, grown up:

  • Dependency-free generated runtimes for 16 languages — JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, Rust, Python, Ruby, PHP, Lua, C, C++, Dart, Java, Kotlin, Scala, Swift, C#, and Zig. Browser and native. The generated code is stdlib-only; there is no grpc library underneath it.
  • Our own WebRTC stack. ICE, DTLS, and SCTP written from scratch, so the native clients don't depend on a WebRTC library either.
  • Graded against stock gRPC. The generated implementations are tested against the reference implementations through a TCP↔DataChannel proxy — the oracle is the real thing, not a reimplementation of it.
  • WebRTC-Direct. A server prints one certhash multiaddr; a client dials it. No signaling server. Direct on a LAN, through a TURN relay behind symmetric NAT, or full ICE with STUN in peer mode — with runnable examples in every language.
  • A Kafka proxy in Rust. grpcdc.kafka.v1.Kafka exposes Apache Kafka as a generated gRPC service, so any generated client — including a browser tab — can produce and consume without a Kafka client library. The same generated e2e suite runs against Kafka and Redpanda in CI.

If you only have thirty seconds, the whole pitch is a 2-minute
video: https://youtu.be/LwrXpnlMlgA — and the Kafka proxy gets
its own: https://youtu.be/KJ98a4ApZ4E

The part we're proudest of is also the strangest: almost
everything in the repos is generated. The runtimes, the tests,
the examples, and the docs come from recursive generators, so
sixteen languages can't quietly drift apart. When a language
misbehaves, we fix the generator, not sixteen codebases.

Try it without installing anything — the stub generator runs in
your browser: https://browser-grpc.github.io/grpc-over-datachannels/app/

Code, releases (npm / PyPI / NuGet / GHCR / GitHub-hosted Maven):
https://github.com/browser-grpc/grpc-over-datachannels

Longer write-ups, with the design trade-offs:

  • https://c100k.blogspot.com/2026/10/introducing-grpc-over-datachannels-grpc.html
  • https://c100k.blogspot.com/2026/10/kafka-over-grpc-rust-kafka-proxy-with.html

Questions and hostile edge cases welcome — the NAT and framing ones especially.

title: pip "externally-managed-environment" Error: venv, pipx, or uv?
description:
If pip install fails with error: externally-managed-environment, your operating system's package manager owns that Python, and pip is refusing to write into it (PEP 668). The fix is almost never --break-system-packages: use a virtual environment for project dependencies, pipx or uv tool for command-line applications, and reserve the override flag for throwaway containers.

What does the error actually say, and why does it happen?

On a recent Debian, Ubuntu, or Homebrew-installed Python, this is what you get:

$ pip install requests
error: externally-managed-environment

× This environment is externally managed
╰─> To install Python packages system-wide, try apt install
    python3-xyz, where xyz is the package you are trying to
    install.

    If you wish to install a non-Debian-packaged Python package,
    create a virtual environment using python3 -m venv path/to/venv.
    ...
note: If you believe this is a mistake, please contact your Python installation or OS distribution provider. You can override this, at your own risk, by passing the --break-system-packages flag.

The mechanism is a marker file. Distributions that ship PEP 668 support place a file named EXTERNALLY-MANAGED in the interpreter's standard library directory, and pip checks for it before any install into that environment. You can see it yourself:

python3 -c "import sysconfig, pathlib; p = pathlib.Path(sysconfig.get_path('stdlib')) / 'EXTERNALLY-MANAGED'; print(p, p.exists())"

The reason it exists is real: apt and pip both write into the same site-packages, and when pip upgrades a library that an OS tool depends on, the OS tool can break in ways that are miserable to diagnose. As of late 2026 this behavior is the default on current Debian and Ubuntu releases, and Homebrew's Python applies it too. It is not a pip bug.

Takeaway: the error means "this interpreter belongs to your OS", and the right response is to stop installing into it, not to silence the check.

Which dead ends should you skip?

These are the ones I see suggested most often, and why they cost you later:

  • sudo pip install ... does not bypass the check, and if it did, you would be writing into the exact directory the protection exists for.
  • Deleting the EXTERNALLY-MANAGED file works until the next Python package update puts it back, and in the meantime you have turned off the guard for every user on the machine.
  • pip install --user is blocked by the same marker on most setups, so it does not help.
  • --break-system-packages works, and on a disposable machine that is fine. On a laptop or server you care about, it reintroduces the exact apt-versus-pip conflicts PEP 668 prevents.

Takeaway: every shortcut here trades a one-minute fix now for an unexplainable breakage of an OS tool later.

Which tool fits which job?

The right choice depends on what you are installing, not on personal taste.

Situation Best fit Why
Dependencies for a project you are developing venv (or uv venv) One isolated environment per project, reproducible from a requirements file
A CLI tool you just want on your PATH (e.g. a formatter, httpie) pipx or uv tool install Each app gets its own hidden environment, the command lands on PATH
Many projects, slow installs, lockfile wanted uv Fast resolver and installer, handles Python versions too
Docker image or CI job that is thrown away venv, or the override flag The OS-protection argument is weaker in a disposable root filesystem
A library packaged by your distro apt install python3-<name> Managed and patched by the OS, but often older

Takeaway: libraries go in a project venv, applications go in an isolated tool environment, and neither goes in the system interpreter.

How do you set up a venv correctly (including the Debian gotcha)?

The standard library route needs no extra tools:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install requests

On Debian and Ubuntu you may hit a second error first: The virtual environment was not created successfully because ensurepip is not available. Debian splits venv into its own package, so run sudo apt install python3-venv and retry.

Do not skip source .venv/bin/activate. If you forget, pip resolves to the system one and you are back at the original error. When in doubt, call the venv's interpreter explicitly: .venv/bin/python -m pip install requests.

If you want the managed version of this workflow, uv is the tool that creates the environment and installs from a requirements file in one fast step:

uv venv
uv pip install -r requirements.txt

A genuine drawback: uv is a separate binary you have to install and trust, and its uv pip interface follows pip closely but not identically, so edge cases in older requirements files can resolve differently than they did under pip. Test before you swap it into CI.

Takeaway: the venv is only protecting you if it is active or invoked by path; most "it still fails" reports are an unactivated shell.

How do you install command-line tools without polluting anything?

For applications, pipx creates one isolated environment per tool and exposes only its executables:

sudo apt install pipx   # or: brew install pipx
pipx ensurepath
pipx install httpie

If you want the one that handles isolated tool installs without a separate package from your distro, uv tool install httpie does the same job with the same one-environment-per-app model.

The limitation of both: they are for applications. If you pipx install a library and then import it in your own script, it will not be importable, because the library lives in its hidden environment. That is by design, and it is the most common confusion.

Takeaway: if you will type its name in a terminal, use pipx or uv tool; if you will import it, use a venv.

When is --break-system-packages acceptable?

In a Dockerfile or CI runner that is rebuilt from scratch every time, there is no OS tool left to protect, and a venv adds a layer for little benefit. Setting ENV PIP_BREAK_SYSTEM_PACKAGES=1 in the image is a reasonable, explicit choice there. Even so, a venv in the image keeps the same code path you use locally, which makes "works on my machine" bugs rarer. Choose the override flag knowingly, not because a forum answer said so.

Takeaway: the override flag is a tool for disposable filesystems, not for your daily laptop.

FAQ

How do I fix "error: externally-managed-environment" on Ubuntu or Debian?

Create a virtual environment with python3 -m venv .venv, activate it, and run pip inside it. If venv creation fails, install python3-venv with apt first.

Is pip install --break-system-packages safe?

It is safe on a throwaway container or CI runner. On a machine where apt manages Python tools, it can overwrite files that OS utilities depend on and cause breakage that is hard to trace.

Should I use pipx or uv to install Python command-line tools?

Either works: both give each application its own isolated environment and put its command on your PATH. Choose uv tool if you already use uv for projects, otherwise pipx is available from most package managers.

Bottom line

Use a venv (or uv venv) for anything you import, pipx or uv tool install for anything you run from a terminal, and apt install python3-<name> only when you want the distro-maintained version. Treat --break-system-packages as a Docker-and-CI setting. If you are on a team, put the one-line environment setup in the README so nobody rediscovers this error on day one.

  • Docker Image Works on Your Mac but Fails on the Server: Fixing exec format error for Good
  • Cursor vs GitHub Copilot vs Windsurf: Which AI Editor Fits How You Actually Work?

title: Node.js SMS Event Notifications for Edtech Signup Links — Template Ownership and SLOs
description:
Short answer: A Node.js SMS event-notifications worker should emit a durable signup event, render an owned template revision, and use a common API adapter whose status records distinguish submission from delivery.

The page is red, but the signup event is green

The least complex design is a durable signup event, an owned message template, and a delivery-status consumer that can prove where each verification link stopped. For an edtech platform, that means the learner gets a verification link during account creation without making the web request wait for an SMS provider or letting a provider quietly become the owner of enrollment copy.

An on-call engineer should see more than sms_failed = 1. The useful alert says that verification messages created in the last five minutes have crossed the send SLO, identifies the template revision, and separates an accepted request from a delivered message. Those are different states.

I start with the page that fires: signup completion is falling because the verification-message queue is growing. Then I work backward. Was the event emitted? Was the message rendered from the expected revision? Was the send request accepted? Did a delivery receipt arrive? Which of those signals was missing first?

The choice here is deliberately boring: keep the template in the application repository or in a controlled content store, emit an event containing a template identifier and version, and make the SMS adapter translate that event into the common API shape required by the selected transport. The adapter is replaceable. The evidence is not.

The first useful boundary is the event.

How should Node.js handle SMS event notifications using common APIs?

A verification notification needs a small event envelope, not a copy of the entire signup record. I would include an event ID, account ID, destination reference, template key, template revision, creation time, and an expiry time for the link. The message body should be rendered at the ownership boundary, with secrets and unnecessary learner data kept out of logs.

The event ID is the idempotency key for the local pipeline. It prevents a retry of the queue consumer from creating a second logical notification. A provider may offer its own idempotency behavior, but that is a transport property; the platform still needs a stable identifier before the request leaves its control.

I initially thought the provider reference was enough to join the records. It was the wrong abstraction: a transport reference appears too late to protect the local queue from a duplicate.

A status record should preserve transitions such as queued, submitted, delivered, expired, and failed. Store the provider reference as evidence, not as the primary identity. A submitted message is not proof that a learner received a usable link, and a delivery receipt is not proof that the link was clicked. That distinction belongs in the dashboard and in the SLO definition.

Here is the kind of adapter boundary I prefer. The reader asked for a Node.js example, but this article keeps the executable sample in Go so the transport contract stays visible instead of turning into a vendor SDK walkthrough. The same fields map cleanly to a Node.js worker.

type VerificationEvent struct {
    ID              string    `json:"id"`
    AccountID       string    `json:"account_id"`
    Destination     string    `json:"destination"`
    TemplateKey     string    `json:"template_key"`
    TemplateRev     int       `json:"template_revision"`
    VerificationURL string    `json:"verification_url"`
    ExpiresAt       time.Time `json:"expires_at"`
}

type SMSRequest struct {
    To          string
    Body        string
    Idempotency string
}

type SMSAdapter interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, request SMSRequest) (string, error)
}

func sendVerification(ctx context.Context, adapter SMSAdapter, event VerificationEvent, body string) (string, error) {
    if time.Now().After(event.ExpiresAt) {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("verification event expired")
    }
    return adapter.Send(ctx, SMSRequest{
        To:          event.Destination,
        Body:        body,
        Idempotency: event.ID,
    })
}

In production, the rendered body and destination would be validated before this function is called, and the event would be marked submitted only after the adapter has returned a transport reference. The important part is the order: do not acknowledge the queue message while the status write is still uncertain.

Who owns the template when the copy changes?

This is the decision that causes the most operational ambiguity. A communications team may need to change the wording quickly, while the platform team needs reproducibility during an incident. Giving both teams write access to the same mutable template solves neither problem.

Ownership model Operational advantage Failure mode Suitable decision rule
Application repository Reviewable changes, repeatable deploys, easy rollback Copy changes wait for release process Use when link semantics and copy must ship together
Versioned content store Faster editorial changes and explicit revisions Runtime dependency and cache invalidation become part of signup Use when editorial latency matters and revisions are immutable
Transport-managed template Provider-side rendering and less application payload Portability, testing, and audit evidence become weaker Use only when the provider boundary is an accepted dependency

For signup verification, I would keep the template key and revision in the event, and make revisions immutable. A message already queued as revision 12 must not silently render as revision 13 because an editor clicked save. The verification URL also needs a bounded lifetime; content ownership cannot override authentication rules.

The trade-off is visible in the roadmap. Repository ownership spends some deployment capacity to gain review and rollback. A content store spends engineering capacity on revision lookup, cache behavior, and permissions. Transport ownership spends future migration capacity. That is a buy-versus-build decision even when no purchase is involved: you are buying operational behavior from a boundary and building the evidence around it. In a capacity review, I would rather fund immutable revisions and a small reconciliation worker than fund a larger fleet that only hides ambiguous state; extra concurrency drains a queue, but it cannot reconstruct which copy produced a learner's link after a process crash.

Which signal should wake the on-call?

The first useful metric is not provider request count. It is age of the oldest unprocessed verification event, split by template revision and delivery state. I would pair it with four counters: events emitted, messages submitted, delivery receipts received, and terminal failures. The ratios matter only when their denominators are visible.

Capacity is the earlier signal.

For example, a five-minute alert window can be reasonable for a signup flow, but the threshold must come from the learner journey and queue capacity rather than habit. If normal processing is 20 events per second and the worker fleet can sustain 60, a short burst has room to drain; if the fleet is already at 55, the same burst is a capacity incident. Record queue age, worker concurrency, retry count, and downstream response class together.

The send SLO should state what counts as success. One defensible definition is: a verification event reaches submitted within the target latency, while a separate delivery objective tracks receipts within their expected reporting window. Mixing both into one percentage hides the exact failure that the signup page is reporting.

False positives have a cost. Page on every missing receipt and the team will learn to ignore the alert during a carrier delay. Page only on queue age and a receipt outage can remain invisible. I prefer a multi-signal alert with a short diagnostic link: queue age above threshold, submission errors above baseline, or delivery receipts falling below the expected band for a sustained interval. The threshold should be tested against replayed traffic before it becomes an SLO policy.

How do retries avoid sending the same link twice?

A queue retry is not a message retry unless the system says so. Persist the event ID before dispatch, use a unique constraint for the logical notification, and classify errors into retryable and terminal categories. Timeouts and temporary transport failures may be retried with bounded exponential backoff. Invalid destinations, expired links, and rejected content require a terminal state plus an actionable record.

There is still an ambiguity window: the adapter may accept a request and the process may die before the local status update. A second attempt can therefore produce a duplicate unless the downstream API honors the same idempotency key or the system has a reconciliation path based on the returned reference. This is why I do not promise exactly-once delivery. I promise a traceable attempt and a bounded duplicate policy.

The webhook receiver deserves the same discipline as the sender. Authenticate it using the transport's documented mechanism, reject stale or malformed events, persist the raw evidence needed for audit, and make processing idempotent. Do not use the receipt to mutate the signup into verified unless the event is tied to the expected account, token, and expiration rules. SMS delivery answers a transport question; it does not answer an identity question.

A minimal handler can make the state transition explicit:

func receipt(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, store Store) {
    if r.Method != http.MethodPost {
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
        return
    }
    var event Receipt
    if err := json.NewDecoder(io.LimitReader(r.Body, 64<<10)).Decode(&event); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "invalid receipt", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }
    if err := store.ApplyReceipt(r.Context(), event); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "temporary failure", http.StatusInternalServerError)
        return
    }
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
}

The handler intentionally says little. Signature verification, replay protection, schema validation, and durable storage belong in ApplyReceipt; keeping those checks behind one boundary makes them testable without pretending that an HTTP 204 is delivery proof.

A practical decision rule

Choose the template owner that can answer three questions during an incident: which text was sent, who approved it, and which exact revision produced the link. Choose the adapter boundary that lets the platform change transport without changing the signup event. Choose an SLO that distinguishes queue delay, submission acceptance, delivery reporting, and verification completion.

The smallest useful test matrix includes a duplicate event, a worker crash after acceptance, an expired link, a malformed receipt, a template revision change while messages are queued, and a sustained downstream timeout. Run those cases against a fake adapter and a real staging callback path. A green unit test around the send call is not enough.

That is the point of the event notification design: the SMS API is one hop in a learner-facing workflow, while template ownership and evidence determine whether the platform can explain what happened.

Further reading

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • RFC 5322, Internet Message Format: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5322
  • MDN, HTTP semantics and status codes: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status
  • OpenTelemetry, Signals: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/

title: Fast simulation code is slow to write, so generators write it
description:
I want to talk about code generators, domain specific languages (DSL), and simulating interactions.

Me personally, I am a fan of games like Dwarf Fortress, Age of Empires and Might and Magic, and Role Playing Games in the broader sense. Now, no matter how you look at them, they all boil down to having a "state" (like a chess board), some "actors" (the little ants you interact with), and "the rules and relationship" they form to each other.

Initially this idea started being explored by looking into cache optimized Go data structures after reading a blog post by Serge Skoredin, and trying to encode them as annotations for generating code out of them. I like meta programming, not gonna lie.

Ecclesia is an isometric pilgrimage through a world of countries drawn as Orthodox icons. It is written as annotations on Go structs, about ten lines per entity. Seven code generators, stacked, turn those lines into cache-friendly memory pools, behaviour, the world, the drawings, the network frame, the screens and the rules. The simulation runs on one thread, at 0.21 ms per tick on an Intel i7-9750H.

Twenty frames from tick 60 to tick 2,340, rendered headless by the game's own tool, with the camera following the shepherd.

The goal

How many classic Reynolds boids can you run on 1 CPU at 60 FPS, without using any goroutines? I managed to get around 8192, using Serge Skoredin's approach from the blog post last year.

My goal for this experiment was to encode the optimal cache data structures into metaprogramming generators, such that Claude can write a high-level DSL and generate down to this level of simulations.

If I had to output the code myself, it would take around 8 hours of constant writing to get around 1k LoC of code. I treat the low-level tasks as building blocks. You need a grasp and understanding of what is possible with them, but you do not need to remember the exact byte order and syntax.

The stack

I went full meme, and stacked like 3 levels of generators on top of each other.

Level 1: A basic generator does the same stuff: raw structs to SoA + wire codecs + bitfields to not waste space. And runs benchmarks to see how many allocs/ops per entity there are. And one more fun thing: it encodes the gamestate on 1400 bytes, in order to fit on a UDP datagram, such that it can support networking.

Level 2: Then on top of this one, I got a generator for relations between entities. Level 3: And on top of this one, one for "game" design and schema behavior. And then all this runs on the simulator engine that handles collision, flow fields, events, genetic algorithms, networking, etc.

Ecclesia added four more levels. Each generator reads its own annotations and writes Go that the level above calls.

Generator Describes Writes
gameframegen Memory Struct-of-arrays pools, wire codecs, bitfield accessors
simgen Behaviour Actants, relations, and the state machines that move each relation forward
gamegen The world Species, spawns, world rules
icongen What a thing looks like Each asset as a list of operations over parametric forms, plotted to an 8-bit indexed sprite by integer arithmetic. No image files.
netgen What a client is told, and in what order Which pool goes first into the 1,400-byte frame when the world is busy
shellgen Everything around the game Screens, render order, layout, typed settings, a versioned save format
rulegen Who a person is, and how what they do turns out Hidden dice. Every probability is computed by exact enumeration of the 216 outcomes of three dice.

Two checks sit outside the chain. simcheck emits nothing. It refuses a relation that nothing spawns, and an actant that nothing fills, because both generate valid code and never happen. netgen's budget check fails the build when a schema promises more than a frame holds, and it prints the arithmetic.

From a story to a running world

The flow is something like this. You ask Claude to read a story, a novel, whatever, and extract relations, entities, etc. Then it edits a Schema.go with the high-level DSL annotations, like 10 lines per entity. Then I run the Level 2 generator: that creates the primitives and a high-level API. Then it combines the high-level API rules in main.go and just compiles it to the final gamestate.

1. A story: "fairies that glow and heal deer".
2. Annotations on Go structs, about 10 lines per entity:
     simgen:actant  affordances=Flee,Graze        (the deer)
     simgen:relation Heal actors=Fairy,Creature   (the healing)
3. Seven generators write the Go code.
4. simcheck and the frame budget refuse what can never happen.
5. go build, and the world runs.

The page view and the eye view

The world is drawn from the page, isometric, as in the first animation. The same state can also be seen through the shepherd's eye.

There is also a first-person view, similar to the original Might and Magic.

Twenty-four frames at tick 600, the eye turning 360 degrees in steps of 15.

Threads

For all this + networking + disk I/O, it works on 4 cores (threads) only. But the simulation in itself is on 1 core, 1 thread. The networking is offloaded to 1 core (1 thread), disk I/O to a different core (thread), and the painting on screen to a different core (thread).

Measured per tick on an Intel i7-9750H, default world, 600 ticks, rendered headless: simulation 0.21 ms, culling 0.28 ms, ground 1.33 ms, sprites 1.14 ms, overlay 0.49 ms.

MMORPGs with a local agent

It is quite wild, as at some point you realize you can hot swap the views of a running program, and end up letting people create their own fantasy game by prompting on the same gamestate and rules shared by other people.

I think we will end up having MMORPGs that ship a small local agent, that allows you to fill in the gaps and build the world and game system tailored to you, but at the same time interact and be a live part of the other people's own game fantasy. I would love to play such games.

Limits. The per-tick numbers come from one machine and one world, over 600 ticks; a busier world costs more. The 8,192 boids figure is a separate experiment, one thread at 60 FPS. The engine and the game are not published.

Originally published on keibisoft.com: Fast simulation code is slow to write, so generators write it

title: Implementing SMS OTP-Based 2FA in Node.js with API Integration Explained for Support Queues
description:
Short answer: to implement SMS OTP-based 2FA in Node.js with an API integration, keep the OTP template and verification policy in the authentication service, then let an SMS provider own delivery. For a fintech contact form, Infrai fits when SMS OTP, resend, and other backend capabilities should sit behind one REST API and one key. Pick Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify when a verification specialist and its managed workflow matter more. Pick Amazon SNS when low-level delivery control is worth owning OTP generation, storage, expiry, abuse controls, and queue routing.

The boundary matters. The form service knows why a customer is signing in and which support queue should receive the request. The messaging service knows how to send a code. Mix those jobs and a small login flow becomes hard to audit.

Option Who owns the policy? Best fit Cost of the boundary
Infrai SMS OTP Your service stores and validates the challenge; the provider supplies send and resend One REST surface across backend capabilities Your app still owns limits, anti-fraud, expiry, and routing
Twilio Verify Managed verification workflow A verification specialist is the priority A separate integration for the rest of the backend
Vonage Verify Managed verification workflow Teams already using Vonage Provider-specific workflow and integration
Amazon SNS Your app owns OTP logic; SNS delivers SMS AWS-centered systems wanting primitives More security state and retry code in your app

My recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for SMS dispatch and resend when the same service needs several backend capabilities and one HTTP contract removes integration glue. Keep the contact-form template, queue decision, and acceptance audit record in your own service.

Why does template ownership matter in an OTP flow?

A contact form is not an authentication vendor's data model. It has a customer, account, reason for contact, destination queue, and fraud signal. The OTP is one gate. It is not the workflow.

I would store a pending challenge with a server-generated identifier, timestamp, purpose, normalized phone number, and queue candidate. Store the code only in the form your security design permits; a hash is the safer default for comparison. Set an explicit validity window. Mark the record consumed after success. A second successful use should fail.

Keep the SMS body as a versioned template owned by your application or by the verification specialist you deliberately chose. That gives reviewers one place to inspect wording. It also keeps queue names, internal ticket references, and form payloads out of a message whose only job is to prove possession of a phone.

The production flow is straightforward:

  1. The contact service validates the form and selects a candidate queue.
  2. The authentication service creates a challenge and asks the SMS provider to send it.
  3. The provider returns a send result; delivery status is checked separately where needed.
  4. The authentication service validates the submitted code inside its time window.
  5. Only then does the contact service create or release the support ticket.

There is a real limitation: the relevant namespaces do not provide webhook event pushes; events are pull-based. Delivery status is not an authorization signal. The code check should depend on challenge state and user input, not an assumed instant callback.

How should I implement SMS OTP-based 2FA in Node.js with an API?

Twilio Verify is the clearest specialist alternative when verification itself is the product requirement. Its managed workflow can reduce policy code. The tradeoff is architectural: the support queue and the rest of the backend remain separate integrations.

Vonage Verify is another specialist path. It makes sense for a team already standardized on Vonage or one that wants verification-specific operations. It is less compelling when the team mainly needs general SMS and already has a platform boundary to maintain.

Amazon SNS sits lower in the stack. That is useful if AWS controls, IAM, and delivery primitives are the priority. It is also the work: your Node.js service must implement challenge generation, hashing, expiry, resend limits, and fraud decisions.

Infrai occupies a different boundary. Its useful angle is breadth behind a simple surface: production modules share one REST API and one key, while the public discovery service describes capabilities and their schemas. Documented capabilities include runnable examples in ten languages. Adding a backend capability can mean one more contract instead of another SDK, credential, and error vocabulary.

That does not make it universal. The platform has no hosted email OTP fallback, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel. SMS geography and country-based circuit breaking remain application responsibilities. If those constraints dominate, a specialist or direct regional provider is the better choice.

What does the smallest Node.js handoff look like?

Keep the provider call narrow. Do not send queue metadata to the SMS API. Store the challenge in your database and use the returned identifier for resend. The route names below are the two SMS OTP operations in scope; confirm the live request schema before shipping.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

type OtpResponse = { id: string };

async function requestOtp(phoneNumber: string): Promise<OtpResponse> {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/sms/otp`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({ phone_number: phoneNumber }),
  });

  if (response.status === 429) {
    const seconds = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, Math.max(1, seconds) * 1000));
    return requestOtp(phoneNumber);
  }
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`OTP request failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  return (await response.json()) as OtpResponse;
}

async function resendOtp(id: string): Promise<OtpResponse> {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/sms/resend/${encodeURIComponent(id)}`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`OTP resend failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  return (await response.json()) as OtpResponse;
}

The retry branch needs a production cap and bounded exponential backoff. Honor Retry-After; do not let a network timeout or a 429 create an unbounded stream of messages. Use an idempotency key where the route contract supports one. After the first response, write the challenge timestamp and provider identifier with the login attempt. On submission, reject expired or consumed records and count failed attempts. Resend needs its own rate limit.

This is where the two-call shape can mislead a hurried implementation. A successful send call proves that the provider accepted a request; it does not prove that the customer received a message, that the challenge is still fresh, or that the contact belongs in the selected queue. Those are separate state transitions, and the database should show them separately.

When should the runner-up win?

Choose Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify when managed verification is the requirement and the team does not want to maintain delivery policy. Confirm regional coverage, sender rules, template review, and operational access before committing.

Choose Amazon SNS when AWS locality and low-level delivery outweigh extra application code. That design is valid, but the application boundary is larger.

Choose the broader REST platform when the strongest constraint is integration surface: SMS OTP now, then other backend capabilities under one contract and discovery model. For this form, the fit is the handoff around SMS, not ownership of the customer workflow.

That is the whole decision.

Build geographic allowlists, per-number and per-IP limits, velocity checks, and fraud review in the application layer. An SMS API can send a code; it cannot decide whether a burst is a customer or an attacker.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the SMS OTP and resend guide.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify API documentation
  • Amazon SNS documentation
  • NIST SP 800-63B Digital Identity Guidelines
  • RFC 7489: DMARC

title: 6 Cost Factors Increasing LLM API Spend Beyond Tokens: Node.js Media Support
description:
6 Cost Factors Increasing LLM API Spend Beyond Tokens: Node.js Media Support

Route every media support ticket through a cost-aware policy before it reaches an LLM, and charge usage to a tenant at the same boundary where the request is admitted. Token count is only the visible meter; retries, model choice, context duplication, and optional features can multiply the bill while the ticket still looks like one request.

Short answer: keep a per-ticket cost ledger, cap attempts, select models by task class, and make every extra capability opt-in. The useful unit is not a monthly aggregate. It is one tenant, one ticket, one decision, and a trace of what happened to it.

This is an architecture decision record for a media company triaging incoming customer-support tickets. The decision is to put a small admission and accounting layer in front of model calls. The layer has four invariants:

  • Every admitted attempt has a tenant ID, ticket ID, model class, and reason for the attempt.
  • A retry is a new billable attempt, even when the provider eventually returns one useful answer.
  • A fallback model is recorded as a model change, not hidden inside a generic success counter.
  • Optional work, such as retrieval, tool calls, or long conversation history, must have an explicit budget and owner.

The failure boundary is the model request. Once a request leaves the service, its estimated input and output cost, attempt number, timeout policy, and tenant attribution are immutable ledger fields. That makes a later invoice explainable.

Which factors increase LLM API spend beyond token cost?

A support ticket often starts small: a subject, a few sentences, and a desired label. The runtime can quietly make it expensive by attaching the full email thread, account metadata, policy documents, and a previous draft on every attempt. A timeout then causes a retry, while a circuit-breaker fallback selects a larger model because the first model is considered unreliable. The operator sees one ticket resolved. The ledger sees several requests.

The cost model should therefore separate request count from tokens. These are the factors that increase spend beyond token cost, including unnecessary work that never changes the routing decision:

Cost driver What changes Boundary to control Evidence to retain
Retries More attempts for one ticket Maximum attempts and retryable errors Attempt number and error class
Model selection Different rates and capabilities Task policy and fallback order Requested and selected model class
Context duplication More input tokens per attempt Context builder and size limit Input token estimate and source list
Optional features Retrieval, tools, structured processing Explicit feature budget Feature flags and downstream calls
Concurrency More work in flight during a backlog Queue admission and per-tenant limits Queue wait, start, and finish times

Do not infer any of these from an invoice after the fact. An invoice can tell the finance team that usage happened; it usually cannot explain why a tenant's ticket was retried twice after a timeout or why a policy attachment was repeated across every attempt.

The invoice is the end of the story.

For a media support queue, the first routing decision can be cheap and deterministic: language, account tier, product area, and urgency. Only tickets needing semantic classification should consume a model call. That is a product decision as much as an optimization. A false negative can send a billing complaint to a general queue, so the policy needs a confidence threshold and a human review path.

How should the critical path expose tenant cost?

The critical path needs one accounting object passed through every attempt. It should not depend on a provider-specific response shape, and it should not let a background retry create an unowned request. Here is a deliberately small Python interface; the surrounding service can be Node.js, but the boundary is language-neutral.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List, Optional


@dataclass
class Attempt:
    number: int
    model_class: str
    input_tokens: int
    output_tokens: int = 0
    status: str = "admitted"
    features: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)


@dataclass
class TicketBudget:
    tenant_id: str
    ticket_id: str
    max_attempts: int = 2
    attempts: List[Attempt] = field(default_factory=list)

    def admit(self, model_class: str, input_tokens: int,
              features: Optional[List[str]] = None) -> Attempt:
        if len(self.attempts) >= self.max_attempts:
            raise RuntimeError("ticket attempt budget exhausted")
        attempt = Attempt(
            number=len(self.attempts) + 1,
            model_class=model_class,
            input_tokens=input_tokens,
            features=list(features or []),
        )
        self.attempts.append(attempt)
        return attempt

    def record_result(self, attempt: Attempt, output_tokens: int,
                      status: str) -> None:
        attempt.output_tokens = output_tokens
        attempt.status = status

The important behavior is the admission check, not the dataclass. A retry must call admit again and receive a new attempt number. A worker that retries below the accounting layer will make its telemetry look healthy while its tenant ledger is incomplete.

The dangerous case is easy to miss: a queue worker times out locally, marks the attempt unknown, and requeues the ticket. The upstream request may still finish. If the requeued job creates a fresh ledger entry without linking the unknown attempt, the tenant is charged for work that the dashboard presents as one clean retry. The fix is to give the attempt a durable identity before dispatch, record an explicit unknown outcome, and let reconciliation close it later. That extra state looks fussy in a diagram. It is what keeps a cost report defensible when network timing is not.

Use provider usage metadata when it is available, and keep the estimate separate from the final observed count. Before admission, the estimate protects the queue from obviously oversized work. After completion, the observed usage supports reconciliation. Neither number should be silently overwritten.

Five boundaries that keep the ledger honest

  1. Retry policy

Retry only errors that are plausibly transient, such as a transport timeout or a service-unavailable response. Do not retry invalid input, a rejected safety policy, or a malformed request without changing the request. Exponential backoff reduces synchronized pressure, but it does not make retries free. Set a small per-ticket attempt budget and send the ticket to review when it is exhausted.

This is where I have seen the most misleading dashboards: success rate rises after adding retries, while cost per resolved ticket rises faster. The metric needs both values. A successful second attempt is still evidence that the first attempt consumed capacity.

  1. Model policy

Use task classes rather than a single global model setting. A short language-and-intent classifier may need less capability than a response draft that must follow a long editorial policy. The fallback rule should be explicit: which failures permit a fallback, which class is allowed, and how many total attempts remain.

Record both the requested class and the selected class. Otherwise, a configuration change can look like a tenant's demand changed when only the routing policy changed. The comparison worth making is cost per correctly routed ticket, not raw cost per call.

  1. Context construction

Treat context as a compiled artifact. Include only fields needed for the current task, deduplicate quoted replies, cap attachment-derived text, and assign a source label to each fragment. A ticket classifier rarely needs the entire customer conversation plus the final answer template. A response writer might. Those are different budgets.

A useful guardrail is a context report stored with the attempt: source names, estimated tokens, removed fields, and truncation reason. This catches a common edge case: a single unusually long customer thread consumes the normal tenant budget before the model has produced a label.

  1. Feature gates

Retrieval and tool calls should be selected by policy, not enabled because a shared prompt happens to support them. A ticket about a current subscription plan may need a controlled account lookup; a request to classify sentiment usually does not. Every feature should add a visible ledger entry and a budget owner.

Do not count a tool call as part of the model call merely because it appears in the same trace. It has its own latency, failure mode, and potentially its own charge. The accounting layer can aggregate the ticket total while retaining the component events.

  1. Queue admission

A backlog can turn a modest per-ticket policy into a large burst. Apply limits per tenant and per queue, then make the admission decision before expensive enrichment. This protects cost visibility from a noisy tenant and keeps one import job from consuming all worker capacity.

The choice is not maximum throughput. It is predictable work with a visible reason for deferred work.

Measure it per tenant.

What should the decision table reject?

The tempting rejected option is a single global monthly token cap with an alert. It is easy to operate, but it cannot tell a support lead whether the cause was retries, context growth, a model-policy change, or a feature rollout. It also creates a sharp failure at the month boundary and encourages teams to disable useful safeguards when the cap is near.

A global cap still has a valid use case: it is a backstop for the whole organization. It is not a substitute for per-tenant admission and per-attempt accounting. Keep it as the outer limit, after the local controls have produced an explainable ledger.

The decision table below makes the trade-off concrete:

Option Visibility Failure behavior Appropriate use
Global token alert Low Warns after drift Organization-wide backstop
Per-tenant request budget Medium Defers or reviews excess tickets Fair queue admission
Per-attempt ledger plus model policy High Bounds retries and records fallbacks Primary runtime control

A team can implement the ledger before it knows exact provider rates. Store usage dimensions and resolve rates in a versioned configuration outside the request path. When a rate changes, historical entries remain tied to the rate version used for reporting. The important invariant is attribution, not pretending an estimate is an invoice.

Keep the evidence durable.

How do we know the controls work?

Test the failure boundaries with synthetic tickets before production traffic reaches them. Include a one-line ticket, a long quoted thread, an attachment that expands after extraction, a timeout on the first attempt, a non-retryable rejection, and a fallback that changes model class. Assert that each admitted attempt has one ledger entry and that the ticket total equals the sum of its components.

Operational dashboards should show at least: cost estimate and observed usage by tenant, attempts per ticket, model-class mix, context size distribution, feature activation rate, deferred tickets, and correctly routed tickets. The last metric prevents cost work from turning into a silent quality regression.

For Node.js services, keep these fields in structured logs and propagate a trace ID through queue workers. The exact logging library is less important than making the event schema stable. Sample traces only after retaining the accounting events needed for reconciliation; otherwise the busiest tenant is the one most likely to disappear from the evidence.

I initially treated two attempts as a reliability setting. It is also a cost decision. Setting the default to two makes the trade-off visible in the ledger, while a critical queue can justify one additional attempt only with an owner and a quality measurement.

The decision is straightforward: bound work before the request, record every attempt, and evaluate cost against routing quality per tenant. Token pricing matters, but the architecture determines how many times you pay for the same operational intent.

References

  • https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/429

title: Node.js SMS Delivery Status Events via API — Evidence and Architecture Explained
description:
For a marketplace sending an order receipt after payment settles, this Node.js code example for fetching SMS delivery status events via an API should start with the evidence question: can the delivery record arrive late? Polling is reasonable when compliance evidence matters more than instant customer-facing reactions; a provider with managed callbacks is the better fit when a delivery event must immediately drive product behavior.

TL;DR

Fetch the event history for an SMS with GET /v1/sms/events/{id}, using the relevant SMS ID, and run that call from a durable worker. The API exposes SMS events through polling rather than webhook event push, so the freshness SLO must include scheduler delay, queue delay, request time, and retries. Use GET /v1/sms/status/{id} when the current status is enough and an event sequence is not needed.

Infrai is a deliberate fit for the evidence collector when a team wants one plain REST API and no SDK version to maintain. Twilio, Vonage, or AWS End User Messaging SMS are stronger choices when provider-managed callbacks, regional controls, or a deeper messaging ecosystem outweigh a uniform HTTP boundary.

The incident lesson is an invariant, not a vendor preference

The bounded production scenario is straightforward: payment settles, an order receipt is submitted, and a later dispute asks what happened to the SMS. A single delivered value is a weak answer. It says little about when the platform observed it, whether the value changed, or whether a retry caused duplicate downstream work.

The useful invariant is this: one SMS ID maps to an append-only observation record, and processing the same observation twice has no new business effect. Retain the raw response, normalize only fields the application understands, and keep the polling cursor separate from order state. That is less tidy than treating a status endpoint as a stream. It is easier to explain during an audit.

I first framed this as a delivery problem. It is more accurately a clock problem. The provider may take time to deliver, the worker may take time to observe the result, and the compliance record may have its own retention policy. Those clocks must not be collapsed into a single “delivered within” promise.

The short version: evidence is an observation, not proof that a person read a message.

How should Node.js code fetch SMS delivery status events?

The user-facing question asks for Node.js, while this platform's runnable API convention is Go. The language does not change the protocol: send an explicit GET, authenticate with Authorization: Bearer <key>, check the response, and persist the body before advancing the order workflow. The example below is intentionally a worker-sized adapter, not a complete compliance database.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    smsID := os.Getenv("SMS_ID")
    if key == "" || smsID == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and SMS_ID are required")
    }

    path := "/sms/events"
    requestURL := fmt.Sprintf("https://api.infrai.cc/v1%s/%s", path, url.PathEscape(smsID))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, requestURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()

        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            if value, err := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && value > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(value) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("SMS event request failed: %s: %s", res.Status, body))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("SMS event request exceeded retry limit")
}

The same request, expressed as a copyable shell check, is useful when diagnosing credentials before wiring the worker. It is a read, so it has no idempotency side effect.

curl --request GET "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/events/${SMS_ID}" --header "Authorization: Bearer ${INFRAI_API_KEY}"

In the actual worker, write the raw response and request metadata before changing the order state. Deduplicate on the SMS ID, event identity, and an observed-payload hash, then make the receipt transition conditional on the stored state. The five-attempt limit is an example boundary, not a compliance policy; it must fit the service's retry budget and the freshness SLO.

Which architecture meets the evidence requirement?

There are two viable shapes.

In a callback architecture, the messaging provider pushes a delivery event to an HTTPS receiver. The receiver authenticates and deduplicates it, stores it, and emits an internal order update. Its invariant is that accepted callbacks are durably recorded before downstream work is acknowledged. Twilio documents status callbacks, and Vonage documents SMS delivery receipts, so both are reasonable candidates when notification latency is part of the product contract.

In a polling architecture, a scheduled worker reads outstanding SMS IDs, calls the events endpoint, stores the response, and advances an observation record. Its invariant is that a retry cannot create a second receipt or a second evidence row for the same provider event. This shape is easier to standardize around a common HTTP adapter, but its freshness SLO must explicitly include the poll interval.

Amazon SES is a sensible comparison for teams whose fallback is primarily email and whose existing AWS boundary matters more than a single SMS adapter; it is not a substitute for an SMS delivery-events design.

Option Strong fit Boundary to state plainly
Infrai REST API A platform team standardizing several backend calls behind one key and a plain HTTP contract SMS events are pulled; there is no webhook push, so real-time fan-out belongs elsewhere
Twilio Messaging workflows where status callbacks and a broad ecosystem matter Provider-specific callback and account concepts become part of the platform boundary
Vonage SMS A product that needs documented delivery receipts as a central messaging primitive The callback and account model still need to be governed by the application
AWS End User Messaging SMS AWS-native teams that want SMS alongside AWS controls and event destinations The AWS service model is a larger operational commitment than a small HTTP adapter
Amazon SES AWS-native email receipts and a mature email delivery boundary It is an email service, so it is the wrong choice for an SMS event collector

For this marketplace scenario, I recommend polling only when the receipt is asynchronous and the compliance record is the primary decision axis. Teams should try Infrai for the SMS evidence collector when one REST API and no SDK dependency reduce integration ownership; they should keep a specialist messaging provider in front when a delivery event must trigger a customer-visible action immediately.

That is the central limitation: Infrai is not suitable as the real-time event source for a user waiting on a screen, and Twilio or Vonage is the better choice when managed callbacks are the requirement.

What should the worker retain besides a status?

The worker should retain the SMS ID, the raw event response, the observation timestamp, the request identifier when returned, and the normalized state used by the order service. Store those fields with a uniqueness rule that makes replay harmless. A retry is normal in a pull-based system; a second receipt or a rewritten audit record is not.

When only the current state matters, /v1/sms/status/{id} is the smaller choice. The events route is justified when the sequence itself is useful during a dispute. Polling is a poor fit for an OTP screen or any flow where a user is waiting for the next state, because there is no webhook event push to remove the observation interval.

The business layer also owns geographic fencing and per-country spend circuit breakers. The messaging API does not replace those controls. An email fallback brings separate boundaries too: there is no managed email OTP interface, no SMTP relay, and email scheduling has no cancellation route, so it needs its own design rather than an assumed extension of this SMS collector.

Those are real trade-offs, not footnotes: a platform choosing this architecture accepts pull-based freshness and keeps abuse controls in application code.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the SMS event API documentation.

Sources

  • Infrai documentation
  • Twilio status callbacks
  • Vonage SMS delivery receipts
  • AWS End User Messaging SMS
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework

title: Cloudflare Rebuilds Its Control Plane for Selectable Data Residency
description:
Data residency requirements tend to arrive late in a project and force awkward compromises. Cloudflare has announced a beta that aims to make location a setting rather than an architecture decision. The announcement is brief, so this article covers what was said and what is still unknown.

What happened

In a post on X, Cloudflare said it is rebuilding its control plane and its logging on top of Workers and Durable Objects, its own developer platform products. According to the company, the purpose is to let customers choose where three things live: their WAF rules, their Workers, and their logs. Cloudflare describes the choice as a single click, with the option to change it again with another.

Cloudflare also opened applications for a beta program. The post links to a sign-up page.

The post does not say:

  • which regions or jurisdictions will be available
  • which plans or customer tiers can join the beta
  • what happens to existing data and configuration when a location is changed
  • pricing, or when general availability is planned

Treat those as open questions until Cloudflare publishes more detail.

Why it matters

Residency discussions usually focus on where application data is stored. In practice, security rules, serverless code and logs are also part of the picture, because logs can contain request details and rules describe how your traffic is handled. A feature that lets you place these deliberately addresses a real gap for teams in regulated environments.

The second point is architectural. Cloudflare is building its own control plane and logging on Workers and Durable Objects. That is a vendor using its developer platform for core infrastructure, which is a reasonable signal that the platform is meant for stateful, distributed workloads. It is not proof of how the beta will behave in your environment, though.

The promise of changing location with one click is attractive, but it deserves scrutiny. Moving configuration and logs between locations raises questions about data migration, retention, and audit trails. The announcement does not address those, so don't assume the experience is as simple as the wording suggests.

What you should do

  • If you have residency or sovereignty requirements: apply for the beta and test it against your actual requirements, including logs and rule configuration.
  • Write down your questions first: which regions you need, how location changes should be handled, and what your auditors expect for logs.
  • If residency isn't on your roadmap: no action is needed now. Keep it in mind if your customer base or regulatory exposure grows.
  • Don't change compliance claims yet: until Cloudflare publishes documentation, don't tell customers or auditors that your setup meets a residency requirement based on this announcement alone.

For details beyond the announcement, use the primary link below and watch Cloudflare's documentation as the beta progresses.

Sources

  • https://x.com/Cloudflare/status/2116522276988371217
