title: Cutting LLM Calls in Incident Triage: Sliding Windows, Log Reduction, and a pgvector Cache
description:
A Kafka-to-WebSocket pipeline where the model is the last resort, not the first step.

The problem

The obvious way to add an LLM to log monitoring is to send logs to a model and ask what is wrong. That breaks quickly. Most log lines are not errors. During an outage, the same error repeats thousands of times with only timestamps, UUIDs and counters changing. A raw stack trace with framework frames is mostly noise. And the same database timeout will show up on orders today and inventory tomorrow, so you pay for the same diagnosis again.

I built telemetry-incident-dashboard around one rule: every step before the model must be cheaper than the model, and must be able to stop the pipeline.

It is a working prototype. I'll say clearly later what has and hasn't been exercised.

Architecture 

flowchart TD
    A[Apps / log shipper] --> K[Kafka topic app-logs]
    K --> C[Spring Boot consumer<br/>virtual threads]
    C -->|every log| W[STOMP /topic/logs]
    C -->|ERROR only| D[Per-service sliding window<br/>10+ errors in 60s]
    D -->|below threshold| X[Stop: no tokens]
    D -->|burst| R[LogPayloadReducer]
    R --> E{Exact fingerprint<br/>in cache?}
    E -->|yes| H[CACHE_EXACT]
    E -->|no| V{pgvector cosine<br/>>= 0.90?}
    V -->|yes| S[CACHE_SEMANTIC]
    V -->|no| L[LLM call via LangChain4j]
    L --> P[(PostgreSQL + pgvector<br/>diagnosis_cache)]
    H --> I[(incidents hypertable)]
    S --> I
    L --> I
    I --> A2[STOMP /topic/alerts]

Stack: Java 21, Spring Boot 3.3, Apache Kafka (KRaft), PostgreSQL with TimescaleDB and pgvector, LangChain4j with OpenAI (gpt-4o-mini and text-embedding-3-small by default), and a React + Vite dashboard.

Step 1: detect bursts without a model

Each service gets its own ErrorWindow. It holds the errors from the last 60 seconds, fires when the count reaches the threshold (default 10), and then stays quiet for a cooldown (default 120 seconds).

synchronized List<LogEvent> record(LogEvent event, long nowMs, long windowMs, int threshold,
                                   long cooldownMs, int maxBuffered) {
    errors.addLast(new Stamped(nowMs, event));
    while (!errors.isEmpty() && nowMs - errors.peekFirst().arrivalMs() > windowMs) {
        errors.pollFirst();
    }
    while (errors.size() > maxBuffered) {
        errors.pollFirst();
    }
    if (errors.size() < threshold || nowMs - lastAlertMs < cooldownMs) {
        return List.of();
    }
    lastAlertMs = nowMs;
    return errors.stream().map(Stamped::event).toList();
}

Info, debug and warning logs never get here. They are counted and streamed to the dashboard, capped at 200 non-error events per second. A malformed Kafka record is counted and dropped. The listener never rethrows, so one bad record can't stall a partition.

Visual instruction: Capture this exact code section in VS Code using the OneDark-Pro theme. Use a readable font size and crop unnecessary editor UI.

The cooldown matters. Without it, a long outage would trigger analysis on every incoming error once the window is full.

Step 2: shrink the burst

LogPayloadReducer turns a burst into a short context string:

  • strips ANSI codes, ISO timestamps, UUIDs and hex addresses
  • drops framework frames (java.base/, jdk.internal., Tomcat, Spring AOP and CGLIB, JUnit)
  • keeps the top 12 stack lines and notes how many were cut
  • groups identical errors by fingerprint and prints them as xN
  • caps the whole thing at 2,000 characters and 5 distinct errors

The fingerprint is a SHA-256 of the text after volatile parts are normalised. Numbers become <n>, so Timeout after 3001ms and Timeout after 9999ms hash the same:

private static String normalize(String s) {
    return NUMBER.matcher(scrub(s)).replaceAll("<n>");
}

For the 15-error connection-pool burst in sample-data/02-db-timeout-burst.ndjson, the README reports the model input going from 8,415 characters (about 2,100 tokens) to 506 characters (about 127 tokens). That is one synthetic burst and the token count is a four-characters-per-token estimate, so treat 94% as an illustration, not a benchmark.

The reduced output looks like this:

service=orders errors=15 distinct=1
[1] x15 ERROR HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30001ms
java.sql.SQLTransientConnectionException: HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30001ms
    at com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.HikariPool.createTimeoutException(HikariPool.java:696)
    at com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.HikariPool.getConnection(HikariPool.java:197)
    at com.shop.orders.Repository.save(Repository.java:48)
    at com.shop.orders.Service.handle(Service.java:71)

Step 3: a two-level cache

LogAnalysisEngine.resolve goes cheapest first.

Exact match. One UPDATE ... RETURNING both bumps the hit counter and fetches the stored diagnosis:

List<String> exact = jdbc.queryForList(
        "UPDATE diagnosis_cache SET hits = hits + 1 WHERE fingerprint = ? RETURNING diagnosis",
        String.class, fingerprint);

Semantic match. If there's no exact hit, embed the context and ask pgvector for the nearest row. A cosine similarity of 0.90 or more counts as a hit. This is what lets a database timeout on inventory reuse the diagnosis made for orders:

SELECT id, diagnosis, 1 - (embedding <=> ?::vector) AS similarity
FROM diagnosis_cache
WHERE embedding IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY embedding <=> ?::vector
LIMIT 1

The table uses an HNSW index with vector_cosine_ops. The schema is 1536 dimensions to match text-embedding-3-small. If you change the embedding model, you change docker/init.sql and EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS together. The engine checks the returned vector length and skips the vector cache on a mismatch instead of failing.

LLM call. Only on a miss. The prompt asks for under 150 words in three headings (root cause with confidence, impact, fix) and says not to invent details. The answer and its embedding are written back, so the next occurrence is free.

Visual instruction: Capture this exact code section in VS Code using the OneDark-Pro theme. Use a readable font size and crop unnecessary editor UI.

Engineering decisions

Single-flight for identical bursts. Two services can hit the same failure at once. diagnoseOnce keeps a ConcurrentMap<String, CompletableFuture<Diagnosis>> keyed by fingerprint. The first caller does the work; the rest join() its future. That avoids paying for duplicate LLM calls in the gap before the first answer lands in the cache.

Never throw from the pipeline. If the cache query, the embedding call, the database or the LLM fails, the incident is still recorded with source FALLBACK and the raw condensed telemetry attached. A flaky dependency degrades the diagnosis, not the stream.

Virtual threads. Each Kafka consumer loop and each analysis task runs on a Java 21 virtual thread. Analysis is blocking I/O (HTTP to a model, JDBC), which is the case virtual threads fit. The analysis is also submitted off the consumer thread so a slow model call can't hold up log ingestion.

Timescale for history. Cached diagnoses live in diagnosis_cache. Every incident, including cache hits, goes into an incidents hypertable with its source, similarity and tokens used, so you can see how often the model is actually needed.

Testing

There are two unit test classes, five tests:

  • ErrorWindowTest: fires at the threshold, respects cooldown, and expires old errors from the window.
  • LogPayloadReducerTest: truncates stacks to 12 lines plus a marker, collapses 200 repeated errors to x200 under the 2,000-character budget, and gives two events with different numbers and UUIDs the same fingerprint.

Nine NDJSON scenarios in sample-data/ cover normal traffic, bursts (DB timeout, NPE, OOM, upstream 502, JWT failures), a similar failure on a second service, malformed lines, and a below-threshold case.

Limitations

I'd rather list these than have you find them:

  • The successful LLM path (real diagnosis written to the cache and then served as a hit) has not been run against a funded OpenAI account. The fallback path, reducer, window logic and the dashboard demo have been run.
  • The dashboard's live mode hasn't been tested against the backend.
  • Kafka offsets auto-commit, so a crash mid-analysis can lose that burst.
  • No auth on the WebSocket endpoint. No cache eviction. Single Kafka broker.
  • No throughput or latency benchmarks.

Try it 

cp .env.example .env            # optionally set OPENAI_API_KEY
docker compose up -d            # Kafka (KRaft) + TimescaleDB with pgvector
set -a; source .env; set +a
mvn spring-boot:run             # http://localhost:8080, STOMP at /ws

cd dashboard && npm install && npm run dev   # http://localhost:5173

scripts/send-sample-logs.sh sample-data/02-db-timeout-burst.ndjson

Without an API key the app still starts, and bursts are stored as FALLBACK. There is also a browser-only demo that simulates the same rules with hand-written diagnoses and is labeled as a simulation. Click "Play the story" to see an LLM call, a below-threshold burst, a similar-error hit and an exact hit.

What's next

Not implemented yet, but the obvious gaps: manual offset commits after analysis, cache eviction, authentication on the WebSocket, and a real run of the LLM path with measured cache hit rates.

Code is on GitHub: axololtos/telemetry-incident-dashboard

If it's useful, a star helps. Issues and PRs are welcome (there's a CONTRIBUTING guide). Follow me here on DEV for more write-ups like this.

title: Getting only the new DOIs from the Crossref API every day: dates, cursors and rate limits
description:
AI disclosure: this post was drafted with AI assistance. I ran every request and every number below myself against the live Crossref REST API on November 1, 2026, and checked the code and tests before publishing.

I wanted a boring thing: every morning, a CSV of the journal articles that got a DOI since yesterday, for a handful of journals, and never the same DOI twice. Crossref's REST API is free, needs no key, and held 188,319,891 records when I asked, so it should be one request. It is close, but it took me a few wrong turns. Here are the ones worth knowing about.

The finished script is about 400 lines of standard-library Python with a daily GitHub Actions workflow. It is my repo, free and MIT licensed: https://github.com/fecklesspleb/crossref-new-works-feed

1. Pick the right date: created, not published, not indexed

/works has four families of date filters, and for "what is new" they give very different answers. Here are the counts for a single day, 30 October 2026, all work types, each filter with from-… and until-… set to that day. The created count is stable; the other three drift a little as records change, so they are rounded:

Filter Works on 30 Oct 2026
from-created-date / until-created-date 86,622
from-index-date / until-index-date about 789,000
from-update-date / until-update-date about 155,000
from-pub-date / until-pub-date about 18,900
  • created is when the DOI was first registered. That is the one you want for "new".
  • index changes whenever Crossref re-indexes a record, including citation counts. Nine times more rows, nearly all old works.
  • update is when the publisher last deposited a change to the metadata.
  • pub-date is the publication date the publisher wrote down. It can be a year, a month, or a print issue date months away. "Published yesterday" misses most of what appeared yesterday and includes old material deposited late.

For scale, type:journal-article with created gave 26,945 on 28 October, 29,785 on 29 October and 26,966 on 30 October. On Saturday 31 October it was 16,641. Filter by journal, publisher or funder unless you really want ~9 MB of CSV a day.

2. Always set both ends of the range

from-created-date:2026-10-30 on its own means "from then until now". That is fine today and silently wrong when you re-run a past day. Set until-created-date too; both ends are inclusive.

The filters also take a time: from-created-date:2026-10-30T12:00:00,until-created-date:2026-10-30T12:59:59 returned 2,829 works for that hour.

3. Page with a cursor, and you can still sort

rows maxes out at 1,000. rows=1001 gets a 400:

Integer specified as 1001 but must be a positive integer less than or equal to 1000.

offset stops at 10,000 (offset must be ... less than or equal to 9999. Use the cursor parameter ...). So use deep paging:

  1. Send cursor=* with the first request.
  2. Read message.next-cursor from the answer and send it back with the next request.
  3. Stop when a page comes back empty.

I was not sure cursors keep a sort order, so I tested it. With sort=created&order=asc and rows=2, three cursor pages came back in ascending created order, with the same DOIs as a single rows=6 request.

Reading oldest first matters for a feed with a cap. If you stop after N new works, the next run can carry on where you stopped instead of rereading the newest ones.

params = {
    "filter": "from-created-date:2026-10-31,until-created-date:2026-11-01,"
              "type:journal-article,issn:0028-0836",
    "rows": 1000,
    "cursor": cursor,                # "*" first, then message["next-cursor"]
    "sort": "created",
    "order": "asc",
    "select": "DOI,type,title,container-title,ISSN,publisher,member,created,published",
}

select= keeps responses small. A field name it does not know returns a 400 that lists the valid ones, which is handy.

4. The 2026 rate limits are lower than old blog posts say

Crossref changed its limits in July 2026. For list and filter requests like these:

  • 1 request per second in the public pool;
  • 3 per second in the polite pool;
  • polite-pool limits counted per mailto email address.

The response headers tell you where you are. On a public-pool request I saw:

x-rate-limit-limit: 1
x-rate-limit-interval: 1s
x-concurrency-limit: 1
x-api-pool: public-array

So my client:

  • sends one request at a time, at most once a second;
  • slows down further if those headers ask for less.

I still hit a real 429. I ran the script twice back to back from the shell, each process started fresh, and the first request of the second came too soon after the last request of the first. The fix is the usual one:

  • honour Retry-After (seconds or an HTTP date);
  • otherwise back off 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds;
  • give up after 5 tries;
  • retry 5xx and network errors the same way.

A 403, or an answer that is not JSON, is different. Stop and write nothing.

5. Say who you are

To get into the polite pool, add mailto=you@example.org to the query string or the User-Agent. I do both, with a User-Agent that names the tool and links to its source:

crossref-new-works-feed/1.0 (+https://github.com/fecklesspleb/crossref-new-works-feed; mailto:you@example.org)

Use your own address. The limit is per email, so a shared one in a popular template would put everyone in the same bucket. I also validate it loosely and drop it if it does not look like an email. (api.crossref.org/robots.txt was a 404 when I checked, which means no rules, but the script checks it anyway.)

6. "New" arrives late, so overlap your window

A DOI's created timestamp is when it was registered, not when the API can serve it. The newest work I could see was 20 to 30 minutes behind its created time. Indexing can take longer on a busy day.

So a daily run should not ask for "yesterday" only. Mine asks for yesterday plus today and lets a seen-DOI list drop repeats. A work is only missed if it reaches the API more than a day late.

7. query is a relevance search, not a filter

query.bibliographic=perovskite solar over two days matched 246 works. Only 29 had both words in the title. If you sort by date (as a feed must), you no longer get the most relevant first, so you get all the loose matches in date order.

My fix was a client-side --title-word check: all the words must be in the title. Rejected works are not marked as seen, in case you loosen the check later.

8. Small normalisation traps

  • ISSNs. issn:0028-0836, issn:00280836 and Nature's electronic ISSN issn:1476-4687 all returned the same 88 works for 25 October to 1 November. Normalise user input to NNNN-NNNC anyway, with an uppercase X check digit.
  • DOIs are case-insensitive. /works/10.1038/S41586-026-11328-3 returns the lower-case DOI. Store them lower-cased, or your dedupe will see two works.
  • Dates come as date-parts. That means [[2026]], [[2026, 10]] or [[2026, 10, 25]]. Keep the precision you were given rather than inventing a day.
  • Titles and ISSNs are lists. A work can have no title or several ISSNs. I join ISSNs with |.
  • Overlapping windows return duplicates by design. Dedupe by DOI before you write, both within a run and across runs.

9. Finding the IDs to filter on

You rarely know a member ID or funder ID by heart. The API has lookups. They are fuzzy searches, so the best match is not always first; check the names in the results:

  • /journals?query=nature gives the ISSNs, used as issn:.
  • /members?query=springer gives member IDs, used as member:.
  • /funders?query=national science foundation gives funder IDs; prefix the id with 10.13039/ for funder:.

What the feed looks like

The first run for Nature over seven days found 88 works with 2 requests (robots.txt plus one page). The second run found 0 new. On the broad side, all journal articles since midnight with --max-works 1000 stopped at 1,000. The next run carried on and wrote the next 1,000, rather than the same ones again.

doi,type,title,journal,issn,publisher,member,published,created,url,first_seen
10.1038/s41586-026-11328-3,journal-article,ctDNA clearance and outcomes for resectable lung cancer from NeoCOAST-2,Nature,0028-0836|1476-4687,Springer Science and Business Media LLC,297,2026-10-25,2026-10-25T07:01:31Z,https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11328-3,2026-11-01T16:37:25Z

The GitHub Actions workflow runs it once a day and commits the CSVs. One catch: GitHub turns off scheduled workflows in public repositories after 60 days without activity.

Code, tests (offline with saved Crossref responses, plus a few live checks) and the workflow are MIT licensed: https://github.com/fecklesspleb/crossref-new-works-feed

Numbers in this post come from requests I made on November 1, 2026; Crossref's counts and limits change, so check the response headers on your own requests.

title: Go 1.24+ Servers Ask Linux for MPTCP: the Precondition for Claude's Root Exploit
description:
• Book: System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

If your Go service runs on Linux and its main module targets Go 1.24 or later, it asks the kernel for a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener. Anthropic wrote on October 27 that Claude, "after initial prompting," built a remote root exploit for "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener." Two days later the Go Security Team sent golang-announce a note on protecting Go programs against CVE-2026-98432 (archived on oss-security). Its message for Go developers: unless you told it not to, a Go 1.24+ server requests exactly that kind of listener.

The Go docs say that since Go 1.24 the multipathtcp setting "defaults to multipathtcp="2", thus enabled by default on listeners." You probably never chose that.

What changed since Anthropic's post

Anthropic's October 27 post described the bug as "a race condition-induced UAF bug in the kernel networking stack" and said it took the model's exploit "48 minutes to leak a kernel pointer and another five minutes to reach the shell command execution." The model is "an unreleased, internal research model," and Anthropic has not published the exploit.

The Go team's October 29 announcement tied the exploit's precondition to Go's default and listed mitigations. On October 30, Red Hat published RHSB-2026-016 and rated the flaw Critical for RHEL 8, 9 and 10 and OpenShift. It lists no fixed kernels yet and says Red Hat "is expediting the release of fixes."

The distributions have split. Debian has fixed kernels for bookworm and trixie. Ubuntu's tracker, last updated October 30, still lists the linux package as vulnerable on every release from 16.04 to 26.10, with work in progress on 22.04, 24.04, 26.04 and 26.10.

The CVE itself is older. Ubuntu lists it as published on October 15 with a CVSS 3 score of 9.8, and Debian's tracker describes IP options being freed while another CPU still reads them during the IPv4 TCP handshake.

Why a Go server meets the precondition

Go 1.21 added Multipath TCP, but only when an application asked for it. Go 1.24 changed the default to multipathtcp=2: MPTCP on for listeners, off for dialers. Every net.Listen("tcp", ...) and every http.ListenAndServe in a program whose main module declares go 1.24 or later (in go.mod or go.work) requests an MPTCP socket from the kernel, unless a godebug setting says otherwise. The toolchain version alone doesn't decide it. Per the GODEBUG docs, a newer toolchain building a module that still says go 1.23 keeps the old opt-in behavior.

Whether the kernel hands one back depends on the host. The kernel switch is net.mptcp.enabled. TuxCare, which sells KernelCare, a live kernel patching service, says Enterprise Linux 8, 9 and 10 ship with MPTCP disabled, so a Go service on a stock RHEL host falls back to plain TCP. Don't assume. Check each host:

# 1 means the kernel will create MPTCP sockets
sysctl net.mptcp.enabled

# listening MPTCP sockets and the process that owns each
sudo ss -Mlnp

If the second command lists your Go binaries, they meet the precondition Anthropic described.

The Go team is careful about what that means. Its announcement says the bug is not specific to MPTCP, and a Go maintainer said the same on the proposal issue. Per Debian's tracker, the root cause is a use-after-free in Linux's IPv4 TCP handling. Turning MPTCP off removes the one path that has been demonstrated. Nobody has said it is the only path.


A Go 1.24+ server asks the kernel for MPTCP on its listeners. The kernel decides whether that lane is open.

Patch first. The Go switches are a stopgap

The Go team calls a patched kernel "the best fix." Debian's fixed builds are 6.12.113-1 for trixie and 6.1.190-1 for bookworm, per its tracker. A new kernel package only protects you after a reboot.

Until then, the announcement lists three ways to keep a Go program on plain TCP. The quickest needs no rebuild. Set it in the service's environment and restart:

GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 ./server

If GODEBUG already holds settings, add this one with a comma. To bake it into the binary, put it in the main module's go.mod:

module example.com/server

go 1.24

godebug multipathtcp=0

Two catches from the GODEBUG docs. Only the main module's go.mod counts, so a library can't set this for you. And when you build inside a workspace, go.mod godebug lines are ignored and go.work is read instead.

The third switch is per listener. ListenConfig.SetMultipathTCP overrides the GODEBUG value for that one socket:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "log"
    "net"
    "net/http"
)

func main() {
    var lc net.ListenConfig
    lc.SetMultipathTCP(false) // plain TCP, whatever GODEBUG says

    ctx := context.Background()
    ln, err := lc.Listen(ctx, "tcp", ":8080")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    log.Fatal(http.Serve(ln, http.NotFoundHandler()))
}

The Go team's own verdict on all three is "a fragile mitigation." One forgotten MPTCP listener on the host, in any language, keeps the precondition alive, and the approach assumes every working exploit needs MPTCP. Red Hat's interim nftables rule, which drops inbound IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options, has the same limit: Red Hat says it "cannot fully prevent it."


GODEBUG covers a process, go.mod covers a binary, SetMultipathTCP covers one listener.

Should Go flip the default back?

A proposal to disable MPTCP by default was opened on October 29 and is still open. Maintainers disagree. One Go maintainer wrote that changing the default now would be "closing the barn door after the horse has left," and asked for a justification of the current default, noting Go seems unusual in having one. Another Go team member wrote: "I don't see any reason that a security issue should lead us to disable it." A Linux kernel MPTCP developer joined to argue for MPTCP's benefits, such as moving a connection between networks without dropping it, and to say listener-side MPTCP has no performance cost for plain TCP clients. The Go team's announcement calls a default change "premature" for now.

Some projects aren't waiting. The Lightning Network daemon lnd merged a change on October 30 that, in an lnd developer's words, "makes plain TCP the default for newly built lnd binaries." The same developer told operators that "Disabling MPTCP removes the prerequisite for the demonstrated exploit," and that they "should still install a patched kernel as soon as one is available."

What to do this week

  1. Run sudo ss -Mlnp on every Linux host that faces the internet. Note which processes hold MPTCP listeners.
  2. Check your distribution's tracker for a fixed kernel: Debian, Ubuntu, Red Hat. Install it and plan the reboot.
  3. Check the go line in each service's go.mod (or go.work). At go 1.24 or later, assume the service requests MPTCP unless a godebug setting turns it off.
  4. Where no fixed kernel exists yet, set GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 on Go services and restart them. Add godebug multipathtcp=0 to go.mod if you don't use MPTCP on purpose.
  5. Look at which kernel completes the TCP handshake with outside clients. If a proxy terminates TCP in front of your Go service, that proxy's host is the one an outside peer reaches first, so patch it first.

If this was useful

The fix for this one is a kernel update and a reboot on every exposed host, and the hard part is doing that across a fleet without dropping traffic. Draining a node behind a load balancer, rolling it, and bringing it back is the kind of building block the System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals walks through. I also build Hermes IDE, a free, source-available desktop app (macOS, Windows, Linux) that runs Claude Code, Codex and other coding agents side by side, and each one can work on its own branch; star it on GitHub if that sounds useful.

title: API Gateways & the Edge
description:
⚡ TL;DR: Give your scattered services one front door. You will know what an API gateway actually handles, which managed options you will meet, and how a WAF guards the edge against the traffic you do not want.

Contents

  • You shipped three services. Now what's the URL?
  • One sentence, then a picture in your head
  • Where it sits
  • What the gateway is actually responsible for
  • What a route + rate-limit policy looks like
  • Managed options you'll actually meet
  • The WAF and the edge
  • Common mistakes that cost hours
  • Takeaways
  • Where to go next

You shipped three services. Now what's the URL?

You split your app into a few services, one for auth, one for orders, one for payments. Each runs somewhere, each has its own host and port. Now your mobile app needs to call them. Do you hand the client three different URLs? Who checks the token? Who stops a bad actor from hammering the login endpoint 10,000 times a second? Who adds CORS headers, strips the internal X-Debug header, and caches that one expensive response?

The honest answer for most teams is: an API gateway. It's the single front door that every request passes through before it reaches a backend service, and once you have one, a whole category of cross-cutting problems stops living in your application code.

📌 Who this is for: Junior cloud and backend engineers who have built an API or two and are now staring down multiple services, public traffic, and the question "where does auth and rate limiting actually go?" No prior gateway experience assumed.

One sentence, then a picture in your head

An API gateway is a reverse proxy that sits in front of your services and handles routing, authentication, rate limiting, transforms, and caching, so each service doesn't have to.

If that still feels abstract, borrow the hotel. Guests don't wander into the kitchen, the laundry, or the manager's office directly. They walk up to the front desk, and the concierge handles everything from there.

In the real world In tech
You check in once at the front desk and get a room key. You authenticate once at the gateway and get a token it validates on every later request.
The concierge sends you to the right floor and room. The gateway routes /orders to the orders service and /pay to payments.
One guest can't monopolize the concierge all day. Rate limiting caps how many requests one client can make per window.
The desk keeps printed maps ready so it doesn't reprint per guest. The gateway caches common responses instead of re-hitting the backend.
A security guard screens people at the entrance. A WAF at the edge filters malicious traffic before it even reaches the desk.

A hotel front desk is an API gateway with a uniform.

Where it sits

The gateway lives between the public internet and your private services. In front of it, at the very edge, sits a WAF and usually a CDN. Behind it, your services stay on a private network and never take traffic directly from clients.

Clients → WAF (edge) → API gateway → private backend services.

  1. Request hits the edge: The client calls one hostname over HTTPS. The WAF inspects it first and drops anything matching known attack patterns.
  2. Gateway authenticates: Clean traffic reaches the gateway, which validates the token or API key. No token, no entry, the backend never sees the request.
  3. Rate limit is checked: The gateway counts requests for this client in the current window. Over the limit returns 429 immediately, sparing the backend.
  4. Route and (maybe) cache: The path is matched to a backend route. If a fresh cached response exists, it's returned without touching the service at all.
  5. Transform and forward: The gateway rewrites headers/paths as needed, forwards to the private service, then shapes the response on the way back out.

What the gateway is actually responsible for

The pitch for a gateway is consolidation: every concern below would otherwise be re-implemented (slightly differently, slightly buggily) in each service. Centralize them once.

Responsibility What it does Why at the gateway
Routing Maps an incoming path/host to a backend service Clients get one stable URL; you can move or split services behind it freely
Authentication Validates tokens, API keys, or mTLS before forwarding Reject unauthenticated traffic once, not in every service
Rate limiting Caps requests per client per time window Protects every backend from abuse and runaway clients in one place
Caching Stores and serves common responses Cuts latency and backend load without per-service cache code
Transforms Rewrites headers, paths, and bodies in/out Hide internal shapes; add CORS; strip debug headers consistently

The five core gateway responsibilities, and why they belong here.

💡 The rule of thumb: Cross-cutting and request-shaped concerns go in the gateway. Anything that needs to know what your business does stays in the service.

What a route + rate-limit policy looks like

Most gateways are configured declaratively, you describe routes and policies, the gateway enforces them. Here's a vendor-neutral shape: a route for the orders service with JWT auth, a per-client rate limit, and a short response cache.

gateway-route.yaml

routes:
  - name: orders
    match:
      path: /orders/*
      methods: [GET, POST]
    upstream:
      service: orders-service.internal
      port: 8080
    policies:
      # 1. Require a valid JWT before forwarding
      auth:
        type: jwt
        issuer: https://auth.example.com
        audience: orders-api
        forward_claims: [sub, scope]

      # 2. 100 requests per minute, per client key
      rate_limit:
        requests: 100
        per: minute
        key: ${request.header.X-Client-Id}
        on_exceeded:
          status: 429
          body: "Rate limit exceeded. Retry shortly."

      # 3. Cache successful GETs for 30s
      cache:
        methods: [GET]
        ttl: 30s
        vary: [Authorization]

      # 4. Shape the request/response
      transform:
        request:
          remove_headers: [X-Debug, X-Internal-Trace]
        response:
          add_headers:
            Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com

Read it top to bottom and you've read the request lifecycle: authenticate, rate limit, serve from cache if possible, transform, forward. No business logic anywhere in here, that's the point.

Managed options you'll actually meet

You rarely build a gateway from scratch. Each major cloud has a managed one, and Apigee is the heavyweight cross-cloud option for serious API programs. They differ in polish and price, not in the fundamentals above.

  • AWS API Gateway, deep integration with Lambda and IAM; REST and HTTP APIs; pay-per-request. The default if you're already on AWS.
  • Azure API Management (APIM), strong policy engine (XML-based transforms), a built-in developer portal, and tiered pricing. Common in enterprise Azure shops.
  • Google Apigee, full API management platform: monetization, analytics, lifecycle, and a polished portal. Heavier and pricier; chosen when APIs are the product.
  • Self-managed (Kong, NGINX, Envoy), open-source data planes you run yourself. Maximum control, you own the upgrades, scaling, and on-call.

The WAF and the edge

A Web Application Firewall sits one hop in front of the gateway, at the edge of your network. Where the gateway asks "who are you and where are you going?", the WAF asks "does this request look malicious?" It inspects requests against rules, known SQL injection and XSS patterns, suspicious user agents, traffic floods, requests from flagged IP ranges, and drops the bad ones before they cost you anything downstream.

The edge is also where your CDN lives, terminating TLS close to users and serving static content from points of presence worldwide. WAF rules typically run right there, so an attack is filtered near its origin rather than after crossing the globe to your gateway. For the CDN side of this story, see CDN & Edge Compute.

📌 Gateway vs WAF, not the same job: The WAF is about threat filtering (is this request hostile?). The gateway is about identity and traffic management (who is this, and where should it go?). You want both, in that order.

Common mistakes that cost hours

  1. Business logic in the gateway. It's tempting to add "just one" pricing rule or order check in a transform. Now your business logic is split across two systems with different deploy cycles. Keep the gateway dumb about your domain.
  2. No rate limiting. Without it, one buggy client or one attacker can take down every service behind the gateway at once. Set sane per-client limits from day one, even generous ones.
  3. Treating the gateway as a single point of failure. Everything flows through it, so if it's one box, it's the outage. Run it across multiple instances and availability zones, and health-check it like the critical infrastructure it is.
  4. Skipping the WAF because "the gateway has auth." Auth checks identity; it does not catch injection or floods. They solve different problems.
  5. Caching authenticated responses without a vary key. Cache a logged-in user's data without varying on their token and you'll serve their data to the next person. Always vary on the auth header.

Takeaways

The whole article in seven lines

  • An API gateway is the single front door: routing, auth, rate limiting, caching, and transforms in one place.
  • It lets clients use one stable URL while you reshape services freely behind it.
  • Cross-cutting concerns go in the gateway; business logic stays in the service.
  • A WAF sits one hop further out at the edge and filters malicious traffic before the gateway sees it.
  • Gateway = identity and routing; WAF = threat filtering. Use both.
  • Reach for a managed option, AWS API Gateway, Azure APIM, or Apigee, before building your own.
  • Always cap rate limits, run the gateway redundantly, and vary cached responses on auth.

Where to go next

The gateway handles the front door, but the contracts your services expose through it matter just as much. Pair this with the design and edge sides of the picture, then put it into practice on the path.

  • Read Secure API Design for the contract and auth patterns the gateway enforces.
  • Read CDN & Edge Compute to go deeper on what else lives at the edge.
  • Practice routing and proxy concepts in the networking lab.
  • Follow the full track on the Cloud Engineer path.

Originally published on TheSimplifiedTech, where this guide is interactive, with in-browser terminal labs and diagrams. Learn cloud and DevOps by doing, no videos.

title: Node.js 26 LTS: planning the Lambda upgrade
description:
Node.js 26 LTS has been official since October 28, 2026, under the codename “Lithium”. For me, an LTS switch like this is always the moment to stop eyeing the next release and write an upgrade plan instead. If you only touch your Lambda functions once the deprecation email from AWS lands in your inbox, you work under time pressure. And time pressure is a pretty bad advisor for runtime upgrades.

On AWS Lambda, the nodejs26.x runtime is already available as a public preview, and according to the documentation AWS is targeting general availability for November 2026. That window is valuable: you can test today without having to switch production today. I will show you what Node.js 26 brings, what breaks when you move from Node.js 22 or 24, and how a small probe function for a fictional bike rental tells you what the new Lambda runtime can really do.

In short

Node.js 26 became LTS on October 28, 2026 and receives updates until the end of April 2029, while nodejs26.x on Lambda is still a preview with a planned launch in November 2026. The most useful addition for everyday work is the Temporal API for dates and times. The biggest pitfall: what works under Node 26 on your laptop is not necessarily enabled the same way in the Lambda runtime, so check features there directly instead of assuming them.

What you will learn in this article

  • What Node.js 26 LTS means for your support timeline on Lambda
  • Which additions such as Temporal and Map.getOrInsert you can use right away
  • Which changes can break when you upgrade from Node.js 22 or 24
  • How to test nodejs26.x next to nodejs24.x with AWS CDK
  • How to find every Node runtime in your AWS account

What Node.js 26 LTS means for your timeline

LTS stands for Long Term Support: a version receives security and bug fixes over a long period, and new features only arrive cautiously. Release 26.13.0, which officially starts Node.js 26 LTS, is purely formal. According to the release notes, it only switches metadata such as process.release to LTS and contains nothing else beyond 26.12.1. Updates for Node.js 26 LTS continue until the end of April 2029.

The Node.js project is also changing its rhythm. Until now, only even-numbered versions became LTS, while odd ones such as Node.js 25 were done after six months (25 reached EOL, or “end of life”, at the end of March 2026). Starting with Node.js 27, there will be one major version per year, and each of them becomes LTS after its six-month Current phase. For teams, that means fewer versions and a predictable cadence.

Here is where Lambda stands at the end of October 2026:

Runtime Node.js line Status on Lambda
nodejs22.x LTS “Jod” Deprecated on Apr 30, 2027, updates blocked from Aug 31, 2027
nodejs24.x LTS “Krypton” Deprecated on Apr 30, 2028
nodejs26.x LTS “Lithium” Public preview, general availability planned for November 2026

For many teams, the date that matters most is the end of nodejs22.x in April 2027.

My take: for many teams, the real deadline is not the launch of Node.js 26 but the deprecation of nodejs22.x. That leaves roughly six months. If you plan now, you can fit the upgrade into your normal sprint cadence.

Node.js 26 LTS features you will notice day to day

Coming from Node.js 24, you get not only the changes in Node.js 26 LTS but also everything from Node.js 25. That intermediate version was never LTS, so many teams skipped it. A few points stand out for daily work.

Temporal: dates and times without the headache

Node.js 26 LTS ships the Temporal API enabled by default, no flag required. Temporal is the new standard for dates and times in JavaScript and fixes the weaknesses of Date: months that start at 0, no real time zone arithmetic, and objects you can mutate by accident. Instead, you get clear types. Temporal.Instant is an exact point in time, Temporal.ZonedDateTime is a point in time in a specific time zone, and Temporal.PlainDate is a plain calendar date.

const pickup = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2026-10-24T10:00[Europe/Berlin]");
const due = pickup.add({ days: 2 });

console.log(due.toString());
// 2026-10-26T10:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]  (same wall-clock time, even though the DST change happens in between)

We will use exactly this example in the probe function later. With Date and “plus 48 hours”, you end up at 9 a.m. instead of 10 a.m. on October 26, because the clocks go back during the night before October 25. I cover how to use Temporal day to day for deadlines, time zones and DynamoDB in detail in Temporal API in TypeScript: deadlines and time zones.

Small helpers: getOrInsert, Iterator.concat and Base64

V8 14.6 adds two small but pleasant functions. Map.prototype.getOrInsert() and getOrInsertComputed() read a value or create it if it is missing. The classic “does this key exist yet?” pattern for grouping shrinks to a single line. Iterator.concat() chains several iterators without building intermediate arrays.

const rentals = [
  { station: "Central Station", bikeId: "city-bike-17" },
  { station: "Old Town", bikeId: "e-bike-03" },
  { station: "Central Station", bikeId: "cargo-bike-02" },
];

const byStation = new Map<string, string[]>();
for (const rental of rentals) {
  byStation.getOrInsert(rental.station, []).push(rental.bikeId);
}
// Map { "Central Station" => ["city-bike-17", "cargo-bike-02"], "Old Town" => ["e-bike-03"] }

Node.js 25 contributed, for example, Uint8Array.fromBase64() and toBase64() (plus hex variants) and a noticeably faster JSON.stringify. In Lambda functions that build lots of JSON responses or encode binary data for API Gateway, that is a nice bonus for free. One observation from my test: with "lib": ["esnext"], TypeScript 7.0.2 already knows the types for Temporal, getOrInsert and fromBase64, but still reports an error for Iterator.concat.

Platform: Undici 8, Web Storage and permissions

Undici, the built-in HTTP client behind fetch, moves to version 8. Since Node.js 25, the Web Storage API is enabled by default, but in Node.js 26 localStorage returns undefined as long as no storage file is configured. Since Node.js 25, the permission model also knows --allow-net, which lets you restrict a process’s network access. On Lambda, that matters more for local tools and CI scripts, because isolation there is handled by IAM and VPC anyway.

What breaks when you move to Node.js 26 LTS

Most projects keep running after the upgrade to Node.js 26 LTS. Still, there are a handful of changes worth checking deliberately before you switch the runtime:

  • The old internal modules _stream_readable, _stream_writable and their siblings are removed in Node.js 26. Older libraries sometimes still import them directly.
  • http.Server.prototype.writeHeader() is gone, use writeHead().
  • Since Node.js 25, fs.F_OK, fs.R_OK, fs.W_OK and fs.X_OK are no longer exported directly from the module. The constants live under fs.constants.
  • SlowBuffer and assert.CallTracker have reached end of life since Node.js 25.
  • Corepack is no longer bundled since Node.js 25. If you enable pnpm or Yarn via Corepack, install it separately in CI.
  • module.register() emits a runtime deprecation warning in Node.js 26, and --experimental-transform-types was removed.
  • Native addons need a rebuild, because NODE_MODULE_VERSION changes to 147.
  • Since Node.js 25, the official Linux binaries are linked against libatomic. Slim container images for CI may be missing that package.

On top of that on Lambda: what has applied since nodejs24.x

If you jump from nodejs22.x straight to 26, you also pick up the Lambda-specific changes AWS introduced with nodejs24.x. Callback handlers are no longer supported, context.callbackWaitsForEmptyEventLoop is removed, and so are context.succeed, fail and done. In addition, Lambda no longer waits for pending promises once your handler returns. Anything you still want to finish has to be completed with await first.

// Before: callback handler (no longer works from nodejs24.x)
export const handler = (event, context, callback) => {
  loadBike(event.bikeId)
    .then((bike) => callback(null, bike))
    .catch((err) => callback(err));
};

// After: async handler, every piece of work is awaited
export const handler = async (event: { bikeId: string }) => {
  const bike = await loadBike(event.bikeId);
  await auditLog.write({ action: "lookup", bikeId: bike.id }); // without await this would get lost
  return bike;
};

One more point is easy to miss: Lambda disables experimental Node.js features by default, such as require() of ES modules and automatic module detection. You can turn them back on via NODE_OPTIONS, but AWS covers such cases with neither support nor the SLA.

nodejs26.x on Lambda: the state at the end of October 2026

The nodejs26.x runtime is available as a public preview, both as a ZIP runtime and as the container base image public.ecr.aws/lambda/nodejs:26-preview. Preview means no SLA, no technical support, and breaking changes are possible. It is explicitly not meant for production workloads. AWS names November 2026 as the launch of the stable version, but only as a non-binding estimate.

The feedback issue for the preview on GitHub is revealing. Users report, among other things, that Temporal is missing in the preview and that process.features.require_module is false. These are community observations, not an official AWS statement, and a lot can change before the stable release. I still think the lesson matters: a Lambda runtime is not automatically identical to the Node.js on your machine. So let us check directly in Lambda.

🎬 Probe function on two Lambda runtimes – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

Step by step: testing nodejs26.x next to nodejs24.x

Our example is a fictional bike rental. A function calculates when a rented bike has to be back: same time of day, a given number of days later, in the time zone of the rental station. It also returns a small report on which features the runtime really provides. If Temporal is built in, the function uses it, otherwise a polyfill steps in. A polyfill is a retrofitted implementation of a standard API for environments that do not support it yet.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 22 or newer locally (thanks to the polyfill, the tests run without Node.js 26 too)
  • AWS CLI v2 with credentials for a test or sandbox account
  • An account bootstrapped with npx cdk bootstrap in your region
  • A region where nodejs26.x is already selectable. You can see that in the Lambda console when creating a function.

Step 1: create the project 

mkdir bike-rental-runtime-check && cd bike-rental-runtime-check
npm init -y
npm install @js-temporal/polyfill@0.5.1
npm install -D typescript@7.0.2 @types/node@26 @types/aws-lambda tsx esbuild aws-cdk-lib@2.275.0 constructs aws-cdk@2.1146.1
mkdir -p bin lib src test

Switch package.json to ES modules and add a few scripts:

{
  "name": "node26-lambda-upgrade",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "scripts": {
    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit -p .",
    "test": "node --import tsx --test test/*.test.ts",
    "synth": "cdk synth",
    "deploy": "cdk deploy"
  },
  "license": "MIT",
  "devDependencies": {
    "@types/aws-lambda": "^8.10.164",
    "@types/node": "^26.6.6",
    "aws-cdk": "^2.1146.1",
    "aws-cdk-lib": "^2.275.0",
    "constructs": "^10.8.1",
    "esbuild": "^0.28.2",
    "tsx": "^4.23.15",
    "typescript": "^7.0.2"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "@js-temporal/polyfill": "^0.5.1"
  },
  "private": true,
  "type": "module"
}

Step 2: configure TypeScript

With "lib": ["esnext"], TypeScript knows the new APIs such as Temporal. noEmit is enough, because esbuild bundles during deployment and tsx runs the tests directly.

// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2024",
    "lib": ["esnext"],
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "types": ["node"],
    "noEmit": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["bin", "lib", "src", "test"]
}

Step 3: write the runtime report

The function checks every feature directly instead of inferring it from the version number. That is more reliable, because a runtime can have a feature disabled despite a matching version.

// src/runtime-report.ts
// Reports which runtime features are actually available in the current Node.js environment.

export interface RuntimeReport {
  nodeVersion: string;
  ltsName: string | null;
  temporal: boolean;
  mapGetOrInsert: boolean;
  iteratorConcat: boolean;
  uint8ArrayBase64: boolean;
  requireModule: boolean;
  lambdaRuntime: string | null;
}

export function collectRuntimeReport(env: NodeJS.ProcessEnv = process.env): RuntimeReport {
  const g = globalThis as Record<string, unknown>;
  const iteratorCtor = g.Iterator as { concat?: unknown } | undefined;

  return {
    nodeVersion: process.version,
    ltsName: process.release.lts ?? null,
    temporal: typeof g.Temporal === "object" && g.Temporal !== null,
    mapGetOrInsert: typeof (Map.prototype as { getOrInsert?: unknown }).getOrInsert === "function",
    iteratorConcat: typeof iteratorCtor?.concat === "function",
    uint8ArrayBase64: typeof (Uint8Array as { fromBase64?: unknown }).fromBase64 === "function",
    requireModule: process.features.require_module === true,
    // In Lambda, AWS_EXECUTION_ENV looks like this, for example: AWS_Lambda_nodejs24.x
    lambdaRuntime: env.AWS_EXECUTION_ENV?.replace("AWS_Lambda_", "") ?? null,
  };
}

Step 4: load Temporal with a fallback 

// src/temporal.ts
// Uses the built-in Temporal if the runtime provides it, otherwise the polyfill.

export type TemporalApi = typeof Temporal;

export async function loadTemporal(): Promise<{ api: TemporalApi; source: "runtime" | "polyfill" }> {
  const builtIn = (globalThis as { Temporal?: TemporalApi }).Temporal;
  if (builtIn) {
    return { api: builtIn, source: "runtime" };
  }
  const polyfill = await import("@js-temporal/polyfill");
  return { api: polyfill.Temporal as unknown as TemporalApi, source: "polyfill" };
}

The dynamic import ensures that the polyfill is only loaded when it is needed. esbuild still bundles it, which makes the package about 150 KB larger. Once Temporal is reliably available in the stable runtime, you can remove the fallback.

Step 5: the rental logic 

// src/rental.ts
// Fictional bike rental: when does a bike have to be back?

import type { TemporalApi } from "./temporal.js";

export interface RentalRequest {
  bikeId: string;
  pickupAt: string; // pickup time as an instant, e.g. "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z"
  days: number; // number of rental days
  timeZone: string; // time zone of the rental station, e.g. "Europe/Berlin"
}

export function validateRental(input: Partial<RentalRequest>): RentalRequest {
  const { bikeId, pickupAt, days, timeZone } = input;
  if (!bikeId || !pickupAt || !timeZone) {
    throw new Error("bikeId, pickupAt and timeZone are required");
  }
  if (typeof days !== "number" || !Number.isInteger(days) || days < 1 || days > 30) {
    throw new Error("days must be an integer between 1 and 30");
  }
  return { bikeId, pickupAt, days, timeZone };
}

// With Temporal, "2 days" means the same wall-clock time two calendar days later, even across a DST change.
export function returnDeadline(T: TemporalApi, req: RentalRequest): string {
  return T.Instant.from(req.pickupAt)
    .toZonedDateTimeISO(req.timeZone)
    .add({ days: req.days })
    .toString({ smallestUnit: "minute" });
}

// The classic Date approach just adds milliseconds. Across a DST change it is off by one hour.
export function naiveReturnDeadline(req: RentalRequest): string {
  const start = new Date(req.pickupAt).getTime();
  return new Date(start + req.days * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000).toISOString();
}

Step 6: the Lambda handler 

// src/handler.ts
// Lambda handler: returns the runtime report and the return deadline for a rental.

import { collectRuntimeReport } from "./runtime-report.js";
import { loadTemporal } from "./temporal.js";
import { naiveReturnDeadline, returnDeadline, validateRental, type RentalRequest } from "./rental.js";

const DEMO_RENTAL: RentalRequest = {
  bikeId: "city-bike-17",
  pickupAt: "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z",
  days: 2,
  timeZone: "Europe/Berlin",
};

// Deliberately async without a callback: since nodejs24.x, Lambda no longer supports callback handlers.
export const handler = async (event: Partial<RentalRequest> = {}) => {
  const rental = validateRental({ ...DEMO_RENTAL, ...event });
  const { api, source } = await loadTemporal();

  return {
    runtime: collectRuntimeReport(),
    temporalSource: source,
    rental: {
      bikeId: rental.bikeId,
      returnAt: returnDeadline(api, rental),
      naiveReturnAtUtc: naiveReturnDeadline(rental),
    },
  };
};

Step 7: tests with the Node test runner

The tests cover the interesting case: a rental across the DST change on October 25, 2026. This shows in black and white why Temporal is worth the switch.

// test/rental.test.ts
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { loadTemporal } from "../src/temporal.js";
import { naiveReturnDeadline, returnDeadline, validateRental } from "../src/rental.js";

const overDstChange = validateRental({
  bikeId: "city-bike-17",
  pickupAt: "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z", // 10:00 in Berlin (summer time)
  days: 2,
  timeZone: "Europe/Berlin",
});

test("Temporal keeps the wall-clock time across the DST change", async () => {
  const { api } = await loadTemporal();
  assert.equal(returnDeadline(api, overDstChange), "2026-10-26T10:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]");
});

test("Date arithmetic ends up one hour early after the DST change", () => {
  // 08:00 UTC on Oct 26 is 09:00 winter time in Berlin, not 10:00
  assert.equal(naiveReturnDeadline(overDstChange), "2026-10-26T08:00:00.000Z");
});

test("without a DST change both approaches agree", async () => {
  const { api } = await loadTemporal();
  const normalWeek = { ...overDstChange, pickupAt: "2026-11-02T09:00:00Z" };
  assert.equal(returnDeadline(api, normalWeek), "2026-11-04T10:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]");
  assert.equal(naiveReturnDeadline(normalWeek), "2026-11-04T09:00:00.000Z");
});

test("invalid rental duration is rejected", () => {
  assert.throws(() => validateRental({ ...overDstChange, days: 0 }), /days must/);
  assert.throws(() => validateRental({ ...overDstChange, days: 1.5 }), /days must/);
});

// test/runtime-report.test.ts
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { collectRuntimeReport } from "../src/runtime-report.js";
import { handler } from "../src/handler.js";

test("report contains the Node version and detects the Lambda runtime", () => {
  const report = collectRuntimeReport({ AWS_EXECUTION_ENV: "AWS_Lambda_nodejs26.x" });
  assert.match(report.nodeVersion, /^v\d+\./);
  assert.equal(report.lambdaRuntime, "nodejs26.x");
});

test("outside of Lambda, lambdaRuntime is null", () => {
  assert.equal(collectRuntimeReport({}).lambdaRuntime, null);
});

test("handler returns report and return deadline", async () => {
  const result = await handler({ days: 3 });
  assert.equal(result.rental.bikeId, "city-bike-17");
  assert.equal(result.rental.returnAt, "2026-10-27T10:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]");
  assert.ok(["runtime", "polyfill"].includes(result.temporalSource));
});

Step 8: the CDK stack with two runtimes

The installed version of aws-cdk-lib (2.275.0) does not ship nodejs26.x as a ready-made constant yet. That is not a problem, because new Runtime(...) lets you define any runtime yourself. The stack creates the same function twice. If you have not used AWS CDK with TypeScript before, my introduction Lambda function with CDK and TypeScript will help.

// lib/runtime-check-stack.ts
import * as path from "node:path";
import { CfnOutput, Duration, RemovalPolicy, Stack, type StackProps } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { Architecture, Runtime, RuntimeFamily } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda";
import { NodejsFunction, OutputFormat } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-nodejs";
import { LogGroup, RetentionDays } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-logs";
import type { Construct } from "constructs";

// aws-cdk-lib does not ship a constant for nodejs26.x yet, so we define it ourselves.
const NODEJS_26_PREVIEW = new Runtime("nodejs26.x", RuntimeFamily.NODEJS, { supportsInlineCode: true });

export class RuntimeCheckStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    const variants = [
      { name: "Node24", runtime: Runtime.NODEJS_24_X, target: "node24" },
      { name: "Node26", runtime: NODEJS_26_PREVIEW, target: "node26" },
    ];

    for (const variant of variants) {
      const logGroup = new LogGroup(this, `${variant.name}Logs`, {
        retention: RetentionDays.ONE_WEEK,
        removalPolicy: RemovalPolicy.DESTROY,
      });

      const fn = new NodejsFunction(this, `RentalCheck${variant.name}`, {
        entry: path.join(import.meta.dirname, "../src/handler.ts"),
        handler: "handler",
        runtime: variant.runtime,
        architecture: Architecture.ARM_64,
        memorySize: 256,
        timeout: Duration.seconds(10),
        logGroup,
        bundling: {
          format: OutputFormat.ESM,
          target: variant.target,
          minify: true,
          sourceMap: true,
          // esbuild needs a require function in the ESM bundle for CommonJS dependencies
          banner: "import { createRequire } from 'module'; const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);",
        },
        environment: {
          NODE_OPTIONS: "--enable-source-maps",
        },
      });

      new CfnOutput(this, `${variant.name}FunctionName`, { value: fn.functionName });
    }
  }
}

// bin/app.ts
import { App } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { RuntimeCheckStack } from "../lib/runtime-check-stack.js";

const app = new App();
new RuntimeCheckStack(app, "BikeRentalRuntimeCheck", {
  env: { region: process.env.CDK_DEFAULT_REGION ?? "eu-central-1" },
});

// cdk.json
{
  "app": "npx tsx bin/app.ts"
}

Step 9: check, deploy and compare 

npm run typecheck
npm test
npx cdk synth
npx cdk deploy

After the deployment, CDK prints both function names. Call both with the same request and compare the responses:

aws lambda invoke --function-name <Node24FunctionName> \
  --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out --payload '{"days":2}' node24.json
aws lambda invoke --function-name <Node26FunctionName> \
  --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out --payload '{"days":2}' node26.json
diff <(jq .runtime node24.json) <(jq .runtime node26.json)

This is the response when I call the bundled package locally under Node.js 22. Under nodejs26.x you expect a 26.x version, and exactly this report tells you which features are true there:

{
  "runtime": {
    "nodeVersion": "v22.23.4",
    "ltsName": "Jod",
    "temporal": false,
    "mapGetOrInsert": false,
    "iteratorConcat": false,
    "uint8ArrayBase64": false,
    "requireModule": true,
    "lambdaRuntime": "nodejs24.x"
  },
  "temporalSource": "polyfill",
  "rental": {
    "bikeId": "city-bike-17",
    "returnAt": "2026-10-26T10:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]",
    "naiveReturnAtUtc": "2026-10-26T08:00:00.000Z"
  }
}

The rental field is what matters: the Temporal calculation returns 10 a.m., while the naive Date calculation lands at 9 a.m. local time. On both runtimes, returnAt has to be identical, no matter whether Temporal is built in or the polyfill does the math.

Common mistakes

  • Runtime rejected: if your region does not offer the preview yet, the deployment fails. For the test, switch to a region where nodejs26.x is selectable in the console.
  • “Dynamic require … is not supported”: this message appears when an ESM bundle contains a CommonJS dependency. The banner with createRequire in the stack prevents it.
  • Callback handlers: old code with (event, context, callback) no longer works from nodejs24.x. Switch to async first.
  • Green locally, different in Lambda: your tests may run with the polyfill locally and with built-in Temporal in Lambda, or the other way round. That is exactly why the report checks every feature in the real runtime.

Cost and security

Two small 256 MB functions that you call a few times cost practically nothing and usually stay within the free tier. With the Lambda cost calculator you can do the math for your real load profiles. Logs are deleted after one week, and npx cdk destroy removes everything again. Do not process real customer data in the preview runtime, since there is neither an SLA nor support for it.

Upgrade checklist for your team

Find the Node runtimes in your account

Before you plan, you need a list. This command shows every function with a Node runtime per region:

for region in eu-central-1 eu-west-1; do
  aws lambda list-functions --region "$region" \
    --query "Functions[?starts_with(Runtime, 'nodejs')].[FunctionName, Runtime]" \
    --output text | sed "s/^/$region\t/"
done

Update TypeScript, bundler and CI

Bump @types/node to version 26, set the matching target in esbuild or on NodejsFunction, and add a Node.js 26 entry to your CI test matrix. Rebuild native addons. And if you use pnpm or Yarn via Corepack, install Corepack explicitly in the pipeline, since it is no longer bundled.

Roll out gradually

Once nodejs26.x is generally available, do not switch all functions at once. I would start with non-critical functions and use an alias with weighted routing to send only part of the traffic to the new version. New runtimes often have somewhat longer cold starts at launch, so keep an eye on error rate and init duration. How to build alarms and dashboards for that is covered in Monitoring Lambda with CDK.

My take

Testing: yes, now. Production on the preview: no. That is my position in a nutshell. The preview is a gift, because you find the surprises while nobody is rushing you yet. If you still run on nodejs22.x today, though, I would not wait for November. The move to 24 brings the biggest Lambda-specific breaks, namely callback handlers and promises that are not awaited. Those affect 26 just the same. Once that is done, the step from 24 to Node.js 26 LTS is small in most projects.

Temporal is what I am looking forward to most. I would rather not count how many time zone and daylight saving bugs I have seen in my career. At the same time, the preview shows that Lambda runtimes are deliberately more conservative than upstream Node.js. For stability, I think that is right, but it can catch you off guard. So my advice: check features in the runtime where your code will actually run. And while you are at it, take a look at your patch routine, because security updates like the one for the Node.js vulnerability CVE-2026-111497 arrive regularly for LTS versions too.

By the way, I like the new annual cadence starting with Node.js 27. A team can schedule one LTS upgrade per year instead of debating every time which version to skip.

FAQ

When will Node.js 26 be generally available on AWS Lambda?

AWS names November 2026 as the planned launch for nodejs26.x, explicitly as a non-binding estimate. Until then, the runtime is a public preview without SLA or support.

How long is Node.js 26 LTS supported?

According to the Node.js project, the 26.x line receives updates until the end of April 2029. When AWS will deprecate the Lambda runtime has not been announced yet.

Can I already use Temporal in Lambda?

Yes, via a polyfill such as @js-temporal/polyfill on any Node runtime. Whether Temporal is built in and enabled in nodejs26.x is best checked with feature detection as in the example.

Do I have to upgrade from Node.js 22 to 24 first?

No, you can go straight to 26. But then you have to handle all changes from 24 and 26 at once. Since nodejs22.x is deprecated in April 2027, going through 24 now is often the more relaxed path.

Your next step

Run the command from the checklist today and count how many functions still run on nodejs22.x. Then deploy the probe function to a sandbox account and check in the report what Node.js 26 LTS really brings in nodejs26.x. I would like to know: which Node runtime are your Lambdas on right now, and what slows you down most when upgrading? Let me know in the comments.

Sources

  • Node.js blog: Node.js 26.0.0 (Current), May 5, 2026
  • Node.js blog: Node.js 25.0.0 (Current), Oct 15, 2025
  • Node.js: releases and release schedule
  • AWS Lambda Developer Guide: Lambda runtimes
  • GitHub: feedback issue for the Node.js 26 preview runtime
  • AWS Compute Blog: Node.js 24 runtime now available in AWS Lambda
  • Tested with Node.js 22.23, TypeScript 7.0.2 (tsc --noEmit), aws-cdk-lib 2.275.0 (cdk synth), @js-temporal/polyfill 0.5.1 and the Node test runner (7 tests). A deployment to AWS and a run under Node.js 26 were not possible in my test environment.

title: Why We Built StatusNow: Stopping the $200/mo Tool Sprawl for Small Teams
description:
If you run a indie project, small SaaS, or boutique dev agency, you’ve probably hit this frustrating wall:

To properly monitor a simple web application, you end up registering for five separate tools:

  1. UptimeRobot or Better Stack to check if your site is online.
  2. Sentry or Logtail to collect application errors and stack traces.
  3. Qualys or an open-source scanner to check for exposed vulnerabilities.
  4. Statuspage.io to show customers your uptime without exposing internal infrastructure.
  5. Notion or GitHub to store server setup scripts and runbooks.

Before you know it, you’re paying $30 to $50 per month per service, managing 5 different passwords, and jumping across half a dozen tabs just to figure out why an alert fired at 2 AM.

We built StatusNow because we were tired of context-switching across fragmented tools—and tired of pricing models that punish small teams.

The Problem with Traditional Ops Tooling for Small Teams

Big enterprises have dedicated SecOps, DevOps, and SRE teams running complex Datadog dashboards. But for a team of 1–5 developers, that level of complexity is overhead you can't afford.

When an incident occurs in a small team:

  • Alerts are disconnected from fixes: An uptime alert tells you api.example.com is down, but you have to log into a separate service to view the stack trace, and a third service to find the baseline PowerShell or Bash script to restart the node.
  • Per-seat pricing scales prematurely: Adding a developer or client to view a status page or error log shouldn't cost an extra $20/month per seat.
  • Vulnerabilities go unnoticed: Small teams rarely run dedicated vulnerability scanners until something breaks or an SSL cert expires, simply because setting up security scanners feels like a separate discipline.

What We Built: 5 Core Tools, 1 Login, Zero Fluff

Instead of building another niche tool, we integrated the five core operational components every site needs into a single product with a single dashboard:

  1. Uptime & SSL Monitoring: Track HTTP 200 responses, SSL certificate expiration warnings, and TCP ports (like database ports).
  2. Vulnerability Scanning: Ownership-verified scanning for misconfigurations and known vulnerabilities, automatically prioritizing actively exploited issues (CISA KEV).
  3. Application Logs: A lightweight, Sentry-compatible log ingest with stack trace grouping and audit logs.
  4. Public Status Pages: 90-day uptime metrics and incident reports that keep your internal server details completely private.
  5. Versioned Runbooks: Store, version, and hash-check server setup scripts so your team always runs verified fixes.

Built with a "Free First, Pay Only for Extra Capacity" Model

We wanted StatusNow to be something any developer could adopt immediately without asking for management approval or putting down a credit card.

  • 10 Uptime Monitors
  • 10 Vulnerability Scan Targets
  • 1 Public Status Page
  • Application Logs & Runbooks Included
  • Unlimited Team Seats & Full API/MCP Access

All $0 forever. No feature gating, no artificial seat limits. When your application grows and you need 30 monitors or 20 scan targets, you simply add lightweight capacity packs ($5–$25/mo) as you need them.

How It Helps Small Teams Act Fast

Having an alert, a finding, and a fix in the same place changes how quickly you recover:


text
[Alert Fired] db.example.com:5432 down (TCP port closed)
 ↳ Associated finding: SSL certificate expires in 9 days
 ↳ Actionable Runbook: "02_restart_postgres_node.ps1" (Hash verified)

title: Reducing AI Chatbot API Token Cost for Repetitive Invoice Queries with Node.js
description:
TL;DR: The least complex way to reduce token cost for repetitive marketplace questions is to answer stable questions from a tenant-scoped cache before calling a model, then retrieve only the invoice fields needed for the current turn. Keep a small, versioned prompt and measure input and output tokens per tenant. A cheaper model is a later decision, not the first control.

For a supplier-invoice chatbot, the bill is usually driven by repeated context: the same supplier rules, the same field definitions, and users asking the same questions about payment terms or tax totals. Sending that context on every turn multiplies the input-token count. The useful change is to stop resending material that has not changed.

That is the boundary.

Which chatbot API minimizes token cost for repetitive questions?

Start with an accounting identity rather than a vendor shortlist:

request_cost_units = (input_tokens * input_rate) + (output_tokens * output_rate)
monthly_units = sum(tenant.request_cost_units for tenant in usage_events)

The rates are provider-specific and can change, so the durable engineering work is measuring the two token counts and keeping the arithmetic outside the application prompt. For each request, record tenant ID, model identifier, input tokens, output tokens, cache hit status, retrieval count, and a prompt-schema version. Do not store the invoice text in a general-purpose cost table. Store a request ID and retention-safe metadata instead.

This accounting makes a common mistake visible: a short user question can still be expensive if the application appends twenty previously retrieved invoices and a long system instruction. Output tokens matter too, but invoice extraction normally benefits from a strict field schema and short explanations. The response contract should make that constraint explicit.

Can a cache answer the repeated question safely?

Yes, for the narrow class of questions whose answer is stable for a tenant and a document version. Examples include “What currency is this invoice in?” after extraction, or “Which fields are available?” A cache key can include tenant ID, invoice version, normalized question, locale, and prompt-schema version. That prevents a value extracted for one tenant or one revision from crossing a boundary.

A cache should not be a blind string lookup. Save the answer, the source field IDs, the extraction version, and an expiry or invalidation reason. If a supplier replaces an invoice, invalidate entries tied to the old document version. If the field schema changes, invalidate by schema version. The operational cost of keeping these links is small compared with debugging a plausible answer that came from yesterday’s document.

In email and OTP systems, I learned to treat a successful delivery as a state transition with evidence, not as a boolean. Use the same discipline here: a cache hit is useful only when it carries enough provenance for the UI and audit trail to explain why it was returned.

How much context should retrieval send?

Retrieve the smallest evidence set that can support the answer. For invoice extraction, that might be the supplier name plus the line-item, tax, total, or payment-term fields requested in the turn. A reranker can help order candidate passages, but ranking does not remove the need to cap the final context. Reranking documentation describes reranking as a relevance step; it is not a substitute for tenant isolation, field validation, or cost accounting.

A practical pipeline is: classify the question, check the exact-answer cache, retrieve candidate fields, apply a token budget, call the model only when needed, validate the structured response, and write a usage event. The token budget should be a policy by question type. “What is the invoice total?” needs less evidence than “Explain every discrepancy across these three invoices.”

Here is a deliberately plain interface for the decision point:

def answer_invoice_question(question, tenant_id, invoice_version):
    key = make_cache_key(tenant_id, invoice_version, normalize(question), PROMPT_SCHEMA_VERSION)
    cached = answer_cache.get(key)
    if cached and cached["schema_version"] == PROMPT_SCHEMA_VERSION:
        return {"answer": cached["answer"], "source_fields": cached["source_fields"], "cached": True}

    fields = retrieve_fields(tenant_id, invoice_version, question, limit=6)
    prompt = build_prompt(question=question, fields=fields, max_output_tokens=240)
    result = model_gateway.complete(prompt)
    answer = validate_invoice_response(result)

    answer_cache.put(key, {
        "answer": answer.text,
        "source_fields": answer.source_fields,
        "schema_version": PROMPT_SCHEMA_VERSION,
    })
    record_usage(tenant_id, result.input_tokens, result.output_tokens, cached=False)
    return {"answer": answer.text, "source_fields": answer.source_fields, "cached": False}

The numbers in this example are policy placeholders, not a claim about a particular API. Set them from evaluation data. A hard limit of six retrieved fields and 240 output tokens is only sensible if the validation and fallback path handle cases that need more evidence. The tradeoff is deliberate: a smaller context lowers token use, but it can lower answer quality when the question spans several invoices.

What should each tenant be allowed to see?

Cost visibility is a tenancy problem as much as a billing problem. Aggregate usage by tenant, workspace, feature, model identifier, and cache outcome. Show both total cost units and the causes: cache misses, average input tokens, average output tokens, retrieval count, and validation retries. A single blended average hides the tenant whose invoices contain unusually long line items.

Put budgets and alerts beside the ledger, not inside the chat prompt. A soft alert can trigger review; a hard policy can route new requests to a smaller context or require an asynchronous workflow. Preserve enough event data to reproduce the calculation, then expire sensitive payloads on a defined schedule. What I would deliberately stop keeping is raw prompt text in the long-lived cost ledger. That makes incident investigation harder, but it reduces the blast radius of a billing table becoming an accidental document archive.

A decision rule that survives model changes

Before selecting an API, replay an anonymized set of representative questions and group results by tenant and question class. Compare answer correctness, cache-hit rate, input-token reduction, output length, validation retries, and observed cost units. The winning configuration is the one that meets the correctness and latency target with an explainable per-tenant bill. A lower advertised token rate can lose if it requires more context, more retries, or longer answers.

Keep the gateway interface provider-neutral. The application should ask for a structured invoice answer and receive usage metadata; it should not know how a specific service counts tokens. Tokenizers differ, so use the gateway’s reported counts for accounting and a tokenizer tool for local estimates. The public tokenizer tool is useful for inspecting how text is split, but production accounting still belongs to the response metadata from the service you actually call.

The simplest cost reduction remains the most durable one: do not ask a model to regenerate an answer that is already valid, do not attach fields unrelated to the question, and make every cache hit attributable to one tenant and one document version. That design keeps the selection decision measurable when models, prompts, and traffic patterns change.

Further reading

  • https://docs.cohere.com/docs/rerank-overview
  • https://platform.openai.com/tokenizer
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
