Per-customer rate limits and 429s in Express and FastAPI
description:
Most rate limiting tutorials limit by IP address. That's the right tool for a login form, and the wrong one for an API that customers pay for. A customer's traffic can come from fifty servers behind fifty addresses, or from one office NAT shared with someone else's script. What you want to cap is the customer: "Acme gets 5 requests per second, however many keys or machines they use."

This post builds that in Express and in FastAPI with nothing but the framework, then covers the 429 response and the parts that tend to go wrong: ordering, retries and running more than one process.

A token bucket per customer

A token bucket is two numbers per customer: how many tokens are in the bucket, and when you last looked. The bucket holds at most capacity tokens and refills at refillPerSecond. Each request takes one token; an empty bucket means 429. A customer who's been quiet can send a burst of capacity requests, then continues at the refill rate.

You don't need a timer. Refill lazily when a request arrives:

// rate-limit.js
// One token bucket per customer. Refilled lazily when a request arrives, so no timers.
export function tokenBucket({ capacity, refillPerSecond, now = () => performance.now() / 1000 }) {
  const buckets = new Map(); // customerId -> { tokens, updatedAt }

  return function take(customerId) {
    const time = now();
    const bucket = buckets.get(customerId) ?? { tokens: capacity, updatedAt: time };
    bucket.tokens = Math.min(capacity, bucket.tokens + (time - bucket.updatedAt) * refillPerSecond);
    bucket.updatedAt = time;
    buckets.set(customerId, bucket);

    if (bucket.tokens < 1) {
      // Round up: a client that retries a moment too early just gets another 429
      return { allowed: false, retryAfter: Math.ceil((1 - bucket.tokens) / refillPerSecond) };
    }
    bucket.tokens -= 1;
    return { allowed: true, remaining: Math.floor(bucket.tokens) };
  };
}

Two details matter here. The clock is performance.now(), which is monotonic, so an NTP adjustment can't refill or drain every bucket at once. And retryAfter is rounded up, because telling a client to come back in 0 seconds produces a retry that fails again.

Express: authenticate first, then limit 

// app.js
import express from "express";
import { tokenBucket } from "./rate-limit.js";

// Stand-in for your key table. Acme has two keys but one bucket.
const KEYS = new Map([
  ["key_acme_1", "acme"],
  ["key_acme_2", "acme"],
  ["key_globex", "globex"],
]);
const CAPACITY = 5;
const take = tokenBucket({ capacity: CAPACITY, refillPerSecond: 1 });

function authenticate(req, res, next) {
  const key = req.get("authorization")?.replace(/^Bearer\s+/i, "");
  const customerId = key && KEYS.get(key);
  if (!customerId) return res.status(401).json({ error: "invalid_api_key" });
  req.customerId = customerId;
  next();
}

function rateLimit(req, res, next) {
  const result = take(req.customerId);
  res.set("RateLimit-Policy", `"default";q=${CAPACITY};w=${CAPACITY}`);
  if (result.allowed) return next();

  res.set("Retry-After", String(result.retryAfter));
  res.set("RateLimit", `"default";r=0;t=${result.retryAfter}`);
  res.status(429).json({ error: "rate_limited", retry_after: result.retryAfter });
}

const app = express();
app.get("/health", (req, res) => res.send("ok")); // before the limiter: never limited
app.use("/v1", authenticate, rateLimit);
app.get("/v1/things", (req, res) => res.json({ customer: req.customerId }));

app.listen(3000);

Send six requests in a row, alternating Acme's two keys, and the sixth gets:

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
RateLimit-Policy: "default";q=5;w=5
Retry-After: 1
RateLimit: "default";r=0;t=1

{"error":"rate_limited","retry_after":1}

Globex is unaffected, because it has its own bucket.

The order of authenticate and rateLimit is the whole point. Authentication runs first for two reasons:

  • The bucket key has to be the customer, not the API key string. Key it on the key and a customer with five keys gets five times the limit. You only know the customer after authentication.
  • Unknown keys should never reach the limiter. If they did, anyone could fill your Map with junk keys. Junk keys get a 401 instead. (If you're worried about key guessing, add a per-IP limit on failed authentications at the edge.)

Also note that Express middleware only applies to routes registered after it. /health above is open on purpose; a router mounted in some earlier file would be open by accident.

FastAPI: dependencies, and why they should be async

In FastAPI the natural place for this is a dependency chain: one dependency resolves the customer, the next one spends a token.

# main.py
import math
import time

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Header, HTTPException

# Stand-in for your key table. Acme has two keys but one bucket.
KEYS = {"key_acme_1": "acme", "key_acme_2": "acme", "key_globex": "globex"}
CAPACITY = 5
REFILL_PER_SECOND = 1.0
buckets: dict[str, tuple[float, float]] = {}  # customer_id -> (tokens, updated_at)


def take(customer_id: str) -> tuple[bool, int]:
    now = time.monotonic()
    tokens, updated_at = buckets.get(customer_id, (CAPACITY, now))
    tokens = min(CAPACITY, tokens + (now - updated_at) * REFILL_PER_SECOND)
    if tokens < 1:
        buckets[customer_id] = (tokens, now)
        return False, math.ceil((1 - tokens) / REFILL_PER_SECOND)
    buckets[customer_id] = (tokens - 1, now)
    return True, 0


async def current_customer(authorization: str = Header(default="")) -> str:
    scheme, _, key = authorization.partition(" ")
    customer_id = KEYS.get(key) if scheme.lower() == "bearer" else None
    if customer_id is None:
        raise HTTPException(401, detail="invalid_api_key")
    return customer_id


# async def on purpose: a plain def dependency runs in a thread pool,
# and two threads could both spend the last token.
async def rate_limited(customer_id: str = Depends(current_customer)) -> str:
    allowed, retry_after = take(customer_id)
    if not allowed:
        raise HTTPException(
            429,
            detail="rate_limited",
            headers={
                "Retry-After": str(retry_after),
                "RateLimit-Policy": f'"default";q={CAPACITY};w={math.ceil(CAPACITY / REFILL_PER_SECOND)}',
                "RateLimit": f'"default";r=0;t={retry_after}',
            },
        )
    return customer_id


app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/v1/things")
async def things(customer_id: str = Depends(rate_limited)):
    return {"customer": customer_id}

Run it with uvicorn main:app and the sixth quick request gets a 429 with the same three headers, and a body of {"detail":"rate_limited"}. FastAPI wraps HTTPException details in detail; add an exception handler if you want the same body shape as the Express version.

Two FastAPI-specific notes:

  • async def is doing real work here. FastAPI runs plain def dependencies in a thread pool. The read-modify-write in take() isn't atomic, so two threads can read the same bucket and both spend its last token. An async def dependency runs on the event loop, and take() has no await in it, so nothing else can run in the middle. If you need a sync dependency, put a threading.Lock around the bucket update.
  • A dependency can't limit what it doesn't run on. Routes that don't declare Depends(rate_limited) aren't limited. If you'd rather cover everything under a prefix, put the dependency on the APIRouter (APIRouter(dependencies=[Depends(rate_limited)])). If you move the check into a middleware instead, remember that middlewares run before dependencies, so the customer has to be resolved in a middleware too.

What the 429 should carry

  • Retry-After in seconds. It tells the client how many seconds to wait before retrying. Seconds don't depend on the client's clock being right, which an HTTP date does.
  • RateLimit-Policy and RateLimit. These come from an IETF draft (draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers). q is the bucket size and w its window in seconds; r is what's left and t is when to try again. It's still a draft and the field names have changed over the revisions, so treat them as a bonus and Retry-After as the one clients should rely on.
  • A machine-readable error code in the body, so clients can tell a rate limit apart from other 429s.

That last point matters more than it looks. If your plans have monthly quotas, "you've used this month's allowance" is often also a 429, and its Retry-After can be days away. A client that sleeps on every Retry-After will park a job for a week; one that ignores it and retries with backoff will keep hammering an answer that won't change. A reasonable client rule:

const wait = Number(res.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
if (wait > 60) throw new Error(`Not retrying: ${body.error}, retry after ${wait}s`);
await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, wait * 1000));

Put the same rule in your API docs, and give the two cases different error codes so people can tell them apart in their logs.

More than one process

Everything above lives in one process's memory. Put four instances behind a load balancer and a customer whose requests spread evenly gets about four times the limit. You have three choices:

  1. Accept it. A per-process cap can be enough to curb runaway scripts, as long as you can live with a customer reaching 4× the configured limit. It won't enforce a per-customer limit you've promised in a contract.
  2. Divide the limit by the number of instances, rounded up and never below 1. That keeps the total close to what you set without any shared state, but you need a reliable instance count, and a client whose keep-alive connection pins it to one instance gets only that instance's share.
  3. Use a shared store such as Redis, with the bucket update in a Lua script so it's atomic. That's exact, at the cost of a network round trip per request and a decision about what happens when Redis is down.

Decide which one you're doing before autoscaling decides for you.

Test it with a fake clock

tokenBucket() takes now as a parameter so tests don't have to sleep. Pass a function that returns a number you control, then check the edges: exactly capacity requests pass, the next one fails with retryAfter: 1, half a token isn't enough, and a long pause refills the bucket to capacity and no further.

I work on UsageRail, which does the per-customer part of this as middleware for Express (and FastAPI, Hono, Fastify, Django and Next.js), with the limits set per plan in a dashboard instead of in code: https://usagerail.com/docs/express

title: How long does a Postgres restore actually take?
description:
When someone asks how long it would take to get the database back, the answer is usually a guess based on the size of the dump. I wanted a real number, so we timed it: one schema at four sizes, from a 400 MB Supabase project up to a 10 GB database with 18.8 million rows, each dump restored into an empty PostgreSQL 17 on a single 2 vCPU / 8 GB VM.

The 10 GB restore took about 12 minutes. Most of those 12 minutes went to rebuilding indexes and foreign keys. Loading the rows was the smaller part, and that changes how you should estimate your own restore.

The numbers

Plain pg_restore with one job, into a fresh PostgreSQL 17 container:

Database Rows Dump Restore
396 MiB (real Supabase Free project) 723,500 74.6 MiB 19.4 s
1.03 GiB 2,172,000 226.5 MiB 65.9 s
5.04 GiB 9,222,000 1.00 GiB 379.8 s (6.3 min)
10.05 GiB 18,822,000 1.74 GiB 725.9 s (12.1 min)

Sizes are pg_database_size of the source. The schema is modeled on a multi-tenant SaaS app with an AI feature: orgs, users, projects, orders, an events table with JSONB payloads, a documents table with 384-dimension pgvector embeddings, 16 indexes, 7 RLS policies, triggers and functions. The three bigger databases are synthetic copies of that schema, and most of their size is event rows.

I also restored every dump twice through the restore drill of BackupDrill, the backup tool I work on. At every size, the restore step of those drills averaged within 5% of the single-job time above. That comparison is the restore alone; a full drill also downloads the dump, starts the database and checks every table.

Two things to keep in mind before you quote any of this:

  1. The target ran with durability turned off: fsync, synchronous_commit and full_page_writes off, wal_level=minimal, shared_buffers at 1.9 GB and maintenance_work_mem at 960 MB. That's fine for a test copy you delete afterwards. It's not how you'd run a database you're recovering production into. In a separate run earlier the same day, the 1 GB restore took 61 seconds with these settings and 110 seconds on stock PostgreSQL settings, about 1.8x slower.
  2. There's no download time in here. The dump sat in a bucket on the same VM; the 1.74 GiB dump came down in 15 seconds. If your backup lives in another region, add however long it takes to move the file.

Where the 12 minutes went

The 10 GB restore, one job, timed step by step from pg_restore --verbose:

Step Time Share
Build the pgvector HNSW index (200,000 embeddings, 384 dimensions) 184.8 s 25%
Build the JSONB GIN index on events 145.5 s 20%
Load the events table (13.5 million rows) 141.3 s 19%
Add the three foreign keys on events 102.8 s 14%
Add the primary key on events 57.7 s 8%
Build the (project_id, created_at) index on events 43.3 s 6%
Everything else: five smaller tables, their indexes and constraints, RLS policies, triggers 50.5 s 7%
Total 725.9 s 100%

Loading the biggest table, 13.5 million rows, took 141 seconds. One HNSW index over 200,000 vectors took longer than that on its own. Averaged over the two drill restores of this database, 77% of the restore (559 of 722 seconds) went to indexes, constraints and foreign keys, and 163 seconds to loading all 18.8 million rows.

That follows from what a custom-format dump contains. It has the rows and the definition of each index, not the index itself. pg_database_size counts index pages; the dump doesn't carry any. Across all four databases the compressed dump came out at 17–22% of the database size, and every index missing from the file gets built from scratch during the restore. Foreign keys get checked again against every row.

Estimate from your schema, not your dump size

Two databases with the same dump size can restore at very different speeds. One with a few large tables and a primary key on each is mostly COPY. One with GIN indexes on JSONB, trigram indexes, a vector index and a dozen foreign keys spends most of its restore in CREATE INDEX and ALTER TABLE.

You can see how much rebuilding is waiting in a dump before you restore anything:

pg_restore --list app.dump | grep -cE ' INDEX | CONSTRAINT | FK CONSTRAINT '

A count won't give you minutes, though. For that, time a restore of your own dump in a throwaway container. This one uses the same kind of tuning as our test target:

docker run -d --name restore-test -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw \
  -p 127.0.0.1:5433:5432 --shm-size=1g postgres:17 \
  -c fsync=off -c synchronous_commit=off -c full_page_writes=off \
  -c wal_level=minimal -c max_wal_senders=0 \
  -c shared_buffers=2GB -c maintenance_work_mem=1GB

Scale shared_buffers and maintenance_work_mem down on a machine with less memory. --shm-size matters because parallel index builds, HNSW builds included, use shared memory, and Docker's default 64 MB can be too small for them. wal_level=minimal only starts with max_wal_senders=0. If your tables have vector columns, swap postgres:17 for an image that ships pgvector, such as pgvector/pgvector:pg17, which is what our test used. Our target also had the extensions the schema needed (pg_trgm, pgvector) and Supabase's auth stubs created before the restore.

Then restore with a timestamp on every line of verbose output:

PGPASSWORD=pw pg_restore --verbose --no-owner --no-privileges \
  -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5433 -U postgres -d postgres app.dump 2>&1 \
  | perl -MTime::HiRes=time -ne 'printf "%.1f %s", time, $_' > restore.log

And list the slowest steps:

awk 'NR > 1 { printf "%6.1fs  %s\n", $1 - prev_time, prev_line }
     { prev_time = $1; $1 = ""; prev_line = $0 }' restore.log | sort -rn | head

With a single job, the gap between one line and the next is roughly how long the step on the first line took, so the top of that list is where your restore time goes. Use a pg_restore of the same major version as the pg_dump that made the file, or newer. If the dump came from Supabase and the restore complains about the auth schema, I wrote up the stubs a plain Postgres target needs a while ago.

What these numbers don't cover

  • More cores. Everything here ran on 2 vCPU. pg_restore --jobs can build several indexes at the same time, so a bigger machine can beat these numbers. We didn't test one.
  • Restoring into a new Supabase project. Speed then depends on the project's compute size and your connection to it.
  • Supabase's own restore from daily backups or point-in-time recovery. The Free plan has neither, so we couldn't time it.
  • Other schemas. More indexes per gigabyte, bigger vector indexes or thousands of small tables will spend the time differently.

Taking the backup was the quick part, at least for the small database: 25 seconds to dump the 400 MB Supabase Free project through the Session pooler from a VM in the same region (Ashburn to us-east-1), for a 75 MB file.

The full result tables, the drill timings, the test setup and the list of what we didn't test are on the benchmark page.

I work on BackupDrill, which runs scheduled backups and restore drills for Supabase projects. The drill timings above come from its open-source CLI; the plain pg_restore numbers don't depend on it.

title: I built Noktiq to make UI changes easier to explain to coding agents
description:
A small UI change should be simple to explain. But when working with coding agents, I kept spending time describing which button, heading, or card I meant.

That’s why I built Noktiq, a visual feedback tool for React and Vue.

Point. Note. Paste.

Noktiq runs on your development website:

  1. Select the element you want to change.
  2. Write a note describing the change.
  3. Copy the request into your existing coding agent.

When available, the request includes the source file, line, and column, alongside a selector and page context.

Noktiq gathers the context. Your coding agent makes the code changes.

What does the copied request look like?

Instead of describing an element’s position from memory, you can give your agent something like this:

Source: components/sections/About/About.tsx:148:17
Page: http://localhost:3000/tr
Selector: #about a
Visible text: "View my CV"
Requested change: "Change the text to Download my CV."

This is a shortened example. Actual selectors may be more specific, especially when similar elements appear more than once.

Source locations point to the code that renders the element. They don't necessarily identify the CSS rule, translation file, or event handler that needs editing, so the agent still needs to verify the target.

React and Vue, the same workflow

Noktiq supports:

  • Individual elements, selected text, multiple elements, and area selection.
  • Numbered pins, target status, and rebinding notes to another element.
  • Copying individual notes or all notes together.
  • Compact, Standard, and Detailed output.
  • A draggable mascot and local browser note storage.

Documented integrations include Next.js, Nuxt, Vite, and Webpack. Compatibility depends on the framework version and project setup; the repository includes tested configurations and limitations.

Getting started 

npm install -D noktiq

Installation alone doesn't display the toolbar. Add the React or Vue component and configure the source integration using the setup guide.

Keep the documented development condition so the toolbar stays hidden in production.

Noktiq doesn't require an AI account or API key, and it doesn't send your notes to an AI service. You review and copy the request into the coding tool you already use.

Why I’m building it

My goal is to reduce repeated explanations and unnecessary code searches when making visual changes.

That could also reduce token usage across a task, but I haven't measured the savings yet. A structured request can be longer than a short prompt—the potential benefit comes from avoiding clarification and correction rounds afterward.

Noktiq is available on npm, and the source code is on GitHub under the PolyForm Shield 1.0.0 license.

  • GitHub and documentation
  • npm package

I'd love to hear your feedback. Would this fit into your workflow, and what would make it more useful?

title: batching in react
description:
Optimizing UI Updates for Performance

Introduction

React is known for its efficient rendering process, and one of the key techniques it utilizes is batching. Batching refers to the process of combining multiple
updates into a single update, minimizing the number of times the real DOM needs to be updated. In this article, we will explore how batching works under the
hood in React and its impact on performance. We will also provide examples to demonstrate the concept.

Understanding Batching

When React renders a component, it doesn’t immediately apply every change to the real DOM. Instead, it batches the updates together and performs them all at
once, resulting in better performance and a smoother user experience. React achieves batching through a technique called “transaction,” which groups related
operations and executes them as a single unit of work.

Example: Updating State with Batching:

Let’s consider an example where a component updates its state multiple times in quick succession. Without batching, React would update the real DOM for each
state change separately, even if the actual value changed only once. This approach would be inefficient.

However, due to batching, React combines these updates into a single transaction. As a result, the real DOM is updated only once after all the state changes
have been processed. This reduces unnecessary DOM updates and improves performance.

To demonstrate this, let’s modify the example code to log the current transaction state:

import React from "react";

function Example() {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    const handleClick = () => {
        console.log("before ", React.__SECRET_INTERNALS_DO_NOT_USE_OR_YOU_WILL_BE_FIRED.ReactCurrentOwner.currentDispatcher);
        setCount(count + 1);
        setCount(count + 1);
        setCount(count + 1);

        console.log("after ", React.__SECRET_INTERNALS_DO_NOT_USE_OR_YOU_WILL_BE_FIRED.ReactCurrentOwner.currentDispatcher);
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <p>Count: {count}</p>
            <button onClick={handleClick}>Increment</button>
        </div>
    );
}

In this modified example, we log the current transaction state before and after the state updates. By observing the logs, we can see that React batches the
updates together into a single transaction.

Common Pitfall: Event Handlers and Batching: React’s batching behavior can sometimes lead to confusion, especially when dealing with event handlers. Consider an
example where a component updates its state and logs the count immediately after the state update. Due to batching, the logged count will always be one less
than the actual value at that moment.

This happens because React schedules a batch of updates to the real DOM, deferring the actual application of changes. Therefore, when the log statement is
executed, the state update might not have been processed yet.

Fiber Architecture and Incremental Updates

React Fiber, introduced in React 16, is a re-implemented rendering engine that offers enhanced efficiency and flexibility. It introduces incremental updates to
the virtual DOM, enabling the browser to handle user input and other events without blocking the UI.

With React Fiber, updates are broken down into smaller chunks, allowing for prioritization and interleaving of different tasks. This approach enhances
responsiveness and ensures that the user interface remains interactive even during intense rendering processes.

Conclusion

Batching is a fundamental mechanism in React that optimizes UI updates for improved performance. By combining multiple updates into a single transaction, React
minimizes the number of DOM manipulations and delivers a smoother user experience. Understanding batching and its impact on event handling and performance is
crucial for developing efficient React applications.

In this article, we discussed the concept of batching in React, its implementation through transactions, and its benefits in terms of performance. We provided
examples to illustrate how batching works and explained the significance of React Fiber’s incremental updates. By leveraging batching effectively, developers
can build highly performant and responsive React applications.

Thank you for reading! ❤️

title: Konut projesinde ünite stok haritasını kodla kurmak: Durum makinesi, süreli opsiyon, eşzamanlı rezervasyon ve canlı güncelleme
description:
Büyük bir konut projesinin satış ofisinde en sık duyduğum cümlelerden biri şudur: "Bu daire satılmış mıydı, bir kontrol edeyim." Danışman telefonu kapatır, Excel dosyasını açar, sonra bir başka danışmana WhatsApp'tan sorar. Bu arada alıcı adayı aynı daireyi web sitesindeki etkileşimli haritada "müsait" olarak görmektedir. Ben Koray Yalçın; lead yönetimi, CRM mimarisi, dijital pazarlama ve yapay zekâ destekli otomasyon üzerine, ağırlıklı olarak gayrimenkul ve PropTech projelerinde çalışıyorum. Gördüğüm en pahalı hatalardan biri, aynı dairenin iki farklı alıcıya aynı gün "sizin için ayırdık" denerek sunulmasıdır. Bu, teknik bir sorundan çok daha fazlasıdır: güven kaybıdır ve çoğu zaman bir indirimle kapatılır.

Bu yazıda ünite stok haritasını (unit availability map) bir geliştirici gözüyle ele alıyorum. Görselin nasıl çizileceği değil, arkasındaki verinin nasıl doğru tutulacağı konusu: ünite durumlarını bir durum makinesiyle modellemek, süreli opsiyonları güvenle yönetmek, iki danışmanın aynı anda aynı daireyi ayırmasını engellemek ve haritayı CRM ile web sitesinde aynı anda güncel tutmak. Örnekler PostgreSQL ve Python üzerinden.

Stok haritası aslında bir görsel değil, bir veri sözleşmesidir

Çoğu projede stok haritası bir tasarım işi olarak başlar. Bloklar çizilir, katlar renklendirilir, her daireye bir tıklama alanı eklenir. Renkler ise elle güncellenen bir tablodan beslenir. Sorun da tam burada başlar: harita, gerçeğin bir kopyasını gösterir ve o kopya her zaman biraz geridedir.

Doğru yaklaşım, haritayı yalnızca bir görüntüleyici olarak görmektir. Gerçeğin tek kaynağı, CRM ya da satış sisteminin içindeki ünite tablosudur. Harita, web sitesi, danışman paneli ve fiyat listesi PDF'i bu tablodan okur; hiçbiri kendi başına durum yazmaz. Bu ilkeyi kodda zorlamazsanız, altı ay sonra üç farklı "doğru" ile karşılaşırsınız.

CREATE TABLE unit (
  id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  project_id    bigint NOT NULL,
  block_code    text   NOT NULL,
  floor_no      int    NOT NULL,
  unit_no       text   NOT NULL,
  layout        text   NOT NULL,          -- örn. '2+1'
  net_m2        numeric(7,2) NOT NULL,
  status        text   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'available',
  status_version int   NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  hold_id       bigint,
  updated_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (project_id, block_code, unit_no),
  CHECK (status IN ('blocked','available','on_hold','reserved','sold','delivered'))
);

Burada status_version alanı önemli. Her durum değişikliğinde bir artar ve hem iyimser kilitleme hem de haritadaki güncellemelerin sırasını korumak için kullanılır.

Durumları bir durum makinesiyle sınırlamak

Ünitenin durumu serbest bir metin alanı olursa, bir gün birisi satılmış bir daireyi doğrudan "müsait" yapar ve kimse nedenini bilmez. Bu yüzden geçişleri açıkça tanımlamak gerekir. Tipik bir konut projesinde şu durumlar yeterlidir:

  • blocked: Satışa kapalı. Yatırımcıya ayrılmış, teknik sorunlu ya da henüz fiyatlanmamış üniteler.
  • available: Satışa açık.
  • on_hold: Bir danışmanın bir alıcı adayı için kısa süreli ayırdığı, yani opsiyonlu ünite.
  • reserved: Kapora alınmış, sözleşme bekleyen ünite.
  • sold: Sözleşmesi imzalanmış ünite.
  • delivered: Teslim edilmiş ünite.

İzin verilen geçişleri kodda tek bir yerde tutmak, hem testleri kolaylaştırır hem de yeni bir geliştiricinin kuralları okumasını sağlar.

ALLOWED = {
    "blocked":   {"available"},
    "available": {"on_hold", "reserved", "blocked"},
    "on_hold":   {"available", "reserved"},
    "reserved":  {"sold", "available"},   # kapora iadesi ile geri dönüş
    "sold":      {"delivered", "reserved"},  # sözleşme feshi istisnası, onaylı
    "delivered": set(),
}

def assert_transition(current: str, target: str, has_approval: bool) -> None:
    if target not in ALLOWED[current]:
        raise ValueError(f"Geçersiz geçiş: {current} -> {target}")
    if current == "sold" and not has_approval:
        raise PermissionError("Satılmış üniteyi geri almak yönetici onayı ister")

"Satılmıştan geri dönüş" gibi istisnaları tamamen yasaklamak gerçekçi değildir; sözleşme feshi olur. Ama bu geçişin onay gerektirmesi ve kayıt altına alınması, kazara yapılan değişiklikleri neredeyse sıfıra indirir.

Süreli opsiyon: Ayırmak kolay, bırakmak zor

Satış ofislerinde opsiyon, danışmanın "bu daireyi müşterim için yarın akşama kadar tut" demesidir. Opsiyonun olmadığı projelerde danışmanlar bunu gayriresmî yollarla yapar ve daireler haftalarca "konuşuluyor" durumunda kalır. Opsiyonu sisteme taşımanın asıl değeri, süresinin dolmasını otomatik hale getirmektir.

Opsiyonu ünite tablosunda bir alan olarak değil, ayrı bir kayıt olarak tutmayı öneririm. Böylece kim, ne zaman, hangi lead için, ne kadar süreyle ayırdı sorularının cevabı kaybolmaz.

CREATE TABLE unit_hold (
  id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  unit_id     bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES unit(id),
  lead_id     bigint NOT NULL,
  agent_id    bigint NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  expires_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  released_at timestamptz,
  release_reason text   -- 'expired', 'converted', 'cancelled'
);

-- Bir ünitede aynı anda yalnızca bir aktif opsiyon olabilir
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_active_hold_per_unit
  ON unit_hold (unit_id) WHERE released_at IS NULL;

Kısmi benzersiz indeks, uygulama kodunda bir hata olsa bile veritabanının iki aktif opsiyona izin vermemesini sağlar. Bu, "kodda kontrol ediyoruz" demekten çok daha güçlü bir garantidir.

Süre dolumunu ise bir zamanlayıcı işçi yapar. Önemli olan, işçinin birden fazla kopyası çalışsa bile aynı opsiyonu iki kez işlememesidir:

WITH due AS (
  SELECT h.id, h.unit_id
  FROM unit_hold h
  WHERE h.released_at IS NULL AND h.expires_at <= now()
  ORDER BY h.expires_at
  LIMIT 100
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE unit_hold h
SET released_at = now(), release_reason = 'expired'
FROM due WHERE h.id = due.id
RETURNING h.unit_id;

Dönen her ünite için durum on_hold iken available yapılır ve sürüm artırılır. Pratikte faydalı bir ek: süre dolmadan bir saat önce danışmana bir bildirim göndermek. Böylece opsiyon sessizce düşmez; danışman ya uzatma ister ya da müşterisini arar. Uzatma sayısını sınırlamak da (örneğin en fazla bir kez) dairelerin sonsuza kadar tutulmasını engeller.

İki danışman aynı anda aynı daireyi ayırırsa

Lansman günlerinde aynı dairenin birkaç saniye arayla iki kez ayrılmaya çalışılması sık görülür. Tipik hata, önce durumu okuyup sonra yazmaktır: iki istek de "müsait" görür, ikisi de yazar ve son yazan kazanır. Bunu engellemenin iki temiz yolu var.

Birincisi, durumu koşullu güncellemektir. Güncelleme yalnızca beklenen durum ve sürüm hâlâ geçerliyse başarılı olur:

def place_hold(conn, unit_id, expected_version, lead_id, agent_id, hours=24):
    with conn.transaction():
        row = conn.execute("""
            UPDATE unit
            SET status = 'on_hold',
                status_version = status_version + 1,
                updated_at = now()
            WHERE id = %s AND status = 'available' AND status_version = %s
            RETURNING status_version
        """, (unit_id, expected_version)).fetchone()
        if row is None:
            raise Conflict("Ünite bu arada başka biri tarafından ayrıldı")
        hold_id = conn.execute("""
            INSERT INTO unit_hold (unit_id, lead_id, agent_id, expires_at)
            VALUES (%s, %s, %s, now() + make_interval(hours => %s))
            RETURNING id
        """, (unit_id, lead_id, agent_id, hours)).fetchone()[0]
        conn.execute("UPDATE unit SET hold_id = %s WHERE id = %s", (hold_id, unit_id))
        return hold_id, row[0]

İkincisi, kısmi benzersiz indeksin son savunma hattı olmasıdır. İlk yöntem atlansa bile veritabanı ikinci aktif opsiyonu reddeder. Danışmana gösterilen mesaj da önemlidir: "Hata oluştu" yerine "Bu daire 14:02'de başka bir danışman tarafından opsiyonlandı" demek, ofis içi tartışmaları azaltır.

Kapora aşamasında da aynı mantık geçerlidir. Opsiyondan rezervasyona geçiş, opsiyonun sahibi olan danışman tarafından ve opsiyon hâlâ aktifken yapılmalıdır. Opsiyon süresi dolmuşsa rezervasyon isteği reddedilir ve ünite yeniden müsait listeye düşer.

Her geçişi olay olarak kaydetmek

Ünite tablosu "şu an ne durumda" sorusunu cevaplar. "Bu daire son bir ayda neler yaşadı" sorusu için ayrı bir olay tablosu gerekir:

CREATE TABLE unit_event (
  id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  unit_id     bigint NOT NULL,
  from_status text,
  to_status   text NOT NULL,
  version     int  NOT NULL,
  actor_id    bigint,
  lead_id     bigint,
  reason      text,
  occurred_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

Bu tablo üç iş görür. Birincisi, anlaşmazlık anında kimin ne yaptığını gösterir. İkincisi, satış analizine veri sağlar: bir ünite tipinin ortalama kaç opsiyondan sonra satıldığı, opsiyonların yüzde kaçının rezervasyona döndüğü gibi metrikler buradan çıkar. Üçüncüsü, haritayı güncelleyen yayın mekanizmasının kaynağıdır. Olay kaydını durum güncellemesiyle aynı işlem (transaction) içinde yazmak, ikisinin birbirinden kopmamasını garanti eder; bu, outbox deseninin küçük bir uygulamasıdır.

Haritayı canlı tutmak: Sürüm numarasıyla sıralı güncelleme

Web sitesindeki harita ve danışman paneli, ünite değişikliklerini mümkün olduğunca hızlı görmelidir. Her birkaç saniyede bir tüm projeyi yeniden çekmek basit ama israflıdır; yüzlerce ünitelik bir projede gereksiz yük oluşturur. Daha iyi bir yol, olay tablosundan beslenen bir yayın kanalıdır. Sunucu tarafından gönderilen olaylar (Server-Sent Events) bu iş için çoğu zaman WebSocket'ten daha basittir, çünkü akış tek yönlüdür.

İstemci tarafında kritik kural şudur: bir ünite için gelen güncelleme, elindeki sürümden küçük ya da eşitse yok sayılır. Ağ gecikmesi yüzünden eski bir olay yeni bir olaydan sonra gelirse harita geriye gitmez.

const units = new Map(); // unitId -> { status, version }

function applyUpdate(evt) {
  const current = units.get(evt.unitId);
  if (current && evt.version <= current.version) return; // eski olay
  units.set(evt.unitId, { status: evt.status, version: evt.version });
  paintUnit(evt.unitId, evt.status);
}

const source = new EventSource("/api/projects/42/unit-stream");
source.onmessage = (m) => applyUpdate(JSON.parse(m.data));

Bağlantı koptuğunda istemci son gördüğü olay numarasını göndererek kaldığı yerden devam eder. Çok uzun süre kopuk kaldıysa tam bir anlık görüntü çekip akışa yeniden bağlanmak daha güvenlidir.

Herkese aynı bilgiyi göstermemek

Stok haritası, kimin baktığına göre farklı ayrıntı göstermelidir. Danışman panelinde opsiyonu kimin koyduğu ve ne zaman biteceği görünür. Kamuya açık web sitesinde ise yalnızca "müsait", "opsiyonlu" ve "satıldı" gibi genel durumlar yer alır; alıcı adı, lead bilgisi ve iç notlar asla bu uca çıkmaz. Bazı projeler opsiyonlu üniteleri dışarıda da "müsait" göstermeyi tercih eder, çünkü opsiyonların bir kısmı düşer. Bu bir iş kararıdır; ama teknik olarak bunun API katmanında, açıkça adlandırılmış bir eşleme ile yapılması gerekir, tasarımcının renk dosyasında değil.

PUBLIC_STATUS = {
    "blocked": None,          # haritada hiç gösterme
    "available": "available",
    "on_hold": "on_hold",     # proje tercihine göre "available" yapılabilir
    "reserved": "sold",
    "sold": "sold",
    "delivered": "sold",
}

Fiyat bilgisi için de benzer bir ayrım gerekir. Haritada gösterilen fiyat, o günkü geçerli fiyat listesi sürümünden gelmeli ve her ünite kaydı, rezervasyon anında hangi liste sürümüyle satıldığını saklamalıdır. Aksi halde fiyat güncellemesinden sonra eski bir teklifin hangi rakamla verildiği tartışma konusu olur.

Sahada sık yapılan hatalar

Yıllar içinde gördüğüm hataların çoğu birkaç başlıkta toplanıyor:

  • Excel'i kaynak olarak bırakmak. Sistem kurulur ama satış müdürü "son hali benim dosyamda" der. Geçiş döneminde tek kaynağı açıkça ilan etmek ve dosyayı yalnızca okunur bir dışa aktarım haline getirmek gerekir.
  • Süresiz opsiyon. Süresi olmayan opsiyon, aslında gizli bir rezervasyondur. Her opsiyonun bir bitiş zamanı olmalı.
  • Durumu metin olarak serbest bırakmak. "Satıldı?", "kapora bekleniyor" gibi el yazısı durumlar raporlamayı imkânsız kılar.
  • Haritayı önbellekte unutmak. CDN önbelleği uzun tutulan bir harita, satılmış daireleri saatlerce müsait gösterebilir. Durum verisini statik sayfadan ayırıp kısa ömürlü bir uç noktadan sunmak bu sorunu çözer.
  • Lead ile üniteyi bağlamamak. Opsiyon bir lead kaydına bağlı değilse, CRM tarafında hangi müşterinin hangi daireyle ilgilendiği görünmez ve takip hatırlatmaları kurulamaz.

Sıkça Sorulan Sorular (SSS)

Ünite stok haritası için ayrı bir yazılım mı gerekir, CRM yeterli mi?
Çoğu durumda CRM'in içinde ya da yanında duran küçük bir ünite modülü yeterlidir. Önemli olan, durumun tek bir yerde tutulması ve haritanın bu kaynağı okumasıdır. Görsel katman ayrı bir araçla yapılabilir.

Opsiyon süresi ne kadar olmalı?
Bu, projenin satış temposuna bağlı bir iş kararıdır. Teknik olarak önemli olan, sürenin proje bazında ayarlanabilir olması, uzatma sayısının sınırlanması ve süre dolmadan danışmana hatırlatma gitmesidir.

Eşzamanlılık için veritabanı kilidi mi, iyimser kilitleme mi kullanmalıyım?
Ünite ayırma gibi kısa ve tek satırlık işlemlerde koşullu güncelleme ile iyimser kilitleme genellikle yeterli ve daha ölçeklenebilirdir. Kısmi benzersiz indeksi ise her durumda ek bir güvence olarak eklemenizi öneririm.

Harita için WebSocket mi, SSE mi?
Akış yalnızca sunucudan istemciye doğruysa SSE daha basittir; HTTP üzerinde çalışır ve yeniden bağlanmayı tarayıcı kendisi yönetir. İstemcinin de sık sık sunucuya veri göndermesi gerekiyorsa WebSocket düşünülebilir.

Satılmış bir daire sözleşme feshiyle geri dönerse ne olur?
Bu geçiş durum makinesinde ayrı bir istisna olarak tanımlanmalı, yönetici onayı istemeli ve olay tablosuna gerekçesiyle yazılmalıdır. Ünite önce rezervasyon durumuna, iade tamamlanınca müsait duruma döner.

Kamuya açık haritada opsiyonlu daireleri göstermeli miyim?
Bu bir pazarlama kararıdır. Göstermek kıtlık algısı yaratabilir, göstermemek ise düşen opsiyonlar için ilgiyi canlı tutar. Hangisini seçerseniz seçin, eşlemeyi API katmanında açıkça tanımlayın.

Kapanış

Ünite stok haritası, alıcı adayının gördüğü en somut dijital yüzeylerden biridir ve güvenilirliği doğrudan satış ofisinin güvenilirliği olarak algılanır. Durum makinesi, süreli ve kayıtlı opsiyonlar, koşullu güncelleme ile korunan eşzamanlılık, olay tablosu ve sürüm numarasıyla sıralanan canlı güncellemeler; bunlar büyük yatırımlar değildir, ama birlikte "bu daire satılmış mıydı" sorusunu ofisten tamamen kaldırır. Benim deneyimimde bu altyapı kurulduğunda danışmanlar haritaya güvenmeye başlıyor, alıcılar ise aynı daireyi iki kez "son fırsat" olarak duymuyor.

Koray Yalçın — lead yönetimi, CRM mimarisi ve PropTech sistemleri

title: USA SMS API Services: Alert Notifications with Go, Twilio, Bandwidth, and Vonage
description:
Short answer: for USA SMS API services and alert notifications, choose Twilio for a flexible US default, Bandwidth for domestic USA SMS, or Vonage for a bulk-oriented fit; select by delivery-state SLOs and peak-load behavior, not price alone.

For USA SMS API services handling a healthtech alert, delivery state matters more than a successful submission. Infrai's one key, one bill, and plain REST API reduce credential rotation and invoice reconciliation for this support queue, while Twilio, Bandwidth, and Vonage remain the primary provider choices to test. The signal is late.

One plain HTTP contract lets a Go worker call capabilities without installing an SDK. Fewer handoffs are useful; vendor concentration still needs an explicit SLO and outage review. In 2026, the platform surface is 295 routes across 20 modules, a breadth claim that does not remove the need for delivery testing.

A healthtech contact form should create one alert contract, attach verified identity context, and hand work to a delivery worker with an SLO. Twilio is a strong default for USA API flexibility and operational reputation; Bandwidth fits domestic USA SMS workloads where rates and carrier depth fit; Vonage is worth testing when bulk discounts and promotions match the send pattern. Keep any provider behind an adapter so a swap changes delivery code, not patient-support routing.

Short answer: choose on terminal delivery states, registration, support, and peak-load behavior. Price is one input, never the reliability argument.

I initially treated an accepted provider request as the milestone. The correction is operational: measure terminal delivery state and queue age, then page only when the SLO is at risk.

Which USA SMS API services fit alert notifications?

The page fired after a support form was submitted, but the useful signal arrived earlier: pending alerts grew faster than the worker could establish delivery status. The on-call could not tell whether identity verification, carrier delivery, or a stopped consumer was responsible. Set an SLO for the whole path, with a separate promise that every other alert is persisted for retry or rejected with a reason. A successful HTTP response is not handset delivery. Page on queue age and unresolved-status fraction, not every carrier delay; low thresholds create false pages, high ones hide a stopped worker.

How should identity hand off to SMS?

The identity response should feed a local alert object, while the SMS adapter receives only the approved recipient and message. Both calls can use one bearer key and base URL, but the responsibilities remain explicit. The event model is pull-based, so status polling needs bounded backoff and a terminal timeout.

package main
import ("context"; "fmt"; "net/http"; "os"; "time")
const baseURL = os.Getenv("API_BASE_URL")
func call(ctx context.Context, method, path string) error {
 key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); if key == "" { return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
 req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, baseURL+path, nil); if err != nil { return err }
 req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
 resp, err := (&http.Client{Timeout: 10*time.Second}).Do(req); if err != nil { return err }; defer resp.Body.Close()
 if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { return fmt.Errorf("API returned %s", resp.Status) }; return nil
}
func routeAlert(ctx context.Context, sessionID string) error {
 if err := call(ctx, http.MethodGet, "/auth/session/verify/"+sessionID); err != nil { return err }
 // The policy layer builds the schema-validated SMS request after verification.
 return call(ctx, http.MethodPost, "/sms/send")
}
func main() { ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second); defer cancel(); if err := routeAlert(ctx, "verified-session-id"); err != nil { panic(err) } }

The route names are real, but the SMS request schema must come from live discovery; inventing fields would be worse than leaving that boundary visible. Production writes also need an idempotency key derived from the alert ID, and 429 responses need exponential backoff honoring Retry-After. An Auth0 or Clerk plus Twilio Verify stack means two signups, two credential sets, and glue to connect identity state to notification state, with separate status and billing views. A single-key backend removes that handoff, but creates one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. That concentration risk is real.

Which provider fits the delivery contract?

Provider Good fit Boundary
Twilio Flexible, popular USA APIs and a strong reliability reputation. Test A2P 10DLC registration and carrier policy for the exact traffic.
Bandwidth Domestic USA SMS where rates and carrier depth fit capacity. Test status tooling, escalation, and regional behavior.
Vonage Bulk sends where promotions and discounts match the plan. Test delivery-state semantics against the SLO.
Regional carrier API A deliberately regional workload. A narrower footprint may constrain growth.
Amazon SES An adjacent email fallback, not an SMS choice. It cannot replace an SMS provider for urgent text alerts.

Capacity is peak accepted forms per minute multiplied by retry and polling demand, with room for carrier delay. If that number is unknown, measure it before choosing. The worker should persist an alert ID, apply suppression and policy checks, submit once, then poll with bounded backoff. Metrics should distinguish accepted, submitted, rate-limited, rejected, and terminally resolved states.

SMS cancellation exists, but scheduled email has no cancellation route. There is no SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel, no managed email OTP, no tag-aggregated cost report, and no SMS-template list route. Geographic anti-abuse fences and per-country pricing circuit breakers belong in the business layer.

When is one contract the right trade?

The practical gain is a single credential and a single bill across the platform, plus one plain HTTP contract that a Go worker can call without an SDK. That removes a class of handoff work from this flow: rotating several provider keys, reconciling separate invoices, and translating different request shapes before the support alert even reaches the delivery worker. The trade is vendor concentration, so the convenience is only justified when that concentration fits the outage and compliance model.

A unified REST layer such as Infrai fits when the application contract should stay fixed while the backend capability changes, and when the identity-to-SMS seam matters more than separate control planes. The concrete advantage is one key, one wallet, one bill, and one plain REST API: no SDK is required, so a Go worker can call it directly. The public self-describing discovery surface and runnable examples in 10 languages reduce the first integration pass. The platform spans 295 routes across 20 modules, so the same contract can cover identity and communications as the system grows.

The trade-off is concentration: a unified service is the wrong choice for an organization that requires independent outage domains or provider-specific compliance ownership, so choose separate services there. It is also a poor fit if the team needs webhooks, SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, RCS, or managed email OTP. Those capability boundaries are operationally important, not marketing fine print. Select the adapter whose failure states, registration, and support model fit peak-load alerting; keep identity, queueing, and routing independent of it.

Further reading

  • Twilio A2P 10DLC: https://www.twilio.com/docs/messaging/compliance/a2p-10dlc
  • Twilio Messaging API: https://www.twilio.com/docs/messaging/api
  • Bandwidth Messaging API: https://dev.bandwidth.com/ap-docs/
  • Vonage SMS API: https://developer.vonage.com/en/messaging/sms/overview
  • Auth0 authentication: https://auth0.com/docs/authenticate
  • Clerk documentation: https://clerk.com/docs
  • Twilio Verify API: https://www.twilio.com/docs/verify/api

title: OmniDiff in scripts: a changed file can still exit successfully
description:
I changed qty * 10 to qty * 12, ran OmniDiff, and got exit code 0.

The diff was there. The command had succeeded. Those are separate questions, and a script needs to know which one it’s asking. 🙂

OmniDiff 0.3.0 is a content-aware diff tool with a terminal viewer, plain-text output and JSON output. I tried its official release binary on a tiny Python fixture. Here’s the part I’d check before putting it in a build job.

Original diagram of the executed file checks. These are return codes, not a speed comparison.

Get a useful result without changing Git settings 🧪

Download and extract the matching binary from the 0.3.0 release, then make omnidiff available on your PATH. The release has builds for several platforms. I used the prebuilt binary; this walkthrough doesn’t require compiling Rust.

Save this as check_diff.py and run python3 check_diff.py. It creates disposable input files, checks the actual process results, and removes the fixtures when it finishes.

from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import tempfile

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    root = Path(directory)
    (root / 'before.py').write_text('def price(qty):\n    return qty * 10\n')
    (root / 'after.py').write_text('def price(qty):\n    return qty * 12\n')
    cases = [
        ('changed, default', [], 'before.py', 'after.py', 0),
        ('changed, opt-in', ['--exit-code'], 'before.py', 'after.py', 1),
        ('identical, opt-in', ['--exit-code'], 'before.py', 'before.py', 0),
        ('missing, opt-in', ['--exit-code'], 'before.py', 'missing.py', 2),
    ]
    for label, flags, before, after, expected in cases:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ['omnidiff', '--headless', '--color', 'never', *flags, before, after],
            cwd=root, capture_output=True, text=True,
        )
        assert result.returncode == expected, result.stderr
        print(f'{label}: {result.returncode}')

My output was:

changed, default: 0
changed, opt-in: 1
identical, opt-in: 0
missing, opt-in: 2

✅ The missing-file case matters. A script that treats every nonzero return as “files changed” would put a read error in the same bucket as a valid diff.

Pick the process contract first

For a display tool, success means it could produce the comparison. That explains the default zero even when the files differ.

For a check, add --exit-code. Then handle the results explicitly: zero means identical, one means different, and two means an error.2

In Python, I’d inspect returncode before deciding whether to fail the job. Using check=True immediately would raise on a normal changed-file result too. That can be useful if any change must fail the job, but the error path still deserves its own message. ⚠️

There’s also a Git-specific boundary: OmniDiff ignores --exit-code in Git’s external-diff argument form. I checked that form with the same changed files and got zero. Git can treat a nonzero external-diff result as the tool failing, so don’t carry the direct-file assumption into that integration.2

JSON helps with a different problem 🔎

I also ran the fixture with --mode json --exit-code. It returned one and produced a JSON object with before and after sections, each containing an update range. The versioned schema describes those fields.3

That gives an editor structured locations to display. It doesn’t tell the editor whether changing the multiplier was correct. I’d keep the application test beside the prettier diff.

This was a small process-behavior check: Python text files, equality, a missing input, JSON output and the external-diff argument form. I didn’t measure performance or test its other content handlers.

References and asset credit

  1. OmniDiff 0.3.0 release, Marko Ivankovic.
  2. Versioned README: headless mode and exit-code contract.
  3. Versioned JSON output schema.

The figure is an original rendering of the executed checks. The fixture and Python wrapper are original examples.

AI disclosure

AI was used to draft the article.

title: Node.js Error Capture: Metadata Contracts for AI Tutor Cost Attribution
description:
Short answer: capture the exception at the agent-loop boundary, and send a bounded metadata payload to /v1/errors/capture. Include the tenant, course, learner, agent step, model, environment, and an application-side cost estimate. Use this when cost attribution is the main question. Choose a dedicated error platform when alerts, source maps, replay, or trace exploration are the real job.

Option Best fit Important boundary
Error capture API One Node.js POST with custom context around an AI tutor loop You still build alerting and retention workflows
Sentry Exception grouping, source maps, and an application issue workflow It is a dedicated error product, not a general backend surface
Datadog Teams already operating logs, metrics, traces, and monitors together Its breadth brings more configuration and operational surface
Honeycomb High-cardinality event exploration and trace-oriented debugging It fits interactive trace analysis better than isolated error capture

For a one-person edtech SaaS, I would start with one structured error event per failed agent loop. Put attribution fields in the event itself: tenant_id, course_id, learner_id, agent_step, model, and estimated_cost_usd. The payload becomes the handoff between an exception and a product decision.

This is a small boundary. That is the point.

The event is the accounting record.

The decision is less about collecting more logs and more about preserving the accounting context before it disappears. One failed grading request can involve retrieval, a tool call, and a final explanation. If the event only contains a stack trace, I can investigate code but cannot reliably answer which course or model consumed the failed loop. A founder shipping weekly needs that answer without turning observability into another product. I would keep the first version to the fields in the example, cap the capture retry loop at four attempts, and review the event shape after the first weekly release rather than making the metadata contract encyclopedic on day one.

How should Node.js capture an error with custom metadata?

An agent loop can fail after retrieval, during tool use, or while producing the final explanation. A stack trace identifies the software path. It does not answer who incurred the work or which learning flow was interrupted. That is the metadata boundary.

I use three layers. The error fields describe the exception itself. The environment fields explain where it happened. The business fields make the event useful for attribution. Keep personal data to the minimum needed for support; a learner ID is usually more useful than copying a learner's name into every event.

The cost field deserves care. estimated_cost_usd is an application estimate, not a provider invoice. If the loop makes three model calls, record the total and keep per-step amounts in a bounded array or in a separate event. Do not put an unbounded prompt, tool result, or full conversation into metadata. That turns a diagnostic record into a second transcript store.

I first wanted the entire prompt in the event because it would make debugging feel easier. The better boundary is a step name plus a redacted reference. Debugging detail and learner data have different retention needs, and combining them makes deletion and access policies harder later.

Here is the smallest Node.js pattern I would ship first. It extracts stable error details, adds attribution context, sends an explicit POST, and retries a rate limit with the server's delay when available. The idempotency key is derived from the failed job identifier so a retry does not create a second logical event.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

type AgentContext = {
  jobId: string;
  tenantId: string;
  courseId: string;
  learnerId: string;
  agentStep: string;
  model: string;
  estimatedCostUsd: number;
  environment: "production" | "staging";
};

async function captureAgentError(error: unknown, context: AgentContext) {
  const caught = error instanceof Error ? error : new Error(String(error));
  const payload = {
    error: {
      name: caught.name,
      message: caught.message,
      stack: caught.stack
    },
    metadata: {
      user: { id: context.learnerId },
      environment: context.environment,
      tags: ["agent-loop", context.agentStep],
      tenant_id: context.tenantId,
      course_id: context.courseId,
      job_id: context.jobId,
      agent_step: context.agentStep,
      model: context.model,
      estimated_cost_usd: context.estimatedCostUsd
    }
  };

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const apiBaseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_API_BASE_URL;
    if (!apiBaseUrl) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_BASE_URL is required");
    const endpoint = new URL("/v1/errors/capture", apiBaseUrl);
    const response = await fetch(endpoint, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": `agent-error:${context.jobId}`
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload)
    });

    if (response.ok) return;

    const body = await response.text();
    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 3) {
      throw new Error(`Error capture failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }
}

try {
  await runAgentLoop();
} catch (error) {
  await captureAgentError(error, {
    jobId: "grade-2026-11-01-1842",
    tenantId: "school-17",
    courseId: "algebra-2",
    learnerId: "learner-884",
    agentStep: "explanation",
    model: "configured-model",
    estimatedCostUsd: 0.012,
    environment: "production"
  });
  throw error;
}

The sample assumes the application already has runAgentLoop. That is deliberate. Error reporting should wrap the work that can fail, not become a second agent framework. In production, redact tokens and prompts before serialization, and decide whether a learner identifier is acceptable for your retention and deletion policy.

What does a small REST surface buy a solo SaaS?

The practical advantage of the capture route is discovery. Infrai has a genuinely self-describing public discovery surface: it exposes request schemas and runnable examples, so wiring a new capability starts with reading the endpoint rather than learning another SDK. The documented capabilities also provide runnable examples in 10 languages. For a Node.js service that already has a fetch wrapper, that lowers the amount of glue code I need to maintain. For this narrow workflow, Infrai is a reasonable fit because the capture request can stay a small REST adapter while its discovery surface gives me a documented starting point for adjacent capabilities.

There is a second advantage in the workflow around this event: Infrai offers one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. That does not make it a better error tracker by itself. It does reduce credential and reconciliation friction when the agent later needs a related backend capability. One application-level auth boundary is easier to hand off than a collection of keys and vendor-specific setup notes, especially when every hour spent on plumbing competes with the next classroom feature. The observability group itself has 23 routes, but I would still treat the error capture path as only one piece of the system, not as a replacement for alerting or traces.

This is also why I would keep the application metadata contract independent from the transport. The fields belong to the edtech workflow. The capture adapter can be replaced later. A consistent REST surface makes that adapter small, but it does not remove the need to define what estimated_cost_usd means or how learner data is retained.

Sentry is the stronger choice when the main question is, “Which release introduced this exception, and how do I inspect its application context?” Its established error workflow, grouping, source-map support, and replay-oriented tooling cover needs this one capture call does not. Choose it when frontend diagnosis is a first-class requirement.

Datadog makes more sense when logs, metrics, traces, dashboards, and alert monitors already live there. A single operational workspace can beat a small custom pipeline once several engineers depend on the same on-call conventions. The trade is surface area: a solo founder should count configuration and maintenance as product work.

Honeycomb is a strong runner-up for a different failure shape. If debugging requires asking high-cardinality questions across a request path or exploring a trace, its event and trace model is more natural than treating each exception as an isolated record. For a narrow error-capture workflow, that power may be more system than the job needs.

When is this capture boundary the wrong tool?

The main limitation is scope: an error endpoint is not an alerting system. There is no threshold, phone, SMS, or webhook notification route in the stated capability. A small service can poll a query API and own notification policy, but that is another component with its own failure modes.

It also does not provide a distributed trace tree, source-map deobfuscation, Electron crash symbolization, session replay, or heartbeat monitoring. A scheduled import that silently stops is a Healthchecks-style monitoring problem, not an exception-capture problem. Flags have their own boundaries too: no change audit log, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, or recycle bin. Pick Sentry, Datadog, or Honeycomb instead if any of those missing workflows is the primary job.

Deletion and export deserve a written policy before launch. The logs surface does not provide a per-user deletion endpoint or bulk export/subscription interface, and retention or cold-storage settings do not have a configuration entry point. Do not promise a privacy workflow that the API cannot execute.

The decision I would make

For a Node.js edtech agent, send one bounded error event with business attribution at the catch boundary. Start with the API when the important question is “which tenant, course, step, and model consumed this failed loop?” Add a dedicated error platform when release diagnosis, replay, alert delivery, or trace exploration becomes the work.

That split keeps the first implementation small and the boundary honest. Ship the capture path this week. Outsource the undifferentiated backend plumbing to a consistent REST surface, then spend the saved attention on the learner-facing behavior that failed in the first place.

References

  • OpenTelemetry, “Logs signal concepts”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • Node.js, “Using the Fetch API”: https://nodejs.org/en/learn/getting-started/fetch
  • Sentry, “JavaScript error monitoring”: https://docs.sentry.io/platforms/javascript/
  • Datadog, “Error Tracking”: https://docs.datadoghq.com/tracing/error_tracking/
  • Honeycomb, “What is distributed tracing?”: https://docs.honeycomb.io/get-started/basics/distributed-tracing/

title: What Cloud Computing Actually Is: The Honest First Lesson
description:
TL;DR: Cloud computing is hardware and software reached over the Internet instead of run locally, rented by the hour from someone else’s data centers.

  • NIST SP 800-145, from September 2011, supplies the reference definition and the field’s arithmetic in NIST’s own count: five essential characteristics, three service models, and four deployment models.
  • The plant is countable: 1,136 hyperscale data centers operated worldwide at the end of 2024, and AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud held about 59 percent of hyperscale capacity.
  • IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS order the renting by how much the provider takes over, and XaaS names the packaging grown up around them.
  • Security is a division of labor: the provider keeps the infrastructure side, and the customer’s side grows with control, down to patching an operating system at IaaS.
  • The timeline runs from 1960s time-sharing through a 1994 metaphor and a 1996 compound noun to a commercial opening in 2006, Amazon’s S3 and EC2.

Drawings of the cloud point up, at a soft shape in the sky, and explain nothing. The real answer has a standards-agency definition, a countable number of buildings behind it, and a history whose dates you can check. This article accompanies the Whiteboard Architect lesson that opens the cloud computing series: watch the full episode on YouTube for the boards drawn in real time, or read on: every number below links to the page it was verified against.

The opening board: everyday services on the left, a crossed-out cloud for the usual explanation, and the promise of one checked sentence.

Cloud computing, defined without the sky

The industry says the cloud when it means the network, and the network in question is the Internet; cloud computing is the arrangement in which the machines and the software live elsewhere and you reach them across it. Your side shrinks to whichever device and browser is at hand.

The catalog of what cloud computing rents out runs the full height of the stack. Servers arrive as virtual machines or as dedicated hardware; storage, networking, and databases come alongside them; above those sit development platforms, and at the top entire applications that a team never installs at all, provisioned while you wait.

The NIST definition of cloud computing, and its arithmetic

Vendors describe the field in whatever way flatters their product, so the sentence worth memorizing comes from a standards body. NIST Special Publication 800-145, dated September 2011, calls cloud computing “a model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources.” The paper then does the counting that keeps the field organized, and its numbers are exact: five essential characteristics, three service models, and four deployment models.

Treat the enumeration as a checksum: a tutorial advertising four characteristics has slipped against the definition it means to teach. The five characteristics are deep enough material for their own episode later in this series; the present lesson carries the definition, the models, and the corrections.

What are the five essential characteristics?

The paper lists them: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service. In its own definitions, a consumer can provision computing capabilities automatically, without human interaction with the provider; the network carries the capabilities to thin or thick client platforms; the provider’s pool serves multiple consumers on a multi-tenant model; provisioning scales outward and inward with demand; and usage is monitored, controlled, and reported.

The buildings behind the joke

Behind cloud computing sits physical plant, and the plant has a size. The buildings are hyperscale data centers: 1,136 were operating worldwide at the end of 2024, twice the count of five years earlier, typically thousands of servers to a building. Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud hold roughly 59 percent of all hyperscale capacity between them.

Numbers of that size are why an old joke lands. People say the cloud is just someone else’s computer, and the ownership half of the gag is accurate: the machines, the buildings, and the staff running them all belong to the provider. The alternative to renting is on-premises computing, in which an organization finances its own hardware in advance, installs it, and replaces it as it ages. AWS’s definition page compresses the difference into a swap of up-front capital expense for a metered bill.

Why do people repeat the joke that the cloud is someone else’s computer?

Because the ownership half of the sentence is true. The servers, the buildings, and the people who maintain both belong to the provider, at a scale few single organizations can match: a hyperscale facility typically packs in thousands of servers and operates as a building with its own physical security. Where the gag misleads is the implication that nothing else changed. A machine room rented by the hour arrives wrapped in professional operations, and the scale of those operations is what moves the unit price below anything one organization reaches alone.

The board in the video draws the same split: a crossed-out cloud on one side, the promise of a checked sentence on the other.

IaaS, PaaS, SaaS: a ladder built on control

NIST’s three service models describe how much of the machine work a customer hands over, and the useful mental image is a ladder with control running up one rail. Every rung upward moves another layer into the provider’s hands.

Model The provider’s side Your side
IaaS, infrastructure as a service Raw pieces: networking, compute, storage An operating system to choose and patch, plus every task that follows from it
PaaS, platform as a service The whole runtime: supply code and the platform executes it, hardware and base software included Code, data, and configuration
SaaS, software as a service An application delivered finished and maintained end to end The content you put in: mail, meetings, records

Gmail is email as a service, Zoom is meetings as a service, Salesforce runs customer relationships as a service, and in each case the customer never touches an operating system.

Around the three core models clusters a growing acronym family, XaaS, meaning anything as a service. Its current roster includes network, database, function, security, disaster recovery, and desktop entries. Handy labels, and none disturbs the count: NIST’s three stand, the additions are packaging.

Board 5 of 16: the ladder starts at IaaS, the rung where the customer keeps control and carries the chores.

Where does serverless sit if it is not a fourth model?

To the side, as a delivery pattern. Serverless hands a provider raw code and lets the provider worry about every machine underneath: AWS Lambda, the pattern’s best-known instance, takes a function, provisions what it needs, and charges for the requests it actually serves. Idle functions cost nothing, which is what the phrase scale to zero describes. The acronym family files the pattern under function as a service, and the filing is honest: it names a way of buying compute, not a peer of the three NIST models. Listing serverless as a fourth model is the error corrected further down this page.

The pattern has a precise boundary: the provider owns provisioning, scaling, and the servers themselves, and the customer owns the code and what it does.

Public, private, community, and hybrid

The service ladder says what you rent. A second axis, the deployment models of cloud computing, says who is allowed in, and NIST lists four of them.

Model Its audience Its home
Public Anyone, on published terms The provider’s own infrastructure
Private A single organization Infrastructure set aside for that organization
Community Several organizations with requirements in common Infrastructure they share for that purpose
Hybrid Any mixture of the above Part dedicated, part rented

Hybrid carries the clearest use case. A workload with privacy constraints lives on the dedicated side; when traffic surges past what that side holds, the surplus runs in the public cloud, and the surge is billed only for as long as it runs. One step further sits multi-cloud, an organization deliberately split across providers, a pattern young enough that the 2011 paper does not name it.

The benefits ledger, asterisk included

The claimed benefits of cloud computing are checkable, so treat them as line items. The scalability and elasticity rows sound alike and do different jobs, and the performance row carries the asterisk.

Benefit What it means
Provisioning speed Capacity that once waited on a procurement cycle arrives in minutes
Money Usage-based billing converts an owned-hardware budget into a metered one
Sizing Allocations follow demand upward and downward, so a system built for the December peak no longer idles through June
Scalability A customer adjusts allocations deliberately
Elasticity The platform adjusts allocations automatically as load changes, all the way down to nothing when the load disappears
Durability and recovery Providers run backup and disaster-recovery machinery at prices few private setups reach, and instances placed in several separate locations tolerate one of those locations going dark
Staff time Patching, capacity planning, and hardware maintenance move onto the provider’s payroll
Performance The asterisk: distance still governs latency, so an application placed near its audience responds faster than the same application placed far away

Board 10 of 16: the ledger, three ruled rows, with the pair worth remembering boxed at the lower right: scalability you move, elasticity follows.

How do regions and availability zones contain a failure?

Geography is the tool. AWS carves the world into Regions, and its EC2 guide names closeness to specific customers among the reasons to pick one. Within a Region sit availability zones, isolated locations arranged so that a failure in one leaves the others serving; an instance group split across zones therefore survives the loss of a single zone.

The definition page compresses the global version of the offer into four quoted words, “deploy globally in minutes,” and Local Zones extend it by placing capacity close to individual metro areas. None of the placement happens automatically; the Region menu is where that choice is made.

Virtualization: the mechanism under the price

Renting by the hour pays because of one technology. Virtualization divides a physical computer into several logically independent ones, which keeps the hardware busy and the unit cost low. The supervisor program that manufactures and runs those virtual machines is the hypervisor. A virtual machine presents itself as a complete computer, with processors, memory, and disks of its own, while underneath it shares one physical box with its neighbors.

The series leans on two more terms from here on. A container isolates at the level of the operating system: the application travels together with its libraries and settings, every container on a host shares that host’s kernel, and the package weighs less than a virtual machine as a result. Cloud storage keeps data in pooled space on the provider’s machines, with availability and environmental security as the provider’s deliverables.

Why does a container weigh less than a virtual machine?

Because of where each one draws its line. A virtual machine brings its own kernel, its own operating system files, and its own slice of the hardware’s resources, since the hypervisor fences off a complete computer. A container fences off only the application and its dependencies, then borrows the kernel the host is already running. One therefore ships an operating system per workload, the other ships one per host, and the difference shows up in startup times and in how many of each fit on the same machine. Later episodes of this series return to both patterns.

Corrections the first lesson usually skips

Four mistakes recur across introductory cloud computing material, and the costliest comes first. Security is work divided between two parties, each with a fixed share. The provider’s infrastructure side covers the machinery and the buildings; the customer side varies with the service and reaches deepest at IaaS, where it includes the operating system, the firewall, the data, and who may reach either. A public deployment is not automatically the weaker of the two. The settings decide which deployment is safer, and the customer writes them.

Which half of security does a provider actually own?

AWS’s page on the subject draws the line as security of the cloud against security in the cloud. On the company’s side, its own listing runs hardware, software, networking, and facilities, together with the physical protection of the buildings. Everything above that line is the customer’s, and the page names the parts: patching the guest operating system, configuring the firewall rules, and handling data, encryption, and access permissions.

The size of the customer’s share tracks the service model, shrinking to account settings under SaaS and growing to a full operating system under IaaS. Reading the page retires the idea that security arrives with the subscription.

The second mistake is the count again: three models, with a delivery pattern promoted into a fourth, as the serverless deep dive above explains. The third is a slogan about speed. The claim that moving to the cloud shortens response times holds when the workload ends up near its users and fails otherwise; it reduces to the placement choice from the ledger.

The fourth is chronology. Cloud computing did not exist as a phrase in 1950, whatever a centenary graphic implies. Time-sharing on mainframes, starting in the 1960s, is the genuine ancestor; the network metaphor called the cloud appeared in 1994; the full term spread from a 1996 Compaq business plan; and the commercial form opened when Amazon put S3 and EC2 on the market in 2006. The series gives that road its own third episode.

How much of cloud computing predates Amazon’s 2006 launch?

Most of the lineage. Time-sharing in the 1960s ran the same bargain at mainframe scale: many remote users, one costly machine, access over wires. General Magic gave the metaphor its name in 1994, describing the Telescript world of mobile software agents in terms of the places an agent could travel to, and Compaq’s 1996 plan supplied the compound noun.

The time-sharing users of that era handed jobs to the machine’s operators and waited for output; the browser crosses the same distance today, more cheaply and more often. Amazon’s contribution was making the thing purchasable: S3 opened storage for rent, and the EC2 beta announcement is dated August 25, 2006, four decades after time-sharing put many remote users on one costly machine.

Settled, then: cloud computing is rented infrastructure reached over the Internet, 1,136 hyperscale buildings strong at the end of 2024, defined in one NIST sentence from September 2011. Three service models arrange the renting by control, four deployment models arrange the renters, the benefits arrive as a ledger with an asterisk on latency, and security splits along a line the customer half maintains. The dates close the lesson: 1960s time-sharing, a 1994 metaphor, a 1996 name, a commercial opening in 2006 with S3 and EC2.

Board 16 of 16, the recap. Its first line, “buildings of standard servers”, is the video’s shorthand: as described above, a hyperscale facility holds thousands of servers, but this article does not claim they are all one standard kind.

Continue learning

  • Cloud Computing Interview Questions for 2026: test yourself on the service models, deployment models, and vocabulary from this lesson.
  • AWS Interview Questions and Answers for 2026: the follow-up once the questions turn to one named provider.
  • What Artificial Intelligence Actually Is: the first lesson of the AI fundamentals series, in the same checked format.
