title: SaaS Usage-Based Billing & Metering Architecture: Event Ingestion, Rollups & Stripe Invoicing
description:
The most common usage-billing design I see in SaaS codebases sends one Stripe API call per customer request. It works in staging. In production it runs into rate limits during traffic spikes, double-counts usage whenever a queue job retries, and cannot answer the question every finance team eventually asks: "Show me exactly which events make up this invoice line." The billing code is short. The cleanup is not.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every command and claim myself against Stripe's current API reference. I run Loop Origin, where we build custom SaaS platforms in Laravel, Node.js and .NET, and metered billing for AI and API products comes up often. This post is the architecture I use: durable event ingestion, hourly rollups you own, and a thin, idempotent reporter to Stripe Billing Meters.

📚 Series Roadmap — Production AI & SaaS Systems Engineering

  • Part 1: Building Production MCP Servers & Tool-Calling AI Agents: Sandboxing, Schemas & Approval Gates
  • Part 2: Zero-Downtime Database Migrations in Laravel & Node.js SaaS: Expand-Contract & Lock Timeouts
  • Part 3: Multi-Tier Caching & Stampede Protection with Redis/Valkey: Singleflight Locks & SWR
  • Part 4 (This Post): SaaS Usage-Based Billing & Metering Architecture: Event Ingestion, Rollups & Stripe Invoicing
  • Part 5: Production Observability on a Budget: OpenTelemetry Traces, Structured Logs & Tail Sampling
  • Part 6: LLM Gateway & FinOps Architecture for B2B SaaS: Semantic Caching, Routing & Tenant Quotas

How should a SaaS product architect usage-based billing with Stripe?

Direct answer: Record every billable action as an immutable event in your own database with a unique idempotency key, roll events up per tenant, meter and hour, then report each rollup (or its delta) to Stripe Billing Meters with a deterministic identifier. Your ledger stays the source of truth; Stripe aggregates, prices and invoices.

What changed in Stripe, and why it matters

If you built metered billing before 2025, you probably used usage records on subscription items. Stripe removed legacy usage-based billing in API version 2025-03-31.basil: metered prices now must be backed by a Meter, and usage is reported as meter events to POST /v1/billing/meter_events. A few properties of that API shape the whole design:

  • Each event carries an event_name, a payload with stripe_customer_id and value, an optional timestamp and an optional identifier.
  • Stripe enforces identifier uniqueness within a rolling period of at least 24 hours. That protects you from quick retries, not from a job that re-runs tomorrow.
  • timestamp must be within the past 35 calendar days and no more than 5 minutes in the future.
  • In live mode the endpoint allows 1,000 calls per second per account, and only one concurrent call per customer per meter.
  • Processing is asynchronous. Invalid events surface later as v1.billing.meter.error_report_triggered events, not as HTTP errors.
  • Usage must arrive before the invoice for that period finalizes. Late events can be accepted without being added to an already-finalized invoice.

The last three points are why "call Stripe on every request" fails in production. The 24-hour dedupe window is why Stripe cannot be your only defense against double billing.


AI-generated image.

The architecture 

 App / API / AI worker
        │  (same DB transaction as the business action)
        ▼
 usage_events  (append-only, UNIQUE(tenant_id, idempotency_key))
        │  every 5 min
        ▼
 usage_rollups (tenant, meter, hour) ── quantity, reported_quantity
        │  reporter job, serialized per customer + meter
        ▼
 Stripe Billing Meter events ──► meter-backed Price ──► Invoice
        │
        └──► nightly reconciliation against meter event summaries

1. Ingest: one immutable row per billable action

Write the usage event in the same transaction as the work it bills for. If the AI completion is saved, the usage is saved. If the transaction rolls back, nothing is billed.

CREATE TABLE usage_events (
  id               bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id        bigint      NOT NULL,
  meter            text        NOT NULL,          -- 'ai_tokens', 'api_calls'
  quantity         numeric(20,6) NOT NULL CHECK (quantity >= 0),
  occurred_at      timestamptz NOT NULL,
  idempotency_key  text        NOT NULL,          -- e.g. request id + step
  properties       jsonb       NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, idempotency_key)
);
CREATE INDEX ON usage_events (meter, occurred_at);

// Node.js (pg-promise): record usage after the model call succeeds
await db.tx(async (t) => {
  await t.none('INSERT INTO completions(id, tenant_id, output) VALUES ($1,$2,$3)',
    [completionId, tenantId, output]);
  await t.none(`INSERT INTO usage_events
      (tenant_id, meter, quantity, occurred_at, idempotency_key, properties)
    VALUES ($1, 'ai_tokens', $2, now(), $3, $4)
    ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, idempotency_key) DO NOTHING`,
    [tenantId, usage.total_tokens, `completion:${completionId}`, { model }]);
});

ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING makes retries harmless. The idempotency key must come from the business action (completion ID, request ID plus step), never from uuid() at insert time, or every retry becomes new revenue and a future refund.

2. Roll up: hourly buckets you can recompute 

-- usage_rollups has UNIQUE (tenant_id, meter, hour)
INSERT INTO usage_rollups (tenant_id, meter, hour, quantity)
SELECT tenant_id, meter, date_trunc('hour', occurred_at), sum(quantity)
FROM usage_events
WHERE occurred_at >= now() - interval '48 hours'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, meter, hour)
DO UPDATE SET quantity = EXCLUDED.quantity, updated_at = now();

Recomputing a 48-hour window each run absorbs late events from mobile clients and delayed queues. The rollup table also powers the customer's usage dashboard, so you never query Stripe to render a chart. If you are adding these tables to a live database, the expand-contract approach from Part 2 applies.

3. Report: deltas with deterministic identifiers

The reporter sends only what Stripe has not seen yet. Because the meter uses sum, a late correction is just another positive event:

// Laravel job, one per tenant + meter
public function middleware(): array
{
    return [(new WithoutOverlapping("meter:{$this->tenantId}:{$this->meter}"))->releaseAfter(30)];
}

public function handle(StripeClient $stripe): void
{
    UsageRollup::where('tenant_id', $this->tenantId)
        ->where('meter', $this->meter)
        ->whereColumn('quantity', '>', 'reported_quantity')
        ->where('hour', '>=', now()->subDays(30))
        ->lazyById(200)
        ->each(function (UsageRollup $r) use ($stripe) {
            $delta = bcsub($r->quantity, $r->reported_quantity, 6);
            $version = $r->report_version + 1;

            $stripe->billing->meterEvents->create([
                'event_name' => $this->meter,
                'identifier' => "{$r->tenant_id}:{$r->meter}:{$r->hour->timestamp}:v{$version}",
                'timestamp'  => $r->hour->timestamp,
                'payload'    => [
                    'stripe_customer_id' => $r->tenant->stripe_customer_id,
                    'value'              => $delta,
                ],
            ]);

            $r->update(['reported_quantity' => $r->quantity, 'report_version' => $version]);
        });
}

Three details matter here. WithoutOverlapping keyed by tenant and meter respects Stripe's one-concurrent-call-per-customer-per-meter limit. The identifier is deterministic, so a crash between the API call and the update() produces a duplicate that Stripe rejects within its dedupe window. The 30-day cutoff keeps timestamps safely inside Stripe's 35-day window. Run these jobs on a dedicated queue with retries and backoff; my notes on running Laravel queues in production cover the Supervisor and failed-job side.

To reverse a wrong event, Stripe offers POST /v1/billing/meter_event_adjustments with type=cancel and the event's identifier. I use it only for mistakes; normal corrections go through the delta path.

4. Reconcile: trust, then verify

Every night, compare your rollups with GET /v1/billing/meters/{id}/event_summaries?customer=...&value_grouping_window=hour. Reporting each event with the hour-start timestamp makes Stripe's hourly buckets line up exactly with yours. Alert on any hour where they differ, and subscribe to the meter error events so a missing stripe_customer_id mapping does not silently drop a tenant's usage.

Choosing an ingestion strategy

Approach Throughput to Stripe Duplicate protection Audit trail Invoice freshness When I use it
Per-request meter event Up to 1,000 calls/s per account, 1 concurrent per customer/meter Stripe identifier only (≥24h window) Only in Stripe Near real time Prototypes, low volume
Hourly rollup + deltas (this post) A few calls per tenant per hour Your unique keys plus Stripe identifier Full, in your DB Within the hour Most B2B SaaS and AI products
v2 meter event streams Up to 10,000 events/s (live mode), 15-minute session tokens Stripe identifier plus your own Only in Stripe unless you also store events Near real time Very high-volume event billing
Own rating engine, Stripe for invoices only One invoice item per period Fully yours Full End of period Complex contracts, credits, committed spend

Pre-launch checklist

  1. Every billable action writes exactly one event with a business-derived idempotency key.
  2. Usage is written in the same transaction as the work it bills.
  3. Rollups are recomputable from raw events for any past window.
  4. Reporter calls are serialized per customer and meter, with deterministic identifiers.
  5. No usage timestamp is older than 30 days when reported.
  6. Usage for a period is reported before the invoice finalizes; you know your grace period.
  7. Nightly reconciliation against meter event summaries, with alerts.
  8. Meter error events are subscribed to and routed to on-call.
  9. Raw events are retained long enough to answer invoice disputes.

FAQ

Should I send raw events or aggregates to Stripe?

For most products, aggregates. Stripe recommends pre-aggregating if you approach the rate limits, and aggregates keep your API calls proportional to tenants, not traffic. Keep raw events in your database for audits.

Why not rely on Stripe's identifier for idempotency?

Because uniqueness is only guaranteed for a rolling period of at least 24 hours. A backfill or replayed job days later would pass. Your own unique constraint has no expiry.

How do I handle refunds or credits for bad usage?

For a wrong event, cancel it with a meter event adjustment. For goodwill credits, use credit notes or customer balance adjustments rather than editing usage, so the usage record stays truthful.

Can usage be reported before the customer subscribes?

You can record it: meters are tied to customers, not subscription items, and Stripe's migration guide lists collecting usage before a subscription exists as a meter feature. Invoices reflect usage only once the customer subscribes to a meter-backed price, so test how early usage lands on the first invoice in a sandbox before relying on it.

What aggregation formula should the meter use?

sum for tokens, calls, GB processed. count when each event is one unit. last (added in the Basil release) suits values like seats or storage snapshots, where you send the current level rather than increments. Deltas only work with sum.

How does this connect to integrations with ERPs or CRMs?

The same pattern applies: an outbox, retries and a dead-letter path. I covered that in Resilient ERP & CRM API Integrations: Retries, DLQs, Replay.

Next in this series, Part 5 covers production observability on a budget, including how to trace a usage event from the API request all the way to the invoice line.

title: Try a React component without creating a project
description:
You want to check how a hook behaves. The usual route is a new project: scaffold, install, start a dev server, delete the boilerplate. That's a lot of ceremony for twenty lines.

Today's twenty lines: a useDebouncedValue hook, the kind you write for a search box so it doesn't filter on every keystroke.

The hook 

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

function useDebouncedValue<T>(value: T, ms = 250): T {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);

  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), ms);
    return () => clearTimeout(id);
  }, [value, ms]);

  return debounced;
}

How it works: every time value changes, the effect starts a timer. If value changes again before the timer fires, React runs the cleanup first, which cancels the old timer. So debounced only catches up once the input has been still for ms milliseconds.

Two details that bite people:

  • The cleanup is the debounce. Without return () => clearTimeout(id), every keystroke schedules an update and you've built a delay, not a debounce.
  • ms belongs in the dependency array. Leave it out and changing the delay does nothing until value changes too.

A component to try it in 

import { useEffect, useMemo, useState } from "react";

// useDebouncedValue from above goes here

const fruits = ["apple", "apricot", "banana", "blueberry", "cherry", "grape", "mango"];

export default function App() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  const debounced = useDebouncedValue(query, 300);

  const matches = useMemo(
    () => fruits.filter((f) => f.includes(debounced.toLowerCase())),
    [debounced],
  );

  return (
    <div style={{ fontFamily: "system-ui", padding: 24 }}>
      <input
        value={query}
        onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)}
        placeholder="Filter fruit"
      />
      <p>
        {matches.length} of {fruits.length} (typed: "{query}", filtering: "{debounced}")
      </p>
      <ul>
        {matches.map((f) => (
          <li key={f}>{f}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </div>
  );
}

Showing both query and debounced on screen is the trick: type fast and you can watch the second one lag behind, then snap into place.

Running it without a project

I ran this in JSLab, a JavaScript & TypeScript scratchpad for macOS. Click + in the tab bar and pick React: JSLab sets the tab's language, runtime and framework, installs the packages it needs, and opens starter code. Paste the file over it.

JSLab renders it into a Web View tile beside the console. Edit the JSX and it rerenders as you type. Change 300 to 1000 and you feel the difference on the next keystroke.

Here's a smaller component running the same way in a real JSLab Browser tab: a Counter mounted with createRoot, ticking in the Web View beside the code.

The console still works alongside it. Add a line like this inside the effect and the logs land in the output panel, tagged with their line:

console.log("debounced →", value);

Want styling? Turn on Tailwind in the status bar and the utility classes your code uses get compiled into the page, with nothing to install.

When to make it a real project

A scratchpad is for the question "does this hook behave the way I think?" Once the answer is yes, move it into your app with its tests. The point is not having to pay for a project before you know you need one.

JSLab launches Nov 15. The Web View and framework docs are here: https://js-lab.app/docs/web-view

title: I built a pixel-art whale that grows with your GitHub commits (Rust, SDFs, Bayer dithering)
description:
Your GitHub profile README is the one page you fully control. Most of us fill it with badges and stat cards. I wanted something alive, so I built GitTulkun: a pixel-art Tulkun (the giant whale-like creatures from Avatar's Pandora) that is generated from your real GitHub activity, swims in a seamless looping GIF, and grows up as your year goes on.

PramudithaN / git-tulkun

Procedural pixel-art Tulkun whale generated from your GitHub contributions and language colors as a looping GIF for your profile README.

git-tulkun

A procedural pixel-art Tulkun leviathan for your GitHub profile README.md that resets to a baby calf every January 1st, grows on a logarithmic scale into an armored adult bull from your contributions, and takes its colors from your top programming languages.


Live git-tulkun generated from @PramudithaN's current-year GitHub activity (1,072 contributions - Stage 3: Adolescent Tulkun)

Quick Start (1-Step Setup)

1. Add this embed snippet to your profile README.md (replace YOUR_USERNAME with your GitHub username):

<p align="center">
  <a href="https://github.com/PramudithaN/git-tulkun">
    <img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/YOUR_USERNAME/YOUR_USERNAME/output/tulkun/tulkun.gif" width="640" alt="git-tulkun swimming" />
  </a>
</p>

2. Create .github/workflows/tulkun.yml in the same repository (the action pushes tulkun.gif, tulkun.png, and share-card.png to an orphan output branch automatically so daily updates never bloat your main commit history):

name: Update Tulkun
on:
  schedule: [{ cron: "0 0 * *
…
View on GitHub

That is my own whale, generated live from my own contributions.

What it does

  • Reads your current-year contributions and top repository languages from the GitHub GraphQL API
  • Maps your contribution count to one of five life stages, from Baby Calf to Adult Male Bull
  • Resets every January 1, so everyone starts the year as a calf
  • Tints the whale with the official GitHub colors of your top three languages
  • Renders a 48-frame, 15 FPS loop that updates daily through a GitHub Action

The five stages

Stage Contributions this year What changes
1. Baby Calf [range] Short, stubby body, blunt snout, cream belly
2. Yearling Calf [range] Longer, slimmer body; kuru whips sprout
3. Adolescent [range] Sensor crest rises; six flippers elongate
4. Adult Female [range] Dark carapace armor, sloped crest, serrated jaw
5. Adult Male Bull [range] Maximum length, hooked hammer-crest, battle scars

How the renderer works

There are no spritesheets. Every frame is computed from a handful of parameters, so one code path draws all five stages and three camera angles.

1. Shape. The body is a spline, with signed distance fields (SDFs) for the head crest, flippers, whips, jaw stripes and flukes. A stage change just moves parameters, such as the spine growing from 64 px to 186 px.

2. Lighting. For each pixel the renderer builds a surface normal from the body's cylindrical profile and lights it with a fixed directional light:

n = (nx, ny, sqrt(1 - nx^2 - ny^2))
light = [-0.30, -0.62, 0.72]

3. Pixel-art look. Brightness is quantized to a 4-shade ramp with a 4x4 ordered Bayer dither matrix, which gives the classic crosshatch of old pixel art. A 1 px dark outline (#0f121a) keeps the whale readable on both light and dark GitHub themes.

4. Language colors. Each top language's hex color becomes a 4-shade ramp (shadow, mid dark, mid light, highlight). Your top language paints the belly, skin and carapace, the second tints the sensor crest, and the third lights its tip. A TypeScript-heavy profile gets a different whale than a Rust-heavy one.

5. Swimming. The loop is 48 frames at 15 FPS (3.2 seconds). A traveling S-wave bends the torso and drives the tail, while the flippers lag behind in phase:

dy(u, t) = A_bob * sin(w*t) * (1 - u)^1.3 + A_tail * sin(2.35*pi*u - w*t) * u^0.92

Here u runs along the body from head (0) to tail (1).

6. No jitter. The camera box is precomputed across the whole stroke, so the whale never clips or bounces the frame. Output is upscaled 2x with nearest-neighbor into a 640x280 GIF, plus a PNG and an HTML preview.

Why Rust and a GitHub Action

The whole thing is one Rust binary with five dependencies (chrono, gif, png, serde, serde_json). The composite GitHub Action downloads a prebuilt binary when one exists and compiles from source otherwise. Data collection shells out to gh api graphql, so the built-in workflow token is enough.

Add your own whale

Create .github/workflows/tulkun.yml in your profile repository:

name: Update Tulkun
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 0 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: write
jobs:
  tulkun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: PramudithaN/git-tulkun@[latest tag, e.g. v1]
        with:
          view: side
          canon: "false"
      - run: |
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add tulkun/tulkun.gif tulkun/tulkun.png
          git diff --cached --quiet || git commit -m "chore: update Tulkun"
          git push

[If you shipped a commit input or an output-branch option, show the shorter workflow here instead.]

Then embed it in your README:

<img src="tulkun/tulkun.gif" width="640" alt="My Tulkun" />

Want a preview without any setup? Run the demo mode locally:

cargo run --release -- demo --commits 145 --view dive --output-dir tulkun-demo

What I learned

[Add 2 or 3 honest lessons here, for example: keeping five stages visually consistent, getting a seamless loop, or the repo bloat from daily GIF commits and how you fixed it. Real stories earn more comments than feature lists.]

What I would love feedback on

  • Should the stages scale differently, or use a rolling 365 days instead of a calendar year?
  • What else should shape the whale: pull requests, reviews, streaks?
  • Which camera angle do you like most?

Drop your whale in the comments, I would love to see them.

Repo: https://github.com/PramudithaN/git-tulkun (if you like it, a star helps others find it).

GitTulkun is an unofficial fan project. Tulkun and Avatar belong to their respective owners, and this project is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

title: Architecture Firm Website Redesign Guide
description:
Architecture Firm Website Redesign Guide

As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, I have witnessed numerous architecture firms struggle to create an effective online presence. The primary culprit behind this struggle is the reliance on standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms, which fail to capture the unique essence and complexity of architectural services. These templates often lack the nuance and customization required to showcase an architecture firm's distinctive style, expertise, and portfolio.

The limitations of generic templates are multifaceted. Firstly, they are designed to cater to a broad range of industries, resulting in a lack of specificity and depth in their design and functionality. Secondly, they often prioritize aesthetics over user experience, leading to confusing navigation and poorly optimized conversion paths. Lastly, these templates rarely provide the flexibility and scalability needed to accommodate the evolving needs of a growing architecture firm.

To overcome these challenges, it is essential to adopt a more tailored and engineering-driven approach to website redesign. Here are three concrete takeaways to consider:

  1. Customized Information Architecture: Develop a bespoke information architecture that reflects the firm's unique services, projects, and values. This involves creating a clear and intuitive navigation system, as well as a robust filtering and search functionality to facilitate easy access to relevant content.
  2. High-Performance Visual Storytelling: Leverage high-quality visuals and immersive storytelling techniques to showcase the firm's portfolio and expertise. This can include interactive 3D models, virtual tours, and responsive image galleries that adapt seamlessly to various devices and screen sizes.
  3. Data-Driven Conversion Optimization: Implement a data-driven approach to conversion optimization, using tools like A/B testing, heat mapping, and analytics to identify areas of improvement and measure the effectiveness of design iterations. This enables architecture firms to refine their website's user experience, enhance engagement, and drive more conversions.

By embracing these engineering principles and moving away from generic templates, architecture firms can create a website that truly reflects their brand and expertise. A well-designed website can serve as a powerful marketing tool, attracting new clients, and showcasing a firm's capabilities to a wider audience.

title: Understanding the CAP Theorem
description:
As developers, we often assume that distributed systems can provide everything at once: perfectly consistent data, high availability, and resilience to network failures. Unfortunately, distributed systems don't work like that.

This is where the CAP Theorem comes in, one of the most fundamental concepts in distributed computing.

What Is the CAP Theorem?

Proposed by computer scientist Eric Brewer, the CAP Theorem states that a distributed system can guarantee only two of the following three properties simultaneously:

  • Consistency (C)
  • Availability (A)
  • Partition Tolerance (P)

When a network partition occurs, you must choose between consistency and availability.

Consistency

Consistency means every node sees the same data at the same time.

If you update a user's account balance, every server should immediately return the updated value.

From the user's perspective:

  • Read after write works correctly
  • No stale data
  • Single source of truth

Availability

Availability means every request receives a response, even if some servers are experiencing issues.

The response might not contain the most recent data, but the system remains operational.

Examples:

  • Social media feeds: If User X updates their profile info, it's just fine if User Y sees the old info for a few minutes.
  • Product recommendations
  • Content Platforms
  • Analytics dashboards
  • Review Sites (Yelp etc.)

These systems often prioritize availability over strict consistency.
We can basically ask ourselves "Would it be catastrophic if users briefly saw inconsistent data?" If the answer is yes, choose consistency. If not, choose availability[1]

Partition Tolerance - Not Optional

A partition happens when nodes cannot communicate because of network failures."Partition Tolerance” is the the ability of a distributed system to continue operating even when a partition occurs.

In modern cloud environments, partitions are not hypothetical events.

They happen because of:

  • Network outages
  • Region failures
  • Router issues
  • Infrastructure maintenance

Since partitions are unavoidable, most distributed systems must support partition tolerance. Because you cannot prevent hardware failures or router crashes.The systems should not be affected by network partitions.
Therefore, any distributed system must be partition-tolerant.

A Real-World Example: The ATM

Imagine you have $1,000 in your bank account and two ATMs connected to different bank servers.

You withdraw $200 from the first ATM, but a network failure prevents the second server from receiving the update 🫣 The second ATM still shows your balance as $1,000.

Now, you try to withdraw another $900 from the second ATM.

  • Consistency (CP): The ATM rejects the transaction because it cannot verify your current balance. The system sacrifices availability to protect data consistency.
  • Availability (AP): The ATM continues processing transactions using its outdated balance, potentially allowing you to withdraw more money than you actually have.

Real banking systems use additional safeguards to prevent such situations.

This example illustrates the fundamental CAP trade-off: when a network partition occurs, a system may need to reject or delay requests to maintain consistency, or continue responding despite the risk of serving outdated data.

The Real Trade-off

The CAP Theorem becomes important when a partition occurs.

At that moment you must decide:

CP Systems

Consistency + Partition Tolerance

The system rejects or delays requests to ensure data remains correct.

Examples:

  • Banking transactions
  • Inventory management
  • Financial systems

Correctness matters more than availability.

AP Systems

Availability + Partition Tolerance

The system continues serving requests even if some nodes have outdated information.

Examples:

  • Social networks
  • Messaging systems
  • Content platforms

Availability matters more than immediate consistency.

What About CA Systems?

Technically, CA systems exist only when partitions never happen.

In real distributed environments, partitions are inevitable.

This is why most cloud-native systems end up choosing either CP or AP behavior during failures.

CAP in Modern Databases

Different databases make different trade-offs:

Database Typical Preference
MongoDB CP
Apache Cassandra AP
DynamoDB AP-oriented
PostgreSQL (single node) CA-like
CockroachDB CP

Understanding these trade-offs helps architects choose the right database for their workload.

Why Developers Still Need CAP

Many developers learn CAP Theorem during interviews or reviewing the interview questions and then forget about it😀

But CAP influences real-world decisions:

  • Designing microservices
  • Choosing databases
  • Building global applications
  • Handling outages
  • Architecting cloud-native systems

Whenever someone says, "Why can't we just keep everything available and perfectly consistent?", they are usually running into the limitations described by CAP.

I think CAP Theorem is not like a database rule. It is a reminder that distributed systems require trade-offs.

As systems scale across regions, clouds, and continents, understanding those trade-offs becomes more important than memorizing any specific technology.

Resources & Further Reading
[1]- Cap Theorem

Understanding CAP Theorem: Basics and Real-World Examples

title: Don't Migrate Logs. Outlive Them.
description:
For two months, every log written into Shipbook was written twice.

Once into the old Elasticsearch cluster, the one we had been running for years. And once, in parallel, into a new one — a different Elasticsearch version, with a completely different way of organizing the data. Dual-write. The standard playbook for moving a database you cannot afford to lose: keep both copies, keep them in sync, prove the new one is right, then flip.

It worked. We are fully on the new cluster now; the old one is gone. But somewhere in the middle of those two months, a much smaller change — one I was forced to handle a completely different way, because dual-write was physically impossible for it — quietly showed me that I had built the entire rest of the migration the hard way.

That smaller change took one line of code and a calendar reminder. The big one took two months of machinery and a steady drip of bugs. They were solving nearly the same problem.

One Dual-Write for Two Changes

I was changing two things at once, and I folded them into a single migration.

The first was the engine: a jump from Elasticsearch 7 to Elasticsearch 9. Years of accumulated reasons — features, a saner storage-tiering model, the end of a version aging out from under us.

The second was the schema. For most of the life of Shipbook — our logging platform — we created one index per customer per day. At our scale that meant thousands of tiny indexes, most nearly empty, all of them taxing the cluster in shard count and metadata churn — the structural problem I wrote about in Driving Our Error Log to Zero. The new shape shares one index across every customer on the same plan, routes writes by account so each customer's data stays together, and gives dedicated indexes only to whale accounts — the handful pushing more than twenty million logs a day.

Both changes went into one dual-write. New cluster, new schema, all at once. Every log landed in the old per-customer index on the old cluster and in the new shared per-plan index on the new one. A backfill job scrolled the entire history across. A flag — readFromNew — kept reads coming from the old, trusted side while the new side filled, ready to flip when I believed it.

That is the textbook approach. The textbook is also where the textbook pain lives.

The Tax on Keeping Two Truths

Dual-write means every write now has two outcomes, and they can disagree.

The secondary write was fire-and-forget — I did not want a hiccup on the new cluster to block a real request on the old one. So when the new cluster pushed back under load, writes to it failed silently. Nothing surfaced, because reads were still served from the healthy old side. The gap only existed on the cluster nobody was reading from yet.

That exact failure became its own story: 1.3 million silent errors a day, accumulating on the secondary side of this very migration, invisible to every customer. It was future damage — fuel loading quietly behind a flag, waiting for the day reads flipped over to detonate as missing sessions and stale fields. We caught it only because Claude could read the production logs and a number on a histogram did not fit the story.

That is the dual-write tax. You are not running one system; you are running two systems and a promise that they match. Every write path carries a branch. Every error makes you ask which cluster it came from. The whole apparatus exists to keep two copies of the truth in sync — and keeping two copies of the truth in sync is one of the genuinely hard problems in computing. We paid the tax for two months. The commit that finally deleted the old cluster's code path is dated almost two months after the one that added the dual-write.

The One Change I Couldn't Dual-Write

In the middle of all that, I needed to add routing to the new per-plan indexes — to tell Elasticsearch to place every account's logs together on the same shard, so a query for one customer hits one shard instead of fanning out across all of them.

And I could not dual-write it. Not because of effort — because it is impossible. Routing is decided at the instant a document is written; it determines which shard the document physically lands on. The logs already written to the new indexes were already placed, scattered across shards by their id. There is no second write that fixes where the first one went. My only options were to reindex everything — expensive, and exactly the kind of bulk data movement I was trying to avoid — or to draw a line.

So I drew a line. One constant:

private static readonly RET_ROUTING_TEMPLATE_CUTOVER = '2026-04-28';

Indexes created before that date are read the old way, without routing assumptions. Indexes created on or after it carry routing. The reader checks the date in the index name and does the right thing for each. And then — because every log has a retention and a nightly job deletes the ones past it — the pre-cutover indexes simply age out. A thirty-day index is gone thirty days later. Once the last one expires, the special case is dead code.

// TODO ~2026-05-28: drop the 30d guard once pre-cutover indexes age out.

That TODO is the entire decommission plan. Not a migration. A reminder. No second write, no backfill, no flag to flip, no held breath. The only cost was patience: for a few weeks, some reads spanned both the old and new index shapes before the old ones evaporated.

It was so much calmer than the thing happening all around it that I almost did not notice it was the same kind of problem.

Where Claude Helped, and Where It Led Me Astray

I did this work in a tight loop with Claude Code, and the honest accounting cuts both ways.

It earned its keep on the hard, fiddly parts. The hot/warm storage tiering — recent data on fast NVMe, older indexes rolled down to cheaper disk — it designed cleanly. When the new per-plan indexes started rejecting writes every midnight, it worked out why: routing by account funneled a burst of high-volume accounts onto one shard the instant each fresh daily index appeared. And it caught a missing shards-per-node cap that had piled a whale's ten shards onto two machines.

It also walked me into walls with total confidence.

It opened by reasoning about Elasticsearch 7 — because it saw 7.17 in our package.json. That was the client library; the cluster was already on 9. Half its early advice applied to a system we no longer ran.

It recommended an index setting to read each index's age from its name. Reasonable, except Elasticsearch's date parser wants hyphens and our names use underscores. It did not fail in review. It failed in production, on all 325 existing indexes at once, every one stuck in an error state until I tore the setting back out by hand.

And for a stretch it argued against the hot/warm tiering I wanted — insisting it would not come out ahead, that there was nothing to gain. The argument rested on a cost calculation, and the calculation was simply wrong: my configuration cost the same either way, and the tiered shape was the right one for the workload. Not a defensible judgment built on a real number — a wrong number, stated with exactly the confidence of a right one.

The lesson is the one from every post I write about this: a confident wrong number reads identically to a confident right one. The model will reason beautifully and calculate badly in the same breath, and my job is to make it show the arithmetic before I act on the conclusion.

And the decision itself stays mine. The model can fetch, calculate, and propose — but the moment you let Claude, or any AI, do the deciding, you have handed the wheel to something that is wrong and right with the same face, and it will walk you off a cliff with perfect composure. For the moment, at least, that is the one job you do not delegate.

What I'd Do Differently

The routing change was forced into the cheap approach. I did not choose the cutoff date because it was elegant; I chose it because dual-write was off the table. And the forced move turned out to be the one I should have made everywhere.

If I ran the cluster migration again, I would not dual-write it. I would give it a cutoff date too. Stand up the new cluster, point new writes at it, leave the old cluster running and serving the logs it already holds. Read from both during the overlap and merge. Then wait — and the day the oldest log on the old cluster passes its retention, the old cluster holds nothing anyone needs, and you switch it off.

No second copy of the truth to keep in sync. No backfill dragging the whole history across the wire. No silent secondary-write failures loading future damage behind a flag. The price is real and worth naming: you keep two clusters running for as long as your longest retention tier — up to a hundred and eighty days for us — instead of cutting over in a weekend. For a dataset that deletes itself, that is almost always the cheaper trade.

I reached for dual-write because that is what you reach for when you migrate a database. But logs are not most databases. They expire. The hard part of a migration is usually moving the history — and with logs there is no history to move, only a present that, left alone, becomes the past and then becomes nothing.

The Dull Work Customers Could Feel

I have spent this whole post second-guessing how I ran the migration. I want to be just as clear about the thing I do not second-guess: running it at all.

After the new infrastructure settled, the feedback started arriving on its own — from several customers, unprompted. The server feels faster. Searches come back quicker. Nobody files a support ticket asking you to reorganize your Elasticsearch indexes — but the speed-up was real enough that they noticed it on their own and told us.

That is the part worth holding onto. Infrastructure work is the least glamorous work there is. It ships no feature, closes no requested ticket, and shows up on no roadmap anyone cheers for. It is dull — right up until you discover that the dull work was what everything visible had been quietly resting on the whole time. The plumbing is invisible until someone notices the water is suddenly faster out of the tap. The schema change I almost talked myself out of as not-worth-it turned out to be something paying customers could feel.

So both things are true at once. I would change how I did it. I would not, for a second, change that I did it.

The one change I could not force into the dual-write was the one that told me the truth. Next time I will draw the line first.

Originally published on the Shipbook blog.

title: Second Highest Salary in SQL: 4 Ways, and Which Ones Quietly Break
description:
"Write a query to find the second highest salary."

If you have prepared for any SQL round, you have seen this one. And you probably memorised an answer.

Here's the thing. Most memorised answers work on the sample table in the tutorial and break on the interviewer's follow-up. Two things trip people up: ties (two people with the same top salary) and no second row (a department with one employee).

So let's do it properly. Same small table, four solutions, and we'll see which ones survive.

The data

I ran everything below in SQLite 3.53. The syntax is standard enough that it works in PostgreSQL and MySQL 8 too, with a couple of small notes where it differs.

CREATE TABLE employees(id INTEGER, name TEXT, dept TEXT, salary INTEGER);

INSERT INTO employees VALUES
(1,'Asha','Eng',90000),
(2,'Ravi','Eng',90000),
(3,'Meera','Eng',75000),
(4,'Kiran','Sales',60000),
(5,'Neha','Sales',55000),
(6,'Tara','HR',50000);

Notice what I did on purpose. Asha and Ravi both earn 90000, so the top salary is tied. Tara is alone in HR.

The correct answer for the whole company is 75000. Keep that in mind.

Way 1: ORDER BY with LIMIT and OFFSET

This is the one most people write first.

SELECT salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;

Output:

90000

Wrong. It sorted the rows 90000, 90000, 75000... and skipped one row, which was the first 90000. The second row is the other 90000.

The fix is DISTINCT, so duplicates collapse before you skip:

SELECT DISTINCT salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;

Output:

75000

Correct now. In SQL Server the same idea is OFFSET 1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY.

Way 2: Max of everything below the max

No sorting, no window functions. Just ask: what is the biggest salary that is smaller than the biggest salary?

SELECT MAX(salary)
FROM employees
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);

Output:

75000

This handles ties without any extra work, because salary < max throws away every row tied at the top. It's also easy to explain out loud, which matters in an interview.

The catch is that it only gives you the second highest. If the interviewer then says "okay, now the 5th highest", you have to nest it again and again. Not nice.

Way 3: DENSE_RANK

This is the version that scales to any N.

SELECT DISTINCT salary
FROM (
  SELECT salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
) t
WHERE rnk = 2;

Output:

75000

Want the 5th highest? Change rnk = 2 to rnk = 5. That's it.

Why DENSE_RANK and not RANK or ROW_NUMBER? Let's look at all three on our data.

name salary ROW_NUMBER RANK DENSE_RANK
Asha 90000 1 1 1
Ravi 90000 2 1 1
Meera 75000 3 3 2
Kiran 60000 4 4 3
Neha 55000 5 5 4
Tara 50000 6 6 5

I ran ROW_NUMBER() and RANK() on this table to get those numbers. (ROW_NUMBER's order between Asha and Ravi can swap, since they tie.)

  • ROW_NUMBER never ties, so "rank 2" is just the other 90000. Wrong.
  • RANK ties, but then skips. After two people at rank 1, the next rank is 3. There is no rank 2 at all, so you get an empty result.
  • DENSE_RANK ties and doesn't skip. Meera is rank 2. Correct.

Rule of thumb: for "Nth highest value", use DENSE_RANK.

Dropping the DISTINCT is also useful: if you want the people earning the second highest salary, just select name too:

SELECT name, salary
FROM (
  SELECT name, salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
) t
WHERE rnk = 2;

Output:

Meera|75000

Way 4: The correlated subquery

You'll see this in older tutorials and some interviews, because it works without window functions.

SELECT name, salary
FROM employees e
WHERE 2 = (
  SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT salary)
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary >= e.salary
);

Output:

Meera|75000

Read it like this: for each employee, count how many distinct salaries are at least as high as theirs. If that count is 2, they are the second highest.

It's correct, and it's also slow on big tables, because the inner query runs once per row. Good to understand, not what I'd write today if window functions are available.

The trap everyone misses: what if there is no second salary?

Our HR department has only Tara. Ask for the second highest salary in HR and see what each method returns.

Way 1 with LIMIT/OFFSET:

SELECT salary FROM (
  SELECT salary FROM employees
  WHERE dept = 'HR'
  ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1
) t;

Output: no rows at all.

Way 2 with MAX:

SELECT MAX(salary)
FROM employees
WHERE dept = 'HR'
  AND salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE dept = 'HR');

Output: one row containing NULL.

These look similar but behave differently. An empty result and a NULL are not the same thing to the application reading your query. Some interviewers specifically ask for "return NULL if there is no second highest salary". If so, wrap the Way 1 query in a subquery in the SELECT list, which turns "no rows" into NULL:

SELECT (
  SELECT DISTINCT salary
  FROM employees
  WHERE dept = 'HR'
  ORDER BY salary DESC
  LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1
) AS second_highest;

Output:

NULL

Good to know before you walk into the room, not after.

Second highest per department

The follow-up that comes right after is almost always "now do it for each department". This is where DENSE_RANK shines, because you only add PARTITION BY:

SELECT dept, name, salary
FROM (
  SELECT name, dept, salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
) t
WHERE rnk = 2;

Output:

Eng|Meera|75000
Sales|Neha|55000

HR doesn't appear because it has no rank 2, which is the right behaviour here. Asha and Ravi both being rank 1 in Eng doesn't push Meera out of rank 2.

What I'd say in the interview

  1. "I'd use DENSE_RANK so ties don't break it, and it works for any N."
  2. "If window functions aren't allowed, I'd use MAX with a subquery on salary < MAX(salary)."
  3. "And I'd ask whether they want NULL or an empty result when there is no second salary."

That third line is what sounds like experience. Asking about the edge case before the interviewer does is a good habit in any SQL question.

Try it yourself

If you want to practise a few more like this, I've put together SQL problems on LakeBench, a platform I'm building. "Top three salaries" is free and is a good warm-up for the ranking idea: lakebench.in/studio/lb-sql-05. The exact "Second highest salary" problem is lb-sql-20. There's also a page of window function problems at akebench.in/learn/sql-warehousing/window-functions.

Which of the four would you have written first? I'd bet on Way 1.

title: pointer-events: none doesn't disable an element. It hands the press to whatever is underneath.
description:
In a fanned hand of cards, I pressed a card I wasn't allowed to play, and the game played a different card: the one lying under it. The click handler was fine. The card I pressed had pointer-events: none, and that property doesn't stop a press. It takes the element out of hit-testing, the step where the browser works out which element is under the pointer, so the press goes to the next element down, and in a fan the next element down is the neighbouring card.

This post has the minimal repro, a table of where the press lands in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit for five ways of switching an element off, and the fix.

The repro 

<!doctype html>
<style>
  .hand { position: relative; height: 140px; margin: 20px; }
  .card { position: absolute; top: 0; width: 80px; height: 120px; }
  .card:nth-child(1) { left: 0; }
  .card:nth-child(2) { left: 40px; }
  .card:nth-child(3) { left: 80px; }
  .off { pointer-events: none; opacity: .5; }
</style>
<div class="hand">
  <button class="card" id="a">A</button>
  <button class="card off" id="b">B</button>
  <button class="card" id="c">C</button>
</div>
<script>
  document.querySelector('.hand').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
    console.log('played', e.target.id);
  });
</script>

Three cards, each covering the right half of the one before it. B is dimmed and has pointer-events: none. Click the strip of B that you can see, between A and C. The console says played a.

You can ask the browser what a press at that spot would hit:

const r = document.getElementById('b').getBoundingClientRect();
document.elementsFromPoint(r.left + 20, r.top + 60).map((el) => el.id || el.tagName);
// ["a", "DIV", "BODY", "HTML"]

B isn't in the list at all. That is what the spec asks for. CSS UI 4 says that with none, hit-testing "acts as if the boxes generated by the element were not there, effectively causing the element behind the pointer-events: none element to become the target of hit-testing-based events instead."

The part I had wrong was "the element behind". It isn't the page background. It is whatever hit-testable box comes next in paint order, and if that box is another live control, the press is now a press on that control.

Five ways to switch B off, in three engines

I disabled B five different ways and pressed its visible strip in Chromium 148, Firefox 150 and WebKit 26.4: once with Playwright's mouse, once with Playwright's emulated touchscreen, and once by tabbing to it from A and pressing Enter. A capturing listener on window logged the target of every pointer, touch, mouse and click event.

B is switched off with pointerdown lands on click, mouse click, touch Tab from A, then Enter
nothing (control) B B B focuses B, clicks B
pointer-events: none A A A focuses B, clicks B
inert A A A skips B, focuses C
disabled B no click no click; A in WebKit skips B, focuses C
aria-disabled="true" B B B focuses B, clicks B

The three engines agree everywhere except the one cell marked WebKit. Four things fall out of it.

pointer-events: none switches off the pointer, not the element. Every event in the sequence, from pointerdown to click, went to A, with the mouse and with touch. The keyboard is untouched: B still takes focus, and Enter clicks it. The spec says so too: "pointer-events: none does not inhibit sequential focus navigation." So a card switched off this way plays its neighbour when you click it and plays itself when you press Enter on it.

inert behaves the same for the pointer. inert is an HTML attribute that switches off an element and everything inside it, and the HTML spec defines it this way. The first rule in its list for an inert node is "Hit-testing must act as if the 'pointer-events' CSS property were set to 'none'." It also takes B out of the tab order, which is why Tab went from A straight to C. It is the right tool for a whole region the user can't reach, such as the page behind a modal, and the wrong one for a single item that sits on top of other live items.

disabled keeps the press on B, but not every event. Hit-testing stops at the disabled button. With the mouse, no engine dispatched a click anywhere, and with touch, Chromium and Firefox didn't either. But pointerdown and pointerup still fired on B in all three engines, so a handler on pointerdown gets no protection from disabled. And with emulated touch in WebKit, pointerdown and touchstart went to B while the mousedown, mouseup and click that follow a tap went to A. That happened when the element under B was another button; with a <div> under B, nothing received a click, even with a click listener on it. disabled also only exists on form controls, so a card built from a <div> can't use it.

aria-disabled changes nothing about the press. Every event landed on B, in every engine, from every input. That is the behaviour you want: the press reaches the element the user aimed at, and your code decides what it means.

The fix

Keep every item hit-testable and refuse the press in the handler. Against the repro, replace the .off rule, mark B with the attribute instead of the class, and check it in the handler:

.card[aria-disabled="true"] { opacity: .5; }

<button class="card" id="b" aria-disabled="true">B</button>

document.querySelector('.hand').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const card = e.target.closest('.card');
  if (!card) return;
  if (card.getAttribute('aria-disabled') === 'true') {
    console.log('refused', card.id);
    return;
  }
  console.log('played', card.id);
});

A press on B's strip now logs refused b in all three engines, with the mouse, with touch, and with Tab and Enter. elementsFromPoint at the same spot returns ["b", "a", "DIV", "BODY", "HTML"]: B is back on top of the stack, with A under it where it belongs. The dimming and the refusal read the same attribute, so they can't disagree.

pointer-events: none is still the right tool when you want the press to go to whatever is underneath: a label floating over a canvas, or a drag preview that follows the pointer while you hit-test for the drop target under it. Use it for things that should be transparent to the pointer, never as a way to say "this control is off".

Two caveats. These are Playwright's synthesized mouse, touch and keyboard input, not a physical mouse or a finger on a phone, so test the devices you ship to. In particular, the WebKit touch result comes from Playwright's WebKit build with emulated touch; I haven't reproduced it on an iPhone, so treat it as a reason to check Safari, not as a fact about it.

How much of a fan it hits

In a fan, most of the part of a card you can see lies on top of the card before it. With pointer-events: none on the cards you can't play, a press on one of them goes to the card underneath, and on down the stack until it reaches a card that takes presses, or the table. It only plays the wrong card when an unplayable card lies on a playable one.

I measured how much of a hand that is in a game of Spades, where the hand is sorted by suit and, when you have the suit that was led, only that suit may be played. I dealt eight hands, four at 1280×900 with the mouse and four at 390×844 with emulated touch, and stopped at the first trick where I had to follow suit. For each card I couldn't play, I sampled its visible area on a 2 px grid with elementFromPoint, then switched back to the old rule, under which only playable cards take presses, and checked what each sampled point hit.

  • In four hands, the playable suit was the last one in the fan. Nothing lay on it, and every stray press fell to the table.
  • In the other four, the card lying on the end of the playable run had 50–89% of its visible area over a playable card. The 50% was the last card in the hand, whose whole face shows.
  • At phone size the fan is tighter, and the card after that one still had 7% of its visible area over the same playable card: a press can fall through two cards.

In all four of those hands, a press on that card played the playable card under it with the old rule, and played nothing with the fix in place. The fixed hand is in this Spades game: when you have to follow suit, a press on a card you can't play does nothing.

Takeaways

  • pointer-events: none doesn't disable an element. A press goes to whatever hit-testable box is underneath, and the keyboard still reaches the element itself.
  • inert does the same to the pointer, by definition, and also removes focus. Use it for whole regions, not single items in a stack.
  • disabled stops click but not pointerdown or pointerup, and exists only on form controls.
  • In any UI where items overlap, keep each item hit-testable and refuse the press in your handler. document.elementsFromPoint(x, y) shows you what a press at a point would hit.

title: React error #418: five hydration bugs I shipped
description:
This post was created with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy before publishing.

If your production console shows Minified React error #418, React is telling you that the HTML the server sent and the first render in the browser did not match. The development build spells it out ("Hydration failed because the server rendered HTML didn't match the client") and shows a diff. The production build gives you a number and a link to react.dev/errors/418.

It is easy to treat it as console noise, because the page still works. It is not free. When hydration fails, React throws away the server-rendered tree and renders the whole root again in the browser. On my site that one error took mobile Total Blocking Time from 0 to 420 ms and the Lighthouse performance score from 96 to 83, and pushed Largest Contentful Paint 1.2 seconds past First Contentful Paint, which had always been equal.

I have shipped this error five different ways on one Next.js site. Here is each one, how it was found, and the fix that stuck.

1. Randomness or time in a useState initializer

The games on the site generate a puzzle, a word or a board. The obvious code seeds state when the component is created:

// Wrong: the initializer runs on the server and again in the browser.
const [puzzle, setPuzzle] = useState(() => generatePuzzle());

The initializer runs twice, once during prerendering and once during hydration, and Math.random() gives a different answer each time. The same thing happened in a lorem ipsum generator, a mock data generator and a password generator. Anything that reads Date.now() or new Date() while rendering has the same problem.

The fix is a deterministic first value, with the random one set after mount:

const [puzzle, setPuzzle] = useState(INITIAL_PUZZLE); // fixed, the same everywhere
useEffect(() => {
  setPuzzle(generatePuzzle()); // runs only in the browser, after hydration
}, []);

The first frame shows the fixed puzzle for an instant. For a game that is fine. For anything where the flash matters, render a placeholder of the same size until the effect runs.

2. Formatting with the machine's locale 

// Wrong
<span>{downloads.toLocaleString()}</span>
<time>{new Date(post.date).toLocaleDateString()}</time>

With no locale argument, toLocaleString() uses whatever the current machine prefers. The server that prerenders the page (on Vercel, en-US in UTC) and a visitor in Germany or India produce different strings, so the text differs and hydration fails. It never reproduces on your own machine if your machine matches the server.

Pass the locale you rendered with, or move the formatting after mount:

<span>{downloads.toLocaleString('en-US')}</span>

To catch this class of bug, load the deployed page in a browser with a different locale and time zone. In Playwright that is two options on the context:

const context = await browser.newContext({ locale: 'de-DE', timezoneId: 'America/Los_Angeles' });

3. Browser-only APIs while rendering

Five tools on the site called something during render that only exists, or only behaves the same, in a browser: DOMParser in an XPath evaluator, document in an SVG animation tool and an HTML-to-Pug converter, and URL.createObjectURL in an SVG viewer. That last one is a good example of why this can hide: on the server it produced nothing useful, in the browser it produced a blob: URL, and the visible symptom was a broken image, not an error.

// Wrong: runs during render on the server too.
const src = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([svg], { type: 'image/svg+xml' }));

The fix is to compute these only after the component has mounted:

function useHasMounted() {
  const [mounted, setMounted] = useState(false);
  useEffect(() => setMounted(true), []);
  return mounted;
}

const mounted = useHasMounted();
const src = useMemo(
  () => (mounted ? URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([svg], { type: 'image/svg+xml' })) : null),
  [mounted, svg],
);

Remember to revoke the URL when nothing can reach it any more, but that is a separate bug.

4. usePathname() in a prerendered component

This is the one that cost the most, because I fixed it and then shipped it again.

The site's navigation highlights the current page. The highlight compared the path:

const pathname = usePathname();
const isActive = pathname === href;

On the deployed homepage this logged #418 on every visit. It never happened locally, with next dev or with a local production build. The comparison for the / link came out differently in Vercel's prerender of the index route than in the browser, so the active class differed between the server HTML and the first client render.

The first time, I fixed it in one header. Later a different navigation design carried the same comparison into a new component, and it went live again. That second time is the one that took Lighthouse from 96 to 83.

The fix that stuck is a shared hook that gates only the / comparison on mount and leaves every other link server-rendered, so the other routes keep their active state from the first paint. Simplified, it looks like this:

export function useIsRouteActive(href: string) {
  const pathname = usePathname();
  const mounted = useHasMounted();
  if (href === '/') return mounted && pathname === '/';
  return pathname === href || pathname.startsWith(`${href}/`);
}

The second part of the fix was making sure it could not come back. The repository has a small script that runs before every build and fails when a client component compares usePathname() directly. A lint rule would do the same job. Writing the lesson down had not been enough.

5. A script that edits <body> before React gets there

The site sets a colour scheme and, on festival days, a few data- attributes on <body> from an inline script, so the right look paints before any JavaScript bundle loads. React then hydrates <body>, finds attributes it did not render, and complains.

This is the one case where suppressHydrationWarning is the right tool:

<body suppressHydrationWarning>

It only silences attribute and text differences on that one element, not its children, which is exactly the scope you want. Two rules keep it honest: only the element the script edits gets it (here <body>, not <html>), and the script only ever sets attributes, never content.

suppressHydrationWarning is not a fix for the first four causes. Those are real differences in what renders, and hiding the warning leaves the re-render in place.

How to find yours

  • Read the console on the deployed site, not just locally. Three of these five never reproduced on my machine.
  • Run the development build once to get the readable message and the diff React prints, which names the element and the two values.
  • Load the page with a foreign locale and time zone. It finds cause 2 and anything else that reads the environment.
  • Search the codebase for Math.random, Date.now, new Date(, toLocale, window., document., DOMParser and usePathname inside components that render on the server.

The common thread is simple: everything a component renders the first time must be computable on the server, from the same inputs, with the same answer. Anything that depends on the browser, the clock, chance or the visitor waits until after mount.
