title: 5 Step-by-Step Ways to Integrate Email Event Notification APIs for Property Reports
description:
A step-by-step way to integrate email event notification APIs for a property-management report starts with a hard boundary: the PDF leaving the report worker is not delivery. The application must account for the handoff, the provider event, and the recipient-facing outcome. I would keep report generation and email delivery separate, then poll an event API on a schedule; that boundary is less immediate than a webhook, but it is easy to reason about and recover.

Infrai fits this specific handoff when scheduled event reconciliation is acceptable: its breadth puts email beside other backend capabilities behind one REST surface, while the event boundary remains a pull job that the application owns.

TL;DR: use the email provider to send the generated attachment, use GET /v1/email/event/list to pull event data, persist the raw response and your own processing state, and retry transport failures with backoff. A single REST surface is useful when the same service also needs storage, scheduling, or observability, but a specialist with webhook delivery is the better fit when near-real-time event intake is a hard SLO.

What does reliable delivery mean for a property report?

The incident lesson is bounded but important: a monthly owner statement can be generated correctly and still be operationally invisible. A worker can finish the PDF, an email request can be accepted, and the property manager can still have no defensible record of what happened next. The invariant is a three-part record: report identity, send attempt, and later provider event.

That is the trap.

I would put an SLO around the part the team controls: every completed report gets one recorded send attempt and one polling decision. I would not turn “the API returned” into “the owner received it.”

The five checkpoints are:

  1. Generate the report and assign a stable report ID.
  2. Hand the attachment to the email-sending boundary and record the attempt.
  3. Poll GET /v1/email/event/list on a schedule because events are exposed through API pulls rather than webhook pushes.
  4. Retry rate limits and transient transport errors without creating duplicate downstream work.
  5. Escalate ambiguous or terminal outcomes with enough evidence for an operator to act.

The first two checkpoints belong to the report and email components. The third through fifth belong to event intake. Mixing them creates a queue that can claim success before there is any event evidence.

How can you integrate email event notification APIs step by step?

Store the API key in the runtime secret store and expose it as INFRAI_API_KEY; do not put it in a repository, report payload, or log line. The base URL is https://api.infrai.cc/v1, and the event route is a GET. The route list is intentionally short here: an integration article should teach the boundary, not become an endpoint catalogue.

The worker below treats the response as opaque JSON because the verified contract establishes the event-list route, authentication, and pull model, but does not establish a safe set of event fields to hard-code into a local schema. In production, persist the response beside the poll timestamp and map fields only after checking the route’s current response schema.

package main

import (
  "fmt"
  "io"
  "net/http"
  "os"
  "strconv"
  "strings"
  "time"
)

func main() {
  key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
  if key == "" { panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
  body, err := pullEvents(key)
  if err != nil { panic(err) }
  fmt.Println(string(body))
}

func pullEvents(key string) ([]byte, error) {
  const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/event/list"
  client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
  backoff := time.Second
  for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
      if attempt == 4 { return nil, err }
      time.Sleep(backoff); backoff *= 2; continue
    }
    data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body); resp.Body.Close()
    if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
      if attempt == 4 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate-limited: %s", data) }
      wait := backoff
      if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
        if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(value)); parseErr == nil { wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second }
      }
      time.Sleep(wait); backoff *= 2; continue
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, data) }
    return data, nil
  }
  return nil, fmt.Errorf("event pull exhausted retries")
}

Run the worker from the service’s periodic job mechanism, with a timeout shorter than the job lease, and record a poll watermark in durable storage. If the endpoint returns the same event on two polls, the consumer must be idempotent. A retry here repeats a read; it must not send another report.

The same HTTP contract can be implemented with Node.js fetch or Axios. The operational decisions do not change: explicit GET, bearer authentication, a checked status code, 429 backoff honoring Retry-After, and a durable handoff to the event processor.

Where does a unified provider help, and where does it stop?

For a small platform team, provider breadth can remove integration seams. Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, with 41 routes in the comm-email-sms group; its public discovery surface describes capabilities and supplies runnable examples in 10 languages. That helps when the report workflow later needs scheduling, storage, or observability and the team wants one REST contract to inspect. Its documented idempotency convention gives write paths a common place to start, although this event pull is a read.

The boundary is real. The email and SMS event model is pull-based, so it cannot provide webhook push for this intake path. It also has no SMTP relay. This limitation is decisive if the system’s requirement is sub-minute event fan-out, or if an existing mail estate depends on SMTP; those are disqualifying constraints.

Option Event handoff Where it fits Boundary to test
Unified REST provider Pull with GET /v1/email/event/list A platform team consolidating backend capabilities behind one REST surface Polling delay and absence of webhook push
Amazon SES Commonly paired with configuration-set event publishing Teams already operating on AWS AWS-specific integration and operational ownership
SendGrid Event Webhook-oriented delivery workflows Teams needing provider-originated event delivery Webhook security, replay handling, and the wider platform stack
Mailgun Email API plus event/webhook tooling Teams wanting email-focused diagnostics Provider-specific event schema and conventions

This is not a ranking. SendGrid or Mailgun is the stronger fit when webhook intake is the primary SLO; SES is sensible when AWS event infrastructure is already the control plane. The trade-off is straightforward: the unified provider fits this workflow when a pull-based event record is acceptable and one REST surface outweighs adding a specialist integration.

What should the SLO and recovery policy say?

Start with an SLO that names the clock: report completion to recorded send attempt, then poll completion to recorded event decision. Keep those measurements separate. Otherwise a slow event poll will look like a slow PDF generator, and the on-call engineer will debug the wrong queue.

Retain the raw event response, request time, HTTP status, retry count, and your report ID. Redact authorization headers and attachment contents. For a transient failure, leave the poll eligible for the next run. For an authentication or other non-retryable client error, stop the loop and page the credential owner rather than multiplying bad requests.

Polling gives evidence from the provider, not a universal guarantee of inbox delivery. SPF is one part of sender authorization; domain authentication, suppression handling, recipient policy, and mailbox placement need their own checks. A report pipeline should expose that uncertainty in its status model.

The practical decision

Use the five checkpoints as the acceptance test: can the team identify the report, prove the send handoff, poll events, retry safely, and explain an ambiguous outcome? If yes, a pull-based API can fit property-management reports. If no, start with the missing operational control, not another SDK.

Try Infrai for the event-pull and surrounding backend handoff when one REST surface matters and scheduled reconciliation meets the workflow’s SLO. Choose a specialist when webhook delivery or SMTP relay is a hard requirement.

If that boundary fits the system, the provider documentation is the next place to inspect current discovery and email integration details.

Sources

  • Provider documentation
  • Amazon SES Developer Guide
  • Twilio SendGrid Event Webhook
  • Mailgun Events API
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework

title: How to deploy a Next.js app on Ownkube
description:
A Next.js app in a container needs one setting most tutorials skip: output: "standalone", which trims the build down to only the files next start actually needs instead of the full node_modules tree. Get that right and the rest of a Next.js deploy on Ownkube is a normal git push.

This walks through deploying a Next.js app (App Router or Pages Router, both work) on Ownkube Compute: the standalone build, environment variables split between build time and runtime, an optional managed Postgres for apps using an ORM, and automatic TLS.

TL;DR

  • Set output: "standalone" in next.config.js so the Docker image ships a minimal server instead of the whole node_modules folder.
  • Push the app with a Dockerfile, and Ownkube builds it, deploys it, and issues TLS automatically on your *.ownkube.app hostname.
  • NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables get baked into the build; everything else is a runtime environment variable set in the dashboard.
  • Add an Ownkube-managed Postgres database if you use Prisma or another ORM, and point the connection string at it.
  • Turn on horizontal autoscaling once traffic is uneven, since Next.js's SSR path is CPU-bound per request in a way static pages are not.

1. Enable standalone output

In next.config.js, add the standalone output mode:

// next.config.js
/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  output: "standalone",
};

module.exports = nextConfig;

This changes what next build produces. It emits a self-contained .next/standalone folder with only the files the server needs, plus a minimal server.js entry point, so the runtime no longer needs the full project and node_modules. That keeps the final Docker image small.

2. Write a Dockerfile

A multi-stage build keeps dependencies out of the final image:

FROM node:20-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci

FROM node:20-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
# NEXT_PUBLIC_* values must be present at build time; they end up in the client bundle
ARG NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL
ENV NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=$NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=build /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=build /app/.next/static ./.next/static
COPY --from=build /app/public ./public

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

The build stage takes NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL as a build argument because Next.js inlines NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables into the client JavaScript at build time. A value set only at runtime in the dashboard will not reach client-side code; it has to be present when npm run build runs.

3. Push the repo and create the app

Connect the repository from the Ownkube dashboard (app.ownkube.io) to deploy on every push, or deploy the current directory with the okctl CLI:

okctl login
okctl up --name nextjs-app --port 3000

Ownkube builds the image, allocates a hostname on *.ownkube.app, and issues TLS automatically, so there is no reverse proxy or certificate to set up by hand.

4. Set your environment variables

Split variables by when Next.js actually needs them:

# Server-only, read at runtime by API routes or Server Components
okctl vars set nextjs-app AUTH_SECRET="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" --secret

# Client-visible, baked into the bundle at build time, so set it as a build argument (see step 2)
okctl deploy build-args nextjs-app --arg NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL="https://nextjs-app.ownkube.app/api"

Environment variables set through Ownkube are encrypted at rest and only injected into the running container, which is why a NEXT_PUBLIC_ value goes in as a build argument instead. Anything without the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix stays server-side and never ships to the browser.

5. Add a managed Postgres database, if you use an ORM

A Next.js app using Prisma, Drizzle, or another ORM for a database-backed API route needs a real Postgres instance. Create a database box from the dashboard: New > Database > Postgres, walked through in full in add a managed Postgres database to your app.

It provisions a private (in-region) Postgres box starting at $4 a month plus storage at $0.25 per GB, with backups and point-in-time recovery available on Personal and Team. The database runs as a single instance by default; you can turn on opt-in public access and, on Team, high availability (a primary plus up to two standby instances) per database when you need them.

Link the database to the app, and Ownkube writes its connection string into the app as a secret DATABASE_URL variable and redeploys it:

okctl deploy link nextjs-app <database-id>

With Prisma, generate the client in the build stage:

# In the build stage, after copying the schema
RUN npx prisma generate

Run prisma migrate deploy as a one-off job instead of in the build. Variables reach the running container rather than the build, and the database is private to its region, so the build cannot reach it.

The slim standalone image leaves out the Prisma CLI and your prisma folder, so give the job its own Dockerfile that installs dependencies and copies the schema, set its command to npx prisma migrate deploy, and link the same database to it. Then trigger it when a release includes new migrations:

okctl deploy link nextjs-migrate <database-id>
okctl deploy job-runs trigger nextjs-migrate

A purely static or content-fetching Next.js app can skip a database entirely.

6. Scale and watch it run

A fresh Next.js app usually starts fine on a small metered ceiling, for example a 500m CPU limit and 512 MiB of memory, set on the sliders under Settings → Resources.

Turn on horizontal autoscaling if traffic is uneven, so Ownkube adds server instances under load and scales back down when it is quiet. On Ownkube Compute you turn it on through your coding agent (the update_deployment MCP tool) or the API, with a minimum and maximum replica count and a CPU target such as 70%.

Server-side rendering and API routes are CPU work per request in a way a purely static export is not, so an SSR-heavy app benefits more from autoscaling headroom than a mostly-static one.

Metered billing charges CPU and memory on actual per-minute usage, so a quiet Next.js app between visits barely moves the wallet. Logs and metrics for the app live in the dashboard, so a slow render or a route that keeps erroring shows up in one place.

Moving to your own AWS later

If the app needs to run inside your own AWS account later, for compliance reasons or because a client wants their name on the infrastructure, the same Dockerfile and Next.js app move over with no rewrite. Ownkube provisions the instance, wires up the same deploy flow, and brings the logs, metrics, and health checks with it.

Railway only runs your app on its own infrastructure. Our Railway alternatives guide compares Railway with the other options.

FAQ

Do I need output: "standalone", or does the default build work?

The default build works, but it expects the full project and node_modules present at runtime, which makes for a much larger Docker image and a slower deploy. Standalone output is the setting almost every Next.js Docker guide converges on, and it is the one used in the Dockerfile above.

Does Ownkube support the App Router and Server Actions?

Yes, both the App Router and the older Pages Router run the same way, since next start in the standalone build serves whatever the app builds. Server Actions run as part of the same Node process and read server-side environment variables normally.

How do I handle a value that is different between preview and production?

Set the environment variable per app in the dashboard or with okctl vars set <app> NAME=VALUE, and use a separate Ownkube app for each environment you want isolated, each with its own hostname, environment variables, and (if needed) database.

What happens if my wallet balance runs out mid-month?

The app pauses and any attached database keeps its data. Adding credit or the next monthly plan load resumes it. Unused wallet credit rolls over and never expires.

Can I use a custom domain?

An automatic *.ownkube.app hostname with TLS is provisioned for every app the moment it deploys, so you always have a working URL with no configuration. On Personal and Team you can also add your own domain to the app. You set two DNS records and Ownkube issues and renews the certificate. See Custom domains.

Should I host Next.js on Vercel instead?

For a personal, non-commercial frontend, Vercel's Hobby plan is free and runs Next.js well. A commercial project needs Pro at $20 per developer seat a month. Is Vercel free? covers the Hobby rules. Ownkube fits when the app needs a long-running server, workers or Postgres next to it.

For the always-current version of this walkthrough, see the Deploy Next.js guide in the docs.

Where Ownkube fits

Next.js wants a slim server image, a clean split between build-time and runtime configuration, and a database only when the app actually uses one, and Ownkube gives you all three without provisioning a cloud account first. Set standalone output, push the Dockerfile, set your environment variables, and the hostname and TLS are already waiting. See Ownkube pricing for the per-minute wallet model, from $5 a month. Deploy my first app.

title: The browser title was correct. The Open Graph title wasn’t.
description:
On 1 November 2026, an audit of the StackEndBox homepage found a small inconsistency that a browser-tab check had missed.

The HTML title already contained the company name. The Open Graph and Twitter titles still said “We design and build the software your business needs.” A separate page extractor returned that generic sentence as its page label. Its output matched the Open Graph field, while the browser tab remained correctly branded.

Both observations were accurate. They described different title sources.

Three fields, two answers

The initial page contained this combination:

<title>StackEndBox | Product Engineering, AI & Custom Software</title>
<meta property="og:title" content="We design and build the software your business needs.">
<meta name="twitter:title" content="We design and build the software your business needs.">

The release aligned the two share titles with the existing HTML title. It preserved the heading, design, canonical URL, robots directive and company schema.

Field Before After
HTML title Branded Branded
Open Graph title Generic sentence Same branded title
Twitter title Generic sentence Same branded title

This is a useful homepage policy when every surface should identify the same company. Other pages can legitimately use different social copy. Agree on a per-page expectation before turning consistency into a release gate.

Why checking only document.title misses the problem

A test that asserts document.title will pass for the initial page above. A test that uses querySelector for each metadata field can also overlook duplicate tags because it returns only the first match.

Collect every matching tag and keep the arrays intact:

const snapshot = await page.evaluate(() => ({
  title: [...document.head.querySelectorAll("title")]
    .map(el => el.textContent ?? ""),
  "og:title": [...document.head.querySelectorAll(
    'meta[property="og:title"]'
  )].map(el => el.getAttribute("content") ?? ""),
  "twitter:title": [...document.head.querySelectorAll(
    'meta[name="twitter:title"]'
  )].map(el => el.getAttribute("content") ?? "")
}));

This collection is read-only. It assumes an existing Playwright-compatible page handle and should run after the application has reached its rendered-ready state. Choose that state for your application instead of adding an arbitrary delay.

The arrays make four separate findings visible: a missing field, duplicate fields, an empty value and a value that differs from the reviewed expectation. DOM values have already decoded HTML entities, so compare the rendered ampersand with an ampersand rather than the source spelling &.

A runnable contract check

The public audit module and instructions contain a dependency-free function and eight synthetic example cases. The function accepts the snapshot above and an expected title:

const result = auditTitleSnapshot(
  snapshot,
  "StackEndBox | Product Engineering, AI & Custom Software"
);

if (!result.ok) {
  throw new Error(JSON.stringify(result.issues));
}

The examples cover aligned values, generic Open Graph copy, missing Twitter metadata, duplicate Open Graph tags, an empty title, three generic fields, surrounding whitespace and a malformed snapshot. All eight passed when executed in a JavaScript isolate. The public file includes the examples so readers can rerun them.

Those examples test the comparison contract. Collecting the correct page and waiting for its rendered state remain responsibilities of the browser test.

Verify the artifact that actually ships

This homepage uses a preserved static release. Editing future application source alone would leave the served artifact unchanged. The correction therefore covered the served response and future source, with validation around the known metadata structure.

The production change went through source checks, canonical release checks, provider preflight and hosted staging before publication. After publication, a browser reload showed exactly one of each title field with the branded value. A fresh independent fetch then returned the branded label too.

For another application, the implementation may simply be a shared metadata object. The acceptance question stays the same: does the response and rendered page that readers receive contain the reviewed values?

Keep search outcomes separate

Google documents Open Graph titles among the sources it can use for search-result title links. That makes the field worth checking alongside the HTML title and visible heading. Google chooses the resulting title automatically and has to recrawl and reprocess updates.

The metadata correction established a consistent page. It did not establish a ranking improvement. The ordinary company-name query still received a spelling substitution immediately after deployment. A title audit cannot measure indexability, Google’s interpretation of a brand query or search position.

A practical release checklist is therefore two-part: verify the page contract you control, then observe search behaviour separately. Passing one check should never silently mark the other complete.

title: How to Retry Email API Calls in Go: Backoff for Signup Verification
description:
Short answer: Use a bounded exponential retry policy for failed email API calls: start at 2 seconds, cap the delay at 32 seconds, stop after 5 attempts, and make every attempt idempotent.

When a signup verification email fails, the useful alarm is not “the API returned 500.” The useful alarm is “the account has not received a link after the retry budget expired.” Keep the signup state idempotent, log every attempt, and inspect the email list or event list afterward for messages that still need action.

This protects deliverability in two directions. A short-lived provider failure gets another chance without a request storm; a permanent failure stops consuming capacity and becomes visible to an operator. The verification template should remain owned by the team that can review its wording, expiry behavior, and abuse controls. Delivery infrastructure can be shared, but the decision about what the user receives should not disappear inside a vendor dashboard.

Keep it finite.

Exactly.

What should the on-call alarm actually say?

Picture the page at 03:10: signup completion is healthy, but the “verification email delivered” counter has fallen below its normal range. The first response is usually to inspect the last request, find a 503 or 429, and restart the worker. That is a noisy response if the worker immediately sends the same request again.

The earlier signal is a growing set of verification records in pending_delivery, partitioned by outcome. For example, a record that receives a 503 on attempt 1 should carry a next retry time near 2 seconds later; a second transient failure should move it toward 4 seconds, and the fifth failure should become an explicit terminal review state rather than another hidden background task. Log at least the account identifier, message identifier, attempt number, HTTP status, provider request ID when available, and the next retry time. Do not log the verification token or the full email address. Those fields help answer two different questions: did the API accept the request, and did the message later reach a useful terminal state? They also let the on-call compare the queue age with the user-facing signup state without opening a provider console and guessing which request belongs to which account. That correlation is the difference between an alert that points to a repair and an alert that merely announces traffic.

I initially treated every non-2xx response as retryable. That was a mistake in the policy, even before it became a production problem: an invalid request can be repeated five times with perfect exponential math and still remain invalid. Retry transient rate limits and server failures; surface authentication, validation, suppression, and other terminal responses for review. A backoff policy is not a substitute for classifying errors.

How should I handle retrying failed email API calls?

Use a capped schedule, not an unbounded formula. With a 2-second base, the nominal delays are 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 seconds. Five attempts give the system a finite boundary. That boundary matters because a signup flow should not keep a worker occupied indefinitely while an upstream service is unavailable.

Honor Retry-After when the server supplies it, but still enforce the local cap. A provider may ask for a delay longer than the workflow can tolerate; the application should record that fact and move the message to a later queue or an operator-visible state rather than sleeping forever. Add jitter in a real queue so many workers do not wake on the same second.

Here is a complete retry wrapper around the verified send route. It takes the request JSON from EMAIL_JSON because the exact message fields belong to the API contract you are using; the retry behavior does not need to duplicate that schema. Set EMAIL_API_BASE_URL to the service base URL in the deployment environment. The program uses a stable idempotency key for the message, checks response bodies on errors, and exits nonzero when the budget is exhausted.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    baseURL := os.Getenv("EMAIL_API_BASE_URL")
    payload := os.Getenv("EMAIL_JSON")
    idempotencyKey := os.Getenv("EMAIL_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" || baseURL == "" || payload == "" || idempotencyKey == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY, EMAIL_API_BASE_URL, EMAIL_JSON, and EMAIL_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY are required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 3*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()

    if err := sendWithRetry(ctx, client, apiKey, baseURL, []byte(payload), idempotencyKey); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

func sendWithRetry(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, apiKey string, baseURL string, payload []byte, idempotencyKey string) error {
    const maxAttempts = 5
    const baseDelay = 2 * time.Second
    const maxDelay = 32 * time.Second

    for attempt := 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, strings.TrimRight(baseURL, "/")+"/v1/email/send", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("build request: %w", err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            if attempt == maxAttempts {
                return fmt.Errorf("attempt %d transport error: %w", attempt, err)
            }
            if err := wait(ctx, baseDelay, attempt, ""); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            continue
        }

        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("read response: %w", readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Printf("email accepted on attempt %d: %s\n", attempt, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
            return nil
        }

        retryable := resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests || resp.StatusCode >= 500
        if !retryable || attempt == maxAttempts {
            return fmt.Errorf("email send failed on attempt %d with HTTP %d: %s", attempt, resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        if err := wait(ctx, baseDelay, attempt, resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    return errors.New("retry loop ended unexpectedly")
}

func wait(ctx context.Context, base time.Duration, attempt int, retryAfter string) error {
    delay := base * time.Duration(1<<(attempt-1))
    if delay > 32*time.Second {
        delay = 32 * time.Second
    }
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(retryAfter)); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
        delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        if delay > 32*time.Second {
            delay = 32 * time.Second
        }
    }
    // Jitter avoids synchronized retries when several workers see the same outage.
    delay += time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(delay / 4)))
    timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
    defer timer.Stop()
    select {
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return fmt.Errorf("retry wait canceled: %w", ctx.Err())
    case <-timer.C:
        return nil
    }
}

The key detail is not the sleep. It is the stable Idempotency-Key. If a timeout occurs after the provider accepted the message, the next attempt must be recognizable as the same operation. Generate that key from the signup verification record, persist it before enqueueing, and reuse it on every retry. A retry without that property can create duplicate links and duplicate messages.

One small Go concern is worth calling out: the jitter expression assumes a positive delay, which this policy guarantees. If you adapt the helper to accept arbitrary durations, guard that random range before calling rand.Int63n. Tiny helpers become incident code surprisingly quickly.

Which service should own the template and delivery path?

The template owner and the transport owner can be different. For a B2B SaaS signup, I would keep the verification template in application-controlled configuration or a reviewed template store, then send through a provider with clear delivery events. The review boundary should include subject, link lifetime, locale, unsubscribe handling where applicable, and the domain authentication setup. SPF is one part of that setup, not a complete deliverability diagnosis.

The practical choices have different operational shapes:

Option Useful fit Boundary to verify
Amazon SES Teams already operating on AWS and comfortable assembling their own email workflow More responsibility sits with the application for templates, event handling, and operational policy
SendGrid A managed provider with broad email tooling and a dashboard-oriented workflow Decide which template changes require code review and how provider-side edits are audited
Mailgun API-first teams that want delivery events and domain-oriented tooling Confirm regional, compliance, and event-retention requirements before making it the only path
Postmark Transactional email teams that want a focused product boundary Check whether its template and stream model matches signup verification and future message types
A unified REST layer such as Infrai A small platform team that wants one key and one bill across backend services, with email as one capability It does not provide SMTP relay or hosted email OTP; events are pull-based, so polling and the application-owned fallback remain your responsibility

There is no universal winner here. SES may fit an AWS-heavy platform; Postmark may be the clearer boundary for a narrowly transactional product; SendGrid or Mailgun may fit teams already invested in their tooling. A unified REST layer is attractive when reducing key and invoice sprawl matters across backend services, but it should not erase ownership of the verification experience.

The trade-off is concrete. A unified layer is a poor fit if your requirement is SMTP relay, hosted email OTP, webhook-driven event handling, or a domestic compliance decision based on a specific pending vendor. In those cases, choose a provider whose documented capability matches the requirement and keep the application-level retry policy anyway.

For the retry workflow, Infrai exposes the send route and list/event routes needed for follow-up inspection, while its event model is pull-based. That means the worker can retry, then a reconciler can poll for messages requiring further action. The limitation is real-time coordination: there are no webhook events in this namespace, so polling needs its own rate limit and checkpoint. It does not turn a provider response into proof that an inbox received the link.

What should happen after the fifth attempt?

Stop retrying. Mark the delivery attempt as needs_review or enqueue it in a controlled recovery queue with a new operator-visible reason. The user-facing signup state should distinguish “account created, verification pending” from “verification request rejected.” Do not silently issue a second token just because the first delivery attempt timed out; that can invalidate a link the user is already opening.

The reconciliation job should inspect the email list and event list, correlate provider IDs with the local verification record, and check suppression or bounce signals where the chosen service exposes them. Since the event surface is pull-based in this scenario, give the poller its own rate limit and checkpoint. Otherwise the recovery job becomes the next source of load during an incident.

Finally, alert on the symptoms that affect the user: pending verification age, terminal send failures by status class, duplicate idempotency keys, and the proportion of records needing review. A high retry count is a useful diagnostic, but it is not the business outcome. The business outcome is a verification link delivered once, with enough evidence to explain what happened when it was not.

Further reading

  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
  • Amazon SES Developer Guide
  • SendGrid Mail Send API
  • Mailgun Sending Messages
  • Postmark Developer Documentation

title: AWS FinOps Field Notes (2026-11-01): Auditing RDS Extended Support Charges with Python
description:
While auditing cloud infrastructure costs this week, recurring configuration gaps continue to quietly inflate monthly cloud bills.

Field Insight: The Hidden Cost Trap

Antonio Augusto Maguelniski: "A client who asked him to halve their AWS bill saw it double from February to March 2025 with no new resources, because the RDS line jumped from about $30 to about $330/month when two PostgreSQL 12 databases left standard support."

When managed resources drift out of standard support windows or detached storage components persist after instance terminations, infrastructure spend spikes without any increase in user traffic or compute demand.

Auditing Outdated RDS Engine Versions with Boto3

Rather than relying on manual console spot-checks across multiple AWS regions, you can automate inspection using a lightweight Python script:

import boto3

def audit_rds_engine_versions(region='us-east-1'):
    rds = boto3.client('rds', region_name=region)
    instances = rds.describe_db_instances().get('DBInstances', [])

    # PostgreSQL <= 12 and MySQL <= 5.7 incur AWS Extended Support charges
    eol_engines = {'postgres': 12.0, 'mysql': 5.7}
    flagged = []

    for db in instances:
        db_id = db['DBInstanceIdentifier']
        engine = db['Engine']
        version_str = db['EngineVersion']
        parts = version_str.split('.')
        major_ver = float(f"{parts[0]}.{parts[1]}") if len(parts) > 1 else float(parts[0])

        for eol_key, max_ver in eol_engines.items():
            if eol_key in engine and major_ver <= max_ver:
                flagged.append({'DBInstance': db_id, 'Engine': engine, 'Version': version_str})
                print(f"[ALERT] {db_id} ({engine} {version_str}) is past standard support! Extended Support fees apply.")

    return flagged

if __name__ == '__main__':
    audit_rds_engine_versions()

Continuous Multi-Account Governance

Running one-off audit scripts in single regions does not scale across enterprise AWS Organizations. Sustained cloud cost management requires cross-account role assumption (sts:AssumeRole), cost anomaly correlation, and automated scheduled auditing.

title: Building a Waitlist with Automatic Promotion in Spring Boot (and Keeping the Queue Gap-Free)
description:
🇺🇸 English version (🇧🇷 versão em português logo abaixo)

The problem: sessions with limited spots

I'm building a tutoring management system with Java, Spring Boot and PostgreSQL. Students can become tutors for a subject, and tutors open sessions with a limited number of spots.

That raised a real business question: what happens when a session is full? I didn't want to just return "Session is full". I wanted an optional waitlist:

  • if there's a free spot, the student is confirmed;
  • if the session is full and allows a waitlist, the student goes to the queue;
  • when a confirmed student cancels, the first in line is promoted automatically and gets notified;
  • the rest of the queue moves up, with no gaps (1, 2, 3... never 2, 3, 5).

Modeling the enrollment

Each enrollment has a status and an optional position in the queue:

  • CONFIRMED → has a spot, queuePosition is null
  • WAITLISTED → waiting, queuePosition is 1, 2, 3...
  • CANCELLED → left the session, queuePosition is null

In the database, I made sure an invalid position can never be saved:

CREATE TABLE enrollment (
    id             UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    status         enrollment_status NOT NULL,
    queue_position INT               CHECK (queue_position >= 1),
    session_id     UUID              NOT NULL REFERENCES session (id),
    student_id     UUID              NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id),
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ       NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

The repository only needs two Spring Data derived queries. No SQL written by hand:

long countBySessionAndStatus(Session session, EnrollmentStatus enrollmentStatus);

List<Enrollment> findBySessionAndStatusOrderByQueuePositionAsc(Session session, EnrollmentStatus enrollmentStatus);

Enrolling: confirmed or waitlisted?

After checking that the session exists, is active and the student isn't already enrolled, the enroll method decides where the student goes:

long confirmedCount = enrollmentRepository.countBySessionAndStatus(session, EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED);

if (confirmedCount < session.getSpots()) {
    Enrollment enrollment = new Enrollment(EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED, session, student);
    return enrollmentRepository.save(enrollment);
}

if (session.isAllowsWaitlist()) {
    long waitlistedCount = enrollmentRepository.countBySessionAndStatus(session, EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED);

    int queuePosition = (int) waitlistedCount + 1;

    Enrollment enrollment = new Enrollment(EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED, session, student);
    enrollment.setQueuePosition(queuePosition);

    return enrollmentRepository.save(enrollment);
}

throw new SessionFullException("Session is full");

If there's no spot and no waitlist, a SessionFullException is thrown, and my @RestControllerAdvice turns it into a 409 Conflict.

Cancelling: promoting the first in line

This is the most interesting part. When a student cancels, three things must happen together:

  1. the enrollment becomes CANCELLED;
  2. if that student had a confirmed spot, the first in the queue is promoted and notified;
  3. the queue is renumbered. 
@Transactional
public Enrollment cancelEnrollment(UUID enrollmentUuid, UUID userUuid) {
    // ... find the enrollment, check permission and status

    EnrollmentStatus previousStatus = enrollment.getStatus();

    enrollment.setStatus(EnrollmentStatus.CANCELLED);
    enrollment.setQueuePosition(null);

    List<Enrollment> waitlist = enrollmentRepository
            .findBySessionAndStatusOrderByQueuePositionAsc(enrollment.getSession(), EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED);

    if (previousStatus == EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED && !waitlist.isEmpty()) {
        Enrollment promoted = waitlist.get(0);
        promoted.setStatus(EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED);
        promoted.setQueuePosition(null);
        Notification notification = new Notification(NotificationEventType.SPOT_PROMOTED,
                "You have been promoted from the waitlist", promoted.getStudent());
        notificationRepository.save(notification);
    }

    // ... renumber the queue (next section)
}

Notice previousStatus: if the student who cancelled was only waiting, no spot was freed, so nobody gets promoted. The queue still has to be renumbered, though.

Renumbering the queue without gaps

After the promotion, the list still contains the promoted student (now CONFIRMED). So I only renumber whoever is still WAITLISTED:

int position = 1;

for (Enrollment waiting : waitlist) {
    if (waiting.getStatus() == EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED) {
        waiting.setQueuePosition(position);
        position++;
    }
}

enrollmentRepository.saveAll(waitlist);
return enrollmentRepository.save(enrollment);

The @Transactional is what makes this safe: cancelling, promoting, notifying and renumbering are all or nothing. If anything fails halfway, nothing is saved, and I never end up with a cancelled spot and nobody promoted.

Proving it with unit tests

I tested the service with JUnit 5 and Mockito. The main scenario: a queue with positions 1, 2 and 3, and a confirmed student cancels. Expected result: the 1st becomes CONFIRMED, the others become 1 and 2, and a notification goes to the right student.

Enrollment enrollmentTest = sessionService.cancelEnrollment(enrollmentUuid, student.getId());

Assertions.assertEquals(EnrollmentStatus.CANCELLED, enrollmentTest.getStatus());
Assertions.assertNull(enrollmentTest.getQueuePosition());

Assertions.assertEquals(EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED, firstWaiting.getStatus());
Assertions.assertNull(firstWaiting.getQueuePosition());
Assertions.assertEquals(1, secondWaiting.getQueuePosition());
Assertions.assertEquals(2, thirdWaiting.getQueuePosition());

ArgumentCaptor<Notification> notification = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Notification.class);
verify(notificationRepository).save(notification.capture());

Assertions.assertEquals(NotificationEventType.SPOT_PROMOTED, notification.getValue().getEventType());
Assertions.assertEquals(promotedStudent, notification.getValue().getReceiver());

ArgumentCaptor was new to me: it lets you grab the object passed to the mock and check what was saved, not only that something was saved.

What I learned and next steps

  • Modeling the states (CONFIRMED, WAITLISTED, CANCELLED) first made the code much simpler.
  • Validating in two places (service + CHECK constraint in the database) protects data even if a bug slips through.
  • @Transactional matters most when one action changes several rows.
  • A next step: enroll checks the count and then saves. Two students enrolling at the exact same moment could both see the last spot free. I want to study locking (for example, a pessimistic lock on the session) to handle that.

The full code is on GitHub: jg-abreu/tutoring-management-system

Thanks for reading! Feedback is very welcome. 🙌

🇧🇷 Versão em português

Criando uma lista de espera com promoção automática no Spring Boot (sem buracos na fila)

O problema: sessões com vagas limitadas

Estou construindo um sistema de gestão de monitorias com Java, Spring Boot e PostgreSQL. Alunos podem virar monitores de uma disciplina, e os monitores abrem sessões com um número limitado de vagas.

Isso trouxe uma pergunta de negócio real: o que acontece quando a sessão lota? Eu não queria só responder "Session is full". Queria uma lista de espera opcional:

  • se tem vaga, o aluno fica confirmado;
  • se a sessão está cheia e aceita lista de espera, o aluno entra na fila;
  • quando um aluno confirmado cancela, o primeiro da fila é promovido automaticamente e recebe uma notificação;
  • o resto da fila anda, sem buracos (1, 2, 3... nunca 2, 3, 5).

Modelando a inscrição

Cada inscrição tem um status e uma posição opcional na fila:

  • CONFIRMED → tem vaga, queuePosition é null
  • WAITLISTED → esperando, queuePosition é 1, 2, 3...
  • CANCELLED → saiu da sessão, queuePosition é null

No banco, garanti que uma posição inválida nunca seja salva:

CREATE TABLE enrollment (
    id             UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    status         enrollment_status NOT NULL,
    queue_position INT               CHECK (queue_position >= 1),
    session_id     UUID              NOT NULL REFERENCES session (id),
    student_id     UUID              NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id),
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ       NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

O repositório só precisa de duas derived queries do Spring Data, sem escrever SQL na mão:

long countBySessionAndStatus(Session session, EnrollmentStatus enrollmentStatus);

List<Enrollment> findBySessionAndStatusOrderByQueuePositionAsc(Session session, EnrollmentStatus enrollmentStatus);

Inscrevendo: confirmado ou na fila?

Depois de verificar que a sessão existe, está ativa e o aluno ainda não está inscrito, o método enroll decide para onde o aluno vai:

long confirmedCount = enrollmentRepository.countBySessionAndStatus(session, EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED);

if (confirmedCount < session.getSpots()) {
    Enrollment enrollment = new Enrollment(EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED, session, student);
    return enrollmentRepository.save(enrollment);
}

if (session.isAllowsWaitlist()) {
    long waitlistedCount = enrollmentRepository.countBySessionAndStatus(session, EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED);

    int queuePosition = (int) waitlistedCount + 1;

    Enrollment enrollment = new Enrollment(EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED, session, student);
    enrollment.setQueuePosition(queuePosition);

    return enrollmentRepository.save(enrollment);
}

throw new SessionFullException("Session is full");

Se não tem vaga nem lista de espera, é lançada uma SessionFullException, que o meu @RestControllerAdvice transforma em 409 Conflict.

Cancelando: promovendo o primeiro da fila

Essa é a parte mais interessante. Quando um aluno cancela, três coisas precisam acontecer juntas:

  1. a inscrição vira CANCELLED;
  2. se esse aluno tinha vaga confirmada, o primeiro da fila é promovido e notificado;
  3. a fila é renumerada. 
@Transactional
public Enrollment cancelEnrollment(UUID enrollmentUuid, UUID userUuid) {
    // ... busca a inscrição, verifica permissão e status

    EnrollmentStatus previousStatus = enrollment.getStatus();

    enrollment.setStatus(EnrollmentStatus.CANCELLED);
    enrollment.setQueuePosition(null);

    List<Enrollment> waitlist = enrollmentRepository
            .findBySessionAndStatusOrderByQueuePositionAsc(enrollment.getSession(), EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED);

    if (previousStatus == EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED && !waitlist.isEmpty()) {
        Enrollment promoted = waitlist.get(0);
        promoted.setStatus(EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED);
        promoted.setQueuePosition(null);
        Notification notification = new Notification(NotificationEventType.SPOT_PROMOTED,
                "You have been promoted from the waitlist", promoted.getStudent());
        notificationRepository.save(notification);
    }

    // ... renumera a fila (próxima seção)
}

Repare no previousStatus: se quem cancelou estava só esperando, nenhuma vaga foi liberada, então ninguém é promovido. Mas a fila ainda precisa ser renumerada.

Renumerando a fila sem buracos

Depois da promoção, a lista ainda contém o aluno promovido (agora CONFIRMED). Por isso só renumero quem continua WAITLISTED:

int position = 1;

for (Enrollment waiting : waitlist) {
    if (waiting.getStatus() == EnrollmentStatus.WAITLISTED) {
        waiting.setQueuePosition(position);
        position++;
    }
}

enrollmentRepository.saveAll(waitlist);
return enrollmentRepository.save(enrollment);

O @Transactional é o que torna isso seguro: cancelar, promover, notificar e renumerar é tudo ou nada. Se algo falhar no meio, nada é salvo, e nunca fico com uma vaga cancelada sem ninguém promovido.

Provando com testes unitários

Testei o service com JUnit 5 e Mockito. O cenário principal: uma fila com posições 1, 2 e 3, e um aluno confirmado cancela. Resultado esperado: o 1º vira CONFIRMED, os outros viram 1 e 2, e uma notificação vai para o aluno certo.

Enrollment enrollmentTest = sessionService.cancelEnrollment(enrollmentUuid, student.getId());

Assertions.assertEquals(EnrollmentStatus.CANCELLED, enrollmentTest.getStatus());
Assertions.assertNull(enrollmentTest.getQueuePosition());

Assertions.assertEquals(EnrollmentStatus.CONFIRMED, firstWaiting.getStatus());
Assertions.assertNull(firstWaiting.getQueuePosition());
Assertions.assertEquals(1, secondWaiting.getQueuePosition());
Assertions.assertEquals(2, thirdWaiting.getQueuePosition());

ArgumentCaptor<Notification> notification = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Notification.class);
verify(notificationRepository).save(notification.capture());

Assertions.assertEquals(NotificationEventType.SPOT_PROMOTED, notification.getValue().getEventType());
Assertions.assertEquals(promotedStudent, notification.getValue().getReceiver());

O ArgumentCaptor era novidade para mim: ele permite pegar o objeto passado para o mock e verificar o que foi salvo, e não só que algo foi salvo.

O que aprendi e próximos passos

  • Modelar os estados primeiro (CONFIRMED, WAITLISTED, CANCELLED) deixou o código muito mais simples.
  • Validar em dois lugares (service + constraint CHECK no banco) protege os dados mesmo se um bug passar.
  • O @Transactional faz mais diferença quando uma ação altera várias linhas.
  • Um próximo passo: o enroll conta e depois salva. Dois alunos se inscrevendo exatamente no mesmo momento poderiam ver a última vaga livre ao mesmo tempo. Quero estudar locking (por exemplo, um lock pessimista na sessão) para tratar isso.

O código completo está no GitHub: jg-abreu/tutoring-management-system

Obrigado por ler! Feedback é muito bem-vindo. 🙌
