title: Queues: at-least-once means never exactly-once
description:
The most useful sentence I've read about queues: at-least-once delivery is easy, exactly-once processing is a property of your handler, not the broker.

Which means every consumer needs to survive a duplicate. The ways I do that, in order of preference:

  1. Idempotent writes. UPDATE ... WHERE version = expected instead of blind writes.
  2. A dedupe key with a unique index. Cheapest and most explicit.
  3. A processed table with a TTL, for handlers with side effects.

The failure mode to design for isn't the duplicate, it's the poison message: one bad event that blocks the partition because the handler retries forever. Give every consumer a max attempt count and a dead-letter queue you actually read.

One more: make the retry delay grow. A flat 1-second retry turns a small outage into a stampede.

What's your dead-letter policy?

title: Why I don't automatically retry timed-out AI video requests
description:
A request times out. The obvious next step is to try again.

For a video generation request, that can be an expensive guess. The provider may already be rendering the first video. You just didn't receive its task ID.

I'm working on AI Effect Studio, where people choose an effect, upload photos, and get a short video. The generation backend has to deal with this gap between sending a paid request and knowing what happened to it.

Here's how the current implementation handles it, including the part that still needs manual review.

The timeout doesn't tell you enough

Imagine this sequence:

  1. Our server sends a generation request.
  2. The provider accepts it and starts work.
  3. The connection drops before our server receives the response.

From our side, the request failed. From the provider's side, there's a video being generated.

Sending the same payload again doesn't necessarily resume that work. Unless the provider supports a documented idempotency mechanism, it may create another paid task.

Exponential backoff changes when that second request happens. It doesn't make the second request safe.

Record the attempt before sending it

Each local job stores a submission timestamp separately from its provider task ID. Before calling the generation API, the worker records that it's about to submit.

That gives the next worker enough information to distinguish these cases:

What the job has What the worker does
No submission marker and no provider ID Claim the job, record the attempt, then submit
A provider ID Query that existing task
A submission marker but no provider ID Hold the job for support review
An output URL already recorded Continue processing or saving that video

The database updates are conditional, and processing uses a short lease so overlapping workers don't casually pick up the same job. The submission marker is checked and written in the database before the external call.

There's an awkward consequence here. If the worker crashes after writing the marker but before sending the request, the job also ends up waiting for review. It might never have reached the provider.

I accept that tradeoff for the expensive generation step. The marker prevents an automatic second submission, but it cannot prove that the first one happened. This is a conservative fallback, and it leaves some real work for support.

A provider-side idempotency key would be a better way to close that gap. A local timestamp can't give us exactly-once execution across two systems.

Retry the stage that failed

A video job keeps going after the model finishes. Depending on the effect, there's a soundtrack step, followed by saving the output to our own storage.

If storage fails, generating another video would be a costly way to retry a file transfer. The job records the source video URL so recovery can continue from the output it already has.

The soundtrack step has a different retry policy. It's much cheaper than generation, so it gets bounded retries. If those are exhausted, the delivery path can fall back to the silent footage. That is a product compromise: the user gets a video, but the soundtrack may be missing. The interface and product description need to make that possibility clear.

Credits need the same care. A confirmed generation failure restores the user's allowance. An ambiguous submission stays reserved while it's investigated, because a timeout alone doesn't tell us whether paid work is still running.

The question I use when reviewing these paths is pretty mundane: if this line runs twice, do we check the same work, or buy more work?

Polling an existing task, copying an existing output, and starting a fresh render deserve different answers. Putting all three behind one generic retry helper would hide the distinction I most need to see.

title: Why an Up-to-Date ECU Database Matters More Than You Think
description:
A tuning business is only as good as its information. New cars arrive, manufacturers revise engine control units, and tools unlock models that were previously out of reach. If the data behind your quotes and calculators is stale, you will promise things you cannot deliver, or miss opportunities for cars you could have helped.

What goes into a gains database

At a basic level, a database links a specific vehicle to details such as:

  • Engine code and displacement
  • ECU and TCU (transmission control unit) type
  • Stock power and torque
  • Typical tuned figures for common stages
  • Which reading and writing tools support it, and by what method

Each of these changes over time. A model year may swap ECU hardware; a software revision may change what tools can do.

The cost of getting it wrong

  • Wrong figures. Quoting gains for the wrong engine variant damages trust.
  • Wrong tool assumptions. Booking a job that your tools cannot actually handle wastes time and annoys the customer.
  • Missed enquiries. If a new model is not in your system, the visitor sees "not found" and leaves.

How to keep data fresh

If you maintain your own records:

  1. Log the outcome of every job: vehicle, ECU, tool, result, and any problems
  2. Review new releases from your tool suppliers regularly
  3. Share information with trusted peers where appropriate
  4. Date-stamp entries so you know how old a figure is

If you use a third-party database or calculator, ask the supplier how often it is updated, where the figures come from and how you can request corrections. For example, the Tuning Tech calculator states that its gains database is continuously updated with new ECUs, brands, models and gain figures, and that larger customers can ask about a dedicated database. As with any supplier, ask for specifics rather than relying on a general claim.

Be honest about uncertainty

No database is perfect. Where data is estimated, say so. Where a model is unsupported, say that too, because customers appreciate honesty far more than a failed job.

Use the database for the customer experience

Good data lets you answer the first question quickly. When a visitor enters a registration and sees stock versus tuned power and torque in seconds, the enquiry that follows is better informed. The same data can support add-on recommendations for the specific vehicle, where legal for road use.

A simple audit

Pick ten vehicles you have worked on recently and check that:

  • the engine and ECU details in your records are correct
  • the gains you quoted match what you delivered
  • the tools and methods recorded still apply

If more than one or two are wrong, your data process needs attention.

In short

Treat your database as a core business asset. Keep it current, label uncertainty and review it regularly.

title: rspec-wasm v0.2.0: Testing Ruby Code That Integrates with JavaScript and WebAssembly
description:
In September 2026, I released rspec-wasm, a tool for running RSpec tests on ruby.wasm, and introduced it in my previous DEV article:

Stop Writing Ruby Tests in JS Template Literals: Meet rspec-wasm

I've now released rspec-wasm v0.2.0, which adds support for asynchronous JavaScript setup and teardown around RSpec execution.

One of the great advantages of building applications with WebAssembly is the ability to combine functionality from different Wasm modules.

However, until now, rspec-wasm had no way to asynchronously initialize an external runtime before running RSpec tests or clean it up afterward.

With v0.2.0, we can initialize external JavaScript or Wasm runtimes before running RSpec, making it possible to test Ruby code that interacts with them.

In this article, I'll demonstrate the new functionality by testing Ruby code that uses a WebAssembly-based MP3 decoder.

Why Use External Wasm Modules with ruby.wasm?

When developing applications with ruby.wasm, building a custom Wasm binary can expand what's possible.

However, if we want to use existing gems with a prebuilt ruby.wasm runtime, we're currently limited to pure Ruby gems.

This can lead to a few challenges:

  • An appropriate pure Ruby gem might not exist for the functionality we need.
  • A pure Ruby implementation might not provide the performance we expect.
  • Our application might be designed to combine multiple Wasm modules from the beginning.

In these situations, using external Wasm modules alongside ruby.wasm can be a practical solution.

For example, we might want to integrate:

  • Image and video processing libraries
  • Databases such as SQLite
  • Python/Wasm runtimes
  • Compression and cryptography libraries
  • Numerical computing or machine learning runtimes

But how can we test Ruby code that depends on these external runtimes?

That's where the new functionality in rspec-wasm v0.2.0 comes in.

Example: Decoding MP3 Audio with WebAssembly

Let's build a small example that initializes a WebAssembly-based MP3 decoder, calls it from Ruby, and verifies the decoded audio information using RSpec.

We'll use the following:

  • Node.js 18 or later
  • rspec-wasm 0.2.0
  • mpg123-decoder 1.0.3

Both ruby.wasm and RSpec are included in rspec-wasm, so we don't need to install them separately.

mpg123-decoder is an MP3 decoder that runs mpg123 through WebAssembly.

1. Create the Project

First, create a new project and install the dependencies.

mkdir rspec-wasm-mp3-example
cd rspec-wasm-mp3-example
npm init -y
npm install mpg123-decoder@1.0.3
npm install --save-dev rspec-wasm@0.2.0

Add the test command to package.json.

{
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "test": "rspec-wasm"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "mpg123-decoder": "1.0.3"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "rspec-wasm": "0.2.0"
  }
}

Our project will have the following structure:

.
├── lib/
│   └── audio_probe.rb
├── spec/
│   ├── fixtures/
│   │   └── tone.mp3
│   └── audio_probe_spec.rb
├── package.json
└── rspec-wasm.config.mjs

2. Prepare an MP3 File for Testing

For this example, we'll use a stereo MP3 file with a sample rate of 44.1 kHz.

Download the test file using the following commands:

mkdir -p spec/fixtures
curl -L https://github.com/eshaz/wasm-audio-decoders/raw/refs/heads/main/test/data/44100.stereo.cbr.mp3 \
  -o spec/fixtures/tone.mp3

This file comes from the test data in eshaz/wasm-audio-decoders, which is distributed under the MIT license.

If you use a different MP3 file, adjust the expected sample rate and channel count in the tests accordingly.

3. Initialize the Wasm Decoder Before Running RSpec

Now comes the main feature introduced in v0.2.0.

Create rspec-wasm.config.mjs to define the setup and teardown operations.

import fs from "node:fs/promises";
import path from "node:path";
import { MPEGDecoder } from "mpg123-decoder";

let decoder;

function summarize(decoded, encodedBytes) {
  const peakLevels = decoded.channelData.map((channel) => {
    let peak = 0;

    for (const sample of channel) {
      peak = Math.max(peak, Math.abs(sample));
    }

    return peak;
  });

  return {
    encoded_bytes: encodedBytes,
    sample_rate: decoded.sampleRate,
    channels: decoded.channelData.length,
    samples_per_channel: decoded.samplesDecoded,
    duration_ms: Math.round(
      decoded.samplesDecoded / decoded.sampleRate * 1000
    ),
    peak_levels: peakLevels,
    errors: decoded.errors.map((error) => error.message),
  };
}

export default {
  async setup({ workspaceRoot }) {
    decoder = new MPEGDecoder();
    await decoder.ready;

    globalThis.audioCodec = {
      async inspect(relativePath) {
        const root = path.resolve(workspaceRoot);
        const filePath = path.resolve(root, relativePath);
        const relative = path.relative(root, filePath);

        if (relative.startsWith("..") || path.isAbsolute(relative)) {
          throw new Error("Audio file must be inside the workspace");
        }

        const encoded = await fs.readFile(filePath);

        try {
          const decoded = decoder.decode(encoded);
          return JSON.stringify(
            summarize(decoded, encoded.byteLength)
          );
        } finally {
          await decoder.reset();
        }
      },
    };
  },

  async teardown() {
    decoder?.free();
    delete globalThis.audioCodec;
  },
};

The setup function initializes the Wasm decoder and waits until it's ready before RSpec starts.

We expose the initialized API through globalThis.audioCodec, allowing Ruby code to access it through the JavaScript bridge.

After the tests finish, teardown releases the decoder.

The execution flow looks like this:

Create Ruby VM
      |
      v
Asynchronously initialize
the MP3 Wasm decoder
      |
      v
Run RSpec tests
      |
      v
Release the decoder

This lifecycle management is particularly useful for external Wasm modules that require asynchronous initialization.

4. Await a JavaScript Promise from Ruby

Next, create lib/audio_probe.rb.

require "json"
require "js"

class AudioProbe
  def self.inspect(path)
    result = JS.global[:audioCodec]
      .call(:inspect, path)
      .await
      .to_s

    JSON.parse(result, symbolize_names: true)
  end
end

The JavaScript inspect function returns a Promise, so we use .await on the Ruby side to wait for the result.

In v0.2.0, rspec-wasm executes RSpec through RubyVM#evalAsync, allowing Ruby code inside specs to await JavaScript Promises.

Another important detail is that the MP3 binary data and decoded PCM data remain on the JavaScript/Wasm side.

Only a small JSON summary is returned to Ruby.

This avoids unnecessarily transferring large binary data across the Ruby–JavaScript boundary.

5. Write the RSpec Tests

Now let's create spec/audio_probe_spec.rb.

require "audio_probe"

RSpec.describe AudioProbe do
  it "decodes MP3 metadata with a WebAssembly codec" do
    result = described_class.inspect("spec/fixtures/tone.mp3")

    expect(result[:encoded_bytes]).to be > 0
    expect(result[:sample_rate]).to eq(44_100)
    expect(result[:channels]).to eq(2)
    expect(result[:samples_per_channel]).to be > 0
    expect(result[:duration_ms]).to be > 0
    expect(result[:peak_levels].first).to be_between(0.0, 1.0)
    expect(result[:errors]).to be_empty
  end

  it "rejects parent-directory traversal" do
    expect {
      described_class.inspect("../outside.mp3")
    }.to raise_error(JS::Error, /inside the workspace/)
  end
end

The first test actually decodes an MP3 file using WebAssembly and verifies properties such as the sample rate, channel count, and audio duration.

The second test verifies that the JavaScript API rejects attempts to access files outside the workspace using ../.

JavaScript exceptions are exposed as JS::Error on the Ruby side, so we can test them using the usual RSpec matchers.

A note about path validation: This example uses lexical path validation with path.relative. If you need to enforce workspace boundaries even when symbolic links are involved, you should also validate the resolved paths using fs.realpath.

For this demonstration, we'll keep things simple.

6. Run the Tests

Finally, run:

npm test

The output should look similar to this:

AudioProbe
  decodes MP3 metadata with a WebAssembly codec
  rejects parent-directory traversal

Finished in 0.10502 seconds (files took 1.3 seconds to load)
2 examples, 0 failures

2 examples, 0 failures!

We've successfully tested Ruby code that calls JavaScript, invokes a WebAssembly MP3 decoder, and returns the result to RSpec.

And we can use ordinary RSpec matchers throughout the process.

What's New in rspec-wasm v0.2.0?

Version 0.2.0 introduces the following features:

  • Configuration through rspec-wasm.config.mjs — Define JavaScript-side initialization and cleanup behavior.
  • Asynchronous setup and teardown — Initialize external runtimes before tests and release resources afterward.
  • Promise support in Ruby specs — Call JavaScript functions that return Promises and wait for their results using .await.
  • Reliable cleanup — Run teardown operations whether RSpec tests pass or fail.
  • Initialization failure handling — If setup fails, RSpec won't start, and the process exits with a non-zero status.

The MP3 decoder example demonstrates the first three features directly.

Conclusion

With rspec-wasm v0.2.0, we can now test more than just Ruby code running entirely inside ruby.wasm.

We can also test Ruby applications that use JavaScript as their host environment and integrate functionality from external WebAssembly modules.

I think combining multiple Wasm modules is one of the interesting possibilities of WebAssembly-based application development.

By supporting asynchronous runtime initialization and Promise handling, rspec-wasm makes it easier to write RSpec tests for these applications without moving test logic into JavaScript.

If you're building applications with ruby.wasm and other Wasm modules, give rspec-wasm a try!

References

  • rspec-wasm on npm
  • ruby.wasm on GitHub
  • RSpec
  • mpg123-decoder on npm
  • My previous DEV article: Stop Writing Ruby Tests in JS Template Literals: Meet rspec-wasm

title: The design system is a contract, not a component library
description:
The component library is the easy part. The contract is what makes a design system survive a team change.

A contract here means: what the component accepts, what it promises, and what you'll never change without a major version.

Practically:

  • Props are public API. Rename one and you've broken someone's page.
  • Deprecation needs a date and a codemod, not a note in a doc.
  • Docs are generated from the code, because handwritten docs drift within a sprint.
  • Version the package, even internally. "Just pull main" is how a design system becomes a fork.

The hard part is saying no. Every component request is a request to own another contract.

The best design systems I've used felt small, and the docs explained the why, not just the props.

Do you version your internal design system?

title: Idempotency keys: the boring header that saves the queue
description:
Every payment API has it, and almost no internal service does. Idempotency keys are the cheapest way to make a queue safe.

The shape I use in Go:

  • the client sends Idempotency-Key with the request
  • a middleware checks a dedupe table keyed by (key, route)
  • if it exists, return the stored response
  • if not, process, store the result with a TTL, then return

The subtle parts: store the response, not just the status; set the TTL to something longer than your retry window; and make the check-and-insert atomic, or two workers will race and both process.

The win is that at-least-once delivery becomes safe without changing the queue. The cost is one small table and a header.

I'd argue every handler that touches money or email should have one. What's the smallest service where you'd skip it?

title: Next.js 16: Fixing "cookies() can't be read inside 'use cache'" (and Caching Public Data Without It)
description:
You turn on Cache Components, add 'use cache' to a data function, and the build fails:

Error: Route "/broken": `cookies()` can't be read inside `"use cache"`. Read it outside the cached function and pass what you need as an argument.
Learn more: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/next-request-in-use-cache
    at h (lib/server-client.ts:6:29)
    at i (app/broken/page.tsx:7:24)

The confusing part is that your cached function might never call cookies() itself. In this example, the call is inside a helper that creates a "server client", the kind of cookie-aware factory that many auth and database SDKs ship for the App Router. The rule follows the call stack, so a cookie read anywhere below a 'use cache' boundary breaks it.

This post shows why that happens and the four patterns that fix it, each built and run on Next.js 16.4.3.

What you'll learn

  • Why cookies(), headers() and searchParams are not allowed in 'use cache'
  • How to cache public data when your SDK's default client reads cookies
  • How to pass a cookie value into a cached function safely
  • Where per-user data should go instead (and the Suspense rule that comes with it)
  • When 'use cache: private' is the right tool, and what it does not do

Prerequisites and versions

  • Next.js 16.4.3 with the App Router
  • React 19.3.1
  • TypeScript
  • Cache Components enabled (below)

Since Next.js 16.0, cacheComponents is a top-level config option. The current docs recommend setting partialPrefetching explicitly alongside it. Leaving it unset logs a warning:

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  partialPrefetching: true,
}

export default nextConfig

Background: why the rule exists

A 'use cache' function's output is stored and reused across requests and users. Its cache key is built from the build ID, a hash of the function's identity, and its serializable arguments (see the use cache reference).

Cookies and headers aren't arguments. If a cached function could read them, the cache key wouldn't reflect them, and one user's cookie-dependent result could be served to someone else. So Next.js forbids request-time APIs inside the cached scope:

Cached functions and components cannot access runtime APIs like cookies(), headers(), or searchParams, and the restriction follows the call stack: a helper the cached function calls that reads one of these fails the same way.

The docs also warn that on a dynamically rendered route this "can pass next build and fail under next start". Don't treat a green build as proof.

Reproducing the error

Here's a stand-in for a cookie-aware SDK factory. Real ones (for example, an auth or database "server client" for the App Router) usually take the cookie store so they can attach the user's session:

// lib/server-client.ts
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'

// Stand-in for a cookie-aware SDK factory such as an auth or database
// "server client". The important part: it calls cookies() internally.
export async function createServerClient() {
  const cookieStore = await cookies()
  const token = cookieStore.get('session')?.value ?? null
  return {
    async getPublicPosts() {
      return [{ id: 1, title: 'Hello' }, { id: 2, title: 'World' }]
    },
    async getMyDrafts() {
      if (!token) return []
      return [{ id: 99, title: `Draft for ${token}` }]
    },
  }
}

And a page that caches "public" posts with it:

// app/broken/page.tsx
import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache'
import { createServerClient } from '@/lib/server-client'

async function getPublicPosts() {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('hours')
  const client = await createServerClient() // calls cookies() inside the cache scope
  return client.getPublicPosts()
}

export default async function Page() {
  const posts = await getPublicPosts()
  return <ul>{posts.map((p) => <li key={p.id}>{p.title}</li>)}</ul>
}

next build fails with the error at the top of this post. The stack trace points to the cookies() call in the helper and to the cached function that called it. That's the fastest way to find the culprit in a real codebase.

The fix, in four patterns

All four patterns below live on one page. Together they built cleanly. Next.js marked the route as Partial Prerender (◐) with Revalidate 1h and Expire 1d, which come from the hours profile.

Pattern 1: Public data uses a client that never touches cookies

If the data is the same for everyone, it shouldn't go through a cookie-aware client at all. Create a separate client for public reads. With real SDKs, this usually means the plain client created with a public/anon key, not the App Router "server client" helper.

// lib/public-client.ts
// Stand-in for a cookie-free client (for example a plain SDK client created
// with a public/anon key). It never touches cookies() or headers().
export function createPublicClient() {
  return {
    async getPublicPosts() {
      return [
        { id: 1, title: 'Hello' },
        { id: 2, title: 'World' },
      ]
    },
  }
}

// 1. Public data: cookie-free client, safe to share across all users.
async function getPublicPosts() {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('hours')
  cacheTag('posts')
  const posts = await createPublicClient().getPublicPosts()
  return { posts, generatedAt: new Date().toISOString() }
}

generatedAt is there to show the caching. With the page served by next start, two requests without cookies and one request with Cookie: locale=fr; session=alice all returned the same generatedAt value. The entry was filled during the build and reused for everyone.

Security note: Only do this for data that really is public. If your database enforces row-level security based on the user's session, a cookie-free client sees what an anonymous user sees. That's correct for public data and wrong for anything personal.

Pattern 2: Read the cookie outside and pass the value in

This is the pattern the error page recommends. The value you pass becomes part of the cache key, so each distinct value gets its own entry.

// 2. Data that depends on one small cookie value: read the cookie outside,
//    pass the value in. The value becomes part of the cache key.
async function getGreeting(locale: 'en' | 'fr') {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('days')
  return locale === 'fr' ? 'Bonjour' : 'Hello'
}

async function Greeting() {
  const raw = (await cookies()).get('locale')?.value
  const locale = raw === 'fr' ? 'fr' : 'en'
  return <p id="greeting">{await getGreeting(locale)}</p>
}

The response without cookies showed Hello. With Cookie: locale=fr it showed Bonjour.

Two design choices here matter:

  • Normalize the value before passing it. raw === 'fr' ? 'fr' : 'en' limits the cache to two entries. If you pass a raw cookie straight through, any client can create a new cache entry by sending a random value.
  • Prefer low-cardinality values such as locale, theme, plan tier or feature-flag variant. Passing a session token or user ID technically works (one entry per user), but at that point you're building a per-user cache. That's usually better handled by Pattern 3 or 4.

Pattern 3: Per-user data stays uncached, inside Suspense

Personal data, like "my drafts", can just stay dynamic. Use the cookie-aware client outside any cache scope:

// 3. Per-user data: not in a shared cache at all. Rendered at request time
//    inside a Suspense boundary.
async function MyDrafts() {
  const client = await createServerClient()
  const drafts = await client.getMyDrafts()
  return (
    <ul id="drafts">
      {drafts.map((d) => (
        <li key={d.id}>{d.title}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  )
}

The full page puts it all together:

// app/fixed/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react'
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'
import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache'
import { createPublicClient } from '@/lib/public-client'
import { createServerClient } from '@/lib/server-client'

// 1. Public data: cookie-free client, safe to share across all users.
async function getPublicPosts() {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('hours')
  cacheTag('posts')
  const posts = await createPublicClient().getPublicPosts()
  return { posts, generatedAt: new Date().toISOString() }
}

// 2. Data that depends on one small cookie value: read the cookie outside,
//    pass the value in. The value becomes part of the cache key.
async function getGreeting(locale: 'en' | 'fr') {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('days')
  return locale === 'fr' ? 'Bonjour' : 'Hello'
}

async function Greeting() {
  const raw = (await cookies()).get('locale')?.value
  const locale = raw === 'fr' ? 'fr' : 'en'
  return <p id="greeting">{await getGreeting(locale)}</p>
}

// 3. Per-user data: not in a shared cache at all. Rendered at request time
//    inside a Suspense boundary.
async function MyDrafts() {
  const client = await createServerClient()
  const drafts = await client.getMyDrafts()
  return (
    <ul id="drafts">
      {drafts.map((d) => (
        <li key={d.id}>{d.title}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  )
}

export default async function Page() {
  const { posts, generatedAt } = await getPublicPosts()
  return (
    <main>
      <p id="generated">{generatedAt}</p>
      <ul id="posts">
        {posts.map((p) => (
          <li key={p.id}>{p.title}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading greeting…</p>}>
        <Greeting />
      </Suspense>
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading your drafts…</p>}>
        <MyDrafts />
      </Suspense>
    </main>
  )
}

The test results: without a session cookie the drafts list was empty. With session=alice it contained Draft for alice. The public posts and their timestamp were identical in both responses.

Why the Suspense boundaries matter. With Cache Components, reading cookies() outside <Suspense> blocks prerendering. This page fails the build:

// app/nosuspense/page.tsx — fails the build with Cache Components
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'

export default async function Page() {
  const session = (await cookies()).get('session')?.value
  return <p>{session ?? 'anonymous'}</p>
}

Error: Route "/nosuspense": Next.js encountered uncached or runtime data during prerendering.
`fetch(...)`, `cookies()`, `headers()`, `params`, `searchParams`, or `connection()` accessed outside of `<Suspense>` prevents the route from being prerendered, blocking the page load and leading to a slower user experience.
Ways to fix this:
  - [stream] Provide a placeholder with `<Suspense fallback={...}>` around the data access
  - [cache] For uncached data (`fetch`, database calls): cache the access with `"use cache"` (does not apply to `connection()`)
  - [block] Set `export const instant = false` to allow a blocking route

Wrapping the cookie-reading component in <Suspense> (as Greeting and MyDrafts are above) is the "[stream]" option. The static shell, which includes the cached public posts, is served right away, and the personal parts stream in.

Pattern 4: 'use cache: private' when you can't refactor

Sometimes the cookie read is buried in code you can't change easily. 'use cache: private' allows cookies(), headers() and searchParams inside the cached scope:

// app/private/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react'
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'
import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache'

async function getDashboard() {
  'use cache: private'
  cacheLife({ stale: 60 })
  const session = (await cookies()).get('session')?.value ?? 'guest'
  return { session, at: new Date().toISOString() }
}

async function Dashboard() {
  const { session, at } = await getDashboard()
  return <p id="dash">{session} @ {at}</p>
}

export default function Page() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading…</p>}>
      <Dashboard />
    </Suspense>
  )
}

The important thing is what "private" means. From the docs: "In production, matching calls within one request can reuse the same result, but Next.js does not store it in a server cache across production requests." The client router can keep the output in browser memory for the stale time.

The test confirmed this. Under next start, consecutive requests with the same session=alice cookie got a different at timestamp every time. So 'use cache: private' deduplicates within a request and feeds the browser's router cache. It does not make repeated server requests cheaper. If you need that, use Patterns 1–3.

Other limits from the docs:

  • connection() is still not allowed inside it.
  • You can't configure custom cache handlers for it.
  • Its stale time feeds the route's client cache. It must be at least 30 seconds for per-link prefetching and at least 5 minutes to be included in the route's App Shell.

Choosing a pattern

Your data Pattern
Same for everyone 1: cookie-free client inside 'use cache'
Varies by a small, known set of values from a cookie/header 2: read outside, normalize, pass as argument
Specific to the signed-in user 3: uncached, in a component wrapped in <Suspense>
Per-user, and the cookie read can't be moved 4: 'use cache: private', but no cross-request server cache

Common mistakes and troubleshooting

  • "My function doesn't call cookies()." Something it calls does. Check the stack trace. The first frame is the actual cookies() call, and the next frames show the path back to your cached function.
  • The build passes, production throws. On dynamically rendered routes, the error shows up when the route runs. Exercise the route under next start before deploying.
  • Passing the whole cookie store or headers() object. Arguments must be serializable, and class instances aren't. Extract the plain values you need.
  • Passing unbounded values. Each distinct argument creates a cache entry. Validate and normalize anything that comes from the client.
  • Using React.cache to smuggle values in. React.cache is isolated inside 'use cache' boundaries. Values set outside aren't visible inside. Use arguments.
  • Module-level promise caches. The error page notes that a cached function can stall if it awaits a promise stored outside the function (for example, in a module-scoped Map). 'use cache' already deduplicates calls with the same arguments, so remove the extra layer.
  • Draft Mode. You can read draftMode().isEnabled inside 'use cache', but cookies() and headers() are still off-limits, even in draft mode.

Limitations and alternatives

  • With the default in-memory cache handler on serverless platforms, runtime cache entries "typically don't persist across requests", although build-time caching works normally. Self-hosted servers keep entries in memory. If you need a shared runtime cache, look at 'use cache: remote', which uses a platform-provided handler and has network and cost trade-offs.
  • Cache entries don't survive a new deploy, because the build ID (or deploymentId) is part of the key.
  • Cache Components needs the Node.js runtime and doesn't support the runtime route segment config. Remove export const runtime = ... from routes when you adopt it.
  • Don't wait for plain 'use cache' to start accepting cookies()/headers(). A reply in discussion #82873 (August 2025) says "There's no plan to allow use cache to access cookies/headers" and suggests using 'use cache' as much as possible and the private variant only rarely. The current docs take the same position.

Conclusion

The error is Next.js protecting you from serving one user's data to another. Most of the time the fix is structural. Keep public reads on a cookie-free client inside 'use cache'. Read cookies at the edge of your component tree, normalize the values, and pass them in as arguments. Keep personal data uncached behind <Suspense>. Use 'use cache: private' only when you can't move the cookie read, and remember that it doesn't give you a cross-request server cache.

Next step: search your codebase for helpers that call cookies() or headers() and check whether any of them run below a 'use cache' boundary. Then run the affected routes under next start, not just next build.

References

  • use cache directive: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache
  • Error: Cannot access request data in use cache: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/next-request-in-use-cache
  • use cache: private: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private
  • use cache: remote: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote
  • cacheComponents config: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents
  • Caching guide: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/caching
  • Blocking prerender error: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/blocking-prerender-dynamic
  • Next.js discussion #82873, "Allow cookies() or headers() in use cache": https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/82873
  • Next.js 16.4 release post: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-4

title: Small design systems: tokens first, components second
description:
Every design system I've built that started with components ended up with a pile of one-off variants. The ones that started with tokens survived.

Tokens are the decisions: spacing scale, type scale, radii, colors, elevation. Components are just the places those decisions show up.

The order that works for me:

  1. Name the scales. 4/8/12/16 is not a system, it's a suggestion. Pick a small set and stop.
  2. Write the tokens as CSS variables. They work in every framework and they make dark mode a variable swap instead of a refactor.
  3. Build one component at a time, and delete variants that aren't used twice.

The last part is the hard one. A variant that exists because one screen needed it is not a design system, it's a bug with a name.

Do you keep tokens in CSS variables, a JS object, or both?

title: The inference endpoint is not the model
description:
Serving a model is a systems problem wearing a machine-learning costume.

The model is maybe 20% of the endpoint. The other 80% is queueing, timeouts, batching, retries, and the failure mode where a 2-second p99 quietly turns into a 30-second one because the batch got too large.

Three things I now do by default:

  1. Bound the batch by time, not just size. A batch that waits for 8 items is a batch that waits forever at night.
  2. Separate the queue from the HTTP request. Return a job id, let the client poll. It makes backpressure explicit instead of mysterious.
  3. Add a fallback that returns a safe default after the deadline. A slower answer is usually better than a hung request.

The model accuracy curve is the interesting part of the job. The p99 is the part that wakes you up.

Curious how other people handle the fallback: cached response, heuristic, or just an error?

title: Balancing Centralized Cloud Computing with Individual Ownership: Addressing Underutilized Resources and User Preferences
description:
Introduction: The Clash of Computing Philosophies

The debate over the future of computing has crystallized into a fundamental conflict: on one side, proponents of centralized cloud computing, exemplified by Sam Altman, argue that underutilized consumer DRAM represents inefficiency, advocating for its consolidation in cloud ecosystems. On the other, self-hosting advocates counter that personal hardware ownership is essential for privacy, autonomy, and resistance to centralized control. Altman’s assertion that consumer DRAM operates at only 5% utilization frames idleness as waste, yet this critique overlooks the systemic implications of relinquishing hardware control—a shift that extends beyond resource allocation to the erosion of individual digital sovereignty.

Altman’s efficiency-centric argument hinges on the volatile nature of DRAM, which, while critical for active computing tasks, remains idle in personal devices during periods of inactivity. However, this idleness is not a defect but a byproduct of ownership. For instance, a self-hosted setup comprising a TrueNAS storage appliance, a Docker-based media server, and a desktop running local large language models (LLMs) exemplifies decentralized control. These systems, powered by hardware like an RTX 3080, process data locally, ensuring that sensitive information remains within the user’s domain. The 5% utilization Altman criticizes is the cost of maintaining this control, a trade-off between efficiency and autonomy.

The push for cloud centralization carries tangible risks. As hyperscale providers such as AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud dominate 67% of global cloud infrastructure, they accrue disproportionate control over resource allocation, dictating the terms of access and usage. Altman’s framing of idle DRAM as waste masks a strategic maneuver to subsume the last vestiges of decentralized hardware. This is not merely resource optimization but a consolidation of power, where individual computing capabilities are subsumed into corporate ecosystems.

Self-hosting, while technically feasible, faces institutional barriers. Challenges such as email deliverability from residential IPs and the complexity of security management persist, yet open-source tools like Nextcloud, Gitea, and Pi-hole have lowered technical entry points. The primary threat lies in the convenience paradigm—a gradual, often imperceptible transfer of ownership through cloud dependencies. Each service adopted cedes a degree of control, incrementally transforming the open web into a relic of the past.

The causal relationship is unambiguous: centralization begets dependency, which in turn erodes autonomy. As cloud providers extend their reach, individuals risk forfeiting not only their hardware but also the ability to compute independently. Altman’s vision of "maximum utilization" envisions a world where personal resources serve corporate interests, not individual needs. In contrast, the idle cycles of a self-hosted RTX 3080 represent a deliberate choice to retain control, prioritizing sovereignty over efficiency.

Scenario Analysis: Six Perspectives on Resource Utilization

The debate between centralized cloud computing and self-hosting transcends mere efficiency—it fundamentally concerns control, ownership, and the trajectory of digital autonomy. Below, we analyze six scenarios that illuminate these trade-offs, grounded in technical mechanisms and causal relationships.

1. The Idle DRAM Dilemma: Efficiency vs. Sovereignty

Sam Altman’s critique of underutilized consumer DRAM centers on its volatile nature: DRAM requires continuous power to retain data, rendering idle memory inefficient. In cloud environments, DRAM is pooled and dynamically allocated via virtualization and workload balancing, maximizing utilization. Conversely, self-hosted setups, such as the author’s RTX 3080-powered LLM machine, prioritize local data processing, ensuring sensitive information remains on-device. The trade-off is clear: lower utilization in exchange for enhanced sovereignty. The critical risk lies in resource monopolization: as cloud providers consolidate DRAM, individual ownership diminishes, and users forfeit the capacity for independent data processing.

2. The Email Deliverability Conundrum: Institutional Barriers in Self-Hosting

Self-hosting email in 2026 is fraught with challenges due to the fragmented nature of email protocols and the blacklisting of residential IPs. Cloud providers like ProtonMail circumvent these issues by operating from dedicated IP ranges with established reputations. The causal mechanism is straightforward: institutional barriers (ISP restrictions, spam filters) → increased technical complexity → user abandonment of self-hosting. This scenario exemplifies how convenience systematically erodes autonomy, one service at a time.

3. The RTX 3080’s Dual Role: Local LLMs vs. Cloud Rental

The RTX 3080 in the author’s setup epitomizes the utilization-ownership trade-off. In cloud environments, GPUs like the 3080 are overclocked and load-balanced across multiple tenants, optimizing efficiency but accelerating hardware degradation and generating excess heat. Locally, the GPU operates at user-defined loads, preserving its lifespan but remaining idle during downtime. The risk lies in cloud providers framing local GPU ownership as inefficient, incentivizing users to adopt rental models that centralize control.

4. The TrueNAS Paradox: Storage Centralization vs. Decentralized Control

TrueNAS, a self-hosted NAS solution, leverages local HDDs/SSDs to avoid cloud providers’ data lock-in mechanisms. However, cloud storage offers redundancy through geographic distribution and automated backups. The trade-off is data sovereignty vs. convenience. The risk lies in cloud providers’ tiered pricing and egress fees, which create economic lock-in, rendering self-hosted storage increasingly impractical over time.

5. The Pi-hole Predicament: DNS Control vs. Institutional Resistance

Pi-hole, a self-hosted DNS and ad blocker, functions by intercepting DNS queries locally, bypassing cloud-based ad networks. However, ISPs and content providers increasingly block residential DNS servers, citing security risks or policy violations. The causal chain is evident: institutional resistance → reduced functionality → user migration to cloud-based alternatives. This scenario highlights how institutional barriers systematically undermine technical solutions favoring decentralization.

6. The Open Web’s Silent Erosion: Convenience as a Trojan Horse

The author’s observation—“We lost the open web to convenience, one login at a time”—encapsulates a causal chain of dependency. Cloud services exploit proprietary APIs and vendor lock-in to consolidate control. For instance, Google Drive’s seamless integration with Gmail and Docs creates a network effect, rendering self-hosted alternatives like Nextcloud less appealing. The risk is clear: as users prioritize convenience, they incrementally surrender ownership, culminating in a centralized web dominated by a handful of providers.

Conclusion: The Mechanisms of Control

Each scenario exposes a mechanism of control: cloud providers leverage efficiency gaps, institutional barriers, and user convenience to centralize resources. Self-hosting, while less efficient, safeguards digital sovereignty through local processing and ownership. The choice is not merely technical—it is existential. As Altman targets your idle DRAM, consider: What are you willing to trade for control?

Conclusion: The Existential Clash Between Efficiency and Autonomy

The debate between centralized cloud computing and individual ownership of computing resources transcends technical considerations—it is fundamentally existential. Sam Altman’s critique of underutilized consumer DRAM underscores a legitimate efficiency concern: DRAM, a volatile memory essential for active tasks, remains idle in personal devices 95% of the time. Cloud providers address this inefficiency by pooling and virtualizing DRAM across thousands of users, achieving economies of scale unattainable by individuals. However, this efficiency is predicated on centralized control. By framing local ownership as "waste," cloud providers not only optimize resource allocation but also redefine the locus of computational ownership, shifting it from individuals to corporations.

The Efficiency Paradox: Short-Term Gains, Long-Term Dependency

Cloud computing’s promise of maximum utilization is undeniable. Hyperscale providers like AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud leverage load-balancing and resource virtualization to extract peak performance from hardware. For instance, a GPU such as the RTX 3080, which might idle 90% of the time in a self-hosted setup, is overclocked and distributed across multiple tenants in the cloud. Mechanistically, overclocking accelerates thermal degradation, reducing the GPU’s lifespan, but it maximizes short-term efficiency. This trade-off commodifies individual hardware, embedding it within corporate ecosystems where users forfeit control over resource allocation and lifecycle management.

Ownership as a Bulwark Against Institutional Capture

Self-hosting champions digital sovereignty, ensuring that data processing and storage remain physically localized. By deploying services like Nextcloud, Gitea, or local LLMs on personal hardware, users retain direct control over their data and workflows. This autonomy extends beyond privacy to resisting institutional lock-in. Cloud providers employ egress fees and tiered pricing models to create economic dependency, exploiting the asymmetry between low-cost data ingestion and high-cost extraction. Mechanistically, these fees disincentivize data portability, making self-hosted alternatives like TrueNAS viable but demanding trade-offs in redundancy and convenience. Self-hosting, therefore, is not merely a technical choice but a strategic act of resistance against corporate capture.

Institutional Barriers: Eroding Autonomy by Design

The push toward centralization is as much institutional as it is technological. Email self-hosting, once a symbol of autonomy, has been rendered impractical by security-patching complexities and blacklisting of residential IPs. Mechanistically, this arises from the need to emulate the reputation of dedicated cloud IPs, a standard residential users cannot meet. Similarly, DNS solutions like Pi-hole are undermined by ISPs blocking residential DNS servers under the pretext of security risks, funneling users into cloud-based alternatives. These barriers are not accidental but deliberate, designed to consolidate control within corporate ecosystems.

Convenience as a Mechanism of Control

Convenience serves as the silent architect of dependency. Cloud providers leverage proprietary APIs and vendor lock-in to create frictionless experiences that mask the surrender of autonomy. Migrating from Google Drive to Nextcloud, for example, requires physical data transfer and workflow reconfiguration—a barrier cloud providers exploit. Mechanistically, this friction stems from the incompatibility between open protocols and proprietary ecosystems. Each interaction with a cloud service incrementally cedes ownership, eroding the open web through cumulative micro-surrenders.

The Future: Navigating the Spectrum of Control

The choice between cloud and self-hosting is not binary but exists on a spectrum. Hybrid setups, such as using Proton for email while self-hosting media stacks (e.g., Sonarr, Radarr), offer a balanced approach. However, the stakes are clear: unchecked cloud consolidation threatens to subsume individual computing capacity into corporate ecosystems. Hyperscale providers already control 67% of global cloud infrastructure, and their leadership openly advocates for greater control over consumer hardware. This is not resource optimization but strategic acquisition of the last hardware they do not yet control.

As you navigate this landscape, scrutinize the mechanisms of control: efficiency gaps, institutional barriers, and convenience traps. Self-hosting is not merely about optimizing idle DRAM—it is about preserving the ability to compute on your terms. The tools for autonomy have never been more accessible, yet the gravitational pull toward centralization has never been stronger. The open web is not being lost in a war; it is being surrendered, one login at a time. The question remains: what are you willing to trade for convenience?

title: Kubernetes manifest settings that affect safety
description:
Which fields in a Kubernetes manifest decide how safe and stable a workload is, what each one changes, and what to write instead of the risky default.

A Kubernetes manifest is safe to apply when the pod cannot gain more power on the node than it needs, when the image you run is the image you reviewed, when memory and CPU have a ceiling, and when the cluster can tell whether the container is alive and ready for traffic. Six groups of fields decide most of that: the securityContext, host access, image references, resource requests and limits, probes, and where secrets come from. None of them is exotic. They are the defaults you leave in place when a manifest is copied from a tutorial, and each one has a small, boring replacement.

Read the full report on AISkills402: https://aiskills402.com/blog/kubernetes-manifest-risks?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social
