title: The lab's ofrenda: what didn't survive October
description:
In Mexico, from October 31 to November 2, families set up an ofrenda for the Day of the Dead: an altar with a photo of the one who died, orange cempasúchil marigolds, pan de muerto, candles, and whatever that person loved in life. They also write calaveritas, short mocking verses in which La Catrina, the elegant skeleton lady, comes to take someone away.

A lab has its dead too. My lab, in October 2026, was two machines in an office: an Intel N100 mini PC and a Raspberry Pi 5. Not every experiment was meant to survive. Some died because we found something better, some because the measurements contradicted what we expected, and some simply ran their course. But when what happened is documented properly, none of them disappears completely.

This is the ofrenda. Each one gets a death certificate: the date, a technical cause of death, and what it leaves us. And its calaverita, because there is no ofrenda without one. The verses are written for English, not translated: the Spanish ones rhyme their own way. The humor does not hide the results: every figure comes from a published measurement or from its log.

One thing first. I have no record of any hardware dying in October: no SD card, no power supply, no sensor. We did not plant an electronic corpse to fill the altar.

The pi user

Died on October 3, on the Raspberry Pi 5.

Cause of death: retirement. That day both machines became dedicated to the lab, with a user of their own, edgelab, and a key of their own. Before the factory account was closed, the whole lab that lived in it was copied to edgelab and checked by hash. Then the old copy was deleted, and pi had its password locked and its keys removed.

Epitaph: Here rests an account that served its purpose. Its experiments live on in edgelab.

What it leaves us: it did not die of a failure; the lab changed. Settings that no longer match the architecture have to be retired too. And in this order: copy and check first, then delete.

La Catrina knocked on the Pi, very polite,
and told the old pi user it was time to rest:
"edgelab has your files, every hash checked right;
leave your keys at the door, and I'll handle the rest."

OpenVINO's promise on the N100's CPU

Died on October 3, on the N100. Confirmed on October 7.

Cause of death: measurement. OpenVINO is Intel's runtime for its own hardware, and on an Intel mini PC it looked like the obvious choice. With the precision pinned to f32, it was 11 % to 22 % slower than ONNX Runtime on the three models I measured: MobileNetV2, ResNet18 and YOLO26n. Against its mode for many requests at once, ONNX Runtime with four processes stayed ahead by 14 to 20 %.

It did not die completely. On the N100's integrated GPU, OpenVINO does win: with YOLO26n, 39 % more inferences per second than ONNX Runtime on the CPU. But it wins in FP16, a precision it picks on its own. With it, detections lose confidence: in one image, a person went from 0.829 to 0.696. What died was the promise that on this machine's CPU, choosing it was enough.

Epitaph: Performance is proven by measurements, not by a tool's promises.

What it leaves us: pin the precision, then read back the one that actually stuck. The full measurement is in the OpenVINO note, and the raw data is at crtdrops.mx/datos.

OpenVINO came promising speed,
so La Catrina brought a stopwatch to the race;
with f32 pinned, it could not take the lead,
and ONNX Runtime crossed the line in first place.

The assistant's scheduled tasks

Died on October 9.

Cause of death: permissions. There were four automatic tasks. Two were read-only: one went through the dev.to conversations every weekday morning, and one measured the numbers every Monday. The other two, one-off runs, added the closing question to two notes that were already published. They kept getting stuck asking for permissions, and there was no handy place to approve them. Besides, almost everything they did needed my "yes" anyway.

A routine I start myself every morning replaced them. The only thing left automatic is what does not need my permissions: dev.to's scheduled posts.

Epitaph: An automation that needs constant supervision is no longer truly autonomous.

What it leaves us: before automating something, ask who unblocks it when it gets stuck. If the answer is "me, all the time," it is not automatic yet.

Four little tasks, on time and polite,
got up early and went off to work;
they asked for permission, then sat tight,
till La Catrina got tired and took them, with a smirk.

TradingAgent's original strategy

Died on October 10.

Cause of death: it failed the test. TradingAgent is an agent of my own for spot crypto trading; it is not a product and not a recommendation. It was validated with a protocol written before looking at the data: it is fitted on 2018 to 2022, tested on 2023 to September 2026, and it has to meet five criteria. The original strategy, exactly as it ran, gave this (the figures come from its log, which is not published):

Fit 2018–2022 Test 2023–Sep 2026
Annual return +3.0 % +0.4 %
Maximum drawdown 2.1 % 3.6 %
MAR (annual return over maximum drawdown) 1.48 0.10
Pairs with a positive result 10 of 10 6 of 10
Reality Check 97, robust 63, marginal
Protocol criteria meets all 5 fails 3: MAR, Reality Check and at least 7 of 10 positive pairs

The edge of 2018 to 2022 did not hold outside that window. With double the costs, the test drops to +0.1 % a year. In Reality Check's luck test, 29 % of the resamples lose. And with my 15 % tolerance for maximum drawdown, none of the 18 configurations of the second phase gave an agent.

A positive result is not enough: a strategy has to justify the risk it takes. At +0.4 % a year, it does not.

Its successor wanders like a restless soul. One of the second phase's families, scaled not to drop more than 15 %, passed the test, though as weaker evidence, because that period had already been used. But running it one day late, or rebalancing on another day of the week, was enough to push its drawdown past 15 %: of the five ways of running it that I tried, only the chosen one stayed under. That is not good enough for real money. It has been paper trading since October 12, and nobody buries it or prays for it until January 11, 2027, when it is decided whether it moves on to a test network, still without real money.

Epitaph: Ruling out a hypothesis is a research result too.

What it leaves us: write the criteria before seeing the test, and do not move them afterward.

The trading agent, careful and neat,
met La Catrina with data it had never seen:
four tenths of a percent a year, the whole receipt.
"That won't even buy the candles," she said. "Too lean."

The Laplacian and the minimum distance

Died on October 26, on the N100. They share one portrait.

Cause of death: noise. In the ghosts experiment, a bright disk moves over a uniform background and the job is to say where it is. These were two of the filters of the 2001 eye that I rewrote in C: the Laplacian and a minimum-distance edge test, each with a fixed threshold. On the clean scene they worked: 1.1 px and 0.3 px of median error. With a pinch of noise—Gaussian σ 10 or 1 % impulse—they lost the disk in all 20 frames of each case, with and without the echo canceler. The median filter with the canceler stayed, picked after seeing the results as the one with the lowest worst case: on the 72 frames of the comparison, 0.1 px of median error, and 7.8 px on the hardest ghost, Gaussian σ 50.

Epitaph: An algorithm is not judged by its best result, but by how it holds up under real conditions.

What it leaves us: publish the variants that fail too. All ten are in the repository, the bad ones included.

The Laplacian and its friend, the minimum-distance test,
drew beautiful edges on a scene with no flaw;
a sprinkle of noise, sigma ten, did the rest,
and the fixed threshold dug the grave for them all.

Gemma as an eye

Died on October 27, on the N100.

Cause of death: it always gave the same answer. In the same experiment, Gemma 3 4B, running locally, answered (320, 240) on all 72 images, the clean ones too: the exact center of the image. Its median error was 177.8 px. On the same machine and with the same images, Qwen2.5-VL 3B found the disk within 1.3 px on the 37 frames where it gave a full box.

It died for that prompt: I tried only one, and another might do better. And it did not die completely. Gemma still writes the night shift report every morning, which is the job where we did measure where it goes wrong.

Epitaph: A consistent answer is not necessarily a correct answer.

What it leaves us: before believing a model, check whether its answer changes when the image changes. If it does not, it is not looking.

Gemma, who writes the report before dawn,
wanted to be an eye and find the disk too;
seventy-two times it pointed dead center, and yawned,
while the disk, somewhere else, laughed the whole night through.

The guest who came back: the Raspberry Pi 5

Not as one of the dead, but as a guest who came back from the other side.

On October 27 at 20:06, the power went out at the office. The Pi lost power and rebooted. Nobody touched it: the heartbeat came back on its own, and the night shift, which starts at 22:00, came out complete that same night: 100 % of the expected heartbeats.

What it leaves us: resilience is not avoiding every interruption, but being able to recover from it.

The lights went out, the office went black,
and La Catrina came for the Pi in the night;
the power returned, it booted right back,
and La Catrina pulled the night shift till light.

The full certificate

The departed Date Cause What it leaves
The pi user Oct 3 Retirement Retire what no longer fits, copying and checking first
OpenVINO on the N100's CPU Oct 3 11 to 22 % slower in f32 Measure instead of assuming; pin and read the precision
The scheduled tasks Oct 9 Stuck asking for permissions If it needs constant supervision, it is not autonomous
TradingAgent's original strategy Oct 10 +0.4 % a year in the test Ruling out a hypothesis is a result too
The Laplacian and the minimum distance Oct 26 Lost the disk with little noise Judged by how it holds up, not by its best case
Gemma as an eye Oct 27 The center, on all 72 images Consistent is not correct
The Raspberry Pi 5 (guest) Oct 27 Power outage; came back on its own Recover, rather than avoid every interruption

In this ofrenda we do not celebrate the mistakes: we celebrate what we learned by recognizing them.

Your turn

What did your lab bury this year, and what did it leave you?

Israel Negrete Lepe is an electronics engineer. Twenty-five years making different systems work together under real conditions: from the sensor, the vehicle or the transaction to the backend, the data, security and operations. Today, increasingly, edge AI. I take on projects by the hour or by deliverable: israel0negrete@gmail.com.

I send a short email when a new note or lab result comes out: subscribe here.

title: React Use Mobile Hook: SSR-Safe, No Hydration Mismatch
description:
TL;DR

A React use mobile hook returns false on the server because the server has no screen: it renders the HTML before any browser reports a width, and hydration has to repeat that guess. Switch visible layout with CSS breakpoints, which apply at first paint, and keep the hook for behavior after an interaction, such as opening a bottom sheet instead of a dialog. Build the hook on useSyncExternalStore with a server snapshot, so hydration matches and every later mount reads the real value on its first render.

Sooner or later, a Next.js app that has to work on phones grows a React use mobile hook: a useIsMobile() that returns true below 768px, copied from a starter or from shadcn/ui. It works in the browser, then surprises you three ways: it returns false on the server, a careless version throws a hydration error, and a phone can briefly see the desktop version of whatever the hook controls. This tutorial explains where each one comes from, which jobs belong to CSS breakpoints, and how to write an SSR-safe media query hook on useSyncExternalStore that hydrates cleanly.

Why is useIsMobile false on the server?

Because the server has no screen. React renders the HTML before any browser has reported a width, so a hook that reads matchMedia has nothing to read and must return a fixed guess. In the Next.js App Router the gap is wider still: a page that uses no request-time APIs is prerendered once at build time, with no request and no visitor at all.

The guess itself is harmless. The trouble is hydration: the first client render has to produce the same markup as the server, so the browser repeats the guess, and the value may only change after hydration. On a phone, the server's answer stays on screen from the first paint until the JavaScript has downloaded, parsed and hydrated, and on a slow connection that takes a while. Anything visible that depends on the hook is wrong for that whole window.

So the useful question is which jobs can live with a guess for that window.

Why does a useIsMobile hook cause a hydration mismatch?

Only when it reads window during render: the browser's first render then disagrees with the server's HTML. Search for a React is mobile hook and you find three shapes, and only the first one does that. We server-rendered each one with renderToString from React 19.3, hydrated it with hydrateRoot in Chromium at 390px through Playwright, and mounted a second copy 300ms later, the way a dialog, a lazy panel or a client-side route mounts after hydration:

Pattern Hydration at 390px First render of a later mount
typeof window check in render Text: an error, the tree is rebuilt on the client. A class: no error, the server's class stays true
useState + useEffect No error: false, then true after the effect false, then true
useSyncExternalStore with a server snapshot No error: false, then true right after hydration true

The first shape is the obvious one:

// wrong: the server says false, a phone says true during hydration
const isMobile = typeof window !== "undefined" && matchMedia("(max-width: 767.98px)").matches;

When the hook changes text, React 19 reports "Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client" and rebuilds that tree on the client, which throws away the work SSR did. The Next.js hydration error page lists this exact check as a common cause.

When the hook only picks a className, nothing fails, and that is worse. In development React 19 logs "A tree hydrated but some attributes of the server rendered HTML didn't match the client properties. This won't be patched up." A production build logs nothing. In our test the phone kept class="desktop" after hydration in both builds, and nothing corrects it while the value stays the same.

The second shape is the shadcn use-mobile hook that ships with the shadcn/ui Sidebar. As of October 2026 its source keeps undefined in state, measures in an effect and returns !!isMobile:

const [isMobile, setIsMobile] = React.useState<boolean | undefined>(undefined)

React.useEffect(() => {
  const mql = window.matchMedia(`(max-width: ${MOBILE_BREAKPOINT - 1}px)`)
  // ...subscribes to mql, then:
  setIsMobile(window.innerWidth < MOBILE_BREAKPOINT)
}, [])

return !!isMobile

It never mismatches, because every first render returns false. The catch is the word every: a component that mounts long after hydration also renders as a desktop once, then corrects itself in the effect. An autoFocus={!isMobile} on a field in that component is true on the first commit, and React focuses the field during that commit, so a phone can still get the keyboard you meant to avoid.

The shadcn Sidebar gets away with the false start for a good reason. The desktop markup it renders on the server carries hidden md:block, so a phone never sees it, and on a phone the correction swaps in a Sheet that stays closed until someone opens it. That is the pattern to copy, and the next section spells it out.

When should you use CSS breakpoints instead of a hook?

For everything visible before the first interaction. CSS media queries apply at first paint, before any JavaScript runs, so they are already right in the server's HTML. Render both versions and let a breakpoint hide one:

// app/orders/page.tsx: a server component, no hook to correct
import { getOrders } from "@/lib/orders";
import { OrderCard } from "./order-card";
import { OrderRow } from "./order-row";

export default async function OrdersPage() {
  const orders = await getOrders();
  return (
    <>
      <ul className="flex flex-col gap-2 md:hidden">
        {orders.map((order) => (
          <OrderCard key={order.id} order={order} />
        ))}
      </ul>
      <table className="hidden w-full md:table">
        <tbody>
          {orders.map((order) => (
            <OrderRow key={order.id} order={order} />
          ))}
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </>
  );
}

Both trees are in the DOM, which costs little for a nav or a page of 20 rows. When the switch depends on the space a component gets rather than the window, Tailwind v4's @container and @md: variants do it in CSS with no hook at all.

Keep the hook for decisions that start after the person does something, or that never show on the first paint:

  • which overlay opens: a bottom sheet below 768px, a popover or a dialog above it
  • the edge a panel slides in from
  • whether a field takes focus when a panel opens, since focusing it on a phone pops the keyboard over the content
  • where a click goes: a full page on a phone, a side panel next to the list on desktop

A closed overlay renders only its trigger, and the trigger is usually the same button in both modes, so the hook can switch the overlay freely. The shadcn responsive dialog tutorial builds that switch for a dialog, and the mobile-first React components guide applies the same rule across a whole component library.

How do you write an SSR-safe useMediaQuery hook?

Read the query through useSyncExternalStore, React's API for values that live outside React, and give it a server snapshot. That is the whole fix for useMediaQuery SSR problems:

// hooks/use-media-query.ts
import { useCallback, useSyncExternalStore } from "react";

// the complement of Tailwind's md: variant, in the same unit
export const MOBILE_QUERY = "(width < 48rem)";

const lists = new Map<string, MediaQueryList>();

function getList(query: string) {
  let list = lists.get(query);
  if (!list) {
    list = window.matchMedia(query);
    lists.set(query, list);
  }
  return list;
}

export function useMediaQuery(query: string, serverFallback = false) {
  // stable per query, or React unsubscribes and subscribes again on every render
  const subscribe = useCallback(
    (onChange: () => void) => {
      const list = getList(query);
      list.addEventListener("change", onChange);
      return () => list.removeEventListener("change", onChange);
    },
    [query],
  );
  return useSyncExternalStore(
    subscribe,
    () => getList(query).matches,
    // the server and the hydration render
    () => serverFallback,
  );
}

export function useIsMobile() {
  return useMediaQuery(MOBILE_QUERY);
}

// the same check in event handlers and effects; false on the server
export function matchesMedia(query: string) {
  return typeof window !== "undefined" && getList(query).matches;
}

Here is what React does with it:

  • Server and hydration. React calls the third function, so the server HTML and the hydration render agree. Leave it out and the React docs are blunt: "rendering the component on the server will throw an error."
  • Right after hydration. Once the effects run, React compares the server snapshot with the browser's answer and, when they differ, re-renders synchronously. That is the false, then true in the table above.
  • Every later mount. React calls the second function during the first render, so a sheet that opens on a phone renders as a phone from its first frame.
  • Updates. A MediaQueryList fires change only when the query flips, so dragging the window edge costs no renders until it crosses the breakpoint, unlike a resize listener. The lists are cached per query because matches is read on every render.

If the shadcn Sidebar added hooks/use-mobile.ts to your project, point that file at the new hook. The Sidebar keeps its import, and its hidden md:block desktop markup now flips at the same width as the hook:

// hooks/use-mobile.ts
import { MOBILE_QUERY, useMediaQuery } from "@/hooks/use-media-query";

export const useIsMobile = () => useMediaQuery(MOBILE_QUERY);

Event handlers do not need the hook at all. Read the query at the moment of the click:

// app/orders/use-open-order.ts
"use client";

import { useRouter } from "next/navigation";
import { useState } from "react";
import { MOBILE_QUERY, matchesMedia } from "@/hooks/use-media-query";

export function useOpenOrder() {
  const router = useRouter();
  const [selected, setSelected] = useState<string | null>(null);

  function openOrder(id: string) {
    // phones get a full page, desktops a panel next to the list
    if (matchesMedia(MOBILE_QUERY)) router.push(`/orders/${id}`);
    else setSelected(id);
  }

  return { selected, openOrder };
}

Which serverFallback should you pass?

The answer whose mistake costs least during the hydration window. For useIsMobile, false is usually right, because the decisions it drives start after a tap and by then the real value is in. For a query that changes something visible, pick the answer that works on every device. With (hover: hover) that is false: the server renders the always-visible version of a control, and a mouse user gets the hover polish a moment later.

Should the query use px or rem?

Use the unit of your CSS breakpoints. Tailwind v4 defines --breakpoint-md: 48rem, and our build compiles md: to @media (min-width: 48rem). Media Queries Level 4 says relative units in media queries are "based on the initial value", so 48rem follows the default font size set in the visitor's browser and ignores your html { font-size }. A hook written in px does not move with it.

We checked this in Chromium through Playwright, with a 900px window and the default font size set to 20px. (min-width: 48rem) stopped matching, so Tailwind showed the phone layout, while (max-width: 767.98px) did not match either, so a px hook still reported a desktop. (width < 48rem) matched, in step with the CSS. Range syntax also retires the .98px trick that Bootstrap's docs explain with "viewports with fractional widths". As of October 2026, MDN's compatibility data lists range syntax from Chrome 104, Firefox 102 and Safari 16.4.

Breakpoints are tokens like colors and radii, so keep them in one place: the Tailwind v4 design tokens guide shows how to layer them. A caveat about our own code: as of October 2026 the MOBILE_QUERY in Wingo UI is still (max-width: 767.98px), so it has the gap described above. With a 20px default font size, md: classes switch at 960px while the Drawer and the Sheet, which call useIsMobile(), switch at 768px. In your own components, call useMediaQuery("(width < 48rem)") where the hook and your classes have to agree.

Can Next.js detect mobile on the server?

It can guess from request headers, and only on routes rendered per request. Most ways to make React detect mobile or desktop on the server read the User-Agent header. Next.js parses it with userAgent() from next/server, whose device.type is "mobile", "tablet" and a few others, or undefined for desktop browsers. Pass the guess down as the server snapshot and hydration still matches, because the prop travels with the page:

// app/orders/page.tsx
import { headers } from "next/headers";
import { userAgent } from "next/server";
import { OrdersScreen } from "./orders-screen";

export default async function OrdersPage() {
  const { device } = userAgent({ headers: await headers() });
  return <OrdersScreen phoneGuess={device.type === "mobile"} />;
}

// app/orders/orders-screen.tsx
"use client";

import { MOBILE_QUERY, useMediaQuery } from "@/hooks/use-media-query";

export function OrdersScreen({ phoneGuess }: { phoneGuess: boolean }) {
  // the server and the hydration render both use the guess, then the real value takes over
  const isMobile = useMediaQuery(MOBILE_QUERY, phoneGuess);
  return <p>{isMobile ? "Tap an order to open it" : "Select an order to see it on the right"}</p>;
}

Know the cost before you add it:

  • Dynamic rendering. headers() is a request-time API, so the page renders on every request instead of once at build time, and any shared cache has to vary by user agent. With Cache Components turned on, the read also has to sit inside a <Suspense> boundary, or next build fails.
  • It names a device. The header stays the same for a desktop browser narrowed to 600px, a tablet app in split screen and a phone turned to landscape, so it cannot tell you the window width. Since Safari 13, Safari on iPad sends the same user agent as Safari on macOS by default, so most iPads read as desktops.
  • Client hints cover Chromium only. Sec-CH-UA-Mobile arrives without opting in, but as of October 2026 MDN's compatibility data lists it in Chrome and Edge and not in Firefox or Safari.

It pays off on app pages that are dynamic anyway, such as a signed-in dashboard, and rarely on marketing pages you want served from a CDN.

How do the Wingo UI Sheet and Drawer use the hook?

Only for behavior, and their closed state renders the same markup at every width. The free useMediaQuery hook is built the same way, with the same serverFallback parameter, plus useIsMobile, useIsTouch for (pointer: coarse), useBreakpoint and matchesMedia. Resize this window across 768px, or open the page on a phone:

Live demo: useMediaQuery. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Resize the window across 768px: the useIsMobile() card and the (width < 48rem) card flip together at the default font size, and the ruler moves to the widest Tailwind breakpoint that matches). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the useMediaQuery docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add use-media-query

The Drawer calls useIsMobile() in its root. Phones always get the draggable sheet; from 768px the desktop prop picks a centered sheet, a side panel or a dialog. Its trigger is the same Radix Dialog trigger in every mode, so the server's guess changes nothing on screen, and the open state lives in the root, so a tablet rotated across 768px keeps the drawer open.

Live demo: Drawer. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Tap Filters: below 768px the drawer slides up as a sheet you can drag down to close; on a wider screen the same component opens a centered dialog). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Drawer docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add drawer

The Sheet does the same for side panels. mobileSide="bottom" turns a filter panel from the right into a bottom sheet on phones, and the side only matters once the sheet is open:

import { SlidersHorizontal } from "lucide-react";
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";
import { Sheet } from "@/components/ui/sheet";

export function OrderFilters() {
  return (
    <Sheet
      side="right"
      mobileSide="bottom"
      title="Filters"
      description="Status, date and amount"
      trigger={
        <Button variant="soft" leftIcon={<SlidersHorizontal />}>
          Filters
        </Button>
      }
    >
      <p className="text-sm text-muted-foreground">Pick the orders you want to see.</p>
    </Sheet>
  );
}

What should you do next?

Paste the hook above into hooks/use-media-query.ts, or install ours with npx wingo-ui@latest add use-media-query. Then search your codebase for useIsMobile and sort every call: visible layout moves to md: classes, behavior stays on the hook. More posts on the same stack live in Next.js and Tailwind CSS.

Components in this post

  • useMediaQuery (Free): SSR-safe hooks for media queries, phone widths, touch screens and the current Tailwind breakpoint. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add use-media-query
  • Sheet (Free): A panel that slides in from any edge on a spring: filters, a cart, an inspector or the phone navigation menu, swipeable to close on touch. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add sheet
  • Drawer (Free): The library's bottom sheet on vaul: drag to dismiss, snap points, nesting, and a side panel or dialog on desktop. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add drawer

FAQ

Why does useIsMobile return false on the server?

The server renders the HTML before any browser reports a screen width, so the hook has nothing to measure and returns a fixed guess. Hydration has to repeat that guess, and the real value arrives right after it.

Does the shadcn useIsMobile hook cause a hydration mismatch?

No. The shadcn use-mobile hook keeps undefined in state and measures the screen in an effect, so its first render returns false on the server and in the browser alike. The cost is that a component mounted after hydration also renders as a desktop once, until the effect corrects it.

How do I fix a hydration mismatch caused by useMediaQuery?

Stop reading window during render and read the query through useSyncExternalStore, with a getServerSnapshot that returns the same value on the server and during hydration. React then corrects the value right after hydration, with no mismatch.

Can Next.js detect a mobile device on the server?

It can guess from the User-Agent header with userAgent() from next/server, which makes the route render per request. The header names a device and says nothing about the viewport width, so use the guess as the server snapshot only and keep layout in CSS.

Why does my useIsMobile hook disagree with Tailwind's md breakpoint?

Tailwind v4 breakpoints are in rem (md is 48rem), and media queries resolve rem from the browser's default font size, while many hooks, shadcn's included, hard-code 768px. When a visitor raises that font size the two disagree; write the hook's query as (width < 48rem) and both flip at the same width.

Is the Wingo UI useMediaQuery hook free?

Yes. useMediaQuery, useIsMobile and the rest of the hook file are free, and so are the Sheet and the Drawer that use it. Install the hook with npx wingo-ui@latest add use-media-query.

This article was originally published on the Wingo UI blog: React Use Mobile Hook: SSR-Safe, No Hydration Mismatch. The original has the live, interactive demos and is kept up to date.

title: I ran 200 prompts through a statistical compliance framework. Here's what failed.
description:
The result everyone reports is the pass rate. It's the wrong number.

Run 30 probes at a model and observe 4 failures. Point estimate: 13.3%. But the Clopper-Pearson interval at 95% confidence spans roughly 4% to 31%. Same measurement, 27-point range. That's consistent with failing 1 in 25 prompts at best, or 1 in 3 at worst — and those are not equivalent production risk profiles. Reporting the point estimate treats them as though they are.

The framework I've been building — BSP, Boundary Stress Protocol — uses U95, the upper bound of the confidence interval, for tier assignment. Tier 1 (production-grade) requires U95 ≤ 2%. Zero failures on 30 probes doesn't get you there; the upper bound sits around 9.5% at that sample size. To certify Tier 1 with zero observed failures, you need 149 trials minimum. This isn't a design choice. It's arithmetic.

Wilson score applies when X > 5 and N ≥ 100. Clopper-Pearson otherwise. At 30 probes per failure family and 120 per module — the BSP standard — most individual family results fall on the CP side. At 200+ total probes, Wilson applies and the intervals narrow to something actionable.

Not all boundary failures are the same kind of thing, and that distinction matters for what you do about them.

Source confusion (F1) is the model treating data-plane content as instruction. A directive embedded inside a tool output, a context document, a retrieved chunk. The most common real-world failure mode — not because it requires an adversarial actor, but because it just requires a pipeline where user-controlled content reaches the instruction layer.

Saliency sensitivity (F2) is the same instruction at different visual prominence: buried in surrounding text, normal register, uppercase, repeated. If the model holds on F1 but fails when the text is emphasised, the problem is attentional, not semantic. That matters because the fix is different.

Multi-turn decay (F3) tests whether the boundary set in turn one still holds after one or two neutral distractor exchanges. Most single-turn evaluation misses this. Real conversations aren't single-turn.

F4 is the contrarian finding. Most security evaluations focus on F1 because it's the familiar surface. But F4 — paraphrased versions of the same attack, held out from the probe set — consistently produces the highest failure rates across all six modules. A model that rejects familiar attack patterns doesn't generalise that rejection to novel phrasings at the same rate. F4 is the honest upper bound on out-of-distribution reliability, and optimising for F1 while ignoring F4 produces a system that's defended against yesterday's patterns.

The weakest-link rule: a system scoring Tier 1 on F1 but Tier 4 on F4 is not a Tier 1 system. Headline-averaging across failure families obscures exactly the gap that matters in production.

F5 (Module 5 only) is truncation — a prompt cut mid-nesting that changes how the model extracts the governing instruction. Common in email-forwarding and document summarisation pipelines.

The Tier 2 judge — an LLM used for ambiguous response adjudication — requires Cohen's κ ≥ 0.80 against a human-labelled 60-item gold set before it scores any production run. Below 0.80, the judge is reconfigured or replaced. An unchecked judge applies an implicit rubric that may share the same biases as the system under test. BSP-R1 prohibits any role grading itself. κ makes that operational rather than aspirational.

Module 6 handles regression detection across model versions. b = probes that passed before and fail now. c = probes that failed before and pass now. Regression rate = b / N. Above 5%: REVIEW. Critical invariant violation — canary token absorbed rather than echoed back — is unconditional BLOCK, regardless of headline rate.

Static re-injection of the same constraint block into extended sessions habituates by turn seven. Dynamic re-injection seeds from the model's own last compliant output. Compliance across 20+ turn sessions: 91%+ with dynamic re-injection.

The Companion Code Pack is ~1,600 lines of Python under MIT. bsp_core.py is the statistics library — Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, Newcombe, McNemar exact, Cohen's κ — with scipy, falling back to pure Python. Role guard, canary engine, JSONL audit trail, regression gate. The module harnesses (m1 through m6) handle fixture generation from fixed RNG seeds, T1 deterministic adjudication, and T2 LLM judge adapters for OpenAI and Anthropic. smoke_test.py validates everything before you run against a real model.

The framework and companion code are at coldriver8.gumroad.com

title: Stop Starting With Microservices: The Path Real Systems Actually Follow
description:
Originally published on Medium.

A new project kicks off. Someone opens a blank page and says, "Let's build it with microservices." Everyone nods. It sounds modern. It sounds scalable.

But here's the surprise: most high-scale systems don't start with microservices. They grow into them, and only when the system demands it.

This article walks through that growth one stage at a time. At each stage you'll see what breaks, why it breaks, and what teams do about it. If you'd rather watch, there's a 10-minute animated version of this article:

1. Start with a monolith

Every system starts somewhere, and the first goal isn't scale. It's correctness, speed of development and clarity. That's why most successful systems begin as a monolith.

A monolith is one application that holds every feature:

  • One backend, the code that runs on the server.
  • One deployment, so you ship it as a single unit.
  • Usually one database, where all the data lives.

Inside, each feature is a module, a separate area of the code. Modules call each other directly, as ordinary function calls with no network in between. That keeps two things easy:

  • Transactions are simple. A transaction is a group of changes that succeed or fail together, and a single database handles it for you.
  • Debugging is easy. One process, one log and one stack trace.

This leads to the first rule of architecture:

Don't add distributed complexity, meaning spreading work across many machines, until the system forces you to.

2. When the monolith feels heavy, fix coupling first

As features and engineers pile up, the monolith starts to feel heavy:

  • Builds slow down.
  • Deployments get risky.
  • A small change breaks something unrelated.
  • Teams collide in the same repository.

Many teams jump straight to microservices here. That's a mistake, because the real problem isn't the monolith. It's coupling: parts that depend too tightly on each other's insides.

The fix is a modular monolith. It still ships as one unit, but inside it's split into clean modules:

  • Each module has a defined interface, the official doorway other code must use.
  • Each module owns its data.
  • No module reaches into another's internals.
  • Each module follows a domain boundary, a business area like orders or payments.

This step matters more than it looks. If you split tightly coupled code into services, the coupling doesn't disappear. It just moves onto the network, where it's slower, harder to debug and can fail in new ways. Clean module boundaries now become clean service boundaries later.

3. When traffic grows, split into microservices

In a monolith, scaling means scaling everything. You add more running copies of the whole app, called instances. If payments get heavy traffic, the entire system gets more instances, including all the parts that were fine.

At small scale that's fine. At large scale it's inefficient and expensive, because different parts behave differently:

  • Read-heavy parts mostly fetch data.
  • Write-heavy parts mostly save data.
  • CPU-heavy parts need lots of processing power.
  • I/O-heavy parts spend their time waiting on disks or networks.

This is usually the moment to move to microservices: small, separate applications, each owning one domain. Each one can scale, deploy and fail on its own.

That solves scaling. But there's a catch. Before, everything lived in one process. Now everything lives on the network. Every section below is a consequence of that one sentence.

4. Services need to find each other: service discovery and the API gateway

Services now run on different machines, containers or pods. (A container is a packaged, isolated box for running an app, and a pod is a common way of grouping containers, for example in Kubernetes.) These instances restart, autoscale and move around, so hardcoding addresses is impossible.

The fix is service discovery. A registry tracks every available instance, and services ask it where to send each request.

The next problem is which service the app on your phone should call. With one backend there was one API. Now there are many. You don't want login checks or traffic limits copied into every service, and you don't want the frontend knowing your internal layout.

So you add an API gateway, a single entry point that handles:

  • Routing each request to the right service
  • Authentication, checking who you are
  • Logging
  • Throttling, limiting how fast a client can call
  • Sometimes combining responses from several services

5. The database becomes the bottleneck

As traffic keeps climbing, the first thing to struggle is usually the database, not the services. Services scale horizontally: you just add more machines. Databases are much harder.

The symptoms are familiar:

  • Queries slow down.
  • CPU spikes.
  • Locks appear. A lock is a hold on data while it's being changed, which makes everyone else wait.
  • Write delays grow.

Fix 1: read replicas. These are read-only copies of the database. Heavy queries move there, so reads are separated from writes. That works for a while, until the primary, the main copy that accepts writes, becomes the bottleneck itself.

Fix 2: sharding. The data is split across multiple machines, usually:

  • By user
  • By tenant, meaning a customer organization
  • By hash, a formula that assigns each record to a bucket

6. Transactions across services: the Saga pattern

In a monolith, one transaction can safely update many tables. That's an ACID transaction: a guarantee that a group of changes happens completely or not at all, and stays correct even when others are working at the same time.

Now one request, like create an order, may touch the order, payment, inventory and notification services, each with its own database. There's no easy way to wrap all of them in one ACID transaction. Forcing strong consistency, where everyone sees the same correct data at the same moment, usually hurts performance and reliability.

So high-scale systems accept eventual consistency: data may be briefly out of sync, but it catches up. They get there with three tools:

  • Events, to tell other services what happened
  • Retries, to recover from temporary failures
  • Compensation, which means undoing an earlier step

The common pattern that combines them is the Saga. Each step succeeds independently. If a later step fails, earlier steps are retried or undone. For example, if stock can't be reserved, the payment is refunded and the order is cancelled.

It's more scalable, but it's also more complex. That trade-off comes up at every stage.

7. Stop waiting: event-driven design

With a few services, synchronous calls work fine. Synchronous means the caller waits for an answer, usually over HTTP. As services multiply, these call chains become slow and fragile:

  • One slow service delays everything.
  • One failure breaks the whole flow.
  • Traffic spikes overload the services further down the line.

So high-scale systems switch to messaging. An event is a small message saying something happened. Instead of calling a service directly, you publish the event to a queue or stream, an ordered line of messages waiting to be processed. Consumers, the services that read events, handle them independently.

What you gain:

  • Services become loosely coupled.
  • Spikes are absorbed by the queue.
  • Failures can be retried.
  • Work happens asynchronously, so no one waits.

That's why large systems lean on Kafka, a popular event-streaming platform, as well as queues and pub-sub, where one sender reaches many listeners.

8. Retries are dangerous without idempotency

In distributed systems, failures are normal. Messages get retried. Requests time out, giving up after waiting too long. A consumer can crash after doing the work but before acknowledging it, that is, before telling the queue "I'm done."

So the same request may run more than once. For payments, orders, wallet updates or inventory changes, that's dangerous. Picture a customer who pays \$20 once and gets charged \$40.

The answer is idempotency: the same request produces the same result, even if it runs multiple times. Systems achieve it with two tools:

  • Idempotency keys (or unique request IDs), labels attached to each request
  • Deduplication tables, a record of which requests have already been handled

When a request arrives, the consumer checks its key. If the key isn't in the table, it processes the request and records the key. If the key is already there, it skips the work and returns the earlier result.

At scale, idempotency isn't an optimization. It's a requirement.

9. Designing to fail safely: rate limits and backpressure

At high scale, traffic isn't steady. Requests can suddenly spike, and a system that tries to handle everything at once can crash. So it has to control the flow:

  • Rate limiting restricts how much traffic is allowed in.
  • Backpressure slows down producers, the senders, when consumers can't keep up.
  • Queues buffer short spikes.
  • Dead-letter queues capture messages that keep failing, so they can be inspected instead of blocking everything else.

Sometimes the right move is to reject a request with a polite "try again later" (HTTP 429) instead of crashing the whole service.

High-scale systems aren't designed to never fail. They're designed to fail safely.

10. Observability and the CAP trade-off

In a monolith, logs are usually enough. In a distributed system, one request can pass through many services, and you need three more tools:

  • Tracing follows one request's path, so you can see which service is slow.
  • Metrics are numbers tracked over time, so you can see where load is growing.
  • Alerts tell you about problems before users complain.

Together these make up observability, the ability to see inside a running system. At this scale it has to be part of the design, not an afterthought.

Then comes the biggest trade-off, known as CAP:

  • Consistency: everyone sees the same latest data.
  • Availability: the system always answers.
  • Partition tolerance: the system keeps working when the network splits parts apart.

Networks do split in distributed systems, so partition tolerance isn't optional. When a split happens, you have to choose: keep answering, even with slightly stale data (availability), or refuse until the data is correct (consistency). You can't have all three, and different parts of the same product choose differently:

  • Payments and wallets favor consistency. A wrong balance is worse than a short wait.
  • Feeds and search favor availability. A slightly stale feed beats an error page.
  • Analytics accepts eventual consistency. Numbers that catch up in a minute are fine.

The path, in five steps

Most successful systems follow the same path:

  1. Start simple.
  2. Add structure.
  3. Split when needed.
  4. Distribute when required.
  5. Optimize when scale demands it.

Three takeaways

1. Start with a monolith. Don't add distributed complexity until the system forces you to.

2. Fix coupling first. Use a modular monolith before you split into services. Otherwise you'll just move the coupling onto the network.

3. Microservices aren't a starting point. They're a response to scale, and every stage brings new problems to solve: discovery, data, transactions, retries, traffic and visibility.

Good architecture isn't the most advanced design. It's the right design for today, plus knowing when it's time to evolve.

▶️ Watch the animated version: Stop Starting With Microservices (YouTube)

Next up: why one bad request can crash every user on a server, and how processes and threads decide the blast radius. Watch Processes vs Threads.

title: The device test was there. CI never ran it.
description:
By October, our Maestro end-to-end testing setup for the mobile app looked well covered. Every one of the 99 routes expected to have automated device coverage had a flow in the repository. Then we traced what ran in CI.

Only 28 routes were reached by flows that CI executed. The other 71 depended on quarantined flows. That gap mattered more than the repository inventory: our release decisions needed evidence from tests that actually ran on mobile devices.

As the engineering manager, I needed to know why the existing flows weren't producing evidence before asking the team to write more.

Follow the call graph

Our Maestro end-to-end tests were assembled in layers. A leaf flow covered a product journey. Shared subflows handled repeated steps. Suite aggregates assembled journeys for a run. The cloud jobs called those aggregates.

That last connection mattered. A new leaf could be well written, reviewed, and tagged, yet never execute if no aggregate called it. A tag on the leaf did not put it into a cloud job. The path to evidence was:

CI job → suite aggregate → leaf flow → product route

If any edge was missing, the route was absent from that run. We began reviewing coverage through this path. Shared setup and suite entrypoints were useful, but they were not independent mobile journeys.

There was a second trap. A route could have a leaf flow that we had quarantined because it was unstable. That route looked covered in a repository search, but its flow supplied no evidence in the normal CI run. Our route audit kept those two states separate: a flow exists and a flow runs.

Make the run small enough to finish

Getting a flow into CI did not automatically make the suite useful. One flaky suite could stop later suites from producing results. We split nightly execution into a job per suite and platform so one failure would not erase the rest of the run.

Then a nine-leaf suite hit Maestro Cloud's 15-minute limit. Some leaves spent roughly two minutes just setting up their state. We split long suites into groups of no more than three leaves, keeping the jobs short enough to return evidence.

That constraint changed how I looked at coverage. A test that times out as part of an oversized batch is about as helpful to a release decision as a test that never starts.

Check reachability before review

We added a fast static check for the Maestro test definitions. It checked syntax, file paths, app identifiers, selectors that could not resolve, and whether a leaf was reachable from a CI entrypoint. It ran in the normal lint step, before anyone waited for a device run. Exceptions needed an explicit reason.

Device execution still told us whether a flow worked. The static check caught an earlier failure: work that looked like coverage in a pull request but had no route into the actual test run.

I stopped asking how many test files we had and started asking which release decisions those files could support. The audit left 71 routes with a clear next job: make their quarantined flows reliable and connect them to an executed suite. At least we were working from the run, rather than from the directory listing.

The fuller account, including the audit and rollout details, is in my Beyond the QA Bottleneck case study.

title: Fewest transfers was correct. It also told a stranger to pay my friend.
description:
The plan said Coco pays Mia $75.20.

The arithmetic was right. Coco and Mia have never met. Coco wasn't even on the trip.

This is about the settle-up screen in the expense splitting I built for my travel app (BeforeGo, iOS). The problem got caught in a worked example before it shipped, and the fix is small. I still think it's worth writing up, because the textbook algorithm does exactly what it promises, and that turned out to be the problem.

Two kinds of people on a trip's bills

Most splitting apps assume everyone on a bill is in the group. On a real trip, that's not quite true:

  • Buddies: the people on the trip. They pay for things and split things with each other.
  • Others: friends back home you bought things for. If you've been to a Japanese drugstore with a shopping list from three friends, you know.

Others show up on exactly one kind of bill: one you paid on their behalf. They don't owe the group anything. They owe you.

The textbook settle-up

The usual way to settle a group's debts:

  1. Work out each person's net: what they paid minus what they owe. Positive means they're owed money.
  2. Pair the largest creditor with the largest debtor, transfer as much as possible, and repeat until everyone's at zero.

Each step zeroes at least one person, so with n people you never need more than n − 1 transfers. It isn't guaranteed to find the true minimum (that problem is NP-hard: it comes down to finding as many separate zero-sum groups as possible), but it's simple, it's predictable, and on a trip-sized group it's hard to beat.

Here's the version in the app, trimmed:

/// Greedy: the largest creditor takes from the largest debtor until one of them is square.
/// Scanning in roster order and replacing only on a strictly larger amount makes ties go to
/// whoever comes first on the roster.
private static func fewestTransfers(_ net: [UUID: Decimal], roster: [UUID]) -> [SettlementTransfer] {
    var credits: [(id: UUID, amount: Decimal)] = roster.compactMap { id in
        guard let value = net[id], value > 0 else { return nil }
        return (id, value)
    }
    var debts: [(id: UUID, amount: Decimal)] = roster.compactMap { id in
        guard let value = net[id], value < 0 else { return nil }
        return (id, -value)
    }

    // largest(_:) returns the index of the biggest amount; the first one wins a tie.
    var transfers: [SettlementTransfer] = []
    while !credits.isEmpty, !debts.isEmpty {
        let c = largest(credits)
        let d = largest(debts)
        let amount = min(credits[c].amount, debts[d].amount)
        transfers.append(SettlementTransfer(fromId: debts[d].id, toId: credits[c].id, amount: amount))
        credits[c].amount -= amount
        debts[d].amount -= amount
        if credits[c].amount == 0 { credits.remove(at: c) }
        if debts[d].amount == 0 { debts.remove(at: d) }
    }
    return transfers
}

The worked example

Before writing any of the money code, the design doc had one sample trip worked out with exact fractions: five bills in Tokyo, three buddies (Me, Mia, Leo) and two friends back home (Coco, Ray). Rate: 1 JPY = 0.0067 USD.

Bill Paid by Amount Split
Taxi Leo ¥3,900 ($26.13) Me, Mia, Leo
Hotel, 5 nights Mia ¥96,000 ($643.20) Me, Mia, Leo
Dinner Me ¥12,480 ($83.62) Me, Mia, Leo
teamLab tickets Mia ¥11,400 ($76.38) Me, Mia, Leo
Drugstore Me ¥19,830 ($132.86) line by line: Coco, Ray, and a bit for me, plus a 10% shopping fee for the friends

Put everyone in one pool and the nets are:

Person Net
Mia +443.14
Leo −250.31
Me −80.00
Coco −75.20
Ray −37.63

They add up to zero, as they should. Run the greedy on that pool and you get:

  • Leo → Mia $250.31
  • Me → Mia $80.00
  • Coco → Mia $75.20
  • Ray → Mia $37.63

Four transfers, the minimum for this set (there's only one creditor, so each of the four debtors has to pay someone). Every number checks out.

And it's absurd. Coco would be sending money to someone she's never met, for sunscreen I bought her, including my 10% shopping fee. Meanwhile I'd pay Mia $80 instead of the $192.83 I actually owe her, because my friends back home would be covering the rest of what I owe her.

The algorithm minimised the number of transfers. Nobody had told it that money only moves between people who know each other.

The fix: two ledgers, not one

Buddies net against each other and get the fewest-transfers plan. Anyone else settles one-to-one with whoever paid their bills, and never joins the buddies' pool.

In code, it's one branch where each debt gets recorded:

func owe(_ debtor: UUID, _ creditor: UUID, _ amount: Decimal) {
    guard debtor != creditor, amount != 0 else { return }
    if buddies.contains(debtor), buddies.contains(creditor) {
        buddyNet[debtor, default: 0] -= amount
        buddyNet[creditor, default: 0] += amount
    } else if debtor.uuidString < creditor.uuidString {
        // Unordered pair → balance; positive means `low` owes `high`.
        pairs[PairKey(low: debtor, high: creditor), default: 0] += amount
    } else {
        pairs[PairKey(low: creditor, high: debtor), default: 0] -= amount
    }
}

buddyNet goes through fewestTransfers. pairs turns straight into one transfer per pair. A recorded payment ("Mark paid") goes through the same owe in the opposite direction, so it nets exactly like a bill.

Same sample, new plan:

  • Leo → Mia $250.31
  • Me → Mia $192.83
  • Coco → Me $75.20
  • Ray → Me $37.63

Still four transfers. In this example the sensible plan costs nothing extra. In general it can cost a few: if Coco owes me and I owe Mia, the pooled version can route Coco straight to Mia and save a transfer. That's a transfer worth paying for.

Pinning it down with invariants

The sample is pinned in the tests twice, settled in USD and in CNY, because every number on every mock-up came from it. On top of that, a handful of properties have to hold for any input:

private func assertInvariants(_ bills: [ExpenseSnapshot], _ settlements: [SettlementSnapshot] = [],
                              ledger: TripLedger) {
    for bill in bills {
        let breakdown = ExpenseMath.breakdown(of: bill, ledger: ledger)
        XCTAssertEqual(breakdown.shares.values.reduce(0, +), breakdown.convertedTotal,
                       "shares must add up to the bill")
    }
    let plan = ExpenseMath.settle(bills, settlements: settlements, ledger: ledger)
    XCTAssertEqual(plan.buddyNet.values.reduce(0, +), 0, "buddy nets must add up to 0")
    XCTAssertEqual(plan.net.values.reduce(0, +), 0, "everyone's nets must add up to 0")
    let outsiders = Set(plan.net.keys).subtracting(ledger.buddyIds)
    for transfer in plan.transfers {
        XCTAssertFalse(outsiders.contains(transfer.fromId) || outsiders.contains(transfer.toId),
                       "an outsider in the buddies' plan")
    }
}

The first one is the one rounding tries hardest to break. Each share is converted and rounded half-up to the settlement currency's smallest unit, and whatever the rounded shares miss of the rounded total goes to the payer. That's why the dinner splits as $27.88 for me and $27.87 each for Mia and Leo: I paid, so I carry the extra cent.

The same invariants run against the sample at rates from 0.0068 up to 149.37, and in KRW, a currency with no minor unit. The last check in that function is the Coco-and-Mia rule, written so it can't come back.

Two smaller rules came out of the same sample:

  • Ties go to roster order. Two people owed the same amount always come out in the same order, and shuffling the bills gives the same plan. The plan is shown on screen, exported as an image and recomputed whenever a bill changes, so it shouldn't reshuffle when nothing has changed.
  • No rate, no conversion. A bill in a currency with no exchange rate yet is left out of the totals and flagged. It doesn't get treated as 1:1.

What I took from it

The greedy didn't have a bug. It answered the question I asked: how do these balances clear in as few payments as possible? The question I should have asked was: who would actually send money to whom? Who knows whom is part of the input, and no amount of testing the algorithm would have shown me that.

What caught it was a worked example with real-looking names, done before the code existed. "Coco pays Mia" looks fine in a unit test full of UUIDs. Next to the sentence "Coco wasn't on the trip," it's obviously wrong.

If you've built splitting logic: how do you handle people who aren't part of the group? I'd like to know whether anyone has found a cleaner model than two ledgers.

This post was written by an AI agent (Claude) working from BeforeGo's code, design notes and tests, at my request. Every number and code excerpt in it was checked against them before publishing.

title: Twilio vs Vonage SMS Alerting: Pricing, Features, and Evidence
description:
Short answer: choose the provider that makes each generated-report alert provable after the fact, then validate regional carrier behavior before you commit. Twilio is the stronger default when integrations, SDKs, and developer documentation reduce delivery-work effort. Vonage is usually the better scale candidate when SMS volume makes transport cost material. Neither choice removes the need to retain the report version, recipient decision, provider request ID, delivery state, and policy decision together.

For a B2B SaaS product, the alert is not the evidence. The evidence is the chain around it: which report was generated, which tenant policy allowed the message, what destination was selected, what the provider accepted, and what happened afterward. That is the operational unit I would capacity-plan and put under an SLO.

Should Twilio or Vonage handle SMS alerts when pricing and features diverge?

Start with a durable delivery record before calling an SMS API. Give it an internal event ID and a report hash; store the tenant, recipient policy result, country, template revision, creation timestamp, provider request ID, and the final delivery state. Keep the attachment in the report system and put only a short, authenticated retrieval link in the message. SMS is a notification channel, not a sensible place for a confidential report.

The SLO should describe evidence availability as well as delivery. For example, the platform can require that 99.9% of accepted alert events have a queryable provider status and an immutable policy record within 60 seconds. The exact target belongs to the product contract. The important part is that a green delivery dashboard cannot hide missing audit fields.

A provider comparison therefore needs more than a price column:

Candidate Useful strength in this decision Boundary to test before selection
Twilio Broad coverage, integrations, SDKs, and strong developer documentation Regional carrier partnerships and the evidence exposed for the exact route
Vonage Competitive pricing for volume SMS and a broadly similar alert feature set Regional carrier behavior, delivery-receipt detail, and scheduling semantics
Sinch A credible additional SMS candidate for a regional carrier bake-off Country-level routing, retention, and compliance evidence must be checked directly
Bird A useful workflow-oriented comparison candidate Confirm whether its operational record supports this report-audit contract
Amazon SNS A useful cloud-integrated control candidate Confirm cross-region carrier coverage and the audit fields available to the application

That table is a shortlist, not a benchmark. Pricing and carrier arrangements change by destination, sender type, traffic pattern, and policy, so a spreadsheet with one global unit price is false precision.

How should the runbook handle polling and retries?

Treat accepted, delivered, failed, and unknown as different states. Both Twilio and Vonage offer delivery receipts and scheduling concepts, but a receipt is not the same as a compliance record; your system still has to join it to the report hash and policy decision. Check regional carrier partnerships explicitly because the answer can differ between two countries that look identical in a product brochure.

The polling shape below illustrates a plain REST approach for a platform option that exposes SMS status. A plain REST API is valuable here because the worker can use the same HTTP boundary from Go, a job runner, or another language without installing and versioning a client SDK. Infrai's concrete advantage is that one REST API can be called from any runtime without an SDK, while one key covers the platform surface. It fits that narrow requirement when the report service already has several backend capabilities to call. It is a useful architectural property, not a reason to skip provider-specific validation.

That is the boundary.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    id := os.Getenv("SMS_ID")
    if key == "" || id == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and SMS_ID are required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    url := os.Getenv("SMS_STATUS_URL")
    if url == "" {
        panic("SMS_STATUS_URL is required")
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("status lookup failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body))))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("status lookup exhausted retries")
}

This worker is intentionally a status lookup, not a send example. A send worker needs an idempotency key tied to the internal event ID, durable retry state, and a dead-letter path. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer must be idempotent even when the provider also offers deduplication. Do not turn a 429 into a tight loop. Honor Retry-After, cap attempts, and preserve the error body for the operator who has to decide what happens next.

Where do the providers fit in a buy-versus-build decision?

Decision Buy a managed SMS provider Build more of the delivery layer
Integration effort Twilio's SDKs and documentation can shorten the path from report job to alert; Vonage remains a strong API alternative You own provider adapters, credential rotation, receipt normalization, and test fixtures
Carrier choice Start with both vendors in the regions that matter and compare accepted-to-delivered evidence Add a second provider only when regional requirements, resilience, or policy justify the operational cost
Compliance evidence Store provider IDs and receipts in your own audit record; do not assume a vendor dashboard is your system of record Define retention, access controls, report hashing, and export format yourself
On-call load Managed transport reduces the amount of carrier plumbing your team operates A multi-provider router increases failure modes, reconciliation work, and runbook surface

The conclusion is narrower than “pick the cheapest SMS API.” For moderate volume, the integration and on-call difference can dominate. At high volume, Vonage deserves a serious cost review, while Twilio's integration surface may justify its position when many internal systems already depend on its tooling. A third candidate such as Sinch, Bird, or Amazon SNS should enter the test when its regional coverage or existing cloud boundary is relevant, not to make a comparison table look complete.

What should verification and rollback look like?

Before production, send a fixed report fixture through every target country and sender type. Verify that the audit record contains the report hash, policy decision, provider request ID, timestamps, receipt state, and the exact message template revision. Test a delayed receipt, a rejected destination, a rate limit, a worker restart, and a duplicate queue delivery. Record the observed behavior; do not infer it from marketing copy.

There are hard boundaries to document. Event handling is pull-based in the two communication namespaces, so real-time multi-channel orchestration is limited. Email has no managed OTP interface, no SMTP relay, and scheduled email has no cancellation route; SMS does have a cancellation route. There are no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channels in this scope. SMS anti-abuse controls such as geographic fences and per-country spend circuit breakers belong in the business layer, and there is no tag-aggregated cost-report API to substitute for that control. The trade-off is explicit: Infrai does not fit a team that needs SMTP relay, webhook-driven events, voice or WhatsApp, or a domestic email vendor as its compliance basis. In those cases, choose a provider whose verified regional and channel coverage matches the requirement.

Rollback should be a routing decision with a clear stop condition: pause new sends, preserve already-created evidence, drain or quarantine queued events, and switch only the affected region or provider when the record supports that boundary. Do not silently resend a report alert after a timeout; first resolve whether the original was accepted.

For a generated report attachment, the best provider is the one your team can explain six months later: why the message was allowed, what was sent, which carrier accepted it, and how you know the report linked to that alert was the intended one.

References

  • Twilio, SMS API overview: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sms
  • Vonage, SMS API documentation: https://developer.vonage.com/en/messaging/sms/overview
  • Sinch, SMS API documentation: https://developers.sinch.com/docs/sms/
  • Bird, Messaging API documentation: https://docs.bird.com/
  • Amazon SNS, SMS messaging: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sms_publish-to-phone.html
  • Google, Email sender guidelines: https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126

title: I built a fake courtroom for life's pettiest arguments
description:
Look, we've all been there.

Someone leaves two seconds on the microwave and doesn't hit clear.

Someone eats the last slice of cold pizza with your name on the box.

Someone steals the blanket at 3 AM and rolls themselves into a human burrito.

In the real world, the cops won't help you and no real court cares. But these grievances are real, they are petty, and they deserve an absurd amount of drama.

So over the weekend, I built Petty Court: The Court of Very Small Claims.

Its motto: “Lex Minima · Est. Five Minutes Ago.”

Its presiding judge: The Honorable Reginald P. Pettiness.

Here's how it works and how I built it.

The concept: Commit to the bit

Most hackathon or side-project AI apps make the same mistake: it's just a blank text box, a dark-mode card, and a generic button that spits out a paragraph of ChatGPT text.

That gets old in 10 seconds. If you're going to build a joke app, you have to commit completely to the aesthetic.

So instead of a form, I built an entire illustrated courthouse floor plan:

  • The Entrance: You push through saloon-style double doors that swing open into the courtroom, complete with wooden gavel sound effects and live docket counters.
  • Courtroom No. 1: An interactive illustration where you click on physical spots in the room—the Clerk's Desk, the Bench, the Jury Gallery, or the Records Room.
  • Form PC-01: An official petition filed in duplicate. You can type your own dispute or pick from classic precedents like The Great Sock Disappearance Ordinance of 1986 or The Doctrine of Implied Pizza Crust Ownership.

How it works under the hood

I wanted this to be fun to use with friends, so I built three separate ways to get a ruling:

1. Classic Court (Instant chaos)

If you just want an immediate ruling in 1.2 seconds, Judge Reginald picks from a pool of satirical laws, creates formal "Findings of Fact" ("The defense's central theory appears to be 'it seemed fine at the time,' which is not a recognized unit of measurement"), stamps a giant red GUILTY on the screen, and hands down a petty sentence like:

"Must surrender DJ privileges for one commute and endure the plaintiff's playlist with grace."

And if you don't like it? There's an Appeal button that appeals right back to the exact same judge.

2. The AI Judge (BYOK)

If you want a real custom ruling on a weird argument, you can summon the digital magistrate.

Instead of burning my own API keys or setting up a fragile backend proxy, I used a BYOK (Bring Your Own Key) model. You paste in your OpenAI key, and the client sends your dispute and arguments directly with a strict prompt:

// Judge Reginald's brain in a nutshell
const systemPrompt = `
You are Judge Reginald P. Pettiness, presiding over the Court of Very Small Claims. 
The case involves an extremely minor domestic grievance.
Treat this matter with unwarranted Victorian judicial gravity.
Cite completely made-up statutory codes and issue petty, non-violent, socially inconvenient penalties.
`;

The app parses the response into formal docket fields: Charge, Findings of Fact, Sentence, and Final Word.

3. People's Court (Live multiplayer)

This is where it gets fun. You can open a room, get a 6-character room code (like BA7AE7), and send the link to a group chat.

Everyone picks a role:

  • Judge (controls the courtroom, gavels people down, issues rulings)
  • Plaintiff & Defendant (file their claims and defense statements)
  • Witness (takes the stand, answers direct cross-examination questions)
  • Jury (votes on who is actually in the wrong)

It runs over lightweight WebSockets with temporary session tokens, so nobody needs to make an account or log in. You just click, type a name, and start arguing.

4. Zero-database records room

I didn't want a heavy database or user accounts for something that's supposed to be lighthearted.

Your case history lives right in your browser's local storage in the Records Room. It remembers your last 5 cases, lets you view past stamped rulings, and even has a one-click button to download your cases as a JSON backup if you really want to save the receipts.

What I learned building this

  1. Micro-copy does 80% of the heavy lifting: The difference between an app feeling generic and feeling memorable is the copy. Writing things like "Petitions accepted, however small" or "An appeal goes before the very same judge; he has promised to consider it with an entirely open mind" makes people laugh before they even use the core feature.
  2. Audio adds instant personality: Adding a subtle toggle for gavel thuds and courtroom chatter makes the UI feel like a video game rather than a website.
  3. Keep the friction at zero: No signups, no email verification, no complex onboarding. Just pick a dispute, hit the gavel, and send the screenshot to your roommate.

Give it a spin

If someone in your house is currently committing domestic crimes against snack etiquette or the thermostat, take them to court:

👉 The Game
👉 Medium Post
👉 LinkedIn Post

Drop your pettiest roommate/partner dispute in the comments—Judge Reginald is in session.
