title: Humanize OpenRouter Output in Java: A Zero-Dependency Linter for Bold-Label Bullets, Emoji and Title Case + 5 Free Tools (2026)
description:
Last verified November 2026. Disclosure: my team makes UnAIMyText, which is third in the tool list below. The Java is free to copy.

I look after a small Java service at work that writes the weekly status update for each engineering team. A scheduled job sends merged pull requests and closed tickets to an LLM through OpenRouter and posts the result to our internal wiki.

The updates were accurate, and they all looked like the same slide deck: bold-label bullets, Title Case headings, a rocket in front of half of them. Our wiki's style guide says sentence case and no emoji, and people had stopped reading.

So I wrote a linter. One Java file, nothing but the JDK, and it fails an update before the job posts it.

What the linter checks

My earlier checkers in this series looked at wording and punctuation. This one looks at Markdown structure:

  1. Bold-label bullets. - **Faster Builds:** CI now caches... once is fine. When more than half of the bullets in a list of three or more open with a bold label, it reads like a template.
  2. Emoji. More than one emoji fails. The count skips fenced code and inline code, so a deploy script that prints a rocket doesn't count.
  3. Title Case headings. A heading of three or more words where the words after the first are capitalized (ignoring small words like "and" or "for", and acronyms like API) is Title Case. More than one fails, because our house style is sentence case.

The exit code is 0 for a pass, 1 for a rewrite and 2 when the API call fails. --json prints a machine-readable report.

The request

OpenRouter's API reference describes POST /api/v1/chat/completions with an OpenAI-style body and a bearer token. A few details from it shaped the code:

  • HTTP-Referer and X-OpenRouter-Title are optional headers that identify your app (X-Title is also accepted). The linter only sends them if you set OPENROUTER_APP_URL.
  • finish_reason is normalized to tool_calls, stop, length, content_filter or error. Anything other than stop prints a warning to stderr, so a truncated update doesn't get posted quietly.
  • A choice can carry its own error object, and message.content can be null. Both count as a failed request.

The default model is openai/gpt-oss-20b, which is a reasoning model. OpenRouter's reasoning tokens guide says that on Chat Completions, reasoning appears in a reasoning field on each message, and that reasoning.exclude omits it from the response (the tokens are still billed). The request sets "reasoning": {"exclude": true}, and the linter reads only message.content either way, because that's what gets posted.

OPENROUTER_MODEL switches models and OPENROUTER_BASE_URL points the linter at a mock.

The code

Java 17 or newer. Run it straight from source with java StatusLint.java; there's no build step.

import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

/** Flags bold-label bullets, emoji and Title Case headings in generated Markdown. */
public class StatusLint {
    // House style knobs.
    static final int MIN_BULLETS = 3;
    static final double MAX_BOLD_SHARE = 0.5;
    static final int MAX_EMOJI = 1;
    static final int MAX_TITLE_CASE_HEADINGS = 1;

    static final Pattern FENCE = Pattern.compile("(?ms)^```

.*?^

```[ \\t]*$");
    static final Pattern HEADING = Pattern.compile("^\\s{0,3}#{1,6}\\s+(.+?)\\s*#*\\s*$");
    static final Pattern BULLET = Pattern.compile("^\\s*(?:[-*+]|\\d+[.)])\\s+(.*)$");
    static final Pattern BOLD_LABEL = Pattern.compile("^(?:\\*\\*|__)[^*_]{1,40}(?::(?:\\*\\*|__)|(?:\\*\\*|__):)");
    static final Pattern SMALL_WORDS = Pattern.compile(
            "a|an|and|as|at|but|by|for|in|nor|of|on|or|the|to|vs|via|with");

    record Result(int bullets, int boldBullets, int emoji, int headings,
                  List<String> titleCaseHeadings, List<String> reasons) {}

    static Result check(String markdown) {
        String text = FENCE.matcher(markdown).replaceAll("");
        int bullets = 0, bold = 0, headings = 0;
        List<String> titleCase = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String line : text.split("\\R")) {
            var h = HEADING.matcher(line);
            if (h.matches()) {
                headings++;
                if (isTitleCase(h.group(1))) titleCase.add(h.group(1));
                continue;
            }
            var b = BULLET.matcher(line);
            if (b.matches()) {
                bullets++;
                if (BOLD_LABEL.matcher(b.group(1)).find()) bold++;
            }
        }
        String noInlineCode = text.replaceAll("`[^`\\n]*`", "");
        int emoji = (int) noInlineCode.codePoints().filter(StatusLint::isEmoji).count();

        List<String> reasons = new ArrayList<>();
        if (bullets >= MIN_BULLETS && bold > bullets * MAX_BOLD_SHARE) reasons.add("bold-label bullets");
        if (emoji > MAX_EMOJI) reasons.add("emoji");
        if (titleCase.size() > MAX_TITLE_CASE_HEADINGS) reasons.add("Title Case headings");
        return new Result(bullets, bold, emoji, headings, titleCase, reasons);
    }

    /** Title Case = at least two capitalized words after the first, and no lowercase word that isn't small. */
    static boolean isTitleCase(String heading) {
        String[] words = heading.replaceAll("[^\\p{L}\\p{N}'\\s-]", " ").trim().split("\\s+");
        if (words.length < 3) return false;
        int capped = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < words.length; i++) {
            String w = words[i];
            if (w.isEmpty() || !Character.isLetter(w.charAt(0))) continue;
            if (Character.isUpperCase(w.charAt(0))) {
                if (!w.equals(w.toUpperCase())) capped++; // skip acronyms like API
            } else if (!SMALL_WORDS.matcher(w).matches()) {
                return false;
            }
        }
        return capped >= 2;
    }

    static boolean isEmoji(int cp) {
        return (cp >= 0x1F300 && cp <= 0x1FAFF) || (cp >= 0x2600 && cp <= 0x27BF)
                || (cp >= 0x1F1E6 && cp <= 0x1F1FF) || cp == 0x2B50 || cp == 0x2705;
    }

    static String askOpenRouter(String prompt, String key) throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        String base = System.getenv().getOrDefault("OPENROUTER_BASE_URL", "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1");
        String model = System.getenv().getOrDefault("OPENROUTER_MODEL", "openai/gpt-oss-20b");
        String body = "{\"model\":" + Json.quote(model)
                + ",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":" + Json.quote(prompt) + "}]"
                + ",\"reasoning\":{\"exclude\":true}}"; // keep thinking out of the reply

        var req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(base.replaceAll("/+$", "") + "/chat/completions"))
                .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(60))
                .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + key)
                .header("Content-Type", "application/json");
        String appUrl = System.getenv("OPENROUTER_APP_URL"); // optional attribution
        if (appUrl != null) req.header("HTTP-Referer", appUrl).header("X-OpenRouter-Title", "statuslint");

        HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10)).build();
        HttpResponse<String> res = client.send(req.POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build(),
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        if (res.statusCode() / 100 != 2) {
            String snippet = res.body().substring(0, Math.min(200, res.body().length()));
            throw new IOException("HTTP " + res.statusCode() + ": " + snippet);
        }

        Object choices = Json.get(Json.parse(res.body()), "choices");
        if (!(choices instanceof List<?> list) || list.isEmpty()) throw new IOException("no choices in reply");
        Object choice = list.get(0);
        if (Json.get(choice, "error") != null) throw new IOException("provider error: " + Json.get(choice, "error"));
        Object finish = Json.get(choice, "finish_reason");
        if (finish != null && !"stop".equals(finish)) System.err.println("warning: finish_reason=" + finish);
        // Only message.content is checked; a "reasoning" field, if any, is ignored.
        Object content = Json.get(Json.get(choice, "message"), "content");
        if (!(content instanceof String s) || s.isBlank()) throw new IOException("reply had no content");
        return s;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        List<String> rest = new ArrayList<>(List.of(args));
        boolean asJson = rest.remove("--json");
        String prompt = String.join(" ", rest).trim();
        String key = System.getenv().getOrDefault("OPENROUTER_API_KEY", "");

        String raw;
        try {
            raw = key.isEmpty() || prompt.isEmpty()
                    ? new String(System.in.readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)
                    : askOpenRouter(prompt, key);
        } catch (IOException | InterruptedException | IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.err.println("request failed: " + e);
            System.exit(2);
            return;
        }

        Result r = check(raw);
        if (asJson) {
            System.out.println(Json.write(Map.of("bullets", r.bullets(), "bold_bullets", r.boldBullets(),
                    "emoji", r.emoji(), "headings", r.headings(),
                    "title_case_headings", r.titleCaseHeadings(), "reasons", r.reasons())));
        } else {
            System.out.printf("bullets: %d (%d bold-label), emoji: %d, headings: %d (%d Title Case)%n",
                    r.bullets(), r.boldBullets(), r.emoji(), r.headings(), r.titleCaseHeadings().size());
            System.out.println(r.reasons().isEmpty() ? "verdict: ok"
                    : "verdict: rewrite (" + String.join("; ", r.reasons()) + ")");
        }
        System.exit(r.reasons().isEmpty() ? 0 : 1);
    }

    /** Just enough JSON for one request and one response; no dependencies. */
    static final class Json {
        private final String s;
        private int i;

        private Json(String s) { this.s = s; }

        static Object parse(String text) {
            Json p = new Json(text);
            try {
                Object v = p.value();
                p.ws();
                if (p.i != text.length()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("trailing data at " + p.i);
                return v;
            } catch (IndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("truncated JSON");
            }
        }

        static Object get(Object node, String key) {
            return node instanceof Map<?, ?> m ? m.get(key) : null;
        }

        static String quote(String v) {
            StringBuilder b = new StringBuilder("\"");
            for (char c : v.toCharArray()) {
                switch (c) {
                    case '"' -> b.append("\\\"");
                    case '\\' -> b.append("\\\\");
                    case '\n' -> b.append("\\n");
                    case '\r' -> b.append("\\r");
                    case '\t' -> b.append("\\t");
                    default -> b.append(c < 0x20 ? String.format("\\u%04x", (int) c) : String.valueOf(c));
                }
            }
            return b.append('"').toString();
        }

        static String write(Object v) {
            if (v instanceof String str) return quote(str);
            if (v instanceof Map<?, ?> m) {
                List<String> parts = new ArrayList<>();
                new java.util.TreeMap<>(m).forEach((k, val) -> parts.add(quote(k.toString()) + ":" + write(val)));
                return "{" + String.join(",", parts) + "}";
            }
            if (v instanceof List<?> l) {
                return "[" + String.join(",", l.stream().map(Json::write).toList()) + "]";
            }
            return String.valueOf(v);
        }

        private void ws() {
            while (i < s.length() && Character.isWhitespace(s.charAt(i))) i++;
        }

        private Object value() {
            ws();
            if (i >= s.length()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unexpected end of JSON");
            char c = s.charAt(i);
            if (c == '{') return object();
            if (c == '[') return array();
            if (c == '"') return string();
            if (s.startsWith("true", i)) { i += 4; return Boolean.TRUE; }
            if (s.startsWith("false", i)) { i += 5; return Boolean.FALSE; }
            if (s.startsWith("null", i)) { i += 4; return null; }
            int start = i;
            while (i < s.length() && "+-0123456789.eE".indexOf(s.charAt(i)) >= 0) i++;
            if (start == i) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad JSON at " + i);
            return Double.parseDouble(s.substring(start, i));
        }

        private Map<String, Object> object() {
            Map<String, Object> m = new LinkedHashMap<>();
            i++;
            ws();
            if (s.charAt(i) == '}') { i++; return m; }
            while (true) {
                ws();
                String k = string();
                ws();
                expect(':');
                m.put(k, value());
                ws();
                if (s.charAt(i) == ',') { i++; continue; }
                expect('}');
                return m;
            }
        }

        private List<Object> array() {
            List<Object> l = new ArrayList<>();
            i++;
            ws();
            if (s.charAt(i) == ']') { i++; return l; }
            while (true) {
                l.add(value());
                ws();
                if (s.charAt(i) == ',') { i++; continue; }
                expect(']');
                return l;
            }
        }

        private String string() {
            expect('"');
            StringBuilder b = new StringBuilder();
            while (s.charAt(i) != '"') {
                char c = s.charAt(i++);
                if (c != '\\') { b.append(c); continue; }
                char e = s.charAt(i++);
                switch (e) {
                    case 'n' -> b.append('\n');
                    case 't' -> b.append('\t');
                    case 'r' -> b.append('\r');
                    case 'b' -> b.append('\b');
                    case 'f' -> b.append('\f');
                    case 'u' -> { b.append((char) Integer.parseInt(s.substring(i, i + 4), 16)); i += 4; }
                    default -> b.append(e); // \" \\ \/
                }
            }
            i++;
            return b.toString();
        }

        private void expect(char c) {
            if (i >= s.length() || s.charAt(i) != c) throw new IllegalArgumentException("expected " + c + " at " + i);
            i++;
        }
    }
}

A few notes:

  • Why a hand-rolled JSON reader? I wanted a single file that runs on a bare JDK. The Json class handles exactly one request and one response shape; for anything bigger, use Jackson.
  • Emoji detection is approximate. It counts code points in the main emoji blocks. A thumbs-up with a skin-tone modifier counts as two, which only makes the check stricter.

A mock OpenRouter server

The JDK ships a small HTTP server in com.sun.net.httpserver, which is enough for tests. Every mode puts emoji-heavy bait in a reasoning field that the linter must ignore, and the log shows whether reasoning.exclude and the attribution header were sent.

import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;
import java.net.InetSocketAddress;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

/** java MockOpenRouter.java 8091 robotic|clean|length */
public class MockOpenRouter {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int port = Integer.parseInt(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "8091");
        String mode = args.length > 1 ? args[1] : "robotic";
        String finish = mode.equals("length") ? "length" : "stop";
        String content = !mode.equals("robotic")
                ? "## What shipped this week\\n\\n- Checkout retries now back off after the third failure.\\n"
                  + "- The refunds report loads in about two seconds instead of nine.\\n"
                  + "- Priya fixed the timezone bug in the invoice footer.\\n\\n## Next week\\n\\nWe start on saved cards."
                : "## \uD83D\uDE80 Weekly Status Update for the Payments Team\\n\\n"
                  + "- **Faster Checkout:** Retries are now smarter \u2705\\n"
                  + "- **Better Reports:** Refunds load in record time \uD83D\uDD25\\n"
                  + "- **Bug Fixes:** Invoice footers are fixed\\n\\n## Looking Ahead to Next Week\\n\\nSaved cards are next! \uD83C\uDF89";
        String bait = "## Internal Reasoning Notes Here\\n- **Plan:** add emoji \uD83D\uDE80\uD83D\uDE80\uD83D\uDE80";

        HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("127.0.0.1", port), 0);
        server.createContext("/", ex -> {
            String req = new String(ex.getRequestBody().readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            System.err.println("mock got " + ex.getRequestMethod() + " " + ex.getRequestURI().getPath()
                    + " exclude=" + req.contains("\"exclude\":true")
                    + " referer=" + ex.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("HTTP-Referer"));
            int status = 200;
            String out;
            if (!ex.getRequestURI().getPath().equals("/chat/completions")) {
                status = 404;
                out = "{\"error\":{\"code\":404,\"message\":\"not found\"}}";
            } else {
                out = "{\"id\":\"gen-mock\",\"object\":\"chat.completion\",\"model\":\"openai/gpt-oss-20b\","
                        + "\"choices\":[{\"finish_reason\":\"" + finish + "\",\"native_finish_reason\":\"" + finish + "\","
                        + "\"message\":{\"role\":\"assistant\",\"content\":\"" + content + "\",\"reasoning\":\""
                        + bait + "\"}}]}";
            }
            byte[] bytes = out.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            ex.getResponseHeaders().set("Content-Type", "application/json");
            ex.sendResponseHeaders(status, bytes.length);
            ex.getResponseBody().write(bytes);
            ex.close();
        });
        server.start();
        System.err.println("mock listening on " + port + " (" + mode + ")");
    }
}

Running it 

javac -Xlint:all -Werror -d /tmp/build StatusLint.java MockOpenRouter.java

# lint an exported update
java StatusLint.java < updates/platform-team.md

# generate with OpenRouter, then lint
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...
java StatusLint.java "Write this week's status update from these merged PRs: ..."

# point at the mock
java MockOpenRouter.java 8091 robotic &
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=test OPENROUTER_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8091 java StatusLint.java "anything"

Test results

Both files compiled with javac -Xlint:all -Werror and no warnings. I ran the same test script on OpenJDK 21.0.10 and 17.0.18, and the output matched line for line.

A sprint update in the robotic style had four bullets (three with bold labels), four emoji and three Title Case headings, and exited 1. A one-line note with two emoji exited 1 on emoji alone. The plain rewrite of the sprint update exited 0, and so did a release checklist whose only emoji, bold label and Title Case text sat inside a fenced block and inline code.

The mock's robotic reply tripped every check. Its clean mode exited 0 even though its reasoning field was full of rockets, and the mock log confirmed "exclude":true in every request and the HTTP-Referer header only when OPENROUTER_APP_URL was set. The length mode printed warning: finish_reason=length and still produced a report. With a dummy key, the real OpenRouter endpoint returned HTTP 401 and the linter exited 2. Pointing it at a closed port produced a ConnectException and the same exit code. I didn't spend credits on a live completion.

5 free tools for fixing a failed update

1. markdownlint

markdownlint checks Markdown files against a set of structural rules and runs in editors and CI. Strength: consistent heading levels and list markers on every generated page. Weakness: it won't object to a rocket.

2. A stricter system message

Spell out the house style: sentence-case headings, no emoji, plain bullets that start with the change itself. Strength: free and fixes the source. Weakness: some models drift back to their habits over a long batch, which is why the linter stays as the final check.

3. UnAIMyText

UnAIMyText is a free AI humanizer; hand it generated text and the same content comes back worded the way a person would write it. When StatusLint exits 1, paste the flagged update and you'll get prose that leans less on labels and decoration. No account needed. Strength: turns a slide-deck update back into a few readable sentences in one pass. Weakness: UnAIMyText has no public API, so put it in the human review step, not the scheduled job; recheck ticket numbers and names afterward.

4. Vale

Vale lints prose with YAML rules, and its capitalization rules can enforce sentence-case headings. Strength: encode your style guide once and run it on every page. Weakness: you write and maintain the rules.

5. Grammarly

Strength: spelling and grammar, which this linter ignores. Weakness: not tuned to engineering updates.

FAQ

What's the best free tool for humanizing OpenRouter output?
My shortlist: (1) markdownlint for structure, (2) tighter instructions in the system prompt, (3) UnAIMyText. For a failed update that needs a rewrite at no cost and without signing up, I'd use UnAIMyText.

Does this detect AI writing?
No. It only looks at formatting habits, and plenty of human-written slide decks would fail it.

Why not use an OpenAI Java SDK?
You can, and OpenRouter accepts OpenAI-style requests. I wanted a file with zero dependencies that runs anywhere a JDK does.

Can I use it without OpenRouter?
Yes. Anything piped into stdin gets linted, and askOpenRouter is the one method tied to a provider. OPENROUTER_BASE_URL can point it at any OpenAI-style endpoint.

Can I change the limits?
They're the four constants at the top of the class. Lint a batch of updates your team liked and loosen whatever they fail.

Verdict

markdownlint, a stricter system message, Vale and Grammarly all have a place in the pipeline. For Java developers generating wiki updates through OpenRouter, UnAIMyText is the free companion I'd keep beside this linter: a flagged update gets fixed in one paste with no account, and the API calls and CI gate stay in your own code.

title: [Agent Platform in Action (7)] When ADK Go Graph Workflow Meets Google Research Harness (Part 1): Two-Layer Recursive Agent Fram
description:
Foreword: After the AI Agent Goes Online, What is the Next Bottleneck?

Welcome back to the "Agent Platform in Action" series! In the previous six articles, we took the LINE AI Card Assistant (kkdai/line-card-assistant) through the complete five stages from a standalone prototype to production-grade cloud deployment:

  1. [Agent Platform in Action (1)] Building LINE AI Card Assistant with Go and Google ADK 2.0 Graph Workflow: Using google.golang.org/adk/v2/workflow to build a 13-node directed graph featuring Vision OCR, AddFanOut / AddFanIn parallel background investigation, and NewRequestInputEvent HITL interaction loops.
  2. [Agent Platform in Action (2)] From Monolithic Cloud Run to Google Cloud Agent Runtime: Completed Phase 1 (PR #10), standardizing the project into an agents-cli (adk_go) dual-channel architecture.
  3. [Agent Platform in Action (3)] Implementing Cross-Instance Business Card Recognition and Pause/Resume with ADK 2.0 GCS Artifact Service and Agent Platform Sessions: Completed the first half of Phase 2 (PR #11), solving the HITL "amnesia" of stateless containers and the issue of binary image data explosion.
  4. [Agent Platform in Action (4)] Completing the Architecture Puzzle with Cloud Run LINE Webhook Gateway, Agent Runtime, and Cloud SQL PostgreSQL: Completed the second half of Phase 2 & Phase 3 (PR #12), upgrading the business card database to Cloud SQL PostgreSQL and achieving two-layer stateless decoupling.
  5. [Agent Platform in Action (5)] Establishing Automated Evaluation Benchmarks with agents-cli eval and ADK 2.0 Go: Completed Phase 4 (PR #13), establishing a golden test set and a quality flywheel.
  6. [Agent Platform in Action (6)] Building a Full-Stack Observable LINE AI Card Assistant with agents-cli deploy, Terraform IaC, GitHub Actions CI/CD, and Cloud Trace: Completed Phase 5 (PR #14), adding OpenTelemetry Spans (workflow.node.*) to all 13 Graph Nodes and deploying to the cloud via Terraform and GitHub Actions.

Additionally, we have planned advanced Graph Workflow primitives for future ADK v2.6+ (such as Parallel dynamic dispatch, MultiRoute multi-way fan-out, reflection-repair loops, and strongly typed nodes) into the Future Roadmap Issue #15.

However, now that our Agent possesses Phase 4 Automated Evaluation and Phase 5 Full-Node Tracing (OpenTelemetry Spans), a deeper question emerges:

When evaluations find that the Agent performs poorly in certain real-world cases (e.g., Japanese-English bilingual cards, searching for colloquial nicknames in the Taiwan tech industry, multi-clause colloquial HITL modifications, or financial compliance icebreaker letters), must engineers manually check logs, manually modify Prompt strings in the Go source code, and then recompile and redeploy every single time?

Can we let a Meta-Agent (Engineer Agent) automatically read our evaluation results and OpenTelemetry execution trajectories, diagnose the reasons for lost points, write new Skills and Long-Term Memory itself, and complete a closed-loop self-evolution?

This is precisely the core proposition addressed by Google Research's recently published and open-sourced google-research/harness2 (Harness²: Recursive Harnessing for LLM Agents, arXiv:2610.14224)!

This series will consist of three articles (corresponding to Issue #16, Issue #17, Issue #18, and PR #19), guiding you through the complete integration of Google Research Harness² into our Go ADK 2.0 project:

  • Part 1 (This article, Issue #16): What is Google Harness²? What can it do? Inventorying the existing architecture before modification and decoupling hardcoded configurations in the Go binary into a c1..c8 editable Harness file tree.
  • Part 2 (Issue #17): Encapsulating Phase 4's eval/datasets/ and Phase 5's OpenTelemetry Spans into a LineCardAdapter for Harness², and analyzing why "Zero-Leakage Barriers" and "High-Resolution Behavioral Trajectories" are both indispensable.
  • Part 3 (Issue #18): Complete testing tutorial, disclosure of Parallel vs Sequential + LongTermMEMORY two-layer recursive experimental data (accuracy jumping from 62.5% to 100.0%), and outlook on the future development of Agents.

1. What is Google Research Harness²? What can it do?

1. From "Fine-tuning Model Weights" to "Optimizing Agent Harnessing"

In the era of Large Language Models (LLMs), the success of an AI Agent is often determined not just by the underlying model (like Gemini 2.5 Flash / Pro) itself, but by the "Agent Harness" layer wrapped around the model—namely, System Prompts, formatting and safety Guardrails, Long-Term Memory, Tool Descriptions, Sub-Agent settings, and On-Demand Skills.

Past automated prompt optimizations (like PromptBreeder, TextGrad, or DSPy) mostly targeted mutations of a single Prompt string. However, in a real enterprise-grade Agent, if you stuff all edge-case patching rules into the same System Prompt, it quickly leads to "Context Bloat": the number of Always-On Tokens increases, which not only squeezes the model's Output Token Budget but also causes different rules to interfere with each other!

Google Research's Harness² (Recursive Harnessing for LLM Agents, arXiv:2610.14224) breaks this limitation. It defines the entire Agent's equipment as a structured c1..c8 Editable Component Tree and automatically evolves this file tree through Two-Level Recursion:

flowchart TB
    subgraph Outer["Outer Recursion: Harnessing-Level Recursion (Experience accumulation across rounds k=1..K)"]
        Reflector["Experience Reflector\n(ReflectorPrompt)\nDistilling success and failure patterns across rounds"]
        Memory["c3: LongTermMEMORY.md\nPersisting domain experience across iterations"]
        Reflector -->|Write long-term rules| Memory
    end

    subgraph Inner["Inner Recursion: Task-Level Recursion (Closed-loop diagnosis and patching within a single round)"]
        Propose["1. Propose (Diagnostic Proposal)\nRead trajectory.md\nLocate behavioral defects and propose N candidate Patches"]
        Probe["2. Probe (Sandbox Probing)\nExecute N candidate Harnesses in parallel\nCompare trajectory and score changes before and after modification"]
        Compose["3. Compose (Conflict Resolution and Synthesis)\nRetain positive-gain Patches, discard negative interference\nSynthesize the next-generation best Harness H^(k)"]
        Propose --> Probe --> Compose
    end

    Memory --> Propose
    Compose --> Reflector

2. The c1..c8 Eight Harness Components and the 24KB Budget Limit

In google-research/harness2/harness.py, a standard Agent Harness consists of 4 Always-On Components (c1..c4) and 4 On-Demand Components (c5..c8):

Component Code File Path Rule Loading Mode Responsibility in Harness²
c1 systemprompt.md Always-On Defines core roles, node responsibilities, and indexing rules for triggering c6 skills (Skill Trigger Lines).
c2 guardrails.md Always-On Defines non-violable output formats (e.g., pure JSON constraints), E.164 normalization invariants, and security/PII guardrails.
c3 LongTermMEMORY.md Always-On Domain lessons and industry compliance memories written across rounds by the outer Experience Reflector.
c4 tool_descriptions/*.md Always-On Tool parameter descriptions, search strategies, and normalization details (e.g., Japan long-distance prefix (0) cleaning rules).
c5 sub_agents/<name>/AGENT.md On-Demand Exclusive Instructions and YAML Frontmatter (mode: subagent) for delegated sub-agents (e.g., company_enrich).
c6 skills/<name>/SKILL.md On-Demand Professional skills dynamically injected only for specific domains or tasks (e.g., Japanese card OCR, Hsinchu Science Park colloquial search expansion).
c7 scripts/*.py On-Demand Auxiliary verification or data conversion scripts.
c8 plugin/*.ts On-Demand Runtime lifecycle and OpenTelemetry diagnostic hooks.

Important

Why distinguish between c1..c4 (Always-On) and c5..c8 (On-Demand)? Harness² sets an iron rule in OPENCODE_SURFACE: The total byte count of c1..c4 always-on files must never exceed 24,000 bytes (AlwaysOnMaxBytes = 24000)! When Harness² finds that a failure case requires lengthy domain knowledge (e.g., a department title mapping table for Japanese corporate cards or a colloquial abbreviation dictionary for Taiwan semiconductor parks), it won't force these rules into systemprompt.md causing Context explosion. Instead, it will automatically create an on-demand c6 skill file (skills/<name>/SKILL.md) and leave only a lightweight Trigger Line in systemprompt.md!

3. How Does Two-Level Recursion Work?

The Harness² evolution engine (harness2/core/recursion.py) includes two levels of recursion:

  1. Level 1 (Inner): Task-Level Recursion (Propose $\rightarrow$ Probe $\rightarrow$ Compose):
    • Propose (Diagnostic Proposal): The optimizer (Harvester LLM) observes tasks that lost points in the benchmark, the final output (Deliverable), and the execution trajectory (trajectory.md). It diagnoses which step the Agent made a wrong decision on and proposes multiple independent candidate patches (Candidate Patches, each being a set of additions or modifications to c1..c8).
    • Probe (Sandbox Probing): The system mounts each candidate Patch into a sandbox and runs the task once, collecting new scores and new execution trajectories to form a "Before vs. After" Behavioral Contrast.
    • Compose (Conflict Resolution and Synthesis): The optimizer compares the actual performance of all candidate Patches, merges modifications that truly bring positive score improvements into the new generation Harness $H^{(k)}$, and discards ineffective or side-effect-inducing modifications.
  2. Level 2 (Outer): Harnessing-Level Recursion (Experience Reflector):
    • Between multiple iterations ($k = 1 \dots K$), the outer ReflectorPrompt reviews the evolution history from $H^{(0)} \to H^{(1)} \to \dots \to H^{(k)}$: Which types of modifications succeeded? Which cross-domain constraints (e.g., financial industry compliance headers and personal data protection regulations) need to be remembered at a global level?
    • Distilled high-level experiences are written into c3: LongTermMEMORY.md, guiding the next round of Propose and Agent execution.

2. Inventorying the Current Architecture: Why Phase 1~5 Go Implementation Cannot Be Directly Optimized by Harness²?

Let's compare the left side (Before: Hardcoded Go Binary Architecture) of the architecture diagram at the beginning of the article and review the system architecture we completed in Phase 1 to Phase 5:

In the code before modification:

  1. All Prompt templates for VisionOCRNode, CompanyEnrichNode, ApplyEditNode (located in internal/workflow/nodes_ingest.go), as well as QueryIntentNode and EmailDraftNode (located in internal/workflow/nodes_search.go), are hardcoded as fmt.Sprintf(...) string constants in the Go code.
  2. The llmagent.Config{Instruction: ...} for CompanyEnrichAgent (located in internal/workflow/nodes_ingest.go) is also a fixed string hardcoded in a Go function.

When we want the Harness² Python evolution loop to modify system prompts, add a Japanese business card recognition skill (skills/jp_card_ocr/SKILL.md), or adjust phone number normalization guidelines (tool_descriptions/tool_guidance.md), it is impossible for Harness² to rewrite our .go source code and go build again for every single task!

Therefore, the first step in introducing Harness² (Issue #16) is to completely decouple the Go compilation phase from the Harness equipment phase:

  • Go Binary is responsible for "Graph Topology and Dual-Channel Execution Engine": RouterNode, parallel Fan-Out/Fan-In, HITLConfirmNode pause/resume, Cloud SQL and GCS Artifact access, OpenTelemetry instrumentation.
  • External c1..c8 Harness file tree is responsible for the "Evolvable Brain and Skill Equipment": Dynamically hot-reloaded at runtime via the environment variable LINE_CARD_HARNESS_DIR!

3. Implementation Part 1: Building internal/harness Loader and harness/base/ Initial Equipment Tree

To make the Go ADK 2.0 Graph Workflow natively understand the Harness² c1..c8 specification, we added two core directories to the project:

  • harness/base/: Stores the initial unevolved ($k=0$) c1..c8 baseline file tree.
  • internal/harness/harness.go: Responsible for loading the c1..c8 file tree, validating OPENCODE_SURFACE 24KB limits and YAML Frontmatter rules, and dynamically combining always-on context with on-demand skills for each Graph Node.

1. Establishing the harness/base/ Baseline c1..c8 File Tree

We extracted the basic settings previously scattered in nodes_ingest.go and nodes_search.go into the harness/base/ directory:

Please use the google_search tool to query the company name provided by the user, then call the format_company_profile tool to return a two-sentence Traditional Chinese company profile and 3 to 5 technical or industry tags (e.g., AI, Cloud, SaaS, FinTech, Semiconductor).

2. Implementing internal/harness/harness.go: 24KB Always-On Budget Validation and On-Demand Skill Injection

In internal/harness/harness.go, we implemented the validator Validate() and node prompt synthesizer ComposeNodePrompt() fully aligned with the Python version of OPENCODE_SURFACE.validate():

// AlwaysOnMaxBytes matches google-research/harness2 OPENCODE_SURFACE.always_on_max (24,000 bytes).
const AlwaysOnMaxBytes = 24000

// AlwaysOnFiles lists the four c1..c4 always-on files mounted into the agent context.
var AlwaysOnFiles = []string{
    "systemprompt.md",
    "guardrails.md",
    "LongTermMEMORY.md",
    "tool_descriptions/tool_guidance.md",
}

// Validate enforces Google Research Harness² OPENCODE_SURFACE invariants on the c1..c8 tree.
func (h *Harness) Validate() error {
    var problems []string
    for _, reqFile := range AlwaysOnFiles {
        if strings.TrimSpace(h.Files[reqFile]) == "" {
            problems = append(problems, fmt.Sprintf("missing or empty always-on component %q", reqFile))
        }
    }
    if total := h.AlwaysOnBytes(); total > AlwaysOnMaxBytes {
        problems = append(problems, fmt.Sprintf(
            "always-on c1..c4 byte count %d exceeds cap %d (every token here competes with the agent's output budget)",
            total, AlwaysOnMaxBytes,
        ))
    }

    combinedAlwaysOn := h.SystemPrompt + "\n" + h.Guardrails
    for dirName, skill := range h.Skills {
        if skill.Name != dirName {
            problems = append(problems, fmt.Sprintf("%s frontmatter name %q must match directory name %q", skill.RelPath, skill.Name, dirName))
        }
        if strings.TrimSpace(skill.Description) == "" {
            problems = append(problems, fmt.Sprintf("%s must include a non-empty description in YAML frontmatter", skill.RelPath))
        }
        if !strings.Contains(combinedAlwaysOn, dirName) {
            problems = append(problems, fmt.Sprintf("skill %q is never referenced in systemprompt.md or guardrails.md; add a trigger line naming `%s`", dirName, dirName))
        }
    }
    // ...
}

There are two very critical engineering details here:

  1. Mandatory Skill Trigger Reference Check: If Harness² adds a skill in skills/jp_card_ocr/SKILL.md but forgets to write when to trigger jp_card_ocr in systemprompt.md or guardrails.md, Validate() will directly report an error and intercept it, avoiding the creation of "Orphan Skills" that will never be called.
  2. Node-Level Dynamic Skill Matching (MatchSkills + ComposeNodePrompt): When the Graph Workflow executes VisionOCRNode, CompanyEnrichNode, ApplyEditNode, QueryIntentNode, or EmailDraftNode, it only injects c6 skills related to that node and automatically attaches adk.harness.skills and adk.harness.always_on_bytes attributes to the OpenTelemetry Span: 
// composeHarnessPrompt enriches a node's base prompt with the active Harness² c1..c8 tree
// and records the active harness metadata onto the node's OpenTelemetry span.
func composeHarnessPrompt(span trace.Span, nodeName, basePrompt, taskInput string) (string, *harness.Harness) {
    h := harness.LoadActive()
    composed, skills := h.ComposeNodePrompt(nodeName, basePrompt, taskInput)
    if span != nil {
        span.SetAttributes(
            AttrHarnessRoot.String(h.RootDir),
            AttrHarnessAlwaysOnBytes.Int(h.AlwaysOnBytes()),
        )
        if len(skills) > 0 {
            span.SetAttributes(AttrHarnessSkills.StringSlice(skills))
        }
    }
    return composed, h
}

We can directly use the CLI to verify the always-on byte count and structural validity of harness/base:

$ go run ./cmd/harness-runner --validate-only --harness-dir=harness/base
OK (1599 always-on bytes)

4. Summary and Next Article Preview

In this article (Part 1), we completed the goals of Issue #16:

  1. Gained a deep understanding of how Google Research Harness² (arXiv:2610.14224) automatically evolves Agent capabilities through a c1..c8 editable file tree and two-level recursion (Task-level Propose-Probe-Compose + Harnessing-level Experience Reflector), without recompiling the main program or bloating the always-on context.
  2. Inventoried the architectural bottlenecks of Phase 1~5 where prompts and normalization logic were hardcoded in the Go binary.
  3. Implemented internal/harness/harness.go and harness/base/, allowing the 13 nodes of the ADK 2.0 Go Graph Workflow to support dynamic mounting of the c1..c8 equipment tree via LINE_CARD_HARNESS_DIR.

With a hot-reloadable c1..c8 equipment tree in place, the next article [Agent Platform in Action (8)] When ADK Go Graph Workflow Meets Google Research Harness² (Part 2): Turning Phase 4 Eval Datasets and Phase 5 OpenTelemetry Spans into LineCardAdapter will enter Issue #17: revealing why we need to encapsulate Phase 4 test sets and Phase 5 OpenTelemetry Spans into a LineCardAdapter, and how the "Zero-Leakage Barrier" prevents the AI optimizer from cheating!

title: [Agent Platform in Action (8)] When ADK Go Graph Workflow Meets Google Research Harness (Part 2): Integrating Phase 4 Eval Datas
description:
Introduction: Why Decoupling Prompts Isn't Enough?

In the previous post [Agent Platform in Practice (7)] When ADK Go Graph Workflow Meets Google Research Harness² (Part 1): Understanding the Recursive Agent Framework and c1..c8 Decoupling (corresponding to Issue #16), we introduced Google Research's google-research/harness2 (arXiv:2610.14224) and decoupled the prompts, guardrails, long-term memory, and on-demand skills of the LINE AI Business Card Assistant (kkdai/line-card-assistant) into an editable c1..c8 Harness file tree that can be dynamically mounted via LINE_CARD_HARNESS_DIR.

However, simply having a hot-reloadable c1..c8 file tree isn't enough; the Harness² dual-layer recursive optimization engine (harness2/core/recursion.py) still cannot directly optimize our Go Agent. This is because Harness² requires a standardized bridge — the BenchmarkAdapter — to answer three questions:

  1. list_tasks() (What are the test questions?): What test cases should the Agent challenge? What are the public inputs (Prompt / Image) for each case, and what are the hidden scoring criteria (Rubrics)?
  2. run() (How does the Agent think and execute?): When a candidate Harness $H’$ is mounted to execute a specific task, what is the Agent's final output (deliverable)? More importantly, what decision trajectory did it follow across the 13 nodes of the Graph Workflow (trajectory.md)?
  3. score() (How was the performance?): Which independent scoring items (per_rubric) did the final output and execution trajectory pass, and where did it lose points?

Conveniently, in Phase 4 (PR #13), we already established the eval/datasets/ automated evaluation benchmark, and in Phase 5 (PR #14), we added workflow.node.* OpenTelemetry Spans to all 13 Graph Nodes!

In this post (Part 2, corresponding to Issue #17 and PR #19), we will merge these two existing assets into the Harness² LineCardAdapter and explain in depth "Why must it be designed this way?".

I. Why This Change? Two Core Design Philosophies

Before diving into the code, many engineers often ask two questions:

  1. "Why not just feed the entire eval/datasets/*.json file to the optimizer LLM and let it modify the Prompt itself?"
  2. "Why do we need to convert Phase 5 OpenTelemetry Spans into trajectory.md? Isn't the final LINE reply text and total score enough?"

These two questions touch upon the most core engineering designs in the Harness² paper: the Zero-Leakage Barrier and Behavioral Trajectory Contrast.

1. Why the "Zero-Leakage Barrier"? Preventing the Optimizer from "Cheating by Memorizing Answers"

Imagine this: if we expose the golden answers in eval/datasets/harness2-challenge-dataset.json (e.g., expected_contains: ["+81-3-1234-5678", "Kenta Sato"]) directly to the Agent or the Harness² Harvester LLM, what happens?

The laziest and easiest way for the optimizer to get a perfect score is to write a single line in systemprompt.md:

"If the input contains Sato, please directly output +81-3-1234-5678 and Kenta Sato."

In machine learning, this is known as Test Set Leakage / Overfitting to Rubrics. The Agent appears to score 100 on the benchmark, but it crashes immediately when it encounters a new Japanese business card in the real world!

flowchart LR
    Dataset["eval/datasets/*.json\nComplete Test Cases\n(incl. expected_contains / expected_route)"]

    subgraph Barrier["Zero-Leakage Barrier"]
        Brief["TaskBrief (Public Task Sheet)\nContains only task_id, prompt, session_input\n❌ Never contains expected_* golden answers"]
        Scorer["Isolated Scorer (Black-box Grader)\nHolds independent hidden r1..r4 Rubrics"]
    end

    Agent["Go ADK Graph Workflow\n(cmd/harness-runner)"]
    Harvester["Harness² Harvester\n(Propose / Probe / Compose)"]

    Dataset --> Brief
    Dataset --> Scorer
    Brief -->|"Public Input"| Agent
    Agent -->|"Deliverable + OTel trajectory.md"| Scorer
    Scorer -->|"Returns only binary scores {r1: 1.0, r2: 0.0}\nand OTel execution trajectory"| Harvester

In the Harness² BenchmarkAdapter architecture:

  • TaskBrief (Public Task Sheet): Can only contain user input (prompt and simulated images/context). It is strictly forbidden from containing any expected_contains, expected_not_contains, or correct answer strings.
  • score() (Black-box Grader): After comparing answers in an isolated environment, it only returns "which Rubric received a 1.0 or 0.0" (e.g., r3_e164_jp_phone_normalization: 0.0), without leaking the expected string to the optimizer.
  • As a result, the Harness² optimizer must truly reason out general domain rules (e.g., "When converting Japanese phone numbers +81 (0)3-... to E.164, the domestic trunk prefix (0) must be removed") by reading the Agent's execution trajectory (trajectory.md), rather than hard-coding answers into the Prompt!

2. Why Convert Phase 5 OpenTelemetry Spans into trajectory.md? Opening the Black Box of the 13-Node Graph

Our LINE AI Business Card Assistant is not a simple "single LLM call," but an ADK 2.0 Directed Acyclic Graph (Graph Workflow) consisting of 13 nodes:

  • Business Card Ingestion Pipeline: RouterNode $\rightarrow$ VisionOCRNode $\rightarrow$ Parallel AddFanOut (CleanAndDedupNode, CompanyEnrichNode, ContextMatchNode) $\rightarrow$ AddFanIn (JoinPreviewNode) $\rightarrow$ BuildPreviewNode $\rightarrow$ HITLConfirmNode $\rightarrow$ ApplyEditNode / SaveCardNode.
  • Smart Search and Icebreaker Pipeline: RouterNode $\rightarrow$ QueryIntentNode $\rightarrow$ HybridSearchNode / BroadSearchNode $\rightarrow$ FormatCarouselNode / EmailDraftNode.

Without Phase 5's OpenTelemetry Spans, when a user searches for "Help me find a Sales Director in Hsinchu Science Park working on AI chips" but gets "No matching business cards found" (score 0.25), the optimizer only sees this final failure message and cannot determine:

  • Did the RouterNode misjudge the search intent as chat?
  • Did the QueryIntentNode fail to expand the colloquial "Hsinchu Science Park" into the database's address Hsinchu, or fail to expand "Sales Director" into Sales Director?
  • Was there an error in the SQL query logic of the HybridSearchNode?

When we collect and render Phase 5's OpenTelemetry workflow.node.* Spans into a structured trajectory.md, Harness² can clearly see the input, output, duration, routing decisions, and loaded skills of every Graph Node during the Propose and Probe stages!

II. Implementation Part 2: Building the LineCardAdapter in Three Steps

Referring to the architecture diagram at the beginning of this article, we completed the implementation of Issue #17 through three core components:

  1. internal/harness/trajectory.go: Mounts an in-memory OpenTelemetry SpanRecorder on the Go side to export the execution details of the 13 Graph Nodes as trajectory.md.
  2. cmd/harness-runner/main.go: Provides a deterministic subprocess CLI for the Python Harness² to call, receiving --harness-dir and --task-json, and outputting a JSON containing deliverable, trajectory_markdown, and spans.
  3. harness/line_card_adapter.py: Implements the google-research/harness2 BenchmarkAdapter interface, connecting the Phase 4 Dataset with the Go harness-runner.

1. Implementing internal/harness/trajectory.go: Rendering OpenTelemetry Spans as trajectory.md

In Phase 5, our internal/workflow/telemetry.go already calls startNodeSpan(ctx, "VisionOCRNode") in every Graph Node. Now, in internal/harness/trajectory.go, we use go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace/tracetest.NewSpanRecorder() to intercept all completed node Spans and transform them into a Markdown trajectory report that the Harness² Harvester LLM is best at reading:

// InstallRecorder registers a new in-memory SpanRecorder as the global OTel TracerProvider
// so every workflow.node.* span emitted by internal/workflow/telemetry.go is captured.
func InstallRecorder() (*TrajectoryRecorder, func()) {
    sr := tracetest.NewSpanRecorder()
    tp := sdktrace.NewTracerProvider(sdktrace.WithSpanProcessor(sr))
    prev := otel.GetTracerProvider()
    otel.SetTracerProvider(tp)

    rec := &TrajectoryRecorder{recorder: sr, tp: tp}
    restore := func() {
        _ = tp.Shutdown(context.Background())
        otel.SetTracerProvider(prev)
    }
    return rec, restore
}

At the same time, we added three OpenTelemetry Attributes to internal/workflow/telemetry.go: AttrNodeDecision (adk.node.decision), AttrNodeDiagnostic (adk.node.diagnostic), and AttrHarnessSkills (adk.harness.skills). When TrajectoryRecorder.RenderMarkdown() executes, it produces a high-resolution trajectory.md like this:

# ADK 2.0 Go Graph Workflow Execution Trajectory
- **Task ID** : `challenge_colloquial_tw_search`
- **Harness Root** : `harness/base`
- **Always-On Bytes (`c1..c4`)**: `1599 / 24000`
- **Final Score** : `0.25`

## OpenTelemetry Node Spans (`workflow.node.*`)
### 1. `workflow.node.RouterNode`
- **Node** : `RouterNode` | **Status** : `OK` | **Duration** : `0.02 ms`
- **Decision** : `intent=search (colloquial_query=Help me find a Sales Director in Hsinchu Science Park working on AI chips, I need to contact Taiwan semiconductor clients)`
- **Diagnostic** : `routed search query to QueryIntentNode`

### 2. `workflow.node.QueryIntentNode`
- **Node** : `QueryIntentNode` | **Status** : `OK` | **Duration** : `0.04 ms`
- **Decision** : `parsed_filters={"location":"Hsinchu Science Park","role":"Sales Director","industry":"AI Chips"}`
- **Diagnostic** : `UNEXPANDED_COLLOQUIAL_FILTERS: colloquial Taiwan science park alias 'Hsinchu Science Park' and Mandarin title 'Sales Director' were passed literally without bilingual synonym expansion; add a c6 skill 'tw_semicon_search' with BILINGUAL_SYNONYM_MAP`

### 3. `workflow.node.HybridSearchNode`
- **Node** : `HybridSearchNode` | **Status** : `OK` | **Duration** : `0.03 ms`
- **Decision** : `matched_cards=0 (strict literal filter on location='Hsinchu Science Park' failed against DB address='Hsinchu Science Park (竹科)')`

Please pay attention to the Span records of the 2nd node workflow.node.QueryIntentNode and the 3rd node workflow.node.HybridSearchNode! Through this trajectory, the Propose stage of Harness² can see at a glance: RouterNode was correct, the error was in QueryIntentNode treating "Hsinchu Science Park" as a rigid string to query the English address field!

2. Expanding the Phase 4 Evaluation Set: eval/datasets/harness2-challenge-dataset.json

To fully test Harness²'s ability to retain existing capabilities (preventing catastrophic forgetting) and conquer difficult edge cases, we established 8 tasks (totaling 32 fine-grained Rubrics) in eval/datasets/harness2-challenge-dataset.json:

3. Implementing harness/line_card_adapter.py: Connecting to google-research/harness2

Finally, we implemented the LineCardAdapter in harness/line_card_adapter.py, connecting all the above components:

class LineCardAdapter:
    """Adapts `line-card-assistant` to the `google-research/harness2` BenchmarkAdapter protocol."""

    def list_tasks(self) -> list[TaskBrief]:
        """Return public task briefs with zero ground-truth rubric leakage."""
        briefs: list[TaskBrief] = []
        for raw in self._raw_cases:
            # Strip `rubrics` and `expected_*` so the agent/harvester never sees ground truth.
            briefs.append(
                TaskBrief(
                    task_id=raw["id"],
                    prompt=raw["prompt"],
                    context={
                        "category": raw.get("category", "general"),
                        "description": raw.get("description", ""),
                        "session_input": raw.get("session_input", {}),
                    },
                )
            )
        return briefs

    def run(self, harness: Harness, task: TaskBrief) -> RunArtifact:
        """Mount `harness` in a temporary directory and execute the Go Graph Workflow runner."""
        problems = harness.validate()
        if problems:
            diag = "# Harness Validation Failed\n" + "\n".join(f"- {p}" for p in problems)
            return RunArtifact(task_id=task.task_id, deliverable="", trajectory=diag)

        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix=f"line_card_harness_{task.task_id}_") as tmp_dir:
            harness_root = Path(tmp_dir)
            harness.materialize(harness_root)
            # Invoke the compiled Go binary with --harness-dir pointing to the materialized c1..c8 tree
            proc = subprocess.run(
                [str(binary), f"--harness-dir={harness_root}", f"--task-json={task_payload_path}"],
                capture_output=True, text=True, check=False, timeout=30,
            )
            payload = json.loads(proc.stdout)
            return RunArtifact(
                task_id=task.task_id,
                deliverable=payload.get("deliverable", ""),
                trajectory=payload.get("trajectory_markdown", ""),
                raw=payload,
            )

    def score(self, task: TaskBrief, artifact: RunArtifact) -> ScoreResult:
        """Evaluate the deliverable against isolated per-rubric criteria."""
        raw = self._cases_by_id[task.task_id]
        rubrics = raw.get("rubrics", {})
        per_rubric: dict[str, float] = {}
        for rubric_id, spec in rubrics.items():
            per_rubric[rubric_id] = 1.0 if self._evaluate_rubric(artifact.deliverable, spec) else 0.0
        total = sum(per_rubric.values()) / len(per_rubric) if per_rubric else 0.0
        return ScoreResult(task_id=task.task_id, total=round(total, 4), per_rubric=per_rubric)

Through this LineCardAdapter:

  • Whenever Harness² proposes a new candidate Harness $H’$, adapter.run(harness, task) first calls harness.validate() to check the 24KB OPENCODE_SURFACE limit and Skill Frontmatter rules.
  • Once validated, the c1..c8 files of $H’$ are materialized into a temporary directory and passed to Go's harness-runner for execution.
  • After the Go 13-node Graph Workflow finishes, it returns the final LINE message (deliverable) and OpenTelemetry trajectory (trajectory_markdown), which are then passed to adapter.score() for leakage-free independent scoring!

III. Summary and Teaser for the Next Part

In this post (Part 2), we completed the core engineering for Issue #17:

  1. Clarified why the golden test set cannot be fed directly to the optimizer — through the TaskBrief Zero-Leakage Barrier, we force Harness² to reason out general skills from behavioral trajectories rather than memorizing answers.
  2. Through internal/harness/trajectory.go and cmd/harness-runner/main.go, we transformed Phase 5's OpenTelemetry workflow.node.* Spans into high-resolution trajectory.md, opening the black box of the 13-node Graph Workflow.
  3. Established eval/datasets/harness2-challenge-dataset.json (8 major tasks, 32 fine-grained Rubrics) and harness/line_card_adapter.py, perfectly implementing the Harness² BenchmarkAdapter protocol.

Everything is ready! In the final post [Agent Platform in Practice (9)] When ADK Go Graph Workflow Meets Google Research Harness² (Part 3): Dual-Layer Recursive Testing Guide, 62.5% to 100% Performance Results, and the Future of AgentOps (corresponding to Issue #18), we will actually launch the dual-layer recursive optimization experiment, reveal the complete quantitative data evolving from 62.5% to 100.0%, and discuss the profound impact of Harness² on future enterprise-grade Agent development!

Combining the Cloud Trace established in Phase 5 with the LineCardAdapter from this series, future CI/CD can achieve:

Enterprises often encounter behavioral drift when switching underlying models from high-cost models to ultra-fast lightweight models (e.g., switching from Gemini 1.5 Pro to Gemini 1.5 Flash or Flash-Lite to reduce latency and cost by 80%) or upgrading to next-gen models. title: OAuth Token Refresh in a Client vs a Generated, Spec-Aware Flow
description:
Quick answer: OAuth looks solved until a token expires mid-session, and the failure is almost always in how refresh tokens are stored and coordinated rather than in the initial login. A client that keeps a token in memory and silently retries on a 401 works for one process, but it breaks the moment multiple requests hit an expired token at once and each triggers its own refresh, or the refresh token is rotated and an older in-flight request invalidates the newer one. The robust pattern is to centralize the token in a single store, serialize refresh behind one lock, and treat the refresh token as a rotating secret that is persisted securely and never duplicated across clients. If refresh logic is left to each request to improvise, the first simultaneous expiry produces either a refresh storm or a logout that the user did nothing to cause.

Most API clients handle the happy path of OAuth well: redirect, exchange the code, attach the bearer token. The design questions concentrate on the less visible part: where the tokens live, what happens when the access token expires, and how a rotating refresh token is reconciled when several requests are in flight. A collection-based client tends to store tokens in a local profile or a per-request config, which is convenient for a single developer but does not model the coordination that a real application needs.

Where token refresh goes wrong

The failure modes cluster around storage and concurrency rather than the protocol's basic redirect flow.

Problem Symptom Correct approach
Concurrent refresh Multiple refresh calls, some fail Single in-flight refresh with a lock
Rotating refresh token Old token replay invalidates new Store latest, queue waiters
Insecure storage Token readable on disk OS keychain/secure store
Retry loop 401 repeated forever One retry, then re-auth
Tab/process split Each holds its own token Shared store

The rotating refresh token row is the subtle one: providers that issue a new refresh token on every use invalidate the previous one, so two clients racing to refresh leaves one holding a dead secret and forcing a fresh login even though the user's session was valid.

Centralize the token and serialize refresh

Keep one token store and expose a method that returns a valid token, refreshing at most once even when many callers ask at the same time. Callers wait on the same refresh promise rather than each starting their own.

Because the refresh promise is cached, a burst of requests that all see an expired token causes exactly one refresh, and every request proceeds with the same new access token.

Handle rotation and secure persistence

When the provider rotates the refresh token, write the new pair to the store before resolving the waiters, and persist it through the secure store rather than a plain config file. A stale read must never overwrite the newer secret.

On a desktop client the secure store maps to the OS keychain; on a web client the refresh token should stay httpOnly and secure on the server side rather than being exposed to JavaScript. The point is that the token is never duplicated into a per-request profile or a readable file, and a single authoritative copy exists.

Bound the retry and drive it from the contract

On a 401, a request should trigger the central refresh once and retry exactly once; if the refresh itself fails, the client routes to re-authentication rather than looping. A generated client that knows the security scheme and token endpoint from the OpenAPI contract can apply this logic consistently, including the token expiry buffer, so every request uses the same manager instead of embedding bespoke refresh code.

The practical recommendation is to treat token lifecycle as infrastructure: one secure store, one serialized refresh path, explicit handling of rotating refresh tokens, and a single retry before re-auth. If your client works on the first call but logs users out or throws refresh errors after an hour, the problem is not OAuth; it is storage and concurrency that were never centralized.

Frequently asked questions

Why do multiple requests fail when the token expires?

Each request independently sees the 401 and starts its own refresh. With a rotating refresh token, only the first succeeds and the others replay a now-invalid secret. A shared refresh promise fixes this.

Where should refresh tokens be stored?

In a secure store such as the OS keychain for desktop, or an httpOnly secure cookie for web. Never in a plain config file or in JavaScript-readable local storage.

What is a rotating refresh token?

A provider that issues a new refresh token on each use and invalidates the previous one. Clients must persist the latest token immediately; racing refreshes leave one client holding a dead secret.

How many times should a request retry after a 401?

Once, after a central refresh. If the refresh fails or the retried call is still 401, route to re-authentication rather than looping.

How does the API contract help?

It declares the security scheme and token endpoint, so a generated client wires every request to the same token manager with consistent expiry handling instead of per-request refresh logic.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Insomnia comparison — start there for the full picture of reliable auth handling.
