title: Accept or Revert: Designing AI Edits as Reviewable Patches on a Real Video Timeline
description:
By Sagar Dey, founder of MirrorCut

Most AI features ship with an all-or-nothing contract. The model does a thing, and you either keep the result or throw it away.

That works for a one-line autocomplete. It falls apart for a video edit, where a single "AI pass" might contain dozens of independent decisions: cut this pause, drop that filler word, keep the second take, caption this line.

When I built MirrorCut, an AI video editor that runs in the browser, I made one rule early: every AI change is a patch on the timeline, and every patch can be accepted or reverted on its own.

This post is about why, and the design constraints that rule creates. It's written for developers building any kind of AI-assisted editor: video, docs, code or design.

Note: the code below is a simplified illustration of the pattern, written for this post. It is not MirrorCut's production code.

The problem with "re-render and replace"

The simplest way to add AI to an editor looks like this:

  1. Send the current state to the model.
  2. Get back a new state.
  3. Replace the old state.

It's easy to build. It's also hostile to the user, for three reasons:

  • No granularity. If the model made ten good decisions and one bad one, the user can't separate them.
  • Lost work. Anything the user did by hand can get silently overwritten.
  • No explanation. The user sees a different result, not what changed or why.

In video, there's a fourth problem: re-rendering is slow and expensive. Throwing away a whole pass because of one bad cut costs real time.

The alternative: edits as small, named patches

Instead of returning a new timeline, the agent proposes a list of small changes against the existing one. Conceptually, each patch carries:

// Illustrative only
type EditPatch = {
  id: string;
  kind: "cut" | "caption" | "reframe" | "graphic";
  range: { start: number; end: number }; // seconds on the timeline
  summary: string; // one human-readable line
  status: "pending" | "accepted" | "reverted";
};

The summary matters more than it looks. In MirrorCut, every AI change is explained in one line, for example "Removing a 0.6 s pause at 0:54". If you can't describe a change in one line, it's probably several changes and should be split.

Rule 1: Show every patch where it happens

Each pending change is outlined on the timeline itself, not buried in a side panel. The user's eyes are already on the timeline, so that's where the review should happen.

This also forces a useful discipline on the agent: every change has to map to a visible location. "Improved the pacing" isn't a patch. "Removed 2.1 s of dead air at 3:12" is.

Rule 2: Accept and Revert are per patch

The whole point is granularity. A pass with ten patches gives the user ten decisions, not one.

// Illustrative only
function revert(patchId: string) {
  const patch = timeline.patches.get(patchId);
  timeline.apply(inverse(patch));
  patch.status = "reverted";
}

The hard part isn't the button. It's making sure patches are independent enough that reverting one doesn't break the others. Cutting 0.6 s at 0:54 shifts everything after it, so later patches need to be expressed in a way that survives earlier ones being reverted.

Rule 3: One undo history for humans and AI

This is the rule people find most surprising.

In MirrorCut, AI edits and manual edits share one undo history. There's no separate "AI layer" or "AI mode." If you trim a clip by hand, then the agent removes a pause, then you press undo, you undo the pause removal, exactly like you'd expect.

Why not keep them separate? Because two histories create two mental models. Users end up asking "which undo do I need?" And they lose trust when the AI's changes behave differently from their own.

A cut is a cut, whoever made it.

Rule 4: Follow-ups patch, they don't restart

When the user asks for a follow-up, like "make the intro faster and add captions", the agent edits the existing timeline instead of regenerating from scratch.

This protects everything the user already accepted or adjusted by hand. A restart would quietly throw that away.

It also keeps responses small and reviewable. The site shows this flow: "Done. Intro trimmed from 4s to 2s and captions added." That's two patches, not a new video.

Rule 5: Expensive operations ask first

Some patches are cheap to preview. Others, like a full-resolution render, take real compute.

In MirrorCut, expensive steps ask before running. The general pattern: separate proposing a change from paying for it. Let the user review the plan before the costly part kicks off.

There's a pricing angle too. On MirrorCut's plans, each request to the agent uses AI credits based on the work it takes, while editing by hand on the timeline uses no credits. That makes "do it yourself" a real, free option for small fixes, and it keeps the agent honest about when it's worth calling.

Where this pattern applies beyond video

Strip out the video specifics and you get a reusable checklist for any AI-assisted editor:

  1. Return patches, not replacement states.
  2. Give each patch a one-line explanation and a visible location.
  3. Make accept/revert granular, and design patches to survive each other's reversal.
  4. Use one undo history for human and AI changes.
  5. Patch on follow-up; never silently restart.
  6. Ask before expensive work.

Try it on your own footage

MirrorCut, AI video editor (mirrorcut.ai), runs in the browser. It cuts dead air, filler words and retakes, adds word-timed captions, reframes to 16:9, 9:16, 1:1 and 4:5, finds Shorts, and adds motion graphics, all as reviewable patches on a real timeline. Exports are MP4 up to 4K, plus SRT and VTT captions.

Every account starts with 7 days of the Creator plan free (card required). After that, it's Creator $10, Pro $30 or Studio $60 a month. MirrorCut launches publicly in November 2026: https://www.mirrorcut.ai

I'd love to hear how you handle review flows for AI output in your own tools. Drop it in the comments.

title: The new machine with the old map: how GitHub routed writes to servers that no longer existed
description:
On October 7, 2026, GitHub broke in a strange, specific way. You could read almost anything. You could not save almost anything.

Push a commit, open a pull request, file an issue, start an Actions run, sign in: those are all writes, actions that save or change data. Reads, looking at code and pages that already existed, were largely unaffected. That split is the first clue, and it is worth sitting with before you look for a cause. When reads work and writes do not, the data itself is probably fine. The road that new data travels is not.

That is the mystery this article works through. It ends with a small guard, in Python, that you can steal for your own routing config. The guard does one job: it refuses to use a map that points to servers that no longer exist.

Clue one: only the writing road was broken

GitHub had two outages that day with the same cause, totalling about 19 minutes. The first ran from 15:06 to 15:16 UTC, about 10 minutes. The second ran from 16:52 to 17:01 UTC, about 9 minutes.

In the first window, 5.6 percent of all web and API requests failed, peaking at 8.9 percent, and more than 12,000 organizations saw failed requests. Up to 26 percent of Git authentication requests failed, and 17 percent of Actions workflow runs failed with infrastructure errors. In the second window, 6.2 percent of web and API requests failed, peaking at 9.3 percent, and more than 11,000 organizations were affected. Up to 25 percent of Git authentication requests failed, and 19 percent of Actions workflow runs failed with infrastructure errors.

No databases lost data, according to GitHub, and operations retried after recovery succeeded. So this was not a story about lost work. It was a story about work that could not find its destination.

GitHub's own status report, posted October 7, 2026, names the affected areas in those windows: Git operations, pull requests, issues, GitHub Actions, the API, webhooks, sign-in and authentication, GitHub Apps and OAuth, code scanning, Codespaces, and Copilot. That list looks random until you ask what those things share. They all need to save something new.

Clue two: a new machine with an old map

To understand the cause, you need three plain ideas.

A database server is a machine that stores data and answers questions about it. A routing config is a list that says which database servers should receive new and updated data. Think of it as a map: it tells each write where to go.

A quorum is a group of machines that must agree before a change counts. A leader is the machine in that group whose word the others accept for now. Leader election is just the process of choosing which machine leads. If a machine with a wrong map becomes leader, its wrong map becomes the map everyone follows.

GitHub relies on an internal service that keeps track of which database servers should receive new and updated data. While replacing machines that run this service as part of regular maintenance, one of the new machines started with an outdated copy of its records. That copy still listed database servers GitHub had already retired. Retired here means taken out of service, gone, not answering anymore.

When this node came online, it incorrectly modified routing configuration with the outdated records, routing write requests to non-existent database servers. Writes were sent to machines that were not there. Reads did not need that road in the same way, so they mostly kept working.

Each outage ended when one of GitHub's established machines, with the correct configuration, became the leader of the quorum and sent the correct configuration. The good map replaced the bad map. That is why the first outage was only about 10 minutes long. The system healed itself, once the right leader was in charge.

Clue three: the pause that was not honoured

Here is the part that should worry you more than the first outage. After the first outage, GitHub's engineers identified the new machine as the source and paused automated maintenance to stop it from being leader again. Then, at 16:52 UTC, an automated maintenance task that did not honour the pause put it back in charge, and the outage happened again.

Read that slowly. The team did the right thing after the first failure. They found the bad machine and they paused the automation around it. But the pause was not honoured by every piece of automation. One task did not know about the pause, or did not check it, and it undid the fix.

GitHub shut that machine down at 17:02 UTC and has since removed it. GitHub also says the automation now honours the pause, and that this failure to honour it was a new regression, a bug introduced by an update to its Puppet infrastructure. Puppet is a tool for managing machine configuration automatically, which is exactly the kind of tool that can quietly reintroduce a problem while nobody is looking.

This is the pattern to remember. The first failure was a stale map. The second failure was a safety control that only some of the system respected. A pause that lives in one place, and is ignored by another, is not a pause. It is a hope.

The guard: never trust a map you have not checked

GitHub says it is now doing several things to prevent a repeat: clearing retired database servers from the service's records before any new machine is added, keeping new machines from being elected leader until their records have been checked, rejecting configuration that points to servers that do not exist and keeping the last known-good settings instead, giving responders a faster way to take a misbehaving machine out of service, and adding alerts so changes like this are spotted within seconds.

You can borrow the middle idea, the one about rejecting a bad map, in a few lines. The rule is simple. Before you apply a new routing config, check every destination against the live inventory, the list of servers that actually exist right now. If even one destination is missing, reject the whole config and keep the last known-good one. Do not apply the good half and skip the bad half. A half applied map is still a wrong map.

def apply_routing_config(new_config, live_servers, last_good_config):
    """Apply new_config only if every destination really exists.

    new_config: a list of server names the new map points writes to.
    live_servers: a set of server names that exist right now.
    last_good_config: the last config we know worked.
    """
    unknown = [server for server in new_config if server not in live_servers]

    if unknown:
        print(f"Refusing bad routing config. Unknown servers: {unknown}")
        return last_good_config

    return new_config

That is the whole guard. The rest is discipline around it. Check the map at the point where it is applied, not only at the point where it is written. A config file can be correct when it is saved and stale by the time it is used, which is exactly what happened at GitHub: the records were outdated when the new machine started.

A boundary test makes the rule concrete. Test three cases: a config with no unknown servers, which should pass; a config with one unknown server among many good ones, which should fail; and a config where every server is retired, which should also fail. The one-unknown case is the important one. It is tempting to let it through, because most of the map looks fine. That temptation is the bug.

live = {"db-a", "db-b", "db-c"}
last_good = ["db-a", "db-b"]

assert apply_routing_config(["db-a", "db-b"], live, last_good) == ["db-a", "db-b"]
assert apply_routing_config(["db-a", "db-gone"], live, last_good) == last_good
assert apply_routing_config(["db-gone", "db-also-gone"], live, last_good) == last_good

Two more checks belong next to this guard, and they come straight from GitHub's own list. First, do not let a new machine become leader until its records have been checked. A new member of a quorum should prove its map is fresh before it is allowed to lead. Second, make a pause a single, checked thing, not a note in one tool. If a maintenance task can run without asking whether it is paused, it will, on the worst day, run at the worst time.

The question

You probably have a map like this somewhere: a config, a service discovery list, a set of connection strings, a deploy script that names servers. When was it last checked against what actually exists?

Find the newest machine in your system, the one added most recently, and ask a blunt question about it. Does it hold a copy of anything that was written before something was retired? If you cannot answer that in a minute, that is the audit, and it is worth doing this week.

When did you last verify that every destination in your routing config still exists?

title: Replit alternatives: where to build and host your app instead
description:
Replit puts three things on one bill: a browser workspace, the Replit Agent that writes code for you, and hosting for the app it builds. The right alternative depends on which of those you want to replace. Lovable and Bolt replace the agent and the workspace. Cursor or Claude Code in your own editor replaces both with tools you run locally. Render, Railway, Fly.io and Ownkube replace the hosting, which is where most of a running app's bill ends up.

Our picks

If you want Pick
Another browser AI builder with hosting included Lovable or Bolt
To write code with an AI agent in your own editor Cursor or Claude Code, deployed anywhere below
The app, workers, cron jobs and Postgres on one prepaid bill Ownkube
A few steady services at flat monthly prices Render
Fast setup for several small services Railway
Servers close to users on several continents Fly.io
A frontend on a global CDN Vercel

What Replit costs

Plan Price What it adds
Starter $0 Daily Agent credits up to a monthly cap, one published app
Core $20 a month, or $18 billed annually Unlimited published apps, Full build, pay as you go past the credits
Pro $100 a month, or $90 billed annually 10 parallel agents, up to 15 collaborators
Enterprise Custom Security and admin controls

The Starter plan's published app goes down after 30 days unless you publish it again, and it carries a Replit badge. Starter also gets Lite build only. Full build needs Core or Pro.

Publishing bills against the plan's monthly credits first, then as usage:

Deployment type Price
Autoscale $2 a month base, $0.60 per million compute units, $0.40 per million requests
Reserved VM $15 a month (0.5 shared vCPU, 2 GB) up to $130 (4 vCPU, 16 GB)
Static Free hosting, $0.05 per GB of transfer
Scheduled $2 a month base, $0.60 per million compute units

A compute unit is 1/18 of a CPU second, or half a GB-second of memory. Agent usage bills by effort, so a long building session draws more credit than a short fix.

Why people look for a Replit alternative

The agent and the app share one balance

Agent work and running apps both draw on the same credits. A busy week of building can use credit that would have kept the app online, and the cost of an Agent session is hard to know before it runs.

The free app expires

On Starter, a published app goes down after 30 days. That works for a demo. For anything people rely on, it means a paid plan or another host.

The region is fixed at publish

Paid plans can pick where an app runs, and Starter apps publish to North America by default. Once an app is published, its geography can't be changed. Moving it means a new deployment.

You want your code in your own tools

Some people start in Replit and then want a local editor, their own git workflow and a coding agent they already pay for. At that point Replit's workspace and hosting are separate decisions.

The alternatives, one by one

Lovable

Lovable is the closest match to the Replit Agent workflow: describe the app in a chat and it builds it, with hosting on Lovable Cloud. The free plan gives 5 build credits a day, up to 30 a month, plus 20 Cloud credits a month. Paid monthly credits expire two months after they are issued. Small apps usually host within the included grant, and larger or busier ones draw from your credit balance. See Lovable's pricing.

Bolt

Bolt builds apps from a prompt in the browser and hosts them on every plan. The free plan has 1 million tokens a month with a 300,000 daily limit, and no custom domain. Pro is $25 a month for 10 million tokens that roll over, and Teams is $30 per member a month. See Bolt's pricing.

Cursor or Claude Code, in your own editor

These are coding agents that work on a repository on your machine. They write and edit code the way the Replit Agent does, but the code lives in your git repo and the hosting is your choice. Both can connect to Ownkube's MCP server and deploy the app, read logs and manage the database from the same session. The setup steps are on the Claude Code and Cursor pages.

Render

Render runs always-on services at flat monthly prices. The Hobby workspace is $0 and compute bills on top: a web service starts at $7 a month for 0.5 CPU and 512 MB, and Postgres starts at $6. A free instance exists for trying things out, and it spins down when idle. Render pricing explained has the full rate card.

Railway

Railway bills usage per second. Hobby is $5 a month and includes $5 of usage, and there is a Free plan with $1 of monthly credit. It is quick to set up several services and a database from one project. See Railway pricing explained.

Fly.io

Fly.io runs machines in many regions, which suits apps whose users are spread across continents. The smallest machine is $2.19 a month for a shared CPU and 256 MB, and managed Postgres starts at $38 a month. See Fly.io pricing explained for the rate card.

Vercel

Vercel is the pick for a Next.js or static frontend. Hobby is free for personal, non-commercial projects, and Pro is $20 per developer seat a month. Server code runs as functions with time limits, so a worker or a long job needs another host. Is Vercel free? covers the Hobby rules.

Ownkube

Ownkube runs the whole app: web services, workers, scheduled jobs, Postgres from $4 a month and a Valkey cache from $2. Compute is metered at about $18 per vCPU a month and $4.50 per GiB, by the minute, or you pick a flat box per app. Apps run in Mumbai or Germany. Ownkube has no AI of its own; you bring the agent.

Replit vs Ownkube

Replit Ownkube
Where you write code Replit's browser workspace Your own editor and repo
AI Replit Agent, billed by effort Your own coding agent, connected through MCP
Always-on app Reserved VM from $15 a month Metered from about $6.75 a month (0.25 vCPU, 0.5 GiB)
Postgres Built in, billed from credits From $4 a month plus $0.25 per GB
Background work Reserved VMs and scheduled deployments Workers and scheduled jobs
Billing Plan credits, then pay as you go Prepaid wallet; apps pause when it runs out

The wallet is the main difference in how the bill behaves. Pay as you go starts with a $5 top-up, Personal is $5 a month and loads $5 of credit, and Team is $20 a month and loads $20. Credit never expires. When it runs out, apps pause and keep their data until you top up, so a month can't cost more than you loaded.

Sleep is opt-in. An idle app bills nothing for compute and a sleeping database bills storage only.

Moving an app off Replit

  1. Push the code from Replit to a GitHub repository.
  2. Copy the values from Replit's Secrets into a note you can paste from.
  3. Create the new app from the repo in the Ownkube dashboard, or run okctl up in the project directory.
  4. Add the secrets as variables on the app.
  5. Create a Postgres database, then move the data with pg_dump and pg_restore.
  6. Point the app's database URL at the new database and redeploy.

When to stay on Replit

Stay if you mostly build with the Replit Agent and like working in the browser. Replit keeps the agent, the workspace and hosting in one place, and splitting them adds steps. A prototype that only needs to run for a demo also fits the Starter plan well.

A checklist before you move

  • Which part do you want to replace: the agent, the workspace, the hosting, or all three?
  • Does the app need to stay online for more than 30 days?
  • Do you need a worker or a job that runs longer than a request?
  • Where are your users, and which regions does the new host offer?
  • Do you want a hard ceiling on what a month can cost?

FAQ

What is the best free alternative to Replit?

For building with an AI agent in the browser, Lovable and Bolt both have free plans. For hosting, Render has a free instance that spins down when idle and Railway has a Free plan with $1 of monthly credit.

Is Replit free?

The Starter plan is $0 with daily Agent credits and one published app. That app goes down after 30 days unless you publish it again.

How much does Replit hosting cost?

A Reserved VM starts at $15 a month for 0.5 of a shared vCPU and 2 GB. Autoscale has a $2 monthly base plus compute units and requests. Static hosting is free with $0.05 per GB of transfer.

Can I export my code from Replit?

Yes. Push it to a GitHub repository and deploy it from there on any host in this list.

Can I keep using an AI agent after leaving Replit?

Yes. Cursor and Claude Code work on your own repo. Both can connect to Ownkube's MCP server, so the agent that writes the code can also deploy it.

Where Ownkube fits

If Replit got your app built and you now want it hosted with its Postgres, workers and cron jobs on one prepaid bill, Ownkube runs it in Mumbai or Germany. Bring the code from GitHub and the agent you already use. Deploy my first app.

title: BarBridge: a Rust core for GS1 Sunrise 2027 barcode pairs, callable from 7 languages over a C ABI
description:
TL;DR

I built and published BarBridge, a language-independent Rust core that generates GS1-compliant 1D+2D barcode pairs for the upcoming GS1 Sunrise 2027 transition. The core exposes a minimal C ABI, and today I finished publishing ready-to-run samples in 7 languages across 6 platform targets (Windows/macOS/Linux × x64/ARM64), plus a dual MIT/Apache-2.0 license.

Repo: https://github.com/acrossreport/barbridge

The problem: GS1 Sunrise 2027

In 2027, GS1 is moving retail POS barcode practice away from 1D-only symbols (EAN/UPC, etc.) toward pairing them with 2D symbols (GS1 QR Code / GS1 DataMatrix). The 2D symbol can carry attribute data — lot number, expiration date — alongside the GTIN, which is great for traceability. But during the transition, retailers and manufacturers need to print both symbol types together, correctly sized and laid out.

That means, for every label:

  1. Keep the barcode's X-dimension (module width) inside GS1's allowed range
  2. Compute the largest GS1-compliant size that still fits a target footprint (e.g. 50mm × 50mm)
  3. Arrange the 1D and 2D symbols together (side-by-side or stacked) for the same GTIN

Reimplementing that math per printer vendor or per language is exactly the kind of thing that quietly drifts out of spec over time. So I pulled it into a single core.

From an ACR feature to a standalone library

BarBridge didn't start as its own project. The first version of this GS1 pairing logic was built as an optional feature inside ACR, our receipt/label rendering engine, specifically to get ahead of GS1 Sunrise 2027 support there. But the moment I got it working, it was obvious the same logic — GS1 size optimization, 1D+2D layout, pairing — had nothing ACR-specific about it. Any POS, ERP, or label-printing tool facing the same 2027 transition would need the exact same math. So instead of keeping it locked inside ACR, I pulled it out and rebuilt it as BarBridge, a standalone Rust core with its own C ABI, so it could be adopted independently of whatever rendering stack a given tool already uses.

Architecture: one Rust core, one C ABI boundary 

request_json (string)
      │
      ▼
barbridge_render_png()   ← Rust core: GS1 size optimization + layout + rendering
      │
      ▼
PNG bytes (caller-owned buffer)

The exposed surface is intentionally small:

Function Description
barbridge_render_png(request_json, &out_data, &out_len) Renders a GS1 1D+2D pair (or a single symbol) to PNG bytes in memory
barbridge_bytes_free(data, len) Frees the returned buffer (always call it)
barbridge_last_error() Human-readable reason for the last failure

Request example:

{
  "data": "(01)04901234567894(10)LOT42(17)271231",
  "mode": "pair",
  "matrix": "data_matrix",
  "arrangement": "auto",
  "max_width_mm": 50,
  "max_height_mm": 50,
  "dpi": 600
}

data accepts either a GS1 AI element string ((01)GTIN(10)LOT…) or a bare GTIN-8/12/13/14. mode is pair (default), linear (1D only), or matrix (2D only).

Everything happens in memory — no temp files, no subprocess, no external CLI tool. The caller's process owns the output buffer, so there's no process-spawn overhead when embedding this in a server or batch pipeline. A WebAssembly build for the browser is planned too.

Today's work: samples for 7 languages × 6 platforms

The bulk of today's push was finishing a consistent sample set so anyone can see exactly how to call the library from their stack of choice, without reading the core source:

barbridge/
├── barbridge.h             # C ABI header (C/C++, cgo, ...)
├── windows-x64/
├── windows-arm64/
├── linux-x64/
├── linux-arm64/
├── macos-arm64/
└── macos-x64/
    ├── native/              barbridge.dll / libbarbridge.so / libbarbridge.dylib
    ├── common/request.json  # shared sample GS1 data
    ├── c/
    ├── python/              ctypes, standard library only
    ├── csharp/              P/Invoke, `dotnet run`
    ├── vb/                  P/Invoke, `dotnet run`
    ├── java/                JNA, `mvn package`
    ├── php/                 built-in FFI extension (PHP 7.4+)
    └── nodejs/              koffi (prebuilt binary, no build toolchain)
Language Binding Run
Python ctypes (stdlib only) python render_sample.py
C / C++ link against barbridge.dll.lib / .so / .dylib see header comment in render_sample.c
C# P/Invoke dotnet run
VB.NET P/Invoke dotnet run
Java JNA mvn package && java -jar target/barbridge-sample-jar-with-dependencies.jar
PHP built-in FFI extension php render_sample.php
Node.js koffi npm install && node render_sample.js

Every sample follows the same four steps: read ../common/request.json, call barbridge_render_png, write output.png, free the buffer. Seeing the FFI boilerplate side-by-side across ctypes/P-Invoke/JNA/koffi/PHP-FFI was honestly useful just for my own sanity-checking of the C ABI design — if one binding felt awkward, that was a signal the header needed adjusting, not the sample.

If you keep the library elsewhere, BARBRIDGE_NATIVE_LIB lets you point at it instead of relying on the relative path.

I also added a dual MIT OR Apache-2.0 license and cleaned up a stale "macOS build planned" note that had been sitting in both README files since the initial concept push.

What's next

  • GS1-128 and GS1 DataBar support for logistics/case labels
  • A WebAssembly sample for the browser
  • Deciding how much of the core implementation itself to open up

Repo: https://github.com/acrossreport/barbridge — issues and feedback welcome, especially from anyone already dealing with Sunrise 2027 compliance on the printing side.

title: Module Federation (Webpack 5)
description:
Taming the Monolith: How Webpack 5's Module Federation is Revolutionizing Frontend Development

Remember the good old days? We’d all pile our frontend code into one giant, glorious monolith. It was simple, it was contained, and it was… a nightmare to manage as it grew. Updates became a game of Russian roulette, teams tripped over each other, and deployment felt like a high-stakes gamble. Thankfully, the frontend world has evolved, and one of the most exciting advancements is Webpack 5's Module Federation.

Think of Module Federation as a secret handshake for your microservices, but for your frontend applications. It’s a powerful feature that allows you to split your application into independent bundles that can be dynamically loaded at runtime. This means different parts of your application can be developed, deployed, and even versioned independently, all while feeling like a single, cohesive unit to the end-user. Pretty cool, right?

Let's dive deep into this game-changer and see how it can help you tame your frontend monoliths.

The "Why": Why Bother with Module Federation?

Before we get our hands dirty with code, let's understand the problems Module Federation aims to solve. Imagine you're working on a large e-commerce platform. You have a product listing page, a shopping cart, a checkout process, and a user profile section.

  • Monolith Headaches:
    • Slow Builds: As the codebase grows, build times can become excruciatingly long. Waiting an hour for a full rebuild? No thank you!
    • Team Dependencies: Multiple teams working on the same large codebase are constantly stepping on each other's toes. A change in one area might inadvertently break another, leading to endless debugging sessions.
    • Deployment Nightmares: Deploying a new feature often means redeploying the entire application. This increases the risk of introducing regressions and makes rollbacks a complex operation.
    • Code Duplication: Sharing common UI components or utility functions across different parts of the application can lead to duplicated code, increasing bundle sizes.
    • Framework Lock-in: Migrating a large monolith to a new framework is a monumental task.

Module Federation swoops in like a superhero, offering a solution to these woes.

Setting the Stage: What You Need to Get Started

Before we start federating, let's ensure you have the right tools in your arsenal.

  • Webpack 5 (Obviously!): This is the bedrock of Module Federation. Make sure your project is using Webpack 5 or a later version.
  • Node.js and npm/yarn: Standard JavaScript development environment.
  • Basic Understanding of Webpack: Familiarity with Webpack concepts like entry points, output, loaders, and plugins will be incredibly helpful.
  • A Willingness to Experiment: Like any powerful tool, there's a learning curve. Be prepared to tinker and explore!

The Core Concepts: Remote & Host

Module Federation revolves around two key players: the Host and the Remotes.

  • Host Application: This is your primary application. It's the one that will dynamically load modules from other applications. Think of it as the conductor of the orchestra, orchestrating the loading of different musical pieces.
  • Remote Application: These are your independent modules or applications. They expose specific components or functionalities that the Host can consume. They are the individual musicians playing their part.

The magic happens when the Host application requests a module from a Remote application. Webpack, with its Module Federation plugin, handles the dynamic loading and integration seamlessly.

Let's Get Our Hands Dirty: The module-federation-plugin

The heart of Module Federation is the webpack.config.js. Here's where we'll configure our federated applications.

1. Installing the Plugin:

npm install --save-dev webpack-cli webpack-dev-server @babel/core @babel/preset-env babel-loader

(Note: You'll also need Babel configured for your project to transpile modern JavaScript.)

2. Configuring the Host Application (webpack.config.js):

Let's imagine our Host application is our main e-commerce website.

// webpack.config.js (Host)
const HtmlWebpackPlugin = require('html-webpack-plugin');
const ModuleFederationPlugin = require('webpack-module-federation-plugin');

module.exports = {
  mode: 'development',
  devServer: {
    port: 3001, // Host runs on port 3001
  },
  plugins: [
    new ModuleFederationPlugin({
      name: 'host', // The name of this application (optional, but good practice)
      remotes: {
        // This tells the host about available remotes.
        // The key 'remote_app' is how we'll refer to it.
        // The value is the URL where the remote app's manifest is served.
        remote_app: 'remote_app@http://localhost:3002/remoteEntry.js',
      },
      shared: {
        // This is crucial! It defines dependencies that will be shared between
        // the host and remotes. This prevents duplicate libraries and ensures
        // consistency. 'react' and 'react-dom' are common examples.
        'react': {
          singleton: true, // Ensures only one instance of react is loaded
          import: 'react',
          shareKey: 'react',
          requiredVersion: '^18.2.0', // Specify the expected version
        },
        'react-dom': {
          singleton: true,
          import: 'react-dom',
          shareKey: 'react-dom',
          requiredVersion: '^18.2.0',
        },
      },
    }),
    new HtmlWebpackPlugin({
      template: './public/index.html',
    }),
  ],
};

3. Configuring the Remote Application (webpack.config.js):

Now, let's create a remote_app that exposes a "Hello World" component. This remote application will run on a different port (e.g., 3002).

// webpack.config.js (Remote)
const HtmlWebpackPlugin = require('html-webpack-plugin');
const ModuleFederationPlugin = require('webpack-module-federation-plugin');

module.exports = {
  mode: 'development',
  devServer: {
    port: 3002, // Remote runs on port 3002
  },
  plugins: [
    new ModuleFederationPlugin({
      name: 'remote_app', // The name of this remote application
      filename: 'remoteEntry.js', // The name of the entry file
      exposes: {
        // This maps a module name ('./HelloWorld') to its path in the remote app.
        // We'll use './HelloWorld' to import this component in the host.
        './HelloWorld': './src/components/HelloWorld.js',
      },
      shared: {
        // Important: Remotes also need to declare shared dependencies.
        // This allows the host to potentially use the same shared instance.
        'react': {
          singleton: true,
          import: 'react',
          shareKey: 'react',
          requiredVersion: '^18.2.0',
        },
        'react-dom': {
          singleton: true,
          import: 'react-dom',
          shareKey: 'react-dom',
          requiredVersion: '^18.2.0',
        },
      },
    }),
    new HtmlWebpackPlugin({
      template: './public/index.html',
    }),
  ],
};

4. Creating the Remote Component (src/components/HelloWorld.js):

// src/components/HelloWorld.js (Remote App)
import React from 'react';

const HelloWorld = () => {
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Hello from the Remote App!</h2>
    </div>
  );
};

export default HelloWorld;

5. Consuming the Remote Component in the Host (src/App.js):

This is where the magic of dynamic import comes into play.

// src/App.js (Host App)
import React, { Suspense } from 'react';
import './App.css';

// Dynamically import the HelloWorld component from the remote_app
const RemoteHelloWorld = React.lazy(() => import('remote_app/HelloWorld'));

function App() {
  return (
    <div className="App">
      <h1>Welcome to the Host App!</h1>
      <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading remote component...</div>}>
        <RemoteHelloWorld />
      </Suspense>
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;

To run this:

  1. Build and run both the host and remote applications in separate terminals.
    • Remote: cd remote_app && npm start (or your build/start command)
    • Host: cd host && npm start (or your build/start command)

You should see "Welcome to the Host App!" followed by "Hello from the Remote App!". This is Module Federation in action!

Key Features and Benefits: Beyond the Basics

Module Federation is more than just dynamic imports. It unlocks a suite of powerful features:

  • Independent Deployments: Each federated application can be deployed independently. Need to update the "product listing" micro-frontend? Deploy only that, and the rest of your application remains unaffected. This drastically reduces deployment risk.
  • Code Sharing and Collaboration: Imagine a design system team building a library of UI components. This library can be exposed as a remote, and all other applications can consume these components, ensuring a consistent look and feel across your entire ecosystem.
  • Dynamic Versioning: You can have different versions of shared libraries (like React) running in different federated applications. This allows for gradual upgrades and migration strategies.
  • Technology Agnosticism (Partially): While the examples use React, Module Federation itself is framework-agnostic. You could have a Vue application consuming a React component, or vice versa, as long as they agree on shared dependencies.
  • Performance Improvements: By splitting your application into smaller, independent chunks, you can achieve faster initial load times. Users only download the code they need for the current view.
  • Team Autonomy: Teams can own and manage their specific micro-frontends with minimal dependencies on other teams, fostering agility and faster development cycles.

Shared Dependencies: The Secret Sauce to Efficiency

The shared option in the ModuleFederationPlugin is arguably one of the most important features. When you declare dependencies as shared, Webpack ensures that only one instance of that dependency is loaded across all federated applications. This:

  • Reduces Bundle Size: Instead of each application shipping its own copy of React, only one copy is loaded.
  • Ensures Consistency: All applications use the same version of shared libraries, preventing subtle bugs due to version mismatches.
  • Enables Runtime Updates: If you update a shared library, all applications using it will automatically benefit from the update without needing to be rebuilt or redeployed themselves (within compatible version ranges).

Example of complex sharing:

// webpack.config.js
...
shared: {
  'react': {
    singleton: true,
    import: 'react',
    shareKey: 'react',
    requiredVersion: '^18.2.0',
    packageDir: './node_modules/react', // Optional: Can help Webpack find the shared package
  },
  'lodash': {
    singleton: true,
    import: 'lodash',
    shareKey: 'lodash',
    requiredVersion: '^4.17.21',
  },
},
...

Potential Pitfalls and Disadvantages

While Module Federation is incredibly powerful, it's not a silver bullet. Here are some things to be mindful of:

  • Increased Complexity: Setting up and managing a federated architecture is inherently more complex than a monolith. You'll need to think about how applications communicate, how dependencies are managed, and how to handle errors across different modules.
  • Build and Deployment Orchestration: While individual deployments are easier, orchestrating builds and deployments across multiple repositories can become challenging. You might need CI/CD pipelines that can handle multiple independent deployments.
  • Debugging Can Be Tricky: Debugging across federated applications can sometimes be more involved, especially when issues arise from interactions between modules.
  • Learning Curve: As mentioned, there's a learning curve associated with understanding the concepts and effectively configuring Module Federation.
  • Runtime Errors: If a remote module fails to load or throws an error at runtime, it can impact the user experience of the host application. Robust error handling and fallback mechanisms are essential.
  • Network Latency: Dynamically loading modules introduces network requests. If the network is slow, users might experience delays in seeing content.

Advanced Features and Considerations

  • shareScopeMap: This advanced option allows you to explicitly control how shared modules are exposed and consumed. It offers finer-grained control over versioning and dependency resolution.
  • eager loading: By default, modules are loaded lazily. You can set eager: true for specific exposes entries to load them eagerly, which might be beneficial for critical components.
  • Remotes as Hosts: A remote application can also act as a host to other remotes, creating a hierarchical structure of federated applications.
  • Server-Side Rendering (SSR): Integrating Module Federation with SSR requires careful consideration and additional setup to ensure modules are rendered correctly on the server.

When is Module Federation a Good Fit?

Module Federation shines in scenarios like:

  • Large, complex web applications: Where breaking down the codebase into smaller, manageable pieces is a necessity.
  • E-commerce platforms: Where different sections (product pages, cart, checkout) can be developed and deployed independently.
  • SaaS applications with distinct modules: Think of a CRM with modules for contacts, deals, and reporting.
  • Organizations with multiple frontend teams: Where teams can own and manage their respective micro-frontends.
  • Applications requiring gradual migration to new technologies: You can gradually introduce new frameworks by migrating parts of your application as remotes.

Conclusion: Embrace the Future of Frontend Architecture

Webpack 5's Module Federation is a paradigm shift in frontend development. It empowers us to break free from the limitations of monolithic applications and embrace a more modular, scalable, and maintainable architecture. While it introduces its own set of complexities, the benefits of independent deployments, enhanced collaboration, and improved performance are undeniable.

By understanding the core concepts, carefully configuring your Webpack setup, and being mindful of potential pitfalls, you can leverage Module Federation to build more robust, agile, and future-proof frontend applications. So, go forth, experiment, and start taming your monoliths! The future of frontend architecture is here, and it's federated.

title: Supabase vs Firebase: database, pricing, auth and lock-in compared
description:
Supabase and Firebase both give a frontend a database, auth, file storage and functions without running a server. The difference starts with the database. Supabase is Postgres, with tables, joins and SQL, and it bills a plan fee plus compute size. Firebase is Firestore, a document store with offline sync, and it bills per document read and write. Pick Supabase if your data is relational or you want to keep the option to leave. Pick Firebase if you are building a mobile app that leans on offline sync and Google's mobile tools.

TL;DR

  • Supabase is Postgres. Firebase's main database, Firestore, stores documents and has no joins.
  • Supabase Pro is $25 a month and includes $10 of compute credit. Firebase Blaze has no base fee and bills each read, write and GB.
  • Both free plans include 50,000 monthly active users for auth. Supabase Free pauses a project after a week of inactivity, and Firebase Spark caps Firestore at 50,000 reads a day.
  • Supabase Pro has a spend cap on by default for usage lines. Firebase has budget alerts, which do not stop spending.
  • Supabase is open source and can be self-hosted. Firebase runs only on Google Cloud.

Supabase vs Firebase at a glance

Supabase Firebase
Database Postgres Firestore (documents), Realtime Database (JSON tree)
Queries SQL with joins Document queries, no joins
Access rules Postgres row level security Firebase security rules
Functions Edge Functions on Deno (TypeScript) Cloud Functions (Node.js, Python)
Offline sync Not built in Built into the Firestore SDKs
Push, crash reports, analytics Not included Cloud Messaging, Crashlytics, Analytics
Pricing model Plan fee plus compute size Pay per read, write, GB and invocation
Self-hosting Yes, with Docker or the CLI No

How do the data models differ?

Supabase: tables and SQL

A Supabase project is a full Postgres database. You define tables, foreign keys and indexes, and query them with SQL or through the API Supabase generates from your schema. A report that joins orders, customers and products is one query.

Postgres extensions come with it. pgvector stores embeddings next to the rows they describe, and PostGIS handles location queries.

Firebase: documents and collections

Firestore stores JSON-like documents in collections. Queries filter and sort within a collection, and there are no joins, so data that would be related in SQL is usually copied into each document that needs it. Updating a customer's name can mean writing to every order that holds a copy.

In exchange, Firestore's mobile and web SDKs cache data on the device, work offline and sync changes when the connection returns. Real-time listeners push updates to every client watching a document.

How does pricing compare?

The two bill in different units, so the cheaper one depends on traffic.

Firebase bills per operation

On Blaze, Firestore bills each document read, write and delete past a daily free quota.

Firestore location Reads per 100K Writes per 100K Storage per GiB a month
Mumbai $0.035 $0.104 $0.104
Frankfurt $0.039 $0.117 $0.117

Every document a query returns is a read, so a list screen with 50 items costs 50 reads each time it opens. Firebase pricing explained covers Functions, Hosting and Storage line by line.

Supabase bills per plan and compute size

Pro is $25 a month per organization and includes $10 of compute credit, which covers one Micro project (1 GB of memory). Bigger sizes cost more: Small is about $15 a month and Medium about $60. Queries are not counted, so the bill follows the size the database needs. Supabase pricing explained has the full compute table.

Pro quota Included Past the quota
Database disk 8 GB per project $0.125 per GB
Egress 250 GB $0.09 per GB
Monthly active users 100,000 $0.00325 per user
File storage 100 GB $0.0213 per GB
Edge Function invocations 2 million $2 per million
Realtime messages 5 million $2.50 per million
Realtime connections 500 concurrent $10 per 1,000

Two example bills

A small app with 6 million Firestore reads, 900,000 writes and 2 GiB of data a month costs about $2 in Mumbai on Firebase. The same app on Supabase Pro is $25, or $0 on Supabase Free if it fits in 500 MB and stays active.

A busy app with 30 million reads, 3 million writes and 5 GiB costs about $12.90 a month in Mumbai on Firestore, with reads making up about three quarters of that. Supabase Pro stays at $25 while the database fits on Micro. Firebase is cheaper at low and moderate traffic. Its read charges grow in step with traffic, while a Supabase bill moves when you change the compute size.

How do the free plans compare?

Supabase Free Firebase Spark
Database Postgres, 500 MB Firestore, 1 GiB
Database limits Two active projects 50,000 reads, 20,000 writes and 20,000 deletes a day
Egress 5 GB 10 GiB a month from Firestore
Auth 50,000 monthly active users 50,000 monthly active users
File storage 1 GB Needs Blaze
Functions 500,000 Edge Function invocations Needs Blaze
Realtime 200 concurrent connections, 2 million messages Listener updates bill as reads
Inactivity Project pauses after a week No pause
Backups None None

Spark has no inactivity pause, which makes it the better home for a small app that gets little traffic. Supabase Free is the better fit when you need file storage or functions without a payment method.

Auth, storage and functions

Both include email, password and social sign-in, and both give 50,000 monthly active users on the free plan. On paid plans, Supabase Pro includes 100,000 and bills $0.00325 per user past that. Firebase bills past 50,000 at Google Cloud rates, and phone sign-in bills per SMS. Supabase's phone multi-factor authentication is a $75 a month add-on for the first project.

Supabase Storage is part of every plan, with 1 GB on Free and 100 GB on Pro. On Firebase, Cloud Storage needs Blaze, and its free amounts only apply to buckets in three US regions.

Supabase Edge Functions run TypeScript on Deno. Firebase Cloud Functions run Node.js or Python on Google Cloud, with 2 million invocations a month free on Blaze, then $0.40 per million plus CPU and memory time.

Spend limits and backups

Supabase Pro has a spend cap, on by default. With it on, usage past a quota stops until the next billing cycle. It covers disk, egress, users, storage, realtime and function invocations. Compute size and point-in-time recovery bill whether the cap is on or off.

Firebase has no spend cap. A Google Cloud budget sends alerts, and stopping the bill means disabling billing on the project or turning services off yourself.

Supabase Pro includes daily backups kept 7 days. Point-in-time recovery is $100 a month per 7 days of retention. Firestore backups and point-in-time recovery have no free usage and bill once enabled.

Regions

Supabase lets you pick a region per project, including Mumbai (ap-south-1), Frankfurt (eu-central-1) and London (eu-west-2). Firestore has locations in Mumbai (asia-south1) and Frankfurt (europe-west3), plus a Europe multi-region (eur3) that costs more. Put the database in the same region as most of your users.

Lock-in

Supabase is open source, and you can run it yourself with Docker. Because the database is Postgres, pg_dump moves the data to any Postgres host, and the SQL and row level security policies come with it.

Firebase runs only on Google Cloud. Moving off Firestore means exporting documents and redesigning them into another data model, and the client code that calls the Firebase SDK changes too.

Which should you pick?

Your app Pick
Mobile app that must work offline Firebase
Uses push notifications, Crashlytics and Analytics Firebase
Relational data, reports or joins Supabase
Vector search next to app data Supabase, with pgvector
Small app with little traffic and no payment method Firebase Spark
Wants a spend cap on usage Supabase Pro
Wants to self-host later Supabase

How Ownkube compares

Ownkube is a different shape from both. It runs your own backend, workers, scheduled jobs and a Postgres database, billed by the resources they use. It has no built-in auth, file storage or client SDK, so you bring a library for each. This fits a project that has outgrown calling the database straight from the frontend.

Postgres starts at $4 a month on a DB 0.5 box, plus $0.25 per GB of storage, and Postgres extensions such as pgvector and PostGIS turn on from the database settings. Compute bills at about $18 per vCPU a month and $4.50 per GiB, by the minute. Apps run in Mumbai or Germany.

Billing works from a prepaid wallet. Pay as you go starts with a $5 top-up, Personal is $5 a month and loads $5 of credit, and Team is $20 a month and loads $20. Credit never expires. When it runs out, apps pause and keep their data until you top up.

Checklist before you pick

  • Is your data relational, or does it fit in self-contained documents?
  • Does the app need to work offline on a phone?
  • How many documents does a busy screen read, and how often does it open?
  • Do you need a hard cap on usage, or are budget alerts enough?
  • Would you want to move the database to another host one day?

For other Postgres hosts, see Supabase alternatives, Neon vs Supabase and managed Postgres pricing.

FAQ

Is Supabase better than Firebase?

For relational data, SQL and a path to self-hosting, Supabase fits better. For a mobile app that needs offline sync, push notifications and crash reporting from one SDK, Firebase fits better.

Is Supabase cheaper than Firebase?

At low traffic, usually not: a small Firestore app often costs a few dollars a month on Blaze or nothing on Spark, while Supabase Pro starts at $25. Firestore bills every read, so a read-heavy app can cost more on Firebase once its traffic grows.

Can I migrate from Firebase to Supabase?

Yes. Firestore documents have to be mapped to tables, the security rules rewritten as row level security policies, and the client code moved from the Firebase SDK to the Supabase client. Firebase Auth users can be exported and imported.

Does Supabase have offline sync like Firebase?

Not built in. Supabase's client libraries query the database over the network. Apps that need offline sync add a separate library for it.

Can I self-host Firebase?

No. Firebase runs on Google Cloud only. The Firebase emulators run locally for development and testing.

Where Ownkube fits

If your app has its own API and uses Supabase or Firebase mostly as a database, Ownkube runs the API, its workers and Postgres together from a prepaid wallet. Deploy my first app.

title: Adaptive Concurrency Limits in Go: Dynamically Protecting Dependencies Under Load
description:
Most services eventually need a concurrency limit.

You might start with something simple:

const maxConcurrentRequests = 100

A semaphore ensures that no more than 100 requests execute simultaneously.

It works. Until the conditions change.

Your service gets more CPU resources after scaling. A downstream database becomes slower. A new deployment changes request processing time. Traffic patterns shift throughout the day.

The limit that worked yesterday might be too restrictive today. Or worse, it might be too high and allow a dependency to become overloaded.

Static concurrency limits are easy to implement, but they require continuous tuning.

What if a service could adjust its concurrency limit automatically based on how the dependency behaves?

That's the idea behind adaptive concurrency limiting.

Instead of relying entirely on a predefined number, the system observes request latency and failure signals, estimates when queueing is happening, and adjusts the number of requests it allows in flight.

In this article, we'll explore:

  • Why fixed concurrency limits eventually become difficult to maintain
  • The relationship between concurrency, throughput, and latency
  • How TCP congestion control inspired adaptive concurrency algorithms
  • How to implement a latency-aware concurrency limiter in Go
  • How to integrate it into an HTTP client
  • How adaptive limits interact with backpressure, bulkheads, and retry budgets
  • What to monitor and test before using adaptive concurrency in production

1. The Problem with Fixed Concurrency Limits

Imagine a Go service that calls an external market data API.

You initially configure a concurrency limit of 50.

limiter := NewFixedLimiter(50)

Under normal traffic, the dependency responds in 40ms.

Everything looks healthy.

Then traffic increases.

The dependency starts processing requests more slowly. Its response time grows to 150ms, then 300ms.

Your service still allows 50 concurrent requests.

The problem is that concurrency and latency are connected.

When requests take longer to complete, existing requests occupy concurrency slots for longer. New requests accumulate, queues grow, and latency increases further.

A fixed limit cannot automatically distinguish between:

  • A dependency that has additional capacity
  • A dependency approaching saturation
  • A dependency already experiencing queueing
  • A dependency recovering from an overload

You can increase the limit manually, but that risks overloading the dependency.

You can decrease it, but that might unnecessarily reduce throughput.

The challenge is finding a concurrency level that allows high throughput without creating excessive queueing.

2. Why Concurrency Matters More Than RPS Alone

Rate limiting and concurrency limiting solve different problems.

A rate limiter controls how many requests can start during a period.

A concurrency limiter controls how many requests can be in progress simultaneously.

Consider two situations:

Scenario Request rate Average latency Approx. concurrency
Healthy dependency 500 req/s 40ms 20
Slow dependency 500 req/s 200ms 100

Both scenarios have the same incoming request rate.

But the second requires five times as many concurrent requests to sustain that throughput.

This relationship is described by Little's Law:

[
L = \lambda W
]

Where:

  • (L) is the average number of items in the system
  • (\lambda) is the average arrival rate
  • (W) is the average time spent in the system

For request processing:

[
Concurrency \approx Throughput \times Latency
]

This explains why a fixed RPS limit is not always sufficient to protect a dependency.

A service can receive an acceptable number of requests per second while still accumulating too many in-flight operations because response times have increased.

Adaptive concurrency focuses on this relationship.

3. The Idea Behind Adaptive Concurrency

The central idea is straightforward:

  1. Measure request latency.
  2. Maintain an estimate of normal, unloaded latency.
  3. Compare current latency against that baseline.
  4. Increase concurrency when the dependency has spare capacity.
  5. Reduce concurrency when latency indicates queueing or failures.

This resembles congestion control in TCP.

TCP does not blindly send unlimited data. It maintains a congestion window and adjusts how much data can be in flight based on network conditions.

Adaptive concurrency applies a similar idea to service requests.

The concurrency limit becomes a dynamic window.

There are several algorithms worth understanding.

AIMD

Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease.

  • Increase the limit gradually when requests succeed.
  • Reduce it significantly when failures or overload signals appear.

For example:

Current limit: 50

Successful samples:
50 → 51 → 52 → 53

Overload detected:
53 → 37

AIMD is relatively simple and works well when the system has reliable failure signals.

However, it may react only after a dependency starts rejecting requests or timing out.

Vegas

Vegas uses latency as an early signal of congestion.

It estimates queueing using the difference between observed latency and a no-load baseline.

A simplified queue estimate is:

[
Q = L \times \left(1 - \frac{RTT_{baseline}}{RTT_{current}}\right)
]

Where:

  • (Q) is estimated queue size
  • (L) is the current concurrency limit
  • (RTT_{baseline}) is the observed no-load latency
  • (RTT_{current}) is the current measured latency

When latency stays close to the baseline, the algorithm can increase concurrency.

When latency grows significantly, it reduces the limit.

Gradient2

Gradient2 compares short-term and long-term latency averages to detect changes in the latency trend.

It is useful when latency baselines drift over time or workloads are bursty.

Instead of relying only on a minimum latency measurement, it uses smoothed averages to identify growing queueing pressure.

For a deeper implementation reference, Netflix's concurrency-limits project is worth exploring:

https://github.com/Netflix/concurrency-limits

For this article, we'll build a smaller Vegas-inspired controller. It is an educational implementation, not a complete reproduction of Netflix's Vegas or Gradient2 algorithms.

4. Building an Adaptive Limiter in Go

Let's implement a limiter that:

  • Tracks in-flight requests
  • Enforces a dynamic concurrency limit
  • Measures request duration
  • Collects latency samples in windows
  • Estimates queueing using a baseline latency
  • Increases or decreases the limit based on observed behavior

We'll use a fail-fast admission strategy.

When the current concurrency limit is reached, the limiter rejects the new request instead of allowing an unbounded queue to form.

Step 1: Define the limiter 

package adaptive

import (
    "errors"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

var ErrLimitExceeded = errors.New(
    "adaptive concurrency limit exceeded",
)

type Limiter struct {
    mu sync.Mutex

    limit    int
    minLimit int
    maxLimit int

    inflight int
    peak     int

    baseline time.Duration

    sampleCount int
    sampleTotal time.Duration
    dropped     bool

    windowSize int

    alpha float64
    beta  float64
}

func New(
    initialLimit int,
    minLimit int,
    maxLimit int,
) *Limiter {
    if minLimit < 1 ||
        initialLimit < minLimit ||
        maxLimit < initialLimit {
        panic("invalid concurrency limits")
    }

    return &Limiter{
        limit:      initialLimit,
        minLimit:   minLimit,
        maxLimit:   maxLimit,
        windowSize: 20,
        alpha:      2,
        beta:       4,
    }
}

The limiter maintains two important pieces of information:

Current limit: The maximum number of requests allowed simultaneously.

In-flight count: The number of requests currently executing.

We also maintain latency statistics and a baseline.

The windowSize determines how many completed requests we collect before updating the concurrency limit.

Using a window helps avoid changing the limit after every individual request.

Step 2: Acquire a permit

The limiter needs to decide whether a new request can execute.

func (l *Limiter) Acquire() (func(bool), error) {
    l.mu.Lock()

    if l.inflight >= l.limit {
        l.mu.Unlock()
        return nil, ErrLimitExceeded
    }

    l.inflight++

    if l.inflight > l.peak {
        l.peak = l.inflight
    }

    l.mu.Unlock()

    startedAt := time.Now()

    var once sync.Once

    done := func(dropped bool) {
        once.Do(func() {
            elapsed := time.Since(startedAt)

            l.mu.Lock()
            defer l.mu.Unlock()

            l.inflight--

            l.recordSample(elapsed, dropped)
        })
    }

    return done, nil
}

The returned function releases the permit and reports the outcome.

For example:

done, err := limiter.Acquire()
if err != nil {
    return err
}

defer done(false)

return callDependency()

If the operation experiences a dependency-level overload signal, we can report that separately:

done, err := limiter.Acquire()
if err != nil {
    return err
}

defer func() {
    done(isOverloadError(err))
}()

err = callDependency()
return err

The sync.Once protects against accidentally releasing the same permit twice.

The caller must invoke the returned function exactly once in normal control flow. The sync.Once makes repeated invocations harmless.

Step 3: Record latency samples

Now we need to collect completed request samples.

func (l *Limiter) recordSample(
    latency time.Duration,
    dropped bool,
) {
    l.sampleCount++
    l.sampleTotal += latency

    if dropped {
        l.dropped = true
    }

    if l.sampleCount < l.windowSize {
        return
    }

    average := l.sampleTotal / time.Duration(l.sampleCount)

    l.updateLimit(average)

    l.sampleCount = 0
    l.sampleTotal = 0
    l.dropped = false
    l.peak = 0
}

Instead of adjusting concurrency after every request, we wait until a complete sample window is collected.

This reduces sensitivity to individual latency spikes.

A production implementation may use more sophisticated rolling windows, exponential moving averages, or percentile-based measurements.

Step 4: Implement the control algorithm

Now comes the interesting part.

We compare the current average latency against the baseline.

func (l *Limiter) updateLimit(
    currentLatency time.Duration,
) {
    if currentLatency <= 0 {
        return
    }

    if l.baseline == 0 ||
        currentLatency < l.baseline {
        l.baseline = currentLatency
        return
    }

    if l.dropped {
        l.decrease()
        return
    }

    queueEstimate := float64(l.limit) *
        (1 - float64(l.baseline)/float64(currentLatency))

    // Increase only when the previous window
    // demonstrated meaningful concurrency usage.
    if l.peak*2 < l.limit {
        return
    }

    switch {
    case queueEstimate < l.alpha:
        l.increase()

    case queueEstimate > l.beta:
        l.decrease()
    }
}

The queue estimate is an approximation of the queueing pressure observed at the dependency.

When current latency is close to the baseline, the estimated queue remains small.

When current latency increases, the estimated queue grows.

We use two thresholds:

  • alpha: Below this value, the dependency appears to have spare capacity.
  • beta: Above this value, queueing pressure is considered too high.

The gap between the thresholds creates a stability region where the limit does not change.

This helps avoid unnecessary oscillation.

Step 5: Increase and decrease concurrency

The final methods enforce the configured boundaries.

func (l *Limiter) increase() {
    if l.limit < l.maxLimit {
        l.limit++
    }
}

func (l *Limiter) decrease() {
    next := int(float64(l.limit) * 0.7)

    if next < l.minLimit {
        next = l.minLimit
    }

    l.limit = next
}

The limiter uses:

  • Additive increase: Grow gradually.
  • Multiplicative decrease: Reduce more aggressively when congestion appears.

This is intentionally conservative.

Increasing the limit by one allows the dependency to demonstrate additional capacity without creating a large traffic spike.

Reducing the limit by 30% provides a faster response to overload.

These values are configuration choices, not universal production defaults.

Step 6: Expose the current limit

We should expose the current state for observability.

func (l *Limiter) Stats() (
    limit int,
    inflight int,
    baseline time.Duration,
) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()

    return l.limit, l.inflight, l.baseline
}

Now we can inspect the limiter without exposing its internal synchronization.

For example:

limit, inflight, baseline := limiter.Stats()

log.Printf(
    "adaptive limiter: limit=%d inflight=%d baseline=%s",
    limit,
    inflight,
    baseline,
)

5. Integrating the Limiter with an HTTP Client

Let's apply the limiter to an external dependency.

type MarketDataClient struct {
    httpClient *http.Client
    limiter    *adaptive.Limiter
}

func (c *MarketDataClient) Fetch(
    ctx context.Context,
    symbol string,
) error {
    done, err := c.limiter.Acquire()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    var dropped bool

    defer func() {
        done(dropped)
    }()

    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(
        ctx,
        http.MethodGet,
        "https://api.example.com/market/"+symbol,
        nil,
    )
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    resp, err := c.httpClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        dropped = isDependencyOverload(err)
        return err
    }

    defer resp.Body.Close()

    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests ||
        resp.StatusCode >= http.StatusServiceUnavailable {
        dropped = true
        return fmt.Errorf(
            "market data dependency returned %d",
            resp.StatusCode,
        )
    }

    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf(
            "unexpected status: %d",
            resp.StatusCode,
        )
    }

    return nil
}

The example classifies overload responses separately from other errors.

This distinction matters.

A validation error, for example, should not necessarily cause the adaptive limiter to reduce its concurrency limit.

Likewise, a network timeout might be an overload signal in one system but a network infrastructure issue in another.

The failure classifier should reflect the dependency's actual behavior.

The HTTP client should also have appropriate timeouts and connection settings. An adaptive concurrency limiter is not a replacement for transport-level protection.

6. What Happens During an Overload?

Let's walk through a simplified scenario.

Assume the limiter starts with a concurrency limit of 50.

The dependency initially responds in 40ms.

As traffic increases, the limiter observes the following:

Stage Average latency Concurrency limit
Initial 40ms 50
Increased traffic 45ms 51
Higher utilization 55ms 52
Queueing begins 120ms 36
Dependency recovers 45ms Gradually increases

The important behavior is not the exact numbers.

The limiter detects that latency is increasing relative to the baseline and reduces the amount of work it allows in flight.

As the dependency recovers, the limiter can gradually explore additional capacity again.

This is a feedback control loop.

However, it is important to understand that the limiter does not instantly discover the perfect concurrency limit. It continuously estimates a useful operating point based on observed signals.

7. Adaptive Concurrency vs. Other Resilience Patterns

Adaptive concurrency is not a replacement for the patterns we've discussed in previous articles.

It complements them.

Mechanism Responsibility
Backpressure Controls incoming work
Load shedding Rejects work when capacity is exceeded
Bulkhead Isolates resources and dependencies
Retry budget Limits additional retry traffic
Adaptive concurrency Adjusts the concurrency ceiling based on observed conditions

Consider a service that communicates with three dependencies:

  • Market Data API
  • Portfolio Database
  • Reporting Service

Each dependency has different latency characteristics and capacity.

Using one global concurrency limit would couple their behavior.

A better approach is to create an independent adaptive limiter for each dependency.

type DependencyLimiters struct {
    MarketData *adaptive.Limiter
    Portfolio  *adaptive.Limiter
    Reporting  *adaptive.Limiter
}

This gives each dependency its own feedback loop.

If the reporting service becomes slow, its concurrency limit can decrease without automatically reducing the capacity available to market data requests.

This is where adaptive concurrency and bulkheads work particularly well together.

8. Important Production Considerations

The example implementation demonstrates the core idea, but a production adaptive limiter needs additional safeguards.

Baseline latency can become stale

A latency baseline is only useful when it represents a reasonably unloaded system.

If the baseline is established while the dependency is already overloaded, the algorithm may incorrectly treat unhealthy latency as normal.

Production implementations should carefully manage baseline updates and resets.

Traffic must be representative

A dependency may expose different latency characteristics for different operations.

For example:

  • Reading a cached market price
  • Fetching historical prices
  • Calculating a portfolio
  • Executing a database aggregation

Combining all these operations into one latency signal can produce misleading results.

Consider separate limiters or traffic partitions when workloads have significantly different behavior.

The algorithm needs enough samples

Adaptive control depends on observations.

A low-traffic service might not generate enough samples to update its limit reliably.

A new instance also needs a warm-up strategy.

Slow start, conservative initial limits, and minimum sample requirements can help.

Avoid uncontrolled oscillation

A limiter that constantly increases and decreases its capacity can introduce instability.

Useful techniques include:

  • Sampling windows
  • Exponential smoothing
  • Separate increase and decrease thresholds
  • Bounded increase and decrease rates
  • Minimum and maximum concurrency limits
  • Jitter when multiple independent clients share a dependency

Local limits multiply across replicas

This is especially important in distributed deployments.

Imagine ten replicas, each with an adaptive concurrency limit of 100.

The dependency may receive up to 1,000 concurrent requests.

Each instance is making decisions based on its own observations. The aggregate behavior is not automatically coordinated.

Local adaptive concurrency is often sufficient for protecting individual instances and reacting to local conditions.

But strict global dependency quotas may require a shared dispatcher, centralized coordination, or provider-side quota enforcement.

Do not confuse concurrency with connection limits

An HTTP transport's connection pool and an application's concurrency limiter protect different resources.

A request may hold an application permit while waiting for a connection. Conversely, HTTP/2 can multiplex multiple requests over one connection.

Configure both based on the actual workload.

9. Testing Adaptive Concurrency

Adaptive algorithms should be tested as control systems, not only as ordinary utility functions.

At minimum, test these behaviors:

  • The initial concurrency limit is respected.
  • Requests are rejected when the current limit is reached.
  • Permits are released exactly once.
  • Successful low-latency windows allow gradual growth.
  • Rising latency causes the limit to decrease.
  • Overload signals trigger a decrease.
  • The limit never exceeds its configured maximum.
  • The limit never falls below its configured minimum.
  • Concurrent acquisitions are race-safe.
  • Insufficient sample windows do not trigger premature changes.

Run the race detector:

go test -race ./...

Also consider deterministic algorithm tests.

Instead of using real HTTP requests and sleeping for arbitrary durations, separate the control algorithm from the admission mechanism.

Feed known latency samples into the controller and verify the resulting limit.

For example:

Baseline: 40ms

Window 1: 42ms → increase
Window 2: 45ms → increase
Window 3: 120ms → decrease
Window 4: 130ms → decrease
Window 5: 45ms → gradual recovery

This makes algorithm behavior easier to reproduce and debug.

Finally, run load tests with changing dependency latency.

A useful test should simulate:

  1. A healthy dependency.
  2. Gradually increasing latency.
  3. Sudden overload.
  4. Partial recovery.
  5. A complete dependency outage.

Measure throughput, p95/p99 latency, rejection rate, and concurrency limit changes.

The goal is not simply to maximize throughput.

The goal is to maintain useful throughput without allowing latency and queueing to grow uncontrollably.

10. Observability

An adaptive limiter introduces a new operational component.

You need visibility into how it makes decisions.

Useful metrics include:

Metric Type Purpose
adaptive_concurrency_limit Gauge Current concurrency ceiling
adaptive_inflight_requests Gauge Active requests
adaptive_request_latency_seconds Histogram Observed dependency latency
adaptive_rejected_total Counter Requests rejected at admission
adaptive_limit_increase_total Counter Limit increase events
adaptive_limit_decrease_total Counter Limit decrease events
adaptive_baseline_latency_seconds Gauge Estimated unloaded latency

These metrics help answer important questions:

  • Is the limiter constantly operating at its maximum?
  • Is the concurrency limit frequently decreasing?
  • Is the dependency latency increasing?
  • Are requests being rejected before reaching the dependency?
  • Is the limiter recovering too slowly?

A particularly useful dashboard plots three signals together:

  1. Current concurrency limit
  2. In-flight requests
  3. Dependency latency

Looking at them independently can hide the relationship between capacity and latency.

Avoid high-cardinality labels such as raw URLs, user IDs, and request IDs.

11. When Should You Use Adaptive Concurrency?

Adaptive concurrency is not necessary for every service.

A fixed limit is often the better choice when:

  • Dependency capacity is stable and well understood.
  • Traffic patterns are predictable.
  • The service has low request volume.
  • The cost of an adaptive control loop is not justified.
  • A simple semaphore already provides sufficient protection.

Adaptive concurrency becomes more attractive when:

  • Dependency capacity changes frequently.
  • Traffic is bursty or unpredictable.
  • Services scale horizontally.
  • Latency is a reliable indicator of queueing.
  • Manual concurrency tuning is difficult.
  • You need to protect dependencies before they start rejecting requests.

Start with a fixed limit if it is sufficient. Introduce adaptive behavior when operational evidence shows that static configuration is becoming a limitation.

Conclusion

A fixed concurrency limit assumes that system capacity is relatively predictable.

In distributed systems, that assumption does not always hold.

Dependencies slow down, traffic changes, instances scale, and resource availability evolves.

Adaptive concurrency provides a feedback loop that adjusts the amount of work allowed in flight based on observed latency and failure signals.

In Go, the core mechanism is straightforward: track active requests, collect latency samples, estimate congestion, and adjust the concurrency ceiling.

The difficult part is not implementing a semaphore.

It is building a stable controller that reacts to real overload without constantly oscillating or making incorrect decisions from noisy measurements.

Don't just limit how much work your service can handle. Let it learn when it should slow down.
