title: With JavaScript off our dark site renders white, and there is no noscript tag on any of its 72 pages
description:
Ask our homepage for its opening tag:

curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/ | grep -o '<html[^>]*>'
# <html data-dpl-id="dpl_..." lang="en">

No class. The <body> that follows it carries two font variables and font-sans antialiased, and no class either. Nothing in the document we serve says this site is dark.

The dark palette is a class in the stylesheet:

:root { --background: 0 0% 100%; --foreground: 222.2 84% 4.9%; }
.dark { --background: 0 0%  9%;  --foreground: 0 0% 98%;      }

next-themes is configured with defaultTheme: "dark" and attribute: "class", and it works by injecting a small blocking script into the head. That script reads localStorage, picks a theme, and sets the class on the documentElement before first paint. With JavaScript enabled there is no flash: the class is there before anything is painted, which is exactly what the script is for.

With JavaScript off, the class never arrives. No class means :root, and :root holds a white background and near-black text. Our dark marketing site renders as a light one, in a palette nobody has looked at in months.

There is one more mismatch stacked on top. The theme colour is a static meta tag:

<meta name="theme-color" content="#171717"/>

That is the dark background, hardcoded, served to everybody. So in the no-JavaScript case, a mobile browser paints its address bar in near black and the page underneath it white.

No noscript, anywhere

I pulled all 72 URLs from the sitemap and counted:

pages fetched              72
<noscript> elements         0
<form> elements             0

Zero of either. The second number is not a bug, it is where the forms are: every form on this site is on /login, /signup, /forgot-password or the password reset page, and those four are deliberately not in the sitemap. The 72 pages we ask Google to rank are documents with links on them.

Which is the nice part of this story. A page of prose with links does not need JavaScript, and 70 of the 72 are static HTML on a CDN. The parts that break without it are smaller than I expected, and more specific.

The five links that are not in the markup

The header has a Resources menu. Here is everything inside the <header> on the homepage, in the HTML:

/           PubTrivia
/features   Features
/solutions  Solutions
/pricing    Pricing
/login      Sign in
/signup     Get started

Six links, and one <button aria-haspopup="menu" aria-expanded="false"> whose five items, Guides, Questions, Compare, Tools and the FAQ, appear nowhere in the document. They are built by the dropdown component when it opens, which is to say by JavaScript. grep Guides against the header markup returns nothing.

So with JavaScript off the header offers six destinations instead of eleven. The site is saved by its own footer, which lists 20 links as plain anchors on every page, including all four clusters the menu was hiding. That is luck rather than design: nobody chose the footer as the no-JavaScript fallback, it just happens to be a list of links.

Sign-in works. Being told you failed does not.

This surprised me. The login form in the served HTML:

<form action="" encType="multipart/form-data" method="POST">
  <input type="hidden" name="$ACTION_ID_00c6919073..." />

That is Next.js encoding a server action for the no-JavaScript path. The form is a real POST to the current URL with the action id in a hidden field, so a browser with scripting disabled can submit it, and the server runs the same action and issues the same redirect. Sign-in is progressively enhanced, and not one line of this app asked for that.

The error path is not. A failed sign-in sets a message in the action's returned state, and the only thing that renders it is a toast fired from an effect. Effects need JavaScript. With scripting off, a wrong password gives you the form again with nothing on it: no banner, no inline message, no change at all.

That is worth a moment, because it is the general shape of the problem. The framework gave us progressive enhancement for the hard half, the mutation, and we gave it away on the easy half by choosing a rendering mechanism, the toast, that only exists on the client.

Three of our four tools are furniture

The four free tools under /tools are client components. Their controls are server rendered, so they are visibly there, and none of them is inside a <form>:

page                    buttons  inputs  selects  forms
team-name-generator           8       0        0      0
scoresheet-generator          2       4        0      0
qr-code-generator             2       2        0      0
round-planner                 8       9        6      0

Those are whole-page counts, so a couple of the buttons are the header's own menu trigger. Either way: with JavaScript off, 15 inputs, 6 selects and the best part of 20 buttons have nothing to submit to. The QR code is drawn in the browser, the scoresheet PDF is generated in the browser, the planner's arithmetic runs in the browser.

Except one. The team name generator server renders its whole corpus:

curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/tools/team-name-generator \
  | grep -o '<li[^>]*>[^<]\{3,60\}</li>' | wc -l
# 111

110 names and one instruction. The button that draws six of them at random does not work, but every name it could ever draw is already in the document, so the tool that needs JavaScript least is the only one of the four that survives without it.

What I would change, in order

  1. Put the class in the layout. <html lang="en" className="dark"> makes the served document state its own theme. next-themes then overrides it for the handful of people who picked something else, and the no-JavaScript case is correct instead of inverted. One line.
  2. Render the menu items. Five anchors in the markup, hidden with CSS and revealed by the component, costs nothing and means the header is a list of links before it is a widget.
  3. Render form errors in the HTML. The toast can stay. The message should also be on the page, next to the field, where it survives both a disabled script engine and a second identical failure.

A <noscript> block is the thing I am least interested in adding. Telling somebody their browser is wrong is not a fallback.

Check it yourself

In Chrome, open DevTools, press Command-Shift-P, run "Disable JavaScript", and reload pub-trivia.app. The page comes back white. Open the header's Resources menu: nothing happens. Scroll to the footer: every link is still there.

Then go to pub-trivia.app/login with scripting still off, submit an email that does not exist, and watch the page tell you precisely nothing.

title: Anchor security checklist: 16 checks before your Solana audit
description:
Anchor turns account validation into declarations, which removes whole classes of bugs. But Anchor only checks what you tell it to check. Run these 16 checks on any Anchor program before sending it to an auditor. This list is preparation for an audit, not a replacement for one.

Accounts and signers

  • [ ] Use Signer for every account that must authorize the instruction. A plain account or UncheckedAccount is not checked for a signature.
  • [ ] Tie stored authorities to the signer with has_one or an explicit constraint, for example #[account(mut, has_one = authority)].
  • [ ] Justify every UncheckedAccount and AccountInfo: validate owner, key or data yourself.
  • [ ] Prevent the same account being passed twice into two mutable slots, for example from.key() != to.key().

PDAs and initialization

  • [ ] Validate PDAs with seeds and bump in the account constraint, and store the canonical bump.
  • [ ] Design seeds so users cannot collide: include the user or the parent account.
  • [ ] Avoid init_if_needed unless you have a reason, and check it cannot reset balances or owners.
  • [ ] Close accounts with the close constraint instead of draining lamports by hand.

Tokens and CPIs

  • [ ] Constrain token accounts by mint and authority (token::mint, token::authority or associated token constraints).
  • [ ] Use Program<> or Interface<> types for programs you call, so the program ID is checked.
  • [ ] Decide on Token-2022 support explicitly and review extensions such as transfer fees and transfer hooks.
  • [ ] Scope PDA signer seeds tightly: separate PDAs for vaults, authorities and configuration.

Math, upgrades and testing

  • [ ] Use checked arithmetic and keep overflow-checks = true in the release profile. Round in the protocol's favour.
  • [ ] Validate remaining_accounts by hand: Anchor does no validation on them.
  • [ ] Plan account layout changes before upgrades: version accounts or reserve space, use realloc carefully.
  • [ ] Test the failure paths (wrong signer, wrong mint, duplicated accounts, zero and maximum amounts) and fuzz the rest, for example with Trident.

What to do with the results

Fix what you find, write down the invariants your program must always keep, and send both to your auditor with a frozen commit. Before mainnet, also go through the pre-launch checklist in the GitHub repository below.

Full article with FAQ: https://orivions.com/blog/anchor-security-checklist
All three checklists on GitHub: https://github.com/JakeMalarczyk/solana-security-checklists

title: Solana pre-launch security checklist: 15 checks before mainnet
description:
An audit is necessary, but it is not a launch plan. Many incidents have nothing to do with a clever exploit in the program: a leaked upgrade key, a compromised frontend, an unaudited last-minute change, or nobody noticing a drain for hours. These 15 checks cover what usually goes wrong around the code. Assign a name to each line: a check without an owner is a check nobody did.

Keys and authorities

  • [ ] 1. Move the program upgrade authority to a multisig (signers on separate devices, never the development agency).
  • [ ] 2. Decide your upgrade policy in public: upgradeable, behind a timelock or immutable.
  • [ ] 3. Review token mint and freeze authorities. Revoke what you do not need, document what you keep and why.
  • [ ] 4. Audit every admin instruction (fees, pauses, parameters, withdrawals): right signer, controlled by the multisig.

Code and deployment

  • [ ] 5. Deploy exactly the audited commit. Anything changed after the audit is unaudited code.
  • [ ] 6. Publish a verifiable build so anyone can confirm the on-chain program matches your public source.
  • [ ] 7. Test failure paths: wrong signer, wrong owner, duplicated accounts, zero and maximum amounts.
  • [ ] 8. Rehearse the launch on devnet with production settings, including multisig steps.
  • [ ] 9. Plan account migrations before you need them: reserve space or version your accounts.

Operations

  • [ ] 10. Set up monitoring and alerts for unusual outflows, failed transaction spikes, admin instructions and authority changes.
  • [ ] 11. Use more than one RPC provider, with a fallback and rate limits.
  • [ ] 12. Protect the frontend and domain: registrar lock, two-factor authentication, restricted deploy access, pinned third-party scripts.
  • [ ] 13. Write an incident response plan: who can pause, how they reach each other, who talks to users, which partners to call.
  • [ ] 14. Launch a bug bounty sized relative to the funds at risk.
  • [ ] 15. Cap risk at launch with deposit caps or rate limits, and raise them as confidence grows.

Verify that deployed code matches the audited code

Build the audited commit and compare it with the program on chain using solana-verify get-program-hash and solana-verify verify-from-repo. Once remote verification succeeds, explorers such as Solana Explorer, SolanaFM and Solscan show the program as verified.

Full article with FAQ: https://orivions.com/blog/solana-pre-launch-security-checklist
All three checklists on GitHub: https://github.com/JakeMalarczyk/solana-security-checklists

title: You Already Use the Cloud Every Day (Without Noticing)
description:
TL;DR: You use the cloud every time an app on your screen reaches a program running on someone else’s machines: browser mail, photo backup, Netflix streams out of Amazon data centers, and games rendered on remote servers all follow one arrangement, a thin client on your side and a shared back end on theirs.

  • Software as a service means the provider’s application runs on their infrastructure and you reach it through a browser; the NIST definition’s own example is web-based email, and Gmail alone has 1.8 billion users.
  • Netflix has run on Amazon Web Services since a 2008 database corruption stopped its DVD shipments for three days; cloud games go further and render on the server entirely.
  • Of the 2010s product shelf, Mailchimp, QuickBooks Online, Box, Toggl Track and Evernote are alive; Mozy shut down in 2019 and Outright in 2022, while their categories carried on.
  • On the phone, you use the cloud through mobile cloud computing: heavy computation moves off the device, paid for in frequent transmissions and wide-area latency.

You use the cloud before breakfast and again on the couch, and almost none of it looks like “cloud computing”: mail loads in a browser tab, a photo you took yesterday is already on your tablet, a show is queued for tonight. This article is the written half of the Whiteboard Architect episode You Already Use the Cloud Every Day (Even If You Never Noticed); it follows the same chapters with the same fact-checks, and it checks the 2010s product lists that most tutorials still repeat.

What it means to use the cloud

Strip the marketing off “the cloud” and one arrangement is left: the provider’s application runs on the provider’s infrastructure, and you reach it through a thin client, usually a browser. That is software as a service, and it is the shape almost every example in this article takes. The NIST definition of cloud computing makes the point with its own worked example: web-based email, the case where the mail program, the storage and the search index all live somewhere else and your browser holds only the front end.

Gmail is that example at full scale. It opened on April 1, 2004, and is now the largest email service worldwide, with 1.8 billion users. Nothing about your inbox runs on your machine: the spam filter, the archive and every attachment sit in Google’s data centers, and any browser that reaches them gets the same inbox. Some services cannot exist otherwise. Apple’s Siri and Google’s Gemini assistant need cloud computing to answer at all, and the browser editors, Microsoft 365 for the web and Google Docs, run their editing surfaces on top of cloud storage, so two people can type in one document from two continents.

Is webmail really cloud computing, or just a website?

It is cloud computing under the definition the field uses. NIST’s service model for SaaS puts the consumer inside applications the provider runs on cloud infrastructure, reached from a client device through a thin client, with the browser as the usual one, and it names web-based email as the example on purpose: mail was the first application most people met that kept its state entirely off their own hardware. Before webmail, “checking your email” meant a program on your disk, a mailbox file it downloaded into, and an ISP server that only held mail until you collected it. Webmail moved the mailbox, the program and the index onto the provider’s machines at once, which is why the definition’s authors reached for it. A modern webmail account also shows the trade you make: your mail is searchable from any device because it is not on any of them, and the provider can read it at rest as easily as you can read it in a browser.

Your day is a cloud tour

Run through an ordinary day and the back ends stack up, mostly unseen. In the morning, photos: Google Photos, launched in 2015, backs your photos up to its cloud service, which makes them accessible from all of your devices. The picture you took on your phone at breakfast is on your laptop before you sit down, with no cable and no copy step, because the library lives on Google’s machines and your devices are all windows onto it.

Board 3 of 13: the day tour, back ends invisible.

In the evening, streaming. Netflix looks like a delivery service for video, and it is, but it runs on Amazon Web Services, and the reason is dated: corruption took out Netflix’s own database in August 2008, DVD shipments stopped for three days, and the company responded by moving its data to AWS and announcing plans to migrate all of its infrastructure there. The app on your TV and the recommendation engine that picked the show are clients of someone else’s data center.

Music and games finish the tour. Spotify has streamed since 2008 on a freemium model, and the catalog it searches holds over 100 million songs; none of them are stored on your phone. Cloud gaming takes the idea one step further, because the work that moves is the game itself: Xbox Cloud Gaming opened for Game Pass Ultimate subscribers in 2020; Nvidia’s GeForce Now, from the same year, does the identical job. Both render the game on distant servers, and your screen receives nothing but video.

How does cloud gaming differ from streaming a film?

The video stream looks the same; the input path is what makes it a different service. When you stream a film, the server plays a finished file at you. When you play a game through Xbox Cloud Gaming or GeForce Now, every button press leaves your device, travels to a remote server, gets applied to a running game, and comes back as changed video, so the round trip sits between your thumb and the next frame. Xbox describes the service as a link between your device and remote server hardware, and the servers themselves are Xbox-based blades, real console hardware stacked in a data center. GeForce Now does the same job from data-center servers of its own and delivers the game through streaming video. That round trip is also why the arrangement lives or dies on network quality: the compute is never the bottleneck, and the radio link usually is.

What did Netflix’s 2008 database corruption actually change?

The incident was small and the decision built on it was not. In August 2008, corruption in Netflix’s database left the company unable to ship DVDs for three days, which at the time was the core of the business. The fix the company chose was to move its data to Amazon Web Services, and it then announced plans to migrate all of its infrastructure there. First, the migration went to a direct competitor in streaming video, which is the kind of decision you only make when the engineering argument is overwhelming. Second, the pattern it produced is now the default: a video service whose own machines hold none of the product, running its whole operation on rented infrastructure, exactly the arrangement this article keeps finding in every category. When a service you use daily turns out to live on somebody else’s computers, Netflix’s three-day outage in 2008 is one of the reasons that arrangement became normal.

The 2010s product shelf, checked

Cloud product lists age badly, and the list most tutorials still quote comes from the 2010s. Checked item by item, it splits into survivors, renames and closures.

Product What it does Where it is now
Mailchimp Email campaign platform Alive; Intuit has owned it since 2021
QuickBooks Online Cloud accounting covering invoicing, expenses, bank reconciliation, reporting and bookkeeping Alive; Intuit’s cloud accounting service
Box File storage for businesses, reachable from any connected device Alive
Toggl Track Time tracking in the browser, from Tallinn, Estonia Alive
Evernote Notes sync against a master copy kept on Evernote’s servers; reads text inside images Alive
Facebook Posting text, photos and multimedia Alive
Google Apps for Business Gmail, Drive and the Docs editors, edited together in real time Renamed G Suite in September 2016, then Google Workspace in October 2020
Twitter Following accounts, posts landing in your feed Renamed X, announced July 22, 2023; following and feeds work as before
Mozy Online backup pioneer Closed in 2019 after passing EMC, Dell, then Carbonite
Outright Small-business bookkeeping Bought by GoDaddy in 2012, discontinued June 18, 2022

In that table the products expired and the categories did not. Mail became a browser window, files became a synced folder, notes became a master copy with devices attached, feeds and music became streams. Every one of those categories settled into one shape, a phone or browser front end over a shared back end in a data center, and when one product closed, another product in the same category took the traffic. When a new app arrives, ask which back end its window opens onto.

Which 2010s cloud products closed, and what replaced them?

The two closures on the list, Mozy in 2019 and Outright in 2022, both arrived through acquisition rather than as independent failures. Mozy, founded in 2005 as an online backup pioneer, passed through EMC in 2007, Dell in 2016 and Carbonite in 2018, and Carbonite shut it down in 2019, folding its customers into Carbonite’s own backup service. Outright, a small-business bookkeeping site, went to GoDaddy in 2012 in a deal worth around twenty million dollars, was rebranded as GoDaddy Online Bookkeeping, and discontinued on June 18, 2022. Neither closure hurt the category it served: online backup is now a large market with several established providers, and cloud accounting is dominated by the very products still listed as survivors above, QuickBooks Online among them. The renames tell the milder half of the story. Google Apps for Business turned into G Suite on September 29, 2016, and then Google Workspace on October 6, 2020, with the same real-time collaborative editors underneath both renames. The rebrand to X was announced on July 22, 2023, and the mechanics its users cared about, following accounts and reading a feed, carried straight through it.

Inside the phone: mobile cloud computing

The phone in your pocket is the cloud client you notice least, because the heavy work it shows you often happens somewhere else. Mobile cloud computing, usually shortened to MCC, is the named field behind that: Wikipedia’s lead sentence says it combines cloud computing with mobile computing, with the computing work running on cloud hardware, not on the handset. A phone with tight limits on power, storage and energy borrows a server’s resources and still runs applications that would swamp it.

The mechanism has a name too: computation offloading. Heavy, resource-hungry tasks get transferred to the cloud, which sidesteps the device’s ceilings on compute, storage and energy, so jobs finish faster and the battery lasts longer. Your phone does not need a fast chip for a task it never runs; it needs a radio and a screen.

MCC runs on frequent transmissions between device and cloud, and long wide-area network latency is one of the field’s named challenges: push the work off the phone, and the radio link is what decides how the app feels. The same challenge list continues past latency, and it is worth reading in the deep dive below, because the entries named there, lock-in among them, are the ones your own apps live with.

Board 8 of 13: the phone borrows cloud muscle.

What problems does mobile cloud computing still have?

The field’s own challenge list is longer than the latency entry. The sourced list names computation offloading itself, mobility management, seamless connectivity, long WAN latency, the device’s energy constraint, vendor lock-in and data lock-in, then security and privacy, and it notes the field still lacks a reference architecture for heterogeneous environments, meaning no settled blueprint for mixing devices, radios and clouds that all differ. One entry deserves unpacking, because tutorials garble it. What some articles call live VM migration is, in the sourced literature, VM-migration-based offloading: the application gets packaged inside a virtual machine, and that VM is migrated to the cloud, where it runs. When researchers diagram MCC’s resources, the taxonomy the field cites lists three resource shapes, hybrids on top: distant immobile clouds, the conventional cloud; proximate immobile entities, machines near you that stay put; and proximate mobile entities, the devices that move. A fourth bucket, distant mobile entities, appears in some summaries but does not verify, so this article leaves it out. For everyday use, two entries from the list matter most: lock-in, because your offloaded work runs on infrastructure you neither own nor can easily leave, and security and privacy, because the data crosses a network you do not control.

Gotchas: dead platforms and overclaims

Three checks apply before you repeat any of it. First, date any product or platform list before you repeat it. The episode’s own source lists five smartphone platforms; three no longer exist: Symbian, whose support ended on January 1, 2014, after the last Nokia Symbian phone shipped in 2012; Windows Mobile, which Windows Phone replaced in 2010 before its own deprecation; and BlackBerry 10, end of life on January 4, 2022, after BlackBerry pivoted to Android. The survivors are Android, the most used operating system worldwide for phones since 2011, and Apple’s iOS. Repeat that list without dates and three of your five platform recommendations point at dead products.

Second, do not repeat the claim that “the phone is just a display.” What the sources support is narrower than that: processing moves off the device, and the device keeps its storage, its apps and its data. Offloading is a decision each app makes, and the borrowed computation is repaid in transmissions and wide-area latency, which is why a phone that renders nothing locally can still feel slow on a weak radio.

Third, know what you are locked into. The MCC challenge list names vendor and data lock-in alongside security and privacy, and by now the reason is concrete: you use the cloud for mail, photos, notes, feeds, music and games, and a handful of other companies hold the back ends. Knowing which company holds which category is the practical version of that caution, and this article’s day tour is the inventory.

In short

You use the cloud every day, from mail in a browser at breakfast to a game rendered on a remote server at night, and the arrangement repeats: your device is a thin client, the application and its data live on a provider’s machines, and the provider’s data center does the work your device displays. The 2010s product shelf expired while its categories carried on, so the question that travels is which back end a new app is a window onto. On the phone, mobile cloud computing trades local computation for transmissions, a good deal until the radio link is the bottleneck.

Board 13 of 13: the recap, sticky note and all.

Continue learning

  • Containers vs Virtual Machines: The Problem Docker Solves: the sibling Whiteboard Architect companion, on the unit of software that makes those provider back ends reproducible.
  • How Spotify Works: the music stop of the day tour, opened up, from its audio CDN to the nightly run that refreshes recommendations.
  • Cloud Computing Interview Questions for 2026: the definitions from this episode in the form interviewers actually ask them.

Disclosure: this article was drafted with AI from the script of my video lesson, then checked against its sources before publishing.

This lesson first appeared on iqraa.tech.

More whiteboard lessons on the Whiteboard Architect YouTube channel.

title: 13.3 per cent of our HTML is class attributes, 324 distinct strings doing it, and the proof tailwind-merge works is a class that is missing
description:
The whole class handling layer of our app is five lines:

import { type ClassValue, clsx } from "clsx"
import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge"

export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
  return twMerge(clsx(inputs))
}

That is lib/utils.ts, the file every shadcn/ui install drops in, used at 54 call sites across 18 files here. Two dependencies, one function, zero configuration. I wanted to know what it actually produces in production, so I fetched all 72 URLs from pub-trivia.app/sitemap.xml and counted.

What 72 pages of Tailwind weigh 

HTML, all 72 pages      5,081,245 bytes
class attributes           13,379
bytes inside them         674,045   (13.3% of the HTML)
distinct class strings        324

Thirteen per cent of every byte we serve is the contents of class. That number sounds like an indictment and is not, because of the third line: 13,379 attributes are built from 324 unique strings. The homepage is 150,475 bytes raw and 16,824 over the wire with brotli, a ratio of about nine to one, and repeated identical strings are exactly what a compressor is for. The cost of utility classes in the HTML is real and it is mostly paid by the compressor, not by the user.

The repetition is heavier than I expected:

1,380  text-sm text-muted-foreground hover:text-foreground transition-colors
  727  text-muted-foreground leading-relaxed
  471  min-w-0
  462  flex gap-4 py-4

The top one is a footer link. It appears about 19 times per page, because that is how many links the footer carries: the nav columns, the three legal pages, Sign in, Sign up, Dashboard. One styling decision, 1,380 copies, 95 KB of the 674.

The missing class

Here is the longest class attribute on the site, 379 characters, from the team name generator page:

inline-flex items-center justify-center whitespace-nowrap text-sm font-medium
ring-offset-background transition-colors focus-visible:outline-none
focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring focus-visible:ring-offset-2
disabled:pointer-events-none disabled:opacity-50 border border-input
bg-background hover:bg-accent hover:text-accent-foreground h-10 px-4 py-2
mt-4 rounded-full

Now here is the start of the base string in components/ui/button.tsx, which every one of those elements is built from:

const buttonVariants = cva(
  "inline-flex items-center justify-center whitespace-nowrap rounded-md text-sm font-medium ..."
)

rounded-md is the fourth class in the base. It is not in the rendered output. The call site asked for rounded-full, and twMerge worked out that the two belong to the same group and dropped the loser before React ever saw it.

That is the only visible evidence tailwind-merge does anything, and you have to look for an absence to find it. So I counted the absences. Of the 13,379 class attributes, 222 are built from the button base, in 10 distinct strings:

occurrences  pages  rounded-md survived?
         69     69  no   (ghost, h-9, rounded-full)
         69     69  no   (default, h-9, rounded-full)
         67     67  no   (default, h-11, rounded-full)
          6      1  yes  (outline, h-9, rounded-md)
          4      2  no
          2      2  no
          2      1  no
          1      1  no
          1      1  no
          1      1  no

Nine of the ten strings had a class removed. 216 of the 222 rendered buttons on this site are the shadcn base with its own border radius deleted, because somebody decided a while ago that our buttons are pills. Without twMerge, every one of those elements would carry both rounded-md and rounded-full, and which one won would depend on the order Tailwind happened to emit them in the stylesheet, not on the order you wrote them in the JSX. That is the actual argument for the dependency: not tidiness, but that CSS specificity does not care about your intent and twMerge does.

The variant inventory

Four files use class-variance-authority: the button, the badge, the toast and the label. The button declares the most:

variants   default, destructive, outline, secondary, ghost, link
sizes      default, sm, lg, icon

Across 75 <Button> call sites, variant="outline" appears 38 times, ghost 8, secondary 3, destructive 2, and link never. Not once. The link variant exists in the file because it exists in the shadcn registry, and this app renders text links as links.

My favourite of the four is the label:

const labelVariants = cva(
  "text-sm font-medium leading-none peer-disabled:cursor-not-allowed peer-disabled:opacity-70"
)

No second argument. No variants, no sizes, no defaults. cva() here is a function call whose only job is to return the string it was given, wrapped so that VariantProps<typeof labelVariants> can be spread into the component's prop type, where it contributes no props. It is the shape of the pattern with the pattern removed, kept because deleting it would make this file different from the upstream one.

One more thing I found in the config

components.json, which shadcn's CLI reads, records the choices made when the components were installed:

"tailwind": { "baseColor": "slate", "cssVariables": true }

Our dark palette in app/globals.css is written in HSL and every colour in it has a hue of zero:

.dark { --background: 0 0% 9%; --foreground: 0 0% 98%; --border: 0 0% 18%; }

Pure neutral grey. Slate is a blue grey, hue 222. The config says one thing and the stylesheet says another, and the stylesheet wins, because baseColor is only read when the CLI generates a new component. It is a record of a decision that was later reversed, in a file nobody reads again after the first install.

Check it yourself 

curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/tools/team-name-generator \
  | grep -o 'class="inline-flex[^"]*"' | head -1

Look for rounded-md in the output. It is not there. Then look at the shadcn button source, where it is.

And if you want to see the footer links that account for 1,380 of those class attributes, they are at the bottom of every page, including pub-trivia.app/features and pub-trivia.app/pricing.

The lesson I took from the measurement: the two dependencies behind cn() do nothing you can see, one of them earns its place 216 times on the page you are looking at, and the other one is mostly there to let you write cn(a, b && c) without a join. Both are load bearing. Neither is visible. That is a slightly uncomfortable thing to say about 13.3 per cent of your bytes.

title: Show HN: OmniDiff – Opensource, super fast, content aware Git difftool, in Rust
description:
I have been researching what the ultimate diff tool would look like, based on actual diffs in open source repositories.

OmniDiff can diff: code (25 languages), config, images, PDFs, archives, cursors, fonts...

It's fast. It can diff C++ files of tens of thousands of lines in under 100ms, on a 2023 ThinkPad T14s.

It's open source. AGPLv3.

It's based on real diffs. I looked at the 7400 repositories that are listed in Gentoo packages, sampled 2000 diffs and solved them manually to get a good understanding of what is needed, before putting together the diff pipelines for each content type. Incidentally, this also forms the basis of the CI pipeline, so the robustness of the codebase is quite high.

I'm still developing it. It's v0.3.0 at this time. But I have been using it daily as my git difftool for months now, and it works well.

AI Disclosure: Yes, I do use AI. No, I do not vibecode.

title: Prop 45 in California could be hiding a loophole for data centers
description: A high-stakes California ballot measure pitched as a fast track for "essential" infrastructure could wind up giving data center developers a loophole to evade public scrutiny, environmental advocates warn. title: We Moved Our Depot Cameras to the Cloud and Every Scanner Waited Behind the Video
description:
Each of our depots has between twelve and twenty security cameras. Until last year they recorded to a box in the comms room at each site, and when those boxes reached the end of their support we replaced them with a cloud video service. No hardware to maintain, footage available from anywhere, and a security manager who could review an incident at any depot without driving to it. On paper it was a good decision, and I still think it was.

We rolled it out to twelve depots over a month. Within a week of each one going live, the depot started complaining that its handheld scanners were slow. A scan that normally confirmed in under a second was taking three or four. Label printing slowed down, and calls on the depot phones began to break up.

Most of those depots are on business broadband with a download speed of about eighty megabits and an upload of twenty. That had always been plenty, because almost everything a depot did pulled data down to it: screens, updates, label files, email. The cameras changed the direction. Sixteen cameras each streaming about two megabits, without a pause, all day and all night, needed thirty two megabits going up a line that could carry twenty.

The line filled, and once the upload is full everything else waits behind it, including the small acknowledgements a scanner sends back for every transaction. The download was nearly idle the whole time, which is why our monitoring, which watched download use, showed nothing wrong.

The cameras now record continuously to storage built into each camera, and only send footage to the cloud when motion is detected or someone asks to see it. That cut the upload by about nine tenths. Depot traffic is prioritised over video on every router, and the five largest depots have moved to fibre lines with the same speed in both directions. Our monitoring now reports upload use separately at every site.

Nobody had asked which way the data would flow, because for fifteen years the answer had always been the same.

Moving a service to the cloud can turn a site from something that receives data into something that sends it, and most of our lines had been bought for the other direction.

– Serguey Shinder

title: Stop Hardcoding Color Variants. Relative Color Syntax Does It.
description:
The PR comment was two words: "wrong blue." Not a bug report, not a reproduction — a designer scrolling through a staging build, stopping on the "Upgrade" button's hover state, and flagging it because something about it felt off against the rest of the rebrand that had shipped two weeks earlier.

They were right, and it took longer than it should have to find out why. The button's resting color matched the new brand blue exactly — that token had been updated the day the rebrand landed. Its hover color was still the old brand blue, darkened. Nobody had touched it, because nobody remembered it existed.

Five variables, one of which actually gets updated

Open almost any design system's color file and you'll find the same shape: one brand color, and a handful of hand-picked variants sitting next to it that all look derived but are actually just... more hex codes.

:root {
  --brand: #3b6fd6;
  --brand-hover: #2f58ab;      /* "a bit darker" — picked by eye, once */
  --brand-active: #244289;     /* "darker still" — same deal */
  --brand-border: #6e92e1;     /* "a bit lighter" */
  --brand-tint: rgba(59, 111, 214, 0.08); /* "faint background wash" */
}

Every one of those four extra values is somebody's good-faith attempt, at some point in the past, to eyeball a lighter or darker or more-transparent version of --brand. They're not wrong on day one. The problem shows up the day --brand changes and the other four don't — because CSS has no idea they were ever related. To the engine, --brand-hover isn't "darker --brand." It's just a string that starts with #2f58ab, full stop.

The "obvious" fix is discipline: a comment reminding whoever edits --brand to also update the other four, or a design-tokens build step that regenerates them from a single source before CSS ever sees them. Both work, right up until the person making a one-line brand tweak six months from now doesn't know the build step exists, or skims past the comment. Discipline that depends on nobody being in a hurry isn't a fix — it's a bet, and the rebrand PR is the bet losing.

The variables were never the problem — storing the relationship was

Here's the reframe that matters: --brand-hover was never really an independent color. It was always a function of --brand — "darker, same hue." --brand-tint was always "the same color, 8% opaque." The relationship was real and well understood by whoever first picked those hex codes. What got lost was that the relationship lived in a person's head for thirty seconds and then evaporated, leaving only its one-time output behind, frozen in a stylesheet forever.

What you actually want is for CSS to store the relationship, not just a snapshot of what it once produced — and that's a genuinely new category of thing for CSS to express. For most of CSS's life, a color value was a dead end: #3b6fd6 tells the renderer what to paint, but nothing about where it came from or how to get a cousin of it. color-mix() loosened that slightly — you can blend two colors — but blending two colors isn't the shape of this problem. You don't have two brand colors to mix; you have one color, and you want its lightness turned down a notch while everything else about it stays put.

Before you keep reading: what would you even call the CSS feature that lets you say "same color, just darker"? It's a fair question, because until relatively recently there wasn't a clean answer.

Relative color syntax: read a color's own channels back out

Relative color syntax lets a color function take another color as input and expose that color's own channels as variables you can do math on, right there in the function call:

:root {
  --brand: #3b6fd6;

  /* "same hue and chroma as --brand, just darker" */
  --brand-hover:  oklch(from var(--brand) calc(l - 0.12) c h);
  --brand-active: oklch(from var(--brand) calc(l - 0.20) c h);

  /* "same color, lighter, for a border" */
  --brand-border: oklch(from var(--brand) calc(l + 0.15) c h);

  /* "same color, 8% opaque" */
  --brand-tint: oklch(from var(--brand) l c h / 8%);
}

Read the oklch(from var(--brand) ...) part literally: "take --brand, convert it to OKLCH, and give me three variables back — l for lightness, c for chroma, h for hue." Whatever you write after that is just CSS math on those three numbers (plus an optional alpha after the slash). calc(l - 0.12) means "this color's own lightness, minus 0.12" — not a hardcoded lightness value, a relationship to whatever --brand happens to be right now.

Change --brand to a rebrand's new blue, or swap it entirely for a dark-mode theme, and every line below it recomputes. There's no second hex code to forget, because there is no second hex code — --brand-hover isn't stored anywhere; it's derived, every time the browser needs it, from the one variable a human actually edits.

This isn't OKLCH-only, either. rgb(), hsl(), and color() all support the same from syntax, exposing whichever channels that color space naturally has:

/* rgb()'s own channels: r, g, b (0–255), alpha */
.badge { background: rgb(from var(--brand) r g b / 15%); }

/* hsl()'s own channels: h, s, l, alpha — s and l come back as plain
   numbers (0-100), not percentages, so the math below uses 10, not 10% */
.link:hover { color: hsl(from var(--brand) h s calc(l - 10)); }

OKLCH is usually the better pick for lightness math specifically, because it's designed so that "lightness" tracks perceived brightness consistently across hues — nudging l down by the same amount darkens a yellow and a blue by roughly the same perceived amount. Nudge hsl()'s l channel the same way and the result can feel inconsistent hue to hue, because HSL's lightness was never built to model human perception in the first place.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The one sharp edge: clamp your math

calc(l - 0.12) is honest math, which means it'll happily produce a number outside the range that makes sense. Pick a brand color that's already quite dark, subtract 0.20 from its lightness, and l can go negative — which isn't a color error so much as a "this doesn't mean anything" result, rendered as whatever the browser decides black looks like.

The fix is the same clamp() you'd reach for anywhere else in CSS, wrapped around the channel math:

--brand-hover: oklch(from var(--brand) clamp(0, calc(l - 0.12), 1) c h);

That one change makes the derivation safe for any input color, including ones your design system doesn't control yet — a user-customizable accent color, say, or a brand color read from a CMS. Skip the clamp and the formula only works for colors in roughly the lightness range you tested it against, which defeats a good chunk of the point: a derivation that only works for some inputs is just a more elaborate hardcoded value.

Is this safe to ship, or is it another flag-gated preview?

Safe to ship — but the rollout order isn't what you'd guess. Safari 16.4 (March 2023) was the earliest browser with something, but it was a partial pass at an older draft of the spec with real parsing bugs; that implementation was later replaced, not extended. Chrome and Firefox did the work of actually matching the final spec through 2024 (Firefox in Firefox 128, July 2024), and Safari didn't catch up — bug fixes included — until Safari 18 in September 2024. So for the exact forms used above, Safari was last to ship the behavior this post describes, not first. Either way, that was over two years ago: by now every major evergreen browser has unprefixed, unflagged, spec-correct support, and there's no realistic "but what about X" objection left to raise for a typical modern browser matrix. If your project still has to support browsers from before that window, the fallback is simple and honest: keep writing literal hex variants for those browsers, and layer the relative syntax on top for everyone else — it degrades to "the hardcoded value you already had," not to a broken page.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

The bug wasn't really "someone forgot to update a hex code." It was that the stylesheet never had anywhere to put the fact that --brand-hover meant "darker --brand" — so that knowledge lived in a person's memory instead, with exactly the shelf life you'd expect. Relative color syntax isn't a shorter way to write the same five hex codes. It's a way to stop writing four of them at all.

Where does your own color system still keep that kind of relationship in a comment instead of in the CSS itself?

title: You're Writing Mouse and Touch Handlers. Pointer Events Does Both.
description:
The demo went great. Drag the card, it follows your cursor, drop it anywhere — smooth, on every laptop in the room. Then someone picks up their phone, drags a thumb across the card — and nothing happens. No movement, no feedback, like the card isn't even listening.

You didn't write a buggy drag handler. You wrote half of one.

box.addEventListener('mousedown', (e) => {
  dragging = true;
  offsetX = e.clientX - box.offsetLeft;
  offsetY = e.clientY - box.offsetTop;
});

box.addEventListener('mousemove', (e) => {
  if (!dragging) return;
  box.style.left = `${e.clientX - offsetX}px`;
  box.style.top = `${e.clientY - offsetY}px`;
});

box.addEventListener('mouseup', () => {
  dragging = false;
});

This is correct, tested, and works on exactly one category of device.

The "fix" that just adds a second bug

The instinct is to bolt on touch support: copy the three listeners, swap mouse* for touch*, convert e.clientX/e.clientY to e.touches[0].clientX/e.touches[0].clientY, and call it done.

box.addEventListener('touchstart', (e) => {
  dragging = true;
  const t = e.touches[0];
  offsetX = t.clientX - box.offsetLeft;
  offsetY = t.clientY - box.offsetTop;
});

box.addEventListener('touchmove', (e) => {
  if (!dragging) return;
  const t = e.touches[0];
  box.style.left = `${t.clientX - offsetX}px`;
  box.style.top = `${t.clientY - offsetY}px`;
});

box.addEventListener('touchend', () => {
  dragging = false;
});

Now it works on a phone, in isolation. But you're maintaining the same drag math twice, in two event systems that don't agree on anything — touch events report an array of active touch points (because a screen can have more than one finger on it at once), mouse events report exactly one cursor. And both paths share a bug neither the original mouse-only version nor this touch-added version ever fixed: drag fast enough, or past the edge of the box, and the "end" event stops firing, leaving the card stuck mid-drag.

That's not a mobile-only bug. It's the same bug on both input types, because mousemove and touchmove share the same design flaw.

Why the drag "sticks"

mousemove only fires on the element it's attached to while the cursor is actually over that element — it's hit-tested live, every event. Flick the mouse fast enough, or drag past the edge of the box, and the browser stops delivering mousemove (and eventually mouseup) there at all; those events go to whatever's now under the cursor instead, which has no idea your drag was in progress. The card is left believing it's still being dragged, because the one event that was supposed to tell it otherwise was never sent to it.

Touch has a related but distinct failure mode: if the OS decides your drag gesture is actually a scroll or a browser gesture (a mid-drag notification pull-down, a back-swipe), it can cancel the touch sequence outright, firing touchcancel instead of touchend — and if you only wired a touchend listener because "that's how the drag ends," it never gets a chance to clean up.

Two input systems, two different reasons, one shared symptom: dragging gets stuck true, because neither API gives the element a reliable way to say "tell me how this interaction ends, every time, no matter what."

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

One event model, built to not have this bug

The Pointer Events API replaces mouse* and touch* with a single stream — pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup, pointercancel — that fires identically whether the input is a mouse, a finger, or a stylus. You write it once:

box.addEventListener('pointerdown', (e) => {
  dragging = true;
  offsetX = e.clientX - box.offsetLeft;
  offsetY = e.clientY - box.offsetTop;
  box.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
});

box.addEventListener('pointermove', (e) => {
  if (!dragging) return;
  box.style.left = `${e.clientX - offsetX}px`;
  box.style.top = `${e.clientY - offsetY}px`;
});

function endDrag() {
  dragging = false;
}

box.addEventListener('pointerup', endDrag);
box.addEventListener('pointercancel', endDrag);

Three things changed, and each one closes a specific gap the old code had:

  1. One set of listeners, no branching on input type. e.clientX/e.clientY work the same for mouse, touch, and pen — no more reading e.touches[0] on one path and e.clientX directly on the other.
  2. box.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId) is the actual fix for the stuck-drag bug. Once an element captures a pointer, every event for that pointer — including pointermove and pointerup — keeps firing on that element, even when the pointer moves outside its boundaries or off the page entirely. The box can't lose track of the drag because the browser is now routing events to it directly, not based on where the pointer happens to be.
  3. pointercancel is the cleanup path the old code didn't have. It fires when the browser interrupts the interaction for its own reasons — a touch sequence hijacked into a system gesture, for instance. Listening for it alongside pointerup means dragging always gets reset, instead of staying stuck on true forever.

One more line matters for touch devices specifically: add touch-action: none in CSS on the draggable element.

.box { touch-action: none; }

Without it, the browser's own scroll/zoom gesture handling can still compete with your drag for the same touch input before your JavaScript gets a say. touch-action: none tells the browser "this element handles its own gestures," which is exactly what you're asking Pointer Events to do.

What you get that mouse-plus-touch never gave you

  • e.pointerType tells you "mouse", "touch", or "pen" when you actually need to branch — for a stylus app that wants pressure (e.pressure) and tilt (e.tiltX/e.tiltY) only from a pen, for instance. You branch when the behavior should differ, not just to read the coordinates.
  • Multi-touch stays sane. Each contact point gets its own pointerId, so a canvas handling two fingers at once tracks two independent pointer streams instead of indexing into a shifting touches array.
  • It's been safe to rely on for years. Pointer Events shipped in every major engine — Safari was the last holdout and added support in 2019 — so this isn't a progressive-enhancement decision anymore; it's the default way to handle pointing input.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Pointer Events quietly fixes two separate bugs with one API. The "nothing happens on a phone" bug goes away because there's only one set of listeners to remember to wire up, not two. And the "drag freezes mid-gesture" bug — the one that was hiding in the mouse-only version from the start, then rode along into the touch-added version unchanged — goes away because setPointerCapture() finally gives the element what neither old API did: a guarantee that it keeps hearing from the pointer until the interaction is actually over.

Go find the component in your codebase with a mousedown handler and a near-identical touchstart handler sitting a few lines apart. How much of that duplication would pointerdown alone have deleted? Tell me what you find.

title: Seventeen words for eight database values, and a dot that only pulses when work is actually running
description:
Nakodo does its work while nobody is watching: it reads a brand's website, finds creators and businesses who fit, writes the first email and handles the replies. The how it works page is the public version of that. The private version is a screen that has to answer, in about four words per row, what is happening right now.

That answer lives in three small files totalling 106 lines. None of them touches the database, and none of the words in them is stored anywhere.

Eight values, seventeen words

The conversation table has a status column and a closed_reason column. Both are plain text with a TypeScript enum over them, because this app has no pgEnum anywhere. The words a human reads are a pair of records:

export const STATUS_LABELS: Record<OutreachStatus, string> = {
  drafting: "Writing",
  review: "To approve",
  queued: "Scheduled",
  contacted: "Contacted",
  talking: "Talking",
  needs_you: "Needs you",
  handed_off: "Introduced",
  closed: "Closed",
};

export const CLOSED_LABELS: Record<OutreachClosedReason, string> = {
  no_reply: "No reply",
  declined: "Declined",
  opted_out: "Opted out",
  bounced: "Address bounced",
  complained: "Marked as spam",
  cancelled: "Stopped",
  suppressed: "Can't be contacted",
  no_email: "No email",
  failed: "Failed",
};

export function threadLabel(t: { status: OutreachStatus; closedReason: OutreachClosedReason | null }): string {
  return t.status === "closed" && t.closedReason ? CLOSED_LABELS[t.closedReason] : STATUS_LABELS[t.status];
}

Seventeen words for what the machine thinks of as eight states, and the reason is the three-line function at the bottom. A closed conversation that knows why it closed never shows the word "Closed", because "Closed" is a true statement that answers nothing. "No reply" and "Marked as spam" and "Opted out" are the same state to a scheduler and three completely different things to the person whose brand sent the email: one is normal, one is a deliverability problem, and one is a person telling you to stop.

Typing both as Record<Union, string> rather than Record<string, string> is the whole safety net. Add a ninth closed reason to the schema and the build fails in this file until it has a word. That is the cheapest possible test for "no state reaches the UI without a human writing a sentence for it".

Five views over eight statuses

The same file groups them, in display order, with satisfies doing the checking:

export const THREAD_VIEWS = [
  { key: "attention", label: "Needs you", statuses: ["needs_you", "review"] },
  { key: "active", label: "In progress", statuses: ["drafting", "queued", "contacted", "talking"] },
  { key: "introduced", label: "Introduced", statuses: ["handed_off"] },
  { key: "closed", label: "Closed", statuses: ["closed"] },
  { key: "all", label: "All", statuses: null },
] as const satisfies readonly { key: string; label: string; statuses: readonly OutreachStatus[] | null }[];
export type ThreadView = (typeof THREAD_VIEWS)[number]["key"];

as const satisfies is the pairing I reach for most often in this codebase: as const keeps the literal types, so ThreadView is "attention" | "active" | ... derived from the data, and satisfies checks every status string against the schema union without widening anything. A plain type annotation would have given me string for the keys and no union to derive.

Two things in that array are decisions rather than data. "Needs you" collapses two statuses, because a first email waiting for approval and a reply the model would not answer are both "a human has to look", and a product that makes you learn the difference before you can act has failed at the one job. And statuses: null for "All" means absent rather than a list of everything, so adding a status never silently drops it out of the one view that promises completeness.

The badge is not a traffic light 

// A conversation's state. Introduced is the one stamp; anything waiting on
// the brand is ochre-outlined; work in flight is plain ink; closed stays
// quiet. No traffic-light colours.
const TONE: Record<OutreachStatus, string> = {
  drafting: "border-dashed border-ink-400 text-muted-foreground",
  review: "border-mark-outline text-foreground",
  queued: "border-dashed border-foreground/50 text-foreground",
  contacted: "border-foreground/60 text-foreground",
  talking: "border-cyano-700 text-cyano-800 dark:border-cyano-300 dark:text-cyano-200",
  needs_you: "border-mark-outline bg-mark/30 text-foreground",
  handed_off: "border-cyano-700 bg-cyano-50 text-cyano-800 dark:border-cyano-300 dark:bg-cyano-950 dark:text-cyano-200",
  closed: "border-ink-400/60 text-muted-foreground",
};

Eight tones, two hues, and no red or green anywhere. The brand document is blunt about why: ochre is "used only for attention marks", so the moment a colour means "danger" or "success" it stops meaning "look here". A closed conversation is not a failure, a reply is not an alarm, and three quarters of the states are neither good nor bad, so the axis the colours actually encode is "does this need you", not "is this going well".

The signals are also doubled on purpose. Only two states get a fill, filled is "waiting on you" and "introduced", and the attention dot used elsewhere carries its own text:

export function AttentionMark({ label, className }: { label: string; className?: string }) {
  return (
    <span className={cn("inline-flex", className)}>
      <span className="inline-block size-[7px] rounded-full border border-mark-outline bg-mark" aria-hidden="true" />
      <span className="sr-only">{label}</span>
    </span>
  );
}

Seven pixels of ochre and a screen-reader sentence. The dot is decoration, the sr-only text is the information, which is the only arrangement that survives WCAG 1.4.1 and a colourblind reader.

The dot that tells you whether anything is happening

A campaign gets a different treatment: one word and a dot, where the dot answers a question the word cannot.

export function LiveDot({ live, label, className }: { live: boolean; label: string; className?: string }) {
  return (
    <span className={cn("inline-flex items-center gap-1.5 text-[13px] text-muted-foreground", className)}>
      <span className="relative inline-flex size-1.5">
        {live && (
          <span className="absolute inset-0 rounded-full bg-cyano-600 motion-safe:animate-[live-pulse_2.4s_ease-out_infinite]" />
        )}
        <span className={cn("relative inline-flex size-1.5 rounded-full", live ? "bg-cyano-600" : "bg-ink-400")} />
      </span>
      <span className={cn(live && "text-foreground")}>{label}</span>
    </span>
  );
}

A solid dot with a pulsing copy behind it, motion-safe so it is a static dot for anybody who has asked for less motion, and the label's own colour as the second channel so the state is legible without the animation.

And then the function that decides live, which is 32 lines and the densest product thinking in the app:

// Campaign status as a live dot and a word. Only running work pulses: a
// campaign with only its emails paused is still searching, and one with
// enough good leads waiting may still be checking what it found.
export function campaignStatus(
  status: string,
  working: boolean,
  pauseMode: PauseMode | null = null,
  enoughLeads = false,
): { live: boolean; label: string } {
  switch (status) {
    case "researching":
      return { live: true, label: "Reading website" };
    case "draft":
      return { live: false, label: "Brief to review" };
    case "active":
      if (enoughLeads) return { live: working, label: "Enough leads" };
      return working ? { live: true, label: "Surveying" } : { live: false, label: "Up to date" };
    case "paused":
      return pauseMode === "emails"
        ? { live: working, label: "Emails paused" }
        : pauseMode === "finding"
          ? { live: false, label: "Finding paused" }
          : { live: false, label: "Paused" };
    case "failed":
      return { live: false, label: "Research failed" };
    default:
      return { live: false, label: status };
  }
}

Four inputs, nine possible labels, six database statuses. The two branches worth staring at are the ones that return live: working rather than true or false.

"Emails paused" with a pulsing dot looks wrong until you remember that pause here has a reason column and three answers: a campaign can be paused for sending while it carries on searching. The word tells you what is stopped, the dot tells you that something is still moving. If live were hardcoded false for every paused campaign, the screen would claim nothing is happening while jobs run, and the next thing that appears would be unexplained.

"Up to date" versus "Surveying" is the same trick with the opposite emphasis: same status, same plan, and the only difference is whether any job is open right now. "Idle" would have been a worse word, because nothing is wrong, and "Active" would have been a worse word, because nothing is happening.

The branch that should not exist 

default:
  return { live: false, label: status };

That line prints a raw database value into the interface. active instead of "Surveying", in lower case, in a dot label. It exists because the first parameter is typed status: string and not the schema's union, so TypeScript cannot see that the switch is exhaustive and insists on a return.

Printing the raw value is the right behaviour for a branch that should be unreachable: it does not crash, it does not say "Unknown", and anybody who sees active on a card knows immediately that a status was added and this file was not told. But the honest fix is one word in the signature. Narrow status to the union, the switch becomes exhaustive, the default goes away, and the next person to add a status gets a compile error in the same place the conversation labels already give them one.

Three files, 106 lines, 26 words, and not one of them in the database. The nearest public equivalent is the glossary, where the same discipline is applied to the words customers meet before they sign up: one definition each, written once, and never two names for one thing.

title: Weekend Apple deals: Apple Watch Ultra 4, AirTag 2, MacBooks, AirPods, more

title: Website Hacked Incident Response Guide
description:
A website hacked incident response plan is crucial to minimize damage and prevent further exploitation, ensuring a swift restoration of your online presence with a structured approach.

Key Takeaways

  • Identify and contain the breach to prevent further damage
  • Conduct a thorough analysis to determine the attack vector and scope
  • Remove malware and backdoors, and restore from backups
  • Implement additional security measures to prevent future incidents
  • Continuously monitor for suspicious activity and update website hacked incident response plans

How Does Website Hacked Incident Response Work?

Website hacked incident response involves a structured approach to contain and eradicate the breach, including identifying the attack vector, removing malware, and restoring from backups, as outlined in the NIST Special Publication 800-61. This approach ensures that the breach is contained and the website is restored to a secure state.

Why Is Website Hacked Incident Response Critical?

Website hacked incident response is critical because it helps contain the breach, reduces downtime, and minimizes the impact on your business and reputation, ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements and reducing the risk of future incidents, which is a key aspect of website hacked incident response. A well-planned incident response plan can help mitigate the effects of a breach and prevent further exploitation.

What Are the Steps in a Website Hacked Incident Response Plan?

A website hacked incident response plan involves several steps, including initial response, analysis, containment, erasure, restoration, and lessons learned, all of which are essential components of a comprehensive website hacked incident response strategy. These steps help ensure that the breach is contained and the website is restored to a secure state.

How Can You Implement a Website Hacked Incident Response Plan?

Implementing a website hacked incident response plan involves developing a structured approach to incident response, including identifying potential vulnerabilities, implementing additional security measures, and continuously monitoring for suspicious activity, as recommended by the OWASP Incident Response Guide. This approach helps ensure that the website is secure and that any potential breaches are detected and responded to quickly.

What Tools Can You Use for Website Hacked Incident Response?

Several tools can be used for website hacked incident response, including security information and event management (SIEM) systems, intrusion detection systems (IDS), and web application firewalls (WAF), which can help detect and prevent potential threats, and are an essential part of a website hacked incident response plan. These tools can help identify potential vulnerabilities and detect suspicious activity, allowing for quick response and mitigation.

How Can You Prevent Future Website Hacks?

Preventing future website hacks involves implementing additional security measures, such as multi-factor authentication (MFA), regularly updating and patching software, and continuously monitoring for suspicious activity, which are all critical components of a website hacked incident response plan. These measures can help reduce the risk of a breach and prevent further exploitation.

What Are the Best Practices for Website Hacked Incident Response?

Best practices for website hacked incident response include having a comprehensive incident response plan in place, continuously monitoring for suspicious activity, and implementing additional security measures to prevent future incidents, all of which are essential for effective website hacked incident response. These best practices can help ensure that the website is secure and that any potential breaches are detected and responded to quickly.

How Can You Restore Your Website After a Hack?

Restoring your website after a hack involves removing malware and backdoors, restoring from backups, and implementing additional security measures to prevent future incidents, which is a critical step in the website hacked incident response process. This step helps ensure that the website is restored to a secure state and that any potential vulnerabilities are addressed.

What Are the Common Challenges in Website Hacked Incident Response?

Common challenges in website hacked incident response include identifying the attack vector, containing the breach, and restoring the website to a secure state, all of which require a structured approach and specialized tools. These challenges can be addressed by implementing a comprehensive incident response plan and using specialized tools, such as SIEM systems and WAFs.

How Can You Ensure Effective Website Hacked Incident Response?

Ensuring effective website hacked incident response involves having a comprehensive incident response plan in place, continuously monitoring for suspicious activity, and implementing additional security measures to prevent future incidents, all of which are essential for effective website hacked incident response. This approach helps ensure that the website is secure and that any potential breaches are detected and responded to quickly.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the common signs of a website hack?

Common signs of a website hack include unusual login attempts, suspicious files or directories, and unexpected changes to website content or behavior, which can indicate a potential security breach. Monitoring for these signs can help detect potential breaches.

How can I prevent my website from getting hacked?

Preventing your website from getting hacked involves keeping software up-to-date, using strong passwords, and implementing additional security measures such as MFA and a WAF, which can help reduce the risk of a security breach. Regularly updating and patching software can also help prevent breaches.

What should I do if I've already been hacked?

If you've already been hacked, act immediately to contain the breach, conduct an analysis, and implement a step-by-step website hacked incident response plan to minimize damage and prevent further exploitation, and consider seeking guidance from the US-CERT Incident Response Guide, which provides comprehensive guidance on incident response.
