title: Prism: Building a Zero-Chromium Browser Engine in Rust — Architecture, Internals, and Implementation
description:
Modern web browsers are among the most intricate software systems in computing history. A functional browser cannot simply display markup; it must ingest network streams, tokenize and parse non-standard HTML, construct a mutable object tree, parse and cascade stylesheets, execute scripting runtimes, compute geometric layouts across multiple rendering paradigms, rasterize primitives into pixel buffers, register spatial interactions, and maintain strict process-level security boundaries.

The vast majority of modern browsers bypass this complexity by wrapping existing engines, predominantly Google’s Chromium codebase or occasionally Apple’s WebKit. Prism takes an entirely different route.

Prism is an independent, modular browser engine written from scratch in Rust. Rather than embedding an existing rendering core, Prism implements its own decoupled pipelines for resource handling, document object model creation, style calculation, display-list generation, software rasterization, and extension sandboxing. Where external technologies are integrated — such as Boa for ECMAScript interpretation and Wasmtime for WebAssembly extension containment — they are isolated within custom coordination layers rather than serving as black-box rendering backends.

The browser engine recently crossed a critical threshold: bootstrapping an end-to-end rendering loop on a live production website (Hacker News), successfully loading network dependencies, building a sanitized DOM, hydrating JavaScript structures, calculating multi-column table layout, and flushing an 800 by 600 framebuffer with hundreds of painted glyphs.

This document breaks down the internal architecture of Prism, tracing how each distinct subsystem is constructed, how data transitions across boundary layers, and where the current limitations lie.

  1. Browser Shell and Application Architecture The browser shell acts as the entry point and supervisor process for Prism. It handles high-level application lifecycles, tab orchestration, navigation events, and the display output interface.

At startup, the shell initializes tab managers and coordinates thread barriers between window events and engine processing tasks. For native display targets, Prism interfaces with the winit crate to manage platform windows, surface creation, and system event loops.

A central engineering requirement for Prism is environment resilience. When executed inside environments devoid of an active display server or Wayland/X11 socket — such as a remote development container or automated Linux CI pipeline — the native compositor path fails gracefully. Prism automatically falls back to an embedded HTTP-based frame-streaming server bound locally to port 3000. This fallback mechanism ensures that the engine can execute its full layout and rasterization sequence headlessly, piping the generated framebuffer bytes directly to a web interface for visual inspection and regression testing without requiring virtual framebuffers like Xvfb.

  1. Network and Resource Loading Pipeline The rendering pipeline cannot operate on isolated markup. A modern web document requires synchronous and asynchronous retrieval of external assets, including stylesheets, external scripts, and vector or raster imagery.

Prism’s resource subsystem is built on top of native Rust asynchronous networking primitives. When a navigation event is dispatched by the shell:

The root document is retrieved, following any HTTP redirects to resolve the final canonical base URL.
The tokenizer and parser run a discovery pass to extract resource dependencies linked via standard tags (, , <img src="...">).<br> Relative resource paths are canonicalized against the base navigation URL.<br> Assets are fetched concurrently through an internal asset-preloading broker.<br> Asset resolution operates symmetrically across HTML attributes and CSS property declarations. Because styles frequently declare resources via url() tokens (such as background graphics), the resource loader maintains an internal registry keyed by both original relative paths and canonical absolute URLs. When layout and rasterization stages demand image bytes, they resolve them directly from this memory-backed asset pool without blocking on redundant network I/O.</p> <ol> <li>HTML Tokenization The entry point of the document pipeline resides in components/dom/src/tokenizer.rs. This component transforms raw incoming UTF-8 byte streams into discrete syntactic tokens without intermediate allocations where possible.</li> </ol> <p>The tokenizer operates via an incremental next_token() interface, supporting both push-based streaming and batch processing over whole documents. It defines a rigorous token set covering:</p> <p>Start tags, capturing the element name, self-closing state, and raw key-value attribute pairs.<br> End tags, marking structural termination.<br> Character data, separating printable text runs from whitespace.<br> Comments, extracting developer annotations without polluting the render path.<br> Doctype nodes, identifying strict or quirks-mode document declarations.<br> End-of-file indicators, terminating state machines cleanly.<br> A critical design challenge in HTML tokenization is the handling of CDATA, raw text, and entity references. HTML is notoriously forgiving to malformed input, necessitating extensive handling for quoted and unquoted attributes, numeric entities, and named character escapes.</p> <p>Crucially, Prism implements strict RAWTEXT state management for <script> and <style> blocks. Within these elements, content cannot be tokenized as standard element markup, because characters such as < and > often represent comparison operators or JavaScript logic rather than tag boundaries. The tokenizer switches into a raw-text capture mode until it encounters a matching closing tag sequence, preserving nested code strings for the script and CSS parsers.</p> <ol> <li>HTML Parser and Stack-Based DOM Construction Tokens generated by the tokenizer are fed directly into the hierarchical document parser located in components/dom/src/parser.rs.</li> </ol> <p>The parser utilizes an explicit open-element stack to reconstruct tree hierarchies. When a start-tag token arrives, the parser instantiates a node, links it to the current stack head as its child, and pushes the new node onto the stack. When a matching end-tag token arrives, nodes are popped until the matching scope is closed.</p> <p>Because real-world markup frequently deviates from valid XML structures, the parser implements standard HTML structural recovery heuristics:</p> <p>Implicit Paragraph Termination: Opening a block-level element inside an active <p> tag automatically generates an implicit closing token for the paragraph.<br> List and Definition Management: Consecutive <li>, <dt>, and <dd> items auto-close preceding siblings without requiring explicit closing tags.<br> Implicit Table Wrapping: The HTML specification requires that <tr> elements residing directly within a <table> must be wrapped inside an implicit <tbody> element. Prism checks table child states and dynamically synthesizes <tbody> nodes on the fly. Real-world sites such as Hacker News depend heavily on this implicit wrapping behavior to ensure table geometries do not collapse.<br> Beyond full-document parsing, the subsystem provides a specialized fragment-parsing path. This allows the JavaScript engine to mutate innerHTML properties dynamically, running partial markup strings through the parser and grafting the resulting subtrees into the live DOM tree.</p> <ol> <li>The DOM Engine Prism’s in-memory document model resides in components/dom/src/lib.rs. It serves as the primary source of truth across the engine, interconnecting the HTML parser, the JavaScript execution context, the CSS style resolver, and the layout tree.</li> </ol> <p>The tree consists of element nodes, text nodes, and comment nodes. Element nodes preserve tag identities, parent pointers, sequential sibling chains, and key-value attribute maps.</p> <p>To avoid stack-overflow crashes when processing deeply nested real-world DOM trees, all critical DOM traversal, node searching, serialization, and mutation functions are implemented iteratively using heap-allocated work stacks rather than naive recursive functions.</p> <p>Prism also introduces a distinct pre-render sanitization phase. To prevent scripts and metadata from bloating layout passes, the engine runs an iterative filter that strips non-visual elements (such as <script>, <style>, <noscript>, and <template>) from the layout tree. Because asset references are harvested during initial parsing, stripping these nodes prior to layout allows the layout engine to focus strictly on structural and typographic nodes.</p> <ol> <li>JavaScript Integration and the INIX Subsystem JavaScript integration in Prism is driven by the INIX subsystem, which pairs the document model with the Boa ECMAScript runtime.</li> </ol> <p>DOM Hydration<br> A browser must bridge the memory model of its native systems language (Rust) with the object model of its scripting language. Prism solves this through an explicit hydration bridge. Rather than wrapping every single Rust node in a heavy FFI envelope during initial parse, the Rust DOM serializes its structural tree into an optimized payload. The INIX runtime consumes this payload on the JavaScript side, iteratively constructing mirrored DOM objects, populating attributes, and linking parent-child associations.</p> <p>The Mutation Interception Bridge<br> To handle dynamic client-side applications, INIX implements an event-driven mutation bridge. When scripts execute operations such as modifying element.className, mutating attributes, or appending children via appendChild, INIX catches these operations through monkey-patched prototypes and native hooks. It serializes mutation records containing:</p> <p>The unique target node identifier.<br> The property or attribute mutated.<br> The updated payload value.<br> Structural metadata for tree rearrangements.<br> These mutation batches are queued and dispatched back across the native bridge into Rust, updating the primary DOM tree and signaling the layout engine that a restyle or reflow is required.</p> <p>Parallel Custom Runtime Path<br> Alongside the integrated Boa engine, the Prism repository contains an independent, custom-built JavaScript toolchain located in src/lexer.rs, src/parser.rs, and src/compiler.rs. This subsystem consists of a hand-written JavaScript lexer, an AST parser, and an experimental bytecode compiler paired with a stack-based virtual machine. While Boa handles active webpage execution today, this internal path represents Prism’s long-term research vector toward a fully unified, zero-dependency browser runtime.</p> <ol> <li>CSS Parsing and Style Resolution The CSS architecture is split cleanly between declaration parsing and selector application.</li> </ol> <p>The stylesheet parser in components/css/src/lib.rs consumes raw CSS text, stripping comments, tokenizing at-rules, and breaking style blocks into structured rulesets containing selector lists and declaration maps.</p> <p>Style resolution takes place in components/layout/src/style.rs. Here, Prism matches the parsed rules against the live DOM tree. The selector engine contains representation logic for:</p> <p>Type selectors (element tag names).<br> ID selectors (#id).<br> Class selectors (.class).<br> Attribute matchers.<br> Combinators (parent, descendant, sibling chains).<br> The resolver constructs an intermediate StyledNode tree, applying computed values and computing basic inheritance rules (such as propagating font colors and typography defaults down from the <body> element).</p> <p>Current Limitations in the Style Engine<br> Diagnostics from production tests reveal that selector matching and cascade resolution remain incomplete. For instance, during the execution of Hacker News, the main content wrapper <table id="hnmain"> failed to receive its authored width rules (width=None), indicating that ID selector specificity weighting or attribute-matching lookups occasionally miss matches during tree walks. Correcting cascade precedence and selector specificity scoring remains an active development priority.</p> <ol> <li>The Layout Engine The layout engine in components/layout/src/lib.rs translates the abstract StyledNode tree into concrete Cartesian geometry, assigning each element an (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) coordinate along with definitive width and height bounding boxes.</li> </ol> <p>Intrinsic Display Roles<br> Prism maps HTML elements to their default structural layout behaviors:</p> <p>Block Elements: Elements like <div> expand horizontally to fill their parent container and stack vertically.<br> Inline Elements: Elements like <span> flow horizontally along the active text line, wrapping when container boundaries are reached.<br> Table Elements: Specialized display types (table, tbody, thead, tfoot, tr, td, th) enter the dedicated table constraint-solving pipeline.<br> Replaced / Inline-Block Elements: Form controls (<input>) and visual embeds (<img>) maintain intrinsic dimensions while participating in horizontal inline flows.<br> Non-Rendered Elements: Tags such as <br> emit explicit line-break commands without generating visual boxes.<br> Table Layout Resolution<br> Because legacy and data-dense websites rely on complex table formatting, Prism includes a dedicated table formatting context. The table solver operates in multi-pass stages:</p> <p>It inspects all child rows and aggregates total column counts across all row fragments.<br> It executes cell measurement passes, calculating both the minimum intrinsic content width (the smallest width an element can adopt without text overflowing) and preferred content width for every cell.<br> It resolves column widths proportionally against available space while respecting explicit author-specified dimension constraints.<br> During execution on Hacker News, Prism successfully identified the main three-column news layout, resolving column widths of approximately 31.3 pixels for ranking indices, 24.3 pixels for voting arrows, and 740.4 pixels for headline/metadata content. This multi-pass algorithm prevents columns from collapsing into equal-width divisions that ruin page readability.</p> <ol> <li>Graphics Engine and Display-List Rasterization Prism enforces a strict architectural boundary between layout computation and pixel manipulation. Located in components/graphics/src/lib.rs, the graphics subsystem does not allow the layout engine to paint directly into memory. Instead, layout generates an immutable, serializable Display List.</li> </ol> <p>Write on Medium<br> A display list is an ordered sequence of draw commands:</p> <p>Solid rectangles for element backgrounds.<br> Styled boundaries for borders.<br> Image blits containing raw pixel buffers and target coordinates.<br> Text commands carrying font handles, glyph positions, and color values.<br> The rasterizer processes these commands sequentially, drawing into an 800 by 600 32-bit RGBA software framebuffer.</p> <p>The Text Rendering Pipeline<br> Prism integrates a CSS-aware glyph rasterizer capable of measuring font metrics and applying typographic rules. While the engine successfully painted 844 glyphs across 420 text commands in production tests, text rendering remains the most visually critical issue.</p> <p>Because coordinate offsets between inline text boxes, containing block wrappers, and rasterizer baseline expectations can drift, glyphs currently exhibit coordinate displacement and overlapping text baselines. The display list is correctly generating rendering commands, but the geometry calculation within the inline layout context requires baseline alignment fixes.</p> <ol> <li>Spatial Hit Testing A browser must map hardware input events back to the appropriate DOM nodes. Prism generates a unified hit-test spatial index during the layout pass.</li> </ol> <p>Each layout object emits an axis-aligned bounding box tied to its originating node reference. During navigation and rendering of Hacker News, Prism generated 1,190 distinct hit-test bounding boxes. This spatial index allows pointer coordinates to be queried against the tree in logarithmic time, providing the foundation for click handling, link navigation, hover states, and future form-control inputs.</p> <ol> <li>Extension Sandboxing via WebAssembly Rather than implementing extensions via high-privilege JavaScript bindings that risk browser security, Prism features an extension sandbox built on Wasmtime.</li> </ol> <p>Extensions are compiled to WebAssembly targets and executed inside deterministic memory sandboxes. The host environment provides a strictly defined native shim interface, limiting extension operations to designated system calls while bounding computation via execution fuel.</p> <p>During live tests, Prism loaded and executed adblock_lite.wasm, an internal ad-blocking extension:</p> <p>The sandbox loaded the 734-byte binary.<br> It allocated an execution fuel budget of 10,000,000 instructions.<br> The extension consumed 159 fuel units, returning 9 active CSS and structural filtering rules targeting ad banners, tracking pixels, sponsored posts, and modal consent overlays.<br> These rules were injected into the layout engine’s rule list to suppress matching nodes before display lists were emitted.<br> This proves the feasibility of running isolated, memory-safe extensions natively within an independent engine core.</p> <ol> <li>The Aegis Security Pipeline Prism incorporates an internal security inspection gate called Aegis, situated directly between the network loader and the parsing pipelines.</li> </ol> <p>Aegis functions as a zero-trust payload verification boundary. Before fetched bytes are allowed to touch the HTML tokenizer or parser, the Aegis pipeline scans document streams, enforces content policies, validates resource origins, and ensures data payloads do not violate boundary constraints. In live testing runs, this clearance pipeline completed in approximately 38 microseconds, establishing an inline security verification layer that introduces near-zero latency to the content pipeline.</p> <ol> <li>Production Milestone: Loading Hacker News To prove the viability of its architecture, Prism was deployed against a live, external web destination: <a href="https://news.ycombinator.com">https://news.ycombinator.com</a>.</li> </ol> <p>The test verified that the browser could navigate the web, retrieve external HTML, download linked CSS (news.css), fetch and decode SVG/PNG image assets, sanitize DOM nodes, hydrate the JavaScript environment, fire its WASM ad blocker, resolve complex multi-column table dimensions, and rasterize a full 800 by 600 framebuffer containing 480,000 pixels.</p> <p>Pipeline Run Metrics<br> Viewport Geometry: 800 pixels wide by 600 pixels high.<br> Document Layout Height: 2,797.4 pixels of vertical content mapped.<br> Rasterized Layout Objects: 429 discrete layout elements.<br> Text Commands Executed: 420 draw calls.<br> Glyphs Processed: 844 individual characters shaped and rendered.<br> Painted Pixel Surface: 26,249 active foreground pixels rendered.<br> External Images Blitted: 2 assets loaded and painted.<br> Hit-Test Geometry: 1,190 interaction regions mapped.<br> Adblock Rules Injected: 9 structural suppression filters applied.<br> While the metrics confirm that data flows cleanly through the entire pipeline, the final rendering exposed the engine’s primary current limitations: text baselines frequently overlap due to inline cursor miscalculations, and certain CSS rules (such as #hnmain table widths) do not yet resolve correctly against the style cascade.</p> <ol> <li>Current Subsystem Status and Next Engineering Steps Prism has completed its proof-of-concept bootstrapping phase. The implementation status of the engine breaks down across its subsystems as follows:</li> </ol> <p>Browser Shell and Tab Orchestrator: Implemented and functional. Manages tabs and provides automatic fallback streaming over local HTTP when headless.<br> Network Pipeline: Functional. Concurrently fetches HTML, linked CSS stylesheets, external JavaScript, and image assets.<br> HTML Tokenizer and Parser: Implemented and functional. Supports streaming tokens, raw-text state isolation, and tree recovery including implicit table structures.<br> DOM Engine: Implemented and functional. Uses iterative traversal and sanitization mechanisms to prevent stack overflows.<br> INIX JavaScript Runtime: Functional for tested workflows. Uses Boa for ECMAScript compliance, supported by custom hydration and mutation interception layers.<br> Internal JavaScript Engine Path: Present. Standalone lexer, parser, compiler, and VM path implemented for research and future integration.<br> CSS Parser: Functional. Accurately extracts rulesets, properties, and values from stylesheets.<br> Style Cascade and Selector Engine: Incomplete. Structural tag matching functions, but ID/class specificity calculations and property inheritance need refinement.<br> Table Layout Engine: Functional. Computes minimum and preferred cell widths to generate accurate multi-column layouts.<br> Block and Inline Layout Engine: Partially functional. Block flows calculate correctly, but inline cursor tracking and text wrapping suffer from coordinate calculation issues.<br> Graphics Rasterizer: Functional. Translates display lists into memory framebuffers, drawing rectangles, borders, images, and text.<br> Hit-Testing Engine: Functional. Produces coordinate-indexed boundaries for mouse tracking and interaction.<br> Wasmtime Sandbox: Functional. Safely runs WebAssembly binaries with strict fuel budgets and native API bindings.<br> Aegis Security Gate: Integrated. Inspects incoming payloads with sub-millisecond execution times.<br> The Next Engineering Target<br> With the end-to-end rendering pipeline proven, development focus shifts away from adding high-level features and toward visual fidelity and layout correctness:</p> <p>Inline Cursor Correction: Refactor components/layout/src/lib.rs to ensure relative inline text coordinates correctly track cumulative parent offsets and baseline alignments.<br> Cascade and Specificity Rectification: Overhaul components/layout/src/style.rs so that ID selectors (#hnmain) and class selectors (.title, .subtext) take proper precedence over generic element styles.<br> Display-List Coordinate Validation: Audit the transformation path between layout box bounds and TextCommand execution in components/graphics/src/lib.rs to eliminate glyph scrambling.<br> Conclusion<br> Prism is an engineering effort to prove that a modern browser engine can still be built from the ground up without relying on the Chromium monoculture. By dividing the problem into modular, decoupled Rust crates — spanning tokenization, DOM engineering, style cascading, table mathematics, software rasterization, and WebAssembly sandboxing — the project establishes that building an independent web engine is not an impossible task.</p> <p>While substantial work remains before Prism can render arbitrary web applications with pixel-perfect standards compliance, the engine has moved past basic architectural theory. It parses real code, runs real logic, computes complex structural tables, and renders live web pages down to the pixel level through a fully self-authored pipeline.</p>

title: **One package for the whole life of a text.**
description:
One package for the whole life of a text.

Publishing a readable article usually means wiring three separate libraries: an editor to write in, a renderer to lay the text out, and something for audio if you bother. Each with its own API to learn and its own version to keep in sync.

editorkit keeps all three in one place. The editor is where you write. The article lays the text out — typography, tables, images. And a player reads it aloud, sentence by sentence, highlighting the sentence as it goes.

That last part is the least obvious. The audio is not a bolt-on: the same document that renders also speaks. One line of code gives you a complete article page, in React, Vue, Svelte or plain JS.

It is safe by default. No reader's text ever executes code, so an article cannot run a script on its page. Multilingual, with audio optional and provided by adapter — no provider imposed.

Licensed MPL-2.0. The live playground runs at lalter.org, source on GitHub.

title: In Cloud Security, Good Enough is Indistinguishable From Failure
description:
✓ Human-authored analysis; AI used for formatting and proofreading.

Cloud failures come from systems that are good enough until they aren't.

The IAM role was good enough for 18 months. Then someone discovered the trust chain it created. The S3 bucket policy was good enough until the VPC endpoint was removed and the condition clause failed silently. The security tooling was good enough. It detected 95% of individual misconfigurations. The 5% it missed were the compound paths where breaches happened.

Good enough is the most dangerous state a safety system can be in. Good enough: functioning well enough that nobody prioritizes replacing it, while silently accumulating the conditions for catastrophic failure.

In cloud systems, good enough safety is indistinguishable from failure that is just delayed. The delay makes it invisible. The failure makes it catastrophic.

The convergence pattern

Every product category goes through the same cycle. Many good enough tools → structural pressure → convergence into one integrated solution:

Domain Good enough era Convergent era
Mobile phones (1990s) Phone + MP3 player + GPS unit + wallet + pager + camera. Each "good enough" at its job. Smartphone subsumes all of them. Not by being better at any one — by being the integrated solution.
Browser plugins (2000s) Flash + RealPlayer + ActiveX + Java applets. Each solving one media problem. Native browser (HTML5/JS). The plugins disappeared not because they stopped working — because the integrated solution made them unnecessary.
Build automation Make + autoconf + custom shell scripts. Each solving one piece of the build. Integrated CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI). The scripts didn't break — they became unnecessary.
Configuration management SSH + custom scripts + tribal knowledge. Each "good enough" for its scope. IaC + GitOps. The scripts were still correct — but the integrated approach was structurally superior.
Cloud security (today) CSPM + SIEM + WAF + IaC scanners + OPA + dashboards. Each "good enough." (Convergence pending)

The pattern is the same every time. The good enough tools work. They work at the wrong level. The convergent solution subsumes them by solving the higher-order job.

The smartphone didn't have a better camera than a dedicated camera. It solved "capture and share a moment" better than camera + USB cable + computer + email. The job was higher-order than any individual tool addressed.

The most dangerous state

For most product categories, good enough is fine. A good enough MP3 player plays music adequately. The worst case: slightly worse audio quality.

For safety systems, good enough is structurally dangerous:

Non-safety system:
    "Good enough" → acceptable → stays acceptable → no problem

Safety system:
    "Good enough" → acceptable today → margin tested over years 
    → margin fails at an unpredictable moment → catastrophic

This is the temporal version of Lamport's safety/liveness distinction. A safety property must hold at ALL TIMES. A good enough safety margin will be tested by every possible configuration, composition and interaction continuously, for years. The margin that was good enough for the first 10,000 configurations meets configuration #10,001 and fails.

The three outages of Cloudflare, CrowdStrike, AWS are each a good enough margin that failed:

  • Cloudflare's feature-file validation was "good enough" until a file exceeded the size the proxy could handle
  • CrowdStrike's schema checking was "good enough" until a file had 20 fields instead of 21
  • AWS's plan versioning was "good enough" until a race condition applied a stale plan

Each system worked correctly for years. The transition from good enough to catastrophic was instant.

The job customers want

The cloud security industry has been selling MEANS:

"We scan!"     → a means, not a job
"We alert!"    → a means, not a job
"We block!"    → a means, not a job  
"We visualize attack paths!" → a means, not a job
"We auto-remediate!"         → a means, not a job

The job customers want:

"Operate distributed systems safely, continuously, and without surprise."

No customer wakes up wanting more scans, alerts, or dashboards. They want the job done: the system stays safe, continuously, without requiring constant human attention.

The means-vs-job distinction separates pre-convergence tools from convergent-era solutions. Pre-convergence tools sell means ("we scan 47 resource types!"). Convergent solutions deliver the job ("the invariant holds against every snapshot, deterministically, before deployment").

Once a credible job-fit product appears, customers switch, but because the new tool solves the job they were hiring the old tools to do.

Perfection

Perfect means: achieving the safety function with zero unnecessary harm.

Function Perfect direction
Safety Always enforced — not "mostly" or "usually"
Cost Only when needed — not running continuously if per-commit is sufficient
Latency Before damage — not after deployment, not after detection
Scope Smallest possible — not "scan everything always" but "evaluate what's changing"
Human effort Near zero — not "faster triage" but "no triage"
Recovery Reversible — not "auto-fix production" but "block the merge before it's irreversible"

Each row is a direction. The product moves toward each direction with every release. "Always enforced" is the limit. Currently, Stave enforces on every CI run, not on every API call. "Near zero human effort" is the limit. Currently, the operator selects a profile and reads an exit code. Each is closer to the perfect direction than the industry default, without claiming perfection.

The Innovator's Dilemma

Incumbent tools look at the convergent-era product and see inferiority:

Incumbent: "We manage 300+ resource types across 5 clouds with runtime monitoring,
            auto-remediation, attack-path visualization, and AI-powered triage."

Convergent product: "We evaluate invariants against snapshots. No runtime monitoring.
                     No auto-remediation. No visualization. No AI."

The incumbent's feature list is longer. The convergent product looks inferior by every metric the incumbent measures.

This is the Innovator's Dilemma. The convergent solution doesn't compete on the incumbent's metrics. It solves a different job at a different level:

Historical parallel Why the "inferior" solution won
VOIP beat telecom Solved "talk to people remotely" at a fraction of the cost. Worse call quality. Didn't matter.
Flash storage beat spinning disks Solved "store data portably." Less capacity initially. Didn't matter.
GitOps beat manual ops Solved "reproducible deploys" at the right abstraction. Less flexibility. Didn't matter.

Each inferior solution won because it solved the higher-order job better than the superior incumbent. The incumbent's features were means. The convergent solution delivered the job.

The cloud-security version:

Incumbent job (means):     "Scan, alert, triage, remediate"
Convergent job (outcome):  "The invariant holds. Deterministically. Before deployment."

The convergent product doesn't scan (the operator's collectors do). Doesn't alert (exit codes replace alerts). Doesn't triage (the verdict is binary). Doesn't remediate (the CI pipeline blocks the merge). Each missing feature is a means the convergent product doesn't need. Because it solves the job differently.

Seven commitments for the convergent era

Each commitment looks suboptimal from the pre-convergence competitive frame. Each is optimal for the convergent-era job:

1. Self-checking yes; self-healing no

Pre-convergence view: "Why can't it auto-fix? Every competitor auto-remediates."

Convergent-era reason: Perfection advances in small reversible steps, not leaps. Auto-remediation is an irreversible mutation of production state. One wrong fix is worse than the misconfiguration it corrected. The convergent product evaluates and blocks. The operator's existing pipeline fixes.

2. Invariants, not rules

Pre-convergence view: "Rules are more flexible. Invariants are rigid."

Convergent-era reason: Invariants compose (Alpern-Schneider theorem). Rules accumulate. 3000+ invariants compose into a global safety guarantee by mathematical theorem. 3000+ rules accumulate into a maintenance nightmare. The convergent product scales through composition.

3. Transitions, not just snapshots

Pre-convergence view: "Just tell me what's wrong right now."

Convergent-era reason: The convergent system asks about CHANGE, not just state. "Does this proposed transition violate an invariant?" is a different question from "is this resource misconfigured?" The first prevents breaches. The second detects them after the fact.

4. Bounded mitigation, not full remediation

Pre-convergence view: "Why doesn't it fix the problem end-to-end?"

Convergent-era reason: Stay outside the runtime mutation path. A product that modifies production state has the same blast-radius risk as the misconfigurations it's supposed to prevent. The convergent product gates. The existing pipeline remediates through the existing change-management process.

5. No replacement of existing tools

Pre-convergence view: "We need a platform that replaces our fifteen tools."

Convergent-era reason: Additive adoption beats rip-and-replace. The convergent product adds one step to the existing pipeline (the CI gate). The fifteen existing tools keep running as the reactive safety net. Adoption friction kills convergent products; zero-friction adoption is the only path.

6. Open-source embedded catalog

Pre-convergence view: "Why give away the controls? That's the IP."

Convergent-era reason: The catalog becomes the convergence substrate like HTTP or the Kubernetes API. When every operator runs the same 3000+ controls, the catalog is the standard. The value accrues to the entity that defined the standard.

7. "One invariant closer" — not "we solve cloud security"

Pre-convergence view: "You need a bigger vision statement."

Convergent-era reason: Engineering claims beat marketing horizon-claims. "We evaluate 3000+ invariants deterministically" is testable. "We solve cloud security" is a hostage to fortune. The convergent product advances step-wise with each invariant added, chain defined, schema extended and the claim is always verifiable.

Four refusals

Each refusal looks like a weakness from the pre-convergence frame. Each is an advantage in the convergent era:

Refusal Why it's correct
Don't replace existing tools Adoption friction kills convergent products. Add one CI step, not a platform migration.
Don't auto-remediate cloud state Irreversible runtime mutation compromises the trust the product is built on.
Don't claim "we solve cloud security" Maximalist claims are hostages to fortune. The claim must be verifiable at every moment.
Don't optimize for current customer feature requests Current requests target the pre-convergence era. The convergent product builds for the job that doesn't have a name yet, until it's the only job that matters.

The strategic dichotomy

"The only strategic choice is whether you lead that convergence or get displaced by it."

There is no third option. Once the structural conditions for convergence are present (the good enough tools have saturated, the failure cost has crossed the threshold, the higher-order job is nameable), convergence happens. The empirical record such as VOIP, Flash storage, GitOps, smartphones, HTML5 is decisive. Incumbent excellence at the pre-convergence job is no defense against displacement when the convergent era arrives.

The conditions are present now in cloud security:

"Good enough" tools have saturated      → 15+ tools per organization, breach rate unchanged
Failure cost has crossed the threshold  → Cloudflare, CrowdStrike, AWS are billion-dollar outages
Higher-order job is nameable            → "The invariant holds, deterministically, before deployment"
Structural forcing function has arrived → Agentic era removes the human from the loop

All four conditions met. The convergence is coming. The question is which product leads it.

The good enough test for your own stack

Look at your cloud security toolstack. For each tool:

1. Is it solving a MEANS or a JOB?

We scan is a means. The system stays safe, continuously, without surprise is the job. If the tool solves a means, it's pre-convergence.

2. Is it "good enough" — or is it structurally sound?

Good enough means: it works for the configurations you've tested. Structurally sound means: it works for every configuration that could exist, by mathematical guarantee (safety composition). Good enough fails at configuration #10,001. Structurally sound doesn't fail.

3. Would the tool survive the removal of humans from the loop?

When agents deploy infrastructure and humans aren't triaging alerts at 3am: does the tool still work? If it requires a human to interpret its output, it's pre-convergence. The convergent-era tool produces machine-readable verdicts that agents and pipelines act on.

Good enough is the state your toolstack is in right now. It works. It detects things. It alerts people. It has worked for years.

It's indistinguishable from failure that is just delayed. The delay makes it invisible. The convergence makes it inevitable.

Built for the convergent era with invariants that compose (not rules that accumulate), transitions evaluated before deployment (not states scanned after), bounded mitigation (not runtime mutation), additive adoption (not rip-and-replace), open catalog as convergence substrate, step-wise verifiable claims. Stave is an open-source Risk Reasoner. The convergence is coming. This is the product built for after it arrives. Try it: bash examples/demo-ai-security/run.sh

title: The home screen of our app stores nothing about itself, and two of its panels can delete themselves
description:
The first screen behind the login in Nakodo is a list of campaigns with a few panels around it: what is waiting on you, how much of your plan you have used, and a getting-started checklist. It is 255 lines of server component, and the thing I like about it is that none of those panels has any state of its own. There is no onboarding_steps table, no dismissed_checklist column, no last_seen_tips JSON. Every tick, every bar and every empty state is computed from rows that exist for another reason.

That is a decision with costs, and the costs are more interesting than the benefits.

The checklist has no table 

const steps: Step[] = [
  { label: "Start a campaign", done: true, href: inSetup(latest) ? `/campaigns/new/${latest.id}` : base, hint: "" },
  {
    label: "Review and launch",
    done: launched,
    href: inSetup(latest) ? `/campaigns/new/${latest.id}` : `${base}/brief`,
    hint: `Check the proposal and anything Nakodo guessed, then launch. Nakodo starts finding ${many}.`,
  },
  ...(launched && !campaigns.some((c) => c.hasOffer)
    ? [{ label: "Save your proposal", done: false, href: `${base}/outreach/proposal`, hint: "..." }]
    : []),
  {
    label: `Wait while Nakodo finds ${many}`,
    done: campaigns.some((c) => c.conversations > 0),
    href: base,
    hint: "It writes to the best fits on its own as they turn up, a few each day.",
  },
];

Four steps, sometimes five. "Start a campaign" is done: true as a literal, because the checklist only renders when at least one campaign exists, so the first step is a fact about the page rather than a question. "Review and launch" is launchedAt !== null. "Wait while Nakodo finds creators" is conversations > 0. The fifth step, approving the first emails, is pushed on only when the account has turned automatic sending off.

The third step is the one worth reading twice. Saving a proposal is normally part of the setup wizard, so for almost everybody it is not a step at all. It only appears for a campaign that was launched without one, which happens if the setup flow was interrupted. A stored checklist would have had to decide at signup whether that row exists. A derived one answers the question at render time and the answer is simply the truth.

Then the whole thing is conditional on two lines:

const next = steps.findIndex((s) => !s.done);
if (next < 0) return null;

and, at the top:

if (!latest || campaigns.some((c) => c.contacted > 0)) return null;

Nothing dismisses it. It disappears when there is nothing left in it, or as soon as anyone has actually been contacted, because at that point the account is past getting started and a tutorial panel on the main screen is noise.

next does double duty: it is the early return, and it is which row gets the ring, the background tint, the hint text and an sr-only "(next)". Only one hint is ever on screen, which is the difference between a checklist and a wall of advice.

The honest cost of deriving it

A derived checklist can come back.

Delete every campaign, start a new one, and you are a beginner again as far as this panel is concerned. A dismissed_at column would have made that impossible: once gone, gone for ever. I think the derived version is right, because the panel answers "what is the next thing to do with this account" and after deleting everything the honest answer is "launch something". But it is a real difference in behaviour that falls out of where the state lives, not out of any product decision, and it is the kind of thing that surprises you in a support thread six months later.

The progress bar has the same property. It is done / steps.length as an inline width, so adding the conditional fifth step moves the bar backwards: four of four becomes four of five when a campaign turns out to need a proposal. Percentages computed from a list whose length can change are always a little bit of a lie, and the alternative, a stored denominator, is a worse lie.

The panel that is rendered twice

The same component appears in two places in the tree:

{/* On phones, anything waiting goes above the campaigns rather than below them. */}
{list.length > 0 && waiting.length > 0 && <WaitingOnYou waiting={waiting} className="lg:hidden" />}

...

{list.length > 0 && (
  <WaitingOnYou waiting={waiting} className={waiting.length > 0 ? "max-lg:hidden" : undefined} />
)}

On a wide screen, "waiting on you" belongs in the right column next to the usage meters. On a phone there are no columns, and a panel in the second column renders under a list of campaigns that can be any length, which is the wrong place for the only thing on the page that needs a human. Moving it with CSS order was not available: the two positions are in different grid children, not siblings in one flow.

So it is rendered twice with mutually exclusive visibility, which costs some duplicated HTML and gains a layout nobody has to scroll to. The display: none means only one copy is in the accessibility tree at a time, so a screen reader hears it once.

The asymmetry in the second line is the part I had to think about. When there is nothing waiting, the phone copy is not rendered at all and the desktop copy loses its max-lg:hidden, which means the empty state exists only in the sidebar. The empty state is a sentence and a drawing of our mascot asleep:

{/* Nothing to do, so Alcy naps. */}
<AlcyAsleep size="m" className="mx-auto -mb-3" />

On a phone, "nothing is waiting on you" is worth zero pixels, because the absence of the panel says it. On a desktop the sidebar would otherwise have a hole in it, and a napping bird is a nicer answer than a hole. Same component, same data, two different judgements about whether nothing is worth saying.

One link, three destinations

Every campaign card is a link, and where it goes depends on how far the campaign got:

const href = inSetup(c)
  ? `/campaigns/new/${c.id}`
  : c.status === "draft" || c.status === "failed"
    ? `/campaigns/${c.id}/brief`
    : `/campaigns/${c.id}`;

with

export const inSetup = (c: { status: string; launchedAt: Date | null }) =>
  c.status === "draft" && c.launchedAt === null;

A campaign still in the wizard reopens the wizard where it left off. One whose research failed opens its brief, which is where the error and the retry live. Everything else opens its results. The rule is "put me back where the work is", and it is three lines of ternary rather than a status-to-route map, because there are three answers and a map of three entries reads worse than the question it answers.

Five queries and one write

The page does its reads in parallel, including the search params, which in Next 16 are a promise like any other:

const [listed, account, waiting, daily, sp] = await Promise.all([
  campaignsNow(),
  accountForPage(user.id),
  threadsNeedingYou(user.id),
  shareCampaigns(user.id),
  searchParams,
]);

and then does something I am still slightly uneasy about:

// Research cut off mid-run is put right only when the list shows some, so
// the page doesn't write on every visit.
const list = listed.some(researchIsStale) && (await recoverStaleResearch(user.id)) > 0 ? await campaignsNow() : listed;

A render that repairs data. The guard is that the write only happens when the already-fetched rows prove there is something to repair, so the common path is a pure read, but a GET that can update rows is still a GET that can update rows. The alternative is a cron that sweeps for interrupted research, and the reason it is here instead is latency: the person looking at the screen is the one who cares that a campaign stopped mid-research, and they are looking at it now.

What the public page says

The how it works page explains eight things the product does. The checklist asks the customer for four, and three of those four are "look at this and press launch". That gap is the whole design brief for a screen like this: the product can be complicated, the list of what you have to do cannot be.

title: Every page on our site but one is styled by a class called legal, and three of them are legal pages
description:
This morning I re-requested every URL in munchable.app/sitemap.xml and grepped the HTML for one string. 516 pages. 515 of them open their content with <main class="legal">. The only page that does not is the homepage.

Three of those 515 are legal pages: the privacy notice, the terms, and the licences page. The other 512 are 461 ingredient answer pages, 38 recipes, 8 condition guides, and a few index and about pages. Open a recipe and the privacy notice in two tabs and view source on both: same class, same column, same typography.

How a class ends up with a wrong name

The first long-form pages on the site were the privacy notice and the terms of service. Both wanted the same thing, which is the oldest layout on the web: one centred column of prose, narrow enough to read, with headings that do not shout. So that got written, and it got called .legal, because at the time the set of pages that needed it was exactly the legal pages.

The shell is two rules and nine lines:

.legal {
  padding: 72px 0 88px;
}

.legal-inner {
  max-width: 720px;
  margin: 0 auto;
}

Then the content pages arrived: condition guides, then a few hundred generated answer pages, then recipes, then a reference page. Every one of them is a column of prose with headings. At that point there are two options. Copy the column rules under a new name per page type and accept that the five copies will drift. Or put class="legal" on a page that has nothing to do with law.

We did the second thing, 11 route files now say className="legal", and I do not regret it. What it cost was one incident.

23 rules, and 12 of them had to be rewritten

Our stylesheet is one hand-written file: 3,145 lines, 444 rules. 23 of those rules mention .legal.

The typography rules were originally written the way you would expect, against the page wrapper:

/* What these used to be */
.legal h1 { ... }
.legal h2 { ... }
.legal p  { ... }
.legal a  { ... }

Then the guide pages grew a closing call to action. It is a shared component: a warm card with a cookie mark, a heading, one sentence, and two store buttons. It already existed because the homepage ends with it, and a guide page needs to make the same point, so the component got reused rather than rebuilt.

That card sits inside <main class="legal"> and outside .legal-inner. The moment it rendered on a guide page, two things broke, for two different reasons.

The heading went flush left. The card's own rule is:

.closing h2 {
  font-size: clamp(34px, 4.6vw, 54px);
  max-width: 16ch;
  margin: 0 auto;
}

.closing h2 and .legal h2 have identical specificity, one class and one element each. When specificity ties, source order decides, and the .legal block sits about 130 lines further down the file. So .legal h2's margin: 40px 0 0 replaced margin: 0 auto, and a 16ch block that is meant to be centred sat against the left edge of a centred card.

The store buttons turned the wrong colour. That one was not a tie:

.store-btn { color: var(--ink); }   /* 0,1,0 */
.legal a   { color: var(--caramel-ink); font-weight: 700; }  /* 0,1,1 */

One class versus one class and one element. The descendant selector wins on specificity regardless of order, so every store button inside a guide page came out caramel and bold instead of ink.

The component was not wrong. It rendered perfectly on the homepage, which is the one page in the site with no .legal on it, which is also why this was invisible until the day a guide page shipped.

The fix was to narrow 12 selectors from .legal to .legal-inner, and to leave the reason in the file so the next person adding a rule here does not undo it:

Scoped to the reading column, not to `.legal`, on purpose.

These are typography rules for a column of prose, and the guide pages now end
with the shared app CTA, which sits inside `.legal` but outside `.legal-inner`.

A page wrapper selector is a contract with components nobody has written yet

That is the part worth taking away from a dull little CSS bug. .legal p is not a rule about the paragraphs on your legal pages. It is a promise about every paragraph that will ever be placed anywhere on that page, including paragraphs inside components that do not exist yet, written by somebody who will never read this file.

Scoping to the column makes a narrower promise that is actually true: everything inside the reading column is prose and is styled by the page, everything outside it is a component and is responsible for its own appearance.

The 11 rules still hanging off .legal are the safe kind, and the difference is instructive. They are .legal .cond-lede, .legal .cond-card h2, .legal .cond-q, .legal .sib h3, .legal .closing. Every one of them names a class that only exists on the page type it was written for. The dangerous selector is the one that names a bare element, because elements are what other people's components are made of.

Is a wrong name worth renaming?

.prose would be the honest name. So would .reading-column. The rename is mechanical: 11 route files, 23 rules, no visual change at all.

I have not done it, and the reason is not laziness, it is that a rename with no behavioural change is a diff nobody can review. You cannot test it, you can only read it, and the failure mode is a page you forgot that silently loses its column. The stylesheet comment carries the truth instead, which is the cheaper half of the fix.

But the cost of the wrong name is real and I would rather state it than pretend it is free: the next person who needs a column of prose will not guess that the class they want is called legal. They will write a second column, under a better name, and the site will have two. Names are documentation, and this one documents the first two pages we happened to write rather than the 515 that use it.

If you want to see the shell doing four different jobs, compare the privacy notice it was named for with a condition guide, a reference list and a recipe. Then scroll to the bottom of any of them and look at the store buttons. They are ink, not caramel, and that is the whole of what twelve rewritten selectors bought.

title: Our two self-hosted fonts hold 222 and 230 codepoints, and the arrow on our homepage is in neither
description:
Two weeks ago I wrote that next/font/google broke on an ampersand, so our two fonts are 59KB in the repo now. That post was about the switch: why the build broke, what the diff looked like, and what weight: "300 700" means next to a variable font.

This one is about what is actually inside the two files, because self-hosting a font changes a subset from something a build step chose into an artifact sitting in your repository that you can open and count. So I opened them.

Notifio is a desktop app that watches rental search pages for new listings. The site in front of it is a Next.js app, and it loads three typefaces: Space Grotesk for headings, DM Sans for body text, and Geist Mono for small labels.

const spaceGrotesk = localFont({
  src: "./fonts/space-grotesk-latin.woff2",
  variable: "--font-space-grotesk",
  weight: "300 700",
  display: "swap",
  preload: true,
});

Two of the three are files in server/src/app/fonts/: 22,320 bytes of Space Grotesk and 36,980 bytes of DM Sans. The third comes from the geist npm package.

What is in the files

Four lines of Python, with fonttools and brotli installed:

from fontTools.ttLib import TTFont
t = TTFont("src/app/fonts/dm-sans-latin.woff2")
print(t["maxp"].numGlyphs, len(t.getBestCmap()))
for a in t["fvar"].axes:
    print(a.axisTag, a.minValue, a.defaultValue, a.maxValue)
Space Grotesk DM Sans
Bytes 22,320 36,980
Glyphs 291 270
Codepoints in cmap 230 222
wght axis 300 to 700, default 300 100 to 1000, default 400
Internal family name Space Grotesk Light DM Sans 9pt

Two things in that table were news to me.

The first is that our declared weight: "300 700" is accurate for Space Grotesk and a deliberate narrowing of DM Sans, whose axis actually runs from 100 to 1000. Narrowing it is harmless here, and I checked rather than assumed: the site uses font-bold 95 times, font-semibold 98 times, font-medium five times and font-light twice, so nothing on any page asks for a weight outside 300 to 700. If somebody adds font-extrabold to a heading, they will get a synthesised bold rather than the 800 the file can genuinely draw.

The second is the internal family names. The Space Grotesk file calls itself "Space Grotesk Light" with a default instance at 300, and the DM Sans file calls itself "DM Sans 9pt", which is the name of one optical size of a font whose optical size axis was dropped on the way out of Google Fonts. None of that matters to next/font/local, which generates its own font-family name and never reads those strings. It matters the moment somebody copies one of these files into a hand-written @font-face and trusts the name in it.

The 20 characters our source actually uses

Before checking coverage I wanted to know what the site asks for. Across 80 source files, the copy and markup contain 20 distinct characters above U+007F. The top one is not close:

Character Uses
U+2500 ─ box drawing 602
U+20AC € 68
U+2013 – en dash 64
U+00A3 £ 60
U+2014 em dash 56
U+00B7 · 23
U+2192 → 11

Then a long tail: …, ², ¥, ä, ó, ú, ö, ©, curly quotes, and one each of ✓, ⋮ and ⚙.

Both fonts cover £, €, the dashes, the middot, the ellipsis, the accented vowels and the quotes. They do not cover five of the characters in that list: ─, →, ✓, ⋮ and ⚙.

The 602 box-drawing characters turned out to be the easiest finding of the week to explain:

{/* ── Hero ── */}
{/* ── Feature demo rows ── spacing matches between all sections */}

They are in JSX comments. The single most common non-ASCII character in the repository never reaches a browser, which is also why nobody has ever noticed that neither webfont can draw it.

The other four do reach a browser. Our 56 em dashes are a different kind of embarrassment, documented separately, since the copy rule for this site says there are not supposed to be any.

The characters that fall back, and where you can see them

Three of the five are in rendered text, and the counts are in the HTML if you want to check them:

  • → in link text: four on the homepage, ten on the comparison hub, six on the help page.
  • ⚙ twice on the help page, in a Gmail instruction that says to click the gear icon.
  • ⋮ once on the help page, for Gmail's three-dot menu.
  • ✓ once on the post-checkout success page, which robots.txt disallows, so nobody but a buyer sees it.

Geist Mono, from the npm package, carries 889 codepoints and has the box drawing character and the arrow. It does not have the tick, the vertical ellipsis or the gear. Those three come from the operating system on every page load, in whatever the browser picks next out of ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif.

This is not a bug. Per-character fallback down the CSS font stack is exactly what should happen, and an arrow in SF Pro next to body text in DM Sans is something I only noticed because I went looking. It is still worth knowing which characters on your own site are not being drawn by the fonts you chose.

The six the repository cannot show you

Here is the part I did not expect, and the reason this is a post rather than a note in a commit message.

Notifio prices in 24 currencies, with the figure on the page being the figure charged. The symbols for those currencies are not in any source file, because Intl.NumberFormat produces them at runtime from a currency code and a locale. A grep of the repo cannot find them, so no amount of auditing the source tells you whether the fonts can draw them.

Formatting the same amount in all 24 and checking each character against both cmaps gives six that neither file covers:

Currency Rendered Missing
PLN 2499 zł U+0142 ł
CZK 2 499 Kč U+010D č
TRY ₺2.499 U+20BA ₺
INR ₹2,499 U+20B9 ₹
JPY ￥2,499 U+FFE5 fullwidth ￥
ILS 2,499 ₪ U+20AA ₪, plus two U+200F marks

The Polish and Czech ones are a subset choice: ł and č live in Google's latin-ext, and we asked for latin, both before and after self-hosting, so this is not something the switch to local files lost. Of the other four, the rupee, lira and shekel signs do fall inside latin-ext's declared unicode range, so that subset might carry them depending on what the font itself draws, and the fullwidth yen sits outside every Latin range there is.

The visible consequence is on the pricing page, where the headline price is rendered at 72px in Space Grotesk. A visitor in India gets ₹ at 72px from a system font, hard against digits at 72px from ours, with whatever difference in weight and stroke that font happens to have. The ¥ that appears three times in our own source is U+00A5, the half-width one, which both fonts do have. Japan gets U+FFE5 from Intl, which they do not.

What I am going to do about it

Not add latin-ext. It fixes two of the six for certain, maybe three more, and charges every visitor the extra bytes to find out.

The fix that matches the problem is to stop relying on the symbol for the currencies where the symbol is ambiguous or missing anyway. The line under every price already names the currency, because $39.99 needs to tell a Canadian which dollar it is. For the six above, rendering the ISO code next to the number is both a legibility win and a coverage win, and it is one branch in one formatter rather than another font file.

The thing I would take from this generally: subsetting is usually discussed as a performance decision, and it is also a decision about which of your strings are allowed to be drawn in your own typeface. The strings that catch you out are the ones your code generates rather than the ones you typed, which means you cannot audit them by reading the repository. You have to format one of everything and compare it against the cmap.

If you want to look at the pages involved, the prices are on the pricing page, the arrows are on the homepage and the comparison pages, and the gear and the three dots are in the Gmail setup steps on the help page. The per-site alert pages are at notifio.app/alerts, and the app itself is on the download page.

title: How Dependency Injection Works in Spring Boot: A Quick Walkthrough
description:
If you have written any Spring Boot code, you have seen this: a class asks for another class in its constructor, and somehow the right object is just there. Nobody called new. Nobody looked anything up. Let's see who does that work, with plain words and a tiny Spring Boot app you can run yourself.

The idea in one minute

  1. You mark classes with annotations like @Service or @Component.
  2. When the app starts, Spring Boot scans your code and creates an object of each one. These managed objects are called beans, and they live in the Spring container (the ApplicationContext).
  3. When a bean's constructor asks for another bean, the container passes it in. That passing-in is dependency injection.

The Spring documentation calls this Inversion of Control: instead of your object building or finding its own helpers, the container creates them and hands them over. Your class just declares what it needs.

Watch the flow

The animation follows the real program below: main() hands control to Spring Boot, the scan finds the two annotated classes, the container creates the GreetingService bean, creates WelcomeRunner while injecting GreetingService into its constructor, and run() uses the injected bean.

Run it yourself

A complete Spring Boot app in one file (run with mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=com.example.di.DiDemoApplication in a project with the spring-boot-starter dependency, Spring Boot 3.5.7):

package com.example.di;

import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@SpringBootApplication
public class DiDemoApplication {

    // 1. A bean the container will create and manage
    @Service
    static class GreetingService {
        GreetingService() {
            System.out.println("[container] created bean: GreetingService");
        }
        String greet(String name) {
            return "Hello, " + name + "!";
        }
    }

    // 2. A bean that NEEDS a GreetingService: constructor injection
    @Component
    static class WelcomeRunner implements CommandLineRunner {
        private final GreetingService greetingService;

        WelcomeRunner(GreetingService greetingService) {   // container injects it here
            this.greetingService = greetingService;
            System.out.println("[container] injected GreetingService into WelcomeRunner");
        }

        @Override
        public void run(String... args) {
            System.out.println("[app] WelcomeRunner.run() called with the injected bean");
            System.out.println("[app] " + greetingService.greet("Spring Boot"));
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("[you] main(): handing control to SpringApplication.run()");
        SpringApplication.run(DiDemoApplication.class, args);
        System.out.println("[you] main(): container shut down");
    }
}

What it actually printed (Spring Boot 3.5.7, Java 21)

Real run, startup banner and framework log lines trimmed:

[you] main(): handing control to SpringApplication.run()
:: Spring Boot ::                (v3.5.7)
... Starting DiDemoApplication using Java 21.0.13 ...
[container] created bean: GreetingService
[container] injected GreetingService into WelcomeRunner
... Started DiDemoApplication in 0.774 seconds ...
[app] WelcomeRunner.run() called with the injected bean
[app] Hello, Spring Boot!
[you] main(): container shut down

Read it in order and you can see the handoff:

  • Your main() does exactly one thing: start the container.
  • The container's log lines come before the app's: it creates GreetingService, then builds WelcomeRunner and passes the service into the constructor. All before "Started DiDemoApplication".
  • Only then does run() execute, already holding a ready-to-use bean. CommandLineRunner is just Spring Boot's way of saying "call this once everything is wired up".

What the docs add

  • Two ways to inject. The Spring Framework docs describe constructor-based and setter-based DI. The rule of thumb they give: constructors for mandatory dependencies, setters for optional ones.
  • Constructor injection is the recommended style. The Spring team advocates it because components stay immutable, required dependencies can never be null, and the object is always fully initialized when you get it. The Spring Boot docs give the same advice: use constructor injection plus @ComponentScan, which @SpringBootApplication already includes.
  • It pays off in tests. Because your class receives its helpers instead of building them, a test can hand it a stub or mock instead of the real thing.

One honest caveat: the container does much more than this tiny demo shows (scopes, lazy init, configuration properties, proxies). But the core loop you saw above - scan, create, inject, use - is the part everything else builds on.

Sources

  • Dependency Injection - Spring Framework Documentation
  • Spring Beans and Dependency Injection - Spring Boot Documentation

Written with AI assistance; code examples were compiled and run on Spring Boot 3.5.7 with JDK 21 before publishing.
