title: DORA and Cloud Exit Strategies: What Financial Companies Must Document
description:
Originally published on moveinfra.eu.

Under Article 28(8) of the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554) and Article 10 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1773, financial entities in the European Union must maintain documented, realistic, and tested exit strategies for every cloud service supporting a critical or important business function. Applicable since January 17, 2025, DORA requires more than a high-level policy statement: companies must document concrete trigger events, verified alternative cloud providers or in-house options, technical data and application migration plans, transition timelines, and contractual termination clauses under Article 30(3)(f), and must review and test these plans periodically.

Key takeaways

  • Who is affected: Banks, payment institutions, e-money institutions, investment firms, crypto-asset service providers (CASPs), insurers, and other regulated financial entities using cloud services for critical or important functions.
  • Four mandatory exit scenarios: Under Article 28(8), your exit plan must address provider failure, deterioration of service quality, business disruption from inappropriate or failed service delivery, and material risks preventing the continued use of the service (including early contract termination).
  • Three layers of documentation: Regulators expect coherence across your ICT third-party policy and technical exit plans (Article 28(8) and RTS 2024/1773), your contractual clauses with the cloud provider (Article 30(3)(f)), and your Register of Information (Article 28(3) and ITS 2024/2956).
  • Testing is mandatory: Paper-only plans do not pass supervisory review. You must periodically review and test your exit plans to prove your team can migrate data and workloads within your stated recovery and transition windows.
  • Data Act alignment: Under Article 29 of the EU Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854), cloud switching charges (including data egress fees for switching) are capped at actual cost until January 12, 2027, and banned entirely from that date onward, removing a major financial barrier to testing and executing cloud exits.

Who needs a cloud exit strategy under DORA?

DORA applies to over 20 categories of regulated financial entities across the EU. For companies with 10 to 300 employees, this typically includes licensed fintechs, payment and electronic money institutions, investment firms, asset managers, insurtechs, and crypto-asset service providers regulated under MiCA.

Not every SaaS tool or cloud account requires a full exit strategy. The requirement under Article 28(8) applies specifically to ICT services supporting critical or important functions. DORA defines a critical or important function as one where a disruption would materially impair the financial performance of the entity, the soundness or continuity of its services and activities, or its ability to comply with regulatory obligations.

For most financial companies, production cloud infrastructure on AWS, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Azure hosts core transaction processing, customer portals, ledger databases, or compliance reporting systems. That places your primary cloud environment squarely inside the scope of Article 28(8).

There is a limited legal exemption: "microenterprises" (defined in DORA as financial entities employing fewer than 10 persons and having an annual turnover and/or annual balance sheet total that does not exceed EUR 2 million) are exempt from the formal requirement to put exit strategies in place under Article 28(8). Once a company crosses 10 employees or EUR 2 million in turnover, the full documentation and testing obligations apply.

What DORA and RTS 2024/1773 require you to document

DORA's rules on exit strategies are split across the main regulation and its secondary technical standards:

  1. DORA Article 28(8) establishes the core obligation to maintain comprehensive, documented, and tested exit strategies.
  2. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1773 (Article 10) sets the Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) specifying the exact contents of your exit plans.
  3. DORA Article 30(3)(f) defines the exit and transition clauses that must exist in your cloud contract.
  4. Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2956 defines the Register of Information (RoI), where you must record substitutability and exit readiness fields for each critical contract.

During national supervisory reviews, authorities check whether these documents match. If your Register of Information claims your cloud provider is easily substitutable, your contract provides a 30-day notice period, and your engineering architecture relies heavily on proprietary cloud services that would take nine months to rewrite, an auditor will flag the contradiction.

1. Trigger events and exit scenarios

Under DORA Article 28(8) and Article 10 of RTS 2024/1773, your exit plan cannot only cover a planned, friendly non-renewal. You must explicitly document how you will handle stressed exits triggered by:

  • Unforeseen and persistent service interruptions (such as prolonged regional cloud outages or infrastructure instability).
  • Inappropriate or failed service delivery (such as persistent SLA breaches, security failures, or compliance violations by the provider).
  • Unexpected termination of the contractual arrangement (whether terminated by you for cause, by the cloud provider, or ordered by a financial supervisor under DORA's oversight powers).
  • Provider failure (insolvency, business closure, or revocation of regulatory authorizations).

For each scenario, you must define measurable internal thresholds that trigger the exit process and specify which roles on your management body have the authority to invoke the plan.

2. Alternative solutions and substitutability assessment

Article 29 of DORA requires you to assess ICT concentration risk and understand how easily a provider can be substituted. In your exit plan, you must identify concrete alternative solutions:

  • Moving to another third-party ICT provider (for example, migrating from a US hyperscaler to an EU cloud provider such as UpCloud, Scaleway, or OVHcloud).
  • Reintegrating the function in-house (rarely practical for small and mid-sized companies using public cloud infrastructure, but required to be evaluated).

You do not need to pay for duplicate idle servers running 24/7 on a second cloud unless your specific business continuity risk requires hot standby. However, your exit documentation must name the target provider(s), verify that they offer compatible compute, database, networking, and compliance capabilities, and confirm where data will be stored and processed in the EU.

Note on sovereignty and concentration risk: using a "sovereign" region from your existing provider (such as the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, which keeps data and operations in the EU but belongs to Amazon, a US company) does not satisfy an exit requirement from that same provider group, as DORA Article 29 explicitly requires entities to assess dependencies across connected providers within the same corporate group.

3. Technical migration and transition plan

Article 10 of RTS 2024/1773 states that exit plans must be "realistic, feasible, based on plausible scenarios and reasonable assumptions, and shall have a planned implementation schedule compatible with the exit and termination terms established in the contractual arrangements."

For a cloud infrastructure exit, your technical documentation should include:

  • Complete asset and dependency inventory: Every virtual machine, Kubernetes cluster, managed database, object storage bucket, load balancer, firewall rule, DNS zone, and encryption key supporting the critical function.
  • Portability vs. lock-in mapping: A clear distinction between portable components (such as standard Linux VMs, Kubernetes manifests, PostgreSQL databases, and S3-compatible object storage) and proprietary services that require code changes (such as AWS DynamoDB, Google BigQuery, Azure Cosmos DB, or proprietary IAM and serverless workflows).
  • Data migration methodology: How databases will be replicated (for example, logical replication for PostgreSQL or MySQL), how object storage will be transferred and verified with checksums, how much bandwidth is required, and how data integrity and encryption will be maintained in transit.
  • Cutover and rollback procedures: The exact sequence for updating CI/CD pipelines, pausing writes during the final cutover window, switching DNS, verifying application health, and falling back to the original provider if checks fail during the transition.
  • Secure data deletion: How you will verify and document that all customer and financial data has been permanently erased from the outgoing cloud provider once the retention and rollback window closes.

4. Roles, budgets, and timelines

An auditor will check whether you have the people and money to execute the plan. Your documentation must define:

  • Internal responsibilities: Who leads the exit on the business, compliance, and engineering sides.
  • Resource and budget estimates: Estimated internal engineering hours, external migration tooling or consulting costs, parallel-run infrastructure costs during the transition month, and any early termination fees.
  • Data egress costs: Under Article 29 of the EU Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854), cloud providers may charge no more than their direct cost for switching-related data egress until January 12, 2027, and switching charges are banned entirely from January 12, 2027. Your budget assumptions should reflect this timeline.
  • Step-by-step schedule: A timeline showing how long it takes to provision the target environment, sync data, test applications, and cut over traffic, proving that the total duration fits inside your contractual notice and transition period.

5. Contractual clauses under Article 30(3)(f)

Your technical plan is only valid if your contract backs it up. For critical or important functions, DORA Article 30(3)(f) requires your cloud contract to include:

  • Clear termination rights and minimum notice periods (including termination scenarios requested by a competent authority).
  • Mandatory obligations for the cloud provider to assist you during an exit at no additional cost, or at a cost determined ex-ante in the contract.
  • A sufficiently long mandatory transition period during which the cloud provider must continue delivering services to reduce the risk of disruption while you migrate to another provider.
  • Provisions ensuring you can easily retrieve all your data in an accessible, machine-readable format.

Most major cloud providers offer a "DORA Financial Services Addendum" to cover Article 30 requirements. You must ensure this addendum is actually signed and referenced in your Register of Information, rather than assuming standard online terms of service cover you.

Practical checklist: DORA cloud exit documentation

Use the table below to verify that your cloud exit strategy covers the requirements of DORA and RTS 2024/1773 before a regulatory audit.

Documentation Area Regulatory Basis Specific Evidence Required Owner
Criticality & Scope DORA Art. 28(1)–(3); ITS 2024/2956 Mapping of business functions to cloud accounts and services in the Register of Information (RoI). Risk / Compliance
Exit Policy & Triggers DORA Art. 28(8); RTS 2024/1773 Art. 10 Documented exit triggers (outage, SLA breach, provider failure, termination) and board/management sign-off process. CRO / Compliance
Substitutability & Target DORA Art. 29; ITS 2024/2956 Assessment of provider lock-in, concentration risk, and named alternative cloud provider(s) with EU data residency. CTO / Architecture
Technical Runbook RTS 2024/1773 Art. 10 Infrastructure-as-Code (Terraform/OpenTofu) inventory, database replication plan, CI/CD update steps, DNS cutover, and rollback plan. DevOps / Engineering
Timeline & Budget RTS 2024/1773 Art. 10 Realistic migration schedule (in days/weeks), estimated parallel cloud costs, and engineering staffing plan. CFO / Engineering Lead
Contractual Alignment DORA Art. 30(3)(f); RTS 2024/1773 Art. 8 Signed DORA addendum with mandatory transition period, fixed exit assistance costs, and data retrieval rights. Legal / Procurement
Review & Test Log DORA Art. 28(8); RTS 2024/1773 Art. 10 Dated records of periodic plan reviews, tabletop exercises, or technical migration tests, plus remediation of any gaps found. CTO / Risk

How to test your cloud exit plan without breaking production

Both DORA Article 28(8) and Article 10 of RTS 2024/1773 require that exit plans be "sufficiently tested" and "periodically reviewed". The regulation applies the principle of proportionality: a 30-person payment institution is not expected to shut down live production traffic to run a multi-million-euro full cutover every year, but a tabletop discussion with no technical verification is rarely enough for critical cloud workloads.

A practical, proportionate testing approach for small and mid-sized financial companies includes three steps:

  1. Maintain Infrastructure as Code (IaC): Keep your network, compute, firewall, and database configurations defined in Terraform or OpenTofu. Audit your codebase twice a year to document any newly introduced proprietary cloud services that would block a clean exit.
  2. Run a dry-run environment build: Once a year, provision a non-production copy of your core infrastructure on your designated alternative EU cloud provider. Deploy your application containers or VMs using your existing CI/CD pipeline to verify that your software builds and starts outside your primary cloud.
  3. Test data restoration and replication: Restore an anonymized snapshot of your production database and a sample of object storage to the alternative cloud environment. Measure the actual data transfer speed, check data integrity, and use those real numbers to update the transition timeline in your exit documentation.

Document the date of the test, the participants, the measured transfer and setup times, any blockers discovered, and the tickets created to fix them. That test report is the exact evidence supervisors ask to see.

Frequently asked questions

Does deploying across multiple AWS or Azure regions count as a DORA exit strategy?

No. Multi-region deployment within the same cloud provider is a business continuity and disaster recovery measure (covered under DORA Article 11), not an exit strategy under Article 28(8). An exit strategy specifically addresses what happens when the provider itself fails, breaches its contract, loses regulatory approval, or must be replaced entirely.

How often must we review and test our cloud exit strategy?

Neither DORA Article 28(8) nor Article 10 of RTS 2024/1773 sets a rigid calendar interval, requiring instead "periodic" review and testing proportionate to the criticality of the service. However, an annual review—and an immediate update whenever you make material changes to your cloud architecture or contract—is the standard practice expected by national supervisors and aligns with the annual ICT risk review cycles in DORA.

What if our cloud architecture uses proprietary services like DynamoDB or BigQuery?

Using proprietary cloud services is not banned under DORA, but you must be honest about it in your documentation. In your Register of Information and Article 29 concentration risk assessment, you must record the lower substitutability and higher migration complexity. Your exit plan must include the time, budget, and engineering steps required to refactor the application to an open alternative (such as PostgreSQL or ClickHouse), and your contractual transition period must be long enough to cover that refactoring work.

Can our cloud provider charge us fees to move our data out during an exit?

Under DORA Article 30(3)(f), any assistance fees from the provider during termination must be either free or clearly set in advance in your contract. Furthermore, under Article 29 of the EU Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854), cloud switching charges—including data egress fees for switching to another provider—cannot exceed the provider's direct cost until January 12, 2027, and are completely prohibited starting January 12, 2027.

Sources

  • Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 on digital operational resilience for the financial sector (DORA) – EUR-Lex
  • Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1773 (RTS on policy regarding contractual arrangements for ICT services) – EUR-Lex
  • Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2956 (ITS on standard templates for the register of information) – EUR-Lex
  • Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on harmonised rules on fair access to and use of data (EU Data Act) – EUR-Lex

Drafted with AI assistance and fact-checked by the MoveInfra team. The original, kept up to date, is at moveinfra.eu. Free tools for pricing a move to an EU cloud: moveinfra.eu/tools.

title: JavaScript (ES6+) for React Developers: The Definitive Guide
description:
React is fundamentally plain JavaScript. If you ever struggle with state updates, unintended re-renders, or props drilling, the issue is rarely React itself—it is usually a missing piece of modern ECMAScript fundamentals.

  1. Modern Variables: const, let, Scoping, and Retiring var In legacy JavaScript, var was function-scoped and subject to unpredictable hoisting behaviors: 
JavaScript
// The legacy problem: var leaks out of block statements
if (true) {
  var framework = "React";
}
console.log(framework); // "React" (escaped block scope)

Modern JS introduces block scoping with let and const:

const: Enforces constant references. Variables cannot be reassigned. Use this by default (roughly 95% of the time in React components).

let: Enables reassignable block-scoped variables (ideal for counters, loops, or flags).

Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ): Unlike var, accessing let or const before declaration throws a ReferenceError rather than returning undefined.

JavaScript
/

/ Modern standard:
const API_URL = "https://api.store.com/v1";
let retryCount = 0;

if (retryCount === 0) {
  const localMessage = "Initial attempt";
  retryCount += 1;
}
// localMessage is completely inaccessible here (ReferenceError)
  1. Arrow Functions and Lexical this Arrow functions (() => {}) give developers a concise syntax and, more crucially, lexical this scoping. They do not bind their own this, arguments, or super.

Concise Syntax & Implicit Returns
In React, implicit returns are frequently used for rendering JSX:

// Explicit return
const UserCard = (props) => {
  return <div>{props.name}</div>;
};

// Implicit return (no 'return' keyword, wrapped in parentheses)
const UserCard = ({ name }) => (
  <div className="card">
    <h3>{name}</h3>
  </div>
);

Lexical this vs Standard Functions
In traditional functions, this is determined by how the function is invoked. With arrow functions, this is bound to the surrounding lexical context:

JavaScript
const counterService = {
  count: 0,
  start() {
    // Normal function inside setInterval would rebind 'this' to window/timeout
    setInterval(() => {
      this.count++;
      console.log(`Live Count: ${this.count}`);
    }, 1000);
  }
};
  1. Essential Array Methods: map, filter, reduce, find, some/every


JavaScript
const products = [
  { id: "p1", title: "Wireless Mouse", price: 30, inStock: true },
  { id: "p2", title: "Mechanical Keyboard", price: 120, inStock: false },
  { id: "p3", title: "USB-C Hub", price: 45, inStock: true }
];

// 1. filter: Available items only
const available = products.filter(p => p.inStock);

// 2. map: Transform to rendered strings / components
const catalogView = available.map(p => `${p.title} - $${p.price}`);

// 3. reduce: Calculate aggregate total
const inventoryValue = products.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.price, 0);

// 4. find: Grab exact target
const keyboard = products.find(p => p.id === "p2");

// 5. some: Availability check
const hasOutOfStock = products.some(p => !p.inStock); // true
  1. Destructuring (Arrays & Objects) and Default Parameters

Destructuring provides syntactic shortcuts to extract nested values directly into clean variables.
Object Destructuring in Props

JavaScript

// Instead of accessing props.theme, props.title, props.isActive
function Button({ theme = "primary", title = "Submit", onClick }) {
  return (
    <button className={`btn btn-${theme}`} onClick={onClick}>
      {title}
    </button>
  );
}

Array DestructuringArray destructuring maps variables based on positional indexing (the exact mechanism powering React's useState hook):

JavaScript
const [selectedTab, setSelectedTab] = ["overview", () => {}];
  1. Rest and Spread Operators (...) While both use three dots (...), their intents are distinct: Spread Operator (...): Expands elements of an array or properties of an object into a new structure. Rest Parameter (...args): Condenses multiple distinct arguments into a single collected array. Immutable State Updates with Spread Never mutate React state directly; always create new copies: 
JavaScript
const userProfile = { id: 101, name: "Ali", settings: { dark: true } };

// Updating user profile immutably
const updatedProfile = {
  ...userProfile,
  name: "Alireza", // overrides 'name'
  role: "Admin"     // appends new field
};

// Adding an item to an array immutably
const cart = ["Mouse", "Keyboard"];
const nextCart = [...cart, "Monitor"];

Rest Parameter in Components

JavaScript
// Collect rest of props to pass through to native elements
const CustomInput = ({ label, ...nativeInputProps }) => (
  <label>
    {label}
    <input {...nativeInputProps} />
  </label>
);
  1. Immutability: Shallow vs Deep Comparison React optimizes renders using shallow equality comparison (Object.is() / ===).

Shallow Copy / Comparison: Compares only top-level references. If an object reference hasn't changed, React assumes its internals haven't changed either.

The Mutation Trap:

JavaScript
// WRONG: Direct mutation does NOT change object reference!
const state = { count: 0, meta: { tags: ["tech"] } };
state.count = 1; 

// If passed to a memoized component or setState:
// previousState === nextState evaluated to TRUE -> NO RE-RENDER!

// RIGHT: Shallow copy creates a new top-level reference
const nextState = { ...state, count: 1 };
console.log(state === nextState); // false -> triggers re-render

// Nested reference gotcha:
// state.meta and nextState.meta still point to the EXACT SAME memory address!
// For nested mutations, you must shallow copy the inner object as well:
const fullyUpdated = {
  ...state,
  meta: {
    ...state.meta,
    tags: [...state.meta.tags, "react"]
  }
};
  1. Async JavaScript: Promises and async/await with try/catch React lifecycles and event handlers communicate with network APIs via asynchronous promises. 
JavaScript
// Standard data fetching pattern with async/await and try/catch
async function fetchProducts(category) {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`https://api.store.com/products?category=${category}`);

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`HTTP Error: ${response.status}`);
    }

    const data = await response.json();
    return { success: true, payload: data };
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Fetch pipeline failed:", error.message);
    return { success: false, error: error.message };
  } finally {
    console.log("Network request completed.");
  }
}
  1. Modular Architecture: Named vs Default Exports JavaScript modules (ESM) enable decoupled, maintainable codebases: 
JavaScript
// mathUtils.js
export const TAX_RATE = 0.09;             // Named Export
export const formatCurrency = (val) => `$${val.toFixed(2)}`; // Named Export

export default class CartEngine {}        // Default Export

JavaScript
// Consumer.js
import CartEngine, { TAX_RATE, formatCurrency } from './mathUtils.js';

Cheat Sheet Reference & Visuals
The premier modern interactive and open-source cheat sheets for modern JavaScript development are:

MDN Web Docs JavaScript Reference: The industry standard for official language specifications and browser compatibility tables.

developer.mozilla.org

Modern JavaScript Cheatsheet (mbeaudru on GitHub): Specifically tailored for developers moving to ES6+ and modern frameworks like React.

mbeaudru / modern-js-cheatsheet

Cheatsheet for the JavaScript knowledge you will frequently encounter in modern projects.

Modern JavaScript Cheatsheet

Image Credits: Ahmad Awais ⚡️

If you like this content, you can ping me or follow me on Twitter 👍

Introduction

Motivation

This document is a cheatsheet for JavaScript you will frequently encounter in modern projects and most contemporary sample code.

This guide is not intended to teach you JavaScript from the ground up, but to help developers with basic knowledge who may struggle to get familiar with modern codebases (or let's say to learn React for instance) because of the JavaScript concepts used.

Besides, I will sometimes provide personal tips that may be debatable but will take care to mention that it's a personal recommendation when I do so.

Note: Most of the concepts introduced here are coming from a JavaScript language update (ES2015, often called ES6). You can find new features added by this update here; it's very well done.

Complementary Resources

When you…

cheatography.com

title: Building an AI reply assistant: deciding what it can see and do
description:
While building an AI reply workflow, I kept coming back to a question beyond whether a model could write a sentence: what should a writing assistant be allowed to see and do?

A reply assistant sits close to somebody else’s words. That makes its trust boundary a product decision, not a footnote.

1. Make the request explicit

The user should start a reply or quote-draft action. Read only the relevant post or email context for that request. If a cloud model generates the draft, explain what text or media is sent and who receives it before use.

A useful test: after a quick look at the screen, can a new user say what context is sent, who receives it, and why? If not, the interface needs to explain it more clearly.

2. Keep “draft” separate from “send”

Return words for the person to review. Editing, inserting, copying, or ignoring a draft are different from publishing it; the person decides whether and when to post or send. Inserting text into a composer is not the same as publishing it, and the interface should make that distinction obvious.

A generated reply is a suggestion, not an action taken on someone’s behalf.

3. Give people controls that change the result

Tone, length, language, and personal writing instructions can be more useful than a dozen novelty modes. They let a person shape a draft while making the limits visible: a model can help with a first pass, but the person still owns the words.

4. Be candid about the tradeoff

Human review does not make a cloud tool private by magic. If a service receives writing context or attached media to generate a draft, say so plainly. If someone would not be comfortable sending a conversation for processing, they should not use that workflow for that conversation.

I’m still working through these design questions. If you build browser tools or AI features, where do you draw the line between helpful context and too much access?

title: Gradle Under the Hood: Fighting Incremental Cache Misses in Bytecode Processing
description:
If you have ever written a custom Gradle task to analyze or process compiled bytecode (like custom linters, schema validators, or metadata generators), you have probably encountered a hidden, silent performance killer: the aggressive compiler erasure.

In this first article of our Gradle Under the Hood series, we’ll explore how we re-engineered the incremental tracking of JPersist (a zero-boilerplate JPA build automation suite) to achieve bulletproof UP-TO-DATE execution states, even when the Java compiler tries to destroy your task's cache.

The Naive Approach to Bytecode Tasks

When building a task that processes compiled .class files, the most intuitive setup is to declare the compiler's output directory as your task's @InputDirectory:

abstract class MyBytecodeTask extends DefaultTask {
    @InputDirectory
    abstract DirectoryProperty getCompiledClassesDir()

    @TaskAction
    void execute(InputChanges inputChanges) {
        // Process altered files...
    }
}

You then wire it in your plugin by binding it to the JavaCompile task:

task.getCompiledClassesDir().set(compileJavaTask.flatMap { it.destinationDirectory })

Why this fails in the real world:
Gradle has a magnificent incremental build engine. However, JavaCompile is highly defensive. When a developer alters even a single line of Java source code, JavaCompile often wipes out its entire destination directory (build/classes/java/main) before rebuilding to guarantee no stale classes remain.

For your downstream bytecode task, this folder deletion is catastrophic. Even though you are using Gradle's InputChanges API, the engine sees that the root directory was destroyed and recreated. It panics, concludes that the historical file snapshot graph is non-linear, and forces inputChanges.incremental to evaluate to false. Your task is forced into a heavy, full-pass execution loop on every minor code tweak.

The Solution: Source-Driven Incremental Tracking

To make our query linters and schema validators truly incremental and immune to compiler erasures, we shifted our architectural paradigm: We stopped tracking the volatile compiler output folder and started tracking the stable source code repository layout instead.

Instead of listening to the .class directory, our tasks now listen to sourceSet.java.sourceDirectories as a flat @InputFiles collection wrapper:

abstract class ValidatePersistenceSchema extends DefaultTask {
    @Incremental
    @InputFiles
    @PathSensitive(PathSensitivity.RELATIVE)
    abstract ConfigurableFileCollection getSourceFiles()

    @InputDirectory // Kept as standard non-incremental input
    abstract DirectoryProperty getCompiledClassesDir()
}

Inside our plugin wiring loop, we feed it lazily while filtering out any intermediate or generated build directories:

task.getSourceFiles().from(project.provider {
    sourceSet.java.sourceDirectories.asFileTree.matching {
        exclude { element ->
            element.file.absolutePath.replace('\\', '/').contains(project.layout.buildDirectory.get().asFile.absolutePath.replace('\\', '/'))
        }
    }
})

Mapping Source Deltas to Bytecode Outputs

Because source directories are managed by the developer and are never aggressively wiped out by a compiler task, Gradle's file system snapshot engine maintains a perfect, unbroken lineage of mutations.

When a developer modifies an entity, InputChanges accurately catches exactly one modified .java file. Inside our @TaskAction, we intercept this .java path, compute its relative package structure, and translate it on-the-fly to find the corresponding compiled .class file inside the freshly compiled folder:

@TaskAction
void validate(InputChanges inputChanges) {
    List<String> affectedEntities = []

    if (inputChanges.incremental) {
        inputChanges.getFileChanges(getSourceFiles()).each { change ->
            if (change.file.name.endsWith('.java')) {
                String relativePath = change.normalizedPath
                // Translate com/example/model/User.java -> com.example.model.User
                String className = relativePath.substring(0, relativePath.lastIndexOf('.java')).replace('/', '.')

                if (change.changeType != ChangeType.REMOVED) {
                    affectedEntities.add(className)
                }
            }
        }

        // Fast-Exit Pass: If no active entities were touched, skip heavy DB bootstrapping!
        if (affectedEntities.isEmpty()) return
    } else {
        affectedEntities.addAll(fullDiscoveredEntityList)
    }

    // Submit isolated work wrapper with precisely filtered entity subsets...
}

The Engineering Win

By decoupling task delta tracking from the volatile compilation output graph, we achieved major engineering victories for the JPersist v1.8.0 release pipeline:

  1. Immunity to Directory Purges: Even if JavaCompile erases and rewrites 5,000 class files, our tasks compare the stable source metadata signatures. If only 1 file changed, we only process 1 class binarized stream via ASM.
  2. The Fast-Exit Optimization: If a developer edits a standard Service, Controller, or Utility class that doesn't hold JPA annotations, our tasks process the change stream in under 5 milliseconds and exit before ever spawning database connections or heavy classloaders.

Stay tuned for Part 2, where we’ll dive into ClassLoader Harvesting and how we forced isolated Gradle workers to run seamlessly on headless CI nodes without ever hitting network lookups or requiring mavenLocal() fallbacks!

What are your thoughts on handling aggressive compiler tasks in custom Gradle plugins? Let's discuss in the comments below!

🔗 Check out the JPersist open-source architecture: https://github.com/jpersist/persistence

title: How Does Rust Code Run on a GPU? Tracing cuda-oxide and PTX
description:
I used cuda-oxide to run a vector addition kernel written in Rust on a GPU.

Pass in two arrays and get back their element-wise sums. The calculation is simple, but I wanted to understand what form that Rust function takes before it reaches the GPU.

Among the files generated during the build was some code called PTX. This time, I will read it to see how Rust's thread indexing and array accesses are represented.

What is cuda-oxide?

cuda-oxide is part of NVIDIA's CUDA Rust project. It provides a compiler and related tools for writing kernels for NVIDIA GPUs in Rust. See the official CUDA Rust repository.

The official book introduces it this way:

cuda-oxide is a Rust-to-CUDA compiler that lets you write (SIMT) GPU kernels in safe(ish), idiomatic Rust.

Source: The cuda-oxide Book.

In other words, you can write the actual function that runs on the GPU in idiomatic Rust and compile it. SIMT stands for Single Instruction, Multiple Threads. It is the programming model used in this example, where many threads execute the same kernel.

As of October 2026, CUDA Rust describes itself as an early-stage research project, with its features and APIs still under development. Here, I will focus on a small vector addition example and look at what the Rust code becomes. See the project status.

As someone who writes Rust, I find this a very intriguing project.

Adding arrays: who computes each element?

Here is the kernel we will inspect. A kernel is a function that serves as an entry point for execution on the GPU.

I verified the code and output on November 1, 2026, under the following conditions. I built the vecadd example from cuda-rust commit a0cc6cc0bc18722ec5cdfbea136c118a7c051977 in a source tree separate from my ongoing changes.

Item Verified environment or setting
Host Linux, x86-64
GPU NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti (Compute Capability 12.0)
NVIDIA driver 595.99.02
Rust toolchain nightly-2026-08-28, rustc 1.100.0-nightly (e457a7b0d)
LLVM Version 23.1.0 bundled with the toolchain
Build Release, target sm_120a, ordinary PTX output with bounds checks enabled 
use cuda_device::{DisjointSlice, cuda_module, kernel, thread};

#[cuda_module]
mod kernels {
    use super::*;

    #[kernel]
    pub fn vecadd(a: &[f32], b: &[f32], mut c: DisjointSlice<f32>) {
        let idx = thread::index_1d();
        let idx_raw = idx.get();
        if let Some(c_elem) = c.get_mut(idx) {
            *c_elem = a[idx_raw] + b[idx_raw];
        }
    }
}

This is based on the vecadd example included in NVIDIA's cuda-rust repository. The original code is published under the Apache-2.0 license. See the cuda-rust source.

The calculation is c[i] = a[i] + b[i]. However, there is no for loop inside the function to traverse the whole array.

On a CPU, we could compute the elements sequentially like this:

for i in 0..n {
    c[i] = a[i] + b[i];
}

In this GPU kernel, each thread works out the index of the element it is responsible for and computes that one element. Many threads execute the same kernel.

Thread responsible for element 0: c[0] = a[0] + b[0]
Thread responsible for element 1: c[1] = a[1] + b[1]
Thread responsible for element 2: c[2] = a[2] + b[2]
...

thread::index_1d() produces this index. Its return value, idx, is not just an integer: it has cuda-oxide's ThreadIndex type. idx.get() extracts the integer used to index the input arrays.

On the output side, DisjointSlice accepts this thread index and provides a mutable reference to the element assigned to the thread. If c.get_mut(idx) returns Some, the thread writes its result to that element. I will leave the details of these types aside for now and focus on which elements each thread reads and where it writes.

On the host, meaning the CPU side, the program transfers the input data to GPU buffers, specifies the thread configuration, launches the kernel, and retrieves the result. We need to distinguish the whole program, including that preparation, from the kernel running on the GPU.

PTX is a representation before GPU machine code

So what is the PTX generated from this kernel?

PTX stands for Parallel Thread Execution. It is a virtual instruction set for NVIDIA GPUs. It is not specific to Rust: compilers for languages such as CUDA C++ generate PTX too. See the NVIDIA PTX specification.

PTX contains instruction names and register-like names, but another conversion step remains before we have the machine code the actual GPU executes. You will also encounter the name SASS for the instructions of the physical GPU.

Here, I will use PTX to see how the Rust expression is broken down into operations. I will not treat it as output that already fixes the final machine-instruction count or physical-register allocation.

The vecadd.ptx file starts with these directives:

.version 8.7
.target sm_120a
.address_size 64

They specify the PTX version, target GPU architecture, and address width, respectively. PTX has version and target requirements, so the same file is not necessarily usable with every NVIDIA GPU or driver.

After these directives come the kernel entry point, .visible .entry vecadd(, its parameters, and register-variable declarations. Let's look at what happens in the body.

Where does cuda-oxide connect to rustc?

Before reading the PTX, let's establish the path from Rust source to this point.

cuda-oxide provides a compiler, libraries, and build tools for writing CUDA kernels in Rust. At its center is rustc-codegen-cuda, a custom code generation backend for rustc.

It uses rustc for tasks such as parsing Rust, type checking, and borrow checking. GPU code generation takes the resulting MIR and proceeds by transforming it into other representations. See the cuda-oxide architecture.

The ordinary PTX generation path we are following can be simplified like this:

Rust kernel
    | rustc performs parsing, type checking, borrow checking, and other work
    v
MIR
    | cuda-oxide transforms it using Pliron IR
    v
LLVM IR
    | LLVM's llc generates code with the NVPTX backend
    v
PTX

Pliron is a framework for building and transforming intermediate representations. cuda-oxide uses it to handle representations of Rust MIR and lower them to LLVM IR.

LLVM produces the PTX at the end of this path. cuda-oxide writes out LLVM IR and passes it to LLVM's code generation tool, llc. Here too, LLVM provides the infrastructure for generating code for a different target.

We can break down the roles as follows:

Name Role in this path
rustc Rust analysis, checking, and MIR processing
rustc-codegen-cuda and related crates Extract GPU-side work and transform MIR into LLVM IR
LLVM's llc and NVPTX backend Generate PTX from LLVM IR
cargo-oxide Provide commands for building and related operations

Host-side code in the same file, such as main, goes to the ordinary LLVM backend and becomes CPU code. In this example, the host executable also contains the GPU's PTX.

Calling the body of a #[kernel] function as an ordinary Rust function on the CPU does not move execution onto the GPU. The host uses a launch API to invoke it as a GPU kernel.

Finding one line of Rust in the PTX

For this verification, I built and ran the example from the cuda-oxide workspace, specifying the example and target. --verbose also displays information such as the tools used to generate LLVM IR and PTX.

cargo oxide run vecadd --arch sm_120a --verbose

The final output was as follows. The program compared the results with values calculated on the CPU, and all 1024 elements matched.

✓ SUCCESS: All 1024 elements correct!

The same build generated crates/rustc-codegen-cuda/examples/vecadd/vecadd.ptx. The following excerpts come from that file, with whitespace adjusted for readability.

Working out the element index

First, let's find the instructions related to thread::index_1d(). Omitting an intervening parameter-load instruction gives us this sequence:

mov.u32      %r1, %ctaid.x;
mov.u32      %r2, %ntid.x;
mov.u32      %r3, %tid.x;
mul.wide.u32 %rd11, %r1, %r2;
cvt.u64.u32  %rd12, %r3;
add.s64      %rd13, %rd11, %rd12;

CUDA groups threads into blocks and arranges those blocks in a grid. In one dimension, the global element index is the block index multiplied by the number of threads per block, plus the thread's index within its block. See CUDA's thread hierarchy.

The first three mov instructions read the values used in that calculation.

Special register Value read
%ctaid.x Block index in the x direction
%ntid.x Number of threads per block in the x direction
%tid.x Thread index within the block in the x direction

For example, with 256 threads per block, block index 2, and thread index 7 within the block, the element index is 2 * 256 + 7 = 519.

In the PTX, mul.wide.u32 multiplies two 32-bit values and places the 64-bit result in %rd11. The next cvt converts the thread index within the block to 64 bits, and add.s64 adds the values. %rd13 now holds the element index.

What was a single function call in Rust has become reads of the block and thread coordinates, a multiplication, and an addition.

Names such as %r1 and %rd13 refer to virtual register variables in PTX. We do not need to interpret their numbers as physical GPU register numbers.

From an element index to a memory location

Next come the array accesses.

The index we just calculated is in %rd13, but the later instructions use %rd14. This instruction sits between them:

selp.b64 %rd14, %rd13, -1, %p7;

selp selects between two values according to a condition. If %p7 is true, it places the value of %rd13 in %rd14; otherwise, it selects -1 as an invalid value. In this output, %p7 represents the one-dimensional launch condition: the y and z dimensions of both the grid and the block must all be 1.

When that condition holds, %rd14 contains the element index calculated earlier. One instruction that uses it is:

shl.b64 %rd15, %rd14, 2;

shl is a left shift. Here, it shifts the element index left by two bits, multiplying it by four.

Each element of these arrays is an f32, which occupies four bytes. For element 519, the distance from the start of the array is 519 * 4 = 2076 bytes.

The PTX also adds that distance to the starting addresses. The relevant instructions are:

add.s64 %rd3,  %rd8, %rd15;
add.s64 %rd18, %rd1, %rd15;
add.s64 %rd19, %rd2, %rd15;

In this output, %rd1 points to the start of input a, %rd2 to the start of input b, and %rd8 to the start of output c. Adding the byte offset produces the addresses to read from and write to.

The compact expression a[idx_raw] hides the element size and the address calculation.

Read two values, add them, and write back

Now that we have the addresses, let's look at the calculation. In the actual output, input-address calculations alternate with loads.

add.s64       %rd18, %rd1, %rd15;
ld.global.b32 %r8, [%rd18];
add.s64       %rd19, %rd2, %rd15;
ld.global.b32 %r9, [%rd19];
add.f32       %r10, %r8, %r9;
st.global.b32 [%rd3], %r10;

ld.global.b32 loads 32 bits from global memory. Square brackets, as in [%rd18], indicate an access to the value at that address. The two inputs are loaded into %r8 and %r9.

Next, add.f32 performs a 32-bit floating-point addition, placing the sum in %r10. The .b32 loads handle 32-bit bit patterns, which the addition interprets as f32 values. There is no integer-to-floating-point conversion in between.

Finally, st.global.b32 writes the result to the output address in %rd3. Unlike a load, the bracketed destination appears on the left.

We can now see the work corresponding to this line of Rust:

*c_elem = a[idx_raw] + b[idx_raw];

The addition itself is one instruction, but the surrounding code computes the element index, calculates memory addresses, and reads and writes the values.

Bounds checks remain as instructions too

Around that calculation are instructions that test conditions and branch.

For example, before accessing input a, we find:

ld.param.b64 %rd4, [vecadd_param_1];
setp.ge.u64  %p13, %rd14, %rd4;
@%p13 bra   $L__BB0_5;

In this output, vecadd_param_1 is the length of input a. It is passed as a parameter separate from the starting address.

setp.ge.u64 tests whether the element index in %rd14 is greater than or equal to the length in %rd4 and places the result in the predicate variable %p13. The next instruction, @%p13 bra, branches to the named label if that condition is true.

What is at the destination?

$L__BB0_5:
    trap;

trap aborts execution and notifies the host of an error. In this output, an out-of-bounds access to input a takes this path. Input b has a similar check. The bounds checks associated with Rust's indexing are visible as PTX comparisons and branches. See the PTX trap instruction.

The output is handled differently: the Rust code writes only when c.get_mut(idx) returns Some. Skipping the calculation when the output index is out of bounds and trapping when an input index is out of bounds are two different paths.

The number of GPU threads can be slightly larger than the number of elements. For example, launching four blocks of 256 threads for 1000 elements gives 1024 threads. The extra 24 threads must not write past the end of the array. These index checks have a practical role.

What remains after PTX is generated?

We have read the PTX, but the journey to GPU execution is not finished.

On the path used here, where PTX is passed to the CUDA driver for loading, the driver's JIT compiler translates it into machine code for the target GPU. It can also cache the compiled result for reuse. See NVIDIA's explanation of JIT compilation.

The overall flow is:

Build time
Rust kernel -> MIR -> Pliron IR -> LLVM IR -> PTX
Rust host code -> CPU code
                      |
                      v
           Embedded in the host executable

Run time
The host program starts
    | Pass PTX to the CUDA driver and load the module
    v
Machine code for the target GPU (using JIT compilation or its cache)
    | Launch the kernel from the host
    v
GPU threads compute and write results to memory
    |
    v
The host waits for completion and retrieves the results

There are also paths that build a GPU binary from PTX ahead of time. Here, I am following the path that loads PTX.

Running Rust code on a GPU involves more than sending the Rust source to it. There is checking in rustc, transformation in cuda-oxide, PTX generation in LLVM, and then GPU-specific compilation and launch work.

What we found in the PTX was thread-index acquisition, element-address calculation, two loads, one addition, and a store. That short array expression is becoming readable as the work each GPU thread performs.

title: How to Learn Rust Ownership and Borrowing (Without Fighting the Borrow Checker Forever)
description:
My first week with Rust, I spent most of an evening on one error. I had a Vec<String>, I passed it to a function that printed it, and then I tried to print it again in main. The compiler told me the value had been moved. I added & in random places until it compiled, felt clever for ten minutes, and hit the same wall the next day with a struct.

That's the usual story. People don't quit Rust because of syntax. They quit because ownership feels like a set of arbitrary rules the compiler enforces with error messages, and they try to memorize the fixes instead of the model behind them.

Here's the order I'd learn it in if I started again.

Get the three rules into your head first

The Rust Book states them plainly, and everything else follows from them:

  1. Each value has one owner.
  2. There can only be one owner at a time.
  3. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped.

That's it. Moves, borrows and lifetimes are all consequences. When an error confuses you, ask which of the three rules you just broke. Nine times out of ten the answer is obvious once you look.

Understand moves before you touch references

This is the code that got me:

fn print_all(items: Vec<String>) {
    for item in &items {
        println!("{item}");
    }
}

fn main() {
    let names = vec![String::from("Ada"), String::from("Linus")];
    print_all(names);
    println!("{:?}", names); // error: borrow of moved value
}

Passing names to print_all hands ownership to the function. When print_all returns, its parameter goes out of scope and the vector is dropped. There's nothing left in main to print.

Notice that the same thing does not happen with an i32. Integers, booleans, char and a few others implement Copy, so passing them copies the bits and the original stays usable. String and Vec own heap memory, so they move. Once that difference clicks, a lot of "why does this work here but not there" goes away.

Then learn borrowing as two kinds of permission

The fix for the code above is to borrow instead of move:

fn print_all(items: &[String]) {
    for item in items {
        println!("{item}");
    }
}

fn main() {
    let names = vec![String::from("Ada"), String::from("Linus")];
    print_all(&names);
    println!("{:?}", names); // fine
}

I find it easier to think of references as permissions rather than pointers. &T means "you can look." &mut T means "you can change it, and nobody else can even look while you hold this." You can have as many look-only borrows as you want, or exactly one mutable borrow, never both at the same moment.

The classic error that teaches this:

let mut scores = vec![10, 20, 30];
let first = &scores[0];
scores.push(40); // error: cannot borrow as mutable
println!("{first}");

It feels pedantic until you realize why. push can reallocate the vector, which would leave first pointing at freed memory. In C that compiles and crashes later. Rust refuses up front.

Since the 2018 edition, borrows end at their last use, not at the end of the block (this is called non-lexical lifetimes). Move the println! above the push and it compiles. That one detail explains a lot of code that "shouldn't" work but does.

Leave lifetimes for later

Beginners often try to learn lifetime annotations in week one, and it's a mistake. Most of the time the compiler infers them. You only need to write 'a when a function returns a reference and the compiler can't tell which input it came from:

fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if a.len() > b.len() { a } else { b }
}

Read that as "the result lives at least as long as both inputs." Learn it when you actually hit the error. Not before.

Read the error messages slowly

Rust's compiler errors are unusually good. They point at where the value was moved, where it was borrowed and where you tried to use it again, often with a suggested fix. I used to skim to the red line and start guessing. Reading the whole message, including the notes, fixed more bugs for me than any blog post.

rustc --explain E0382 (or whatever code you got) prints a longer explanation with examples. Worth doing for the first few errors you see repeatedly.

Practice on small programs that force the issue

Toy exercises help. Rustlings has a whole section on move semantics, and it's the fastest way to get reps. After that, build something small where data has to be shared:

  • A to-do CLI that loads tasks from a file into a Vec<Task> and lets you edit them.
  • A word counter that returns a HashMap<&str, usize> borrowing from the input text.
  • A tiny linked list. It's painful on purpose, and it teaches you why Box, Rc and RefCell exist.

When you reach for .clone() to make an error go away, write down why. Sometimes cloning is the right call. Often it's a sign you wanted a borrow.

Make the model stick

My real problem wasn't understanding ownership once. I'd get it after a weekend, take two weeks off for work, and come back to the same moved-value error as if I'd never seen it. The rules are short, but the instinct for applying them fades fast if you don't revisit it.

What helped was keeping a short list of the ideas that kept tripping me up (moves vs Copy, shared vs mutable borrows, borrows ending at last use, when lifetimes need writing) and going back over them after a day, then a few days, then a couple of weeks. That's spaced repetition, and for a mental model like this it beats rereading chapter four every time you get stuck.

I build Recl, and this is the kind of learning it's for. You save a Rust talk from YouTube, a chapter of the Book or a blog post about the borrow checker, it writes a summary of the key points, files it under a topic like "Rust", and brings it back on a spaced repetition schedule so you get quizzed before you forget. A plain notes file and calendar reminders do the same job if you'd rather not use an app. The point is to see it again before the compiler has to remind you.

I build Recl, an AI learning app that saves the videos, reels and articles you learn from, summarizes them, sorts them into topics, and uses spaced repetition so you actually remember them.

title: What Is React?
description:
What Is React?

React is a JavaScript library used to build user interfaces (UI).

It is mainly used to create interactive and dynamic web applications.

For example, websites and applications often have:

  • Buttons
  • Forms
  • Navigation bars
  • Product cards
  • User profiles
  • Interactive pages

React helps developers build and manage these user interfaces more easily.

Why Do We Use React?

When building a large website using only HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, managing the code can become difficult.

React helps by dividing the user interface into smaller, reusable parts called components.

For example:

Website
   │
   ├── Navbar
   ├── Product List
   │      ├── Product Card
   │      ├── Product Card
   │      └── Product Card
   │
   └── Footer

Each part can be created as a separate component.

What Are Components?

A component is a reusable piece of the user interface.

For example:

function Welcome() {
    return <h1>Hello, World!</h1>;
}

This creates a simple React component.

We can use components to build different parts of a website.

React Uses JSX

React commonly uses JSX.

JSX allows us to write HTML-like code inside JavaScript.

Example:

function App() {
    return <h1>Hello, React!</h1>;
}

Although it looks similar to HTML, JSX is written inside JavaScript.

React Can Update the UI

React helps update the user interface when data changes.

For example, if a user clicks a button and a value changes, React can update the relevant part of the screen.

This makes it useful for building interactive applications.

Popular Uses of React

React can be used to build:

  • E-commerce websites
  • Social media applications
  • Dashboards
  • Portfolio websites
  • Single-page applications
  • Interactive web applications

title: Why I replaced looping MP3s with live Web Audio API math for my focus timer (Cadenzato)
description:
Every developer knows the pain of trying to get into a deep coding flow state, throwing on a 3-hour rain or brown noise stream, and getting hit with two problems:

  1. A sudden loud mid-roll ad that shatters your mental stack right when you are debugging a race condition.
  2. Audio loop fatigue. Most ambient focus apps and streams just loop a 60-second MP3 file. Because the human auditory cortex is wired to detect patterns, the moment your ear subconsciously catches the loop seam repeating, your brain wakes up on alert.

On top of that, most visual study timers run unthrottled canvas loops in the background, eating 25% of your GPU and spinning up your laptop fans while your IDE is open.

So I built Cadenzato (https://cadenzato.com), a free, zero-signup focus sanctuary in the browser that solves both problems using pure math and the Web Audio API.

How the procedural audio engine works:

Instead of fetching and looping static audio files, Cadenzato synthesizes every sound wave live in the browser using a custom Web Audio API graph:

  1. Live Brownian Noise (-6dB/octave):
    White noise has equal energy across all frequencies, which sounds like a harsh high-pitched hiss after 20 minutes. By integrating white noise samples over time inside a Float32Array buffer (with a leaky integrator to prevent DC offset drift), we get deep Brown Noise that rolls off high frequencies at -6dB per octave. Because the samples are calculated dynamically, it never repeats a loop.

  2. Procedural Rain & Hearth Fire:
    Rainfall is synthesized by routing pink-filtered noise through dual BiquadFilterNode bandpass stages with randomized micro-transients for individual droplet acoustics. Hearth fire layers low-frequency rumble below 180Hz with stochastic high-passed crackle envelopes.

  3. 40Hz Gamma Binaural & Isochronic Pulse:
    For heavy architectural work, a pair of precision Sine Wave OscillatorNodes (200Hz left ear, 240Hz right ear) creates a gentle 40Hz gamma frequency differential without fatiguing the ear.

How we kept background CPU/GPU at 0%:

A focus tool should never slow down your compiler or IDE. Cadenzato includes 5 live 60fps HTML5 Canvas scenes (Warm Cafe, Botanical Grass, Ocean Drift, Rainfall, and Obsidian), but listens to the browser Page Visibility API (document.hidden). The instant you Alt+Tab back to VS Code or switch windows, the canvas render loop suspends completely to 0% GPU usage while the Web Audio synthesizer continues running on its dedicated audio thread.

No accounts, no ads, no paywalls:

You can open it, press Space to start a 50/10 or 90/15 deep work block, mix your audio channels, and get straight to coding.
