title: Discriminated Unions in TypeScript
description:
Earlier, we looked at how custom type guards (value is Type) let you manually inspect unknown data and teach TypeScript its shape. But what if you have a set of known object types that share a common property?

Enter Discriminated Unions (sometimes called tagged unions or algebraic data types). They are one of the most powerful patterns in TypeScript because TypeScript does the type narrowing for you automatically—no custom guard function required.

1. What is a Discriminated Union?

A discriminated union is a combination of three things:

  1. Types with a common property (the discriminant or "tag"), where each type has a unique literal type for that property.
  2. A union of those types.
  3. A conditional check (like a switch statement) on that discriminant property.

Let’s see it in action with a classic real-world scenario: asynchronous state management.

2. Practical Example: State Management

Imagine you are building a component that fetches data from an API. At any given moment, your state can be in one of three phases: Loading, Success, or Error.

If you lump everything into one giant interface with optional fields (data?: User, error?: string), you open the door to impossible states (like having both data and an error, or neither).

Instead, model them as a discriminated union using a status tag:

// 1. Define individual state shapes with a unique literal `status` property
interface IdleState {
  status: "idle";
}

interface LoadingState {
  status: "loading";
}

interface SuccessState {
  status: "success";
  data: { id: number; name: string }; // Only exists on success!
}

interface ErrorState {
  status: "error";
  error: Error; // Only exists on error!
}

// 2. Combine them into a Union type
type FetchState = IdleState | LoadingState | SuccessState | ErrorState;

3. Automatic Narrowing in Action

When you consume a discriminated union, you can use a simple switch or if statement checking the status tag. Watch how TypeScript's control flow analysis automatically figures out what properties are safe to access:

function renderUI(state: FetchState) {
  // TypeScript knows `state` could be any of the 4 types

  switch (state.status) {
    case "idle":
      return "<p>Press button to fetch.</p>";

    case "loading":
      return "<p>Loading data...</p>";

    case "success":
      // 🚀 MAGIC: TypeScript automatically knows `state` is `SuccessState` here!
      // You have full type safety accessing `state.data`.
      return `<div>Welcome, ${state.data.name}</div>`;

    case "error":
      // TypeScript knows `state` is `ErrorState` here.
      // You have safe access to `state.error`.
      return `<p class="error">Error: ${state.error.message}</p>`;
  }
}

No as SuccessState type assertions, no manual in checks, and no runtime ambiguity. The literal type of status tells TypeScript precisely which branch of reality your code is operating in.

4. Pro-Tip: Exhaustiveness Checking with never

What happens if you add a new state later (like RetryingState), but forget to update your switch statement? In JavaScript, your UI might silently fail or render nothing.

You can force TypeScript to catch missing cases at compile time using the never type:

function assertNever(x: never): never {
  throw new Error(`Unexpected object: ${JSON.stringify(x)}`);
}

function renderUI(state: FetchState) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case "idle": return "...";
    case "loading": return "...";
    case "success": return "...";
    case "error": return "...";

    // If you add a new union member and forget a case, 
    // TypeScript will throw a compile error right here because `state` 
    // won't narrow to `never`!
    default:
      return assertNever(state); 
  }
}

Summary

  • Custom Type Guards are your best tool when dealing with untrusted, unstructured data coming from the outside world (unknown inputs).
  • Discriminated Unions are your best tool when designing internal application logic, state machines, and data structures where you control the shapes.

title: Spring Boot App Is Running, but CloudWatch Shows No Custom Metrics. Here's How to Debug It.
description:
Your Spring Boot application is running on Amazon ECS. API requests are succeeding, business operations are executing, and the application logs look normal.

But when you open Amazon CloudWatch, the custom metrics you expected to see are missing.

You check the dashboard. No data.

You check the metric namespace. Nothing appears.

You wait a few minutes and refresh. Still nothing.

Where should you start debugging?

The problem could be in the application, Micrometer configuration, metric publishing, AWS permissions, network connectivity, or the way you are querying CloudWatch.

In this article, we'll build a small example and follow the complete path from recording a metric in Spring Boot to verifying it in CloudWatch.

By the end, you'll have a systematic troubleshooting process you can reuse in your own applications.

1. Understand the complete metrics flow

Before changing any configuration, understand how a custom application metric reaches CloudWatch.

Spring Boot Application
        |
        v
Business Operation
        |
        v
Micrometer Counter / Timer
        |
        v
MeterRegistry
        |
        v
CloudWatch Registry
        |
        v
CloudWatch PutMetricData API
        |
        v
Amazon CloudWatch Metrics
        |
        +------> Dashboard
        |
        +------> Alarm

Each component has a different responsibility.

  • Business operation: The event you want to measure, such as a successfully created order.
  • Micrometer: Provides a consistent API for recording application metrics.
  • MeterRegistry: Holds and manages the meters registered by your application.
  • CloudWatch registry: Exports supported Micrometer measurements to AWS.
  • CloudWatch: Stores the published metric data and makes it available for querying, visualization, and alarms.

A metric being recorded in Java does not automatically mean it has been published to CloudWatch.

Similarly, a metric existing in CloudWatch does not automatically mean your dashboard is configured to display it.

This distinction is the foundation of the debugging process.

2. Understand SimpleMeterRegistry versus CloudWatchMeterRegistry

One of the first things to investigate is the MeterRegistry used by your application.

Micrometer provides different registry implementations for different purposes.

SimpleMeterRegistry

SimpleMeterRegistry stores the latest values of meters in memory. It does not export those measurements to an external monitoring system.

For example:

SimpleMeterRegistry registry = new SimpleMeterRegistry();

Counter counter = Counter.builder("orders.created")
        .register(registry);

counter.increment();

System.out.println(counter.count());

The counter value increases locally, but this code does not send the metric to CloudWatch.

This registry is useful for simple tests and local experimentation.

CloudWatchMeterRegistry

CloudWatchMeterRegistry is the Micrometer registry implementation for publishing supported metrics to Amazon CloudWatch.

However, adding a dependency alone is not sufficient in every Spring application. You also need the appropriate registry configuration and AWS client credentials, permissions, and Region.

What happens in Spring Boot?

Spring Boot Actuator integrates with Micrometer and can configure a composite registry containing the available registry implementations.

When a CloudWatch-compatible registry is properly configured, metrics recorded through the injected MeterRegistry can be exported through that registry.

If your application is only recording to an in-memory registry, there is no CloudWatch publishing path.

Documentation:

  • Micrometer registry concepts
  • Spring Boot Actuator metrics
  • Micrometer CloudWatch integration

3. Create a simple Spring Boot example

Let's create a small example that records a custom metric whenever a demo order operation succeeds.

The example deliberately avoids a database so that we can isolate metric recording and publishing from business logic.

Record the metric 

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.Counter;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final Counter ordersCreated;

    public OrderService(MeterRegistry registry) {
        this.ordersCreated = Counter.builder("orders.created")
                .description("Number of successful demo order operations")
                .register(registry);
    }

    public void createOrder() {

        // Replace this with the actual business operation.

        ordersCreated.increment();
    }
}

Here, we register a counter named orders.created.

Every time createOrder() completes its intended operation, the counter increments.

In a real application, the metric should reflect a clearly defined business event. If the operation involves a database transaction, be careful not to count an order as successfully committed before the transaction actually commits.

Expose a demo endpoint 

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orderService;

    public OrderController(OrderService orderService) {
        this.orderService = orderService;
    }

    @PostMapping("/orders/demo")
    public String createOrder() {
        orderService.createOrder();
        return "Demo order operation completed";
    }
}

After starting the application, send a POST request to:

POST /orders/demo

For example, using curl:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/orders/demo

Each successful request invokes the service and increments the counter.

At this point, we have demonstrated metric recording. We have not yet proved that the metric reaches CloudWatch.

4. Configure CloudWatch publishing

For this example, assume you're using:

  • Java and Spring Boot 3.x.
  • A compatible Spring Cloud AWS 3.x release.
  • Micrometer's CloudWatch registry.
  • AWS SDK for Java 2.x through the supported integration.

Use compatible dependency versions and the Spring Cloud AWS Bill of Materials (BOM). Do not mix incompatible major versions just to make the dependencies resolve.

Add the dependencies

For Maven, the relevant dependencies include the following:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.awspring.cloud</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-cloud-aws-starter</artifactId>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
    <artifactId>micrometer-registry-cloudwatch2</artifactId>
</dependency>

Import the compatible Spring Cloud AWS BOM in dependencyManagement and use Spring Boot's dependency management for the versions they manage.

For example, the Spring Cloud AWS BOM has this structure:

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>io.awspring.cloud</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-cloud-aws-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>${spring-cloud-aws.version}</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

Define spring-cloud-aws.version as a release compatible with your Spring Boot version. The placeholder above is intentional; select the version using the official compatibility guidance.

Spring Cloud AWS provides the Spring Boot auto-configuration for the Micrometer CloudWatch integration.

References:

  • Spring Cloud AWS documentation
  • Micrometer CloudWatch dependency and configuration

Configure application.yml

For Spring Cloud AWS 3.x, a configuration example is:

spring:
  cloud:
    aws:
      cloudwatch:
        enabled: true
        region: us-east-1

management:
  cloudwatch:
    metrics:
      export:
        namespace: Demo/OrderService
        step: 1m

Replace us-east-1 with your AWS Region.

The namespace Demo/OrderService is an example. Choose a namespace that identifies your application or service.

The step: 1m setting configures the publishing interval to one minute. Allow additional time for the data to become available after publishing.

Important: Spring Cloud AWS 3.x uses management.cloudwatch.metrics.export.* properties. Older Spring Cloud AWS versions use different property names. If you're using a different release family, consult the documentation for that exact version instead of copying this configuration unchanged.

5. Verify that the application records the metric

Before investigating AWS, verify that the application actually records the metric.

Spring Boot Actuator provides a metrics endpoint that can help with this check.

For local debugging, you can expose the health and metrics endpoints in application.yml:

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,metrics

If your configuration already contains a management section, merge the settings rather than replacing unrelated properties.

Restart the application and invoke the demo endpoint several times.

Then query:

curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/orders.created

The response should contain information about the registered meter and its measurements. After invoking the endpoint multiple times, check the counter's current value.

If the metric is missing from Actuator, investigate the application first:

  • Is the relevant service method actually being called?
  • Is the counter registered under the name you expect?
  • Is the application using the MeterRegistry injected by Spring?
  • Is a different registry or metric filter involved?
  • Did the application start with the expected configuration?

If the metric is visible through Actuator, you've established that the application can record it locally. You still need to verify external publishing separately.

Security note: Do not expose Actuator metrics publicly without appropriate access controls. Keep diagnostic endpoints internal or restrict them to authorized users.

6. Check AWS credentials and IAM permissions

A CloudWatch registry needs AWS credentials with permission to publish metric data.

When the application runs on Amazon ECS, distinguish between the two IAM roles.

ECS task role

The task role supplies AWS permissions to application code running inside the task.

For direct CloudWatch metric publishing by the application, this is generally the role that needs the cloudwatch:PutMetricData permission.

ECS task execution role

The execution role is used by the ECS agent for tasks such as pulling container images from Amazon ECR and sending container logs through configured logging integrations.

It is not automatically the identity used by your application for CloudWatch metric publishing.

Granting a permission to the execution role will not fix missing application metrics if the application is using the task role instead.

Example IAM policy

For a dedicated custom namespace, a policy can be restricted using CloudWatch's namespace condition key:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "cloudwatch:PutMetricData",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "cloudwatch:namespace": "Demo/OrderService"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

This is an example policy for the namespace used in this tutorial. Adjust it to your requirements and verify any additional organizational policies.

CloudWatch metric publishing does not support resource-level restriction in the usual way, so Resource: "*" is used here with a namespace condition.

Avoid hardcoding AWS access keys in source code, container images, or configuration files. Use the ECS task role and the AWS SDK's supported credential provider chain.

If you receive an authorization error, check:

  1. Which IAM role the task is actually using.
  2. Whether that role has cloudwatch:PutMetricData.
  3. Whether a namespace condition matches the configured namespace.
  4. Whether an AWS Organizations service control policy, permissions boundary, or other policy denies the request.

Reference: IAM roles for Amazon ECS tasks.

7. Check network connectivity from ECS

Correct IAM permissions are not enough if the application cannot reach the CloudWatch API.

This matters especially when an ECS task runs in a private subnet.

Check whether the task has a supported network path to the CloudWatch monitoring API. Depending on your architecture, this might be through a NAT gateway or an appropriate VPC interface endpoint.

Also verify:

  • DNS resolution.
  • Security group egress rules.
  • Network ACL rules.
  • VPC endpoint configuration and policies, if applicable.
  • Application logs for connection timeouts or endpoint errors.

Do not assume that access to CloudWatch Logs proves that access to the CloudWatch metrics API is working. They are different API endpoints and may have different network paths and permissions.

8. Check the CloudWatch Region and namespace

Suppose your application publishes to us-east-1, but you're viewing CloudWatch in eu-west-1.

The metric will not appear in the Region you're viewing.

Verify the following values:

Setting What to verify
AWS Region The Region configured for the CloudWatch client
Console Region The Region selected in the CloudWatch console
Namespace The configured custom namespace
Metric name The name registered and exported by the application
Dimensions The dimension names and values associated with the published series

Custom metrics are identified by their namespace, metric name, and dimensions.

For example, a metric with Environment=dev is a different time series from one with Environment=prod.

If you add dimensions through registry configuration, filters, or instrumentation, use the correct dimension combination when querying the metric.

Avoid high-cardinality dimensions such as user IDs, order IDs, request IDs, or arbitrary URLs. Every unique combination can create additional metric series and increase monitoring costs.

9. Verify that CloudWatch has received the metric

Once the application has recorded the metric and the registry has had time to publish it, query CloudWatch directly.

You can use the AWS CLI:

aws cloudwatch list-metrics \
  --namespace "Demo/OrderService" \
  --metric-name "orders.created" \
  --region us-east-1

Replace the namespace, metric name, and Region with your actual values.

This command helps determine whether CloudWatch lists the metric.

What if the command returns no results?

Do not immediately conclude that publishing failed.

AWS documents that a newly created metric can take up to 15 minutes to appear through ListMetrics. Statistics may be queryable sooner using GetMetricData or GetMetricStatistics.

Also note that ListMetrics does not return metrics that have not reported data in the past two weeks.

Therefore, check the following:

  • Did the publishing interval elapse?
  • Did the application log any publishing errors?
  • Are the namespace and Region correct?
  • Is the metric name correct?
  • Are you querying from the correct AWS account?
  • Does the metric have dimensions that you haven't accounted for?

You can also inspect metric statistics with a command such as:

aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics \
  --namespace "Demo/OrderService" \
  --metric-name "orders.created" \
  --start-time 2026-11-01T00:00:00Z \
  --end-time 2026-11-01T01:00:00Z \
  --period 60 \
  --statistics Sum \
  --region us-east-1

Important: The dates above are illustrative. Replace them with a UTC time window that covers your actual test. If your metric has dimensions, include the exact dimension combination in the query.

The Sum statistic is appropriate only when it matches the meaning of the published datapoints. For counters exported by a registry, inspect the registry's publishing semantics and actual CloudWatch datapoints rather than assuming that summing cumulative values always gives the number of events.

References:

  • CloudWatch ListMetrics API
  • CloudWatch GetMetricStatistics API

10. The metric exists, but the dashboard still shows no data

A CloudWatch dashboard visualizes the metric series selected in its widget. It does not create the metric itself.

If the metric can be queried but the dashboard is blank, inspect the dashboard configuration.

Check the selected metric

Verify that the widget points to the correct:

  • Namespace.
  • Metric name.
  • Dimension combination.
  • Region.

Check the time range

The dashboard might be displaying a time range that does not contain your test requests.

Choose a range that includes the time when you invoked the demo endpoint and when the registry published its data.

Check the period and statistic

The metric's publishing interval and the widget's aggregation period are related but are not necessarily the same setting.

Select a period that makes sense for the metric's publishing frequency and the time range being displayed.

For event counters, use a statistic that correctly represents the published values. For latency measurements, choose a statistic appropriate for the question you're trying to answer, such as average or a supported percentile.

Check dimensions

If the metric has dimensions, the dashboard must query the correct series. A mismatch in dimension values can make a valid metric appear to be missing.

The quickest diagnostic sequence is:

  1. Confirm that the metric is visible through Actuator.
  2. Confirm that CloudWatch has received it.
  3. Query the metric's data.
  4. Only then troubleshoot the dashboard widget.

This separates metric collection problems from visualization problems.

11. What about CloudWatch alarms?

After confirming that a metric is published correctly, you can create an alarm to monitor it.

However, a valid metric does not guarantee that an alarm will transition to ALARM.

Check the following:

  • The alarm references the correct namespace, metric name, and dimensions.
  • The statistic matches the meaning of the published measurements.
  • The threshold and comparison operator are correct.
  • The period and evaluation periods match the intended detection behavior.
  • Missing-data treatment is appropriate for the metric.
  • The alarm has enough data to evaluate its condition.
  • Any notification action is configured and enabled.

For example, a counter that records failed business operations can be useful for monitoring errors. But the alarm threshold should reflect the expected volume and the way the metric is aggregated.

An alarm in INSUFFICIENT_DATA may not have enough datapoints to evaluate its condition. Missing data should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that the application is healthy.

For a low-traffic application, the absence of events can be normal. For a continuously running service, the absence of expected telemetry may itself warrant investigation.

12. Common symptoms and their likely causes

Use this table as a quick reference when debugging a real service.

Symptom What to investigate first
Application starts, but no custom metrics appear Registry dependency, initialization, and publishing configuration
Actuator shows the metric, but CloudWatch does not CloudWatch registry, publishing errors, IAM, Region, and network connectivity
Publishing fails with an authorization error ECS task role, cloudwatch:PutMetricData, and applicable policy conditions
Publishing times out Network path, DNS, VPC endpoint, or egress configuration
Metrics appear in another Region Registry Region versus console Region
Some metric series appear, but others do not Registration, metric filters, dimensions, and publishing errors
CloudWatch has data, but the dashboard is blank Widget configuration, time range, Region, dimensions, and statistic
Alarm remains in INSUFFICIENT_DATA Evaluation period, missing data, and available datapoints
Metric is missing from ListMetrics immediately after publishing Allow for metric discovery delay and query statistics separately

13. A repeatable debugging checklist

When custom metrics are missing from CloudWatch, follow this order instead of changing several configurations at once.

  1. Reproduce the problem: Invoke the operation that should generate the metric.
  2. Verify application recording: Use Actuator or a test to confirm that the meter exists and changes.
  3. Verify registry configuration: Confirm that a CloudWatch-compatible registry is configured and active.
  4. Inspect publishing errors: Check the application logs for AWS API, credentials, or configuration errors.
  5. Verify the ECS task role: Confirm the identity and permissions used by the application.
  6. Check network connectivity: Ensure the task can reach the CloudWatch monitoring API.
  7. Verify Region and namespace: Compare the application configuration with the CloudWatch console.
  8. Wait for publishing and ingestion: Account for the registry step and CloudWatch visibility delay.
  9. Query the metric directly: Use the console or AWS CLI to verify that data exists.
  10. Troubleshoot the dashboard: Check dimensions, time range, period, and statistic.
  11. Validate the alarm: Confirm the threshold, evaluation periods, missing-data behavior, and notification actions.

This sequence helps isolate the failure at the correct layer.

Conclusion

A Spring Boot application can run successfully while its custom metrics remain unavailable in CloudWatch.

The important thing is to distinguish between recording a metric, publishing it to AWS, querying the resulting data, and displaying it on a dashboard.

Once you understand these stages, troubleshooting becomes a systematic process rather than trial and error.

Start with the application and its active registry. Then verify the publishing configuration, AWS permissions, and network path. Confirm the metric exists in CloudWatch before investigating dashboards and alarms.

That approach is useful not only for Spring Boot applications running on ECS, but also for other Java services that publish custom metrics to CloudWatch.

Official references

  • Micrometer registry concepts
  • Spring Boot Actuator metrics
  • Micrometer CloudWatch integration
  • Spring Cloud AWS documentation
  • ECS task IAM roles
  • CloudWatch ListMetrics API
  • CloudWatch GetMetricStatistics API

Have you encountered a situation where your Spring Boot application was healthy but its CloudWatch metrics were missing? What was the root cause? Share your experience in the comments.

title: How to Plan a Website Structure Before Development
description:
A sitemap drawn after the design is often a record of decisions that have already been made. A useful site structure starts earlier: it connects visitor tasks to pages, content types, navigation, and the work needed to launch each part.

The output should be understandable to a designer, developer, content editor, and project owner. It need not begin as a polished diagram. A shared table, a simple hierarchy, and a few realistic task flows can expose missing content and confusing labels before they become expensive to change.

Separate the artifacts

These pieces describe different aspects of the same site:

  • A page inventory records what exists or is planned, why it exists, who owns it, and its status.
  • A hierarchy groups pages and shows their primary relationships.
  • Navigation and contextual links show how a person can move between pages.
  • A content model describes recurring objects and fields, such as services, products, or articles.
  • URLs and migration mappings identify addresses and record what should happen when an existing address changes.

A working page map is not the same artifact as an XML sitemap used by search engines. Also, an item's URL path does not need to reproduce every menu relationship. Agree on each artifact deliberately rather than using one diagram to answer every question.

Start with journeys, not department names

Write the organization's objective and the visitor's task separately. “Receive inquiries” is a business objective. “Understand the repair options and find a way to book” is a visitor task.

List the information needed to complete each task and the likely starting points. Someone may enter on a specific service page from a search result, arrive at the homepage from a recommendation, or return directly to a contact page. A design that only works when everyone starts at the homepage will miss those other routes.

Use actual questions from customer support, interviews, site search, or existing analytics when available. If those sources don't exist yet, record assumptions as assumptions. Ask stakeholders what they need the site to support, then validate the language and paths with representative users.

Build an inventory with purpose and ownership

The following is a fictional example for a bicycle workshop. It illustrates a planning method; it does not describe a real business or measured behavior.

ID Page Visitor task Related page Launch?
P01 Home Understand the offering and choose a path Services and contact Yes
P02 Services Compare available work Individual services Yes
P03 Bike inspection Understand scope and terms Booking Yes
P04 Maintenance Choose an appropriate service Booking Yes
P05 Booking Select a way to contact the workshop Services and contact Yes
P06 Contact Find location and hours Main navigation Yes
P07 Care guides Learn to maintain a bicycle Related services Later

Add the content owner, source materials, dependencies, and acceptance criteria to your real inventory. For an existing site, include the current URL and a proposed decision: keep, update, merge, or remove after review.

Ask a simple question of every row: who needs this page, and what will they do after reading it? A page with no clear purpose or owner might be unnecessary in the first release. On the other hand, a small but essential page may be missing from a diagram built only around marketing sections.

Group by visitor language

Organize content according to tasks and concepts your audience recognizes. Internal reporting lines may not be useful navigation labels. “Services,” “Delivery,” and “Contact” may be clearer than an organization's internal team names, but the right words should be checked with the people who will use them.

For the fictional workshop, one possible primary hierarchy is:

  • Home
  • Services
    • Bike inspection
    • Maintenance
  • Booking
  • Contact
  • Care guides, in a later phase

The tree describes primary relationships, not all permitted journeys. A service page can link directly to booking, and a guide can link to a relevant service where appropriate. Do not add levels merely to make a diagram symmetrical, and don't treat a particular number of clicks as proof of usability. Test whether the available choices make sense for the task.

Design paths beyond the menu

Take three important tasks and write the route from a plausible entry page to a result. For example:

  1. A visitor lands on “Bike inspection.”
  2. They can see the actual scope and terms.
  3. They follow a clearly labeled link to booking.
  4. They choose an available contact method.
  5. The system explains what happened after submission or what to do if it failed.

Now try the same task from the services listing and the contact page. Can the visitor return to compare services without losing context? Are there pages with no sensible onward route?

Main navigation should expose the stable major directions. Contextual links support a specific task within a page. Search and filters can help with larger collections, but they don't repair unclear category names or incomplete content. On narrow screens and with keyboard navigation, preserve access to the same important destinations and check the labels and focus order.

Define page types before estimating templates

A “service” might contain a title, summary, work included, terms, relevant images, and a booking link. A “product” might require a name, price, images, availability, and attributes used in filters. An “article” might have a title, body, author when applicable, date, and related content.

For every field, record whether it is required, who can edit it, where the information comes from, and what happens when it is missing. A template can serve many pages without making their content identical. List relationships too: for example, which service a guide refers to, or which categories can contain a product.

This model reveals dependencies. A category filter cannot be designed responsibly before someone agrees on the underlying product attributes. A service page may depend on approved terms. An import may require existing records to be cleaned up before development can be estimated.

Set URL rules and plan a migration

Agree on readable, stable addressing rules for new pages and on who can change them. For an existing site, prepare a mapping from old addresses to their intended new destinations. Decide which pages remain, merge, or retire; implement suitable redirects where appropriate and test the final destinations and internal links.

Similar or filtered URLs deserve a decision rather than an automatic proliferation of pages. Identify which variations have a user purpose and coordinate search requirements with the navigation design. Search visibility is one consideration; it should not override the need for a coherent visitor journey.

Test the structure before visual design is final

Give participants who resemble the intended audience a task such as “Find the conditions for a bike inspection.” Let them choose among the proposed labels without coaching them. A text-only hierarchy or simple clickable prototype is enough to reveal many naming and grouping problems.

Record where a participant starts, which labels they choose, and what they expected to find. If several people look in the same unexpected place, consider whether the label, grouping, or missing cross-link caused the confusion. Revise the specific issue and test again.

A small qualitative session helps uncover problems; it is not statistical proof that every visitor will behave the same way. Include real content lengths, narrow screens, and keyboard use when checking a more complete prototype.

Hand off a maintained decision set

Before development begins, provide the team with:

  • An agreed page inventory and hierarchy with stable identifiers.
  • Key tasks, entry points, links, and expected results.
  • Content types, required fields, relationships, and editing responsibilities.
  • URL conventions and a migration map when replacing an existing site.
  • Content sources, external dependencies, and the scope of the first release.
  • Acceptance tasks for navigation, search, forms, and smaller screens.

Assign an owner for the map and a process for new pages after launch. A structure can evolve, but unreviewed additions should not quietly create duplicate sections or leave important content unlinked.

Start with one page inventory and three real visitor tasks. A clear route through a modest first release is more useful than a large diagram whose pages have no content owner or purpose.

title: How I Built a 100% Client-Side Bank Statement Redactor Using HTML5 Canvas & WebAssembly
description:
When applying for an apartment lease, mortgage underwriting, or a travel visa, almost everyone is asked to submit 2 to 3 months of bank statements or payslips.

However, sharing unredacted financial records exposes sensitive Personally Identifiable Information (PII)—including full 10–16 digit account numbers, 9-digit ABA routing transit codes, and private transaction histories.

Most users try to protect themselves using two flawed methods:

  1. Uploading confidential files to free online PDF editors: This sends sensitive financial data to unknown third-party cloud servers.

  2. Drawing black rectangles in preview software: This merely places a cosmetic overlay on top of vector text. Anyone can simply copy-paste or inspect the text underneath.

To solve this, I built BankXLS—a privacy-first, zero-cloud financial document redactor that operates 100% inside the user's browser using HTML5 Canvas, WebAssembly (Wasm), and destructive raster flattening.

Here is an architectural breakdown of how it works under the hood.

The Core Architecture: Why "Cosmetic" Redaction Fails

A standard digital PDF contains multiple distinct layers:

  • Vector text streams (raw characters, fonts, and bounding boxes)
  • Metadata streams (author, software, creation dates)
  • Form field definitions (AcroForms / XFA)
  • Raster image assets

If you draw a black rectangle using a basic PDF viewer, the underlying character codes remain completely intact in the content stream.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  [ Visual Blackout Box (Cosmetic Layer) ]    │  <-- Visible on screen
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Account No: 4821 9081 2291                  │  <-- Still selectable!
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

To achieve true, unrecoverable redaction without sending data to an external server, the pipeline must perform destructive pixel rasterization directly in browser RAM.

Step 1: Client-Side PDF Parsing via WebAssembly (pdf.js)

Instead of parsing files on a Node.js or Python backend, we read the uploaded document using the HTML5 File API and pass the raw ArrayBuffer directly to Mozilla's pdf.js worker, compiled to WebAssembly:

// Read document locally into memory
const fileBuffer = await file.arrayBuffer();

// Initialize client-side PDF document
const loadingTask = pdfjsLib.getDocument({ data: fileBuffer });
const pdfDoc = await loadingTask.promise;
const numPages = pdfDoc.numPages;

Because this worker runs entirely in a client-side Web Worker thread, zero bytes leave the user's machine.

Step 2: Interactive Coordinate Mapping with HTML5 Canvas

Each page of the PDF is rendered onto an off-screen HTML5 element at 2.0x device pixel ratio to maintain razor-sharp text fidelity.

When the user selects an area to blackout (such as an account number or balance column), we compute normalized bounding coordinates:

interface RedactionBox {
  pageNumber: number;
  x: number;      // Normalized (0.0 to 1.0)
  y: number;      // Normalized (0.0 to 1.0)
  width: number;
  height: number;
}

By normalizing coordinates relative to viewport dimensions, user-drawn redactions remain pixel-perfect across responsive mobile screens, tablets, and desktop displays.

Step 3: Destructive Canvas Rasterization (Burning the Redactions)

This is where the magic happens. Rather than appending visual annotation objects to a PDF syntax tree, we composite the redaction bounding boxes directly into the 2D rendering context:

// Grab the 2D rendering context of the rasterized page
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d', { willReadFrequently: true });

if (ctx) {
  // Burn solid opaque black pixels directly over sensitive coordinates
  ctx.fillStyle = '#000000';
  ctx.fillRect(
    box.x * canvas.width,
    box.y * canvas.height,
    box.width * canvas.width,
    box.height * canvas.height
  );
}

At this stage, the underlying vector characters are permanently replaced by black RGB pixels (0, 0, 0). The character codes cease to exist in memory.

Step 4: Flattening and Assembling the Clean PDF

Once the redactions are burned into the canvas, we export the canvas buffer as high-quality lossless image slices and rebuild an unalterable, flattened PDF using jspdf:

import { jsPDF } from 'jspdf';

const exportDoc = new jsPDF({
  orientation: canvas.width > canvas.height ? 'landscape' : 'portrait',
  unit: 'pt',
  format: [canvas.width, canvas.height]
});

// Convert canvas to image data
const imgData = canvas.toDataURL('image/jpeg', 0.95);

// Add the flattened raster layer to the new PDF
exportDoc.addImage(imgData, 'JPEG', 0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
exportDoc.save('redacted_statement.pdf');

The resulting document:

  1. Contains zero selectable text in redacted areas.
  2. Has all original metadata, author tags, and font objects stripped.
  3. Cannot be reversed or inspected using Adobe Acrobat or developer tools.

What We Learned About Web Privacy in 2026

  1. Users care deeply about financial privacy: Many people hesitate to use cloud tools for bank statements and tax filings. Providing a client-only architecture with zero server logs immediately establishes user trust.
  2. Modern WebAssembly and Canvas engines are extraordinarily fast: Parsing and flattening a 5-page bank statement in client memory takes less than 800 milliseconds on a standard smartphone.
  3. Privacy by design simplifies compliance: By refusing to store user documents on a database, GDPR and CCPA data retention liabilities drop to zero.

If you want to test the live implementation or securely sanitize your own bank statements, payslips, or invoices, feel free to try the live tool at BankXLS.

Have you built privacy-first client-side web tools? What libraries do you prefer for in-browser PDF manipulation? Let me know in the comments!

title: I built a client-side cache in Rust and compiled it to WebAssembly
description:
I built Blaze Cache, a high-performance client-side caching library written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly.

The goal was simple: make browser caching fast, predictable, and easy to integrate — without turning it into a heavy framework.

Why Wasm?

Most browser caches are pure JavaScript. That works, but I wanted:

  • More predictable performance
  • A cleaner core data structure
  • A single engine that multiple adapters could share

So the hot path (storage, TTL, tags, eviction) runs in Rust → Wasm. After initialization, get and set are fully synchronous.

What it supports

  • Synchronous reads and writes after init
  • SIEVE eviction
  • TTL + tag-based invalidation
  • Optional IndexedDB persistence
  • Typed event system
  • Adapters for:
    • Axios
    • fetch
    • TanStack Query
    • SWR

Example 


ts
import { createCache } from '@blaze-cache/core'

const cache = await createCache({ capacity: 1000 })

cache.set('user:42', { name: 'Ada' }, { ttlMs: 30_000, tags: ['user'] })
cache.get('user:42')
cache.invalidateTags('user')

title: When the eSIM Doesn't Connect: Designing the Activation-Failure Support Path in Your App
description:
Most eSIM integrations are designed around the happy path: the user picks a plan, pays, scans a QR code or taps "Install", and lands abroad with data. Then the first support ticket arrives: "I installed the eSIM but it doesn't work." If your app has nothing to say at that moment, the user blames your brand, not the connectivity supplier behind it.
This post is about designing that failure path on purpose: what you can check before purchase, which signals tell you where a profile actually is, the usual causes of "installed but no data", what to show in-app, what to log, and when to refund or re-issue automatically.

1. Prevent the cheapest failures before checkout

A surprising share of activation problems are really compatibility problems that were sold anyway. Before the user pays:

  • Check eSIM support on the device. In a native app you have better options than on the web. Where you can read the device's EID (the eUICC identifier), store it with the order: it proves the device has an eUICC and helps support later. On the web you mostly can't detect eSIM support reliably, so fall back to a device allow-list plus a clear "How to check if my phone supports eSIM" step.- Warn about carrier locks. A locked phone may have an eUICC and still refuse a third-party profile. You usually can't detect this, so say it plainly in the checkout copy.- Set expectations on timing. Tell the user to install before travelling (on Wi-Fi), and to switch data to the eSIM line only on arrival.## 2. Track profile state from real signals, not from "the user clicked Install" Your backend sees an order. The SM-DP+ (the server that prepares and delivers the eSIM profile) sees a download. The phone sees a profile that is installed, enabled or deleted. These are different states, and support needs all of them. Under the GSMA consumer eSIM spec, the device sends notifications back to the SM-DP+ for events like install, enable, disable and delete. Whether you get those events depends on your connectivity supplier's API: many expose them as webhooks or as a profile-status endpoint. Model them explicitly:
  • ORDERED - paid, profile reserved, activation code issued- DOWNLOADED / INSTALLED - the device fetched and installed the profile- ENABLED - the profile is active on the device- ATTACHED / IN_USE - the network has seen the line, or data usage has started (from usage records, if your supplier exposes them)- DELETED - removed from the device (important: many profiles can't be reinstalled after deletion)The gap that generates tickets is between INSTALLED and IN_USE. If a profile was installed hours ago, the user's trip start date has passed, and no usage has appeared, that's your trigger to reach out proactively instead of waiting for an angry email. ## 3. Know the usual causes of "installed but no data" In practice, most cases fall into a short list, and almost all are device settings rather than network faults:
  • Data roaming is off on the eSIM line. Travel eSIMs usually connect as roaming, so this is the number-one cause.- The wrong line is selected for mobile data. The profile is enabled, but the phone still uses the home SIM for data.- APN not set or wrong. Most profiles set it automatically; some devices or plans need it entered manually.- Network selection. Automatic selection picked a network the plan doesn't support; manual selection fixes it.- Not yet in the destination, or the plan's validity window hasn't started.- Profile deleted while "troubleshooting", which often turns a settings issue into a re-issue.Only after these does it make sense to escalate a genuine network or provisioning problem. ## 4. Put the troubleshooting inside the app A help-center article is a fallback. A better pattern is a guided checklist inside the order screen, ordered by likelihood and specific to the platform:
  • "Is data roaming turned on for this eSIM?" with the exact settings path for iOS and Android- "Is this eSIM selected for mobile data?"- "Are you in [destination] now?" with the plan's validity dates- A big "Don't delete the eSIM" warning, because that step is often irreversible- Only then: "Still not working? Contact support", with the order context pre-attachedBanks adding travel eSIM inside their apps follow the same idea: BBVA's announcement for its Italian app lists usage tracking, usage alerts, buying more data and contacting technical support side by side in the app (BBVA's announcement). Support isn't a separate channel; it's part of the product screen. ## 5. Log what support will actually need When a ticket reaches a human, they should not have to ask the user for screenshots of settings. Attach to every order:
  • ICCID of the profile and EID of the device (if captured)- Device model and OS version- Timestamps for order, profile download, install/enable notifications, and first usage- Last network or country seen, if your supplier exposes it- Which checklist steps the user already confirmed in-appTreat ICCID and EID as personal data: restrict access, and don't send them to analytics tools that don't need them. ## 6. Decide refund and re-issue rules before launch Write the rules down as code, not as agent judgment:
  • Never downloaded and the trip hasn't started: refund automatically on request.- Downloaded, then deleted, no usage: re-issue a new profile if your supplier allows it; otherwise refund per policy.- Installed, no usage, checklist completed, user in destination: escalate to the supplier with the logged context, and offer a fallback (re-issue or refund) within a defined time.- Usage started: it's a network or plan question, not an activation one; route it differently.Clear rules keep refunds predictable for finance and fast for the user, which matters most when they're standing in an airport. ## 7. Agree who owns tier 1 and tier 2 If you're a bank, travel app or MVNO reselling someone else's connectivity, settle this in the contract:
  • Tier 1 (your brand): in-app checklist, settings guidance, refund and re-issue decisions within policy.- Tier 2 (connectivity supplier): profile state, provisioning faults, network attach problems, coverage issues.- The handoff: which fields you send (ICCID, timestamps, country), the expected response time, and how the answer flows back to the user.Without this, the user gets bounced between "contact your eSIM provider" and "contact the app you bought it from". ## Wrapping up Activation support is where an embedded eSIM either earns trust or loses it. The checklist is short: check compatibility before payment, track real profile state, guide the user through the common fixes in-app, log the identifiers support needs, automate refund and re-issue rules, and draw a clear line between your support and your supplier's. If you're adding branded eSIM to a travel, mobility or fintech product and want the provisioning, portal and support layer handled for you, that's what we're building at One-eSIM: One-eSIM for travel, mobility and fintech. Disclosure: I work on One-eSIM (1-esim.com), a B2B eSIM platform.

title: Self-Taught Programmer Seeks Advice on Transitioning from Java to Go for Backend Development Career
description:
Introduction: The Transition from Java to Go

At 17, with no prior tech experience, a self-taught programmer stands at a crossroads: continue with Java or pivot to Go. This decision isn’t just about language preference; it’s a strategic career move. Go’s simplicity and efficiency make it a rising star in backend development, particularly in microservices and cloud-native architectures. However, transitioning from Java—a statically-typed, object-oriented language—to Go—a statically-typed, procedural language with concurrency features—requires unlearning Java-specific paradigms and adopting Go’s idiomatic style. Without a structured roadmap, this shift risks inefficiencies in learning, missed foundational skill-building, and delayed career entry.

The Problem: A Strategic Shift with High Stakes

The programmer’s attraction to Go’s philosophy is valid. Go’s goroutines, channels, and memory management offer unique advantages for backend development. However, the transition must be guided by a goal-oriented roadmap. A 1-2 year timeline demands prioritization: mastering Go’s core features, building a portfolio, and aligning skills with backend roles. Failure to structure this process could lead to superficial understanding, inability to solve complex problems, and a weak GitHub portfolio—critical for junior/internship applications.

Key Factors Driving the Decision

  • Attraction to Go’s Philosophy: Go’s simplicity and concurrency features align with modern backend demands, but require focused learning to avoid confusion with Java’s object-oriented paradigms.
  • Career Alignment: Go’s role in emerging technologies like Kubernetes and Docker makes it a strategic choice, but only if skills are mapped to backend roles and demonstrated through projects.
  • Self-Study Effectiveness: Relying on free resources (documentation, open-source projects) can be as effective as paid courses, but demands consistent practice and community engagement for mentorship and code reviews.

Typical Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

Common mistakes include overlooking foundational concepts in Go, leading to an inability to solve real-world problems. For example, failing to grasp goroutines and channels can result in inefficient concurrency implementations. Another risk is neglecting networking, which limits access to mentorship and job opportunities. To avoid these, the roadmap must include:

  • Project-Based Learning: Build applications that demonstrate Go’s unique features, such as a RESTful API with goroutines for concurrency.
  • Community Engagement: Contribute to open-source Go projects to gain visibility and feedback.
  • Mentorship: Use AI tools like ChatGPT for guidance, but supplement with human code reviews to correct bad habits.

Rule for Decision-Making: If X, Then Y

If the goal is a backend developer role within 1-2 years, prioritize Go’s backend-specific features (e.g., concurrency, memory management) over Java’s object-oriented depth. Use self-study with a focus on hands-on projects and community engagement. Avoid expensive courses unless they offer mentorship or certification that directly enhances employability. This approach ensures efficient learning and a demonstrable skill set for junior/internship roles.

Evaluating the Benefits of Go for Backend Development

Switching from Java to Go isn’t just about swapping syntax—it’s a strategic pivot toward a language designed for modern backend demands. Let’s break down the mechanics of this transition, focusing on Go’s advantages, potential pitfalls, and how they align with your career goals.

Go’s Core Advantages Over Java in Backend Development

Concurrency Mechanisms: Goroutines vs. Java Threads

Go’s goroutines are lightweight threads managed by the Go runtime, not the OS. Unlike Java’s threads, which require significant memory (1MB+ per thread), goroutines start at 2KB and grow as needed. This efficiency allows Go to handle thousands of concurrent tasks with minimal overhead. For backend systems, this translates to higher throughput in I/O-bound tasks like handling HTTP requests. Mechanism: Goroutines multiplex onto OS threads via a scheduler, avoiding context-switching costs.

Memory Management: Garbage Collection Trade-offs

Go’s tri-color mark-and-sweep GC pauses execution less predictably than Java’s generational GC, but it’s simpler and faster for small-to-medium workloads. In backend systems, this trade-off often favors Go when latency isn’t mission-critical (e.g., microservices). Mechanism: Go’s GC pauses all goroutines during collection, but its efficiency in small heaps reduces pause times.

Simplicity in Syntax and Tooling

Go’s minimal syntax (no classes, inheritance) reduces cognitive load compared to Java’s object-oriented complexity. This simplicity accelerates development speed—critical for rapid iteration in backend projects. Mechanism: Fewer keywords and enforced code style (via gofmt) reduce debugging time and improve readability.

Where Go Outperforms Java in Backend Scenarios

Microservices and Cloud-Native Architectures

Go’s binary compilation produces statically linked executables, eliminating dependency hell common in Java deployments. This makes Go ideal for containerized environments (Docker, Kubernetes). Mechanism: Statically linked binaries reduce container size and startup time, critical for scaling microservices.

API Development: Speed and Efficiency

Go’s standard library includes robust HTTP handling, while Java relies on frameworks like Spring. For lightweight APIs, Go’s native tools reduce latency by bypassing framework overhead. Mechanism: Direct use of net/http avoids abstraction layers, reducing request processing time.

Potential Pitfalls of the Transition

Unlearning Object-Oriented Paradigms

Go’s procedural nature lacks inheritance and method overloading. Misapplying Java OOP patterns in Go leads to verbose, non-idiomatic code. Mechanism: Attempting to replicate Java’s class hierarchies in Go ignores its composition-over-inheritance philosophy, causing inefficiencies.

Concurrency Mismanagement

Goroutines and channels are powerful but unforgiving. Improper use (e.g., unbuffered channels in high-throughput systems) causes deadlocks. Mechanism: Unbuffered channels block sender/receiver goroutines indefinitely if not synchronized correctly.

Decision Dominance: When to Choose Go Over Java

Optimal Conditions for Go

  • If X: Your backend projects prioritize concurrency, low latency, and deployment simplicity.
  • Use Y: Transition to Go, focusing on mastering goroutines, channels, and memory management.

Suboptimal Conditions for Go

  • If X: Your target roles require deep Java ecosystem knowledge (e.g., Android backend, legacy enterprise systems).
  • Use Y: Stick with Java, but supplement with Go for side projects to test its fit.

Practical Roadmap for Go Mastery (1-2 Years)

Year 1: Foundations and Backend Basics

  1. Months 1-3: Learn Go syntax, interfaces, and error handling via The Go Programming Language (book) + small CLI projects.
  2. Months 4-6: Build a RESTful API using net/http, integrating a SQL database (e.g., PostgreSQL) and basic authentication.
  3. Months 7-9: Implement concurrency patterns (worker pools, fan-out/fan-in) in a real-time chat application.
  4. Months 10-12: Deploy a microservices project using Docker and Kubernetes, exposing Go’s deployment advantages.

Year 2: Specialization and Portfolio Polishing

  1. Months 1-6: Contribute to open-source Go projects (e.g., gin-gonic, echo) to refine idiomatic coding.
  2. Months 7-12: Build a production-grade backend system (e.g., e-commerce platform) showcasing Go’s scalability features.

Final Judgment: Is the Transition Worth It?

For a 17-year-old targeting backend roles, Go’s alignment with cloud-native technologies and its learning curve (steeper than Python but gentler than C++) make it a high-ROI choice. However, success hinges on:

  • Avoiding Java-to-Go paradigm mismatches through project-based learning.
  • Leveraging Go’s community (e.g., Gophers Slack) for mentorship.
  • Prioritizing backend-specific skills (Kubernetes, gRPC) over generalist knowledge.

Rule of Thumb: If your goal is backend development in modern architectures, switch to Go now—but treat Java as a foundation, not a crutch. The transition’s efficiency depends on unlearning Java’s OOP habits and embracing Go’s procedural, concurrency-first design.

Structuring a 1-2 Year Self-Study Roadmap for Go

Transitioning from Java to Go is a strategic move for backend development, but it requires a structured, goal-oriented approach. Below is a detailed roadmap tailored to your goal of securing a junior/internship role within 1-2 years. This plan leverages Go’s strengths in concurrency, simplicity, and backend-specific features while avoiding common pitfalls.

Year 1: Foundations and Backend Essentials

Months 1-3: Master Go’s Core Syntax and Idioms

  • Mechanism: Go’s procedural nature and concurrency features (goroutines, channels) differ fundamentally from Java’s OOP. Focus on unlearning Java-specific paradigms like inheritance and method overloading.
  • Resources: Use The Go Programming Language book and official documentation. Build CLI projects to practice interfaces, error handling, and gofmt for enforced code style.
  • Risk: Misapplying Java OOP patterns leads to verbose, non-idiomatic Go code. Solution: Regularly review Go’s idiomatic style via go vet and community code examples.

Months 4-6: Build a RESTful API with Backend Integration

  • Mechanism: Go’s net/http package avoids framework overhead, making it ideal for lightweight APIs. Integrate with an SQL database (e.g., PostgreSQL) to handle data persistence.
  • Project: Create a CRUD API with authentication (JWT). Use gorm for ORM to understand database interactions.
  • Risk: Overlooking database indexing or inefficient queries leads to performance bottlenecks. Solution: Profile queries using pprof and optimize based on real-world load.

Months 7-9: Implement Concurrency Patterns in Real-Time Applications

  • Mechanism: Goroutines and channels enable efficient parallel processing. Build a real-time chat app to practice worker pools, fan-out/fan-in patterns, and deadlock avoidance.
  • Project: Use websocket for real-time communication. Implement rate limiting to prevent abuse.
  • Risk: Unbuffered channels block indefinitely if not synchronized. Solution: Use select statements with timeouts and buffered channels for controlled flow.

Months 10-12: Deploy Microservices with Docker and Kubernetes

  • Mechanism: Go’s statically linked binaries reduce container size and startup time, making it ideal for Kubernetes deployments. Learn Docker for containerization and Kubernetes for orchestration.
  • Project: Deploy a multi-service application (e.g., user service, order service) on Minikube. Use k8s.io/client-go for custom controllers.
  • Risk: Misconfiguring Kubernetes manifests leads to resource wastage or downtime. Solution: Use Helm charts for templated deployments and linters like kubeval.

Year 2: Advanced Skills and Production Readiness

Months 1-6: Contribute to Open-Source Go Projects

  • Mechanism: Engaging with the Go community provides mentorship and real-world problem-solving experience. Contribute to projects like gin-gonic or echo to understand production-grade codebases.
  • Outcome: Build a GitHub portfolio showcasing collaborative work and problem-solving skills.
  • Risk: Superficial contributions (e.g., fixing typos) add little value. Solution: Focus on meaningful issues (e.g., performance optimizations, feature additions) and document your process.

Months 7-12: Build a Production-Grade Backend System

  • Mechanism: Apply all learned skills to a complex project (e.g., e-commerce platform). Incorporate gRPC for inter-service communication, caching with Redis, and monitoring with Prometheus.
  • Project: Include features like payment gateways, inventory management, and user authentication. Deploy on AWS/GCP with CI/CD pipelines.
  • Risk: Overlooking scalability leads to system failures under load. Solution: Use load testing tools like k6 and implement horizontal scaling with Kubernetes.

Decision Dominance: Self-Study vs. Paid Courses

Optimal Choice: High-quality self-study + strong GitHub portfolio is sufficient for securing a job offer. Paid courses are unnecessary unless they offer mentorship or certifications that enhance employability.

  • Mechanism: Employers value practical skills and problem-solving ability, which are best demonstrated through hands-on projects and open-source contributions.
  • Rule: If a course offers mentorship or certification that aligns with backend roles (e.g., Kubernetes, gRPC), consider it. Otherwise, allocate resources to self-study and community engagement.
  • Typical Error: Spending on expensive courses without clear ROI. Mechanism: Lack of mentorship or certification limits the course’s impact on employability.

Final Judgment

Switching from Java to Go is a high-ROI decision for modern backend development, especially in cloud-native architectures. Success hinges on:

  • Unlearning Java OOP habits and adopting Go’s idiomatic style.
  • Leveraging Go’s community for mentorship and open-source contributions.
  • Prioritizing backend-specific skills like Kubernetes, gRPC, and concurrency patterns.

Rule of Thumb: If your goal is a backend developer role within 1-2 years, prioritize Go’s backend-specific features and use self-study with hands-on projects. Avoid expensive courses unless they offer mentorship or certification enhancing employability.

Real-World Applications and Case Studies

To understand the strategic value of transitioning from Java to Go for backend development, let’s examine real-world applications where Go’s unique features—concurrency, memory efficiency, and simplicity—have been leveraged effectively. These case studies not only demonstrate Go’s practical utility but also provide a blueprint for the projects you should aim to build in your 1–2 year roadmap.

1. Uber’s Transition to Go for High-Throughput Geocoding Services

Uber initially relied on Python for its geocoding services, but as the system scaled, it faced latency issues due to Python’s Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), which limits concurrent execution. Uber migrated to Go, leveraging its goroutines and channels to handle thousands of concurrent requests with minimal overhead. The result? A 30x reduction in latency and a 99% decrease in server count for the same workload. (Mechanism: Goroutines multiplex onto OS threads, enabling efficient parallel processing without the overhead of traditional threads.)

Practical Insight: In your roadmap, prioritize building a real-time geocoding API using net/http and goroutines to simulate high-throughput scenarios. This project will not only demonstrate Go’s concurrency but also align with industry demands for scalable backend systems.

2. Twitch’s Use of Go for Low-Latency Video Streaming

Twitch, a live streaming platform, adopted Go to handle its real-time chat and video streaming infrastructure. Go’s statically linked binaries and efficient memory management allowed Twitch to deploy microservices with minimal container size and startup time, critical for low-latency applications. (Mechanism: Go’s garbage collector optimizes memory usage, reducing pauses in I/O-bound tasks like video streaming.)

Practical Insight: In Months 7–9 of your roadmap, implement a WebSocket-based chat application with buffered channels and select statements to manage concurrency. This project mirrors Twitch’s use case and reinforces your understanding of Go’s backend-specific features.

3. Docker’s Foundation in Go for Containerization

Docker, the de facto standard for containerization, is written in Go. Its statically linked binaries and efficient resource utilization make Go ideal for building tools that require portability and performance. (Mechanism: Go’s compile-time optimizations and lack of runtime dependencies reduce container size and improve startup speed.)

Practical Insight: In Months 10–12 of Year 1, deploy a microservices architecture using Docker and Kubernetes. This project not only demonstrates Go’s role in cloud-native technologies but also prepares you for backend roles that increasingly require Kubernetes expertise.

4. Open-Source Contributions: Gin and Echo Frameworks

Open-source projects like Gin and Echo are widely used in the Go community for building RESTful APIs. Contributing to these projects not only enhances your GitHub portfolio but also exposes you to production-grade codebases and community best practices. (Mechanism: Engaging with open-source projects accelerates learning by forcing you to adhere to idiomatic Go and solve real-world problems.)

Practical Insight: In Year 2, focus on contributing to performance optimizations or new features in these frameworks. This aligns with the Decision Dominance rule: If your goal is to demonstrate backend expertise, prioritize open-source contributions over superficial projects.

Edge-Case Analysis: Pitfalls and Solutions

While Go’s simplicity is a strength, it can also lead to superficial understanding if foundational concepts are overlooked. For example, mismanaging concurrency—such as using unbuffered channels without timeouts—can lead to deadlocks. (Mechanism: Unbuffered channels block indefinitely if not synchronized correctly, halting goroutines.)

Solution: In your projects, always use buffered channels and select statements with timeouts. For example, in a real-time chat application, implement a worker pool pattern to manage concurrent message processing. This not only prevents deadlocks but also demonstrates a deep understanding of Go’s concurrency model.

Decision Dominance: Self-Study vs. Paid Courses

Given your resource constraints, self-study is the optimal choice for mastering Go. However, avoid the typical error of relying solely on tutorials without building projects. (Mechanism: Employers prioritize practical skills, and projects serve as tangible proof of your ability to solve real-world problems.)

Rule of Thumb: If your goal is a backend developer role within 1–2 years, use self-study with a focus on hands-on projects and open-source contributions. Invest in paid courses only if they offer mentorship or certifications that directly enhance employability (e.g., Kubernetes, gRPC).

Conclusion

Transitioning from Java to Go is a high-ROI decision for aspiring backend developers, provided you follow a structured roadmap. By studying real-world applications like Uber, Twitch, and Docker, and by prioritizing project-based learning and community engagement, you can efficiently master Go’s backend-specific features. Avoid pitfalls by focusing on foundational concepts and leveraging open-source contributions to build a strong portfolio. With this approach, you’ll not only transition successfully but also position yourself for junior/internship roles within your desired timeframe.

Conclusion: Next Steps and Continuous Learning

Transitioning from Java to Go is a high-ROI decision for aspiring backend developers, but success hinges on a structured, project-driven approach. Here’s how to move forward, grounded in the analytical model and practical insights:

1. Start Your Go Journey Now—But Strategically

Go’s concurrency mechanisms (goroutines, channels) and memory management (tri-color GC) outperform Java in I/O-bound tasks, making it ideal for microservices and cloud-native architectures. However, unlearning Java’s OOP paradigms is critical. Start by mastering Go’s syntax and idioms via The Go Programming Language book and official docs. Use go vet to avoid non-idiomatic code. Mechanism: Go’s procedural nature and enforced code style (gofmt) reduce debugging time, but misapplying Java patterns (e.g., inheritance) leads to verbose, inefficient code.

2. Build a Portfolio That Demonstrates Backend Proficiency

Employers prioritize practical skills over language expertise. Focus on projects like a RESTful API with net/http, a real-time chat app using WebSocket, and microservices deployed via Docker/Kubernetes. Mechanism: Go’s statically linked binaries reduce container size, enabling faster deployments. For example, Uber’s migration to Go for geocoding services achieved a 30x latency reduction by leveraging goroutines for parallel processing.

3. Leverage Self-Study Over Paid Courses—Unless Specific Conditions Apply

Decision Dominance: Self-study + GitHub portfolio is optimal for job offers. Paid courses are only justified if they offer mentorship or certifications (e.g., Kubernetes). Mechanism: Employers value problem-solving skills demonstrated through open-source contributions. For instance, contributing to gin-gonic or echo frameworks accelerates learning by enforcing idiomatic Go and solving real-world problems.

4. Stay Updated with Go’s Ecosystem and Backend Trends

Go’s role in emerging technologies (Kubernetes, gRPC) makes continuous learning essential. Follow Go’s release notes, engage with the Go community, and experiment with tools like Prometheus for monitoring and k6 for load testing. Mechanism: Go’s ecosystem evolves rapidly; for example, generics introduced in Go 1.18 enhance type safety and code reusability. Ignoring updates risks falling behind in modern backend practices.

5. Avoid Common Pitfalls by Focusing on Foundations

Typical failures include superficial understanding of concurrency (e.g., deadlocks from unbuffered channels) and neglecting networking. Use buffered channels and select statements with timeouts to prevent deadlocks. Mechanism: Mismanaging concurrency blocks goroutines indefinitely, degrading system performance. Engage with mentors or code reviews to identify and correct bad habits early.

Rule of Thumb: If your goal is backend development in modern architectures, transition to Go. Focus on hands-on projects, community engagement, and unlearning Java OOP habits. Avoid expensive courses unless they enhance employability.

Start today—Go’s simplicity and efficiency will position you for junior/internship roles within 1–2 years, provided you follow this structured roadmap.

title: Ảnh mà Google không thấy: CSS background, lazy load sai cách và cách audit thẻ img
description:
Developer thường tối ưu ảnh theo hướng hiệu năng: nén, lazy load, chuyển sang ảnh nền cho dễ căn chỉnh. Một số lựa chọn trong đó làm ảnh biến mất khỏi Google Hình ảnh mà không ai để ý. Bài này đi qua những gì tài liệu Google Search Central nói về cách Google tìm và hiểu ảnh, và một script audit thẻ img trên trang.

Google tìm ảnh ở đâu

Google tìm ảnh trong thuộc tính src của thẻ <img>, kể cả khi thẻ đó nằm trong <picture>. Ảnh đặt bằng CSS background-image thì Google không lập chỉ mục. Đây là lỗi hay gặp ở theme bán hàng: ảnh sản phẩm trong lưới danh mục được render bằng div có ảnh nền để dễ cắt khung.

<!-- Google không lập chỉ mục ảnh này -->
<div class="thumb" style="background-image:url(ao-thun-den.webp)"></div>

<!-- Dùng img với object-fit để có cùng hiệu ứng cắt khung -->
<img src="ao-thun-den.webp" alt="Áo thun nam cổ tròn màu đen, mặt trước"
     width="600" height="600" style="object-fit:cover" loading="lazy">

object-fit: cover cho kết quả hiển thị gần như giống ảnh nền, mà ảnh vẫn nằm trong img có alt.

Google hiểu ảnh bằng gì

Theo hướng dẫn SEO cho Google Hình ảnh: văn bản thay thế (alt) cùng thuật toán thị giác máy tính và nội dung trang; thông tin từ chú thích và tiêu đề trang; còn tên file chỉ là "gợi ý rất nhẹ". Hệ quả cho cấu trúc HTML: dùng figure và figcaption để chú thích gắn rõ với ảnh, và đặt ảnh gần đoạn chữ liên quan thay vì gom hết vào một gallery cuối trang.

<figure>
  <img src="yoast-o-seo-title-va-meta.webp"
       alt="Ô SEO title và meta description trong Yoast SEO trên WordPress">
  <figcaption>Thanh xanh cho biết title và mô tả nằm trong giới hạn hiển thị.</figcaption>
</figure>

Script audit ảnh trên một trang 

import re
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

DUOI_HOP_LE = {"bmp", "gif", "jpg", "jpeg", "png", "webp", "svg", "avif"}
TEN_CHUNG = re.compile(r"^(img|image|dsc|screenshot|pic|anh|hinh)[-_ ]?\d*", re.I)

def audit_anh(html: str) -> list:
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
    loi = []
    for el in soup.select("[style*=background-image]"):
        loi.append(f"Ảnh nền CSS (không được lập chỉ mục): {el.get('class')}")
    for img in soup.find_all("img"):
        src = img.get("src") or ""
        ten = src.rsplit("/", 1)[-1].split("?")[0]
        if not src or src.startswith("data:"):
            loi.append(f"img không có src thật (lazy load?): {img.get('data-src') or img}")
            continue
        if img.get("alt") is None:
            loi.append(f"Thiếu thuộc tính alt: {ten}")
        if TEN_CHUNG.match(ten):
            loi.append(f"Tên file chung chung: {ten}")
        duoi = ten.rsplit(".", 1)[-1].lower() if "." in ten else ""
        if duoi and duoi not in DUOI_HOP_LE:
            loi.append(f"Định dạng lạ: {ten}")
    return loi

Kiểm tra src rỗng hoặc data: bắt một lỗi lazy load phổ biến: thư viện cũ để ảnh thật trong data-src và chỉ gán vào src khi cuộn tới. Nếu Google không render tới bước đó, ảnh không có src thật. Thuộc tính loading="lazy" gốc của trình duyệt không gặp vấn đề này, và WordPress đã tự thêm nó cho ảnh trong nội dung.

Định dạng và kích thước

Google hỗ trợ BMP, GIF, JPEG, PNG, WebP, SVG và AVIF, và đuôi file phải khớp với loại ảnh. WordPress tự sinh nhiều kích thước và khai báo srcset, nên phần cần làm thủ công là cắt ảnh về đúng kích thước hiển thị trước khi tải lên. Với ảnh đại diện, Google khuyên rộng ít nhất 1200 pixel cho Discover.

Phần dành cho người viết nội dung, gồm vai trò của 4 ô alt, title, caption, description trong WordPress và ví dụ metadata theo ngành, có trong bài Tối ưu hình ảnh chuẩn SEO trên Onic.vn.

Bài gốc: https://onic.vn/kien-thuc/toi-uu-hinh-anh-chuan-seo/
