title: Bun runtime now supports large functions and extended max duration
description:
The Bun runtime on Vercel Functions now supports larger package sizes up to 5GB uncompressed and extended max duration for up to 30 minutes, two betas that previously ran on Node.js and Python only.

Large functions raise the standard 250MB package size limit to 5GB, and extended max duration raises the generally available 800-second ceiling to 1800 seconds for Pro and Enterprise teams. Both features require Fluid compute to be enabled. New projects are enrolled in the large functions beta automatically, while existing projects created before July 2026 opt in by adding VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_FUNCTIONS=1 as an environment variable in your project settings, then redeploying. Durations above 800 seconds are set per function in vercel.json rather than as a project-level default:

The server.ts entry point serves the long-running route with Bun:

During the beta, these features are unavailable on projects using Secure Compute or Static IPs.

Read the large functions and extended max duration documentation.

Read more

title: Environment variables now use Config and Secret types
description:
When you add or edit an environment variable in Vercel, you now choose Config or Secret instead of using the Sensitive toggle. Existing variables marked Sensitive are automatically treated as Secrets and continue to work without migration.

  • Config: The value remains readable after saving for members with access. Use Config for non-sensitive values you may need to inspect later, such as variables with a public framework prefix.

  • Secret: The value remains available to your deployments and can be replaced, but members cannot view or retrieve it after saving. Use Secret for passwords, API keys, and tokens.

You can select an environment or Preview branch for each value. The environment variable list in the dashboard shows each variable’s type and where it applies.

Team policy changes

The Enforce Sensitive Environment Variables team policy is deprecated with this update. When enabled, it required every environment variable created by a team member to be Sensitive, including non-sensitive configuration. With Config and Secret types, members can choose the appropriate type for each variable.

A new Separate Production Secret Values policy is available in your Security settings. When enabled, the Production value for a Secret must differ from the values used for the same key in Preview, Development, and custom environments.

If your team had the legacy policy enabled, confirm whether the Separate Production Secret Values policy should be enabled for your team. The deprecated policy is no longer enforced by the Vercel CLI.

Set variable types from the CLI

To choose whether an environment variable is a Config or Secret from the CLI, pass --type config or --type secret to vercel env add or vercel env update:

The existing flags continue to work. When --type is omitted, --no-sensitive maps to Config and --sensitive maps to Secret. After adding or updating a variable, the CLI output shows its type under Type.

Learn more in the Environment Variables documentation.

Read more

title: Vercel Sandbox is now globally available
description:
Vercel Sandbox now runs globally, starting with four regions: iad1 (Washington, D.C.), sfo1 (San Francisco), cle1 (Cleveland), and cdg1 (Paris).

iad1 remains the default. Support for all Vercel regions is coming soon.

Choose a region close to the databases, object storage, and other services your sandboxes access to reduce latency. Region selection is available on all plans.

Pro and Enterprise teams can also configure failover regions. If the primary region is unavailable, new sandboxes start in the closest configured failover region. Failover only applies to regions you configure; without it, a sandbox starts in its selected region, or the project default.

Update the SDK or CLI you use to the latest version:

Configure the default region and failover regions from Settings > Sandboxes in your project, or with the Vercel CLI:

Those defaults apply to every sandbox. To override them for a single sandbox, pass region and optionally failoverRegions at create time with the SDK:

Or with the CLI:

Learn more in the Sandbox regions documentation.

Read more

title: Elastic build machines now use Turborepo cache hits to prevent downgrades
description:
Elastic build machines now consider Turborepo cache hits when deciding whether to use a smaller build machine. A warm-cache build no longer triggers a downgrade.

A warm-cache build can use less CPU and memory than the same build with a cold cache. Downgrading based on that lower usage could leave a later cold-cache build without enough resources to complete successfully.

This change applies automatically to all builds using Elastic build machines. No action is required. Learn more in the build documentation.

Read more

title: Chat SDK now supports XChat
description:
You can now build bots that hold end-to-end encrypted 1:1 and group conversations on XChat with the new XChat adapter for Chat SDK.

The adapter handles all encryption, key management, and signature verification automatically. Bots can also message users first, as long as the user has encrypted chat set up and follows the bot.

XChat has no markdown rendering, so the adapter falls back automatically: URLs and @mentions render as tappable links, tables as ASCII code blocks, and cards as text with a link preview. Streaming works through message edits.

Read the XChat adapter documentation to get started.

Read more

title: Bring your agent to Notion with Chat SDK
description:
Your team already works in Notion. Now your agent can too.

With the new Notion adapter for Chat SDK, the same agent you run on Slack, Discord, GitHub, Teams, or WhatsApp can join comment discussions on your Notion pages, no separate codebase required.

Each Notion page maps to a channel and each comment thread to a thread, so replies stay threaded automatically.

The adapter supports mentions, message editing, conversation history, and up to three file attachments. By default, your bot replies when @-mentioned and where mentions aren't available in a workspace, it can trigger on a keyword or on all comments instead.

Notion doesn't support buttons, modals, or reactions, and cards render as markdown. Discussions can start at the page or block level, but not on inline text ranges. History fetches return only open comments.

Read the documentation to get started, browse the directory, or build your own.

Read more

title: Vercel Connect now supports Linq
description:
Vercel Connect now includes a managed connector for Linq, so your apps and agents can send and receive messages over iMessage, RCS, and SMS.

As a Vercel Managed Connector, Vercel can create a Linq account and phone number for you, or link an existing account. You never manage credentials yourself.

Create a connector from the dashboard or Vercel CLI:

Give your eve agent a phone number

The connector powers the new Linq channel in eve.

Run eve add channel/linq, choose Vercel Connect, and eve wires up the connector, phone numbers, and webhook for you:

The channel marks accepted messages as read and continues the same eve session for every message in a Linq conversation. Out of the box, the channel supports read receipts, typing indicators, and mid-conversation steering for a more natural messaging experience.

Use the connector in any project

Call getToken with your connector, and the @vercel/connect SDK exchanges your Vercel deployment's OIDC identity for a short-lived Linq token.

Pass it as the bearer token on any Linq Partner API request:

Linq delivers each message over the best protocol the recipient supports, starting with iMessage, then RCS, then SMS. The same token works across the full Linq API, including group chats, reactions, rich media, and typing indicators.

Read the Vercel Connect documentation, view details about the Linq connector in the Vercel Connect catalog, or create a Linq connector to get started.

Read more

title: Chat SDK now supports Slack Enterprise Grid
description:
Chat SDK's Slack adapter now supports Slack Enterprise Grid.

Bots installed org-wide work across every workspace, with correct token resolution, tenant-scoped caches, and event retry deduplication.

The adapter now stores org-wide installations by enterprise ID. This matches how tokens are resolved for incoming events, slash commands, and interactive payloads. SlackInstallation records the new identity fields:

Token resolution behaves the same over HTTP webhooks and Socket Mode. Events route by the installation identity in the envelope's authorizations field, which keeps routing correct for Slack Connect shared channels.

The adapter is also hardened for multi-workspace deployments:

  • User profile and mention caches are scoped per installation, so one tenant's data never resolves for another.

  • API calls made with an org-wide token pass the event's team_id automatically, which Slack requires for workspace-scoped methods.

  • Retried event deliveries are deduplicated for 24 hours, covering Slack's Delayed Events redeliveries.

  • Outgoing mentions accept W-prefixed Grid user IDs alongside U-prefixed IDs.

Single-workspace installations are unaffected, and getInstallation and deleteInstallation work unchanged for both install types.

Read the Slack adapter documentation to get started.

Read more

title: Vercel Connect is now generally available
description:
Vercel Connect is now generally available on all plans and in v0. Instead of storing long-lived provider secrets, your code requests short-lived, scoped tokens at runtime. Deployments authenticate with their existing Vercel OIDC identity. Each token is scoped to the task, refreshed automatically, and expires on its own.

Any service with one command

Register a connector once from the CLI. Pass the service name and the CLI pre-populates the brand name, icon, auth type, and MCP or discovery URL, then prompts for any credentials the service requires:

Connect ships with 100+ preset connectors for tools like Notion and Workday, managed connectors for Slack, GitHub, Linear, Salesforce, Snowflake, and Microsoft, plus generic OAuth, API key authentication, and MCP servers.

Tokens at runtime, not secrets at rest

Request a token only when your code needs one, with getToken:

Switch the subject from the app to a named user and the token acts on that user's behalf, triggering the authorization flow when consent is needed.

Access your team can inspect and prove

New at GA:

  • Fine-grained RBAC controls who can create and manage connectors

  • Audit logs record authorization and connector activity

  • Token and trigger observability shows how tokens are used across projects

Together with per-environment attachment, including Custom Environments, and one-command revocation, external access becomes something your team can inspect, prove, and cut off in seconds.

Triggers without stored webhook secrets

Triggers deliver provider events to your app without a stored secret. Vercel Connect verifies signatures server-side, re-attests each event using an OIDC identity, and forwards the event to your project, even when Deployment Protection is enabled.

Connect also manages private keys and the full credential lifecycle, so you get standards-compliant OAuth without building the infrastructure yourself.

Works with your stack

Connect works wherever your functions run and is supported in v0, eve, and Chat SDK. Adapters are available for the auth libraries and agent tooling you already use:

  • Better Auth: @vercel/connect/betterauth

  • Auth.js: @vercel/connect/authjs

  • AI SDK: @vercel/connect/ai-sdk

  • MCP clients: @vercel/connect/mcp

  • eve: @vercel/connect/eve

  • Chat SDK: @vercel/connect/chat

Securely connect your AI SDK agents to MCP servers

The AI SDK adapter authenticates MCP clients with tokens minted at runtime. In this example, the agent gets read-only Linear access issued for a single user, so downstream actions carry that user's identity:

Give your GitHub agents only the access they need

GitHub Tools, our open source tool layer for GitHub agents, plugs into eve through Connect via an eve extension. Presets like code-review map to Connect scopes automatically, so tokens carry only the permissions the toolset needs:

Pricing and availability

Vercel Connect is available on all plans, with pricing based on token requests and trigger events. Hobby includes 500 token requests and 1,000 triggers per month at no additional cost. Pro is billed at $3 per 1,000 token requests and $0.95 per 1,000 triggers, with custom pricing on Enterprise.

Get started

  • Deploy a software factory template with Vercel Connect or browse the source

  • Follow the complete guide in the knowledge base or read the launch blog post

  • Hand the prompt below to your coding agent to set up Vercel Connect:

title: AI Gateway now supports asynchronous video generation
description:
Video generation on AI Gateway can now run asynchronously.

By default, generateVideo keeps one HTTP request to AI Gateway open until the result is ready. Because video generation can take seconds or minutes, that request can exceed request timeouts.

With asynchronous generation, your application can receive a webhook, poll for completion, or start a generation and retrieve the result in a later request.

Choose an option based on whether your process can keep running and whether your application can receive webhooks:

Existing generateVideo calls continue to work as before. All four options support text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video, and other video inputs.

Upgrade the SDK

Install the latest versions of the AI SDK and AI Gateway provider:

Use asynchronous video generation

Wait for completion in a Workflow

An easy way to consume the completion webhook is a Workflow SDK. The workflow creates its own webhook URL, passes it to startVideo, and suspends until AI Gateway delivers the completion event. Install the Workflow SDK alongside the AI SDK:

While the video renders, the workflow run is suspended and resumes when AI Gateway delivers the terminal event.

Use a webhook with generateVideo

Pass webhook to generateVideo to wait for a completion event without polling. AI Gateway sends an event when the job completes or fails. The SDK waits for that event, fetches the generated videos, and resolves the original generateVideo call.

The calling process and webhook handler need a shared token and store so the delivery can be matched to the correct generation. generateVideo does not expose the signing secret for this job. See the webhook verification documentation for the complete receiver pattern.

Both the polling and webhook options for generateVideo return result.videos as GeneratedFile objects. The SDK downloads provider-hosted videos, making uint8Array, base64, and mediaType available in either job.

Poll with generateVideo

Add poll to an existing generateVideo call:

AI Gateway starts an asynchronous job, and the SDK sends a short status request at each interval until the job finishes. The calling process must remain running until generateVideo resolves, but no individual request to AI Gateway stays open for the full generation.

Start a job and retrieve it later

startVideo returns an operation as soon as AI Gateway accepts the job, without waiting for rendering to finish. Store that operation and pass it to getVideoStatus later from the same process or another one:

The operation is JSON-serializable, so it can be stored in a database or passed through a queue. Your application controls how long to keep checking the job because it has no built-in timeout.

You can also pass webhookUrl to startVideo to receive a completion event instead of checking the status. The start response includes the signing secret needed to verify the webhook.

Unlike generateVideo, getVideoStatus does not download hosted videos. It returns provider URLs or inline bytes. Hosted URLs can expire, so download any videos you need to keep.

Monitor asynchronous jobs

Every asynchronous generation appears on the AI Gateway Logs page as soon as it starts. Jobs show as Running while generation is in progress and update when they complete or fail.

Under Request Mode, select Async to show only asynchronous jobs. Opening an entry shows the job ID and the request details.

Only asynchronous requests create jobs. A standard generateVideo call appears as a single completed request after the video is ready.

For size limits, idempotency for retried job starts, webhook delivery retries, and other operational details, read the asynchronous video generation documentation or browse all video models.

title: Updates to Hobby and Pro Terms of Service
description:
We are updating the Terms of Service for Hobby and Pro customers, effective October 19, 2026. The updates clarify some existing Vercel practices, expand terms on topics such as managed accounts and credits, and reflect applicable legal requirements, including certain cancellation and service-change rights for eligible consumers in the UK and EU.

Credits and billing

A new section sets out how credits work: plan-included credits expire at the end of the subscription term and purchased credits expire one year after purchase unless stated otherwise in the relevant credit purchase terms. Credits can only be used to pay Vercel fees, have no cash value, and are nontransferable. Credits are generally nonrefundable, but unused purchased credits are refunded if Vercel terminates your account without cause.

The Terms also clarify that credit purchases are billed in advance, subscriptions auto-renew unless you turn off renewal, and third-party pass-through rates may change when provider rates change. ⁠⁠

Managed accounts

The Terms now have a dedicated section for accounts that use a company email domain (e.g., work email), clarifying that the company can manage only the Projects you create inside its Team. We also clarified that if your company wishes to manage your account using your company work email, Vercel will now notify you first and give you a reasonable amount of time to move your personal content to an account with a different email address

Renewal and cancellation

You can turn off auto-renewal and cancel or downgrade through account settings or Support. Cancellation or downgrade generally takes effect at the start of the next renewal period. The Terms also explain statutory withdrawal and refund rights for eligible consumers.

Service changes

Eligible consumers in the UK and EU may cancel the affected subscription free of charge if a change has more than a minor negative impact on their access to or use of the Services. They have 30 days from notice or the change, whichever is later, and may receive a prorated refund of prepaid amounts for the remaining period.

Other updates

The service-specific provisions have been moved to a dedicated Service Terms page. The Terms also clarify sanctions-related obligations, including that use of the Services must not be in connection with or for the benefit of a sanctioned person under applicable laws.

Read the full Terms of Service and Service Terms for details.

title: Death to long-lived static credentials
description:
Fifteen years ago, TLS was something you'd use to protect the most sensitive areas of your app. Then Google, Let's Encrypt, the EFF, and others led the push for HTTPS everywhere, making encryption the default for every request. Without it, anyone between the browser and server can read and tamper with the traffic.

OAuth, OIDC, DBSC, and related standards already provide building blocks for secure authentication, but standards alone do not make secure methods the norm. HTTPS needed tooling that made encryption easy and a sustained push that made it expected. Machine-to-machine authentication still resembles HTTPS in 2010, with some vendors and enterprises leading the way while long-lived static credentials remain the default for many SaaS vendors and infrastructure providers.

At Vercel, we want to make fast and secure the default across the web, including in our own services and the integrations in our Marketplace. We’ve built OIDC UI, a shadcn/ui registry that gives providers trust-policy forms and token verification code. We’re expanding OIDC support across Vercel and setting new authentication requirements for Marketplace providers.

Long-lived static credentials are insecure

Long-lived static credentials are secrets such as API keys and database passwords that applications keep reusing, often with no expiration. As agents take on more useful work, we give them access to our systems, tools, and data through credentials that can grant permissions far beyond the task at hand.

Those credentials can leak into a code repository or chat, be stolen when a service or dependency is compromised, or be exposed when prompt injection leads an agent to reveal them. However it happens, an attacker can use the credential with the permissions it grants until it expires or is revoked. Recent credential-theft and supply-chain incidents across the industry show why encryption at rest isn’t enough when malicious code can read an application’s credentials in production.

Rotating exposed credentials takes time and coordination across the systems that use them, and mistakes can disrupt production. At Vercel, we’ve previously spent thousands of engineering hours on multiple, very painful key rotations out of an abundance of caution, and we never want to have to do this again.

Better solutions already exist

With OIDC, your application can authenticate without storing a long-lived provider key. A trusted issuer provides a signed, short-lived token identifying the application, and the receiving service verifies that token before deciding what access to grant.

A stolen token stops working when it expires, limiting how long that copy can be used even if the leak goes unnoticed. Your application can obtain fresh credentials programmatically, removing the need to distribute and manually rotate a persistent provider key across the systems that use it.

We’ve been prioritizing OIDC across Vercel so applications can access Blob, AI Gateway, and Sandbox without storing long-lived keys for those services. Our OIDC federation has been generally available since 2024, letting applications running on Vercel exchange Vercel-issued identity tokens for temporary AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials under configured project and environment trust policies. But for developers to stop managing long-lived keys, that support has to extend to all the services their applications depend on.

The rest of the web hasn’t followed

We surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported secure authentication methods.

But getting vendors to support secure authentication is only part of the problem. Even when a service offers a secure method, developers often choose a static key because it can be simpler to use. We see three main barriers to broader adoption:

  • Tooling and setup that make secure authentication more complicated than using a static key.

  • Added latency from fetching or exchanging tokens on the request path.

  • Weak incentives for vendors to offer and prioritize secure authentication.

Our goal is to make secure authentication the default on Vercel, while also using our Marketplace to help push more vendors to support it.

Our commitment to a more secure web

We have a responsibility to make this change practical across the services we run, the tools developers use, and the integrations we build with partners.

Make secure authentication easier to use

Using a secure token has to be easier than pasting a key, or developers will keep pasting keys. On Vercel, code retrieves an OIDC token with a function call, and a custom audience specifies the service intended to receive it.

With Vercel Connect, applications and agents use their deployment identity to request provider tokens at runtime, without having to store long-lived provider secrets in environment variables. Once the connector is configured and linked to the project and the user’s account is connected, code can request a token for that user with scopes the provider supports.

We’re also extending OIDC support across the Vercel API and CLI to remove the need for long-lived Vercel tokens in deployment workflows.

OIDC UI for API providers

OIDC UI is a shadcn/ui component registry with a trust-policy configurator and a server-side token verifier. It includes provider forms for Vercel, GitHub, GitLab, Google, Bitbucket, AWS, Azure, and custom OIDC issuers. A provider can let customers configure trust for a particular Vercel project’s production environment, then verify incoming tokens against that policy without building the configuration interface and verification code from scratch.

Reduce the performance cost of secure authentication

A static key in an environment variable is already available when a function runs, so reading it requires no network request. Fetching a token or exchanging it for provider credentials can add network latency, so reducing those calls is part of making secure authentication practical.

Vercel Functions receive a platform-issued token in the request header, which the SDK reads without fetching another. The platform reuses unexpired tokens, while Vercel Connect caches provider tokens in process and refreshes them near expiry. Custom-audience and provider exchanges require network calls.

For example, an application can use the Azure SDK to access Cosmos DB with temporary credentials instead of a database key. With Azure configured to trust the Vercel project and its default token audience, the callback supplies a Vercel OIDC token to ClientAssertionCredential, which exchanges it for the Azure access token used by CosmosClient.

Give providers an incentive to support secure authentication

The Vercel Marketplace offers access to third-party databases, content management systems, observability tools, and more. Our goal is for all of these vendors to support short-lived, identity-based authentication, whether they accept OIDC tokens directly or exchange them for temporary credentials. We’re working to make integrations configure that authentication automatically when developers connect a service, so it does not require a separate setup step.

HTTPS everywhere did not win on ergonomics alone. Chrome put a “Not secure” label on plain HTTP, and then it set deadlines. Now we are setting ours. By November 30, 2026, vendors who do not support OIDC auth from Vercel to their services and use long-lived secrets for authentication will have a similar “Not secure” message on their listing. By January 2027, vendors who do not offer secure auth will be delisted. We are holding the Vercel API and our own native integrations to the same bar.

From static to dynamic

Fifteen years ago, encrypting every request felt like overkill. Today, the padlock is so normal that we only notice when it's missing. Secure authentication between services should become just as routine, so developers can connect the systems they need without storing another long-lived secret. Going from static to dynamic has always been the Vercel mission. It started with pages, and now it’s credentials.

Additional resources

  • OIDC federation covers how deployments get short-lived identity tokens, with guides for AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own API.

  • Custom OIDC token audiences scopes each token to the one service meant to receive it.

  • Vercel Connect requests short-lived, scoped provider tokens at runtime, so code and agents never store credentials.

  • Vercel Connect guides walk through building agents this way, from Slack bots to GitHub agents.

Read more

title: How Interfaze serves 50 million requests a month on Vercel
description:
Interfaze on Vercel

  • 50 million requests a month

  • Backend running on Fluid compute

  • Multiple model providers behind one fallback layer with AI Gateway

Interfaze builds models for deterministic work that general-purpose LLMs handle poorly: document processing, OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification.

As founder Yoeven Khemlani puts it, "Most models aren't deterministic by nature. That's fine when you're drafting an essay. But when a hospital or a legal team needs to process documents, you don't reach for an LLM." Ask an LLM for the total on an invoice and you get a number with no easy way to check where it came from. Interfaze's models return the number along with a bounding box showing where on the page it came from and a confidence score for how sure the model is. Every result can be checked, and the models still take prompts the way an LLM does.

Everything around Interfaze's models runs on Vercel, including the backend. That spans the API serving 50 million requests a month, the sandbox that executes code the model writes, and the routing that keeps data preprocessing running when a third-party model provider goes down.

The backend required no infrastructure work

Interfaze's frontend and backend both run on Vercel. The backend handles every request to Interfaze's API, whether a customer is calling the model or uploading a file. All of it runs as serverless functions in the same codebase as the frontend. When a request needs computation, the model hands the code to Vercel Sandbox, which runs it in isolation. There was no separate infrastructure to set up.

Fluid compute handles the heavy jobs

Scalability was Yoeven's top requirement. The goal is serving the model to millions of users, and Fluid compute scales with traffic on its own. Heavier work runs there too. Vercel's memory and timeout limits are high enough that Interfaze's web scraping, which runs on Puppeteer, works out of the box.

AI Gateway makes model routing reliable at scale

Interfaze pushes large volumes of data cleaning through open source models hosted by third-party providers. A single provider is a weak link. Providers hit rate limits or go down, and when one does, the cleaning stops unless traffic moves somewhere else.

The providers are also not interchangeable. Two of them can claim to host the same open source model and serve it at very different quality.

When a provider fails or throttles, AI Gateway fails requests over to the next provider automatically. It also lets Interfaze choose which provider serves a given model, so the team can run the same workload through each one, see which performs well, and send traffic there.

Workflow SDK runs email sequences over months

Interfaze runs its lifecycle email system on the Workflow SDK, with sends conditioned on product usage. The system tracks which API a customer called, at what volume, and how that compares against their first week. Retries are handled automatically, so one failed step doesn't take down the sequence.

The part Interfaze needed most was durable execution. A workflow can pause a step and pick it back up months later with its state intact, which the team found other systems could not do for long.

Preview deployments carry new model versions to customers

Interfaze runs more than one version of its model at a time, each at its own URL. When an error comes in, the team has to know which version produced the error before they can fix anything. On Vercel every URL is its own deployment with its own logs, so the error is already filed under the version that caused it. There was no separate logging vendor to set up.

Those same preview URLs are how a new model version gets to customers before it ships. The Vercel side of a release builds in about three minutes. Hosting the weights on GPUs is the slow part.

What's next

Interfaze recently released Interfaze 1 Lite, an open-weight version of its model that runs on a single GPU and is served through the same API. Next is a gateway for web search, one API that routes to whichever search provider a developer picks, the way AI Gateway does for models. It launches on the same Vercel backend as everything else.

About Interfaze: Interfaze builds models for deterministic tasks, including OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification. Its customers are engineering teams in legal, healthcare, and finance.

title: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
description:
An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve.

Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes.

The plan determines the permissions

For a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision.

Access is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy:

Plan

Work

Requested scope

Investigate the failure

Inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last successful one

read:deployment

Redeploy the last known-good build

Create a deployment

read-write:deployment

A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically.

The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do:

  • Intent: The outcome the user asks for.

  • Work: The tasks Vercel Agent proposes to achieve it.

  • Access: The scopes those tasks require.

  • Enforcement: The credentials and API checks that enforce access limits.

Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan.

The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with read:. Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless.

Vercel Agent can only use permissions the user already has

Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the user’s existing permissions, so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have.

The Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits.

A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions.

Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions.

Approval determines which permissions Vercel Agent can use

When a user approves a plan that needs additional Vercel access, its requested scopes are checked again and a token is prepared containing the read-only baseline plus the approved permissions. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. That credential remains subject to its scopes, team, the user’s permissions, and expiry.

The credential used depends on the work:

Work

Credential

Read-only investigation

A baseline token with read-only scopes

Approved Vercel changes

A token with baseline scopes plus the approved additional scopes

External actions

Credentials and permissions specific to that provider

The model’s instructions tell it when to propose a plan and request approval. If it attempts an operation outside the token’s permissions, Vercel APIs reject the request, even if the model considers the action necessary to complete the task.

A single plan can include Vercel changes and a GitHub pull request. The user reviews both in one plan, while each provider uses separate permissions and credentials. GitHub pull-request access is tied to an owner and repository, so approval to open a pull request in acme/storefront applies to that repository even if the user also has access to acme/payments. Opening a pull request there requires its own approval.

Plans and tokens use the same permission definitions

A proposed plan can request a permission that has been renamed or removed. We initially maintained a separate permission list for Vercel Agent, which could fall out of sync with the OAuth service that issues its tokens. We moved to the same scope definitions so those mismatches could be caught during planning.

At session setup, Vercel Agent loads those definitions from the Vercel scope registry into an in-memory catalog. Fetching the registry requires authorization for the team, while the scope definitions themselves are shared across teams. The catalog supplies the definitions used at three stages:

  • Plan validation: Requested scopes are normalized, and unknown or malformed names are rejected before the plan is stored or presented for approval.

  • Approval: The requested scopes determine whether the plan fits within the read-only baseline or needs additional access.

  • Token preparation: Valid scopes define the credentials for approved work.

For example, a task to update firewall rules might request an outdated scope. The system rejects the proposed plan and returns valid scopes so Vercel Agent can correct it before requesting approval. This catches the mismatch during planning and requires an explicit correction instead of a fallback to broader access.

Fetching the registry adds latency and a service dependency, so Vercel Agent caches the catalog and uses that copy to check stored plans when they are loaded. Those checks reflect the cached definitions until the catalog is refreshed with changes from the registry.

Resuming work requires an active, approved plan

Vercel Agent may receive approval after the original chat request has ended, or lose its connection before carrying out an approved redeploy. The stored plan includes its state, who approved it, and when, alongside its tasks and requested permissions. That record connects the proposed work to the access the user authorized and allows the approval to be checked when work resumes.

Before resuming, the runtime reloads the plan and checks that it is active before selecting a credential with its approved permissions. A stopped plan fails that check, even if its token has time remaining before expiry.

If approval and a request to stop arrive together, the plan can move from waiting for approval to active only if the stop has not already changed its status. The runtime then checks again that the plan is active before using the approved credential.

If the investigation reveals that the current plan needs replacing, Vercel Agent can propose another. A replacement requesting elevated access needs its own approval, giving the user a chance to review the revised work and permissions together.

Where permissions need more precision

As Vercel Agent reached more of the platform, we had to correct access rules for actions that involve multiple resources or have different consequences. Attaching a domain can require both domain and project permissions, while staging a firewall rule and publishing it need different levels of access. Scopes need to capture these distinctions while keeping each plan’s access request manageable.

Matching those scopes to a proposed fix requires care throughout planning:

  • Choosing scopes: Vercel Agent chooses scopes with incomplete information, so it can request too little access and leave a task blocked, or too much and grant more authority than the work needs. Task-level guidance helps it choose, while validation catches invalid scope names. Even a valid scope can grant broader access than necessary.

  • Describing the work: “Redeploy the last successful build” gives the user a concrete action to assess, while scope names alone leave them to work out the consequences. The plan needs to explain the intended change and make clear which limits the token actually enforces.

  • Understanding denials: A denied operation could indicate a missing scope, an incorrect resource, or an operation that should remain blocked. Vercel Agent needs to distinguish those cases before requesting additional permissions.

Even with the right permissions, a redeploy requires judgment about whether the selected commit is safe to ship. That depends on the application, the failure, and the proposed fix. The user needs enough information to assess the choice, and Vercel Agent still has to execute it correctly.

Read-only investigation also needs controls for the information it retrieves, including sensitive project configuration and operational details. We chose a read-only baseline so Vercel Agent can investigate before asking for approval, and that choice needs continued review as scopes and the information they expose change. Other systems may need a narrower baseline. Separate controls must govern how retrieved information is handled and where it can go.

Vercel Agent can make a wrong decision or encounter malicious instructions in content it reads, such as build logs. Scoped credentials limit which operations it can perform in either case, but permitted operations can still cause harm. Plans therefore work alongside sandbox isolation, network policy, secret handling, rate limits, audit logs, and service authorization. Our work on security boundaries in agentic architectures explains the separation between an agent, its credentials, and the code it executes.

From investigation to approved action

Authority stays attached to the work that required it. The runtime selects the approved credential for an active plan, and its scopes define the operations Vercel Agent can perform. With the investigation already done, the user can assess a proposed fix and its requested access together.

Try Vercel Agent to investigate an issue in your project. Review what it finds and, if it proposes a change, assess the plan and requested access before approving it.

title: Introducing Vercel CI
description:
Coding agents are opening more pull requests than ever, and each one waits on CI before anyone can review or merge it. Most CI systems run the entire workflow on every push, even a one-line change. The more your agents push, the more time you spend waiting on CI.

Today, we're announcing Vercel CI in Beta. It runs only the tasks affected by your code change, and spins up only the compute those checks need, the same way Fluid compute scales with your traffic.

At Vercel, our CI now keeps up with our coding agents. Time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x faster than it was before.

How it works

Vercel CI uses Turborepo to understand your tasks and which ones depend on each other. It reads turbo.json, so if you're already using Turborepo, there's no separate CI config to write.

If you're not on Turborepo yet, add turbo.json and the turbo package. It works in single-package repos too.

Then tag the tasks you want Vercel CI to run.

"tags": ["ci"] is all you need to get started. No workflow YAML to maintain, no drift between your CI config and turbo.json, and Remote Cache is on by default.

When you or your agent push code, Vercel CI determines which tasks need to run based on the change. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come from cache. The remaining tasks each run on their own machine, powered by Hive, Vercel's compute layer, and start as soon as their dependencies finish.

Vercel CI gives each task the compute it needs and nothing more.

Running your CI on Vercel

To get started, follow the documentation or prompt your agent from your repo:

Once set up, you or your agent can watch and inspect CI through the Vercel dashboard, Vercel CLI, or Vercel MCP. When something fails, go straight to the failing task, see what's blocked behind it, and open its logs, or search across recent runs to see whether a test has been flaky all week.

Vercel CI posts a check to your pull request on GitHub, so your existing branch protection rules can block merges on failure, the same way they do today.

Closing the loop

Vercel CI has already completed nearly 8 million tasks across our own repositories and the private beta, and we're just getting started. We're working to keep shrinking the time between writing code and running it in production.

As we work toward general availability, we plan to add:

  • Advanced observability

  • A vc ci CLI command for distributed execution before pushing code

  • More granular test selection

Vercel CI is available in Beta today on all plans. Read the docs and try it on your repository.

Read more

title: Introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway
description:
Today, we are introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway.

Virtual Models are an abstraction of the model string and configurations your apps and developers use. With a single virtual model ID, you can change and update models, configure fallbacks and priority, and enforce Zero Data Retention centrally. The virtual model configuration applies wherever the ID is used.

Assign a virtual model ID to an agent task, and pass it as the model string wherever that task is called. You can then change the model and settings behind the virtual model ID in AI Gateway, and your apps and agents will pick up the new configuration automatically, without code changes or redeploys.

New models use the same virtual model ID

In the last 90 days, 125 new models from more than 10 labs became available on AI Gateway. That adds up to about 10 a week. AI Gateway already makes switching a one-line change. You call any of those models by ID, and AI Gateway routes each request to a healthy provider and can fall back to others when one fails.

That one line still lives in your code, so switching usually means a redeploy.

Virtual Models move model selection and configuration to AI Gateway. You create an ID for a task, like vmc/coding-agent, and then configure the model and the settings it should use:

You can then use that virtual model ID as the model string wherever the task runs:

For coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and others, connect them with vercel ai-gateway setup, then select your virtual model in each harness's model picker or configuration.

When a different model is available, including one from another provider, edit the virtual model. Every app and agent that calls vmc/coding-agent picks it up within a few minutes, with no code change or deployment needed:

Give each task its own model

An agent task like support ticket triage can run hundreds of times an hour and needs to be cheap. Other tasks, like legal contract review, may only run a few times a day, but require a high level of reasoning.

You can now give each task a purpose-built virtual model and easily evolve that model and configuration over time:

Settings such as fallbacks, Zero Data Retention, and tags stay with the virtual model when you switch models. Provider options apply per provider, so an Anthropic-specific setting stops applying when you point the virtual model at an OpenAI model. Review your provider options whenever you switch providers.

Before you switch a virtual model that serves production traffic, point a second one, like vmc/coding-agent-candidate, at the new model and run your evals against it. If quality drops after the switch, point the original back at the previous model.

Govern which models your team uses and how

Anyone on your team can call a virtual model, and team roles control who can make changes to it. Platform and security teams can centrally govern and test models and settings, while still easily giving teams access to new models as they are released.

Settings on a virtual model win over the same settings in a request, so callers can't override the provider order, fallbacks, or service tier you chose. For example, you can configure the fallback models for vmc/storefront-assistant centrally, and every app using that virtual model ID will use the same failover configuration, even if a request specifies different fallbacks.

If a virtual model requires Zero Data Retention or providers that don't train on request data, those configurations are enforced even if a request explicitly sets zeroDataRetention or disallowPromptTraining to false.

Tags on a virtual model replace any tags sent with the request, so spend lands on the task no matter how each app tags its calls. The Virtual Models page shows requests, spend, and success rate for each task.

Get started

Create a virtual model from your team dashboard or with the Vercel CLI.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

Virtual Models work with every model type on AI Gateway, including image, video, speech, embedding, and realtime models, and with the AI SDK and the OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs. See the Virtual Models documentation for every setting.

title: CodeBoo: Exorcising Your Codebase’s Hidden TODOs and Haunted Bugs
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

We’ve all left a line like // TODO: fix memory leak before launch in a file, closed the editor, and promptly forgotten it ever existed. Over time, repos turn into digital haunted houses—populated by lingering code debt, unindexed security hazards, and ghost functions abandoned three years ago.

CodeBoo is a lightweight, local AI tool that brings those spectral bugs out of the shadows.

Point CodeBoo at any local directory or public GitHub repo link, and it scans the codebase to surface hidden TODOs, potential memory leaks, unhandled errors, and security issues.

Instead of dumping a terrifying, dry terminal log, CodeBoo ranks the issues by urgency and renders them as interactive, spooky-cute ghosts:

  • 👻 Harmless Spirits (Low Urgency): Cute, friendly little ghosts for routine TODO comments and cosmetic cleanups.
  • 🧟 Creepy Specters (Medium Urgency): Slightly unhinged ghosts for unhandled exceptions or inefficient loops.
  • 🎃 Nightmare Phantoms (High Urgency): Genuinely spooky, dark spirits for critical memory leaks, exposed keys, or potential null-pointer crashes. It turns technical debt triage into something clear, visual, and oddly charming.

Demo

Code

How I Built It

CodeBoo was built to run entirely on a mid-range developer machine (designed to consume under 5 GB of system memory, leaving plenty of room within an 8 GB free RAM budget).

  • The Model: Qwen2.5-Coder:7b (or gemma2:9b / gemma4:2b) running locally via Ollama. Code-focused open models are fantastic at reading multi-file context, understanding syntax semantics, and returning structured JSON without needing a cloud API key.
  • File Parser & Aggregator: A lightweight backend written in Python that walks through code files, strips non-essential whitespace to stay within model context limits, and flags candidate blocks.
  • Severity Ranking Engine: The LLM evaluates every discovered issue and assigns it an urgency rating (1 to 5), an issue category (Security, Leak, Refactor, TODO), a plain-English explanation (keeping jargon accessible), and a recommended fix.
  • Visual UI: A single-page web dashboard using CSS animations to display issue "cards" inside animated ghost sprites whose expressions and dark glow scale with the severity of the bug.

Limitations

  • Repository Size: Extremely large repos (thousands of files) must be scanned module-by-module to keep context window usage within RAM bounds.
  • Static Analysis Edge Cases: While local open-weight models excel at finding logic flaws and written TODOs, full runtime memory profiling still requires dedicated profilers.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • Codebase Confidentiality: Scanning code for security bugs or unhandled edge cases using a closed cloud API means sending your proprietary context to external servers. Local open-weight models guarantee your code never leaves your device.
  • Unrestricted Code Scans: You can run CodeBoo against massive personal repos or multiple commits without worrying about token limits, rate caps, or monthly bills.
  • Customizable Parsing: Because the inference runner and prompts are completely transparent, developers can swap out models or fine-tune prompt constraints for their specific language stack.

The Spirit of It

title: DAYBACK: An AI time machine that finds the receipts of your past, reconstructs what happened, and never makes up a memory
description:
DAYBACK: Yesterday Is Not Finished

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Some moments are too important to live only in memory. The night a country won a World Cup, the hours after a result nobody expected. People remember how those moments felt, but the voices, headlines and videos that surrounded them are scattered across the web.

DAYBACK takes one sentence and turns it into an entire remembered experience. You type a moment, for example "Argentina wins the 2022 FIFA World Cup", and DAYBACK:

  1. Works out what the event actually was (date, place, people involved).
  2. Plans a spread of searches across the four phases of any historical moment: the anticipation, the moment, the aftermath and the legacy.
  3. Gathers real, source-linked artefacts: YouTube films, news coverage and web pages.
  4. Listens separately to public conversation on Reddit and X and curates a small set of human voices.
  5. Lays the four most prominent memories on a digital ofrenda, a Día de los Muertos altar, where each framed hole in the altar opens a memory.

The ofrenda is not decoration. In Día de los Muertos, we keep the dead present by placing what mattered to them where everyone can see it. DAYBACK applies the same ritual to collective memory: the moments that shaped us deserve an altar, a candle and a place to return to.

Two principles run through every design decision:

  • Never fabricate the past. DAYBACK only shows material it actually retrieved, always links to the original source, and labels everything unverified until a human confirms it. If an API key is missing, it shows the query plan and invents nothing.

  • Fail softly. Every AI and network dependency has a fallback, so a missing model or a rate-limited API degrades the experience rather than breaking it.

Demo:

DAYBACK turns a single historical moment into an explorable archive of the digital traces it left behind.

1. Start with a moment

Enter a historical event, such as Argentina winning the 2022 FIFA World Cup.

DAYBACK uses an AI-powered research workflow to resolve the event, identify its important phases, and generate targeted searches across relevant platforms.

2. Watch the research unfold

The research workflow breaks the event into platform- and phase-specific queries rather than relying on one generic search.

It retrieves relevant material through SerpApi and the YouTube Data API, collecting source-linked videos, news coverage, and other indexed web content.

Each result retains its original source link and provenance information.

3. Explore the historical archive

Once research is complete, DAYBACK organizes the retrieved material into an event-focused experience.

Explore the event overview, its recovered digital artefacts, and the different perspectives surrounding the moment.

The goal isn't to generate a fictional reconstruction of history. It's to make real, discoverable traces of the past easier to explore.

4. Enter The Voices Archive

DAYBACK also performs a separate social research pass to discover public Reddit discussions and X posts related to the event.

These results are independently curated and displayed in The Voices Archive, bringing together reactions and conversations from people who experienced the moment.

This research runs independently of the main archive, so a social-search failure cannot prevent the core experience from loading.

5. Follow the evidence

Every displayed result links back to its original source.

DAYBACK labels retrieved material as unverified until a human confirms it. It does not present search snippets or AI classifications as verified historical facts.

If an API key is unavailable, DAYBACK displays the research plan instead of fabricating results.

The idea is simple: don't invent the past. Recover what can actually be found, preserve where it came from, and let people explore it.

Code:

sherwinkumar2004 / dayback

An interactive digital memorial that brings cherished memories back to life.

DAYBACK

Yesterday is not finished.

What if you could relive a moment in history, not just remember what happened, but experience how the world reacted to it?

DAYBACK is an AI-powered historical memory archive that transforms an event into an immersive, interactive experience. Give it a moment in time, and it gathers the news, videos and public reactions surrounding it, bringing them together in a digital Día de los Muertos Ofrenda.

Instead of another page of search results, DAYBACK gives history a place to live.

Live demo · DEV Challenge post · GitHub repository

The Experience

  • The Memory Altar: An interactive, pixel-art Ofrenda featuring four carefully selected memories. Each frame opens a different fragment of the event.
  • Four Chapters: Explore the anticipation, the moment, the aftermath and the legacy of an event.
  • The Archive: Discover news coverage, web articles and YouTube videos, organised into an interactive collection.
  • The Newspaper: News…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

1. The open-source AI

The language model runs locally through Ollama. The model is configured through an environment variable, making it possible to experiment with alternative models without rewriting the workflow.

It powers two important capabilities:

  • Event resolution: Turns a one-line input into a JSON brief (title, dates, location, aliases, confidence). It is told to use null rather than guess, and every model-supplied date is flagged for human review.

  • Social curation: Reads up to 60 public Reddit and X candidates and keeps at most 20 that add a distinct perspective, with a one-line reason for each.

2. Agent orchestration

Mastra orchestrates the main dayback-research-workflow. The Voices Archive operates through a separate research pipeline, so social discovery doesn't block the main archive.

The workflow has three primary steps:

  • resolve-event – Understands and structures the historical event.
  • plan-research – Generates up to 14 independent, platform- and chapter-specific search queries.
  • collect-sources – Retrieves, normalizes, and deduplicates the resulting artefacts.

3. Research integrations

  • SerpApi for web, news, Reddit, X, and YouTube discovery.
  • YouTube Data API v3 for video discovery.
  • SerpApi's YouTube engine as a fallback.

4. Making a 4B model dependable

Small local models misbehave, so the guardrails are the interesting part:

  • Strip Qwen3's <think> block and code fences, extract the outer JSON, default every missing field, then validate with Zod.
  • If Ollama is down, a rule-based fallback builds an honest brief that says resolution was unavailable.
  • The curator treats every post as untrusted data and may only return IDs from the candidate list; categories and chapters are checked against fixed lists. A local relevance ranker takes over if the model is unreachable.
  • The Voices Archive is a separate request, so a failure there never touches the main archive.
  • verificationStatus is the literal type unverified, so no code path can claim a source is verified.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A memorial cannot be built on a model you cannot inspect, and it must never rewrite the past. Open weights let me use a model for the one job it should have here, deciding what to look for and what to keep, while the remembering stays with real, linked sources.

Open worked better than a closed API in five places.

  1. The curator reads strangers' posts, so it should run where I can contain it. It reads up to 60 public posts per search, any of which could carry instructions aimed at the model. Running Qwen3 locally let me wrap it tightly (untrusted-data prompt, ID whitelist, validated outputs) without sending that text to a third-party model.

  2. The model call is free, so the budget goes to the archive. Each search already spends up to 14 planned metered search queries plus 6 for the Voices Archive. A hosted model would have added two more metered calls and a per-token bill on 60 posts.

  3. I could see the reasoning. Qwen3 writes its chain of thought in a <think> block. Because I run it myself, I log the raw output, strip the block, and fix the parser when a 4B model wanders, instead of guessing at a black box.

  4. One variable swaps the model. Both agents read OLLAMA_MODEL. Trying a larger Qwen3 or a Gemma model is a one-line change with no change to routes, workflows or contracts. A model on disk stays what it was when I tested it; a hosted one can change under me.

  5. A small, imperfect model forced a design nothing can break. The defaults, schemas and fallbacks I wrote for Qwen3 mean DAYBACK still works with no model running, and improves when a stronger one is plugged in.

The deeper reason is that the model never writes history. A model asked to recall a moment gives a fluent, plausible, sometimes invented account. Mine only answers narrow questions, and every item shown is a real URL marked unverified. That job does not need a frontier model, so an open 4B model on a laptop is enough.

The Spirit of It

Día de los Muertos holds that the dead are not gone while someone still tells their story. Moments work the same way. The day a country won, the night a wall came down, the evening you and a stranger both screamed at the same screen: they fade unless somebody sets a place for them.

That is why DAYBACK ends in an altar and not a results page. Four frames force a choice about what mattered most. The marigolds, the candles and the papel picado are the rest of the archive, the offerings around the centre. And the Voices Archive keeps the part history books skip: ordinary people, in their own words, in the hours when it all happened.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Mastra

  • Orchestrates DAYBACK's multi-stage historical research workflow through dayback-research-workflow.
  • Resolves a user's moment into a structured event brief and generates up to 14 targeted research queries.
  • Coordinates source discovery, retrieval, deduplication, and organization into a unified historical archive.
  • Keeps social discovery in a separate pipeline, so Reddit and X conversations can be curated independently without disrupting the main research workflow.

Best Use of SerpApi

  • Powers DAYBACK's web discovery engine, finding historical coverage and sources related to a user's moment.
  • Uses up to 14 targeted queries instead of relying on a single generic search.
  • Helps bring together scattered articles, webpages, and historical references into one research archive.
  • Complements the dedicated Reddit and X discovery pipeline, keeping historical reporting and public conversations distinct.

Built in collaboration with harish_gs_145

title: Building an In-Browser 478-Point Facial Landmark & Symmetry Analyzer (Zero Cloud Uploads)
description:
Most facial measurement and "rating" applications on the market today share two huge flaws:

  1. They charge aggressive subscription fees.
  2. They upload users' personal biometric selfie photos to centralized cloud servers.

I built FaceIQ as an open web application that executes 100% client-side in the browser.

How It Works Under the Hood

Using Google's MediaPipe 478-point landmark topology and WebAssembly/WebGL, the application computes:

  • Bilateral Cranial Symmetry: Evaluates lateral deviation across 32 anatomical mirror pairs.
  • Palpebral Canthal Tilt: Accurately measures inner-to-outer canthus inclination in degrees.
  • Facial Thirds & FWHR: Bizygomatic cheekbone width to midface height proportions.
  • Golden Ratio (Phi 1.618): Mathematical alignment against classical neoclassical cannons.
  • PSL Scale Rating Calculator: Quantitative facial harmony scoring.

Because the entire inference model runs in local browser memory via WebAssembly, zero bytes of photographic data ever touch a remote server.

Check out the live web app: Link

Would love to hear technical feedback and suggestions for additional craniofacial ratios to implement!

title: DEAD AIR: I Built a 3D Mystery Experience Powered by Local Gemma 4 AI 👻📻
description:
DEAD AIR: I Built a 3D Mystery Experience Powered by Local Gemma 4 AI 👻📻

What if you discovered a radio transmission that nobody should be able to hear?

What if the only way to understand it was to enter an abandoned observatory, discover its secrets and communicate with the mysterious signal itself?

For Hacktoberfest Week 4, I built DEAD AIR — The Last Frequency, a first-person 3D mystery experience powered by Gemma 4 running locally in the browser.

This is my interpretation of the theme Ghost in the Machine.

1. What I Built

DEAD AIR takes place inside an abandoned radio observatory.

At 03:17 AM, an impossible transmission begins broadcasting.

The player must explore the observatory, investigate an incident log, discover hidden signal fragments, tune a radio transmitter and reconstruct the final transmission.

But there is something unusual about this experience.

The mysterious entity communicating through the radio is powered by a real open-weight language model running locally in the browser.

No backend. No API key. No remote inference service.

Key Features

  • First-person 3D exploration with WASD and mouse controls.
  • Procedurally generated observatory environment.
  • Interactive incident log, signal monitor and radio transmitter.
  • Frequency-tuning puzzle with dynamic audio and visual feedback.
  • Evidence collection and a six-step investigation progression.
  • Local Gemma 4 AI assistant called THE SIGNAL.
  • Evidence-grounded AI responses with citations.
  • Deterministic mystery reconstruction and validation.
  • Scripted preview when WebGPU or model loading is unavailable.

2. Demo

The project has been built and tested locally.

A video walkthrough and hosted browser demo are not included in this initial submission. The repository includes screenshots, including evidence of the successful real Gemma inference run, and instructions for running the experience locally.

Real Gemma 4 inference:

More screenshots and setup instructions are available in the repository.

3. Code

GitHub Repository:

https://github.com/TechGenDM/Hacktoberfest-Week-4-2026

Branch: main

Commit: 19aa676

4. How I Built It

The application uses:

Technology Purpose
Vite 8 Development and production builds
TypeScript 7 Application logic
Three.js 0.187 3D environment
Transformers.js 4.3.2 Browser-based model inference
Gemma 4 E2B Local language model
WebGPU Hardware-accelerated inference
Web Workers Background model processing
Web Audio API Procedural ambient audio

The environment is constructed using procedural geometry and textures rather than relying on downloaded 3D assets.

The interesting engineering decision

I deliberately separated the mystery-solving system from the language model.

The game itself controls the evidence, puzzle progression and final answer.

Gemma does not decide what happened. It investigates the evidence available to the player and helps interpret it.

Every response passes through a deterministic validation layer.

The validator checks:

  • Whether sentences include evidence citations.
  • Whether the cited evidence has actually been discovered.
  • Whether numerical claims appear in their cited evidence.
  • Whether named entities appear in the discovered evidence.

Responses receive one of four verdicts:

VERIFIED · PARTIAL · REJECTED · NO SIGNAL

Unsupported sentences can be struck out with an explanation.

This is not a guarantee of semantic correctness, but it provides a deterministic first layer of protection against unsupported AI responses.

Real Gemma 4 inference results

I tested actual inference in headless Chrome on macOS using WebGPU and the q4f16 model path.

Measurement Result
Initial load, including download and shader warm-up 279 seconds
Model download Approximately 3.38 GB
Generation speed 28–33 tokens/second
Response time 1–2.5 seconds

I tested several questions.

Question: Where is the carrier coming from?

Result: Three evidence-cited sentences. All were marked VERIFIED.

Question: Who sent the signal from Mars?

Result: NO SIGNAL ON THAT BAND.

Question: What frequency should I tune TX-2 to?

Result: The response repeated a cited sentence. It was accurate but not sufficiently helpful. This is a known limitation.

Testing

The following checks passed:

  • TypeScript compilation.
  • Production build.
  • Complete automated game playthrough.
  • All eight evidence items discovered.
  • Incorrect reconstruction order rejected.
  • Correct reconstruction accepted.
  • Ending sequence completed.
  • Scripted fallback verified.
  • No runtime errors during the automated playthrough.

Browser compatibility beyond Chrome on macOS and low-memory GPU configurations remains untested.

5. Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

I wanted to explore what happens when an AI-powered interactive experience does not depend on a centralized AI service.

DEAD AIR uses an open-weight Gemma model with browser-based inference.

The model runs on the user's hardware rather than sending every conversation to a remote inference API.

This offers several advantages:

  • Conversations can remain on the user's device.
  • No application backend or AI API key is required.
  • The model can be downloaded and used locally.
  • The system does not depend on a proprietary inference endpoint.
  • The application combines an open-weight model with transparent, application-level validation.

One important distinction: the initial model download requires an internet connection. After the weights are cached, inference can run locally without a remote AI service.

For me, open innovation is not just about accessing a model. It is about having the freedom to run, inspect, adapt and build around the technology.

6. What I Learned

The most interesting part of this project was not getting a model to generate dialogue.

It was learning how to build an experience where the model has boundaries.

A language model can produce convincing answers even when it does not have enough information. In a mystery game, that can completely destroy the experience.

Separating deterministic game logic from AI interpretation made the system more predictable.

I also learned how important browser GPU support, model quantization, Web Workers and initial model-loading performance are when building local AI applications.

7. Prize Categories

Gemma — Best Use of Gemma

The project uses Gemma 4 E2B as its central conversational AI model, running locally through Transformers.js and WebGPU.

Final Thoughts

DEAD AIR started as an idea: what if we could build an entire interactive mystery world where the intelligence behind the experience lives inside the browser?

It became an experiment in combining 3D environments, open-weight AI, local inference and deterministic engineering.

There is still plenty to improve. This is an initial prototype, not a finished commercial game.

But it works, the real Gemma inference has been verified, and the mystery can be completed.

Sometimes the most interesting thing is not the signal itself.

It's what happens when somebody finally answers it.

Built for the Hacktoberfest 2026 DEV Challenge — Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.
