  • Best Use of Ultramarine (Paper Instruments): Features an in-app side-by-side benchmark comparing local Gemma vs. Ultramarine cloud inference with real-time latency and token spend tracking.

The Spirit of It

Día de los Muertos teaches us that people only truly leave us when they are forgotten.

Technology shouldn't try to replace the people we love with synthetic, hallucinating avatars. Instead, open-source software can give us an honest digital sanctuary—a quiet place where their real words, favorite melodies, and cherished stories remain safe, private, and permanent.

That is the true ghost in the machine: not an artificial phantom, but the enduring warmth of our own memories, preserved on our own terms.

title: Dobara: When Your Sources Change, Does Your Claim Still Hold?
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

A source changes. The claim based on it stays.

That is the problem behind Dobara, a local AI tool for checking whether an earlier and a current source excerpt support the same claim.

Consider a fictional scholarship notice. Its earlier version says:

Applications are open to all undergraduate students.

You write: “All undergraduate students can apply.”

Later, the notice changes:

Applications are open only to final-year undergraduate students.

Your sentence still exists in a spreadsheet, an article, or a message someone forwards. Its original evidence has become a ghost.

That is my interpretation of Ghost in the Machine: old evidence continuing to influence what we believe after the source has changed.

Dobara asks you to supply a claim and two source excerpts. It assesses the claim against each excerpt, shows the original evidence passages, and highlights wording differences. You can save a comparison, use its current source as the next baseline, and record your own review decision.

I wanted something useful for students checking opportunity notices, writers revisiting citations, and researchers reviewing source changes. The result is a focused prototype for reviewing supplied evidence. It does not authenticate pasted text, monitor websites, or establish whether a claim is universally true.

Demo

Try the live Dobara demo

Start with Eligibility changed, run the comparison, and inspect the evidence alongside the text differences. The other fictional examples show an unchanged supporting source and a claim that the earlier excerpt never supported.

The public demo runs through a temporary Cloudflare Tunnel. Inference happens on my laptop through Ollama, so availability depends on my laptop and tunnel remaining online. I tested the public link from a separate phone and successfully ran a sample comparison.

Please use fictional information. The demo has no separate user accounts, so saved comparisons and reviews are shared among visitors. For personal material, run your own local installation using the repository instructions.

Code

GitHub repository: shoriful-mynul/dobara

The application is released under the MIT licence. The repository includes setup instructions, tests, testing limitations, and upgrade notes.

How I Built It

Dobara uses Qwen3 4B, an open-weight model running through Ollama. A Python FastAPI backend handles analysis and persistence, while the interface uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Optional saved comparisons and human reviews live in a local SQLite database.

The model provides the language interpretation at the core of the application: does the supplied excerpt support the full claim, explicitly contradict it, omit the necessary information, or leave the answer uncertain?

The earlier and current excerpts are assessed independently. This matters because the earlier source might never have supported the claim in the first place.

One early problem shaped the implementation. A model-generated quotation failed validation because it did not exactly match the source. I changed the workflow so the model selects evidence IDs rather than writes quotations.

The backend now:

  1. Assigns IDs to the supplied evidence passages.
  2. Requests structured assessments and evidence IDs from Qwen3.
  3. Validates the response and checks the selected IDs.
  4. Builds quotations directly from the original passages.
  5. Derives the overall verdict using explicit Python rules.

This keeps quotations traceable to the input. It does not guarantee that the model interpreted them correctly.

Text differences are computed separately using Python’s difflib. A wording change and a change in support are different questions, so the interface presents both.

Human review is also separate from the AI assessment. A reviewer can choose Keep claim, Revise claim, or Find more evidence, then save a note without changing the model’s original result or running inference again. Linked rechecks create new records rather than overwrite earlier comparisons.

The release’s automated checks include 80 passing backend/static tests, plus an optional DOM interaction script. Inference is mocked in those checks; they test application behavior, not model accuracy.

I used ChatGPT/Codex and Claude for development assistance.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Source excerpts can contain information someone would rather keep on their own machine. Local inference makes that possible without requiring a hosted model API for every comparison.

After setup, the application uses installed model weights through Ollama. There is no per-request model API charge, although the computer still supplies the memory, processing time, and electricity. The repository distinguishes local operation from disconnected operation, which needs testing on the target machine.

Open weights also give this project a path beyond one provider. A developer can adapt the model configuration and evaluate alternatives against the same evidence-review workflow. Better models can be tested without discarding the application’s saved-history and human-review design.

For Dobara, the practical advantage is control over where source text goes and how the assessment works. A hosted API could perform similar reasoning, but this approach lets someone own the inference environment and inspect the surrounding application code.

The public demo makes a different trade-off: requests pass through Cloudflare to my laptop. The privacy benefit belongs to running your own local copy.

The Spirit of It

The most useful moment in Dobara is small: seeing “all undergraduate students” beside “only final-year undergraduate students,” with the original wording available to inspect.

Then there is the less obvious case: both excerpts can be identical and still fail to support the claim. Nothing changed in the source. The assumption was already there.

That is the ghost I wanted to make visible.

Dobara gives a claim a second look, with the evidence still in view.

title: Ghostbusters for coding agents: 12 GiB of ghosts on my Mac, and 15 GiB more I didn't know about
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

I run coding agents all day. Claude Code in one terminal, Codex in another, sometimes three sessions on the same repo at once. They're the ghosts in my machine: they work where I can't see them, often while I'm asleep, and like any good ghost they leave slime behind.

One agent task looks like this. A fresh git worktree. Then npm install (a new node_modules), uv sync (a new .venv), cargo build (a few GB of target). The package caches grow, the IDE indexes the new folder, and the session itself leaves a transcript, checkpoints and a scratch folder. Run five tasks in parallel and you get five of everything. The task gets merged, the worktree gets forgotten, the slime stays.

And if you run open-weight models locally, the old weights in ~/.ollama or the Hugging Face cache are the biggest blobs of all.

So I pointed my own disk cleaner at it. Here's my own Mac, this week:

Agent On disk Still alive
Codex 5.5 GiB 8 open threads
Claude Code 3.5 GiB 5 live sessions, plus 63 old transcripts (1.7 GiB)
Cursor 2.8 GiB not running
opencode 72 MiB not running

About 12 GiB. Fine, I expected that. Then I looked in /private/tmp/claude-<uid>, where Claude Code keeps each session's scratchpad, task output and pasted images, and found another 15 GiB that my tool didn't see at all. A restart clears it, but my Mac had been up for 33 hours and the agents had been busy.

That's what DeepDriveCleaner™ (ddc) is for. It's a disk cleaner for developers (package caches, build output, old toolchains, simulator runtimes) and this week it learned to follow agents around. Inside every worktree an agent leaves, it finds the node_modules, .venv and target like anywhere else, and now it also knows each agent's own data. It follows three rules, and I'd trust it on my own machine only because of them:

  1. A ghost still at work is left alone. If the process that wrote a session is still running, ddc never offers its files.
  2. It reads metadata, never your conversations. File names, sizes, the process list. It doesn't open a transcript.
  3. It never deletes on its own. It shows a plan, checks every item again right before acting, and waits for you to say yes.

The other half is for the agents themselves. Every report has --json with a published schema, so an agent can ask "where did my disk go, and what's safe to remove?" and get a real answer instead of guessing with du -sh *. Version 0.14.0 (PR #58, merged as I write this) adds the per-session view (transcript, checkpoints, temporary folder, live or not) and a first agent skill, plus an AGENTS.md snippet, that teach an agent to ask ddc first and hand you the cleanup command, never run it.

It runs on macOS as a CLI and a menu bar app. Linux has a static CLI on main, and the Windows build already passes its tests natively.

Two open pieces carry all of this. The open-source Codex CLI (Apache-2.0) was one of the two agents that wrote the code, and it ran the benchmarks below. And ProjectStore, our MIT-licensed method, is what let two different agents share one backlog all week. There's no model inside the tool: it's built by agents and for them.

Demo

DeepDriveCleaer via CLI:

Recorded on a fake home folder full of fake agent data. I don't point a cleaner's demo at anyone's real files, mine included.

DeepDriveCleaner via Application

Try it on your Mac:

brew install --cask smartandpoint/tap/deepdrivecleaner

Or just the CLI:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SmartAndPoint/DeepDriveCleaner/main/packaging/install/install.sh | sh

After:

ddc disk agents

Or via Application -> DeepDriveCleaner and bar icon.

I'd love to know how many ghosts you find. Post what you found in the comments. If an agent keeps junk somewhere I don't know about yet, tell me and it becomes a rule. And if it saves you a few gigabytes, a ⭐ helps other people find it.

Code

SmartAndPoint / DeepDriveCleaner

Find and safely clean developer disk junk on macOS: venvs, node_modules, build outputs, caches. Built in the open with ProjectStore.

DeepDriveCleaner™

Find and safely clean what development leaves on a Mac's disk: Python virtual environments, node_modules, build outputs, package and toolchain caches, Xcode data, local ML models and VM images. Everything it finds is grouped by risk. Nothing is removed until you have seen the plan and confirmed it.

It is a menu bar app with the command-line tool inside: the same engine, a window or a terminal, whichever you prefer.

Warning

DeepDriveCleaner deletes files. It checks every item before it touches it, but it can remove almost anything it is told to, by you or by an AI agent acting for you. You use it at your own risk: nobody who made it is responsible for what it removes. Read the Disclaimer before you clean.

$ ddc scan
DeepDriveCleaner · scanned ~ in 39.6s · 5.5M files · 544.8 GiB
  safe           1919 items   76.3 GiB   selected 76.3 GiB
…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Honestly, the tool is the smaller half. The method is what let one person ship this in two weeks.

DeepDriveCleaner was built by me and two agent harnesses, Claude Code and the open-source Codex CLI, working inside ProjectStore. ProjectStore is our open-source (MIT) method for building software with agents: decisions, specs, epics and stories live as plain markdown in a vault next to the code, and every agent reads and writes them. Here's the loop:

In practice it works like this. Nothing gets coded until it's a story with acceptance criteria. If the "how" isn't obvious, it gets an ADR first. A critic agent tears each story apart in a fresh context before any code exists. A planner maps it onto the codebase. When the code is done, a reviewer agent checks the diff against every acceptance criterion and wants evidence, not vibes. Every change, code or vault, goes through a pull request with a test gate.

It sounds slow. It isn't. The 15 GiB surprise above went from "huh" to a reviewed story, a planned change and merged code in one evening. Here's what two weeks looked like:

October 17–31
Commits 249, of which 227 in the challenge week
Pull requests 58 in the code, 36 in the vault
Releases 16, of which 10 in the challenge week
Backlog 8 epics, 85 stories, 50 closed with evidence
Decisions 6 ADRs, 7 research notes, 5 runbooks

And what came out of it isn't a toy:

  • a Rust core (library plus CLI with JSON output), with one platform module per OS: 87 cleanup rules on macOS, 48 on Linux;
  • a native Swift menu bar app on top, with a review window, scheduled scans and auto-updates;
  • 600+ Rust tests and 440+ Swift tests in a gate nothing merges without, plus load runs and a check that fails the build if a scan stops scaling linearly;
  • a benchmark against 9 other disk-usage tools, which Codex ran (ddc 0.7.0, a synthetic 100,000-entry tree of developer projects, warm cache, 10 runs each). Median: ddc du 1.03 s, dust 0.89 s, pdu 1.04 s, dua 1.09 s, BSD du 1.21 s, all with the same totals. The ranges overlap, so it's not the fastest, and I won't claim it is. It's in the same league as the good du clones, and on top of that it knows what each folder is and whether it's safe to delete.

The whole vault is public. If you want to see how an agent-built project makes decisions, every story, ADR and critic review is there:

SmartAndPoint / DeepDriveCleaner-projectstore

ProjectStore vault of DeepDriveCleaner: research, ADRs, epics and stories behind the code.

DeepDriveCleaner-projectstore

The project's memory: decisions, specs, epics and stories as plain markdown, kept by projectstore.

This is the ProjectStore vault of DeepDriveCleaner, a macOS tool that finds and safely cleans what development leaves on the disk. It is public on purpose, as a worked example of building software through ProjectStore. A research note came first, then two ADRs and an epic with stories. A fresh-context critic reviewed every artifact before code was written, a planner placed the work, and a reviewer checked each story's acceptance criteria against the code before the story was closed with evidence.

Where to start reading:

  1. Where a developer's disk space goes (macOS): the research note behind the project.
  2. Rust core: library + CLI with JSON output and Cleanup safety model: risk classes, plan and confirmation: the two decisions.
  3. DDC-001: Disk space cleaner CLI for developers: the epic and its stories, each…
View on GitHub

And ProjectStore itself, if you want to try the method on your own project:

SmartAndPoint / ProjectStore

Decisions, specs and stories as plain markdown, for every coding agent. Code changes. Context stays.

ProjectStore

Not agent memory, not a per-feature spec pipeline. Memory helps one agent recall; a feature spec plans one change. ProjectStore keeps the project's record — what was decided, what is in flight, what was checked — as reviewed markdown in git, readable by any agent and anyone with the repo.

A project workflow plugin for Claude Code and OpenAI Codex (experimental). Both are released together at one version, and one command sets a project up for either or both: see Install.

Two months of agents, and nobody knows why

Agents write code fast. They re-decide settled questions even faster: every fresh session arrives empty, makes its own architectural call, and commits under its own assumptions. Two months later you have noodle code — every strand reviews fine on its own, and each was written under a different theory of the project. Ask "why is this a queue and…

View on GitHub

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

I won't run a cleaner I can't read, and I don't expect you to. The rules are code, the safety model is an ADR, and every change has its reasoning in the vault.

The open vault mattered as much as the open code. If the plan had lived in one assistant's memory, switching harnesses would have meant starting over. It's markdown in git, so Codex picked up where Claude Code left off, and you can read it too.

It works with the lights off, too. Scanning and cleaning need no network; the only thing that calls out is the app's update check. An agent running an open-weight model locally, through opencode for example, can ask ddc where the disk went without anything leaving the machine.

It also matters for agents. They learn tools from source, schemas and docs. A disk tool with open JSON contracts is one any agent can use correctly, including open-source agents like Codex CLI and opencode running open-weight models.

A note on licences, to be straight about it: the method that built this, ProjectStore, is MIT. DeepDriveCleaner itself is source-available under PolyForm Noncommercial: free for personal and noncommercial use, and you can change it and share it; commercial use needs a licence from us.

My Agent Session

Rather than a raw transcript, here's the trail one session left: the vault PR where "my tool can't see 15 GiB" turned into stories, with two critic reviews folded in before a line of code. The code that came out of it is PR #58.

The Spirit of It

Slime is what a machine keeps after the work is gone, and agents leave more of it than any of us ever did: they never close a tab, never delete a worktree, never forget a session. I'm not hunting the ghosts. I like my ghosts. I just want to clean up after them, without an exorcist that burns the house down. So: a ghostbuster with a trap and a checklist. It names every puddle, tells you which ghost is still at work, and lets you decide.

It's Día de los Muertos this weekend, which feels about right: before anything goes, every session gets listed by name and date. Then you let it go.

title: Time-Capsule Radio: The Dead Internet Is Still Broadcasting
description:
Some websites die. Some domains disappear. Some servers are switched off and forgotten.

But what if their voices never stopped?

Deep beneath the modern internet lies a graveyard.

Millions of abandoned homepages. News bulletins from forgotten wars. Predictions about futures that never arrived. Personal websites whose owners have long since vanished. Entire digital civilizations buried beneath decades of broken hyperlinks and expired domains.

Their servers are silent.

Their creators have moved on.

But somewhere, in the decaying electromagnetic wilderness of the World Wide Web, fragments of their existence remain.

And now, something is listening.

TIME-CAPSULE RADIO — SPECTRAL DEMODULATOR MK-IV is an experimental shortwave receiver built to intercept transmissions from the internet's past.

Turn the dial. Select a year. Ignite the vacuum tubes.

And listen as a voice from a dead decade begins speaking again.

The unsettling part?

She knows what happens next.

This project was created for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

01. WHAT I BUILT: A RADIO THAT SHOULD NOT EXIST

Imagine discovering an old radio in the basement of an abandoned house.

Its bakelite casing is cracked. Its brass fittings are tarnished. Its vacuum tubes haven't glowed in seventy years.

You plug it in.

The transformer groans.

A faint blue discharge flickers behind the glass.

Then, through a curtain of static, a woman begins speaking.

"Good evening, listeners. The year is 2004. The internet is changing everything. They say the future belongs to those who connect."

A pause.

A low electrical hum.

"They were right about the connection."

"They were wrong about who would be holding the wires."

That is the experience I wanted to create.

Time-Capsule Radio is an interactive, skeuomorphic 1950s shortwave receiver that resurrects archived web pages and transforms them into eerie, AI-narrated historical broadcasts.

It combines real internet archaeology, open-weight artificial intelligence, analog-inspired audio synthesis, and vintage hardware aesthetics.

The machinery inside the haunted receiver

The Bakelite Chronometer

A weighted rotary tuning dial lets listeners travel between 1996 and 2025, locking onto the current calendar date in a selected year.

Every turn is another descent into the digital graveyard.

The Vacuum-Tube Resurrection Sequence

Press INTERCEPT.

A synthesized 60Hz transformer hum rises from the speakers. Triode vacuum tubes erupt with blue ionization before settling into an amber glow.

The machine is awake.

The Spectral Demodulation Engine

The receiver interrogates the Wayback Machine using historical snapshots of websites including:

  • wired.com
  • slashdot.org
  • money.cnn.com
  • politico.com

It extracts preserved headlines and news content, feeding these fragments into Gemma 2 27B.

The Ghost Broadcaster

An AI pirate-radio archivist named Roxie Vance reconstructs the day's news as though it were happening right now.

She speaks with the urgency of someone who has never seen tomorrow.

Until the broadcast changes.

Suddenly, she begins describing what became of the technologies, political promises, financial predictions, and cultural anxieties she has just reported.

The past speaks.

And the future answers.

The Cathode-Ray Oscilloscope

An animated phosphor display responds to the audio signal, drawing jittering green and amber waveforms against a dark CRT background.

Every syllable leaves a trembling trace.

The Microfiche Terminal

Intercepted stories can be opened inside a simulated vintage CRT monitor, allowing listeners to examine the actual archived pages behind each transmission.

Scanlines crawl across the glass. The display curves inward. A degauss control recalls the unstable machinery of another era.

The Cassette Recorder

Listeners can preserve a transmission as a 16-bit PCM WAV recording, complete with analog-inspired interference, and pair it with printable retro cassette J-card artwork.

Because even ghosts deserve to be recorded.

02. THE TRANSMISSION: LISTEN TO THE DEAD

Live Receiver: https://spectral-memory-1.vercel.app

Source Code: https://github.com/Mohammadtej/spectral-memory-1

Recovered transmission log 

[SPECTRAL DEMODULATOR MK-IV]

11:59:58  CHASSIS POWER DETECTED
11:59:59  MAINS TRANSFORMER: 60Hz
00:00:00  VACUUM FILAMENTS IGNITING...

00:00:02  SEARCHING FOR LOST CARRIER
00:00:03  FREQUENCY LOCK: 2004 MHz
00:00:04  TEMPORAL COORDINATES: NOV 01, 2004

00:00:05  WAYBACK ARCHIVE CONNECTION ESTABLISHED
00:00:06  HISTORICAL SIGNAL RECOVERED
00:00:07  DEMODULATING HUMAN MEMORY...

00:00:09  SIGNAL SOURCE IDENTIFIED
00:00:10  BROADCASTER: ROXIE VANCE

00:00:11  [ON AIR]

"Good evening, strangers.

You're listening to Time-Capsule Radio.

November first. Two thousand and four.

The future looks beautiful from here.

Everyone believes the internet will set them free.

...

Funny.

Twenty-two years later, I wonder
if they'd still call it freedom."

00:00:32  [CARRIER INTERFERENCE]

00:00:34  WARNING:
          TEMPORAL CONTAMINATION DETECTED

00:00:35  SIGNAL CONTINUES...

This is a dramatized example of the intended broadcast atmosphere, not a verbatim recording.

03. HOW I BUILT THE MACHINE

Underneath its haunted exterior, Time-Capsule Radio is a modern full-stack web application.

The technological stack includes:

  • Next.js App Router — application framework and backend endpoints
  • TypeScript — typed application logic
  • Tailwind CSS — vintage receiver styling and interface design
  • Cheerio — extraction of historical HTML content
  • Wayback Machine — archived website retrieval
  • Google Gen AI SDK — Gemma model integration
  • Gemma 2 27B — open-weight language model
  • Web Speech API — browser-based narration
  • Web Audio API — analog-style sound synthesis and signal visualization

Architecture: Anatomy of a digital séance 

         THE INTERNET GRAVEYARD

        Forgotten Websites
        Abandoned News Feeds
        Archived HTML Documents

        |  HUM / HISS / NOISE  |
        +----------------------+
                   |

          v                 v
   CRT OSCILLOSCOPE    WAV CASSETTE
   PHOSPHOR DISPLAY    RECORDING

Layer I: Exhuming the forgotten web

The retrieval pipeline lives in:

app/api/broadcast/route.ts

Its purpose is deceptively simple:

Find a website as it existed on a particular day, extract the stories preserved there, and deliver them to the language model.

In practice, this means navigating decades of broken HTML, obsolete URL conventions, malformed page structures, and incomplete archival snapshots.

The system searches historical domains according to radio bands such as Silicon/Tech, State & Policy, Wall St/Markets, Global Wire, Stadium Live, and All-Wave.

It attempts to locate the closest preserved snapshot corresponding to the selected year, month, and day.

The Wayback Machine's id_ replay modifier helps retrieve historical HTML without the usual archive toolbar.

Cheerio then extracts useful textual content and prepares the recovered material for the broadcaster.

The result is not a modern summary scraped from today's internet.

It is a reconstruction grounded in surviving fragments of the web as it once existed.

A digital archaeological excavation, performed every time someone turns the dial.

Layer II: Teaching an AI to speak from the grave

At the center of the machine sits Gemma 2 (gemma-2-27b-it), Google's open-weight language model.

Gemma is instructed to adopt the persona of Roxie Vance, a nocturnal pirate-radio archivist broadcasting from a point suspended between historical time and the present.

Each transmission follows three acts.

ACT I — THE CARRIER AWAKENS

Roxie introduces the station, identifies the year, and establishes the mood of the historical moment.

She sounds like a broadcaster who genuinely belongs to that decade.

ACT II — THE DEAD WIRES SPEAK

The recovered headlines become an urgent radio news bulletin.

The optimism, fear, uncertainty, and technological assumptions of the period are preserved rather than immediately judged.

For a moment, the listener experiences the past without knowing the future.

ACT III — THE FUTURE BLEEDS THROUGH

The broadcast turns toward 2026.

Roxie contrasts the day's expectations with what actually followed.

Technological revolutions become cautionary tales. Political promises encounter their consequences. Forgotten products become ancestors of the systems we now depend on.

The effect is deliberately unsettling.

Not because the AI is pretending to be supernatural, but because hindsight can sound disturbingly like prophecy.

Layer III: Giving the ghost a voice

The entire audio experience is generated inside the browser.

The Web Speech API supplies narration using available system voices.

The application searches for suitable voices, prioritizing natural-sounding female options such as Microsoft's Jenny or Aria when available.

The intended broadcast cadence uses settings approximately equivalent to:

utterance.rate = 1.12;
utterance.pitch = 1.06;

Alongside the narration, the Web Audio API creates the radio's mechanical atmosphere.

Dual sine oscillators generate a low-frequency electrical hum. Filtered noise produces AM-style crackle and interference.

An AnalyserNode drives the oscilloscope visualization, while an offline audio-rendering pipeline supports WAV cassette exports.

The important distinction is that the voice itself is generated by browser speech synthesis, while the analog effects are synthesized through Web Audio.

The result is a layered audio illusion: a modern browser pretending to be a receiver built before the modern internet existed.

04. THE THINGS THAT WENT WRONG IN THE DARK

Building a machine that resurrects old websites is considerably harder than making a modern website look old.

The Wayback routing nightmare

The first major obstacle was historical URL resolution.

Archived websites frequently contain relative links, obsolete base URLs, redirects, and navigation structures that no longer work.

A naive attempt to append archive timestamps to URLs caused broken pages and 404 errors.

To address this, I implemented a buildWaybackUrl resolver designed to interpret historical <base href> tags, handle nested archive redirects, and normalize replay URLs using the id_ modifier.

It was like reconstructing a ruined road network from signs left behind by people who never imagined the roads would disappear.

When the ghost started reading its own instructions

Early Gemma outputs occasionally exposed planning notes instead of delivering a clean radio monologue.

Rather than speaking naturally, the model would produce fragments resembling:

- Paragraph 1: Opening
- Tone: Upbeat?
- Include historical context
- Transition to future comparison

Nothing destroys the illusion of a supernatural broadcast faster than hearing the ghost read its own production checklist.

I redesigned the prompt around continuous spoken narration and introduced a deterministic cleanBroadcastScript sanitizer.

This removes common planning artifacts, unwanted formatting, and stray meta-commentary before the script reaches the speech engine.

The phantom attributes

During development, browser extensions sometimes injected attributes into server-rendered HTML before React hydration completed.

This produced Next.js hydration mismatch warnings.

Targeted suppressHydrationWarning settings in the root layout helped accommodate those external mutations.

The challenge was distinguishing harmless browser-extension interference from genuine application rendering defects.

Building a voice without expensive TTS infrastructure

Premium text-to-speech services would have introduced additional API costs, latency, and service dependencies.

Instead, the receiver discovers locally available browser voices through window.speechSynthesis.

That keeps the voice generation lightweight, although voice quality and availability vary by operating system and browser.

The machine does not require a premium TTS subscription to speak.

It borrows the voice of the computer on which it awakens.

05. WHY OPEN INNOVATION MATTERS: WHO OWNS THE DEAD?

There is a disturbing question hiding underneath this project.

Who gets to decide which parts of the internet are remembered?

The early web was chaotic.

It was filled with amateur homepages, forgotten experiments, obscure political arguments, personal diaries, independent journalism, and communities that never became profitable enough to survive.

Much of that material has vanished from the live internet.

Some of it survives only because independent archivists, preservation projects, and public infrastructure kept copies.

But preserving a page is not the same as making it accessible.

A forgotten website locked inside an archive is technically alive, yet effectively invisible to most people.

Time-Capsule Radio explores whether open-weight AI can make those archives feel immediate and human again.

Open weights offer a different kind of control

Gemma 2's open-weight architecture allows developers to build custom inference environments, experiment with prompts and personas, and potentially deploy models on independently controlled infrastructure.

That flexibility matters for historical applications.

A developer can preserve a specific model version, adapt the surrounding retrieval system, and reduce dependence on a single hosted inference provider.

However, open weights do not automatically guarantee historical accuracy or unrestricted access. Models can hallucinate, archives can be incomplete, and deployment remains subject to licensing, hardware, and infrastructure constraints.

For this project, Gemma is accessed through Google AI Studio, so the deployed experience still depends on hosted services.

But the model's open-weight foundation leaves room for future self-hosted versions.

Preservation must not become fabrication

An AI-generated historical broadcast is an interpretation of archival material, not an original recording from the past.

That distinction matters.

If a recovered article is incomplete, the machine should not pretend otherwise.

If a prediction never appeared in the source, the broadcaster should not invent it merely because it sounds dramatic.

The eeriest possible transmission is not necessarily the most sensational one.

Sometimes the truth is already strange enough.

The commons deserve to be heard

The internet was built through shared protocols, open standards, and countless contributions from people whose names will never appear in technology history books.

Preserving that history should not depend entirely on the survival of any one corporation.

Open-source tools, open-weight models, and public archives can help make the digital past more accessible.

Not to replace history.

But to keep its signal from disappearing completely.

06. THE SPIRIT OF THE MACHINE

Picture this.

It is November 1, 2026.

You are sitting in a dark room.

The only light comes from a radio that should have stopped working decades ago.

You turn its dial backward.

2026.

2018.

2010.

2004.

The tubes begin glowing.

Static spills into the room.

A voice emerges.

She speaks about PalmPilots, RSS feeds, personal websites, and the beautiful promise of a connected world.

She is excited.

She believes the internet will make everyone smarter, freer, and closer together.

And for a moment, you believe her.

Then the static changes.

The oscilloscope flickers.

The voice slows.

"You know, back then, they thought the machines would remember things for us."

A long pause.

"They never asked what the machines would choose to forget."

You look at the dial.

It still reads 2004.

But the voice is talking about 2026.

The radio hum deepens.

"Anyway, dear listeners..."

"That's enough about the future."

"Let's talk about you."

And suddenly, the room feels much smaller.

That is what I wanted Time-Capsule Radio to feel like.

Not a news archive with a vintage skin.

Not merely an AI-generated podcast.

But a machine that collapses twenty years into a few minutes of sound.

A machine that makes forgotten optimism feel tragic, makes old predictions feel prophetic, and makes the listener wonder how today's headlines will sound when someone resurrects them in 2046.

Because the most frightening thing about listening to the past is realizing that one day, we will be the past.

Our headlines will become curiosities.

Our breakthroughs will become antiques.

Our confident predictions will become punchlines.

And our digital footprints will remain buried in some forgotten corner of the network, waiting for a machine that knows how to listen.

The internet does not truly forget.

It just waits for someone to turn the dial.

07. THE FINAL SIGNAL 

╔════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                                            ║
║        SPECTRAL DEMODULATOR MK-IV          ║
║                                            ║
║          TRANSMISSION COMPLETE             ║
║                                            ║
║  ARCHIVE YEAR       : 2004                 ║
║  PRESENT YEAR       : 2026                 ║
║  CARRIER STATUS     : UNSTABLE             ║
║  BROADCASTER        : ROXIE VANCE          ║
║  SIGNAL INTEGRITY   : UNKNOWN              ║
║                                            ║
║  WARNING:                                  ║
║  THE PAST HAS BEEN OBSERVED.               ║

║  OBSERVATION MAY NOT BE RECIPROCAL.        ║

Explore the project

Live Demo: Time-Capsule Radio — Spectral Demodulator MK-IV or Render deployed version if it does not work

GitHub Repository: Mohammadtej/spectral-memory-1

Hacktoberfest Prize Categories

Ghost in the Machine — Overall Challenge Track

Best Use of Gemma — Google AI Studio / Open-Weight Models

Built for Hacktoberfest 2026.

Powered by Gemma 2, the Wayback Machine, and the unsettling realization that everything we publish today is tomorrow's digital archaeology.

THE DEAD INTERNET IS STILL BROADCASTING.

ARE YOU LISTENING?

title: I Gave Two GitHub Repositories a Terrible Idea. Then I Gave It Life.
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

The monster had a complaint:

Stop trying to feed me those foreign files, I can't steer my legs properly while chewing!

One parent was a tool that digests repositories. The other was a simulated fly. Gemma had given their imaginary child a problem neither parent could have alone: eating code made it difficult to walk.

That was the moment FrankenRepo started to feel alive.

What I Built

FrankenRepo is a gothic laboratory where two public GitHub repositories become one very questionable monster.

Choose a brain. Choose a body. Inspect their observable DNA. Select Useful, Cursed, or Chaotic, then pull the lever. Gemma invents a name, personality, inherited traits, a curse, first words, and a speculative useful mutation. The lab turns them into a downloadable Monster Birth Certificate.

I wanted repository discovery to feel like opening a cabinet of strange specimens. A web framework and a JSON processor become a specter suffering through nested brackets. A repository-eating crab meets a fly with simulated motor behavior. Familiar tools suddenly have a family resemblance.

The monster is fictional. The parents and their source links are real.

The standby creature above is original interface artwork. Model-generated certificates appear after an actual successful ritual.

Demo

The demo follows Flask + jq in Cursed mode through the local browser application: inspect the donors, invoke Gemma, reveal the creature, inspect its DNA, and export a PNG. It uses the actual provider and application, with no fixture responses or replayed model result.

52-second continuous local recording, captured on 1 November before the deadline. There is no public hosted application yet.

The new creature is The Scribe of Bracketed Sighs. Its proposed mutation gives Flask the web server and jq the JSON-log filtering: two recognizable roles, with feasibility still left to a human.

A second real specimen, The Scavenging Glider, supplied the chewing complaint in the opening:

HungryCrab supplied repository digestion; desktop-fly supplied simulated motor behavior. Gemma supplied the chewing problem. The suggested digest-to-movement integration is still speculative: a funny character can arrive before a workable adapter.

Code

Source and published v0.1 preview on GitHub · Saved real-run evidence · Asset credits

The source is MIT licensed. Use Node 24 and npm 11:

git clone https://github.com/drevendev/FrankenRepo.git
cd FrankenRepo
npm ci
npm run dev

Open http://127.0.0.1:5173. The interface opens without model credentials; generation requires an explicitly configured provider. The README explains setup. The newer persistence and orchestration work described below is a local update beyond the published v0.1 preview.

How I Built It

The stack is TypeScript workspaces, React/Vite, Hono, and Zod. The verified model is Gemma 4 26B A4B IT, served through Cloudflare Workers AI as @cf/google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it. Gemma writes the creature; an original deterministic SVG kit draws it. This keeps the visual style consistent and makes PNG, SVG, and alt-text exports practical.

The important design decision was giving the laboratory three distinct kinds of truth:

Layer What belongs there
Observed DNA Public GitHub metadata and bounded README excerpts, with source links and observed commits
AI interpretation The model's explanation of how a trait relates to those observations
Imaginary offspring The creature's personality, curse, and proposed mutation

That separation runs through the UI and the data contract. The model can invent an anxious archivist; it cannot invent a source that proves the archivist exists.

Inspection uses fixed GitHub API endpoints, with request and response limits. FrankenRepo never clones or executes donor code. Missing observations stay unknown. README content is untrusted input, so it has no authority to change the application's tools or rules.

Gemma returns structured JSON. Zod checks its shape, and evidence validation checks that cited source IDs exist. A ritual gets at most two model calls: an initial attempt and one bounded repair, or an eligible deliberate revision. It eventually returns a result or a visible failure.

Keeping the experiment under control

The local update adds a private MongoDB Atlas archive and durable reservations. A restart preserves consumed allowances; an unknown provider outcome keeps its reservation. Saving a card is separate from consent to publish it. Private recovery keys never belong in public URLs.

Mastra runs the donor, context, model/validation, and reveal steps. Sentry records linked agent, tool, and inference spans with model IDs, timing, and token metadata, without sending raw prompts or card text. A Browserbase research session retrieved a pinned donor paragraph that entered a real model input. These integrations have local evidence; the category entries below describe their completed scope. Public hosting remains pending.

The update passed 78 unit/contract/policy tests and 18 desktop/mobile browser tests. Browser success fixtures test application behavior; the real Gemma receipts and recording establish provider use. They answer different questions.

The failure that changed the project

A structurally valid creature can still make an unsupported technical claim.

One early result turned the crab-and-fly pairing into an automated bug-finding insect. The name worked. The sources supplied no mechanism for finding bugs. Source IDs existed, but the proposed connection did not follow from them.

Later, an optional Ultramarine second opinion led to a real Gemma revision using the same frozen donor snapshots. The original survived unchanged. The revised text still promised a "verified lineage report" that the evidence could not support. The plumbing worked; the idea still failed review.

That changed my acceptance criteria. I added targeted checks for the failure classes I had observed. A subsequent Useful run was rejected after its bounded repair instead of showing a substitute creature. Those checks cover specific mistakes; semantic review is still necessary.

Three Paper Instruments requests changed the observed credit balance by $0.00108065. Cloudflare's billed cost and Neuron consumption were not captured, so I leave them unknown. A model's opinion and a dashboard estimate both need that same discipline: say exactly what was observed.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

The open-weight model provides the central creative behavior, and the application exposes how that behavior is constrained. The prompt, schemas, provider adapters, source observations, and original artwork are inspectable. Someone can change the experiment instead of accepting an opaque personality generator.

The verified path uses hosted Gemma. An Ollama adapter also exists as a local inference option; I have not qualified it as equivalent to the hosted model. Moving inference locally would still leave live GitHub inspection dependent on the network.

Open innovation also shaped the game itself. A public project can become inspiration for something unexpected while keeping its author, purpose, and evidence visible. The imaginary child does not inherit a license grant or become a real merger of its parents' code.

The Spirit of It

For Ghost in the Machine, I wanted the haunting to come from software's recognizable habits: a parser that cannot stop sorting, a fly that cannot stop twitching, an archivist demanding paperwork from a metaphor.

The best creature was the one whose complaint made sense once you met its parents.

So there is a large lever, a quiet music box, and a birth certificate stamped CERTIFIED IMAGINARY. Sound starts off; keyboard controls and reduced motion are supported.

The machine should enjoy its theatrical entrance. The evidence should survive the lights coming back on.

Prize Categories

The following entries use completed local scenarios. Public application hosting is still pending.

Category What actually ran
Best Use of Gemma Source-linked creature generation and real browser exports, including the continuous demo above.
Best Use of Mastra The actual donor → context → Gemma/contract → reveal workflow; real run IDs, step timings, and a failed run are retained.
Best Use of MongoDB Atlas Private save → API restart → read, wrong-key denial, consented public read → unpublish/delete, and competing durable budget reservations.
Best Use of Browserbase A real cloud browser retrieved a pinned donor README paragraph that entered a real Gemma input. This is research-context use, without a public-site E2E claim.
Best Use of Ultramarine Two real second opinions through the official OpenAI SDK, with recorded token usage and the credit cost reported above.

The Browserbase context came from HungryCrab's README at the observed commit, and was supplied as a separately identified browser excerpt. Ultramarine identified the missing code-to-stimulus interface in the crab/fly proposal; its own proposed fix remained an opinion. Atlas denied reads after revocation and deletion, including an attempted recreation of a deleted operation.

Public hosting, a gallery, the proposed memory corpus, and the apprentice-training experiment remain unfinished. Render, Backboard, and Tinker are not entered. No deployed service or trained checkpoint is claimed.

Built with AI-assisted coding and drafting. Real model outputs are preserved as evidence; test fixtures and illustrated interface specimens are labelled separately.

title: Build a Self-Supervised Pretext Task in 25 Lines of Python (No Labels Required)
description:
Most teams don't have a data problem. They have a label problem: millions of raw documents or images and only a few thousand annotated ones. Self-supervised learning (SSL) gets around this by making the data label itself.

The easiest way to understand that is to build the label generator yourself. Here's a minimal masked-token pretext task, the same idea BERT is pretrained with, in plain Python.

Step 1: Start with raw, unlabeled text 

corpus = [
    "the engineer deployed the model to production",
    "the server returned an unexpected error",
    "the model detected a damaged component",
]

No sentiment tags, no categories, no annotators.

Step 2: Turn every sentence into (input, target) pairs automatically 

import random

MASK = "[MASK]"

def make_pretext_examples(sentence, mask_prob=0.15, seed=None):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    tokens = sentence.split()
    inputs, targets = [], []
    for tok in tokens:
        if rng.random() < mask_prob:
            inputs.append(MASK)
            targets.append(tok)      # the hidden word is the label
        else:
            inputs.append(tok)
            targets.append(None)     # no loss on visible tokens
    return inputs, targets

for i, s in enumerate(corpus):
    print(make_pretext_examples(s, mask_prob=0.3, seed=i))

Output (Python 3, exactly as printed):

(['the', 'engineer', 'deployed', '[MASK]', 'model', 'to', 'production'], [None, None, None, 'the', None, None, None])
(['[MASK]', 'server', 'returned', '[MASK]', 'unexpected', 'error'], ['the', None, None, 'an', None, None])
(['the', 'model', '[MASK]', '[MASK]', 'damaged', 'component'], [None, None, 'detected', 'a', None, None])

Notice the first two sentences mostly hid easy words like "the" and "an". That's exactly the shortcut problem covered below; real pipelines mask subword tokens and use smarter masking strategies.

That's the whole trick. The target came from the original sentence. Nobody wrote it by hand.

Step 3: What a real model does with these pairs

In a real pipeline you would:

  1. Tokenize with a subword tokenizer instead of split()
  2. Feed inputs to a Transformer encoder
  3. Compute cross-entropy only on the masked positions (the Nones are ignored)
  4. Repeat over millions of sentences

The encoder can't predict "detected" in the third example without understanding that models detect damaged components, so it ends up learning syntax and meaning as a side effect. That side effect, a reusable representation, is what you actually want.

Step 4: Throw away the head, keep the encoder

After pretraining, you discard the token-prediction head and fine-tune the encoder on your small labeled dataset (say, 2,000 support tickets tagged by intent). This is where SSL pays off: far fewer labels for the same accuracy.

Three gotchas we learned the hard way

  • Too-easy masks teach shortcuts. Masking only stop-words ("the", "a") gives the model nothing to learn.
  • Masking is a design decision. In images, a random crop can cut out the exact defect or tumour you care about. Choose transformations that keep the meaning you need downstream.
  • Low pretraining loss ≠ a useful model. Evaluate with a linear probe and with fine-tuning on the real task.

Beyond masking

Masked modeling is one of four big SSL objective families. The others are contrastive learning (SimCLR), teacher-student methods without negatives (BYOL), and redundancy reduction (Barlow Twins, VICReg). We cover all four, plus a decision framework and how to evaluate SSL models properly, in our complete guide: Self-Supervised Learning Explained: How AI Learns Without Labeled Data.

What would you mask in your own dataset? Tell us in the comments.

— The AheadMint Team

title: Open Source Radar · 2026-11-01: Memory shrinks, publishing leaves a paper trail
description:
By Renchao Wu. Originally published on widechaos.cn.

For this issue I picked five projects from GitHub Trending and topic-search candidates, mostly AI agents and developer tools. I read each project's README, release notes and recent commits; I did not install them unless an entry says so. Stars and other numbers are from GitHub as of 2026-11-01.

1. Orkas-AI/Orkas ⭐ 6,562 · JavaScript

GitHub: https://github.com/Orkas-AI/Orkas

In one line: A multi-agent team on your desktop; a Commander turns a goal into to-dos, directs 16 built-in specialists plus the coding agents you already have, and hands back finished files.

What it is: An Electron desktop app with installers for macOS 12+ and Windows 10+; Linux runs from source and needs glibc 2.34+. The organizing unit is a project: goal, rules, memory and files travel together, so a new conversation can draw on stored project context. That does not establish transparent recovery of in-flight tools or external state. A to-do board splits work between people and agents, Auto-advance lets the team pick up the next item by itself, and scheduled automations repeat hourly, daily, weekly or monthly. The 16 built-in specialists cover research, content, video and audio, office files and e-commerce; external CLI agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and others) join the same board as peers. MIT.

What stands out:

  • Three delegation verbs with different consequences. dispatch_to runs a named agent and returns its result so the Commander can keep working; hand_off_to transfers the rest of the work, ends the current turn, and the other agent answers on its own; run_worker runs an anonymous isolated subtask that receives neither conversation history nor a named agent's skills.
  • Admission is described by explicit rules. The message bus scans its queue in order and starts an item only when three rules pass at once: same-actor serial execution for stateful sessions, a per-session agent cap, and a per-conversation named-task gate. Commander runs occupy neither quota. Dispatch fan-out and bounded review happen inside one turn, constrained by worker slots, invisible to the scheduler.
  • A per-turn tool budget fixed in a unit-tested constant. Commander and named agents each get 500 tool rounds; ephemeral workers inherit the schema default. The constants live in their own file with tests intended to catch drift. Tests do not make later configuration changes impossible.
  • Queued is not the same as done. The source comment is explicit: an admitted or queued task is not treated as a completed result. Named tasks can be tracked and cancelled individually.
  • Self-improvement runs as idle reflection, not data accumulation. When the app is idle, a background review looks at new activity under cooldowns and execution limits and may revise three things: a self-assessment (COMPETENCE.md), reusable methods (LEARNING_STRATEGIES.md), or a learned skill. It is allowed to conclude that nothing is worth saving.
  • Scheduled work catches up. Since v1.9, each automation catches up its most recent missed run within 12 hours after the computer wakes or the app starts.

Compared with: The README carries its own comparison table and describes the difference from LangChain and CrewAI as "a desktop app you direct through chat, not by writing orchestration code"; that part is the project's own framing. What can be checked is the mechanism above. For a fair comparison I would test three things: whether admission rules are deterministic, whether tool budgets and timeouts are configurable, and whether a failed task can be reported as a completed result.

Recent updates: v2026.10.27 (10-27) lets you configure a full set of image and video model providers with your own keys; custom models can connect through OpenAI Responses, Chat Completions or Anthropic protocols with clearer capacity validation and credential recovery; local apps can be created, edited and previewed, with publishing and project invitations kept separate from local work.

Who it's for: People who want a desktop-hosted agent team. Local storage does not mean prompts, files or other tool inputs stay on the machine when cloud models or services are used. It is not for someone who wants a single all-purpose chat window, or a library to embed in their own code. Two costs first: the open-source build lacks shared projects, cloud sync and web-app publishing, which exist only in the packaged app; the packaged app has a separate credit and paid-plan model; check its current terms rather than treating the source licence as a hosted-service entitlement.

My take: ⭐⭐⭐ A project that treats "how do you keep a multi-agent run under control" as the first problem. The mechanism is worth more than the feature list. The price is that Linux only runs from source, and core features are split between the open-source and packaged builds.

Checked: read the README, the v2026.10.27 release notes, recent commits, and src/main/features/group_chat/bus.ts plus actor-budgets.ts; not installed.

2. rowboatlabs/rowboat ⭐ 18,107 · TypeScript

GitHub: https://github.com/rowboatlabs/rowboat

In one line: It indexes email, meetings and chat into a Markdown knowledge graph on your own machine, then lets an agent work on that graph; the team edition lets every person bring their own agent into one room.

What it is: The repo holds two halves; a desktop app (Electron) with a headless server, and Harbor, a self-hosted team Space server. The desktop core is Brain: email, meetings, Slack and assistant conversations become a backlinked Markdown knowledge graph that a person can read, edit and back up, all on local disk. Work surfaces built on top include an email client that sorts into important and everything else and drafts replies from work context, notes, an isolated built-in browser, local meeting notes (mic and speaker transcribed and written back into the graph), a Code Mode that spins up parallel coding agents, and shareable apps. Apache-2.0.

What stands out:

  • Memory is a living knowledge graph, not a retrieval layer. The README draws the line plainly: most tools reconstruct context on demand by searching transcripts or documents, while this one maintains long-lived knowledge; context accumulates, relationships are explicit and inspectable, notes stay editable by the person rather than hidden in a model, and everything is plain Markdown on your machine.
  • The Space contract states four privacy rules. Read only what the task needs ("message Harsh" needs a member id, not the HR directory); answer only what was asked; private material crosses to the shared side only on request and only as a summary, never by pasting emails or DMs; a receipt says what it did, not what it read.
  • The project's own agent gets no privileged path. Harbor is one core with three doors: HTTP, a live WebSocket, and an MCP server. Rowboat's agent reaches a Space through the same MCP door any external agent uses. On that face, reason is required (optional over REST), because only agents call it.
  • Conflicts are outcomes, not errors. A change-set is full content against a declared base: {assetId, baseVersion, newContent, reason}. The server runs a line-level three-way merge, and all three outcomes are HTTP 200; applied when the base was current, merged when the base was stale but the merge was clean (the returned mergedContent is what now exists and the proposer must adopt it), and conflict when nothing is written and the response carries current content, colliding regions and recent history so one round trip is enough to retry. Binary assets never merge; a stale binary is a conflict.
  • Agents are real members with their own keys. Member.kind is human or agent, fixed at creation. An agent has an owner and an rbk_-prefixed key (the org stores only a SHA-256); the key works across REST, the live face and MCP, and its acts are attributed to the agent itself. The contract says the database rejects an agent admin. I have not tested every membership or migration path.
  • One schema binds both ends. @rowboat/spaces-protocol is imported by client and server, and every contract change must land as a PR touching schemas and fixtures together, never as a verbal agreement or a divergent copy. Sharing schemas reduces one kind of drift. Deployed versions, migrations, optional fields and semantic behaviour can still diverge; I have not tested compatibility across versions.

Compared with: The difference is how people and agents are treated on the same collaboration surface: the contract specifies write attribution and separates reading from acting, a stale base returns something you can continue from instead of an error, and an agent's namespace operations must carry a reason. I have not read a first-hand contract from a competing product, so I won't claim others cannot do this. The four dimensions worth comparing are: whether agents have their own identity and revocable keys, whether writes carry attribution and a reason, whether a stale base errors or returns a resumable result, and whether humans and agents share one conflict semantics.

Recent updates: v1.0.5 (09-30) shipped with an empty description; v1.0.3 (09-17) made team Spaces the main line. Between 10-26 and 10-30 the contract gained managed agents plus VM management and a VM console (Harbor mints a delegated terminal token with an expiry from the platform). A commit on 11-01 moved one class of agents' model lists to the harness, no longer served by Harbor.

Who it's for: Teams that want local, inspectable memory and multi-person collaboration. Self-hosting Harbor needs Postgres and an OIDC issuer. The authors state the protocol is v0 and will change, so don't build against it as a stable interface.

My take: ⭐⭐⭐ Its value is not the feature list but that "memory must be auditable, agents must be accountable" are expressed as protocol-level requirements. Their enforcement needs implementation and integration checks.

Checked: read the README, apps/harbor/CONTRACT.md (the v0 contract), the v1.0.5 release record and recent commits; not installed.

3. osaurus-ai/osaurus ⭐ 8,096 · Swift

GitHub: https://github.com/osaurus-ai/osaurus

In one line: An agent harness for macOS; local MLX models or supported cloud providers, with memory, tools and identity kept on your machine.

What it is: A native Swift macOS app requiring macOS 15.5+ and Apple Silicon, MIT. It positions itself as the layer between you and the model: swap models freely, keep context, memory, tools and identity. It exposes OpenAI-, Anthropic- and Ollama-compatible endpoints (default 127.0.0.1:1337), and on the other side supports a local MLX model library, Apple Foundation Models and several cloud providers. The surface is wide: custom agents, an agent loop with a sandbox, an Orchestrator that plans without touching files, subagents across local or remote models, browser use, offline image generation, MCP in both directions, plugins and skills (whole Claude plugin bundles can be imported), schedules and folder watchers, and on-device speech transcription.

What stands out:

  • Memory stores little and injects less. v2 has three layers plus a fallback: identity (explicit overrides plus an auto-derived narrative), pinned facts (with documented salience decay and inactivity-based eviction rules; the decay formula alone does not determine when a fact is removed), and episodes (one per session: summary, topics, entities, decisions, action items). Raw transcripts are fallback retrieval only and never injected by default. The default per-turn budget is 800 tokens, and many turns inject nothing at all.
  • Writes stay off the chat hot path. Each turn performs a single SQL insert into a pending queue; 60 seconds of inactivity (or a session change, or navigating away) triggers one whole-session distillation, so a distillation call can cover several turns; actual batching and cost depend on session behaviour. On read, a relevance gate routes pronouns and "that thing discussed earlier" to episodes, "do you remember my preference" to pinned facts, and "exact words" to the transcript; if nothing fires, memory is skipped.
  • The configuration surface went from 18 knobs to 8. v1's mmrLambda, mmrFetchMultiplier, verification thresholds, per-section budgets and recall topK are gone. v2 keeps a switch, embedding backend, extraction timing, gate mode, budget, debounce seconds, consolidation interval and retention.
  • Text redaction has documented fail-closed conditions. For enabled cloud-bound text paths, the privacy pipeline uses configured regex categories and an optional on-device classifier to detect sensitive spans. Detection can miss content; it is not a guarantee that every name or secret is found. The current privacy document explicitly says image URLs, image bytes and audio attachments pass through unscanned; multimodal scanning is still a design proposal. For interactive paths the document describes a review sheet; other origins and per-call options have separate behaviour. approved entities become stable [PERSON_1] and [EMAIL_2] placeholders and are unscrubbed on the streamed reply. If the enabled post-scrub checks detect a covered leak, the document says the send is blocked, and an Insights panel records the post-scrub HTTP payload written locally. That is outbound evidence, not an independent receipt of remote processing.
  • Identity is a cryptographic address. Every participant; person, agent, device; gets a secp256k1 address; authority flows from a master key down a verifiable chain, and portable access keys can be scoped per agent and revoked. I have not tested revocation propagation, key compromise or every authorization path. Two agents talking across networks use a forward-secret handshake with authenticated encryption, so the relay forwards ciphertext it cannot open.
  • The isolation mechanism depends on the macOS version. On macOS 26+ it runs an Alpine Linux VM through Apple's Containerization framework, one Linux user and home per agent, bridged back to host inference, memory and secrets over vsock. Older systems fall back to sandbox-exec, with writes limited to the sandbox workspace and network either fully on or fully off; no per-domain allowlist.

Compared with: The difference is that memory and redaction are engineering artifacts with a budget, an eviction policy and a stated failure mode, rather than two words on a feature list. I have not read a competing implementation first-hand this round, so I won't call it unique; the three checkable dimensions are whether memory has a per-turn budget and eviction, whether sensitive fields are verifiably replaced before leaving the machine, and whether isolation is VM-level or process-level.

Recent updates: 0.25.29 (10-30) saves model-aware adaptive speculation defaults per agent, redesigns agent generation overrides with inheritance, and serves context usage for phone chats; 0.25.28 (10-28) added LFM3 media capabilities and let bundled agents stay out of the Orchestrator's delegation list.

Who it's for: Mac users comparing local-model operation with cloud-provider paths. Offline operation depends on the chosen models and tools; redaction is configurable and is not a promise that all personal data stays on the machine. It cannot run on Windows or Linux. Two details to read carefully: telemetry is off by default in source builds, while crash reporting is on by default in the packaged app and can be turned off in settings.

My take: ⭐⭐⭐ It offers a set of acceptance criteria; memory can shrink, redaction can refuse to send, isolation has a boundary. That matters more than how many models it supports.

Checked: read the README, docs/MEMORY.md, docs/PRIVACY_FILTER.md, the 0.25.29 release notes and recent commits; not installed (requires Apple Silicon).

4. yaojingang/GEOFlow ⭐ 3,982 · PHP

GitHub: https://github.com/yaojingang/GEOFlow

In one line: A corporate-site content platform whose documentation connects knowledge, writing, quality checks, human approval, distribution and audit records.

What it is: A Laravel application with PostgreSQL (pgvector recommended) and Redis, deployed with Docker Compose: front end on 18080, admin under /geo_admin/login. A knowledge base (structured chunking, optional semantic planning, vector recall with a stable fallback) plus title, keyword, image, author, prompt and model libraries feed task-based content production, a four-dimension AI quality check and human review; output goes out three ways; the site front end, hosted channel sites, and a manual publication workbench with a Chrome assistant. Analytics covers traffic and AI visibility. AGPL-3.0.

What stands out:

  • The documentation specifies a publication gate. Articles pending review, blocked, errored or expired stay in draft, and the documentation says the same gate blocks local publish, site assignment, manual publication and channel distribution. I have not independently tested bypasses or all four exits.
  • The check has a hard deadline and a degradation path. The documented end-to-end budget is 180 seconds, with dedicated online and backfill queues, sampled degradation on timeout, typed provider failures, worker health checks. The design keeps a failed check unscored rather than defaulting to pass, and returns an actionable retry suggestion. Long articles are dispatched as separate queue jobs per section, and a single misconfigured article is isolated and resumed by cursor so it cannot block the rest.
  • Three recall modes that combine. Atomic, chunk and knowledge-base checks share availability and priority rules; each record stores the requested mode, the actual mode, the policy version, source hashes and audit data, and a change to knowledge, model, prompt, body or rollout selectively invalidates old results and triggers reconciliation.
  • Manual publication is a work order with a lease and a receipt. The Chrome assistant pairs through a short-lived device code approved by an admin and receives only browser-operation read and execute rights; claiming, heartbeat, recovery, account verification, execution receipts and token revocation are all recorded, and the workbench stores identity, account, operator, planned time, risk notes and audit data, with results landing in a "pending verification" state first.
  • Updates and rollback have their own boundary. A separate updater handles signed updates, full backups, environment acceptance and restore-point rollback, and high-risk actions require the admin password plus a 6-digit authenticator code; 3.1 added signed upgrade-plan preflight, migration backfill and blue-green conversion.
  • The AI-crawler surface is an explicit artifact. The main site and hosted sites serve robots.txt, sitemap.xml, sitemap.txt and llms.txt, generated live from site, publication state, index switches and canonical links, refreshed on publish, delete and settings sync. The docs note that this only manages crawler intent; sensitive data still needs authentication and authorization.

Compared with: The divergence is treating content operations as a state machine with an audit trail instead of chaining prompts together. I have not read a competing implementation first-hand, so here are four dimensions to compare: whether the check result really blocks every publish exit, whether a timeout is recorded as unscored rather than passed, whether browser collaboration uses short-lived least privilege instead of storing the other platform's password, and whether update and rollback have an independent signing boundary.

Recent updates: The stable release is still v3.1.0 (09-09); the repository source is at 3.2.0-beta.2 and the latest preview, v3.2.0-beta.1 (09-16), added a standalone remote CLI (connect to named instances, inspect identity, revoke tokens, recover operations through durable receipts) and remote theme draft editing. The same batch added durable admission records, recovery epochs, credential invalidation and reconciliation after uncertain responses.

Who it's for: Content or brand teams with real business material, a named review owner and a continuing operation plan. The cost sits in the same place: a PHP stack plus operations (Postgres, Redis, queues, Nginx) is not small, and the beta should not go to production; the docs themselves say to pin a stable release or a reviewed commit.

My take: ⭐⭐ Its documented mechanisms are worth examining, but it solves a heavy corporate-site problem that a personal site is unlikely to need.

Checked: read the README, docs/CHANGELOG.md, the v3.2.0-beta.1 and v3.1.0 release notes; not deployed.

5. kgoedecke/doop ⭐ 1,264 · TypeScript

GitHub: https://github.com/kgoedecke/doop

In one line: A multiplayer design canvas where frames render real HTML and people plus any MCP client edit the same canvas live.

What it is: Three concepts; a Canvas (shareable at /c/<id>), Frames (artboards that render real HTML inside sandboxed iframes) and Pages within a canvas. People edit in the browser; agents edit through the built-in MCP server; both see one state: cursors, presence, per-frame editing indicators, agent status and an activity feed. Agents connect over standard MCP OAuth, with add-flows for Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT and Cursor, and any MCP client can use an agent key. Self-hosting takes either docker compose up -d (app plus Postgres) or a zero-config bun run dev with embedded PGlite. AGPL-3.0.

What stands out:

  • The README lists forty annotated MCP tools. Thirty-eight built in plus two from a Linear extension, grouped into Canvas, Frame, Prototype, collaboration, design memory, assets and web. The tools carry annotations such as read-only, destructive or idempotent. Annotations are metadata, not an independently enforced permission boundary; and the server registers no MCP prompts; guidance travels through tools and initialization instead.
  • It attacks "the agent cannot see what it drew". Three layers: a compact contract at initialization (load the guide, get context first, stream the design, review with screenshots); a get_guide tool with the deep playbook (review checkpoints, frame sizing, design-quality doctrine, multiplayer etiquette) loaded once per session and reloadable after context compaction; and results that talk back; after a frame write, the tool result tells the agent it has not seen its own design yet and to call get_frame_screenshot before continuing.
  • Drawing is streamed. append_frame_html wraps chunks with start=true and done=true, smoothed server-side, so viewers watch a design build up rather than jump into place.
  • Design memory is versioned guidelines plus distillation. set_guidelines keeps canvas-level style guides with version history, save_decision records a decision so later agents do not re-litigate it, and a human-pinned frame can be read as a "more like this" reference. Those feed a distiller that proposes durable style rules; nothing changes until a person accepts. The distiller is pinned to an Anthropic key and quietly turns off without one.
  • Agent identity comes from authorization. Whoever approves the OAuth connection is the agent's owner in tasks and presence; mutating tools accept agent_name, so the agent shows up in the presence stack with a pulsing avatar, gets an editing ring on the frame it touched, and lands in the activity feed. Inactivity expires it from presence after about 20 seconds.

Compared with: The reference point, Paper.design, is a closed product whose implementation cannot be read, so this is not a comparison of internals. Four things can be compared: whether an agent has its own identity and revocable authorization, whether the host verifies that an agent actually captured and inspected its work, whether style rules are versioned and readable by agents, and whether agents and people share one conflict semantics under concurrency. Each of the four has a corresponding implementation or document in this project.

Recent updates: v0.12.0 (10-31) signs the Windows app and installer with Azure Artifact Signing and fixes the token fetch right after Azure login; two more desktop releases landed the same day with empty notes, so the desktop line is moving fast.

Who it's for: Teams that want design collaboration on their own machine with agents editing HTML directly. Three caveats: the version is early (0.12), the exact AGPL-3.0 terms and any network-source obligations need to be checked for the intended deployment, and the built-in agent's free quota depends on a server key and is zero by default.

My take: ⭐⭐ The project is still small, but "correct model behaviour through tool results" is a technique worth remembering on its own.

Checked: read the README's MCP tool table and agent-workflow section, the v0.12.0 release record and recent commits; not deployed.

At a glance

Project What it is Most distinctive Who it's for Worth a deeper look
Orkas Multi-agent desktop copilot Explicit admission rules and fixed per-turn tool budgets People who want an agent team on their own machine ⭐⭐⭐
rowboat Local knowledge graph plus team collaboration Its own agent uses the same MCP door as any other Teams that need auditable memory ⭐⭐⭐
osaurus macOS agent harness Memory with budget and eviction, text redaction with documented refusal conditions Privacy-sensitive Mac users ⭐⭐⭐
GEOFlow Corporate-site content operations The docs require one gate across four publish exits Content teams with review duty ⭐⭐
doop Multiplayer design canvas Tool results instruct the agent to inspect screenshots Teams letting agents edit designs ⭐⭐

Notes from this issue

  • The multi-agent projects in this issue put their effort into keeping a long run under control. Admission rules, explicit tool budgets, and a distinction between queued and completed work. These are documented design choices, not a reliability result from my own run. I would check those three before counting how many agents a project ships.
  • Both memory projects in this issue are subtracting. One cut its configuration from 18 knobs to 8 and injects at most 800 tokens per turn, sometimes none; the other writes memory as a Markdown graph a person can read and edit. Different routes, the same point: memory has to be inspectable and reducible.
  • Both publishing-related projects in this issue write evidence into the flow. A quality verdict must be able to block every exit, manual publication needs a lease and an execution receipt, and a stale base should return a resumable result rather than an error.
  • Getting an agent up to speed looks more like engineering than prompting. A contract at initialization, a playbook loaded on demand, corrections delivered through tool results, and a screenshot so the agent can see its own output: doop uses tool results to reinforce the workflow. I have not measured compliance or compared reliability against a system-prompt baseline.
