title: My Pool Has 4 Threads, DNS Gets 2
description:
In Node, the word "asynchronous" does not describe a single thing. Some calls
really are handed to the kernel and come back when the operating system is
ready; others are placed on one of four background threads and wait their turn.
The second kind is libuv's work pool, its size is four, and that number appears
in Node's documentation in a single aside: "its current default value".

What led me to that number was my cover generator. In batch mode
generate-hero.ts drains its queue with four workers — a hard-coded 4 inside
the script — and each worker is one sharp call. In a separate run, in a
separate process, my social posting script names nine external hosts in its
source. Both are "asynchronous", both sit on their own four threads, and I had
no idea how much of those four either one was holding. I wanted to measure this
properly, once. The result was sharper than I expected: dns.lookup can never
take more than two of those four threads, and neither libuv's documentation
nor Node's mentions that limit.

Who lands in the pool

Node's command-line documentation spells out the list: all fs calls except the
file watchers and the explicitly synchronous ones, asynchronous crypto calls
such as crypto.pbkdf2, scrypt, randomBytes and generateKeyPair, all
zlib calls except the explicitly synchronous ones, and dns.lookup. The
warning that follows is fair: because the pool has a fixed size, if one of these
takes a long time, other "seemingly unrelated" ones get slower.

The sneakiest member of that list is dns.lookup, because you are usually not
the one deciding to call it. In Node's lib/net.js, the connect path says it in
one line: const lookup = options.lookup || dns.lookup;. So net.connect,
http, https and fetch — undici, which sits underneath fetch, uses
net.connect for plain HTTP and tls.connect for TLS, and both pass through
that same line — resolve names through dns.lookup unless you supply your own
resolver. The first step of every outbound HTTP request queues on the same four
threads as your file reads.

The dns.resolve* family is not on that list. Node's documentation draws the
line clearly: those functions do not use getaddrinfo(3), they always query
over the network, and they do not use libuv's threadpool. Keep that distinction
in mind; we will come back to it with a measurement at the end.

The lab: my own resolver, a fixed 300 ms

Measuring against a real DNS server is pointless; if the latency moves, you
cannot read the table. So I wrote a 49-line UDP server: it holds every incoming
query for exactly 300 ms, then answers 127.0.0.2, sets TTL zero (no caching),
and most importantly it counts how many distinct names are in flight at the
same time. Instead of guessing concurrency from the client side, I let the
resolver count it.

The lab ran in a node:26-alpine container: Alpine 3.24, Node v26.13.0, libuv
1.52.1, aarch64, 14 cores. /etc/resolv.conf has one line: nameserver
127.0.0.1. The client calls dns.lookup for 24 distinct names at once, with
family: 4, so each name sends a single A query and the resolver's A/AAAA
behaviour stays out of the table. The numbers below are medians of three runs.
Alpine uses musl; since the limit measured here lives in libuv, the resolver
library does not change the result, but the nsswitch.conf argument later in
this article applies to glibc setups.

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE Concurrent queries counted by the resolver 24 names, total
unset (4) 2 3,695 ms
1 1 7,414 ms
2 1 7,427 ms
3 2 3,703 ms
4 2 3,712 ms
6 3 2,480 ms
8 4 1,859 ms
16 8 934 ms

The second column is exactly half the pool size, rounded up.

What amuses me most in this table is the relationship between the second and
third rows. Going from one thread to two moves the total for 24 names from 7,414
ms to 7,427 ms — that is, nowhere. I doubled the threads and what I gained on
the DNS side is smaller than the measurement noise. But going from two to three
cuts the time in half. Adding one thread buys nothing once and a factor of two
the next time.

The reason sits in libuv's source, on line 46 of src/threadpool.c:

static unsigned int slow_work_thread_threshold(void) {
  return (nthreads + 1) / 2;
}

libuv sorts work into three kinds: UV__WORK_CPU, UV__WORK_FAST_IO and
UV__WORK_SLOW_IO. src/unix/getaddrinfo.c submits its request as
UV__WORK_SLOW_IO; src/unix/fs.c submits every file operation as
UV__WORK_FAST_IO, and user code calling uv_queue_work submits as
UV__WORK_CPU. Slow-I/O work piles up in a separate queue and only a single
"there is slow work" marker goes into the main queue. When a thread picks up
that marker and starts running slow work, a counter goes up; if the counter has
reached the threshold, the thread pushes the marker back to the tail of the
queue and looks for other work.

So this is not an accident but a deliberate guard: it exists so a slow name
lookup cannot swallow the whole pool and block file reads. I have no objection
to the logic. My objection is that the limit is written down nowhere. libuv's
own documentation covers the default, the absolute maximum, and that the pool is
global and shared across all loops; for its scope it says "all file system
operations, as well as getaddrinfo and getnameinfo requests". Not one sentence
about the half-pool threshold. Node's UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE section does not have
it either: there the advice is simply to set a value greater than 4.

Follow that advice and DNS can use at most half of whatever you set. Write 8 and
the ceiling on your name-resolution concurrency is 4. It is a ceiling, not an
allocation: when there is no DNS work those slots do not sit idle, they take
other work.

Who starves whom

The direction of the threshold matters, because it is asymmetric. Two scenarios,
both with the pool at its default four threads:

A) With 32 pending dns.lookup calls (each answered by my 300 ms resolver)
I squeezed in one fs.readFile and one pbkdf2. The fs.readFile waited 0 ms,
the pbkdf2 2 ms. Thirty-two names are queued and the file read goes straight
through. The guard works.

B) With 32 pending pbkdf2 calls — a computation that takes 208 ms on its
own — I squeezed in one dns.lookup and one fs.readFile. The fs.readFile
waited 1,719 ms, the dns.lookup 2,018 ms.

The arithmetic of that second line lands exactly: 32 × 208 ms on four threads is
a 1,664 ms queue, and the measurement is 1,719 ms. DNS's 2,018 ms comes from the
same place — 1,719 ms of queue plus my resolver's fixed 300 ms, totalling 2,019
ms. The resolver answers in 300 ms while dns.lookup takes two seconds, and 85
percent of that has nothing to do with resolving a name.

The lesson here runs the other way: some investigations that start with "our DNS
is slow" are looking in the wrong place. What fills the pool is not name
resolution but the crypto, compression or image work in the same process. The
slow-I/O threshold stops DNS from choking everyone else; nothing stops everyone
else from choking DNS.

Where the threshold sits on my own pipeline

The same question goes to my cover generator, since that is where it started.
came from. generate-hero.ts makes a single sharp call: it rasterises the SVG
at 200 dpi, fits it to 1200×630 and writes a PNG with compressionLevel: 9. On
my Mac (Node v22.16.0, libuv 1.49.2, sharp 0.35.5, libvips 8.18.7, 14 cores)
that call takes 75 ms on its own. On an idle pool an fs.readFile takes 0.2 ms.

I started the same call N times concurrently and squeezed in a read of a real
article file:

Concurrent covers How long fs.readFile waited
1 0 ms
2 0 ms
3 0 ms
4 9 ms (three runs: 1 – 31 ms)
8 62 ms (three runs: 56 – 69 ms)

The threshold is exactly at four. Up to three there is still a free thread in
the pool, so the read never waits; the moment a fourth cover enters, it starts
waiting. I will not lean on the 9 ms in the fourth row — across three runs it
wandered between 1 and 31 ms, because the instant a thread frees up is a matter
of chance. At eight the number is steady: about 60 ms.

Something caught my eye here. My script does not only write two PNGs per article
and exit; in --all mode it drains the queue with four workers, and that four
is a constant I put there myself: Array.from({ length: 4 }, ...). The comment
next to it says it "gains parallel I/O". So when I rebuild the covers for all
2,772 posts I fill the entire pool, and the fourth row of the table is exactly
that point. When I wrote that 4 I did not know the pool was also four; the two
numbers matching is a coincidence, what follows from it is not — during an
--all run every fs read and every dns.lookup in the same process queues
behind it.

The absolute values are small, I know. What interests me is not the absolute
value but that the threshold is visible at all. And one more thing: there is not
a single line in my repository that mentions UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE. Not in the
scripts, not in the systemd units, not in the workflows. I have been running
on four threads and until today I had not chosen that deliberately.

When exactly is the pool born

Node's documentation says that setting process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE "is not
guaranteed to work" and gives a reason: the pool would have been created "as
part of the runtime initialisation much before user code is run". The warning
itself is right; the reason does not hold on the Node in this lab.

libuv's pool is lazy. The first line of uv__work_submit is uv_once(&once,
init_once) — the pool is born when the first piece of work is submitted. We can
count it from outside, because since libuv 1.50.0 the threads are named
libuv-worker:

# process is up but nothing has hit the pool yet
$ ls /proc/<pid>/task/*/comm | xargs cat | grep -c libuv-worker
0

After a single dns.lookup, that same count returns whatever
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE says — 4 if you wrote 4, 128 if you wrote 128, for one
request. That is precisely libuv's sentence about preallocating the maximum
number of threads allowed. Five rows, same lab, on where the value is set:

Where it was set Concurrency counted by the resolver 24 names
nowhere (default 4) 2 3,695 ms
first line of the JS: process.env... = '16' 8 930 ms
the same line after one fs.readFile 2 3,720 ms
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16 in the shell 8 923 ms
node --env-file=uv.env 8 934 ms

The third row vindicates the documentation's warning, but for a different
reason: the setting is not missed because the runtime built the pool early; it
is missed because someone submitted work to the pool before you did. A library
that reads a file with top-level await, or a dependency that calls
randomBytes, quietly makes your setting irrelevant. So the advice stands: do
not set this value from inside your code. The two honest paths in the table
above are the shell environment and --env-file; both land before the first
job.

The bill for growing it

The ceiling is 1024 (libuv 1.30.0 raised it from 128) and each thread wants an 8
MiB stack (since 1.45.0; before that it was the platform default). Readings from
the container's /proc/<pid>/status after a single dns.lookup:

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE libuv-worker VmSize VmRSS Total threads
unset (4) 4 848 MiB 61 MiB 11
8 8 880 MiB 61 MiB 15
128 128 1,841 MiB 61 MiB 135
1024 1024 9,021 MiB 75 MiB 1,031

Going from four to eight adds 32 MiB to VmSize: four threads × 8 MiB, exact.
At 1024 the virtual size reaches 9 GiB while resident memory stays at 75 MiB —
the stacks are paged lazily, just as libuv's documentation says. So the thing to
worry about is not RSS; it is virtual address space in an environment capped by
ulimit -v, and a scheduler that now has 1,031 threads to deal with.

My decision: for a process like my blog pipeline, which writes a couple of
images per article and talks to five platforms, 16 is more than enough. Values
in the hundreds only make sense in a process that genuinely makes hundreds of
concurrent slow calls, and even there the real question is not the pool size but
why those calls are concurrent.

How to leave the limit behind entirely

The cleanest exit is not to grow the pool but not to use it. dns.resolve4 runs
on c-ares; the query happens on the event loop, not in the pool. I asked the
same 24 names of the same 300 ms resolver, with the default four-thread
pool:

Method Concurrent 24 names
dns.lookup 2 3,695 ms
dns.resolve4 24 312 ms

All twenty-four in flight, and the total is the duration of one query. More than
an eleven-fold difference, and I never touched the pool.

It is not free, of course. Node's documentation states the difference honestly:
dns.resolve* does not read /etc/hosts, and it does not use nsswitch.conf
and resolv.conf the way dns.lookup does. So there is no guarantee it gives
the same answer as ping. In a container, service names written into
/etc/hosts, mDNS, search domains — all of that disappears on this path. The
middle ground the documentation points to is more sensible: resolve the name
with dns.resolve() and use the address, or replace the lookup option that
APIs such as socket.connect() and dgram.createSocket() accept with your own
implementation — which is also exactly where a cache belongs.

Questions to ask about your own setup

  • How many distinct hosts does your process talk to? Each one means a default dns.lookup, and they all share at most two threads.
  • Does the same process do image processing, zlib, pbkdf2 or heavy file reads? If so, what fills the pool is probably not DNS but those.
  • Is UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE set from inside the code? If you cannot prove no work hit the pool before that line, the setting may be ignored.
  • Do you know how many threads your pool opened with? On Linux, counting libuv-worker in /proc/<pid>/task/*/comm takes two seconds (libuv 1.50.0 and above); on macOS you need sample or vmmap.
  • If you have a slow-resolver problem, should the answer be dns.resolve? Yes if you have no dependency on /etc/hosts and nsswitch; otherwise your own lookup.
  • If your traffic goes through global fetch, how do you hand it a lookup? fetch takes no such option; the path runs through undici's dispatcher — setGlobalDispatcher(new Agent({ connect: { lookup } })).
  • You opened eight worker_threads and assume you have eight pools? The thread count and the queues in threadpool.c are static: there is one pool per process. Eight workers share the same four threads and the same two DNS slots.
  • What happens when your nameserver dies? A getaddrinfo that has already started cannot be cancelled — uv__work_cancel can only pull work that has not begun off the queue — so two threads stay pinned for as long as timeout × attempts in resolv.conf says.

Limits without counters

Not one measurement in this article produces an alert. There is no counter that
goes up when the pool fills. The tooling is not entirely absent: perf_hooks
has a 'dns' entry type that tells you how long dns.lookup took, and the gap
between the node.threadpoolwork.async and .sync traces gives you the time
spent queueing. But the first one does not tell you why it took that long, and
the second is never emitted by the pool's two busiest customers — dns.lookup
and fs — because neither goes through the code that emits it. The limit is
there; in practice the only evidence is in your p99.

I ran into the same shape in the CPU quota
article: a process using
seventeen percent of its quota, throttled half a million times in ten days,
invisible to every dashboard that looks at averages. In the keepalive
article the
setting was right but almost no application read it. Here is a third variant:
the setting is documented, it is recommended, and half of the recommendation is
lost on the way — and the place it is lost is written on line 46 of the source.

Two threads out of four. If you did not choose that deliberately, libuv chose it
for you.

Official Sources

  • Node.js — UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (CLI documentation)
  • Node.js — DNS: Implementation considerations
  • libuv — src/threadpool.c (v1.x branch)
  • libuv — Thread pool work scheduling documentation
  • libuv — src/unix/getaddrinfo.c (v1.x branch)
  • Node.js — lib/net.js (main branch)

title: How to Export Google Ads Transparency Center Data (with Ad Copy) in Python
description:
I wanted something simple: every Google search ad a competitor is running, how long each one has been running, and the actual ad copy — in a spreadsheet.

Google already publishes all of this in the Ads Transparency Center (Google's answer to Meta's Ad Library). It just has no export button and no API. So I scraped it, and ran into something I didn't expect: for most big advertisers, the ad copy isn't there as text at all.

The surprise: most text ads are stored as images

When you open a text ad in the Transparency Center, Google renders it in one of two ways:

  1. A text preview — the headline and description exist as text (in a small JS preview), easy to parse.
  2. A screenshot — a PNG of the ad, nothing else. The words only exist as pixels.

I pulled the first 30 text ads of five large advertisers on Nov 1, 2026 and counted how many had a text version:

Advertiser Text ads checked With a text version
booking.com 30 0
expedia.com 30 0
hubspot.com 30 1
samsung.com 30 7
nike.com 30 21
Total 150 29 (19%)

So if a tool only reads the text preview, the best it can do here is copy for about 1 ad in 5 — and for booking.com and expedia.com, nothing. That's a big hole if "what are my competitors saying?" is the whole point.

Reading the screenshots (the DIY version)

The fix is OCR. Each ad record links to its snapshot image (tpc.googlesyndication.com/archive/simgad/...), and a basic version with Tesseract is a few lines:

import io, requests, pytesseract
from PIL import Image

def read_ad(image_url):
    img = Image.open(io.BytesIO(requests.get(image_url, timeout=20).content)).convert("L")
    img = img.resize((img.width * 2, img.height * 2))          # small text OCRs better when upscaled
    data = pytesseract.image_to_data(img, config="--psm 6", output_type=pytesseract.Output.DICT)
    words = [(w, float(c)) for w, c in zip(data["text"], data["conf"]) if w.strip() and float(c) >= 0]
    text = " ".join(w for w, _ in words)
    confidence = sum(c for _, c in words) / max(len(words), 1)
    return text, confidence

That gets you a blob of text. Turning it into headline / description / display URL reliably took most of the work. The traps I hit:

  1. Not everything in the image is the ad. Many snapshots include a product thumbnail or sitelink buttons on the right. OCR happily reads those and mixes them into the description. Detect and crop them first.
  2. Headline vs. description. Google draws the headline in blue and the description in dark grey, so splitting by color before OCR works far better than guessing from line positions afterwards.
  3. Language. The same advertiser runs ads in dozens of languages. Picking the Tesseract model from the countries the ad ran in (Korean, Japanese, Thai, Arabic, Cyrillic…) fixes most of the garbage.
  4. Trust the confidence score — strictly. My first threshold was 70. At 77, one booking.com description came out as "Book a Hotel near Universal Studios. HEHHE HAHA Quick, Easy Booking." Above 90 the text was mostly clean, apart from cut-off words. Anything lower should be flagged, not trusted.
  5. Some words are simply cut off. The screenshot crops long headlines, so you'll get "Hotels in Downtown Chica…". Nothing to fix there — just know it.
  6. Be gentle with Google. The listing endpoints rate-limit quickly (429s and CAPTCHA pages). Retry a couple of times, then stop — don't hammer.

The no-maintenance version

I packaged all of this as an Apify Actor (Google Ads Transparency & Ad Library Scraper), so I don't have to babysit OCR models or rate limits. Here's how I find a competitor's long-running search ads — the ones they keep paying for:

from apify_client import ApifyClient
import pandas as pd

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")

run = client.actor("datalume/google-ads-transparency-scraper").call(run_input={
    "domains": ["nike.com"],
    "region": "US",
    "platform": "search",
    "format": "text",
    "minDaysRunning": 30,          # skip short tests
    "sortBy": "longestRunning",
    "maxAdsPerTarget": 50,
})

df = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items())
good = df[df["copyStatus"] == "ok"]   # high-confidence copy only
good[["daysShown", "firstShown", "headline", "regionCount"]].head(10)

Here's what came back for nike.com (US, search, text ads, run on Nov 1, 2026) — 50 ads, copy for all 50 (38 from the text preview, 12 by OCR, all above 90 confidence). A slice of the longest-running ones:

Days shown First shown Advertiser Headline Countries
1,833 2021-10-25 WPP Media (agency) Zapatillas Air Max 90. Nike MX 8
1,794 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV Nike - Onlineshop Deutschland 46
1,794 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV Nike: zapatillas, ropa y más 51
1,793 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV Nike UK - Online Store 44
1,792 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV The Official Nike Site - Nike: Shop The Collection (OCR) 39
1,735 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV NIKE — onlinebutik - Officiella Nike-webbplatsen (OCR) 29
1,384 2022-11-30 Nike, Inc. Training & Gym Equipment. Nike.com (OCR) 1
1,384 2022-11-30 Nike, Inc. (dynamic — Google writes it) 1

A few things jump out in under a minute:

  1. The longest-running ads weren't placed by Nike's own account but by an agency account (WPP Media). A domain search returns every advertiser whose ads point at the domain — useful, but filter by advertiser if you only want the brand itself.
  2. Nike's European "brand" ads have been running since at least October 2021, in roughly 30–50 countries each, with the same handful of lines ("The Official Website. Home Of Everything Nike. Shop The Latest Releases."). That's what a proven, evergreen brand ad looks like.
  3. In the US, 28 of the 31 ads from the Nike, Inc. account have no fixed headline — they're Dynamic Search Ads, where Google writes the headline from the landing page. Nike US leans on DSA and only controls the description. You'd never see that pattern by clicking through ads one at a time.

Also note daysShown is the number of days the ad actually ran, not just last-minus-first: three ads that all "started" on 2021-10-25 show 1,833, 1,794 and 1,688 days.

What else is in each row

  • firstShown, lastShown, daysShown, isActive — how long the ad has been running and whether it's live
  • regions — every country the ad ran in, with the last date shown there
  • headline, description, displayUrl, plus copySource (text or ocr) and copyConfidence
  • transparencyUrl — a link back to the ad on Google's site, so you can check anything by eye

You can also pass advertiser names or IDs instead of domains, filter by country / platform / date, and set onlyNewAds on a daily schedule to get just the new creatives.

Caveats (read these before you trust the numbers)

  • firstShown has a floor. The oldest ads I've seen all show 2021-10-25, which looks like where the Transparency Center's history begins. Read it as "running since at least then", not as the real start date.
  • OCR isn't perfect. Even high-confidence rows can contain a wrong letter ("Al" for "AI") or a cut-off word. Low-confidence rows are kept but marked lowConfidence.
  • Domain searches include other advertisers — agencies, resellers, or anyone whose ads link to that domain or its subdomains (like the WPP Media rows above). Use an advertiser ID if you need exactly one advertiser.

Cost

The Actor charges per ad: $2.00 per 1,000 ads, or $3.50 per 1,000 for text ads where high-confidence copy was extracted (instead of, not on top of, the $2). Countries are included, and rows Google fails to load are free. The 50-ad run above cost $0.18 (50 ads with copy × $0.0035) and took about a minute; with onlyNewAds on a schedule, you only pay for ads you haven't seen before.

Disclosure: I run datalume, the publisher of the Actor used here. Both the Actor and this article were built with AI assistance; every number above comes from real runs on Nov 1, 2026 and was checked against the raw data. Questions welcome in the comments.

title: Un pipeline de clima del Perú con dbt, DuckDB y GitHub Actions, sin AWS
description:
Introducción

Un proyecto de ingeniería de datos puede empezar con una necesidad concreta y pocas herramientas: obtener datos públicos, transformarlos de forma reproducible y facilitar su consulta. Para este proyecto individual elegí comparar el clima de Lima, Arequipa y Cusco mediante una ventana de 30 días.

El código está en el repositorio público data-engineering-pipeline y el reporte puede consultarse en GitHub Pages. Ambos enlaces fueron comprobados después del primer despliegue.

Video de presentación

En este video muestro la funcionalidad de la solución: la consulta del reporte, la comparación entre ciudades, la descarga de datos y la actualización automatizada.

Ver la demostración funcional en YouTube.

El problema

Las respuestas de una API son útiles, pero no bastan para analizar datos de forma repetible. Pueden faltar fechas, aparecer nulos o acumularse duplicados si cargamos varias veces el mismo período. Además, una comparación entre ciudades necesita unidades, fechas y reglas de cálculo consistentes.

Mi objetivo fue construir un flujo pequeño que convierta respuestas meteorológicas en dos productos: una tabla diaria limpia y un resumen por ciudad. El resultado se exporta a un reporte HTML y archivos CSV.

Arquitectura y herramientas 

Open-Meteo → Python → JSON crudo + DuckDB raw.weather
                              ↓
                       dbt stg_weather
                              ↓
                       dbt city_summary
                              ↓
                    pruebas de calidad
                              ↓
                   HTML + CSV + metadatos
                              ↓
                   GitHub Pages, tras CD
  • Python 3.12 extrae respuestas HTTP, valida los datos y exporta los resultados.
  • DuckDB almacena tablas analíticas en un archivo, sin administrar un servidor.
  • dbt Core y dbt-duckdb gestionan las transformaciones SQL, sus dependencias y las pruebas.
  • GitHub Actions ejecuta CI, la actualización diaria y el despliegue.
  • GitHub Pages es el destino configurado para alojar el reporte estático públicamente.

No se utilizan servicios ni credenciales de AWS. La arquitectura usa GitHub como plataforma SaaS y no necesita un proceso Python funcionando permanentemente. Para esta escala, dbt permite demostrar transformación y calidad sin desplegar un orquestador de larga duración.

Implementación

1. Extraer una ventana consistente

La fuente es la API histórica de Open-Meteo. Para cada ciudad se solicitan temperatura máxima, mínima y precipitación diaria. La ventana termina siete días antes de la fecha actual en Lima para dejar margen a la disponibilidad del histórico.

Antes de cargar, Python comprueba las 30 fechas esperadas, las longitudes de las listas, valores numéricos finitos, coherencia entre mínima y máxima y precipitación no negativa. Cada petición tiene un timeout y hasta tres intentos. Si falla, la ejecución termina con error: no reemplaza los datos reales por datos sintéticos.

2. Cargar sin duplicar

Después de validar las tres ciudades, una transacción reemplaza raw.weather en DuckDB. Es una reconstrucción completa de una ventana pequeña. Repetir una ejecución no debe multiplicar registros.

Se conservan también las respuestas JSON para inspeccionar la fuente. Este diseño no pretende guardar un histórico incremental ilimitado: prioriza que el proyecto pueda entenderse, ejecutarse y evaluarse con facilidad.

3. Transformar con dbt

stg_weather tipifica los campos. city_summary utiliza ref('stg_weather'), por lo que dbt conoce el orden de construcción:

select city, min(date) as start_date, max(date) as end_date,
       count(*) as days,
       round(avg((temperature_max + temperature_min) / 2), 2) as mean_midpoint_c,
       round(max(temperature_max), 2) as highest_c,
       round(min(temperature_min), 2) as lowest_c,
       round(sum(precipitation_mm), 2) as total_precipitation_mm
from {{ ref('stg_weather') }}
group by city

El indicador mean_midpoint_c es el promedio del punto medio entre mínima y máxima diaria. Lo etiqueté así porque no equivale a calcular una media de temperaturas horarias. La fuente contiene reanálisis; tampoco debe presentarse como medición de una estación local.

4. Probar y generar la salida

dbt build construye dos modelos y ejecuta nueve pruebas de datos: campos obligatorios, unicidad, duplicados, rangos y continuidad de la ventana. Solo después se exportan el reporte y los CSV.

Las pruebas unitarias de Python cubren respuestas válidas, mediciones inválidas, fechas incorrectas y fallos de red. El modo --offline usa una fixture sintética identificada como TEST y escribe en otra carpeta. CI lo ejecuta dos veces para comprobar idempotencia y agregados conocidos.

Para reproducirlo en Linux o macOS con Python 3.12:

python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
python -m pipeline.run --offline --end-date 2026-01-30
python -m pipeline.run

El README incluye los comandos equivalentes para PowerShell. El reporte real queda en site/public/index.html.

Despliegue y automatización

El workflow versionado separa tres trabajos. test ejecuta pruebas y datos sintéticos. build depende de las pruebas y utiliza la API real. deploy publica exclusivamente site/public en Pages y comprueba el endpoint público por HTTP.

Las PR solo ejecutan pruebas. Un push a main, una ejecución manual o la programación diaria producen una nueva actualización real. La programación está configurada a las 06:17 de Lima; GitHub puede retrasar ejecuciones programadas.

Para activar la publicación hay que seleccionar Settings → Pages → Source → GitHub Actions en el repositorio y ejecutar el workflow. No se necesita guardar un token personal: Actions usa sus credenciales automáticas con los permisos específicos de Pages. Open-Meteo no necesita una clave para este uso no comercial.

Pages está disponible en repositorios públicos gratuitos; la API tiene condiciones y límites de uso. El diseño requiere normalmente tres peticiones diarias y runners estándar. Las condiciones deben revisarse antes de ampliar el alcance: Pages, Actions y Open-Meteo.

Solución publicada: verificada con HTTP 200, descarga del CSV y consulta de metadata.json. Los metadatos del primer despliegue identificaron el commit 27263e7db878d735305ba78006d770919a249847, 90 filas y origen real Open-Meteo.

Ejecución exitosa de CI/CD: los jobs test, build y deploy terminaron correctamente. El workflow también comprueba por HTTP que el sitio sirve metadatos del commit que acaba de desplegarse.

Resultados comprobados

En la ejecución local del 1 de noviembre de 2026, el pipeline recuperó 90 registros reales para el período del 26 de septiembre al 25 de octubre de 2026: 30 por ciudad. Construyó los dos modelos y superó las nueve pruebas dbt. También pasaron cuatro pruebas unitarias y la comprobación de idempotencia con agregados sintéticos conocidos.

La ejecución remota también completó las pruebas y publicó el mismo período. La consulta directa del CSV público devolvió estos resultados:

Ciudad Días Promedio del punto medio diario (°C) Precipitación acumulada (mm)
Arequipa 30 17.48 1.1
Cusco 30 14.30 17.7
Lima 30 22.74 7.7

Son una instantánea del período 2026-09-26 a 2026-10-25, no valores permanentes. El reporte permite descargar el detalle y el resumen; sus metadatos indican el origen, las fechas, el momento de generación y el commit. Las pruebas locales y la comprobación HTTP del despliegue aportan evidencias separadas del funcionamiento.

Conclusión

El proyecto recorre el ciclo de un pipeline ELT: extracción, almacenamiento, transformación, validación, exportación y despliegue automatizado comprobado. Su tamaño permite explicar cada decisión y repetir el proceso sin administrar servidores.

La solución ya puede consultarse públicamente y actualizarse con cada ejecución exitosa del workflow. Como mejoras futuras quedan un histórico incremental, alertas ante fallos y pruebas sobre cambios de esquema en la API.

Datos de Open-Meteo, con atribución bajo CC BY 4.0.

title: CI Can Be Green While the macOS Installer Fails: Stage-by-Stage Acceptance from a Real Controller Migration
description:
This is the English edition of an article first published in Japanese on Zenn: https://zenn.dev/asagiman/articles/macos-installer-actual-acceptance

Even after CI turns green, the macOS Installer can stop. This happens at the final real-machine acceptance step even when development relies on AI agents. The tests have passed and no problem has been found in the built package. Yet a product cannot ship until the user's Mac accepts the installation and the authorized work actually runs.

During the migration of the Controller that Netsujo is developing, the internal records show that, within the two days of October 16 and 17, 2026 alone, we ran the real macOS Installer eleven times. Four runs succeeded (three generation-update stages and one limited diagnostic without authentication) and seven failed (three generation-update stages and four stages involving the administrator's own authentication). All seven failures passed preinstall and then stopped in postinstall, and the operating system recorded a failed installation. In one of the authentication runs, part of the changes had already been applied to the machine when the run failed. There were also real-machine failures and successes before and after these two days. On October 30, 2026, another installation stage succeeded on the real machine and passed readback, but a normal authenticated AI job had not yet been accepted.

Below is a way to record evidence so that the next decision can be made without losing the proof of stages that did succeed, separated into five boundaries: source (including CI), package, OS installation, authorization, and a real AI job. It ends with a check you can run quickly with a disposable test package.

The two-day real-machine results are based on internal records from October 16–17, 2026. The October 30 result and the current status were confirmed by checking the same internal records on November 1, 2026. As of November 1, 2026, the overall Controller migration and acceptance of a normal authenticated job are still in progress. Credentials, internal recovery procedures, secrets, and confidential configuration values are excluded.

What happened: a built package stopped in postinstall

CI runs tests against a specified source, environment, and input. It can find many problems that are reproducible on the development side in advance: types, unit tests, static checks, and package generation.

When the macOS Installer is involved, the existing OS state, pre- and post-install scripts, the actual user and permissions, the administrator's own authentication, and migration state from earlier generations all affect the result. Some of these conditions cannot be fully reproduced in a CI environment.

In the Controller recovery work, we used the real installation logs to separate the progress of preinstall from the later postinstall failure. In the failed runs, postinstall returned an error, and the OS recorded the installation failure together with a PackageKit error (PKInstallErrorDomain Code=112). A separate diagnostic that succeeded is valid only for the diagnostic's own scope; the failed package stays on hold and needs its own acceptance.

The first thing a developer needs to establish is which candidate, which stage, and which recorded outcome were involved. Fixing on a single cause too early risks treating failures from different generations as the same phenomenon.

Sorted by type, the records showed that different candidates succeeded at different stages

The table below organizes the observations by type, within what can be published. The rows are not in chronological order. "Observed evidence" shows what an actual record exists for; "Supported conclusion" shows what that record supports.

Stage (by type) Observed evidence Supported conclusion
Source and CI checks Test and CI success records for the target candidates Source accepted within the specified check scope
Limited unauthenticated diagnostic Record of Installer success on the real machine, with its output read back Processing on macOS confirmed under the diagnostic conditions
Generation-update stage Records of both success (3 runs) and postinstall failure (3 runs), depending on the candidate Only the candidates that succeeded met OS acceptance for that stage
Authentication-related stage Records in which the authentication child process did not finish normally and the Installer also failed (4 runs) The authentication-dependent sequence remained unaccepted
State inspection after failure In one failed run, part of the changes had already been applied to the machine Partially applied changes exist
Real AI job No complete authorized launch, delivery, durable record, and independent acceptance Final acceptance of the Controller migration remains open

The real logs tell us the terminal state of each stage. Even when an authentication-related process fails, an OS denial or nearby warning that appears in the log at the same time cannot simply be taken as the root cause. Establishing causality requires a safe reproduction that isolates the failure conditions.

We therefore adopted a rule: a stage that succeeded for one candidate is never reused as a success for another candidate. The evidence of the successful diagnostic is preserved, and a new package requires new acceptance evidence.

First, identify "the same subject"

In long-running development, conversations, PRs, CI, release files, and host logs are each updated at different times. Even after a commit moves on following review, a package built from an older revision can remain on disk. When this happens during incident response, it becomes easy to attach past check results to the current candidate by mistake.

So we pin the identity of the subject being accepted.

Subject Main information to retain Question answered
Source Repository, commit SHA, reviewed changes Which code was evaluated?
CI Target SHA, job, result, timestamp Which checks passed against which code?
Package Hash, size, build origin, signature and composition checks Do the delivered file and the checked file match?
OS execution Scope of execution authority, real-machine result, log, partial state Was the package actually applied?
Authorization and use Valid authority, real job result, saved output, independent acceptance Can the intended work be completed through the legitimate path?

For example, a package's SHA-256 can confirm file identity: it checks that the file a reviewer approved matches the file a user is about to install. Even when the hash matches, the postinstall terminal status and authentication success must be confirmed separately.

When reporting a single failure, save at least "the candidate identifier, the stage executed, the observed terminal status, and the remaining unknowns" in the same record.

Why a simple retry is dangerous

An installer may update some files or state before it fails. In our records, too, there was a run that failed after part of its changes had been applied. A rerun then starts from a different initial state. Even if only the second attempt succeeds, the cause of the first failure can be lost.

Privileged operations and authentication add a question of authorized scope. If an operation run under a one-time approval fails, treat that approval as used and stop. If a developer removes a protection through an environment variable or a different execution path, the result may look like a technical success, but the legitimate permission model breaks.

After a failure, our practice is to review the preserved logs and remaining state, organize the source, and re-confirm the target file and authorization before rerunning the same operation. The eleven runs above are records of different packages; none of them is a rerun of the same package.

What to check after a failed stage

  • Which terminal state the OS recorded: success, failure, or interruption.
  • Whether any changes were applied before the failure, and how far to preserve the parts that cannot be confirmed.
  • Whether the next run would make additional changes to existing data or managed state.
  • Whether the existing approval was consumed by the run, and who decides the next authorization.
  • Whether a local reproduction environment exists where the same input can be tested safely.

Checking these five points lets you explain why the next operation is needed, even during an urgent recovery. Retrying without checking adds one more partial state of unknown cause.

Put a safe preflight first to make failure cheap

Some operations change the environment's state the moment they succeed. Separating the conditions that can be inspected read-only before execution reduces failures that happen after irreversible changes.

As a general design, consider the following order.

  1. Fix the input and the subject: identify the acceptance candidate, the package to run, and the authorized scope.
  2. Static checks: inspect composition, dependencies, format, and hash.
  3. Non-destructive environment checks: confirm the required OS conditions and readable state within the authorized scope.
  4. Recovery assessment: evaluate in advance what state remains after an interrupted run and how to reconcile it.
  5. Authorized change: execute according to an approval that matches the subject and the operation.
  6. Real-machine readback: compare the OS terminal record with the durable result.
  7. Normal job acceptance: confirm authentication and roles, shutdown, output persistence, and independent review.

This order is a design proposal. We do not claim that the current Controller implementation follows it. Acceptance of a normal job remained incomplete as of November 1, 2026.

What RED→GREEN should confirm

What follows is a generalized approach, not a result carried out on the Controller. Once you find a failure condition, first pin a local counterexample. For example, remove an environmental condition that the package-building logic assumes, using a safe fixture, and confirm that the preflight stops correctly. That is the RED state.

Next, add the minimum condition check or recovery and confirm that the same fixture turns GREEN. Loosening a protection mechanism for testing at this point can weaken the production permission guarantee. Keep the operations that must be refused refused, and give a reason only to the operations that are needed. Testing only the happy path is not enough; include the conditions that must fall explicitly into a hold.

Abnormal case Expected behavior
Package hash mismatch Do not proceed to the real-machine operation; hold
Execution authority expired or mismatched with the subject Stop and await a new, correctly scoped approval
Inconsistent existing-generation information Preserve history and investigate the cause
Preflight finds a missing condition Report the failure before any state change
postinstall exits nonzero Save the OS result as a failure and inspect partial state
Child-process termination unconfirmed Stop promotion to SUCCESS
Real job output cannot be saved Hold job acceptance and inspect the durable record

This table generalizes the refusal and stop conditions to aim for. When applying it to a real product, build tests that fit the assets being protected and the OS specification.

Keep acceptance as a record per stage

Bringing AI into the development process increases the number of times an agent reports "implementation complete" or "tests passed". If the granularity of those reports is vague, a source fix gets taken as a successful start of operations.

We treat each stage as an independent unit of acceptance. The following is a generalized design example. It was constructed to explain the stages and is separate from the actual state names of any product. There are six state names, and they map to the five boundaries from the introduction as follows: SOURCE_REVIEWED and CI_ACCEPTED are "source", PACKAGE_VERIFIED is "package", OS_INSTALL_ACCEPTED is "OS installation", and AUTHORIZED_REAL_JOB_ACCEPTED covers "authorization" and "a real AI job". The final INDEPENDENT_OPERATIONAL_REVIEW is not a boundary but an independent check of the whole.

SOURCE_REVIEWED
      |
      v
CI_ACCEPTED
      |
      v
PACKAGE_VERIFIED
      |
      v
OS_INSTALL_ACCEPTED
      |
      v
AUTHORIZED_REAL_JOB_ACCEPTED
      |
      v
INDEPENDENT_OPERATIONAL_REVIEW

For each stage, record the subject identifier, the observed result, who authorized it, and when it ran. If a stage fails, mark it HOLD and keep the evidence of the earlier stages that succeeded. When the candidate changes, re-examine the stages affected by the change. Keep unknowns visible as unknowns until an authorized observation resolves them.

Example acceptance record 

{
  "candidate": "example-source-revision",
  "packageDigest": "example-package-digest",
  "check": "os_install",
  "observed": "failed",
  "partialState": "requires_reconciliation",
  "authorization": "consumed",
  "realJobAccepted": false,
  "nextGate": "independent_review_before_new_approval"
}

This is fictional data for explanation. It contains no real identifiers or credentials. The record keeps failure and uncertainty as values and does not promote them to success. Any mechanical judgment also needs a design that never promotes an ambiguous value to success.

What to ask an independent review for

An independent review confirms what each piece of evidence actually proves. A review of source changes and tests looks at reproduction of the problem, the changed code and its impact, and boundary conditions including abnormal cases. A review of the package and the real machine looks at the identity of the target bytes, the actual macOS Installer result, and whether anything was partially applied. A review of security and operations looks at the permission boundary and validity of approval, and at output persistence, shutdown, and independent acceptance of the formal job.

The role of an independent review is less about running more tests and more about verifying assumptions the implementer may have missed. For operations that change permissions and OS state in particular, confirm that the reviewed source matches the actual subject of the operation that is later approved.

A minimal check you can run yourself

You can observe what does not become "success" when postinstall fails, using a test package that contains nothing confidential. The steps below were run and confirmed on macOS 26.6.2 on November 1, 2026. They use no administrator privileges and target the user's home directory. The package is empty, and no files are installed.

  1. Create and enter a temporary directory, then create scripts/postinstall and make it fail on purpose. 
work=$(mktemp -d) && cd "$work" && mkdir -p scripts
printf '#!/bin/sh\necho "demo postinstall: failing on purpose" >&2\nexit 1\n' > scripts/postinstall
chmod +x scripts/postinstall
  1. Build the package and record its hash. 
pkgbuild --nopayload --scripts ./scripts --identifier com.example.demo --version 1.0 ./demo.pkg
shasum -a 256 demo.pkg
  1. Install into the user domain and record the exit status and the log. 
installer -pkg demo.pkg -target CurrentUserHomeDirectory; echo "exit=$?"
grep 'com.example.demo\|demo.pkg' /var/log/install.log | tail -5

In our run, installer printed "The install failed" and ended with exit=1, and /var/log/install.log recorded PKInstallErrorDomain Code=112 (the explanatory text in parentheses depends on the display language; if you cannot find the log line, search for Code=112). If you cannot read the log, the exit status alone is enough to identify the failure. For comparison, rebuilding with exit 0 instead of exit 1 gave exit=0 and "The install was successful". An empty package does not appear in the list of installed packages (pkgutil --pkgs) even when it succeeds, so its absence from that list cannot be used as evidence of failure.

  1. In the same shell as step 1, delete the temporary directory. /var/log/install.log keeps a record of the run, which is an ordinary system log entry. 
[ -f "$work/demo.pkg" ] && cd / && rm -rf "$work"

What this confirms is the gap that a package whose identity is confirmed by its hash can still fail OS installation. One observation is complete when you write "observed": "failed" in the acceptance record above and inspect the remaining state before any rerun.

Where to start when applying this to another product

First, write down the scope your usual CI protects. Then list the execution environments outside CI. For the macOS Installer, that is the OS installation result; for a web service, the deployment target and the anonymous production page; for an AI agent, legitimate authentication and the completion of a real task.

You do not need to build a large management platform from the start. Linking the source SHA, check results, release file, and real-environment acceptance result for a single change into one record is enough to make it easier to see where the work stopped. Next, add the person responsible for each stage and its stop conditions.

When a check fails, look at that record before starting any additional run. Reuse valid results for subjects that have not changed, and safely isolate only the parts whose cause remains.

Summary: the last thing to confirm is whether the work actually ran

The Controller migration confirmed that failures can remain in the OS installation and authentication stages even after CI succeeds. The fact that the unauthenticated diagnostic succeeded is kept as valid evidence, while the authenticated stages and the real job need additional acceptance. Work that is still in progress as of November 1, 2026 is not treated as a completed result.

Completing real operations requires evidence that the machine accepted the specified package, started the work with legitimate authority, and finished output persistence, shutdown, and review. Even when AI raises development speed, responsibility for this final confirmation stays with the development team.

Go one step beyond source and CI acceptance: include real-environment and real-use confirmation in the plan, with separate evidence for each stage.
That is the lesson that generalizes from these failures and the recovery process.

title: Next.js Prefetching in App Router: How `<Link>` Partial Prefetch Works and Why Your Pages Still Feel Slow
description:
Next.js Prefetching in App Router: How <Link> Partial Prefetch Works and Why Your Pages Still Feel Slow

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Developers adopt Next.js App Router expecting server components to eliminate client-side waterfalls and prefetching to deliver instant navigation. The reality surprises them: links feel sluggish, dynamic routes block for seconds, and the DevTools network tab shows requests firing only after the user clicks. The prefetch happened, the data arrived, but the navigation still waits.

The confusion stems from three behaviors that collide in production: partial prefetch stops at the first Suspense boundary instead of loading the full page, the router cache expires prefetched data after 30 seconds for dynamic routes, and the client cannot render anything until the server responds with the missing pieces. The result is a server-driven app that feels slower than the client-side SPA it replaced.

Next.js 16.3 introduces partial prefetching as an opt-in feature, giving developers fine-grained control over what loads before navigation. Combined with the new cache components primitive, teams can mark reusable UI as cacheable and let Next.js extract loading shells from any route, not just routes with a loading.tsx file. The client now has enough data to render an instant transition, and the server streams dynamic content as it resolves.

This post explains how App Router prefetching works under the hood, why the default behavior creates slow navigations, and how to adopt the new primitives to make every link click feel instant without breaking dynamic content.

Key Takeaways

  • Next.js App Router partial prefetch (the default) stops at the first Suspense boundary, not the full page, causing slow navigations when routes lack explicit loading shells.
  • The router cache expires prefetched data after 30 seconds for dynamic routes and 5 minutes for static routes, triggering re-fetches on click if the user waits too long.
  • Next.js 16.3's partial prefetching and cache components let developers mark reusable UI as cacheable and control exactly what loads before navigation.
  • Instant Insights in the Next.js DevTools automatically surfaces slow navigations during development, eliminating guesswork about which links need optimization.
  • Full prefetch with prefetch={true} loads the entire destination page ahead of time, but costs bandwidth and can serve stale personalized content if cached data expires.

How Next.js Link Prefetching Actually Works in App Router

The <Link> component in Next.js App Router triggers prefetching when it enters the viewport or when the user hovers over it. The exact behavior depends on the prefetch prop and whether the destination route is static or dynamic.

By default, <Link> uses prefetch="auto", which means Next.js decides what to prefetch based on the route type. For static routes, the full route loads. For dynamic routes, Next.js fetches the route down to the first loading.tsx boundary, a behavior called partial prefetch.

The distinction between static and dynamic routes matters because Next.js treats them differently at build time. A route is static if it contains no dynamic segments (like [id]), no generateStaticParams is missing, and it does not read request-specific data like cookies or headers. Everything else is dynamic.

// app/blog/page.tsx - static route
export default function BlogPage() {
  return <div>Blog posts render at build time</div>;
}

// app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx - dynamic route
export default function PostPage({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }) {
  // Reads dynamic segment, so Next.js treats this as dynamic
  return <div>Post: {params.slug}</div>;
}

When a user hovers over a <Link href="/blog/post-1">, Next.js sends a request to the server. For a static route, the server returns the pre-rendered HTML and RSC payload. For a dynamic route, the server returns only the layout and any shared UI down to the first Suspense boundary, then stops. The page component itself does not load until the user clicks.

The official Next.js documentation (as of version 16.3) describes this behavior in the prefetch prop reference: "For dynamic routes, the partial route down to the nearest segment with a loading.js boundary will be prefetched." If no loading.tsx file exists, the prefetch ends at the layout, and the navigation blocks until the server responds with the page.

The router cache stores prefetched data with a time-to-live (TTL) that depends on the route type. Static routes cache for 5 minutes. Dynamic routes cache for 30 seconds. After the TTL expires, clicking the link triggers a new server request even if the prefetch completed successfully.

This explains why navigations sometimes feel instant and sometimes block. If the user clicks within 30 seconds of hovering, the cached data is fresh and the navigation completes immediately. If the user waits 31 seconds, the cache expires, and the client must wait for the server to re-render the route before the navigation can proceed.

Partial Prefetch vs Full Prefetch: What Gets Loaded When

The prefetch prop on <Link> accepts three values: "auto" (the default), true, and false. Each produces different behavior and costs.

prefetch="auto" defers to Next.js to decide what to load. For static routes, this means the full route. For dynamic routes, this means a partial prefetch that stops at the first loading.tsx boundary. The goal is to balance performance with bandwidth: prefetch enough to make navigation feel instant without loading content the user may never see.

prefetch={true} forces a full prefetch for both static and dynamic routes. The client downloads the entire page, including all data-fetching and rendering, before the user clicks. This guarantees instant navigation but wastes bandwidth if the user never visits the link. It also introduces stale data problems for personalized routes: if the prefetched page contains user-specific content, and the user waits long enough for the cache to expire, clicking the link shows stale content until the server responds with fresh data.

prefetch={false} disables prefetching entirely. The client requests the route only after the user clicks. This saves bandwidth but guarantees a slow navigation because the client must wait for the server to render the page before the transition can complete.

Next.js 16.3 changes the behavior when partial prefetching is enabled via partialPrefetching: true in next.config.ts. With this flag, prefetch="auto" now prefetches the route's app shell (the static and cached content) instead of stopping at the first loading.tsx boundary. The app shell includes layouts, templates, and any components marked with 'use cache', giving the client enough data to render a loading state immediately on click.

Prefetch value Static route behavior Dynamic route behavior Router cache TTL Best for
"auto" (default) Full route Partial (to first loading.tsx) Static: 5min, Dynamic: 30s Most links
true Full route Full route Static: 5min, Dynamic: 30s Critical navigation paths
false No prefetch No prefetch N/A Rarely-visited routes, infinite scroll lists
"auto" (with partialPrefetching: true) App shell + cached content App shell + cached content Configurable per cache tag Next.js 16.3+ apps

The tradeoff between partial and full prefetch becomes clear in a dashboard app. A sidebar contains 20 links to different reports. Full prefetch downloads all 20 pages when the sidebar renders, consuming megabytes of bandwidth and server resources even if the user only views one report. Partial prefetch downloads the shell for each page (layouts, navigation, headers) but waits to load report-specific data until the user clicks. The navigation feels instant because the shell paints immediately, and the data streams in as it resolves.

// app/dashboard/layout.tsx
export default function DashboardLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <div className="dashboard">
      <nav>
        {/* Partial prefetch: loads shell, not data */}
        <Link href="/dashboard/sales">Sales Report</Link>
        <Link href="/dashboard/inventory">Inventory</Link>
        <Link href="/dashboard/analytics">Analytics</Link>
      </nav>
      <main>{children}</main>
    </div>
  );
}

The diagram shows why partial prefetch feels faster for the initial shell render but slower for the complete page, while full prefetch either delivers the entire page instantly or serves stale content if the cache expired. Choosing the right strategy depends on whether the route contains dynamic content that changes frequently.

The Router Cache Problem: When Prefetched Data Goes Stale

The router cache in Next.js App Router exists to avoid redundant server requests. When a prefetch completes, Next.js stores the result in memory with a TTL. Subsequent navigations to the same route read from the cache instead of hitting the server, making back-and-forth navigation instantaneous.

The problem surfaces when the TTL expires before the user clicks. For dynamic routes, 30 seconds is short enough that normal user behavior (reading content, scrolling, comparing options) exhausts the cache before the navigation happens. The user clicks, the cache check fails, and the client blocks while waiting for the server to re-render the route.

This behavior surprises developers because the prefetch succeeded. The DevTools network tab shows the request completing with a 200 status. But when the user clicks 35 seconds later, a second identical request fires, and the navigation waits for that response before proceeding. The prefetch wasted bandwidth and delivered no performance benefit.

The stale data problem is worse for personalized routes. Consider a product page that shows the user's cart count in the header. If the page prefetches when the user hovers the link, and the user adds items to the cart before clicking, the prefetched page shows the old cart count until the new server response arrives. The transition looks instant, but the cart count is wrong for 200-300ms, creating a flicker as the correct data streams in.

Next.js addressed this in 16.3 by tying cache invalidation to the 'use cache' directive. When a component or function is marked with 'use cache', Next.js generates a cache key based on the function's arguments and the user's session. If the arguments or session change, the cache key changes, and the cached data is no longer valid. This lets developers opt specific components into granular caching while keeping the rest of the page fresh.

// app/dashboard/sales/page.tsx
import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';

async function getSalesData(userId: string) {
  'use cache';
  const response = await fetch(`/api/sales?user=${userId}`);
  return response.json();
}

export default async function SalesPage({ params }: { params: { userId: string } }) {
  const data = await getSalesData(params.userId);

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Sales Report</h1>
      {/* This data is cached per user and stays fresh across navigations */}
      <pre>{JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)}</pre>
    </div>
  );
}

The official Next.js 16.3 release notes state: "It's more explicit and composable than our previous server-side caching APIs, and now, it also brings client-side caching to Next.js for the first time." The 'use cache' directive integrates with prefetching by letting the router cache store function-level results instead of full routes. When a prefetch happens, Next.js extracts the cached data, bundles it with the shell, and sends it to the client. The user clicks, the shell renders instantly, and only the non-cached dynamic data requires a server round-trip.

The cache key mechanism solves the stale data problem but introduces a new complexity: cache invalidation. If the sales data changes server-side while the client holds a cached copy, the user sees outdated information until the cache expires or the route re-validates. Next.js provides revalidation APIs (revalidatePath, revalidateTag) to expire caches on demand, but developers must call them explicitly when data changes.

Router cache diagram showing TTL expiration and re-fetch behavior

The image illustrates how the router cache expires after the TTL and triggers a new server request, even when the original prefetch completed successfully. The gap between prefetch and click determines whether the navigation feels instant or blocks.

Controlling Prefetch Behavior: Practical Code Examples

Developers control prefetching at three levels: per-link via the prefetch prop, per-route via loading.tsx files, and globally via next.config.ts flags.

The prefetch prop is the most direct control. Setting prefetch={false} disables prefetching for a specific link, useful for links in infinite scroll lists where prefetching would waste bandwidth. Setting prefetch={true} forces a full prefetch, useful for critical navigation paths like the main call-to-action on a landing page.

// app/components/product-list.tsx
'use client';

export default function ProductList({ products }: { products: Product[] }) {
  return (
    <div className="grid">
      {products.map((product) => (
        <Link
          key={product.id}
          href={`/product/${product.id}`}
          // Disable prefetch for long lists to save bandwidth
          prefetch={false}
        >
          {product.name}
        </Link>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

The loading.tsx file provides a route-level loading shell that prefetching uses to render an instant transition. When a dynamic route includes a loading.tsx file, partial prefetch stops at that file and sends the loading component to the client. The user clicks, the loading state renders immediately, and the page content streams in as the server resolves data-fetching.

// app/blog/[slug]/loading.tsx
export default function Loading() {
  return (
    <div className="blog-post-skeleton">
      <div className="skeleton-title" />
      <div className="skeleton-author" />
      <div className="skeleton-content" />
    </div>
  );
}

Without loading.tsx, partial prefetch has nothing to send, so the navigation blocks until the full page arrives. The Next.js DevTools Instant Insights panel highlights this as a slow navigation and suggests adding a loading file.

Next.js 16.3 adds two config flags that change prefetching behavior globally. Setting cacheComponents: true enables the new cache components primitive, letting developers mark reusable UI with 'use cache' and have Next.js extract it during prefetch. Setting partialPrefetching: true changes the default prefetch="auto" behavior from "stop at first loading.tsx" to "prefetch app shell plus cached content."

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  partialPrefetching: true,
};

export default nextConfig;

These flags unlock fine-grained control over what loads before navigation. A product page can mark the header, footer, and navigation as cached, while leaving product-specific content (price, availability, reviews) dynamic. The prefetch sends the shell, the user clicks, the shell renders instantly, and the dynamic content streams in.

// app/product/[id]/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react';

async function Header() {
  'use cache';
  return <header>Site Header</header>;
}

async function ProductDetails({ id }: { id: string }) {
  const product = await fetch(`/api/products/${id}`).then(res => res.json());

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>{product.name}</h1>
      <p>{product.price}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

export default function ProductPage({ params }: { params: { id: string } }) {
  return (
    <>
      <Header />
      <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading product...</div>}>
        <ProductDetails id={params.id} />
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}

The cache components approach solves the stale data problem by caching at the component level instead of the route level. The header never changes, so it stays cached indefinitely. The product details change frequently, so they skip the cache and fetch fresh data on every navigation. The user sees an instant shell render followed by a smooth stream of dynamic content, no flicker, no stale data.

Next.js 16.3 Instant Navigations and the Future of Prefetching

Next.js 16.3 introduces Instant Navigations, a suite of features designed to make server-rendered apps feel as responsive as client-side SPAs without sacrificing the benefits of server rendering. The headline feature is partial prefetching, which builds on the cache components primitive to extract loading shells from any route, not just routes with a loading.tsx file.

The official Next.js 16.3 announcement states: "Next.js can extract this UI and load it into the client prior to a navigation, making your app feel as snappy as an SPA once users start clicking around it." The key word is "extract." Instead of requiring developers to manually define loading shells in separate files, Next.js analyzes the route's component tree, identifies cached components, and bundles them with the prefetch response. The client receives a ready-to-render shell even if the route has no loading.tsx file.

Partial prefetching also changes how prefetch payloads are structured. In prior versions, a prefetch request returned a monolithic RSC payload containing the entire route. In 16.3, the payload includes three layers: the app shell (layouts, templates, cached components), URL-specific data (dynamic segments, search params), and truly dynamic content (user-specific data, real-time updates). The client renders the app shell immediately, paints URL-specific data as it arrives, and streams dynamic content last.

This staged handoff eliminates the binary choice between instant-but-stale full prefetch and accurate-but-slow partial prefetch. The app shell is always safe to cache because it does not depend on user state or request timing. URL-specific data caches per route, so navigating between products on the same site reuses the shared shell and only fetches product-specific content. Dynamic content bypasses the cache entirely, guaranteeing freshness at the cost of a small delay.

// app/dashboard/[reportId]/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react';

async function DashboardShell() {
  'use cache';
  return (
    <div className="dashboard-layout">
      <nav>Dashboard Navigation</nav>
      <aside>Filters</aside>
    </div>
  );
}

async function ReportData({ reportId }: { reportId: string }) {
  const data = await fetch(`/api/reports/${reportId}`).then(res => res.json());

  return <div>{JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)}</div>;
}

export default function ReportPage({ params }: { params: { reportId: string } }) {
  return (
    <>
      <DashboardShell />
      <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading report...</div>}>
        <ReportData reportId={params.reportId} />
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}

The diagram below shows the execution flow when partial prefetching is enabled. The prefetch extracts the app shell, the user clicks, the shell renders instantly, and the report data streams in as the server resolves the fetch.

The Instant Insights panel in the Next.js DevTools automatically detects slow navigations and suggests fixes. If a route lacks a loading shell, the panel shows a warning and generates a prompt that teaches AI agents how to add one. If a route has a loading shell but still feels slow, the panel identifies which components are blocking the critical path and suggests marking them with 'use cache'.

The official documentation (Next.js 16.3 release notes) describes Instant Insights as "a new devtool that automatically surfaces slow navigations." The panel runs in development mode only, monitoring every client-side transition and measuring the time from click to first paint. If the time exceeds a threshold (currently 300ms), the panel flags the navigation as slow and logs the component stack that blocked rendering.

This eliminates the guesswork that plagued prior versions. Developers no longer need to profile every link manually or instrument their code with performance marks. The DevTools highlight the problem, explain the root cause, and provide a concrete fix. All without leaving the browser.

Instant Insights panel in Next.js DevTools showing a slow navigation warning

The image shows the Instant Insights panel flagging a navigation to /dashboard/sales as slow because the route lacks a loading shell. The panel suggests adding a loading.tsx file or marking reusable components with 'use cache' to unlock instant navigation.

Debugging Slow Navigations: Finding the Real Culprit

Slow navigations in Next.js stem from four common causes: missing loading shells, expired router cache, blocking data fetches, and oversized prefetch payloads. Identifying the root cause requires inspecting the network tab, the React DevTools profiler, and the Next.js Instant Insights panel.

The network tab shows when prefetch requests fire and how long they take to complete. A prefetch that completes in 50ms but triggers a second identical request on click indicates a cache expiration problem. The user waited longer than the TTL, so the router cache invalidated the prefetched data and fetched it again.

The React DevTools profiler shows which components are blocking the critical path. If a navigation waits 2 seconds before painting anything, the profiler flame graph reveals which component is running slow. The usual suspects are data-fetching components that call fetch without Suspense boundaries, heavy computations in the render phase, and third-party libraries that block the main thread.

The Instant Insights panel ties these signals together by showing the full navigation trace. The panel logs the click event, the prefetch check, the cache hit or miss, the first paint, and the final layout shift. If the navigation is slow, the panel highlights the step that took the longest and suggests a fix.

The diagram shows the decision tree the router follows during navigation. If the cache is valid, the render happens immediately. If the cache expired, the navigation blocks while waiting for the server response. The gap between cache check and server response is where slowness accumulates.

Fixing slow navigations requires matching the solution to the root cause. If the cache expired, either shorten the time between prefetch and click (by prefetching on hover instead of on viewport entry) or extend the cache TTL by marking components with 'use cache'. If the navigation blocks on data fetches, wrap the slow components in Suspense boundaries and add a loading fallback. If the prefetch payload is too large, reduce it by setting prefetch={false} on low-priority links or splitting the route into smaller chunks.

The useLinkStatus hook (introduced in Next.js 16.2) provides immediate feedback during navigation. When a user clicks a link, the hook returns { pending: true } until the navigation completes, letting developers show a loading indicator without waiting for the server response.

'use client';

import { useLinkStatus } from 'next/link';

export default function NavigationIndicator() {
  const { pending } = useLinkStatus();

  if (!pending) return null;

  return (
    <div className="fixed top-0 left-0 right-0 h-1 bg-blue-500 animate-pulse" />
  );
}

The hook debounces fast navigations by adding a 100ms delay before returning pending: true. This prevents the loading indicator from flashing on screen for navigations that complete in under 100ms, reducing visual noise for instant transitions.

The official Next.js documentation (version 16.3) recommends combining useLinkStatus with CSS transitions to create a smooth loading experience: "You can 'debounce' the hint by adding an initial animation delay (e.g. 100ms) and starting as invisible (e.g. opacity: 0)." This gives the server time to respond before showing any feedback, avoiding flicker on fast networks.

For further reading on Next.js caching and performance, see the related posts Next.js 15 Caching Changes, Next.js App Router Layouts and Templates, and Next.js Caching Mental Model 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my Next.js link prefetch but still feel slow when clicked?

The router cache expires prefetched data after 30 seconds for dynamic routes. If the user clicks after the TTL, the client fetches the route again even though the prefetch completed. Use 'use cache' to extend the TTL or reduce the delay between prefetch and click by prefetching on hover.

What is the difference between partial prefetch and full prefetch in App Router?

Partial prefetch loads the route down to the first Suspense boundary, sending the layout and loading shell but skipping page-specific data. Full prefetch loads the entire page including all data. Partial prefetch saves bandwidth but may feel slower if no loading shell exists. Use prefetch={true} to force full prefetch on critical links.

How does Next.js 16.3 partial prefetching change the default behavior?

In Next.js 16.3, enabling partialPrefetching: true makes prefetch="auto" send the app shell plus cached components instead of stopping at loading.tsx. This gives the client enough data to render an instant transition without requiring a separate loading file for every route.

When should I disable prefetching with prefetch={false}?

Disable prefetching for rarely-visited routes, infinite scroll lists, and links that appear in large quantities (like a product catalog with 1000 items). Prefetching wastes bandwidth if the user never clicks the link, and disabling it has no downside if the route is not performance-critical.

How do I debug which component is blocking a slow navigation?

Use the Instant Insights panel in the Next.js DevTools to identify slow navigations, then inspect the React DevTools profiler to see which component is blocking the critical path. The profiler flame graph shows render times per component, revealing bottlenecks like unwrapped data fetches or heavy computations in the render phase.

Making Next.js Navigations Feel Instant Without Breaking Dynamic Content

Next.js prefetching promises instant navigation but delivers slow transitions when the defaults collide with dynamic routes, expired caches, and missing loading shells. The confusion stems from partial prefetch stopping at Suspense boundaries, router cache expiration after 30 seconds, and the client blocking until the server responds with missing data.

Next.js 16.3 fixes this with partial prefetching, cache components, and Instant Insights. Developers mark reusable UI with 'use cache', and Next.js extracts it during prefetch, giving the client enough data to render an instant shell. Dynamic content streams in as the server resolves it, and the DevTools highlight any navigation that takes longer than 300ms, eliminating guesswork about which links need optimization.

Adopting the new primitives requires enabling two flags in next.config.ts and marking cached components with 'use cache'. The payoff is a server-rendered app that feels as responsive as a client-side SPA, with no stale data, no flicker, and no guesswork about when prefetches expire.

title: Why Most Directories Fail Developers with 14-Day Queues (And How We Engineered an Instant-Live Launchpad)
description:
If you’ve ever launched a developer tool or side project, you know the dread of the Directory Holding Pattern.

You spend months building your product. You polish the UI, fix the edge cases, write clean docs, and submit your link to five different software launchpads.

Then, you wait.

One directory asks for $49 to "skip the queue." Another takes 17 days to approve your listing. And the third one silently goes live on a random Sunday night while your entire audience is asleep — completely burning your launch momentum.

Makers shouldn't be penalized because an admin queue is backed up.

That’s why I spent the last few months building Astro Discover — an open, hype-free product launchpad with a guaranteed 24-hour spotlight and zero queue delays.

💡 The Core Problem: The Launch Day Limbo

Traditional launchpad moderation models have two major flaws:

  1. The Ghosting Trap: Submissions get buried in queues for weeks. By the time the product is approved, the maker has already moved on to other marketing initiatives.
  2. The Pay-to-Win Fast Track: Platforms create artificial delays just to monetize expedited review tiers.

We wanted to engineer a platform where the maker’s launch day is sacred and protected.

🛠️ The Architectural Solution: 24–48 Hr Turnaround + The "Pending Review" Fail-Safe

Here is the exact mechanism we implemented on Astro Discover:

1. 24–48 Hour Maximum Human Verification

Every submission is screened by a human to prevent malicious phishing, direct executable downloads, and broken links. We keep our queue lean and mean with a 24 to 48-hour SLA.

2. The Auto-Live Fail-Safe (No Lost Launches)

Here’s our biggest innovation: Makers schedule their exact launch day in advance.
