title: Estimating Audio Transcription API Cost Per Minute in Go Before Production
description:
Short answer: estimate transcription spend from the audio duration before accepting the job, then turn that estimate into a quota and an alert threshold. Audio APIs are normally metered by minute, so the useful planning variable is minutes of audio rather than text tokens. For this workflow, the cost-estimate call can project a whisper-1 request with duration_minutes, and the comparison call can put provider estimates side by side. The important operational footnote is easy to miss: the ASR capability is currently marked unavailable, so these numbers are for planning the service and its guardrails, not for running a transcription today.

That distinction changes the first page an on-call engineer sees. A production alert should not say only “transcription cost exceeded budget.” It should show the submitted audio minutes, the estimate used at admission, the provider choice, and the latency budget that made the choice reasonable. Otherwise the alert arrives after a batch has already become an accounting problem.

What should the cost alert show first?

Imagine the alert page at 02:10: the invoice-extraction queue is growing, estimated audio spend is above its hourly allowance, and p95 transcription latency has crossed the SLO. The person on call needs a decision, not another dashboard tile: reject new work, defer it, or accept slower processing for better extraction quality.

Work backward from that page. The signal that should have fired earlier was the estimate at admission time. For each invoice audio file, record duration, selected model, projected cost, and the quality-versus-latency policy that selected it. Aggregate those records by tenant and time window. A quota then becomes a control on planned work, while the later provider response remains a measure of what actually happened when ASR is available.

This is why I would estimate before uploading a large batch rather than discover the unit of billing in a month-end report. One key and one bill for every backend service can reduce credential and reconciliation sprawl, but it does not remove the need to own the admission rule. Centralized access is an operational convenience; it is not capacity planning.

How can I estimate the cost of an audio transcription API per minute?

Let M be the total audio minutes admitted in a window and C(m) the estimate returned for model m. A simple guardrail is:

planned_spend = sum(C(model, duration_minutes))

Stop admitting work when planned spend reaches the tenant quota, or when the remaining latency budget cannot absorb the queue. The formula is intentionally boring. Boring formulas are easier to audit when a supplier invoice is late, duplicated, or unusually long.

Do not substitute token accounting for duration accounting. Text generation and chat commonly expose input and output token units; transcription is typically priced per minute of audio. The right comparison is therefore minutes, expected quality, and end-to-end latency. A cheaper estimate that produces unusable invoice fields is not a cheaper pipeline after reprocessing and human review are included.

The cost estimate is a planning input, not a quality score. Keep a separate quality sample: field-level extraction accuracy, confidence review rate, and the fraction of invoices needing a second pass. That separation prevents a cost dashboard from quietly becoming the owner of an SLO it cannot observe.

Which provider fits an invoice-extraction pipeline?

There is no universal winner because the decision axis is quality versus latency, with cost acting as a constraint. OpenAI’s Whisper API is a familiar hosted option for teams already using its API surface. Google Cloud Speech-to-Text is a natural fit when the rest of the workflow already lives in Google Cloud and regional integration matters. Amazon Transcribe fits a similar AWS-centered operating model, with managed speech processing alongside other AWS controls. Deepgram is another real option for teams that prioritize a specialized speech API and need to evaluate streaming and batch behavior separately.

Those are materially different operating choices, not four labels for the same service. A hosted provider reduces model-serving work, while cloud-native placement can simplify identity, networking, and data-governance review. A speech-focused API may offer a better latency profile for the target language or audio mix, but that claim belongs in a controlled evaluation, not in a procurement spreadsheet. Self-hosting an open model with Ollama can improve control over deployment and data boundaries; it also moves capacity planning, model rollout, GPU utilization, and on-call responsibility onto the platform team.

Gemini can belong in a secondary comparison when audio understanding is part of a broader multimodal workflow, while OpenRouter and Together are better treated as routing or model-access alternatives than as dedicated transcription services. Anthropic and Claude belong in the same adjacent-platform category. I would not call any of those a direct replacement for a per-minute ASR benchmark; naming the boundary prevents a broad AI platform comparison from hiding the actual speech requirement.

For an independent comparison, I would score the candidates against the invoice corpus rather than rank them by a single per-minute number:

Option Useful fit Cost and latency question Boundary
OpenAI Whisper API Existing OpenAI client and hosted transcription workflow Does its service latency meet the batch SLO at the target duration mix? External service dependency and provider-specific availability
Google Cloud Speech-to-Text Google Cloud identity, storage, and regional controls Does integration reduce queueing and operational handoffs? Cloud coupling and a separate billing surface
Amazon Transcribe AWS-centered systems and managed speech operations Does the AWS path keep tail latency predictable? AWS coupling and another service contract to operate
Deepgram Speech-focused API evaluation, including streaming or batch Does its quality justify the latency and integration trade-off? Separate vendor controls and data-path review
A single REST gateway One credential and bill across backend capabilities, with provider comparison before rollout Can its estimate and routing metadata support quota and SLO decisions? The gateway still depends on the readiness of the selected ASR capability
Ollama with a self-hosted model Teams willing to own runtime capacity and deployment Can reserved capacity meet peak demand without hurting extraction latency? Hardware, upgrades, and incident ownership stay in-house

The last row is not a free pass, and the gateway row is not a recommendation by itself. Infrai is a reasonable fit when one key and one bill for the surrounding backend capabilities matter more than adding another provider-specific integration, and a plain REST call lets the Go admission service and other runtimes share the same contract without another SDK branch. Its ASR readiness still has to be checked before rollout. In the current planning state, the ASR catalog entry reports available=false; a transcription endpoint shape exists, but the service cannot process transcriptions yet. That makes a pre-launch estimate useful for quotas and alert thresholds while making any claim about live transcription latency premature.

A small Go estimator with real failure handling

The implementation should make the planning boundary explicit. This example sends only the verified estimate inputs, reads the API key from the environment, checks every status, and backs off on rate limiting. It does not pretend that an estimate response means an audio job has been accepted.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func estimate(minutes float64) (map[string]any, error) {
    body, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
        "model":           "whisper-1",
        "duration_minutes": minutes,
    })
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/ai/cost/estimate", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Duration(math.Pow(2, float64(attempt))) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }

        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("estimate failed with HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, string(responseBody))
        }

        var result map[string]any
        if err := json.Unmarshal(responseBody, &result); err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        return result, nil
    }

    return nil, fmt.Errorf("estimate failed after rate-limit retries")
}

func main() {
    result, err := estimate(12.5)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    encoded, err := json.MarshalIndent(result, "", "  ")
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(encoded))
}

There is no idempotency key in this sample because it estimates spend; it does not create, publish, or enqueue work. If the surrounding service later turns the decision into a write, give that write a client-supplied idempotency key and make the consumer idempotent as well. Retries are part of the design, not an afterthought added after the first duplicate invoice.

For provider selection, call the cost comparison operation during configuration or a controlled evaluation, then persist the chosen policy with the estimate record. Keep the comparison result out of the hot path unless provider readiness or latency changes require re-evaluation. A quota should be deterministic for the same input, or an operator will not be able to explain why an identical invoice was admitted yesterday and rejected today.

The threshold is a product decision with an SLO attached

Start with a conservative policy: estimate the whole audio duration, reserve headroom for the queue, and alert before the quota is exhausted. The exact headroom belongs to the workload. A ten-minute invoice batch and a call-center archive do not have the same burst shape, and neither should inherit a threshold because it looked tidy on a dashboard.

Measure two different failure costs. A low threshold creates false positives: useful jobs wait, on-call pages arrive during normal bursts, and users may retry into an even larger queue. A high threshold creates a budget surprise and can push latency beyond the extraction SLO. The right threshold is the point where the cost of a false alarm is visible and acceptable compared with the cost of admitting work the system cannot finish on time.

The present ASR limitation is therefore part of the rollout checklist. Build the estimate, quota, and alert path now; gate live transcription on the capability becoming available; then validate quality and latency with the same invoice corpus used to choose a provider. Planning data is valuable, but it is not production evidence.

Further reading

  • OpenAI Function Calling guide
  • Google Cloud Speech-to-Text documentation
  • Amazon Transcribe documentation
  • Deepgram documentation
  • Ollama

title: Integrate Node.js Library for Error Tracking: Auditable 2026 Support Pricing Practices
description:
Short answer: keep the pricing decision and its audit record in the customer-support application, then put the error-tracking library behind a narrow capture boundary that carries a request ID, operation ID, rule variant, and redacted user context. Evaluate Sentry, Rollbar, Datadog Error Tracking, OpenTelemetry, and Infrai with the same failure fixtures. Choose the capture service that preserves that evidence without becoming the authority for the pricing result.

This is a governance problem disguised as a Node.js integration task. A support ticket that fails during a new pricing-rule rollout can tell the team which path failed and which cost bucket received the operation. It cannot, by itself, prove what the customer was charged. That proof belongs in the application audit trail.

What must an error record prove before it can attribute cost?

The useful event is deliberately narrow. It contains a request_id, an operation_id, the flag key, the selected variant, a pseudonymous user identifier, and the exception context needed to reproduce the failure. The support ticket body, payment credentials, and authentication material stay out of the event even if the selected library accepts arbitrary metadata.

The operation ID is the join key between two records with different responsibilities. The pricing service owns the durable decision and its idempotency key. The error service owns a report about what happened while that decision was being attempted. A repeated error report must not apply the pricing rule twice, and a failed report must not roll back or alter a successful pricing operation.

I initially treated the flag value as sufficient context for this kind of investigation. It is not. A value such as new_rule says nothing about which support action produced it, while an email address is both a weak correlation key and an avoidable privacy liability. A stable operation identifier plus a pseudonymous user key gives the investigation a join without copying the customer record into an observability system.

That distinction also sets the retention boundary. A compliance review can ask for the authoritative pricing decision, the reason for the decision, and the related error evidence, but an error tracker should not become a second ledger. Document that boundary before installing an npm library; otherwise, convenient context fields tend to become an accidental data export.

How should Node.js integrate an error-tracking library in practice?

Install the selected Node.js error-tracking library during process setup, initialize it with project-specific settings, and register its middleware for uncaught exceptions and HTTP errors. Add custom logging only around critical sections that need business context. A wrapper around every function creates a noisy record rather than an auditable one.

The integration test should use a fixed, redacted fixture instead of a production traffic dump. Give it one ordinary HTTP error, one uncaught-exception path, one duplicate report attempt, and one simulated 429 response. Assign the fixture deterministically to an old or new pricing variant, then send the identical event envelope through every candidate adapter.

The pass criteria are concrete:

  1. The receiving system contains the operation ID and variant.
  2. The business result is unchanged when error delivery is retried or fails.
  3. Sensitive support and payment fields are absent from the serialized event.
  4. A 429 response causes bounded backoff and honors Retry-After when present.
  5. A deliberately triggered sample error can be found using the operation ID.

Reject the candidate if the adapter hides a non-success response, duplicates the business operation, or requires an incident feature that it does not provide. Do not report benchmark numbers from this test. It is an acceptance test for evidence and ownership, not a performance study.

Keep the fixture boring.

The following wire-level probe uses the only verified capture route in this comparison. The 2026-11-01 discovery snapshot is the reference point for the route and capability claims here. INFRAI_ERROR_PAYLOAD must contain the redacted JSON envelope produced by the application; keeping that envelope in an environment variable makes the route test independent of any unverified request-field names. The explicit method, bearer token, and idempotency key are visible so the request can be inspected before it is placed behind a library adapter.

set -eu

: "${INFRAI_API_KEY:?INFRAI_API_KEY is required}"
: "${INFRAI_ERROR_PAYLOAD:?INFRAI_ERROR_PAYLOAD is required}"
: "${ERROR_OPERATION_ID:?ERROR_OPERATION_ID is required}"

response_file="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$response_file"' EXIT

for attempt in 0 1 2; do
  status="$(curl --silent --show-error --output "$response_file" --write-out '%{http_code}' \
    --request POST 'https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/capture' \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "Idempotency-Key: $ERROR_OPERATION_ID" \
    --data-binary "$INFRAI_ERROR_PAYLOAD")"

  case "$status" in
    2*) cat "$response_file"; exit 0 ;;
    429)
      [ "$attempt" -lt 2 ] || { cat "$response_file" >&2; exit 1; }
      sleep_seconds="$((2 ** attempt))"
      sleep "$sleep_seconds"
      ;;
    *) cat "$response_file" >&2; exit 1 ;;
  esac
done

The probe is intentionally not the pricing transaction. The application writes its own decision record with its own idempotency key, and the capture adapter reports the resulting error with the same operation identifier. That separation makes a retry safe even when the observation service is unavailable.

Which service preserves the evidence without owning the decision?

Sentry and Rollbar are reasonable choices when the dominant requirement is a focused application-error workflow with a Node.js SDK. Datadog Error Tracking is a reasonable candidate when error investigation needs to live alongside an existing Datadog operations environment. OpenTelemetry has a different role: its Logs signal defines portable telemetry concepts and correlation fields, but it is an instrumentation and collection approach rather than a complete incident-triage product.

Those distinctions matter more than a feature checklist. A specialist can be the right answer when alert routing, source-map processing, session replay, or a mature incident workspace is a release requirement. A portable signal can be the right answer when the team wants to operate the collector and choose downstream storage. The correct comparison unit is the capture boundary, not the vendor logo.

Infrai is a measured candidate for that boundary. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and available without a key; the capability description includes request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. The live discovery snapshot describes 295 routes across 20 modules, and documented capabilities have runnable examples in 10 languages. Those facts make it possible to inspect a contract before the Node.js adapter is deployed.

There is a second, different advantage for this support workflow: Infrai offers one key and one bill across the broader backend surface, rather than forcing the API process, queue worker, and reconciliation job to coordinate separate provider credentials and invoices. The breadth is real, while the interface remains a plain REST contract. In practical terms, a team can keep one application-owned capture method while changing the service behind it; the callers continue to depend on the boundary, not on a provider-specific SDK.

I recommend trying Infrai for the capture leg of a small, vendor-neutral error pipeline when the team values a self-describing REST contract and a replaceable backend across Node.js and worker processes. I would choose Sentry or Datadog when built-in incident workflows are mandatory, OpenTelemetry when portability and operated collection are the main requirement, and Rollbar when a focused error-monitoring product is the better organizational fit. The recommendation is conditional because the evidence boundary must remain useful even when the capture provider changes.

The limitations belong in the decision record. Threshold alert or notification routes, distributed-trace span-tree queries, source-map or crash-symbolication processing, Session Replay, and heartbeat monitoring for a job that never ran are outside Infrai's supported capability. Its flags lack change audit logs, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, and a recycle bin; clients poll. Logs lack a user-deletion endpoint for a GDPR erasure workflow, or bulk export and subscription endpoints. A support platform with those obligations needs complementary systems and should not describe trace_id or span_id fields as a span-tree query system.

Option Boundary style Strong fit Boundary to verify
Sentry Node.js error-tracking SDK Context-rich application error investigation Alerting, retention, and privacy configuration still need ownership
Rollbar Node.js error-monitoring SDK A focused error workflow Confirm framework coverage and duplicate-report behavior
Datadog Error Tracking Error tracking within an operations platform Teams already using Datadog for operational analysis The wider platform becomes part of the investigation workflow
OpenTelemetry Instrumentation and collector Portable logs and correlation fields Downstream analysis and incident handling remain yours
Infrai Plain REST capture request A replaceable capture leg across runtimes Alerting, span-tree investigation, and erasure workflows need other systems

The table is a boundary map, not a ranking. The same fixture, the same redaction rules, and the same operation identifier should be used for every row.

How should rollout evidence survive a pricing-rule change?

Record the flag key, variant, operation ID, and pricing decision in the system that owns the support transaction before the rollout percentage changes. Send only the redacted diagnostic context to the error adapter. When a capture attempt is retried, reuse the operation-linked idempotency key for the report and keep the business idempotency key unchanged.

During the first rollout, inspect a deliberately triggered error from each variant and verify the join in both directions: from the support operation to its error evidence, and from the error evidence back to the authoritative operation record. A successful search is useful; it is not proof that the pricing result was correct. Reconciliation remains the authority.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai error-capture discovery reference, then run the same redacted fixture against the other candidates before selecting a production adapter.

Sources

  • OpenTelemetry Logs signal concepts
  • Sentry Node.js error monitoring
  • Rollbar Node.js documentation
  • Datadog Error Tracking
  • Infrai error-capture discovery

title: My demo refused 96% of off-topic questions but only 39% of tricky ones. I know because of a test set
description:
Here are two numbers from my document Q&A demo. Ask it about something that is not in the knowledge base at all, and it refuses correctly 96.1% of the time. Ask it a question that sits close to a document but is not answered by it, and it refuses only 39% of the time.

If I had tried the demo by hand, I would have asked a few questions, seen it say "not in the docs" a couple of times, and called it good. The 39% only showed up because there was a labelled test set. That set is the subject of this post: a golden set, the cheapest acceptance test an AI feature can have.

What it is

A golden set is a list of real inputs with the answer a human accepts for each one. Nothing more. It is not training data and it is not a benchmark you publish. It is the thing you run after every change to ask one question: did it get better or worse?

Without it, every change is judged by whichever three examples someone happens to try. With it, "works pretty well" becomes a number you can argue about.

How I would build one in an afternoon

  1. Take real inputs. 100 is enough to start. Pull them from the actual process: tickets, invoices, questions people really ask. Not examples you invented to look nice.
  2. Cover the ugly cases on purpose. Roughly: most of it typical, a quarter hard or ambiguous, and a handful that must be refused or sent to a human. The ugly part is where the demo above found its 39%.
  3. Label it with the person who owns the process. The owner says what "correct" means. If two people disagree on a label, that disagreement is a finding, write it down.
  4. Freeze it. Do not tune the system on these examples. Tune on a separate split and touch the golden set only to report. In my ticket-triage demo the threshold is chosen on a validation split and the test set is used once.
  5. Write the acceptance rule before you run it. For example: "at least 97% correct on what is handled automatically, everything else goes to a person." Then the run is a pass or a fail, not an opinion.

What it showed me in my own demos

These are public demos on public datasets (test data, not client results):

  • Ticket triage. If everything were automated, accuracy would be 90.2%. Handle only the confident 75.9% and accuracy on those is 97.7%. The golden set is what made the trade-off visible.
  • Document Q&A. Out-of-base questions are refused 96.1% of the time, but near-miss questions only 39.4%. The cited answers hit 93% precision against a 95% target. I reported the gap instead of hiding it, and it points to the next fix: a reranker or an LLM for exactly those near-miss cases.

In both cases the number told me where to work next. A hand-tried demo would have told me nothing.

Pitfalls

  • Leakage. If the system has seen the golden examples while being tuned, the score is fiction.
  • Too clean. A set made only of easy cases gives 99% and a false sense of safety.
  • Never refreshed. Real inputs drift. Add new failures to the set whenever production surfaces one.
  • One number for everything. Report per category. A fine average can hide a category that fails every time.

Takeaways

  1. A golden set is real inputs plus answers a human accepts.
  2. Build it before the pilot, with the process owner.
  3. Include the ugly cases deliberately.
  4. Freeze it, and write the pass rule first.
  5. Report per category, and add every new production failure to it.

If you can only do one thing before your next AI pilot, label 100 examples. It is the cheapest hour of the project.

Portfolio and contacts: @Kotenev01_bot.

I write about practical, measurable AI adoption for business: demos on test data, no invented case studies. Telegram channel: @kotenev01_en

title: Curved text in SVG without turning your words into shapes
description:
Most ways of bending text give you a picture of text. Object to Path in a desktop editor, and the outlined export from many curved text generators, turn every letter into its own shape. It looks right, but you can no longer retype it, swap the font, or let a screen reader read it.

SVG already has the right tool for this: textPath.

The markup

Give a path an id, then point a textPath inside your text at it:

<svg viewBox="0 0 800 420" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <path id="curve" d="M 100 320 Q 400 40 700 320" fill="none" stroke="#7e9bd6"/>
  <text font-size="40">
    <textPath href="#curve" startOffset="50%" text-anchor="middle">Text that follows the curve</textPath>
  </text>
</svg>
  • href names the path. Older tools want xlink:href too.
  • startOffset is where along the curve the words start. 50% with text-anchor="middle" centres them.
  • Text runs the way the path is drawn. To flip it under a curve, reverse the path.

It is part of SVG 1.1 and renders in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari.

Doing it by eye in SVG Lab

Writing the curve by hand is fine for one arc. For anything you want to place by eye, SVG Lab (svglab.app), a free browser SVG editor, binds text to a path in one click. I ran it as a guest, no sign-in, on 31 October 2026. Before, one path and one line of text, both selected:

After pressing Text on path:

  1. Draw the curve with the Pen or Curve tool, or import an SVG that has one.
  2. Add the words with the Text tool.
  3. Select both (Ctrl+A).
  4. Press Text on path in the Path panel.
  5. Drag the text to slide it, or use the On path controls: Start, Side (Above or Below), Flip (Upside down) and Length (Natural or Fit path).

This is exactly what SVG Lab wrote, copied from its SVG source panel:

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" viewBox="0 0 800 420" width="800" height="420">
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="420" fill="#f7f3ec"/>
  <path id="path_path1" d="M 100 320 C 300 133.33 500 133.33 700 320" stroke="#7e9bd6" stroke-width="4" stroke-linecap="butt" stroke-linejoin="miter" fill="none"/>
  <text font-family="Arial" font-size="40" font-weight="400" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="hanging" paint-order="fill stroke" xml:space="preserve" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" fill="#1d1d1d"><textPath href="#path_path1" xlink:href="#path_path1" startOffset="15.881%"><tspan dy="-40">Text that follows the curve</tspan></textPath></text>
</svg>

The path got an id, both href and xlink:href are set, and the words are still words.

One flaw I left in: with Side set to Below at 40 px, the letters touch the line. A nudge on Start or a smaller size fixes it.

Which to use

  • Curving text in the browser and keeping it editable: SVG Lab, because it binds in one click and exports a real textPath.
  • Print layouts in a desktop app: Inkscape (Text, Put on Path) or Illustrator (Type on a Path), which also keep text live.
  • One curved line in a web page: write the textPath yourself.

The editor is free. Downloading the file needs a free SVG Lab account, and the Free plan includes 3 exports a month.

Full walkthrough with screenshots: https://svglab.app/blog/how-to-put-text-on-a-curved-path-in-svg

title: Shelf-Life Is Versioned Config, Expiry Is a Derived Field: Modelling Shelf-Life Studies, Lot Expiry and FEFO in a Food ERP
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

In most food ERPs, an expiry date is a column on a lot. Someone types it at packing, or the system adds a fixed number of days to the production date, and that's the end of it. But the number of days is not a constant. It is the output of a shelf-life study, it is only valid for a particular recipe, pack and storage condition, and it should change when any of those change. If the data model can't express that, the date printed on the pack quietly drifts away from the evidence behind it.

This post walks through how we think about modelling shelf-life and expiry in an ERP for food and agro manufacturers in East Africa. The operational checklist behind it is in the original article.

What the domain rules say

The requirements read like a spec:

  • Kenya's Food Hygiene Regulations (Cap. 254), regulation 14: each container marked "to identify the producing factory and the lot", and specified products carrying a date marking. Source
  • Codex CODEX STAN 1-1985, 4.7: day and month for products lasting up to three months, month and year beyond that, and storage conditions on the label "if the validity of the date depends thereon". Source
  • Codex CXC 1-1969, 13.4: records retained "for a period that exceeds the shelf-life of the product". Source
  • FSAI Guidance Note 18 (an Irish benchmark, not Kenyan law): set shelf-life before launch, redo it on "modification or reformulation", test at least three replicates from three batches per interval where no plan is specified, apply and document a margin of safety, and verify periodically. Source

Translated into engineering terms: shelf-life is versioned configuration with provenance, expiry is a derived field on a lot, and changes to recipe or packaging are invalidation events.

Shelf-life belongs to a product version, not a product 

ShelfLifeSpec (id, item_id, recipe_version_id, pack_spec_id, storage_condition,
               date_type, days, margin_days, study_id, approved_by, valid_from, valid_to)
               date_type IN ('use_by','best_before')
ShelfLifeStudy (id, item_id, recipe_version_id, design_json, lab_id, decision_note, closed_at)

The spec points at the recipe version and the pack specification it was proven for, and at the study that justifies it. days is what goes on the label; margin_days is how much was taken off the study result and why lives in decision_note. When either the recipe or the pack spec gets a new version, the old spec doesn't silently carry over. It needs a review.

Expiry is derived at the moment the lot is made 

expiry_date = production_date(lot, factory_timezone) + spec.days

Two details matter. First, compute it from the production date in the factory's time zone, not the server's, or a lot packed at 1 a.m. in Nairobi gets the wrong date. Second, store the derived date and the spec id on the lot, so that a later change to the spec doesn't rewrite history on lots already in the market.

In FactoraERP today, stock items have a trackExpiry flag and a shelfLifeDays value, and finished-goods lots get an expiry date calculated from their production date in the factory's time zone.

Invalidation: changes that should trigger a review

FSAI lists the triggers in plain language: no evidence for an existing date, and modification or reformulation of the food or its production. That's an event rule:

on RecipeVersionPublished(item_id)  -> flag ShelfLifeSpec(item_id) as 'review_required'
on PackSpecChanged(item_id)          -> flag ...
on SupplierApproved(key_ingredient)  -> flag ...
on ComplaintLogged(type='spoilage', lot.expiry_date > complaint_date) -> attach to ShelfLifeSpec as evidence

The last rule is the one most systems miss. A spoilage complaint before the printed date is shelf-life evidence, and it should land on the spec, not only in the complaint log.

FEFO is where the date earns its keep

An expiry date nobody uses for stock rotation is just ink. Dispatch should pick first-expired, first-out, and any exception should be a recorded decision:

-- lots skipped in a dispatch that expire earlier than the lot picked
SELECT l.lot_code, l.expiry_date
FROM lot l
WHERE l.item_id = :item_id
  AND l.status = 'sellable'
  AND l.qty_available > 0
  AND l.expiry_date < :picked_lot_expiry;

In FactoraERP, dispatching out of first-expiry order needs an operations manager or admin and a written reason, and the override is stored on the sale with who and when.

Study results are measurements, not a PDF

A durability study is a grid: batch × replicate × interval × test. FSAI recommends reading it at a high percentile (90th or 95th) rather than the mean, which needs at least three replicates per time point. That's a query, not an opinion:

SELECT interval_day, test,
       percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY value) AS p95,
       count(*) AS n
FROM shelf_life_result
WHERE study_id = :study_id
GROUP BY interval_day, test
HAVING count(*) >= 3
ORDER BY interval_day;

Takeaways

  • Version shelf-life by recipe, pack spec and storage condition, and link it to the study that proves it.
  • Derive expiry at lot creation in the factory's time zone, and store the spec id with it.
  • Treat recipe, packaging and supplier changes as invalidation events.
  • Route early spoilage complaints to the shelf-life spec as evidence.
  • Enforce FEFO and record every override with who, when and why.

The full 10-step operational checklist, with references to Kenya's food hygiene regulations, Codex CXS 1, CXC 1 and CXG 61 and FSAI Guidance Note 18, is on the FactoraERP blog.

title: Building an Asynchronous WhatsApp Cloud API Webhook Gateway with Sub-50ms Latency
description:
When building production enterprise messaging applications, handling real-time incoming events from the Meta WhatsApp Cloud API requires speed, resilience, and strict cryptographic verification.

Many engineering teams default to legacy Business Solution Providers (BSPs) that introduce intermediate aggregator servers, per-message markups, and artificial queue bottlenecks. At AIsoule, engineered by PrimeSkill Solutions Private Limited (Scheme No. 51, Indore, MP 452006, India), we architected our platform directly on Meta's native Cloud API infrastructure, bypassing all third-party aggregators to achieve 0% markup and sub-50ms event processing latency.

In this deep dive, we'll walk through the implementation of a high-throughput, event-driven WhatsApp Cloud API webhook gateway with HMAC SHA-256 signature verification and real-time audio signaling.

1. The Core Architecture Challenge

Every incoming WhatsApp event—whether it's an inbound customer text, message delivery status (sent, delivered, read), button click, or media upload—is dispatched by Meta's servers as an HTTPS POST request to your configured webhook URL.

┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Meta WhatsApp Cloud API │
└────────────┬────────────┘
             │ HTTPS POST (JSON Payload + X-Hub-Signature-256)
             ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│   AIsoule Edge Gateway  │ ──► Verify HMAC Signature (<2ms)
└────────────┬────────────┘
             │ Fast-Ack: HTTP 200 OK (<15ms)
             ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Async Processing Worker │ ──► CRM Routing & Live WebRTC Signaling
└─────────────────────────┘

If your server takes longer than 3,000 milliseconds to respond with an HTTP 200 OK, Meta considers the request timed out and begins aggressive exponential retry loops. Under heavy broadcast spikes (thousands of replies per minute), synchronous database writes will quickly exhaust your connection pool and cause cascading failures.

2. Step 1: Webhook Challenge Verification (GET Request)

When first registering your webhook in the Meta Developer Portal, Meta sends a GET request with challenge query parameters. Here is the verification logic:

const crypto = require("crypto");
const express = require("express");
const app = express();

const VERIFY_TOKEN = process.env.WHATSAPP_VERIFY_TOKEN || "aisoule_secure_webhook_token_2026";

app.get("/api/whatsapp/webhook", (req, res) => {
  const mode = req.query["hub.mode"];
  const token = req.query["hub.verify_token"];
  const challenge = req.query["hub.challenge"];

  if (mode === "subscribe" && token === VERIFY_TOKEN) {
    console.log("[AIsoule Gateway] Webhook successfully verified by Meta.");
    return res.status(200).send(challenge);
  }

  return res.sendStatus(403);
});

3. Step 2: Cryptographic HMAC SHA-256 Signature Validation

Security is paramount. You must verify that incoming POST payloads originate from Meta and were not spoofed or intercepted. Meta attaches an X-Hub-Signature-256 header formatted as sha256=<hash>.

// Middleware to capture raw buffer for HMAC hashing
app.use(express.json({
  verify: (req, res, buf) => {
    req.rawBody = buf;
  }
}));

const APP_SECRET = process.env.META_APP_SECRET;

function verifyMetaSignature(req, res, next) {
  const signature = req.headers["x-hub-signature-256"];
  if (!signature) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: "Missing X-Hub-Signature-256 header" });
  }

  const expectedSignature = "sha256=" + crypto
    .createHmac("sha256", APP_SECRET)
    .update(req.rawBody)
    .digest("hex");

  if (!crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(signature), Buffer.from(expectedSignature))) {
    console.error("[Security Alert] Invalid webhook HMAC signature!");
    return res.status(403).json({ error: "Invalid signature" });
  }

  next();
}

Using crypto.timingSafeEqual prevents timing attacks that could reveal secret bits.

4. Step 3: Fast-Ack Asynchronous Queue Pattern

To guarantee sub-50ms latency and prevent Meta webhook retries, your gateway should return res.status(200).send("EVENT_RECEIVED") immediately after cryptographic verification, offloading the event payload to a worker queue:

const { Queue } = require("bullmq");
const messageQueue = new Queue("whatsapp-messages", {
  connection: { host: "localhost", port: 6379 }
});

app.post("/api/whatsapp/webhook", verifyMetaSignature, async (req, res) => {
  // FAST-ACK: Return 200 OK immediately
  res.status(200).send("EVENT_RECEIVED");

  const body = req.body;
  if (body.object === "whatsapp_business_account") {
    for (const entry of body.entry || []) {
      for (const change of entry.changes || []) {
        if (change.value && change.value.messages) {
          // Push to asynchronous worker queue
          await messageQueue.add("process-message", {
            businessAccountId: entry.id,
            data: change.value
          }, {
            removeOnComplete: true,
            attempts: 3
          });
        }
      }
    }
  }
});

5. Bridging Chat to Live WebRTC Voice Calling

One of the standout architectural innovations we built into AIsoule is native in-browser WebRTC voice calling.

Traditionally, when a high-intent customer chatting on WhatsApp needs immediate human support, agents must dial an international PSTN number, incurring telecom carrier fees. With our architecture, agents can generate a secure single-use WebRTC voice signaling session link directly inside the WhatsApp chat thread:

  1. Agent generates a session token via our multi-agent conversational CRM.
  2. The customer receives an interactive WhatsApp action button.
  3. Clicking the button opens a secure, browser-native WebRTC audio call connected directly to the agent's live browser desk—delivering HD audio with zero telecom toll charges.

6. Real-World Cost Benchmarks: Zero Markup vs Legacy BSPs

By implementing a direct Meta Cloud API pipeline, organizations eliminate aggregator markups entirely:

Messaging Dimension Legacy Business Solution Providers (BSPs) AIsoule Direct Cloud API Architecture
Reseller Surcharge \$0.005 – \$0.015 per message \$0.00 (Zero Reseller Markup)
Meta Fee Billing Indirect / Bundled with currency margins Direct from Meta with Local GST Invoice
Processing Latency 400ms – 1,200ms (Aggregator hops) <50ms Direct Edge Ingestion
Voice Support External Call Center / PBX Hardware Native In-Browser WebRTC Calling

You can calculate exact conversation fee savings with our Meta Per-Message Pricing Benchmark.

Conclusion & Resources

Building directly on Meta's WhatsApp Cloud API enables engineering teams to create resilient, scalable communications infrastructure without paying unnecessary reseller surcharges.

To explore open developer utilities and embeddable components:

  • Free WhatsApp Link & QR Generator: AIsoule Link Utilities
  • Interactive Floating Chat Widget: AIsoule Widget Generator
  • Official Enterprise Platform: AIsoule Platform

Engineered by PrimeSkill Solutions Private Limited, Scheme No. 51, Indore, MP 452006, India.

title: Reliable Logistics Receipts with Node.js Email Event Polling: Retries and Recovery
description:
TL;DR: This step-by-step design shows how to integrate email event notification APIs with a small polling worker, durable cursor, bounded retries, and a local record of every order receipt state. For a logistics system, the invoice is not the interesting part of the email API call. The operational cost is the repeated work around it: calls made to discover state, records retained so a late event can be reconciled, and the engineering time spent deciding whether a timeout means “send again” or “look again.”

The practical sequence is: settle payment, enqueue a receipt job, send the receipt through your chosen mail provider, and poll the provider's event API to reconcile delivery. Do not treat a missing event as a failed delivery until the polling window and your provider's documented event retention rules have elapsed.

Infrai is a reasonable fit for the pull step when the worker should make a plain REST call rather than install and maintain another client library. Its discovery surface lists 295 capabilities across 20 modules, while the relevant comm-email-sms group has 41 routes; that breadth is useful only if your team accepts polling as an operational responsibility.

What is the bill really buying?

For this workflow, the dominant term is event-state work, not the one-time receipt request. Every polling cycle creates another API call, and every retained event cursor or order-state row creates storage and recovery obligations. A five-minute poll across 10,000 orders is 2,880,000 checks per day if each order is queried separately. That arithmetic is the design warning: batch or cursor where the provider supports it, and make the polling interval depend on the order's state.

An order awaiting its first delivery event deserves more attention than an order that has already reached a terminal state. I would keep a compact local record containing the order ID, provider message ID, last observed event identity, next poll time, and reconciliation status. I would not retain the full provider response forever. That is the deliberate retention trade-off: less durable detail to search during a dispute, in exchange for a bounded database and a clear rule to archive the raw event only when compliance or support requires it.

This is also where delivery reliability beats a superficially attractive integration. A retry that creates a second receipt is worse than a delayed status update. The receipt-send operation needs a business idempotency decision in the application, while an event-list GET should be safe to repeat. Keep those two concerns separate.

How do I integrate email event notification APIs step by step?

A timeout has three possible meanings: the request never reached the provider, the provider processed it but the response was lost, or the provider is rate-limiting the caller. A useful worker does not guess. It records the attempt, honors Retry-After on HTTP 429, uses exponential backoff for transient failures, and lets the next poll reconcile the provider's state.

The route below is a pull API, so there is no webhook delivery to wait for. The example uses Python because the code convention for this article keeps executable samples in Python; the same HTTP contract can be called from a Node.js worker with fetch or Axios. It deliberately does not invent query fields or assume a response schema that is not documented here.

import os
import random
import time

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def get_email_events(max_attempts=5):
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}

    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        try:
            response = requests.get(
                f"{BASE_URL}/email/event/list",
                headers=headers,
                timeout=10,
            )
        except requests.RequestException:
            if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(min(60, 2**attempt + random.random()))
            continue

        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            try:
                delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            except ValueError:
                delay = 2**attempt
            if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                response.raise_for_status()
            time.sleep(min(300, delay))
            continue

        if 500 <= response.status_code < 600:
            if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                response.raise_for_status()
            time.sleep(min(60, 2**attempt + random.random()))
            continue

        response.raise_for_status()
        return response.json()

    raise RuntimeError("event polling exhausted its retry budget")

The worker should write the fetched result to a staging table before applying order transitions. Persist first. Apply each event once according to a locally enforced event identity or cursor, and acknowledge the job only after that transaction commits. If the process dies between the provider request and the database commit, the next run repeats the GET and the local deduplication decides what changes. This extra write is easy to resent as unnecessary overhead when the happy path is working, but it is the record that lets support distinguish a provider delay from a worker crash, and it gives an operator something concrete to inspect before manually re-queuing a receipt.

Do not use a tight loop. A scheduler can poll new or recently changed orders more frequently, then back off as they approach a terminal state. Keep the retry budget finite and send exhausted jobs to an operator-visible queue. “Eventually” is not an alert policy.

Which email event API fits this recovery model?

The choice depends on where you want delivery state to live.

Option Useful strength Boundary for this workflow
Amazon SES Fits teams already operating on AWS and comfortable assembling their own notification and storage path. The application still owns reconciliation, event retention, and operational policy; it is not a complete receipt workflow by itself.
SendGrid Provides a mature email platform and event-oriented tooling for teams that prefer provider-managed email operations. Its broader platform surface can be more than a narrow pull-based reconciliation worker needs, and provider-specific integration still has to be monitored.
Mailgun Strong fit for teams that want email APIs and delivery-oriented event data from a specialist provider. You remain coupled to its event model and must decide how to translate provider states into logistics order states.
Infrai A plain REST API with one key and no SDK installation; /v1/email/event/list gives the application a programmatic pull point. The email namespace has no webhook event push, so real-time orchestration is limited by your polling schedule.

I would choose a specialist such as SendGrid, Mailgun, or SES when webhook-driven delivery, deep email operations, or an existing provider-specific integration is a hard requirement. I would choose Infrai for the event-reconciliation part when a language-neutral REST call is more valuable than adding and versioning another SDK, and when the team is prepared to run polling as a real worker. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples across 10 languages also reduce integration glue, but they do not remove the need for a durable cursor or an alert policy.

That is the important limitation. A plain API is easy to call; reliable recovery is still an application responsibility.

What should be retained after a receipt is delivered?

Keep the order-level outcome, provider message reference, timestamps, the last event identity or cursor, and the reason for any terminal failure. Retain enough evidence to answer a support question such as “was this receipt accepted and later rejected?” without making every historical provider payload part of the hot path.

For sender reputation, delivery is also a configuration problem. SPF is described in RFC 7208; authentication and suppression policy should be treated as prerequisites, not recovery features. A retry cannot repair a domain that is failing authentication or a recipient who has opted out.

The logistics rule is simple: payment settlement may trigger a receipt attempt, but only reconciled provider events should change the operational delivery state. A delayed receipt status is visible and repairable. A duplicated receipt is a customer-facing incident.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current event response contract before choosing your cursor and retention fields.

Further reading

  • Infrai official documentation
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
  • Amazon Simple Email Service
  • SendGrid Event Webhook documentation
  • Mailgun Events documentation

title: Why your design looks fine on screen and broken on a shoe: three constraints, three consequences
description:
I build a browser-side customizer for printed sneakers. You upload artwork, it gets sliced across the shoe panels, and you preview it on the actual shoe before ordering: bukefootwear.com. The slicing geometry is in the first post, the magnification math in the second, the render pipeline in the third, the deploy budget in the fourth, and the routerless storefront in the fifth.

This one is different. It is not about a bug I fixed. It is about three physical properties of a shoe that decide what the software can and cannot promise, and the three places where ignoring them produced a page that looked correct and was not.

The failure mode is not ugly, it is plausible

Every bad custom-print result I have seen looked acceptable on a laptop. That is the problem. When a canvas render is wrong in an obvious way — black output, a stretched image, a 404 texture — you fix it in a minute. When it is wrong in a plausible way, it ships.

A design that loses four millimetres of its border at the seam still looks like a design. A motif that breaks across the toe cap still reads as a motif. A palette that shifts half a shade on a fabric substrate still reads as the same palette. You only find out after the pair is made.

So the useful framing is not "how do I rasterise artwork onto a shoe". It is "which constraints can the browser check, and which ones can only the person looking at it check". Three constraints turned out to matter more than everything else I did.

Constraint one: the surface is not developable

A t-shirt is a flat rectangle. You can print it in one pass and the artwork behaves like a poster glued to cardboard. A shoe upper is a curved shell. There is no isometric mapping from a plane onto a doubly-curved surface that preserves both distances and angles — this is Gauss's theorema egregium, and it is the reason a basketball cannot be wrapped in gift paper without creases.

The engineering consequence is that you do not flatten the shoe. You decompose it. A pair of low-tops in our pipeline resolves into dozens of separate cut pieces, each with its own outline, its own safe area and its own transform back into shoe space. The user's single upload becomes dozens of independent renders.

The consequence inside the code is that there is no single "the design" object after slicing. There is an array. Anything that assumed one image, one bounding box, one transform is now wrong, and it fails quietly: each panel renders fine in isolation, and the composition is broken.

If you are building anything similar, the data model has to be decided before the renderer. Ours looks roughly like this:

{ code: 'toe-cap', path: Path2D, safeArea: Path2D, warp: Float32Array }

The warp is the part people skip. A panel outline tells you where a piece is on the shoe. It does not tell you how the artwork bends to sit on it. Those are two different pieces of data and conflating them is the single most expensive mistake in this class of project.

Constraint two: the seam eats the edge

Panels are joined by stitching, and stitching needs material to hold. Every panel therefore carries a seam allowance — a strip along its outline that will be folded under or consumed by the join. Artwork placed there is not printed, or is printed and then hidden.

This converts a design problem into a clipping problem, and the clipping is where the silent failure lives: an out-of-bounds design gets cropped, and cropping is not an error. A drawImage call whose destination rectangle extends past the canvas does not throw, does not warn, and does not return a status. It draws what fits.

I have written about the mask layer specifically elsewhere, but the general lesson is worth stating plainly: in a canvas pipeline, geometry violations are not exceptions. The only way to catch them is to compare the intended area against the safe area yourself, before drawing, and to surface the result to the user as a number or a highlighted region — not as a console message nobody reads.

The practical rule I ended up with: never let the renderer be the first thing that discovers a bounds problem. Validate the placement against the safe area on input, and treat the renderer as an optimiser for a decision already made. This is the same reasoning as validating a form on submit rather than trusting a database constraint to reject it later.

Constraint three: the substrate is not paper

Paper holds ink on the surface. A shoe upper is a textile or a synthetic leather: it absorbs, it stretches over a last, and it moves with the foot. Three things follow, and none of them are visible in a canvas preview:

Colour shifts. Ink on a woven or microfibre surface sits differently than ink on a coated paper. A mid-tone that reads neutral in sRGB can go warm or muddy on a warm-grey substrate. There is no browser API for "how will this CMYK-adjacent stack land on this material" — the material sample is the oracle.

Edges soften. Small type and one-pixel hairlines do not survive the transfer intact. This is not a resolution problem in the usual sense; it is a material problem. Our answer was to stop specifying DPI and start specifying pixels against a measured magnification factor, which is what the second post covers.

The preview can only be honest about the first two constraints. A canvas render can show you cropping and composition truthfully. It cannot show you colour on material or edge softening. Any claim otherwise is a lie dressed up as a feature, so the preview needs to say what it does not model — and that statement belongs on the page, not in a FAQ.

What the constraints cost in pixels

Once the surface is non-developable and the pieces are small, magnification does the budgeting for you. Measured across panels, a single uploaded image is stretched by a factor between roughly 2.9× and 4.8× depending on where the panel sits. Working backwards from a target print resolution gives a hard floor on upload size rather than a preference: around 2,000 px lands near 78% of target, 2,400 px near 98%, and about 2,916 px clears it.

That number is not interesting on its own. It is interesting because it is derivable, and because it can be shown to a user before they upload anything. "Minimum 2,900 pixels on the long edge" is a rule a person can act on. "High resolution required" is not.

The acceptance problem

Put the three constraints together and you get a class of defect that no unit test catches: each panel is individually correct, the composition is wrong. The only reliable check is a human looking at the assembled result.

So the thing I actually shipped for this is not a spec sheet, it is an acceptance surface. There is a page that renders one artwork across the panel set at real proportions, side by side with an assembled preview, so a person can see whether the pattern breaks at a seam or loses its border: panel-preview. It is the same data the customizer uses, presented so that the failure is visible instead of plausible.

The written version of the same reasoning — why an eighteen-panel curved shell is a genuinely different problem from a printed t-shirt, and what that means for what you can promise a customer — is at why shoes are harder than shirts.

What this changes about the build

None of this is exotic graphics programming. It is constraint accounting. The three things I would tell anyone starting a project that maps flat artwork onto a curved, seamed, non-paper object:

  1. Decide the panel data model before the renderer. Outline, safe area and warp are three separate facts. Conflating them produces a renderer that cannot be fixed, only rewritten.
  2. Treat geometry violations as validation, not exceptions. Canvas will happily crop your design out of existence and return success.
  3. Be explicit about what the preview does not model. Colour on substrate and edge softening are outside the browser's knowledge. Say so.

The results, if you want to see whether the constraints are actually being respected rather than just described, are four prints on four different base shoes — a woven geometric, a botanical, a chain motif and a tonal Art Deco fan — each with the full seven-view set on its own page. They are collected at the featured designs gallery; Onyx Deco is the clearest test of the third constraint, because a tonal print with almost no contrast is exactly the case where a colour shift stops being subtle.

And if you want to test the whole pipeline against your own artwork, the customizer is the same one I have been describing: design your own.

The numbers in this post come from measurements on our own panel set, not from a general model. If your panel count, seam allowance or substrate differ, the constants move — the constraints do not.

title: Exploring tenant isolation with Spring Boot, OIDC, and PostgreSQL RLS
description:
A multi-tenant API needs to answer two separate questions: who is making the request, and what may that identity do inside the selected tenant?

Spring Boot SaaS Starter is an open-source backend MVP I maintain to make those boundaries easier to inspect. It provides a Projects API with tenant membership, role checks, optimistic concurrency, and audit records.

The current stack uses Java 25, Spring Boot 4.1.2, PostgreSQL, JDBC, and Flyway. Docker Compose includes Keycloak for local development.

Authentication establishes identity

The API accepts bearer tokens through Spring Security’s JWT resource server support. Its configuration validates the signature and issuer, requires an audience match, and checks for a nonblank subject and an expiration claim.

The subject identifies the caller. Memberships associate that subject with a tenant and a role in the application database.

This distinction matters: a valid token alone does not establish membership in a particular tenant. The tenant UUID in a request selects the tenant to access; authorization still happens in the service layer.

See the implementation in SecurityConfig.java.

Follow the tenant boundary into the database

The starter uses a shared schema with complementary application and database checks:

  1. A transactional service checks and locks the caller’s membership row.
  2. It verifies the role required for the operation.
  3. It sets transaction-local database context for the tenant.
  4. Queries include explicit tenant predicates.
  5. PostgreSQL enforces row-level security on projects and audit events.

TenantAccess.java activates the context using a parameterized query:

SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', ?, true)

The final argument makes the setting local to the transaction. The design therefore avoids leaving tenant state attached to a pooled connection after the transaction finishes.

The database migration enables and forces row-level security on both protected tables. Policies compare each row’s tenant_id with the current transaction’s tenant setting, including checks on writes.

Tenant and membership tables have a different role: they support onboarding and membership discovery across tenants. Their authorization boundary is enforced in services.

The application also uses restricted runtime database credentials, separate from schema migration credentials. Startup checks reject unsafe database privileges or missing RLS enforcement.

These layers help defend against accidentally omitted tenant predicates. They do not make a compromised application or arbitrary SQL execution harmless. The architecture guide explains that boundary explicitly.

Keep permissions specific to each tenant

The role model is deliberately small:

Capability OWNER ADMIN MEMBER
Read projects and list members Yes Yes Yes
Create, update, or delete projects Yes Yes No
Read audit events Yes Yes No
Manage non-owner memberships Yes No No

An authenticated identity can create a tenant and becomes its owner. Ownership transfer and owner removal are outside this MVP.

A caller who is not a tenant member receives 404 for tenant resources. A member who lacks the required role receives 403.

Make conflicting writes explicit

Projects carry a version number. Updates match the tenant, project ID, and expected version, then increment the version. Deletions also require the expected version.

For example, after updating version 0 successfully, a deletion that still supplies version 0 receives 409 Conflict.

The client should reload the project and reconcile changes before retrying. Automatically substituting the latest version would defeat the purpose of detecting a stale write.

Project mutations and their audit records occur within the same transaction. See ProjectService.java and the API walkthrough.

Run the local example

The README’s container-based path requires Git, a POSIX shell, Docker Engine with Compose v2, OpenSSL, and Python 3.9+. On Windows, use WSL with Docker access. Ports 8080, 8081, and 5432 must be available.

A host JDK is unnecessary for this path:

git clone https://github.com/chafian/spring-boot-saas-starter.git
cd spring-boot-saas-starter
./scripts/init-env.sh
docker compose up --build -d
python3 scripts/smoke.py

The setup script generates local credentials. The smoke script waits for readiness, signs in as the demo identities, and exercises the API.

It checks that an outsider cannot access the tenant’s projects, that adding the identity as a MEMBER enables reading, and that the same member still cannot create projects. It also exercises updates, stale-write rejection, deletion, audit events, and requests without authentication.

Successful completion produces:

PASS: real OIDC login, tenant isolation, membership, RBAC, CRUD, conflicts, and audit

Windows/WSL troubleshooting: On my machine, Docker could not bind host port 5432. I changed the PostgreSQL port mapping in compose.yml from 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 to 127.0.0.1:5433:5432, then reran docker compose up -d. The application’s internal database connection remained unchanged, and the smoke test passed.

Each run creates a fictional tenant and retains its audit history. Use docker compose down to stop the services while preserving the database volume.

Keycloak runs in development mode and is ephemeral. Follow the README’s reset guidance if it is recreated, because identity subjects may change.

Test and extend the example

For development, install JDK 25 and unzip, keep Docker running, and use:

./mvnw verify
python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts -p 'test_*.py'

The documented Java verification path uses a real PostgreSQL Testcontainer. CI is configured to run verification and the Compose smoke example.

To add another tenant-owned resource, follow the extension guide and preserve the membership, transaction, tenant-context, and database-policy boundaries.

The current scope excludes billing, a frontend, email invitations, tenant deletion, and ownership transfer. Production deployment also requires environment-specific work such as TLS, production identity configuration, tenant-creation quotas or rate limits, backups, monitoring, and secret management. The local Keycloak setup is a development convenience.

If you work with Java SaaS backends, I’d welcome feedback on the isolation model and the setup experience.

Explore the repository and try the example

title: stageshow skill: How to Make Clean Product UI Demos With Your AI Coding Agent
description:
The stageshow skill is a new add-on for AI coding agents that helps them build "faux UI": simplified product screens, feature cards, bento grids and short cursor animations for landing pages and docs. It was released on 31 October 2026 by designer Benji Taylor, and if you run a small product or make content about software, it's worth a look. This is a research-based walkthrough based on the project's GitHub repo and the author's launch write-up.

What problem it solves

Most small teams need product visuals: a hero animation, a feature card, a "here's how it works" clip. You can ask an AI agent to mock one up, but as the author puts it, the results "often look sloppy and heavy-handed." Stageshow writes down the many small design decisions so the agent can make them too.

The skill is built around one rule from its SKILL.md: "It reads as a real product, simplified to what the viewer needs, framed with intent, and every motion has a cause." It also lists five common failures to avoid: too much detail, a bare wireframe, a whole window "boxed" into a card, a flat layout where nothing stands out, and a bland look that ignores the brief.

How to install it

From your project, run:

npx skills add benjitaylor/skills --skill stageshow

The author says this works with common coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Gemini. Then ask for something small: one interaction, in one product, at one size. The write-up's own example prompt is:

A small looping demo for our homepage hero: someone assigns an issue to a teammate.

The agent reads the skill, starts from the closest example, builds the demo, then films it and fixes what it finds. What you get is an ordinary React component you can drop into your site.

What's inside

  • SKILL.md: the core idea, the failure list and a seven-step workflow (medium and place, look, story, start from an example, and so on).
  • kit/: a small set of React parts (stage, windows, phones) that supports React 18 and later, with no third-party animation runtime.
  • examples/: dozens of "gold" examples, including studies of real products like Figma, Linear, Slack and Raycast.
  • scripts/: film.mjs records a demo and makes a contact sheet so the agent can check its own work, plus checks for one-frame jumps and text that doesn't fit.

There's also a local playground. It needs Node 20.19 or later:

npm install
npm run dev

A practical setup for a small team

  1. Install the skill in the repo where your marketing site lives.
  2. Pick one feature you explain often, like booking, invoicing or a dashboard view.
  3. Ask for a 10 to 16 second loop (the length the skill recommends) at the size it will actually appear.
  4. Ask for a compact phone version too; the skill designs a separate 358px-wide layout rather than squeezing the desktop one.
  5. Review the motion yourself. The README is clear: "No automated clean result replaces watching the motion."

Honest caveats

The author warns it "still may not nail it in one shot," and most demos take a few rounds of feedback. These are illustrations, not automation: a scripted click only draws the cursor pressing. And the repo notes that each skill carries its own licence and third-party asset notices, so check those before using real brand marks.

We cover new AI tools for small businesses and creators in plain English at AI News. If you'd rather have the automation built for you, see AIFix.

title: Secure Amazon S3 Buckets Using IAM Policies and Bucket Policies
description:
Introduction

Amazon S3 is one of the most widely used AWS services, and also one of the most common sources of data leaks. Almost every S3 breach in the news comes down to one thing: a misconfigured access policy.

In this article, I'll explain the two main ways of controlling access to S3, IAM policies and bucket policies, show when to use each, and walk through a hands-on example you can try in your own account.

How S3 Access Is Evaluated

Before writing any policy, it helps to know how AWS decides whether a request is allowed:

Everything is denied by default.
An explicit Allow in a relevant policy grants access.
An explicit Deny always wins, no matter what else says Allow.
For requests within the same account, access is granted if either the IAM policy or the bucket policy allows it (and nothing denies it).

Remember this rule: Explicit Deny > Allow > Default Deny.

IAM Policies vs Bucket Policies
Feature IAM Policy Bucket Policy
Attached to IAM user, group, or role The S3 bucket
Answers the question "What can this identity do?" "Who can access this bucket?"
Has a Principal element No Yes
Cross-account access Needs help from the other side Supported directly
Best for Managing permissions for your users and roles Bucket-wide rules, cross-account access, enforcing conditions
Size limit 2 KB (users), 6 KB (groups), 10 KB (roles) 20 KB

Simple way to remember it:

IAM policy = identity-based ("what can I do?")
Bucket policy = resource-based ("who can touch this bucket?")
Hands-On: Secure a Bucket Step by Step
Step 1: Create a Private Bucket
Open the S3 console and choose Create bucket.
Give it a unique name, for example vishal-secure-demo-bucket.
Keep Block all public access turned ON.
Enable Bucket Versioning.
Enable Default encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS).
Choose Create bucket.

Tip: Block Public Access is your first line of defense. Leave it on unless you have a very specific reason to turn it off.

Step 2: Create an IAM Policy (Least Privilege)

Let's give a user read and write access to only one bucket, nothing more.

json
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "ListBucket",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": "s3:ListBucket",
"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket"
},
{
"Sid": "ReadWriteObjects",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": [
"s3:GetObject",
"s3:PutObject"
],
"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket/*"
}
]
}

Why two statements? s3:ListBucket applies to the bucket itself, while GetObject and PutObject apply to the objects inside it (/*). This is a very common mistake for beginners.

To apply it:

Go to IAM → Policies → Create policy → JSON and paste the policy.
Name it S3-DemoBucket-ReadWrite.
Attach it to a user, group, or (better) a role.
Step 3: Add a Bucket Policy to Enforce HTTPS

Now let's add a rule at the bucket level. This policy denies any request that doesn't use HTTPS:

json
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "DenyInsecureTransport",
"Effect": "Deny",
"Principal": "",
"Action": "s3:",
"Resource": [
"arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket",
"arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket/*"
],
"Condition": {
"Bool": {
"aws:SecureTransport": "false"
}
}
}
]
}

To apply it: S3 → your bucket → Permissions → Bucket policy → Edit → paste → Save.

Step 4: Restrict Access to a Specific IAM Role

You can also lock the bucket so that only one role can access it. Replace the account ID and role name with your own:

json
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "AllowOnlyAppRole",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Principal": {
"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/AppServerRole"
},
"Action": [
"s3:GetObject",
"s3:PutObject"
],
"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket/*"
}
]
}

This is useful when an EC2 instance or Lambda function needs access to the bucket. Use roles instead of long-term access keys.

Step 5: Require Encryption on Upload

This policy blocks any upload that isn't encrypted with SSE-KMS:

json
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "DenyUnencryptedUploads",
"Effect": "Deny",
"Principal": "",
"Action": "s3:PutObject",
"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket/",
"Condition": {
"StringNotEquals": {
"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption": "aws:kms"
}
}
}
]
}
Step 6: Test Your Setup
Try uploading a file with the IAM user: it should succeed.
Try accessing the bucket over plain HTTP: it should be denied.
Try accessing the bucket with a different user that has no permissions: you should see Access Denied.
Use the IAM Policy Simulator or IAM Access Analyzer to validate your policies.
S3 Security Best Practices
Enable Block Public Access at both the bucket and account level.
Follow least privilege. Grant only the actions and resources that are needed.
Use IAM roles, not long-term access keys.
Enforce HTTPS with aws:SecureTransport.
Encrypt data at rest (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS).
Enable versioning and consider MFA Delete for critical data.
Turn on logging with S3 server access logs and CloudTrail data events.
Use IAM Access Analyzer to find buckets shared outside your account.
Avoid "Principal": "" with Allow unless you really mean public access.
Review policies regularly and remove permissions that are no longer used.
Common Mistakes to Avoid
Using "Action": "s3:" and "Resource": "" in IAM policies.
Forgetting the / on the resource ARN for object-level actions.
Making a bucket public "temporarily" and forgetting about it.
Hardcoding access keys in application code.
Not testing policies before applying them in production.
Conclusion

Securing S3 isn't about picking IAM policies or bucket policies. The strongest setups use both:

IAM policies control what your users and roles can do.
Bucket policies enforce rules at the bucket itself, like HTTPS-only access, encryption, and cross-account permissions.
Block Public Access, encryption, and logging add extra layers of protection.

Start with least privilege, test your policies, and review them regularly. Your data will be much safer for it.

dev.to: @vishal_patil_aws
