title: Case Converter: Batch-Renaming PascalCase React Components to kebab-case Without Breaking Imports
description:
Last Tuesday we agreed on a file naming rule. Components move to kebab-case, so ChatWidget.tsx becomes chat-widget.tsx, and the old PascalCase files disappear.

The trigger was mundane. Two teammates on macOS kept hitting broken checkouts because DateRange.tsx and daterange.tsx are two files in CI on Linux, but a single file on their laptops. Same repo, two views of it.

Eleven components. Sounds like one slow afternoon.

I spent most of that afternoon on three problems that have nothing to do with converting case: imports pointing at old paths, Git refusing to notice half my renames, and XMLHttpRequestPanel.tsx coming out of my first script as xmlhttprequestpanel.tsx.

Here is what worked, in Python 3.11.1 and Node v22.13.1, plus the shortcut for small batches.

Method 1: a Python 3.11.1 script that keeps Git history

Plain mv loses the fact that a rename happened. git mv keeps it. My script runs git mv per file, then rewrites every import that points at an old name.

import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

SPLITTER = re.compile(r"(?<=[a-z0-9])(?=[A-Z])|(?<=[A-Z])(?=[A-Z][a-z])")

# Digits next to acronyms: the splitter cannot guess these.
OVERRIDES = {
    "UserAvatar2FA": "user-avatar-2fa",
    "OAuth2Callback": "oauth2-callback",
}

root = Path(sys.argv[1])
plan = {}
for src in sorted(root.glob("*.tsx")):
    target = root / f"{OVERRIDES.get(src.stem) or '-'.join(p.lower() for p in SPLITTER.split(src.stem))}.tsx"
    if target.name != src.name:
        plan[src] = target

for src, dst in plan.items():
    subprocess.run(["git", "mv", str(src), str(dst)], check=True)
    print(f"{src.name:26} -> {dst.name}")

edited = 0
for path in root.glob("*.tsx"):
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    for old, new in ((s.stem, d.stem) for s, d in plan.items()):
        text = re.sub(rf"([./]){old}(?=\")", rf"\g<1>{new}", text)
    if text != path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"):
        path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
        edited += 1

print(f"\nrenamed {len(plan)} files, rewrote imports in {edited} files")

Run it against the component folder, then check that nothing still refers to the old paths.

$ python3 rename_components.py src
ChatWidget.tsx             -> chat-widget.tsx
DateRange.tsx              -> date-range.tsx
Grid2Col.tsx               -> grid2-col.tsx
HTTPClientErrors.tsx       -> http-client-errors.tsx
InvoiceLineItemV2.tsx      -> invoice-line-item-v2.tsx
OAuth2Callback.tsx         -> oauth2-callback.tsx
PDFViewer.tsx              -> pdf-viewer.tsx
SideNavBar.tsx             -> side-nav-bar.tsx
UserAvatar2FA.tsx          -> user-avatar-2fa.tsx
Utils.tsx                  -> utils.tsx
XMLHttpRequestPanel.tsx    -> xml-http-request-panel.tsx

renamed 11 files, rewrote imports in 11 files

$ grep -rn 'from "./[A-Z]' src/*.tsx || echo "(none)"
(none)

Every import got rewritten, so the grep comes back clean, and git mv keeps the batch as 11 renames rather than 11 deletions plus 11 untracked files.

The splitter does the real work. (?<=[a-z0-9])(?=[A-Z]) cuts between a lowercase letter or digit and an uppercase one. (?<=[A-Z])(?=[A-Z][a-z]) cuts before the last capital of an acronym run, which is what turns XMLHttp into XML-Http. Both are zero-width assertions, documented in the Python re reference.

Two names refuse to cooperate. UserAvatar2FA splits into user-avatar2-fa and OAuth2Callback into o-auth2-callback, because the digit rule cannot tell whether a digit attaches forward (2FA) or backward (OAuth2). I gave up on solving that inside the regex and pinned both names in OVERRIDES.

Method 2: the same batch rename in Node v22.13.1

No Python on the machine? The logic ports over directly.

import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";
import { readdirSync, readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";

const root = process.argv[2] ?? "src";
const OVERRIDES = new Map([
  ["UserAvatar2FA", "user-avatar-2fa"],
  ["OAuth2Callback", "oauth2-callback"],
]);
const SPLIT = /(?<=[a-z0-9])(?=[A-Z])|(?<=[A-Z])(?=[A-Z][a-z])/;
const toKebab = (stem) =>
  OVERRIDES.get(stem) ?? stem.split(SPLIT).map((p) => p.toLowerCase()).join("-");

const candidates = readdirSync(root, { encoding: "utf8" })
  .filter((name) => name.endsWith(".tsx"))
  .sort();

const mapping = new Map();
for (const name of candidates) {
  const stem = name.slice(0, -4);
  const target = `${toKebab(stem)}.tsx`;
  if (target === name) continue;
  execFileSync("git", ["mv", path.join(root, name), path.join(root, target)]);
  mapping.set(stem, target.slice(0, -4));
  console.log(`${name.padEnd(26)} -> ${target}`);
}

let edited = 0;
for (const name of readdirSync(root, { encoding: "utf8" })) {
  if (!name.endsWith(".tsx")) continue;
  const file = path.join(root, name);
  const before = readFileSync(file, "utf8");
  let after = before;
  for (const [from, to] of mapping) {
    after = after.replaceAll(new RegExp(`([./])${from}(?=")`, "g"), `$1${to}`);
  }
  if (after !== before) {
    writeFileSync(file, after);
    edited += 1;
  }
}

console.log(`\nrenamed ${mapping.size} files, rewrote imports in ${edited} files`);

String.prototype.split accepts lookbehind in V8, so both assertions work unchanged (MDN covers the lookbehind syntax). The output matched Python line for line: 11 renames, 11 files rewritten, zero leftover imports.

Spot-check the odd names against the Utilvy case converter before trusting either script. If it disagrees with your expectation, the script is usually the wrong one.

Method 3: convert names in a browser tab

Two or three files? Skip the script entirely. Paste the component names into a free case converter, pick kebab-case, copy the result, and pair them up by hand.

It handles whole lists in one paste, so ten names are no slower than one. It runs locally in the tab, which matters on an unreleased branch.

Above a handful of files, go back to a script. The browser gives you the new names, but someone still has to rewrite eleven import blocks, and a web page cannot do that part.

Three things that cost me the afternoon

Straight lowercasing destroys acronym boundaries

My very first line was this:

>>> "XMLHttpRequestPanel".lower()
'xmlhttprequestpanel'

Same for HTTPClientErrors turning into httpclienterrors and PDFViewer into pdfviewer. Every word boundary vanishes, and there is no way back from a flattened string. This browser-based tool keeps those boundaries intact, which makes it a decent oracle when you want to argue with your own regex. Split first, lowercase second.

Renaming the file is only half the job, and the failure is silent

My first rewrite used a guard I thought was clever:

text = re.sub(rf'(?<!/){old}(?=")', new, text)

Every import path in a TypeScript file starts with ./. The guard rejected all of them, and the script printed:

renamed 11 files, rewrote imports in 0 files

Eleven renames, zero rewrites, exit code 0. Nothing broke visibly until the next build. Use a capture group instead of a lookbehind, then grep for from "./[A-Z] before you commit.

Case-insensitive filesystems hide case-only renames

Utils.tsx to utils.tsx changes nothing but case. Fine on Linux, invisible on macOS and Windows, where Git is configured with core.ignorecase. Here is the reproduction on an ext4 disk:

$ git config core.ignorecase true
$ mv Utils.tsx utils.tsx
$ git status --short
 D Utils.tsx

Only a deletion. git ls-files still lists Utils.tsx, while import Utils from "./utils" points at a file Git no longer tracks. Flip the flag and Git sees both halves:

$ git config core.ignorecase false
$ git status --short
 D Utils.tsx
?? utils.tsx

On macOS, step through a temp name: git mv Utils.tsx tmp-utils.tsx && git mv tmp-utils.tsx utils.tsx. Or do the whole batch in CI where the filesystem takes casing seriously.

Pick your approach

Scenario Approach Handled 11 files in
Whole repo to migrate Python 3.11.1 script + git mv one run, imports rewritten
Python unavailable Node v22.13.1 equivalent one run, identical output
Two or three names Browser-based kebab conversion under a minute

Verify in this order: grep for leftover PascalCase imports, then read git status on a case-sensitive filesystem, then commit.

More free browser-based utilities at utilvy.com

title: Make AI API Operations Idempotent
description:
Disclosure: I work on Modelflare, an OpenAI-compatible AI API gateway. The canonical version of this article lives on modelflare.dev.

Make AI API Operations Idempotent: a production guide with an explicit decision, reusable artifact, failure tests, operating signals, and source-qualified limits.

The operating rule

Make AI API Operations Idempotent should be implemented as a reliability control contract, not as a one-off configuration. Freeze the protocol, ownership, evidence, and rollback condition before traffic moves. The concrete control points in this guide are logical_request_id, idempotency_key, request_digest, durable_result.

Make side-effecting AI operations idempotent at the application boundary. Bind a caller-supplied idempotency key to one authenticated principal, operation, and canonical request digest; reserve the operation atomically; persist terminal success or failure; and return the same durable result on replay. Model call IDs are correlation data, not a substitute for this ledger.

Draw the failure boundary first

Separate the reader-facing task from the control-plane work behind it. Client setup owns the local file or environment variable; the gateway owns authentication, routing, limits, accounting, and attempt records; the provider owns its native protocol and volatile capability contract. A passing text prompt proves only that one path worked once.

Reliability controls must be defined on attempts and terminal states, not on a vague notion of a request “working.” Preserve the caller deadline, distinguish overload from permanent errors, and make rejection, cancellation, retry, fallback, and settlement observable as separate outcomes.

The owner record for this page is ai-api-idempotency; its frozen controls are logical_request_id, idempotency_key, request_digest, durable_result. Every value is reviewed at the wire or durable-state boundary and never inferred from a marketing label.

State and control contract: Make AI API Operations Idempotent

Use the following review record as the deployable artifact. Technical values are intentionally explicit so a reviewer can compare configuration, wire evidence, and durable state without relying on a screenshot or a successful-looking outer response.

Control point Fixed decision Evidence to retain
key_scope principal_plus_operation_plus_idempotency_key principal_id + operation + key
request_binding canonical_digest_must_match request_digest + schema_version
reservation atomic_pending_record_before_side_effect unique_constraint + created_at + owner
replay same_key_same_digest_returns_durable_result original_result_id + replay_count
conflict same_key_different_digest_rejected conflict_status + both_digests_without_payload
recovery stale_pending_requires_owned_reconciliation lease + side_effect_receipt + terminal_write

Exercise the critical transition

The example uses placeholders and deterministic inputs. Replace identifiers with reviewed values, never with credentials or customer content. Preserve the exact configuration snapshot alongside the probe result.

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO operation_ledger
  (principal_id, operation, idempotency_key, request_digest, status)
VALUES
  (:principal, :operation, :key, :digest, 'pending')
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
-- only the transaction that owns the new row may perform the side effect
-- persist terminal result before returning it to the caller
COMMIT;

Verify behavior under failure

Run the ladder in order. A later check cannot compensate for a missing earlier boundary, and every attempt must remain attributable to one logical request.

  1. Freeze the current client, gateway policy, model alias, route set, and observable baseline. Evidence record for key_scope: enforce principal_plus_operation_plus_idempotency_key and retain principal_id + operation + key.
  2. Run one deterministic positive probe and capture the client-visible response, request ID, selected route, terminal state, and usage. Evidence record for request_binding: enforce canonical_digest_must_match and retain request_digest + schema_version.
  3. Run the paired negative, limit, or disconnect case and verify that it fails in the intended layer. Evidence record for reservation: enforce atomic_pending_record_before_side_effect and retain unique_constraint + created_at + owner.
  4. Repeat the probe through the actual protocol surface; do not infer native support from a neighboring compatibility endpoint. Evidence record for replay: enforce same_key_same_digest_returns_durable_result and retain original_result_id + replay_count.
  5. Roll out to a bounded cohort with an explicit owner, expiry time, stop threshold, and prepared rollback. Evidence record for conflict: enforce same_key_different_digest_rejected and retain conflict_status + both_digests_without_payload.
  6. Re-read durable configuration and accounting after the test, then remove temporary access or test data. Evidence record for recovery: enforce stale_pending_requires_owned_reconciliation and retain lease + side_effect_receipt + terminal_write.

Failure amplification to prevent

Treat each item below as a release blocker. A 200 response, attractive dashboard, or single successful demo does not override these failure conditions.

  • memory_only_deduplication — Process memory cannot protect retries after restart, failover, or concurrent execution on another node.
  • key_without_digest — Reusing a key for a different payload can return the wrong result or hide a caller bug.
  • check_then_act_race — Reading for an existing record and writing later allows two workers to perform the same side effect.
  • model_call_id_as_key — A model-generated call ID may change across retries and does not define the authenticated business operation.

Trip signals, denominators, and stop conditions

Monitor success and harm together. The threshold is a policy input, not a universal benchmark; choose it from the workload SLO and record the denominator before the observation window begins.

Signal Decision threshold Action
duplicate_side_effect_count 0 stop_operation_and_reconcile
idempotency_digest_conflicts review_each_event reject_and_alert_owner
stale_pending_age <_owned_recovery_deadline reconcile_with_external_receipt
replay_result_mismatch 0 disable_endpoint

Modelflare boundary and limitations

Modelflare can centralize OpenAI-compatible and native-protocol routing, scoped keys, groups, usage records, and failure handling. A configured channel is not proof that every optional field, model alias, retention promise, region, or fallback is supported. Verify the selected route with its native protocol, preserve explicit zero values, and use the final durable settlement as billing truth.

Idempotency does not mean every model generation becomes identical. It means the protected business operation has one durable outcome for the same authenticated request. Read-only generation may be retried under a budget, while payments, messages, database mutations, and tool actions need operation-specific keys and reconciliation.

Continue through the topic cluster

Use the linked parent for the broader decision, the sibling for the next implementation step, and the documentation route for current client configuration. These body links are deliberate because managed CMS articles do not currently carry a separate related-slug field.

  • Parent decision guide
  • Next implementation guide
  • Current setup documentation

Frequently asked questions

Is an HTTP POST automatically non-idempotent?

HTTP method semantics and application idempotency are related but different; the ledger defines replay behavior for the business operation.

Can the gateway invent the key?

The layer that understands the business operation should define it. A gateway request ID alone may not identify the user-visible side effect.

How are stale pending rows handled?

Use an owned recovery lease and external receipt lookup; never blindly repeat the side effect.

Sources and verification date

Sources were checked on 2026-08-07. They establish external contracts and engineering principles; they do not prove an untested route or future provider state.

  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
  • OpenAI API reference: request IDs
  • OWASP: Transaction Authorization Cheat Sheet

Originally published at modelflare.dev. Current models and prices: modelflare.dev/pricing · Docs: docs.modelflare.dev.

title: I wanted Copier in Rust, so I wrote rootstock
description:
I write Rust for a living, and over the last couple of years the tools around me quietly turned into Rust too. On the frontend, Biome does what ESLint and Prettier used to. In Python land it's Ruff and uv. They're fast, they ship as one binary, and there's nothing to set up besides the binary itself.

Project templates were the exception. The best tool I know for them is Copier, and it's genuinely good. But it's Python, so every machine and every CI job that touches a template needs Python and pipx first. I wanted the same thing as one binary. That's rootstock.

Creating a project is the easy part

Plenty of tools can create a project from a template: cargo-generate, kickstart, cookiecutter. They render the files and that's it. From then on the project and the template live separate lives.

That's fine for a one-off. It hurts when the template keeps changing. Think shared CI workflows, lint configs, a service skeleton your team uses everywhere. Someone fixes the CI in the template, and now there are twenty projects with the old version, each with its own local edits. Copying the fix by hand gets old fast.

Copier's answer is to remember how the project was made and replay the template's changes on top of it. rootstock does the same.

What an update looks like

rootstock new renders the template and writes a small record, .rootstock.toml, next to your files: the template source, the tag and exact commit, your answers, and the list of files it wrote.

$ rootstock new gh:acme/service-template my-app --data project_name=my-app --defaults
created my-app from gh:acme/service-template v1.0.0

Later the template ships v1.1.0. It bumps actions/checkout in CI and adds --all-targets to the test and lint targets in the Makefile. Meanwhile you've added a fmt target and made clippy stricter.

$ rootstock update
updated to v1.1.0
markers Makefile
1 conflict

The CI bump and the new test line went in on their own. Your fmt target is still there. The one line you both changed is marked:

lint:
<<<<<<< project
    cargo clippy -- -D warnings
=======
    cargo clippy --all-targets
>>>>>>> template v1.1.0

You fix it, run rootstock check, commit. The update is a plain diff in git, so it's easy to review and easy to throw away.

How the merge works

Under the hood rootstock renders the template twice in temp directories: the old version with the answers from the record (the base), and the new version with the current answers (the target). Then it goes path by path and compares base, target and what's in your project.

If only the template changed a file, you get the template's version. If only you changed it, nothing happens. If both did, the text goes through git merge-file, which is what Copier uses too. I picked the git CLI over a merge library on purpose: the result matches Copier, the markers look like the ones everyone already knows, and your own git config doesn't leak into it.

Some cases can't be merged at all, and rootstock doesn't pretend they can. A binary file you edited keeps your copy and gets the template's version next to it as name.rootstock-new. A file you deleted but the template changed stays deleted and gets reported. Files marked as starter (a README, say) are written once and never touched again.

Want to change an answer later? rootstock update --data ci=false renders the base with the old answers and the target with the new ones, even when the version stays the same.

Conflicts are an exit code

Every case that needs a human ends with exit code 2 and one line per problem on stdout: markers Makefile, binary logo.png and so on. Everything else goes to stderr.

That makes it easy to automate. My harness template (agent tooling, hooks and CI for my projects) has a daily workflow in each project that runs rootstock update, opens a PR and labels it when the exit code is 2. Clean minor and patch updates merge themselves once CI is green. The conflicting ones wait for me.

rootstock check runs in CI without network access and fails on leftover markers or side files, so a half-resolved conflict can't slip into main.

Coming from Copier

rootstock import-copier converts a Copier template, a project generated by Copier, or both if they live in the same directory. It writes nothing unless the whole conversion succeeds. Old template tags don't need converting – update reads versions that only have copier.yml and converts them in memory.

For harness I checked that the converted template renders byte for byte like Copier 9.19 for every combination of its answers. That was my bar for calling the import done.

What it doesn't do (yet)

rootstock supports the part of Copier my templates use. _migrations, Jinja extensions and some question types aren't there, and the import stops with the full list if your template needs them. It's v0.1.0, so expect rough edges.

Try it 

cargo install rootstock --locked

There are also prebuilt binaries for Linux (static, musl), macOS and Windows on GitHub Releases. The only thing it needs at runtime is git.

If you maintain templates and something here doesn't fit how you work, open an issue. I'd like to hear about it.

bodasooqa / rootstock

Create projects from versioned git templates and update them by three-way merge, without losing the project's edits. A single Rust binary, like Copier.

Project templates that keep growing after you use them.

Create a project from a versioned git template, then update it to every new template version
with a real three-way merge: your edits stay, the template's improvements arrive, conflicts are never silent.

Website · Install · Quick start · How updates work · Commands · Writing a template · Coming from Copier

In grafting, the rootstock is the root system, and the scion is the branch grafted onto it. The scion grows its own way, and the root keeps feeding it. A rootstock project works the same way. The template is the root and the project is the scion: the project goes its own way, and improvements to the template keep reaching it.

Why rootstock

Most scaffolding tools stop once the project is created. That is fine for a one-off, but not for a template that keeps changing: shared CI, lint…

title: Your AI Portal Is Live. Why Do Users Still Get Lost?
description:
A white-label AI portal can be technically online and still feel completely unusable.

That is the awkward gap many teams discover after launch. The domain resolves, the dashboard opens, and the models respond, yet new visitors hesitate. They cannot tell what the product is for, which tool to try, whether the price is predictable, or who will help when something breaks.

The usual reaction is to add more: more navigation items, more models, a louder hero banner, and a longer feature list. That often makes the problem worse. A portal does not earn trust by showing everything it can possibly do. It earns trust by helping a visitor complete one useful task without getting lost.

Treat the homepage like the start of a journey

Before changing colors or uploading a logo, open the site in a private browser window and pretend you know nothing about it.

Within a few seconds, the page should answer three ordinary questions:

  • What can I make here?
  • Where should I begin?
  • What will it cost me?

That does not require a grand slogan. A sentence such as “Create product images and short campaign videos from a prompt” is much more helpful than a vague promise about transforming creativity.

The same principle applies to navigation. A catalog of every available capability may impress the person who configured the site, but it gives a first-time user too many decisions. Put the main workflow first. If the portal is built for marketing teams, image creation, copy generation, and video production probably deserve the most visible positions. Secondary tools can remain available without competing for attention on the opening screen.

A useful test is to ask someone unfamiliar with the project to find the primary feature while sharing their screen. Do not guide them. The pause before their first click is valuable product research.

Branding is mostly consistency

A memorable name and a crisp logo help, but branding falls apart when the details disagree. The browser title uses one name, the login page uses another, and the support documentation points to a third domain. Each mismatch creates a small reason to distrust the site.

Keep the logo simple enough to survive at favicon size. Check it on both light and dark backgrounds, and inspect the mobile header instead of relying on the admin preview. A wide logo with tiny lettering may look fine in the source file and become unreadable once the interface scales it down.

The hero image deserves the same restraint. It should reinforce one job the visitor can perform, not carry the entire business plan. Text baked into an image is especially fragile because responsive layouts may crop it. Important claims and calls to action are safer as real page text.

Login is part of the product, not an admin setting

Authentication is often configured from the administrator's point of view: enable a provider, save the form, and move on. Users experience a longer chain. They click, leave the site for an identity provider, return, and expect to land somewhere sensible.

Test that whole chain while signed out. Try it on a phone. Check what happens after a cancelled login and whether an error offers a practical next step. The best default method is usually the one the target audience already uses, but convenience only matters if the redirect and return path work reliably.

It is also worth checking the first minute after registration. A successful login that drops a new user into an empty, unexplained dashboard is technically correct and emotionally disappointing. A short starter prompt, a sample project, or a direct link to the main tool can make the first session feel intentional.

A custom domain needs an end-to-end check

Adding a domain in an admin panel is only half the work. DNS still has to direct that hostname to the service, and HTTPS has to work once the record propagates.

For an Ace Data Cloud subsite, the documented CNAME target is platform-proxy.acedata.cloud. A typical record for ai.example.com would look like this:

Type:   CNAME
Name:   ai
Target: platform-proxy.acedata.cloud

Before adding it, look for an existing A, AAAA, or CNAME record using the same hostname. Conflicting records can produce confusing results that appear to work for one person and fail for another because of resolver caches.

You can inspect the public result from a terminal:

dig ai.example.com CNAME +short
curl -I https://ai.example.com

Do not stop when dig returns an answer. Open the actual URL, verify that it reaches the correct tenant, and check that the browser reports a valid certificate. Repeat the test away from the network where the site was configured if possible. DNS propagation and local caching have a habit of making the administrator's laptop look healthier than the rest of the internet.

Pricing copy should remove surprises

A pricing table is not clear simply because it contains numbers. Users need to know what the unit represents. A price per generated image, per second of video, per request, and per bundle of credits are not interchangeable.

Work backward from a realistic task. If someone wants a ten-second clip, what is the likely total rather than the smallest unit price? If retries consume credits, say so. If quality or resolution changes the cost, show that relationship close to the selector.

This is also where sustainable operation matters. Pricing below the underlying cost may attract early usage, but it turns every successful customer into a larger problem. Pricing far above it without explaining support, curation, or convenience creates a different trust problem. The interface should make both the unit and the value understandable before the user clicks generate.

Documentation should follow the moment of confusion

Most users do not read a manual from beginning to end. They look for help when something interrupts them. Good documentation mirrors those moments:

  • signing in for the first time
  • choosing the right tool
  • understanding credits and charges
  • improving a weak result
  • reporting a failed task

A short answer with the exact interface label and a current screenshot is often better than a long tour of every feature. Support conversations are an excellent backlog for documentation. When the same question appears twice, turn the answer into a page and link to it from the place where the confusion happens.

Privacy information deserves the same practical treatment. Describe what the site actually collects, which third-party services are involved, how long relevant data is kept, and how a user can ask for help. Copying another company's policy without adapting names, contacts, and data flows is worse than having a shorter policy that reflects reality.

Launch with a small acceptance script

The final review should not happen inside the admin session. Log out and walk through the product as a stranger. Then do it again on a narrow mobile screen.

A lightweight launch script can be written in plain language:

Open the homepage from the public domain.
Understand the main use case without opening a menu.
Create a new account with the default login method.
Find the primary tool and run a small task.
See the price or credit impact before and after the task.
Open help from the point where a beginner would hesitate.
Find a real support contact and the privacy terms.
Repeat the critical path on mobile.

This is not a one-time ceremony. Run the same path after changing authentication, navigation, pricing, or DNS. It catches the kind of breakage that monitoring dashboards often miss because every individual service can be healthy while the user journey is broken.

The strongest portal is rarely the one with the most crowded homepage. It is the one that feels obvious. A visitor arrives, understands the promise, trusts the domain, signs in without friction, predicts the cost, and finishes a useful task. Once that path works, adding more capability becomes an improvement instead of another layer of confusion.

Reference

Original Ace Data Cloud guide

title: Node.js Example OpenAI GPT API Integration for Product Text Summarization
description:
The hard part of using a Node.js example to integrate the OpenAI GPT API for text summarization is not producing one short paragraph. It is keeping the catalog pipeline portable when a provider changes its client library, authentication model, or output behavior. My default is to isolate summarization behind a small adapter, use a chat-completion interface for the first useful result, and keep the input contract provider-neutral.

For a team already standardized on OpenAI, the direct OpenAI API is the shortest path. For a team testing several vendors, Infrai is a reasonable integration layer to try because its public discovery surface exposes schemas and runnable examples before a key is required. That matters when adding a capability should involve inspecting one contract rather than learning another SDK. It is a fit for the adapter boundary, not a reason to pretend every model is interchangeable.

What does portability require in a catalog pipeline?

Start with the data boundary. A catalog record should hand the model a bounded description and a precise instruction: preserve factual attributes, remove sales language, and return a concise summary. The application should own truncation or chunking for long descriptions; letting an SDK silently decide what to drop makes later provider comparisons hard to interpret.

The output should be treated as generated text, not as the source of truth for price, dimensions, or compliance claims. Store the original description beside the summary, record the provider and model selected, and validate the result before publishing it. This is more operational work than calling a model once. It is also what makes a migration measurable.

The useful first test is deliberately small: one record, one bounded prompt, one summary, and a saved request identifier. I initially thought the provider choice would dominate the design. The adapter contract does. If the rest of the catalog service knows a vendor-specific message shape, portability has already been lost.

Keep it boring.

The first failure mode I test is silent truncation: a 12,000-character bound can remove a specification table, while a 45-word output limit can hide a required attribute. I keep those numbers in application configuration, preserve the original description, and compare a direct result with a chunked result before changing providers. That is a concrete boundary, not a benchmark claim.

Which integration path reaches a useful summary fastest?

Option Credentials and setup SDK surface Boundary
OpenAI API One OpenAI API key and the OpenAI client pattern A focused chat-completion call Best when the catalog team already owns this provider and wants the fewest moving parts
Anthropic API A separate provider credential and its messages-oriented client pattern A different request and response contract Good for teams willing to maintain a second adapter and evaluate its output separately
Google Vertex AI Google Cloud project and platform authentication Cloud-platform configuration plus model invocation Useful when identity, governance, and deployment already live in Google Cloud
Infrai One Infrai key for the unified surface A plain REST surface with public discovery and runnable examples Useful when provider portability and capability discovery outweigh direct-vendor simplicity

These are different operational choices, not four interchangeable model names. Direct OpenAI has the cleanest match to the question this article starts from: authenticate with an OpenAI key, instruct a chat model to summarize, and tune temperature and max_tokens. Anthropic and Vertex AI are credible alternatives, but each adds a distinct credential or client contract that the adapter must absorb. Infrai reduces that particular discovery friction across a broad surface: its live discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules, with schemas and runnable examples exposed per capability.

The trade-off is worth stating plainly. A unified layer adds one more boundary to understand, and a direct provider may be preferable when a team needs provider-specific controls or the specialist's native feature set. Portability is valuable only if the boundary preserves the controls the workload actually needs.

How should a Node.js service integrate OpenAI GPT API text summarization?

The following example keeps the provider-specific work in one function. A Node.js service can use axios or the openai npm package against the same contract; this Python sample keeps the HTTP method, URL, headers, status handling, and retry behavior visible. The model name is a configuration choice; do not treat it as a promise that every model has identical context or output behavior.

import os
import random
import time

import requests


def summarize_description(description: str) -> str:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    bounded_description = description[:12000]
    prompt = (
        "Summarize this product description in 45 words or fewer. "
        "Keep factual product attributes, remove promotional claims, and "
        "do not invent missing information.\n\n"
        f"Product description:\n{bounded_description}"
    )

    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            response = requests.post(
                "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/chat/completions",
                headers={
                    "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                    "Content-Type": "application/json",
                },
                json={
                    "model": "deepseek-v4.1-flash",
                    "messages": [
                        {
                            "role": "system",
                            "content": "You produce factual e-commerce catalog summaries.",
                        },
                        {"role": "user", "content": prompt},
                    ],
                    "temperature": 0.2,
                    "max_tokens": 180,
                },
                timeout=60,
            )
            if response.status_code == 429:
                if attempt == 3:
                    response.raise_for_status()
                retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
                delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
                time.sleep(delay + random.random())
                continue
            if not response.ok:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"Summarization failed with HTTP {response.status_code}: "
                    f"{response.text}"
                )
            content = response.json().get("choices", [{}])[0].get("message", {}).get("content")
            if not content:
                raise RuntimeError("The provider returned no summary text")
            return content.strip()
        except requests.RequestException as error:
            if attempt == 3:
                raise
            time.sleep((2**attempt) + random.random())

    raise RuntimeError("Summarization retry loop ended unexpectedly")

This is intentionally not a bulk-ingestion worker. For long descriptions, split on meaningful boundaries, summarize chunks, then summarize the chunk summaries; otherwise a truncation rule can silently remove the specifications that customers care about. For a large catalog, queue the records, make the consumer idempotent, and retain the original input so a prompt or provider change can be replayed.

Where does the unified layer help, and where does it stop?

The strongest argument for the unified layer here is integration friction. Its API is self-describing, and the discovery result includes request schemas, response schemas, billing metadata, and runnable examples. That lets an engineer inspect a capability before installing a vendor SDK. The supporting benefit is a consistent credential and REST boundary while the catalog service experiments with providers, instead of distributing provider keys and client conventions through every worker.

I would recommend Infrai to a catalog team that expects to test multiple AI providers and wants discovery plus a runnable request to be part of the integration workflow. I would choose direct OpenAI for a single-provider implementation whose main requirement is the OpenAI chat-completion contract, and I would choose a specialist when its native controls or model behavior are a hard requirement.

The capability boundary also matters. Audio transcription is listed but currently unavailable; real-time voice session keys are pending and limited to the western region; there is no dedicated moderation endpoint, so text or image moderation needs a chat model with a JSON schema fallback; and image upscaling is limited to Lanczos. None of those blocks catalog summarization, but they are reasons to keep capability selection explicit instead of assuming the unified surface covers every adjacent workload.

A controlled rollout is the portability test

Begin with a small evaluation set containing short descriptions, long descriptions, missing attributes, and aggressively promotional copy. Compare summaries for factual retention, length, and unacceptable invention. Keep the prompt stable while changing providers; otherwise a provider result and a prompt change become one indistinguishable experiment.

Then ship the adapter behind a feature flag. Record the chosen provider, model, latency, and failure class, but do not publish generated text before validation. A 429 should delay and retry; a malformed or empty response should be visible as a failed record, not converted into a blank catalog field. The operational detail is unglamorous. It is also where portability either survives or disappears.

For one product record, that means retaining the raw description, the normalized prompt version, the provider name, the model name, the response text, and the validation result as separate fields. If the response is too short, contains a missing required attribute, or arrives after a retry, the worker should preserve the response and mark the record for review rather than overwrite the last accepted summary. If a provider is unavailable, the adapter can route the next attempt according to an explicit policy, but the policy must be visible in the record so a later comparison does not confuse provider selection with prompt quality. I would also keep the chunking decision beside the input: a single bounded request and a multi-chunk reduction are different transformations, even when they produce similar prose. That small amount of bookkeeping is the difference between a portable pipeline and a collection of irreproducible calls.

If this boundary matches your system, start with the capability manifest and inspect the available contract before wiring the worker.

References

  • OpenAI Batch API guide
  • OpenAI API documentation
  • Anthropic Messages API
  • Google Vertex AI generative AI documentation

Sources

  • Infrai AI-readable capability manifest
  • OpenAI Batch API guide

title: SMS OTP Resend API Errors: Unified Handling or Specialist Routes in Node.js
description:
Short answer: For SMS OTP resend API handling in Node.js, record the message ID, classify errors, retry 429 responses with backoff, and choose a unified backend such as Infrai when the identity and SMS evidence must share one credential boundary; choose a specialist route when carrier controls matter more.

An Infrai-backed customer-support system still needs more than a second send attempt. It needs a message ID, a bounded retry policy, a visible state transition, and an evidence trail that can answer who requested the code and what happened to it. A specialist is the better choice when carrier tooling, regional controls, or independently operated authentication are the requirements.

The practical rule is simple: record the original SMS message ID, call POST /v1/sms/resend/{id} only after a genuine non-receipt report, and classify the response before deciding whether another attempt is safe. A retry is not a user experience. It is a state machine.

What does the on-call page actually show?

The page fires after a support agent reports that a customer cannot finish 2FA. The on-call view should show the support case, the identity reference, the original message ID, the resend attempt number, the last response class, and the timestamp. It should not show a raw phone number in every log line.

Work backward from that page. The signal that should have fired earlier is not merely resend failed; it is otp_delivery_evidence_missing after the product's waiting window, with a correlation ID that joins the identity lookup, the original send, and the resend. On each send event, store a unique message ID and the identity reference returned by the auth system. On a resend, append an event rather than overwriting the original. That distinction matters during a compliance review because the latest status is not the same thing as the history.

The threshold has a cost on both sides. Fire too early and agents create duplicate codes while the first carrier attempt is still moving. Fire too late and a legitimate customer is blocked. I would start with a deliberately boring waiting interval chosen from observed delivery behavior, then review false positives against the support queue; the interval belongs to the product's risk model, not to the vendor's marketing page.

How should Node.js handle SMS OTP resend API errors?

The seam between authentication and messaging is where portability is won or lost. An auth record supplies the stable user reference; the SMS operation supplies the message ID. Keep both in your own audit event, and pass the same configured base URL and API key to the client that reads the identity record and resends the message. With Infrai, the relevant auth surface includes GET /v1/auth/user/get/{user_id}, while the SMS resend surface is POST /v1/sms/resend/{id}. The route list is intentionally short.

Here is the error-handling core in Go. The caller has already loaded the identity record and stored the original message ID; Identity.UserID is the first capability's output feeding the audit record for the second capability. The client uses https://api.infrai.cc/v1, Authorization: Bearer <key>, an explicit POST, a stable idempotency key, status checks, and bounded exponential backoff.

package otp

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Client struct {
    BaseURL string
    APIKey  string
    HTTP    *http.Client
}

type Identity struct {
    UserID string
}

const infraiBaseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
const resendRoute = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/resend/{id}"

func (c *Client) Resend(ctx context.Context, identity Identity, messageID string) error {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost,
            strings.Replace(resendRoute, "{id}", messageID, 1), nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+c.APIKey)
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "otp-resend-"+identity.UserID+"-"+messageID)

        resp, err := c.HTTP.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("otp resend failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if attempt == 3 {
            return fmt.Errorf("otp resend throttled after retries: body=%s", body)
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("otp resend exhausted")
}

func example(ctx context.Context, identity Identity, messageID string) error {
    client := &Client{APIKey: os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), HTTP: http.DefaultClient}
    return client.Resend(ctx, identity, messageID)
}

The code treats a 429 as a pacing signal, not as proof that delivery failed. Other 4xx and 5xx responses become visible errors, and the caller can persist the response class alongside the identity and message IDs. In production I would also make the resend command single-flight per identity, enforce a business-level resend limit, and return a neutral UI message such as “We could not send another code yet.” Do not reveal whether a phone number is registered.

The user interface should have explicit states: waiting, resend accepted, throttled, and failed. A successful HTTP response still means the resend request was accepted; it does not prove the handset displayed the code. That is why the evidence record needs the request ID and later status information, and why delivery evidence should not be inferred from email open metrics.

Four attempts is a policy boundary, not a delivery guarantee.

Which boundary survives a vendor change?

There are four credible shapes for this system, and they make different promises.

Option What it does well What your team still owns Best boundary
Infrai unified auth and SMS One key and one bill across the identity and sender surfaces; its public discovery surface describes capabilities, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in ten languages One vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface; SMS anti-abuse geography and country-based circuit breaking remain application work A support platform that values one correlation path and wants a replaceable adapter around the REST contract
Twilio Verify A focused verification product with a mature specialist workflow and broad messaging ecosystem Auth-provider integration, evidence normalization, and the relationship between the identity record and verification record Teams that need messaging specialization and are comfortable operating the auth seam themselves
Auth0 or Clerk plus Twilio Verify Established identity-management workflows paired with a dedicated verification service At least two signups, two credential sets, cross-vendor correlation, retry policy, audit storage, and the glue that maps an auth user to a verification attempt Organizations that already standardize on one of these identity providers and accept the additional boundary
Direct carrier or regional SMS provider Maximum control over regional routing, contracts, and carrier-specific operations Template, throttling, fraud controls, delivery normalization, and a complete audit model Teams with compliance or carrier requirements that make a general API insufficient
SendGrid, Postmark, Mailgun, or Amazon SES Stronger choices for email compliance notices and mailbox delivery workflows They are not an SMS OTP replacement; the SMS evidence path and identity handoff remain separate Teams whose notice channel is email and whose OTP is handled elsewhere

The unified option does not remove operational responsibility. Infrai's documented auth and SMS surfaces still leave SMS geofencing and per-country pricing circuit breakers to the business layer; its communication namespaces also use pull-based event access rather than webhook event pushes. Those limits matter for a compliance notice workflow that expects near-real-time orchestration. Email is not a silent fallback here either: there is no managed email OTP interface, and a domestic Tencent email vendor is still pending, so that route cannot be treated as domestic compliance evidence.

Infrai's limitation is clear: it concentrates provider trust in one boundary, and it does not supply the regional anti-abuse policy that this workflow may require.

I would try Infrai for the identity-to-SMS handoff when one key, one bill, and a plain REST contract reduce the amount of migration glue the platform team must later replace, especially when the application owns the audit event and can poll for the evidence it needs. I would choose Twilio Verify or a regional specialist instead when carrier-level controls, independent vendor failure domains, or a mature verification policy outweigh the value of a single credential boundary. That is the honest trade: fewer credentials to reconcile, but more reliance on one provider.

Make the migration reversible

Do not let a vendor response become your domain model. Store identity_id, message_id, attempt, requested_at, result_class, and a redacted provider request ID in your own event table. Put the provider call behind an interface with one method for “request resend” and one method for “read status”; keep the provider's body available for restricted diagnostics, but map user-visible errors to your own finite set.

The adapter should also own the provider URL, authorization header, idempotency key construction, retry budget, and response parsing. That makes a later move to Twilio Verify or a regional service a replacement of one adapter plus a migration of evidence records, rather than a rewrite of login controllers and support tooling. Test the adapter with a 2xx, a throttled 429 with Retry-After, a permanent 4xx, a transient 5xx, and a cancelled context. Test the audit event separately.

A useful SLO is therefore wider than SMS acceptance: measure the percentage of resend requests that produce a correlated audit record within the support workflow's deadline, and track the rate of duplicate resend commands per identity. Those indicators expose the real failure mode: a system that sends codes but cannot explain them.

The decision is narrower than “which SMS API is best.” Pick the unified route if the identity-to-message evidence chain is the main constraint and you can tolerate one provider boundary. Pick a specialist if delivery controls or independent failure domains are non-negotiable. In either case, keep the message ID and retry policy inside your application, where the compliance record can outlive the vendor.

If this boundary fits the system, the relevant implementation reference is 2FA SMS with resend and cancel.

Further reading

  • Twilio Verify documentation: twilio.com/docs/verify
  • Auth0 authentication documentation: auth0.com/docs
  • Clerk documentation: clerk.com/docs
  • SendGrid API documentation: docs.sendgrid.com
  • Postmark developer documentation: postmarkapp.com/developer
  • Apple Mail Privacy Protection guide: https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/use-mail-privacy-protection-iphf084865c7/ios

title: Wall Street investors demand proof of sustainability for AI spending
description:
An analysis of Big Tech financial results highlights contrasting approaches to AI capital expenditures.

While Microsoft and Oracle gained market confidence by balancing investments without continuous borrowing, companies like Alphabet faced heavy stock corrections after spending over 100% of operating cash flows on infrastructure.

Microsoft and Oracle have won investors’ trust by demonstrating better management. Microsoft posted strong free cash flow of $18,6 billion in the fiscal first quarter, beating estimates, with its Azure cloud storage and computing service up 48%. At the same time, the company allocated 68% of its operating cash flow to infrastructure investments, maintaining lower debt exposure than its competitors. Oracle, meanwhile, announced plans to limit external financing, estimating positive cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028, which pushed its stock higher.

In contrast, Alphabet was punished by the markets with its stock plunging more than 12% as it allocated 121,4% of its operating cash flow to capital expenditures in the September quarter, burning through $9,07 billion in cash. At the same time, Google's search revenue growth slowing to 12% intensified concerns that competition from automated chat systems is affecting the company's main source of revenue. Amazon also fell, burning through cash and announcing a subdued outlook despite strong revenue growth from cloud services and triple-digit growth in artificial intelligence.

title: How to Create an SVG Icon Sprite for Your Website
description:
Build a small navigation example with Home, Search, and a dismiss button using three icons from the same set. You will paste SVG code into the free SVG Sprite Generator, copy its output, and use the resulting symbols in a web page. No framework or build plugin is needed.

Once the generated sprite is included in your page, a visible icon needs only a reference to its symbol. Here is the Home link used in this example:

<a href="#home">
  <svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">
    <use href="#icon-home"></use>
  </svg>
  Home
</a>

.icon { width: 1em; height: 1em; fill: currentColor; }

This short snippet assumes icon-home is already defined in the document. The steps below create that definition; section 3 contains the complete page you can copy.

When a sprite fits

A sprite defines each icon once inside a <symbol>. An <svg> containing <use> draws an instance wherever you need it. This is useful for repeated icons in plain HTML, server templates, and documentation. A small, deliberately chosen set is easier to maintain than a bundle of every available icon.

Sprites can reduce repeated markup, but they do not always improve performance. An inline sprite adds bytes to each HTML document; an external sprite needs a request but can be cached. Unused symbols still cost bytes. Measure your own pages. Separate SVGs or components may fit better when icons need different animations, per-instance path changes, or individual imports.

1. Choose three matching icons

Use the 24-pixel solid variants from HeroIcons: home-solid, magnifying-glass-solid, and x-mark-solid. Keep the same variant and grid rather than mixing outline, 16-pixel, and solid artwork.

On each icon page, use the basic Copy to Clipboard → SVG action. Basic SVG copying is available without signing in; the separate download action requires a verified Member account. Neither an account nor Pro is required to use this generator. See Copy SVG code for that workflow.

The reproducible inputs below come from the same set's official Heroicons v2.2.0 sources. They use a 0 0 24 24 viewBox. Heroicons is distributed under the MIT license; retain its copyright and permission notice with redistributed copies. Save a copy of the linked license alongside your example as LICENSE-heroicons.txt. The generator does not create a license manifest for you.

For an exact reproduction, paste these complete SVG documents into separate input blocks:

Name: home 

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" aria-hidden="true" data-slot="icon">
  <path d="M11.47 3.841a.75.75 0 0 1 1.06 0l8.69 8.69a.75.75 0 1 0 1.06-1.061l-8.689-8.69a2.25 2.25 0 0 0-3.182 0l-8.69 8.69a.75.75 0 1 0 1.061 1.06l8.69-8.689Z"/>
  <path d="m12 5.432 8.159 8.159c.03.03.06.058.091.086v6.198c0 1.035-.84 1.875-1.875 1.875H15a.75.75 0 0 1-.75-.75v-4.5a.75.75 0 0 0-.75-.75h-3a.75.75 0 0 0-.75.75V21a.75.75 0 0 1-.75.75H5.625a1.875 1.875 0 0 1-1.875-1.875v-6.198a2.29 2.29 0 0 0 .091-.086L12 5.432Z"/>
</svg>

Name: magnifying-glass 

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" aria-hidden="true" data-slot="icon">
  <path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M10.5 3.75a6.75 6.75 0 1 0 0 13.5 6.75 6.75 0 0 0 0-13.5ZM2.25 10.5a8.25 8.25 0 1 1 14.59 5.28l4.69 4.69a.75.75 0 1 1-1.06 1.06l-4.69-4.69A8.25 8.25 0 0 1 2.25 10.5Z" clip-rule="evenodd"/>
</svg>

Name: x-mark 

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" aria-hidden="true" data-slot="icon">
  <path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M5.47 5.47a.75.75 0 0 1 1.06 0L12 10.94l5.47-5.47a.75.75 0 1 1 1.06 1.06L13.06 12l5.47 5.47a.75.75 0 1 1-1.06 1.06L12 13.06l-5.47 5.47a.75.75 0 0 1-1.06-1.06L10.94 12 5.47 6.53a.75.75 0 0 1 0-1.06Z" clip-rule="evenodd"/>
</svg>

2. Generate the sprite

  1. Open the SVG Sprite Generator. It starts with two blocks named icon-1 and icon-2.
  2. Replace the first name with home and paste the home SVG. Name the second magnifying-glass and paste its SVG.
  3. Click Add SVG Icon +. Name the new block x-mark and paste the third SVG. Use Remove for unwanted blocks; a named empty block prevents generation.
  4. Under Options, keep ID prefix as icon, Default size as 24, and HTML mode as Decorative. Leave Hide sprite by default and currentColor CSS helper checked.
  5. Click Generate Sprite. Check the previews and any errors or warnings. The output should contain icon-home, icon-magnifying-glass, and icon-x-mark.
  6. Select the Sprite tab and click Copy output. The other tabs are HTML snippet, CSS, and React. Copy each snippet you need.

This interface accepts pasted SVG markup, not uploaded files or a selection from Collections. It processes the markup in your browser. There is no file download button: you copy text and save files yourself. Load example set replaces the inputs with the tool's own samples; Clear restores two empty blocks. After editing names, SVGs, or options, click Generate Sprite again before copying to avoid stale output.

3. Use the output in a web page

Save the following as index.html. The hidden SVG is the actual generated sprite. It belongs once inside the document body; the visible SVGs reference its symbol IDs. The Home and Search icons repeat link text, so they are decorative. The icon-only dismiss button has its accessible name on the button and actually hides the notice.

Complete example: index.html

<!doctype html>

:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #b45309; outline-offset: 4px; }
.icon { width: 1em; height: 1em; fill: currentColor; vertical-align: -.125em; }
.icon-button .icon { width: 24px; height: 24px; }
.large { font-size: 32px; color: #9f1239; }
.dark { margin-top: 1rem; padding: 1rem; color: #e2e8f0; background: #172033; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<!-- Heroicons v2.2.0, MIT; see LICENSE-heroicons.txt. -->
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false" style="position: absolute; width: 0; height: 0; overflow: hidden;">
  <symbol id="icon-home" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
      <g xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" fill="currentColor">
        <path d="M11.47 3.841a.75.75 0 0 1 1.06 0l8.69 8.69a.75.75 0 1 0 1.06-1.061l-8.689-8.69a2.25 2.25 0 0 0-3.182 0l-8.69 8.69a.75.75 0 1 0 1.061 1.06l8.69-8.689Z"/>
        <path d="m12 5.432 8.159 8.159c.03.03.06.058.091.086v6.198c0 1.035-.84 1.875-1.875 1.875H15a.75.75 0 0 1-.75-.75v-4.5a.75.75 0 0 0-.75-.75h-3a.75.75 0 0 0-.75.75V21a.75.75 0 0 1-.75.75H5.625a1.875 1.875 0 0 1-1.875-1.875v-6.198a2.29 2.29 0 0 0 .091-.086L12 5.432Z"/>
      </g>
    </symbol>
  <symbol id="icon-magnifying-glass" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
      <g xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" fill="currentColor">
        <path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M10.5 3.75a6.75 6.75 0 1 0 0 13.5 6.75 6.75 0 0 0 0-13.5ZM2.25 10.5a8.25 8.25 0 1 1 14.59 5.28l4.69 4.69a.75.75 0 1 1-1.06 1.06l-4.69-4.69A8.25 8.25 0 0 1 2.25 10.5Z" clip-rule="evenodd"/>
      </g>
    </symbol>
  <symbol id="icon-x-mark" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
      <g xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" fill="currentColor">
        <path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M5.47 5.47a.75.75 0 0 1 1.06 0L12 10.94l5.47-5.47a.75.75 0 1 1 1.06 1.06L13.06 12l5.47 5.47a.75.75 0 1 1-1.06 1.06L12 13.06l-5.47 5.47a.75.75 0 0 1-1.06-1.06L10.94 12 5.47 6.53a.75.75 0 0 1 0-1.06Z" clip-rule="evenodd"/>
      </g>
    </symbol>
</svg>

<h1>SVG sprite demo</h1>
<nav aria-label="Demo navigation">
  <a href="#home"><svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="#icon-home"></use></svg> Home</a>
  <a href="#search"><svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="#icon-magnifying-glass"></use></svg> Search</a>
  <button class="icon-button" type="button" aria-label="Dismiss notice"
    onclick="document.getElementById('notice').hidden = true"><svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="#icon-x-mark"></use></svg></button>
</nav>
<p id="notice">This is a dismissible demo notice.</p>
<section id="home"><h2>Home</h2><p>One sprite, three reusable symbols.</p></section>
<section id="search"><h2>Search</h2><p>This link is a navigation example, not a search engine.</p></section>
<p class="large"><svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="#icon-home"></use></svg> A larger, differently colored instance</p>
<div class="dark"><svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="#icon-magnifying-glass"></use></svg> The same icon on a dark background</div>
<p>Icons: Heroicons by Tailwind Labs / Refactoring UI Inc, MIT. Keep LICENSE-heroicons.txt with redistributed copies.</p>
</body>
</html>

The generator produces the sprite and small snippets, not the surrounding page, navigation, or dismiss behavior. The example above supplies those parts. The generated wrapper is absolutely positioned with zero width and height, keeping referenced definitions available; its symbols are referenced by the visible SVG instances. Test this pattern with your target browsers, especially if you introduce gradients or filters.

4. Control size and color

The viewBox describes the artwork's coordinate system, not its displayed pixel size. Keep it on each symbol. The CSS helper sets width and height to 1em, so these icons follow their element's font size. The 24-pixel width and height attributes in a generated snippet are overridden by that CSS. Our button deliberately overrides the helper with 24-pixel dimensions; the larger paragraph uses a 32-pixel font size.

fill: currentColor makes this solid artwork follow CSS color. Change the surrounding text color to recolor its icons. The helper does not rewrite hard-coded colors inside paths, and it is a fill helper, not a stroke conversion. Keep intentional multicolor artwork unchanged. See MDN's currentColor reference.

Outline icons keep their paint settings. Supported root presentation attributes, including fill="none", stroke="currentColor", and stroke-width, are preserved on an internal group. Child shapes can still override them. Paste the complete SVG; no manual group wrapper is needed. The fill helper does not turn a preserved outline into a filled icon.

The preview renders the generated symbol. Root style and class are not copied; use explicit SVG presentation attributes. Root viewport effects such as clip-path, mask, filter, transform and vector-effect are not transferred and produce warnings. Review those warnings and the final appearance for complex artwork.

5. Optionally save an external sprite

Save the copied Sprite output as sprite.svg next to your HTML. Remove the inline sprite from that page and use a filename plus a fragment:

<svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">
  <use href="sprite.svg#icon-home"></use>
</svg>

Keep the same CSS. Serve both files from the same origin using your project's local development server. Do not test external references by double-clicking the HTML file: file:// restrictions can prevent the SVG from loading. If Python is installed, run this command in the folder containing both files:

python -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/index.html. Stop the server with Ctrl+C. An external sprite requires deployment of the asset as well as the HTML; check its URL, response type, caching, and your browser support. Do not assume a sprite on another domain will work just by enabling CORS. MDN documents external use references and same-origin restrictions.

Common problems and fixes

  • No output: remove unused empty blocks and paste one complete, valid SVG document per input. Fix the reported XML error before generating again.
  • Blank icon: compare the exact href fragment with the generated ID. A name like “Home Icon” becomes icon-home-icon, not icon-home. Keep input names unique and inspect final IDs; do not rely on suffixing to resolve every possible collision.
  • Wrong size or clipping: preserve the source viewBox and check CSS dimensions. The tool can infer a viewBox from positive numeric width and height (including px), but it cannot recover arbitrary missing coordinate information.
  • Black or missing outline: check the source fill and stroke settings and any generator warnings. A fixed fill on a child path will also override inherited color. Verify both light and dark backgrounds.
  • Broken gradients or masks: review rewritten internal IDs and every reference. This tool removes some obvious unsafe content but is not a comprehensive sanitizer for untrusted SVG. Use reviewed sources.
  • External sprite missing: use HTTP, check the request succeeds, and keep the asset on the same origin. Recheck the deployed path after moving files.
  • Repeated or missing accessible labels: hide decorative SVGs and name their controls. If you choose Labelled mode for a meaningful standalone icon, adapt its title and make title IDs unique for every repeated instance. The generated title IDs are based on symbol names. See the WAI button pattern and SVG icon accessibility guide.

Keep the workflow small

Start with three icons, review their actual use sites, and keep the source SVGs and license notice beside your generated output. Try the SVG Sprite Generator with your next small set of interface icons.

For more options, read the generator documentation. If your project needs automated generation, see Build an SVG Sprite for Modern Vite, React, and Vue Apps. For per-icon components, see Use SVG Icons in React with Vite and SVGR or the [SVG to Component Converter](https://svgicons.com/tools/svg-

title: My AI directory has 92 categories. Ten of them hold 37% of the listings.
description:
I ran one query against my AI tools directory last night, and the result explained why some of its pages get crawled while others sit ignored.

Category Tools
RIP AI 405
Video Generators 294
Image Generators 269
Productivity 253
Developer Tools 247
Education / Studies 245
Business 233
Image editing 230
LLM models 208
Life Assistants 192

Those ten categories hold 2,576 of 7,006 category assignments — 36.8% of the whole taxonomy. The directory has 4,323 tools across 92 categories.

That last number is not the problem. The tail is.

14 categories have ten tools or fewer

  • New AI Tools: 0
  • AIxploria Selection: 0
  • Programming: 0
  • AI Presentations: 2
  • AI Music: 4
  • AI Education: 4
  • AI 3D: 4
  • AI Research: 4
  • AI SEO: 5
  • AI Translation: 7
  • AI Chatbots: 8
  • AI Image Generators: 8
  • AI Social Media: 8
  • AI Customer Support: 10

Three of those are empty, and they are also the most tempting pages to publish, because the names sound valuable: "New AI Tools" and "Programming" are exactly what a searcher types. So I checked what the site actually returns for them:

$ BASE=https://aiverse.mindutil.com
$ curl -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "$BASE/category/last-ai-en"
404
$ curl -s "$BASE/category/last-ai-en" | grep robots
<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow"/>

And the sitemap filter is one line:

where: { tools: { some: {} } }

So 89 of 92 categories ship in the sitemap. The three empty ones do not.

Why a 404 beats an empty page

An empty category that returns 200 with "0 tools found" is a page a crawler can index. Do that twenty times and you have told a search engine your site has twenty useless URLs before it has read a single tool page. The 404 does the opposite: it says this hub does not exist yet.

None of this is free. A user who bookmarked the page gets a dead end, and the internal link from the categories index has to be removed or the link graph starts leaking 404s. The trade is simple: a little maintenance for the absence of thin pages. On a directory where the median tool page is still fighting for its first indexing, that trade is worth taking.

Category is not a tag

4,323 tools produce 7,006 category assignments, an average of 1.62 per tool. Exactly 2,100 tools (48.6%) sit in two or more categories. That overlap is real — a video editor can be "Video Editing", "Productivity", and "Business" without stretching any of those labels.

Overlap is also what keeps category pages from being template clones: each one is a different basket of results. Directory sites get flagged as doorway pages when the only unique word on 92 pages is the category name. The fix is not fewer categories. It is making each category page answer something the tool pages cannot: which five of these should I try first, and why.

The 405-tool graveyard

RIP AI is the largest bucket in the whole directory: 405 tools, 9.4% of everything, 236 of them marked free. These are discontinued or dead products. Publishing that number is useful — a directory that never deletes anything is lying by omission — but RIP AI is not a category. It is a status.

Mixing the two is how you end up with a tool that is both "RIP AI" and "Video Generators", an empty "Programming" bucket, and all three looking equally important in a sitemap.

Four rules I am adopting

  1. A category ships only if it has at least one tool. Zero-tool hub gets a 404 and noindex, never a 200 with an empty state.
  2. A category with fewer than 10 tools does not get its own indexable template until it reaches 10. Until then it is a filter on the parent listing.
  3. Statuses — dead, free, new, verified — stay filters, not categories.
  4. Every category page needs a hand-written shortlist paragraph. If I cannot write one, the category is not ready to be indexed.

Only the first rule is already live. The other three are the work for the next few weeks.

The part that surprised me

The top ten are not the categories I would have guessed. I expected "AI Chatbots" to lead; it has 8 tools. Video Generators has 294. The taxonomy drifted toward whatever the crawler found in bulk rather than toward what people actually search for. That is a data problem wearing a design problem's clothes, and it is the next thing on the list.

If you want to see the current state of the catalog, including the free and paid filters, it is here: https://aiverse.mindutil.com/free-ai-tools?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=topic
