title: Create a Blob-URL Image Fallback System for Canvas
description:
Build a Blob-URL Image Fallback System for Canvas

When working with the HTML5 Canvas API, handling image loading failures is crucial to maintaining a smooth user experience. A Blob-URL image fallback system ensures that if an image fails to load, a default transparent asset is used instead. This guide provides a step-by-step approach to implementing such a system using TypeScript. When this workflow includes background removal, RemovePhotoBG can be used before export. Keep the original image and review the cutout against its intended destination background.

1. Create a Default Transparent Image

Before handling image loads, create a default transparent image that will be used if the primary image fails to load. This image should be a small transparent PNG file. You can generate this image using a canvas element or use a pre-existing transparent image.

2. Load the Primary Image Using Blob-URL

Load the primary image using the Blob-URL method. This method allows you to create a URL for a Blob object, which can be used as a source for an image element. Use the fetch API to retrieve the image data and create a Blob object.

3. Set Up an Image Element with the Blob-URL

Once the Blob is created, use it to set the src property of an image element. This image element will be used to draw onto the canvas. If the image fails to load, the fallback system will activate.

4. Implement an Image Load Fallback Logic

Add an event listener to the image element to detect if the image has failed to load. If the image fails to load, replace it with the default transparent image. This can be done by updating the src property of the image element with the URL of the default image.

5. Draw the Image onto the Canvas

Once the image has been successfully loaded, draw it onto the canvas using the drawImage method. This ensures that the image is rendered correctly on the canvas.

6. Test with Intentional Failure Cases

To ensure the fallback system works as expected, test it with intentional failure cases. For example, use a broken image URL or a corrupted image file. The fallback system should automatically replace the failed image with the default transparent image.

7. Clean Up Resources

After the image has been drawn onto the canvas, clean up the resources by removing the image element and the Blob object. This helps to prevent memory leaks and ensures optimal performance.

TypeScript Example

Here is a TypeScript example that demonstrates the Blob-URL image fallback system:

const canvas = document.getElementById('canvas') as HTMLCanvasElement;
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');

const defaultImage = new Image();
defaultImage.src = 'default.png';

const primaryImage = new Image();
primaryImage.src = 'primary.jpg';

primaryImage.onload = () => {
  ctx.drawImage(primaryImage, 0, 0);
};

primaryImage.onerror = () => {
  ctx.drawImage(defaultImage, 0, 0);
};

This example creates a default transparent image and a primary image. If the primary image fails to load, the default image is used instead. The image is then drawn onto the canvas using the drawImage method.

By following these steps, you can create a reliable Blob-URL image fallback system for Canvas that ensures a smooth user experience even when image loading fails.

title: Show Dev: JPersist v1.8.0 — Hardening Gradle Build Sandbox & ClassLoader Engineering for JPA
description:
Hey everyone,

We just published version v1.8.0 of JPersist, an open-source ecosystem of highly optimized, Configuration Cache-compliant Gradle plugins designed to automate enterprise Jakarta Persistence (JPA) configurations.

In this release, we didn't just add features (like full Apache OpenJPA toolset orchestration) — we deep-dived into advanced Gradle task engineering to fix common continuous integration pain points.

The Problem: Aggressive Compiler Erasures & CI Pipeline Crashes

When writing custom incremental tasks that process bytecodes, pointing your task @InputDirectory to the compiler's output directory (build/classes/java/main) creates an incremental bottleneck. Why? Because whenever a single file changes, JavaCompile wipes out the whole folder, destroying Gradle's historical file snapshots and causing an incremental cache miss.

Furthermore, running isolated worker actions by injecting text coordinates (group:artifact:version) frequently crashes headless CI nodes if those artifacts aren't fully synchronized on Maven Central yet or if mavenLocal() access is disabled.

How JPersist v1.8.0 Solves This:

  1. Source-Driven Incremental Auditing: Our verification tasks (validatePersistenceSchema and lintNamedQueries) now track flat file collection streams from sourceSet.java.sourceDirectories. Because source folders are never deleted by the build, our delta tracking remains 100% stable and fast.
  2. ClassLoader Harvesting: Our plugins now dynamically query their own active ClassLoader at execution time to harvest the physical .jar file protection domains of our tools API. We pass these raw file handles directly to the isolated WorkerExecutor. Zero network calls, zero resolution exceptions.
  3. Container-Friendly Scopes: We restricted dynamic injection to compileOnly and annotationProcessor. Your packaged WAR and EAR files remain clean, lightweight, and completely free of runtime classpath pollution.

If you are dealing with complex multi-module setups, multi-tenant databases, or looking to streamline your build performance, we'd love for you to check it out!

🔗 Main Repository & Templates: https://github.com/jpersist/persistence

title: I Built DTDb — An IMDb for Developer Tools
description:
We developers have strong opinions about the tools we use every day.

Vim vs. VS Code. PostgreSQL vs. MySQL. Ubuntu vs. Arch. Python vs. Go. And now, with AI coding agents becoming part of everyday development, there are even more tools to compare.

But where can you actually see what developers think about these tools?

There are plenty of comparison articles, sponsored rankings, benchmarks, and opinionated blog posts. But I wanted something a little different.

So I built DTDb — Developer Tools Database.

👉 https://dtdb.dev

What's the idea?

Think of IMDb, but instead of movies, we're ranking developer tools.

The concept is simple:

  • Developers rate the tools they actually use.
  • Tools are organized into categories.
  • Each month, ratings are frozen into a ranking.
  • You can follow how rankings change over time and see which tools are gaining or losing popularity.

The goal is to create a community-driven picture of the developer tools ecosystem.

What can you find there?

I've started with several categories:

  • Database engines — PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle Database, and others.
  • Linux distributions — Ubuntu, Debian, Arch Linux, etc.
  • Programming languages — Python, JavaScript, Java, and more.
  • AI coding agents — Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, etc.
  • IDEs and code editors — VS Code, Visual Studio, Notepad++, and others.

This is just the beginning. There are plenty of categories and tools I'd like to add.

Why monthly rankings?

I didn't want DTDb to become just another leaderboard where positions constantly fluctuate.

Freezing ratings into monthly snapshots makes it possible to look back and understand how developer preferences evolve.

For example, it'll be interesting to see how AI coding agents compete over the coming months, or whether developers' preferences for programming languages and databases actually change.

What's next?

There are plenty of things I'd like to improve:

  • More categories and developer tools.
  • Better ways to explore historical rankings.
  • More community participation.
  • Improvements based on actual user feedback.

But before going too far, I'd love to hear what other developers think.

I'd love your feedback!

A few questions I'm particularly interested in:

  1. Does the IMDb analogy make sense for developer tools?
  2. What categories would you like to see?
  3. Which tools do you think are missing?
  4. Would you actually use something like this to discover or compare developer tools?

This is an independent project, and I'm still figuring out the best direction for it.

Check it out: https://dtdb.dev

Any feedback, criticism, or suggestions are very welcome!

title: Screen recording or UI animation for your dev tool demo?
description:
Both formats show your product. They differ in control, cost and how long they stay accurate.

Screen recording

  • Pros: honest, fast, shows the real product.
  • Cons: tiny text, shaky cursor, loading delays, and it goes stale after the next release.

UI animation

  • Pros: zooms, highlights and clean transitions. You can show a feature before it ships.
  • Cons: more design and motion work, and it needs good design files.

How to choose

  • Tutorial or docs video? Record it.
  • Homepage or launch video? Animate it.
  • UI changing soon? Animate from separate layers so one screen can be swapped.

A blended video often works best: a polished animated overview, then a short real clip to prove it is the actual product.

More detail: UI animation vs screen recording.

title: I built a globe where every country is a separate piece you can pull out 🌍
description:
Hey everyone 👋

Most web globes are a texture wrapped around a sphere. You can spin them, and that's about it.

I wanted one where every country is a real object: its own plate, set into the ocean ball like a puzzle piece. So I built it.

mahmad.me / blocks/interactive/world-globe

It's all SVG and a bit of math, with no WebGL and no canvas.

What you can do 🎮

  • Drag to turn the globe any way
  • Click a country to pull it out of its socket
  • Break the whole map apart with one button, then let it settle back

Pull out a big country like Canada, the US or Pakistan and it splits into its states or provinces, each one a plate with its name on it.

How it works 🛠️

  1. The ball is a projection. Natural Earth's outlines go through a d3-geo orthographic projection. When you drag, nothing moves: the globe rotates and every country is projected again.
  2. Each country is its own plate. It has a top, walls, a socket it leaves behind and a shadow, so it can lift out on its own spring while the others stay put.
  3. SVG has no depth buffer. So every frame the plates are sorted by how much they face you, and drawn back to front.
  4. Provinces load on demand. The split data is one small file per country, fetched only the first time you pull that country out.

Try it 🌐

👉 mahmad.me/blocks/interactive/world-globe

Break the map apart, then try to put it back together by hand

Country outlines and borders are from Natural Earth, which is public domain.

title: I Built PosterPilot: A Cloudinary-Powered Tool to Adapt University Event Posters Without Cropping Important Details
description:
University societies and event organizers regularly create posters for seminars, workshops, competitions, hackathons, and other campus activities.

However, sharing one poster across different platforms can become challenging. Instagram posts, Instagram Stories, and website previews all require different dimensions. Simply resizing an image can crop important information, such as event titles, dates, venue details, or sponsor logos.

To explore how image transformation can solve this problem, I built PosterPilot, a Cloudinary-powered web application that helps users adapt one uploaded event poster into multiple formats.

What is PosterPilot?

PosterPilot is a web-based image adaptation tool designed with university societies and event organizers in mind.

Users upload an event poster once and generate different output formats using Cloudinary image transformations.

The main idea is simple: make poster adaptation easier while giving users control over whether the entire image should remain visible or fill the selected dimensions.

🌐 Live Demo: https://posterpilot.vercel.app
💻 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/alpha5-rdx/posterpilot

The Problem I Wanted to Solve:

Imagine a university society has designed a poster for an upcoming technology event. The society wants to share it in three places:

  • Instagram Square post
  • Instagram Story
  • Website or social media preview

Each platform requires a different image size. Cropping the original poster to fit these dimensions can remove important information.

I wanted to build a simple solution that could generate these formats without requiring users to manually edit the same poster multiple times.

Technology Stack

I used the following technologies:

  1. React: Building the user interface and reusable components.
  2. Vite: Development environment and production build tooling.
  3. JavaScript: Application logic and interactions.
  4. CSS: Responsive styling and layout.
  5. Cloudinary: Image uploading, transformation, delivery, and optimization.
  6. Vercel: Deploying and hosting the application.

The project uses a frontend-only architecture. Cloudinary handles image storage and delivery, so I did not need to build a separate backend for this version.

How Cloudinary Powers PosterPilot?

Cloudinary is the central part of the application.

I integrated Cloudinary's Upload API using an unsigned upload preset. This allows the frontend to upload an image without exposing the Cloudinary API Secret. The application sends the selected image and upload preset to the Cloudinary image upload endpoint: https://api.cloudinary.com/v1_1//image/upload

After a successful upload, Cloudinary returns information such as:

  • Secure image URL
  • Public ID
  • Image dimensions
  • File format
  • File size
  • Asset version

PosterPilot uses the returned image information to generate transformed image URLs.

This approach allows the application to work with one original uploaded image and dynamically generate different versions through Cloudinary transformations.

Five Output Formats

PosterPilot currently supports five predefined formats:

Format: Innsta Square Dimensions: 1080 x 1080
Format: Innsta Story Dimensions: 1080 x 1920
Format: Web/Social Preview Dimensions: 1080 x 1080
Format: LinkedIn Portrait Dimensions: 1080 x 1350
Format: LinkedIn Square Dimensions: 1080 x 1080

Users can preview the generated versions before copying their URLs or downloading the images.

*My Main Feature: No-Crop vs Crop-to-Fill
*
One of the main features I wanted to explore was the difference between preserving the complete image and filling a target canvas.

1. No-Crop Mode

For this mode, I used Cloudinary's c_pad transformation.

Example transformation: c_pad,w_1080,h_1080,b_white/q_auto/f_auto

This transformation fits the original image inside the specified dimensions while preserving the entire image. If the aspect ratios differ, padding is added to complete the canvas.

This is useful when the poster contains important information that should remain visible.

2. Crop-to-Fill Mode

For the alternative mode, I used Cloudinary's c_fill transformation with center gravity.

Example transformation: c_fill,g_center,w_1080,h_1080/q_auto/f_auto

This fills the target dimensions by cropping the image where necessary.

It is useful when users prefer a completely filled canvas and accept that some parts of the original image may be cropped.

Image Optimization and Delivery

I also used two useful Cloudinary transformation parameters:

  • q_auto: Automatically selects an appropriate image quality setting.
  • f_auto: Automatically selects a suitable delivery format based on browser support.

These transformations help optimize image delivery without requiring users to manually create multiple optimized files.

Other Application Features

In addition to image transformations, PosterPilot includes:

  1. Drag-and-drop image upload.
  2. File browsing and image validation.
  3. JPG, PNG, and WebP support.
  4. A 10 MB client-side upload limit.
  5. Upload progress and error handling.
  6. Image replacement and reset functionality.
  7. Copy transformed image URL.
  8. Download transformed images.
  9. Responsive user interface.

Testing and Deployment

After development, I tested the application locally and deployed it using Vercel. I also tested the live application to verify that:

  • Image uploads work with Cloudinary.
  • All three output formats generate correctly.
  • No-Crop and Crop-to-Fill modes update the previews.
  • Generated image URLs can be copied and opened.
  • Transformed images can be downloaded.

The live application is available here: (https://posterpilot.vercel.app)

What I Learned?

Building PosterPilot gave me practical experience with Cloudinary's image upload and transformation capabilities. Some of the important concepts I explored include:

  • Integrating an external image service into a React application.
  • Using unsigned uploads without exposing API secrets.
  • Generating image variations through dynamic transformations.
  • Understanding the difference between padding and cropping.
  • Optimizing images for web delivery.
  • Deploying a frontend application with environment variables.

I also learned that a useful project does not always need a complicated architecture. Sometimes, combining the right service with a focused real-world problem can produce a practical solution.

*What's Next?
*
PosterPilot is an initial version, and there is room for improvement. Some possible future enhancements include:

  • More social media presets.
  • Custom width and height controls.
  • Background color selection for padded images.
  • Batch poster processing.
  • Additional image editing options.

*Final Thoughts
*
PosterPilot started with a simple campus-related problem: adapting event posters into different formats without unnecessarily losing important information.

Through this project, I explored how Cloudinary can make image uploading, transformation, optimization, and delivery easier to integrate into a modern web application.

I'm excited to continue learning, building, and exploring more practical applications of Cloudinary.

I'd appreciate your feedback and suggestions!

title: Would You Rather Have a Dumb Component or a Smart Component?
description:
A Component Doesn't Have to Be Dumb to Be Reusable

There's a long-running idea in frontend architecture:

Keep components dumb.

Let them receive data, render the UI, and leave everything else to something higher up the tree.

It sounds clean. And often, it is.

But there's a trade-off we don't always consider:

Making a component simpler can make the surrounding architecture more complicated.

Let's look at both approaches.

🔴 The Problem

Imagine a component that displays a list of users.

It needs to fetch the data, filter the results, and render them.

One approach is to put everything inside UserList.

function UserList() {
  const [users, setUsers] = useState<User[]>([]);
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => {
    getUsers().then(setUsers);
  }, []);

  const filteredUsers = useMemo(
    () => users.filter((user) => user.name.includes(query)),
    [users, query],
  );

  return (
    <section>
      <input value={query} onChange={(event) => setQuery(event.target.value)} />

      {filteredUsers.map((user) => (
        <div key={user.id}>{user.name}</div>
      ))}
    </section>
  );
}

This is a smart component.

It knows where its data comes from, manages its own state, handles filtering, and decides how everything is displayed.

Using it is simple:

<UserList />

But what happens when another part of the application already has the users?

Or when the same UI needs to display data from a different source?

Now the component's built-in behavior becomes a limitation.

🟢 The Other Extreme

We could separate those responsibilities.

The container handles the data. The presentational component handles the UI.

function UserListContainer() {
  const [users, setUsers] = useState<User[]>([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    getUsers().then(setUsers);
  }, []);

  return <UserList users={users} />;
}

function UserList({ users }: { users: User[] }) {
  return (
    <section>
      {users.map((user) => (
        <div key={user.id}>{user.name}</div>
      ))}
    </section>
  );
}

Now UserList doesn't care where the data comes from.

It can render users fetched by a parent, loaded from a cache, or passed in by a test.

That's a real benefit.

But splitting components isn't free.

The container needs to pass data down. Additional behavior may require additional props. And if the presentation component is only ever used in one place, the extra layer might not make the code any easier to understand.

We haven't necessarily removed complexity. We've moved it.

🔵 Reusability Has a Cost

A dumb component is often easier to reuse because it depends on fewer things.

It doesn't need to know about an API, a router, a global store, or a particular data-fetching library.

But reusability isn't the only thing that matters.

Sometimes, keeping behavior close to the UI makes a component easier to understand.

Consider a search box.

If its value, filtering logic, and displayed results always belong together, extracting every small piece into separate components and hooks can make a simple feature harder to follow.

On the other hand, if multiple screens need the same filtering behavior or visual list, separating those responsibilities may be worthwhile.

The useful boundary isn't necessarily between smart and dumb components.

It's between responsibilities that belong together and responsibilities that benefit from being independent.

🟣 So Where Should the Logic Live?

There isn't one rule that works for every component.

A few questions can help:

  • Does the component need to work with different data sources? Separating data access from presentation may help.
  • Does the behavior only make sense for this component? Keeping it local may make the code clearer.
  • Is the component coordinating several unrelated concerns? That may be a sign it has too many responsibilities.
  • Are you extracting something just to make a component smaller? Smaller doesn't automatically mean simpler.

You can also mix the approaches.

A component can own its local interaction state while receiving data from a parent. It can use a shared hook for behavior without becoming purely presentational.

These aren't mutually exclusive architectures.

🟠 What About Consistency Across a Codebase?

So far, we've looked at individual components.

But components don't always exist in isolation. They're part of a larger codebase, often maintained by multiple developers.

Imagine a team decides that components should follow a consistent architecture:

  • Components don't fetch data directly.
  • Shared state is accessed through established abstractions.
  • Business logic lives in hooks, services, or other dedicated modules.
  • Components receive the data they need through props.

There are good reasons to do this.

Developers know where to look for things. Responsibilities are predictable. Moving between different parts of the application feels familiar.

But there's a trade-off.

Some components might genuinely be simpler if they handled their own behavior.

Forcing them into the same structure could mean creating unnecessary hooks, adding extra layers, or splitting closely related logic across several files.

You gain consistency, but potentially lose simplicity.

And that's not necessarily a bad decision.

In a large team, predictable code can be more valuable than making every individual component follow its locally simplest implementation.

The important distinction is between consistent principles and identical implementations.

A codebase can have clear architectural rules without forcing every component to have exactly the same structure.

After all, you're maintaining a codebase, not just individual components.

⚡ The Takeaway

Smart and dumb components aren't competing goals.

A dumb component can be wonderfully reusable, but separating every bit of behavior can create unnecessary indirection.

A smart component can be convenient and cohesive, but accumulating unrelated responsibilities can make it difficult to change.

Neither approach is inherently better.

Don't optimize for dumb components. Don't optimize for smart components.

Optimize for clear responsibilities.

title: Building a browser .io strategy game with a Go server
description:
I'm building Warhex.io, a free .io strategy game that runs in the browser. You build a base out of walls, turrets, snipers and barracks, defend key positions and fight players from all over the world in real time. This post is about how the game is put together, in case you are thinking about making a multiplayer browser game of your own.

If you used to play bloble.io or similar base-building .io games, Warhex.io is made for that kind of player. It is an independent project and is not affiliated with bloble.io.

The shape of the stack

  • Server: Go. One authoritative game loop owns the whole match, and clients only send intentions (place a building, move units, buy an upgrade).
  • Transport: WebSockets with a small binary protocol. Every message is one type byte followed by a compact payload, so a camera update or a unit position costs a handful of bytes.
  • Client: plain JavaScript, a canvas renderer and webpack. No game engine. The renderer only draws what the server says exists.
  • Accounts and data: Supabase for login (Discord only) and for things that must survive a restart, like progress and ranking.
  • Community: a Discord bot in Node that syncs the global top 10 to server roles.

Why Go for the game server

A match is a lot of small updates: bullets, units, buildings and health bars changing many times per second. Go gives cheap concurrency (one goroutine per connection, one loop for the world) and predictable memory use, which matters when you want a cheap server to hold many players.

The important rule is that the server decides everything. The client can ask "place a turret here", and the server checks the cost, the position, the limits and who owns the space before it replies. That one rule removes most of the cheating you would otherwise have to chase.

A tiny binary protocol

Text JSON is easy, but at a few hundred updates per second it gets expensive. Our messages look like this:

[ type: 1 byte ][ playerID: 1 byte ][ payload ... ]

On the client a worker decodes each frame by type and hands plain objects to the game. Rarely sent things (a clan list, a chat line) can still use JSON inside the same envelope, so you only pay for binary where it matters.

Boss fights as a game design tool

The most fun feature to build was three world bosses. Each boss is a fortified base made of the same pieces players use, with a shield made of generators. You have to break the shield generators first, then the core. Because bosses reuse the normal building and damage code, there was almost no special-case logic, and balancing them is just changing numbers.

What I would tell my past self

  1. Make the server authoritative from day one.
  2. Keep the protocol small before you need to.
  3. Reuse your own game rules for new content (bosses, events, tutorials).
  4. Put the moderation tools (chat filter, rate limits) in early.
  5. Ship the community (Discord, wiki, guides) alongside the game, not after.

You can play Warhex.io for free at https://warhex.io and join the community at https://discord.gg/CsVHA7R7Vx. There is also a wiki with a full guide at https://warhexio.fandom.com/pt-br/wiki/Warhex.io

Questions about the netcode or the Go server? Ask in the comments and I will answer.

title: 5 Sites I Use So My Vibe-Coded Apps Don't Look AI-Generated
description:
I teach AI and web development, and the most common thing I see in vibe-coded apps is that they all look the same: same gradients, same cards, same "AI default" feel. The fix isn't a better model. It's better references and better components. Here are the five I keep coming back to.

1. 21st.dev

What it is: A large library of React + Tailwind CSS components, templates and shadcn themes made by design engineers, with a CLI (npx @21st-dev/cli add) and an MCP server so your AI agent can find and install components.
Use it when: You want polished, real-world sections (heroes, AI chat UIs, pricing, sign-ins) and you're working with Cursor, Claude Code or another MCP client.
Free vs paid: A free account can copy 2 components a day. Paid plans remove the limit.

2. React Bits (reactbits.dev)

What it is: Free animated React components: text animations, backgrounds and micro-interactions. Pick JavaScript or TypeScript, with plain CSS or Tailwind, then copy the source or install it with the CLI.
Use it when: Your UI works but feels flat and you want a bit of motion that you fully own and can tweak.
Free vs paid: The main library is free. React Bits Pro (pro.reactbits.dev) is a paid one-time purchase that adds blocks, app UI and templates.

3. Magic UI (magicui.design)

What it is: 150+ free, open-source animated components built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Motion, designed as a companion to shadcn/ui.
Use it when: You're building a landing page and already use shadcn/ui.
Free vs paid: The components are free. Magic UI Pro (pro.magicui.design) sells landing-page templates and sections for a one-time fee.

4. Uiverse (uiverse.io)

What it is: A community-made, open-source library of UI elements such as buttons, cards, loaders and inputs. Copy them as HTML/CSS, Tailwind, React or Figma.
Use it when: You need one small element that looks hand-made, even without React.
Free vs paid: The site says it's 100% free for personal and commercial use.

5. Mobbin (mobbin.com)

What it is: Not a component library. It's a UI/UX reference library of screens from real, shipped mobile and web apps.
Use it when: You need to see how real products design onboarding, paywalls or settings before you prompt your AI.
Free vs paid: Joining is free, with limited access to apps and sites. Flows, animations and search need a paid plan, and there's a student/educator discount.

Quick tip

Don't ask your AI for "a modern UI". Pick one real reference screen from Mobbin, choose one component library (mixing five libraries is how apps start looking generic), and give the AI your brand colours, font and spacing scale. Consistency is what makes an app look designed.

What's on your list? Drop it in the comments.

— KD Jayakody

title: I made my tmux sessions reachable from a 2002 Nokia
description:
I run my work in tmux: builds, logs, servers, and lately a lot of AI coding agents. The thing about an agent in a pane is that it stops and waits for me. "May I run this?" "Which of these three?" "Done." And I am never at that keyboard when it asks. I am in the kitchen, on the train, on a walk.

So I built muxway: a small Go agent next to tmux on each machine, a hub, and clients. The clients got out of hand. There is a browser one, an Android one with a Wear OS watch face, one for Even Realities G2 glasses, and a Java ME MIDlet that runs on a Nokia 6310i from 2002.

That phone has a 96 by 65 pixel screen, GPRS, and cannot do modern TLS. It reads Claude Code and answers it. This post is about why the Nokia was the useful one to build, not the silly one.

The agent calls you

The part I use most is the notification. Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity tell muxway, through their hooks, when they ask a question, want a permission, go idle, or finish. The pane lights up in every client, the phone and the watch buzz, the glasses show a banner at the foot of whatever I am reading. Then I answer from wherever I am: a tap, Enter, y, a number, a few words, or I hold the microphone and say it. The hub transcribes, the words land on the input line, and nothing is sent until I confirm.

In the browser I get up to four tiles from any mix of machines, all live and typable. Drag a header to swap, drag a divider to resize, and tiles that are one tmux window's panes move that window on the host as I rearrange them.

A lens for tiny screens

A terminal does not fit on a watch or a pair of glasses, and certainly not on 96 by 65 pixels. What does fit is the conversation. A lens knows what an agent's screen looks like and reshapes it: the box drawing, the status line and the spinner go, the question and the prompt stay. On the glasses that is eight short lines. On the Nokia it is whatever the screen holds, and you scroll with a key. Whatever the agent suggests in its input box is offered as the first answer, so most of the time the reply is one key.

The lens is also why the Nokia was worth doing. If the API is small enough that a MIDP 1.0 phone can be a client, in under 30 KiB of JAR, then anything can. The protocol has a plain text mode: one authenticated GET returns a pane wrapped to the width you ask for. A phone of that age cannot speak current HTTPS, so it goes through a small relay that terminates TLS for it. The MIDP 2.0 build, on a Nokia 7310 from a few years later, adds colour, Unicode and the camera: take a photo of a whiteboard, it lands in an inbox on the host, and the path is typed into the reply for the agent to read.

It is a remote shell, so build it like one

Whoever can type into a tmux pane owns that machine. I did not want a "trusted network" bypass or a convenience mode that becomes the default.

  • Panes are opt-in. Nothing is reachable until its owner marks it with muxway expose.
  • A token names which hosts and panes it may read, and separately which it may type into. Read and write are different grants.
  • Input is text and a fixed grammar of named keys. Clients never send raw escape sequences.
  • Every authentication step is rate limited and locked out. Secrets are hashed, compared in constant time, never logged.
  • Every write to a pane is audit logged on the host: who, when, which pane, how many bytes.
  • The agent dials out to the hub over a signed, encrypted WebSocket. Nothing listens on your machines, and clients never reach them directly.
  • One static Go binary per role, one third party dependency, no cgo.

The hub signs people in with OpenID Connect if you have an identity provider, or with tokens if you do not. It serves the web client from files embedded in the binary, so there is nothing else to deploy.

Getting it running 

go install github.com/notmarkopadjen/muxway/cmd/muxway@latest

# on the hub
muxway hub serve --listen 127.0.0.1:7600 --public-url https://hub.example.com --trust-proxy &
muxway hub pair-code --host alice-laptop

# on the machine with tmux
muxway agent pair <code>
muxway agent run &
muxway expose -t work:1.0 --write --name build
muxway hooks claude-code

# back on the hub: a token for a client
muxway hub token create --name phone --read 'alice-laptop/*' --write 'alice-laptop/@build'

Open the hub in a browser and paste the token. For a script or your own client, a pane is one request away:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Accept: text/plain" \
  "https://hub.example.com/v1/panes/alice-laptop/@build?width=40&lines=20"

Build your own client

That last request is the whole point. The protocol is documented with examples and a diagram for every flow: bearer tokens, JSON and text mode, long polled events, the key grammar, rate limits, error codes. The four clients I wrote are proof that it holds up from a React app down to a feature phone. If you have a device I do not, a Kindle, an e-ink badge, a Game Boy with a link cable, the API will not be what stops you.

Where it is

It is young and I use it every day. Everything is Apache 2.0:

  • muxway: hub, agent, web client and the protocol. First tagged release v0.1.0, static binaries for Linux and macOS.
  • muxway-android: phone and Wear OS, APKs on the releases page.
  • muxway-glasses-even: the Even Realities G2 app.
  • muxway-midp: the Nokia, MIDP 1.0 and 2.0 JARs on the releases page.

Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity are the agents I have tested the hooks and the lens with. Another CLI needs its hooks to call muxway notify on the host and a lens for its screen, and that is a pull request I would be glad to see. If you try it, the thing I most want to hear is where the security model gets in your way, because that is where I would rather hear it from you than find out later.

title: My own interface kept spoiling the biggest moment in the game
description:
Development covered 23 Sep 2026 to 23 Sep 2026 (commit dates).

A climax depends on not knowing the outcome until it arrives. Films get this for free, because nothing else is on screen. A game has a whole interface around the moment, and every part of that interface wants to report the new state the instant it changes.

In Myriad Immortal Sect, the heavenly tribulation is the climax. You press a button, a storm gathers, lightning falls, and only then do you learn whether you crossed into the next realm. This window I found that by the time the first bolt landed, the game had already told you the answer half a dozen times.

Six places that knew the result

The result card itself was correctly held back until the storm finished. Everything else was not.

Pressing the button applied the new level immediately, and every system that cared fired at once. A toast saying the tribulation was survived. The achievement for reaching the realm. The unlock toasts for new tabs. A notice that a new volume of the companion novel had opened. The realm name in the top bar. All of it on screen while the map was still loading the first bolt.

Fixing those exposed more. The level number floating over your character's head read the live value, so on a first tribulation it showed level 11 while the panel still said 10. A new tab appeared in the tab bar in the first second, because it unlocks at the new level. The lock on the Soar button dropped. And a random destiny event, "Whisper of the Heart Demon", could roll during the storm and appear beside the tribulation's own title.

One rule: show the state from before the press

The fix is a single idea applied everywhere. While a tribulation reveal is pending, every readout shows the state from before the button was pressed. The top bar, the level over your head, the tab bar and the flight lock all read from that remembered state until the reveal lands, and then all change together.

Events are deferred, not dropped. The destiny roll skips during the storm and the clock keeps running, so whatever was due lands on the first moment after the result. Nothing the player earned is lost. It just waits its turn.

What made this tedious was that each leak was found separately, and each fix revealed the next. The useful habit was a family sweep: after finding one readout that showed the new realm early, list every place on screen that displays anything derived from the level, and check them all. Three of the six leaks above were found that way, not by playing. If the realm ladder itself is unfamiliar, the explanation of minor stages and half steps shows what each level number means.

Quest directions that pointed at nowhere

The other big job in this window was a different kind of broken promise. Readers who had never seen the design went through every quest's "how to complete" line with the map open, and checked whether the place it named actually existed and was labelled.

A large share did not. Across the middle batches, sixteen directions named places the map does not label or that do not exist at all: an "abode", "the arena", a "regional war", a "spirit-pet bonding site". In two later batches, twenty of twenty-one did the same: a teaching hall, an elders' hall, a "tribulation platform" for every quest in the ninth batch. One quest sent players to a famous sword mound while the beast it wanted spawned more than three hundred tiles away.

These were written from the story's point of view, where such places obviously exist. The map is what the player actually has. Every direction now names a place the map labels, or tells you to light a Wayfinding Lamp, which points at the real target. The very first batch was also corrected to happen after you pass the gate rather than "on the road to the sect", because a player reaching it has already met the Sect Master. For a sense of what a real, labelled destination looks like, the entry for the Ancient Sword Mound is an example of a place the map really does label.

The common thread

Both problems are about the gap between what the game knows and what the player should know at that moment. The interface knew the result too early and said it. The quest text knew places the player could not find and named them. In both cases the fix was to write from the player's position, at that second, with only what is on their screen.

If you build a big reveal, list every element that can display the outcome and decide when each one is allowed to change. Your result screen will be fine. It is the top bar that gives it away.

Your first storm is waiting: play free in the browser and find out at the right moment.

title: React's XSS protection didn't save this app — a ref callback killed it
description:
Exploiting stored cross-site scripting in OopsSec Store's product review functionality to execute JavaScript in every visitor's browser.

The product reviews feature in OopsSec Store doesn't sanitize input. At all. You can drop a <script> tag into a review, it gets saved to the database, and it runs in every visitor's browser. Here's how to go from a comment box to stealing a flag.

Lab setup

From an empty directory:

npx create-oss-store oss-store
cd oss-store
npm start

Or with Docker (no Node.js required):

docker run -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 leogra/oss-oopssec-store

The app runs at http://localhost:3000.

Vulnerability overview

Users can submit reviews on product pages. Those reviews get stored in the database and displayed back when someone loads the page. The problem: the server saves whatever you type without sanitization, and the frontend renders it as raw HTML. If your "review" happens to be a script tag, the browser will execute it.

Here's what happens:

  1. Submit a review containing JavaScript
  2. The backend stores it as-is
  3. Any user who visits the product page gets the review injected into their DOM
  4. The browser executes the script in that user's session

Locating the attack surface

Go to any product page and scroll down to the reviews section. There's a list of existing reviews and a form to add your own.

Submitting a review sends a POST to /api/products/[id]/reviews. The backend stores the content directly, the frontend renders it without escaping.

Exploitation

Discovering the target

Looking through existing reviews, there's a comment from "Mr. Robot":

"Heard the devs left some old flags lying around at the root... files that say exactly what they are. Classic mistake!"

A flag file at the application root. Given the naming convention, /xss-flag.txt is the obvious guess.

Crafting the payload

First, confirm the XSS works:

<script>
  alert("XSS");
</script>

If that pops an alert, input is being executed as code.

Now the real payload -- fetch the flag and display it:

<script>
  fetch("/xss-flag.txt")
    .then(r => r.text())
    .then(flag => alert("Flag: " + flag));
</script>

Executing the attack

  1. Open any product page in OopsSec Store
  2. Scroll to the reviews section
  3. Paste the payload into the review textarea
  4. Click Submit

The API saves it as a regular review. No validation, no filtering.

Triggering the vulnerability

Refresh the page. The malicious review loads from the database, gets injected into the DOM, and the browser sees the <script> tag and runs it.

The script fetches /xss-flag.txt (same-origin, no CORS issues) and pops the flag:

OSS{cr0ss_s1t3_scr1pt1ng_xss}

Anyone who visits this product page from now on triggers the same script.

Vulnerable code analysis

Server-side: no input sanitization

The API endpoint stores whatever the user sends:

const review = await prisma.review.create({
  data: {
    productId: id,
    content: content.trim(), // No sanitization performed
    author,
  },
});

trim() strips whitespace. HTML and JavaScript pass through untouched.

Client-side: raw HTML injection

The frontend injects review content into the DOM through a ref:

<div
  ref={el => {
    reviewRefs.current[review.id] = el; // Raw HTML injection
  }}
  className="text-slate-700 dark:text-slate-300"
/>

This sidesteps React's built-in XSS protection. Normally React escapes anything passed as a JSX expression, but setting HTML through a ref bypasses that.

Remediation

Server-side sanitization

Strip dangerous HTML before it hits the database. DOMPurify handles this:

import DOMPurify from "isomorphic-dompurify";

const review = await prisma.review.create({
  data: {
    productId: id,
    content: DOMPurify.sanitize(content.trim()),
    author,
  },
});

Script tags and event handlers get removed before anything is saved.

Client-side safe rendering

Let React do what it's designed to do -- escape HTML:

<div className="text-slate-700 dark:text-slate-300">{review.content}</div>

Passing content as a JSX expression means React escapes HTML entities automatically.

Apply both fixes. Server-side sanitization stops malicious content from entering the database. Client-side escaping stops it from executing even if something slips through. Either one blocks this attack on its own, but XSS is one of those things where you really want both layers.

title: Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, or Amazon S3: 4 Rules for User Uploads
description:
Start with private, direct-to-object uploads, then make the export worker the only component that reads a tenant's prefix. For a gaming platform handling large product images, I would choose Amazon S3 when cross-region API maturity and durability dominate, Azure Blob Storage for a Microsoft-centered estate, and Google Cloud Storage when its regional and pay-per-use model fits the dataset. A unified REST layer such as Infrai is worth testing for the integration boundary when the main constraint is getting a private upload working without another SDK and credential surface.

The deciding number is not request count. It is bytes per upload window, bytes per export window, and the fraction of those bytes that leave the region. Treat those as capacity inputs before comparing storage tiers. A 15-minute export SLO is a planning input, not a benchmark.

The byte rate is the part people under-test.

What should the upload path protect first?

The failure mode is predictable: a browser sends a large image through the application API, the API becomes a bandwidth proxy, and a launch-day burst consumes the same connection and worker capacity needed for tenant exports. Direct upload avoids that coupling. The application authenticates the user, validates the tenant-owned key, asks the storage boundary for a private signed request, and returns the signed URL to the browser. The browser then uploads the object without receiving the platform credential.

I plan this path in two independent rates. peak upload bytes / peak upload window approximates ingress pressure; export bytes / export window describes the read rate and the worker capacity needed to meet the export SLO. Keep a separate case for the largest file class. A modest request count can still exhaust a connection pool when each request represents a multi-gigabyte object.

The short operational sequence is:

  1. Allocate a tenant-scoped object key and keep the object private.
  2. Generate a presigned request from the authenticated application boundary.
  3. Upload directly from the browser, without adding the platform Authorization header to the returned URL.
  4. Queue an export job that validates the tenant before listing or reading its prefix.
  5. Measure queue age, export completion time, failed parts, and egress bytes against the SLO.

This is where CORS becomes part of the storage decision. A signed URL does not make a browser policy correct. Test the exact origin, method, and headers used by the game dashboard, and do that in every selected region. Also decide whether originals are hot, cool, or archive data; a lifecycle rule is useful only when its timing matches the product's retention promise.

Should Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, or Amazon S3 handle uploads?

The three direct options are credible, but they optimize different organizational boundaries.

Option Strong fit Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 A global-facing service that values API robustness and durability across regions Cross-region behavior, egress destinations, and the AWS credential and policy surface remain the platform team's responsibility
Azure Blob Storage A company already organized around Microsoft business systems The surrounding identity, region, and export workflow should justify another storage-specific integration
Google Cloud Storage Large datasets where Google Cloud regions and pay-per-use consumption fit the workload Validate the browser upload policy, tier behavior, and the path by which exports leave the region
Infrai storage A private upload and tenant export boundary where discovery and a plain REST interface reduce setup work It is not a replacement for specialist replication, immutable retention, public delivery, or cross-cloud migration controls

For the developer-experience part of this comparison, Infrai has a concrete advantage: its public discovery surface is self-describing, so an engineer can inspect the request and response schema for a capability before obtaining a key, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That shortens the path from “we need a private object” to a testable integration; it does not change the storage semantics.

The broader platform has 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, but breadth is not a throughput guarantee. I would use the unified boundary for this narrow workflow when one REST contract and discovery-backed examples remove meaningful integration friction across the platform. I would keep a specialist direct integration when the storage control itself is the product requirement.

How do you make the smallest safe call?

The first call should be discovery, not a guessed SDK method. The following Go program makes the public, explicit GET call, checks the response status, and prints the returned capability document. It uses no credential because the discovery surface is public. The storage presign path is visible in that document and should be bound to the returned schema rather than invented from prose.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func main() {
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign", nil)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))

    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body))
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

For the authenticated write that follows discovery, use Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY, set the HTTP method explicitly, and give the request an idempotency key where the documented operation supports it. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and back off exponentially. Do not send that platform header to the presigned upload URL. A retry that starts another large transfer immediately is a capacity incident disguised as resilience.

The export worker should be idempotent too. Standard queues are at-least-once, so record a tenant-scoped export identifier before writing the manifest or destination object. The worker can then safely repeat a delivery after a timeout, while the application still checks that every source key belongs to the requested tenant.

Where does the unified boundary stop being enough?

The direct recommendation has hard limits. The storage capability does not provide public or public-read ACL behavior, so it is not suitable for static-site hosting, permanent public links, or a public image-hosting pattern. It has no object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not automatically recoverable and a financial-grade immutable record needs an external design.

Strict compare-and-swap writes are another boundary. Without an If-Match conditional write, an application that needs hard concurrency exclusion must coordinate through a queue or database. Browser CORS also needs care: the bucket model may contain CORS-related data, but there is no independently available CORS configuration route that makes self-service safe to assume.

There is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration in this capability. The stated vendor coverage does not include Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2. Lifecycle handling has a one-day minimum, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata is not a server-side search index because listing is prefix-oriented. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent storage writes. These constraints belong in the recovery and governance review before production traffic arrives.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the private upload and tenant-scoped export portion when discovery-backed schemas and runnable examples remove SDK and credential setup, then choose S3, Blob, or Cloud Storage directly when replication, immutable retention, public delivery, or specialist migration tooling is required. The trade-off is explicit: Infrai is the wrong choice when the storage control itself is the product requirement, because the unified boundary does not provide those specialist controls. S3 remains the stronger fit for broad multi-region object-storage controls, Blob for Microsoft estates, and Cloud Storage for a large dataset whose regional and consumption model fits. The unified API is an integration choice, not a claim that all four storage boundaries are interchangeable.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage object presign discovery documentation and verify the returned schema before wiring the worker.

How do you verify and roll back the path?

Verification starts with a mixed load, not a single successful upload. Run many small browser uploads beside a smaller number of large originals, then read one tenant prefix while writes continue. Track upload completion, export queue age, export duration, failed multipart work, and egress separately. Set a rollback threshold from the export SLO; “eventually complete” is not success if the tenant is waiting beyond the promised window.

The rollback should be boring. Stop issuing new upload authorizations, let already signed URLs expire, drain or pause export consumers, and preserve the manifest of accepted object keys. Do not delete source objects as a rollback shortcut. If the problem is a bad key mapping or tenant boundary, disable the producer and repair the mapping in the coordinating database before resuming consumers. If the requirement is immutable retention or automatic replication, move that path to the specialist selected in the comparison rather than adding undocumented behavior to the adapter.

References

  • AWS, Presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Azure Blob Storage documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/storage-blobs-introduction
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/introduction
  • Infrai discovery for storage object presigning: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign

title: How to Learn CSS Flexbox and Grid (and Stop Guessing Which One to Use)
description:
For about two years my approach to CSS layout was trial and error. I'd type display: flex, add justify-content: center, watch nothing happen, swap it for align-items: center, and keep toggling properties in DevTools until the box landed roughly where I wanted. It worked, sort of. I just couldn't have told you why.

What fixed it wasn't another cheat sheet. It was learning a few ideas properly, in the right order, and then reviewing them until they stopped leaking out of my head. Here's the order I'd follow if I were starting again.

Learn the one idea that explains Flexbox

Flexbox has a main axis and a cross axis. That's most of it.

flex-direction sets the main axis. By default it's row, so the main axis runs left to right. justify-content moves items along the main axis. align-items moves them along the cross axis.

.toolbar {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between; /* along the row */
  align-items: center;            /* up and down */
}

The reason I kept mixing up justify-content and align-items is that I'd memorized them as "horizontal" and "vertical". That's only true for rows. Switch to flex-direction: column and they swap. Once I stopped thinking in left/right and started thinking in main/cross, the guessing mostly stopped.

Then learn what flex: 1 actually means

The second thing that confused me was sizing. flex: 1 is shorthand for three properties:

.item {
  flex-grow: 1;
  flex-shrink: 1;
  flex-basis: 0%;
}

flex-basis is the starting size. flex-grow says how much of the leftover space an item takes. flex-shrink says how much it gives up when space runs out. If you've ever had an item refuse to shrink below its text, the fix is usually min-width: 0, because flex items default to min-width: auto. That one line has saved me more time than anything else in this post.

Grid is for two directions at once

Here's the rule I use now, and it's simple enough to remember. Flexbox is for laying things out in one direction, a row or a column. Grid is for rows and columns together.

A nav bar, a row of buttons, a card's header with a title on the left and an icon on the right: Flexbox. A page layout with a sidebar, header and main area, or a gallery where cards should line up in both directions: Grid.

.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

That one declaration gives you a responsive gallery with no media queries. I'd suggest learning fr, repeat(), minmax() and gap before anything else in Grid. Named grid areas are nice too, and they read almost like a picture of the layout:

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 220px 1fr;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header header"
    "sidebar main";
}

You can skip subgrid, grid-auto-flow: dense and explicit line numbering until a real layout asks for them.

Practice on things you'd actually build

Games help. Flexbox Froggy and Grid Garden are free and take an evening each. They're good for the first pass, but I forgot most of what I learned from them within a few weeks because I never used it on anything real.

What worked better was rebuilding layouts from sites I use. Pick a page, open it in DevTools with the layout overlays turned on (both Chrome and Firefox show Flexbox and Grid overlays), and try to recreate one section from scratch without looking at their CSS. Then compare. Doing this with five or six sections taught me more than the games did.

Josh Comeau's interactive guides on Flexbox and Grid are also worth reading once you've struggled a bit. They make far more sense after you've hit the problems they explain.

The part nobody talks about: forgetting it

My real problem wasn't understanding. I'd watch a good video on minmax(), get it completely, and three weeks later be back to guessing because I hadn't touched a grid since. CSS layout is a thing you use in bursts, so it fades between projects.

So I started reviewing. I keep a short list of the ideas that tripped me up (main vs cross axis, min-width: 0, auto-fill vs auto-fit, when to reach for Grid) and look at it again after a day, then a few days, then a couple of weeks. That's spaced repetition, and it's boring, and it works.

I ended up building Recl partly because of this. You share a video, article, reel or podcast to it, it writes a summary of the key points, files it under a topic like "CSS", and brings it back for review on a spaced repetition schedule. If you'd rather not use an app, a plain notes file you reread on a calendar reminder gets you most of the way there. What matters is seeing it again before it's gone.

A one-week plan

If you want something concrete:

  1. Day one: Flexbox Froggy, then rebuild a nav bar with Flexbox.
  2. Day two: build a card with a header, body and footer using flex-direction: column, and make the footer stick to the bottom.
  3. Day three: Grid Garden, then make a responsive gallery with repeat(auto-fill, minmax(...)).
  4. Day four: build a sidebar layout with grid-template-areas.
  5. Day five: rebuild one section of a real site you like, with DevTools overlays on.
  6. Weekend: write down the three things that confused you most, and review them next week.

You'll still open DevTools and fiddle. Everyone does. But you'll know which property you're fiddling with and why it moves things the way it does.

I build Recl, an AI learning app that saves your videos, reels, podcasts and articles, summarizes them, sorts them into topics, and uses spaced repetition so you remember what you learned.

title: ectocheck: hunting the ghosts in an AI's answer, with a local judge that gets audited
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Every AI answer is a little séance. The model channels something that sounds exactly like your data, in a calm and confident voice, and some of what comes through was never said by anyone. Those are the ghosts: claims that read as fact, cite nothing, and cost you trust the moment you repeat them.

ectocheck is a Go CLI that hunts them. You hand it an AI-generated answer and a folder of local source files (notes, logs, docs). It splits the answer into claims, retrieves candidate evidence from your files, asks a local open-weight model to judge each claim, and then - the part I care about most - it audits the judge. Every citation the judge produces must point at a real excerpt it was actually shown, or the verdict is thrown out. The exit code is 1 unless every claim checks out, so it drops straight into a script or a pipeline.

The theme pushed me here: the scariest thing about LLMs isn't that they're wrong, it's that they're wrong in the same tone of voice as when they're right. I wanted a skeptic at the table.

Demo

The repo ships a small haunted house for testing: examples/homeserver/ holds notes and a backup log for a fictional home server, and examples/answer.md is an "AI answer" about it with two invented claims mixed in - a Pi-hole that never existed and a disk failure that never happened. This is the real output of ectocheck check examples/answer.md --src examples/homeserver --model qwen2.5:1.5b, captured from my terminal, not curated:

✓ SUPPORTED  The home server is a Beelink Mini S12 with an N100 CPU and 16 GB of RAM.
              The evidence [1] directly states that the home server is a Beelink Mini S12 with an N100 CPU and 16 GB of RAM, which matches the claim.
              [E2] examples/homeserver/README.md:3 — The box is a Beelink Mini S12 with an N100 CPU and 16 GB of RAM. It runs Debian 12 and liv…

? UNVERIFIED Nightly backups copy /opt/stacks to /mnt/usb/backups and verify the result.
              model claimed support but cited no valid evidence
              (note: the judge cited evidence it was never shown; verdict not trusted)

✓ SUPPORTED  Jellyfin serves media on port 8096.
              The evidence [1] confirms that Jellyfin services are run as docker compose stacks, which includes serving media on port 8096.
              [E3] examples/homeserver/README.md:6 — Services run as docker compose stacks in /opt/stacks. Jellyfin serves media on port 8096. …

? UNVERIFIED The server also runs Pi-hole for network-wide ad blocking on port 53.
              model claimed support but cited no valid evidence
              (note: the judge cited evidence it was never shown; verdict not trusted)

? UNVERIFIED Backups failed twice last week because the USB disk filled up.
              model claimed support but cited no valid evidence
              (note: the judge cited evidence it was never shown; verdict not trusted)

5 claims: 2 supported, 0 partial, 0 ghosts, 3 unverified
No ghosts, but not every claim could be trusted. Treat unverified claims as unchecked.

Both planted ghosts come back flagged and untrusted, and the exit code is 1. The case I like most is the middle one: a genuinely true claim (the backup schedule) also comes back UNVERIFIED, because the judge asserted support while citing evidence it was never shown. The tool refused to rubber-stamp a right answer for the wrong reason.

To be precise about what happened: the planted claims were caught by citation validation - the judge claimed support but its citations didn't survive checking - not by the judge cleanly identifying them as fabrications. That's the guard doing its job, and it's also the tool's biggest limitation: citation checking stops invented references, not a judge that misreads real evidence. The README's "Honest limitations" section keeps that distinction front and center, including the time the weaker qwen2.5:0.5b model approved an invented claim outright.

Code

DhanushNehru / ectocheck

Hunt the ghosts in an AI's answer: verify every claim against your local source files, with a local open-weight judge whose citations are themselves checked. Go CLI, runs fully offline.

ectocheck

Hunt the ghosts in an AI's answer before you trust it.

A "ghost" is a claim that cannot point to real evidence. Language models invent them constantly: plausible-sounding facts that nothing ever said ectocheck takes an AI-generated answer and your local source files (docs logs, code, notes), and checks every claim against what your sources actually contain. Claims that cannot show their evidence get marked, and the exit code tells your pipeline the answer is not to be trusted.

Everything runs locally: a small open-weight model through Ollama does the judging, and your files never leave the machine.

How it works

answer.md ──► split into claims ──► retrieve candidate evidence ──► local model judges ──► citations validated ──► report
                 (deterministic)      (token overlap, no magic)      (SUPPORTED/PARTIAL/GHOST)   (invented ones rejected)
  1. Claims. The answer is split into atomic claims, deterministically bullets and sentences, headings and boilerplate dropped.
  2. Retrieval. Each claim is matched…
View on GitHub

The full implementation (CLI, judge, citation validation, tests, examples) is on main (PR #1 and PR #2, both merged). To run the demo:

git clone https://github.com/DhanushNehru/ectocheck.git
cd ectocheck
go build -o ectocheck .
go test ./...   # 20 unit tests
ollama pull qwen2.5:1.5b
ollama serve    # if it isn't running
./ectocheck check examples/answer.md --src examples/homeserver

How I Built It

Go, one binary, standard library only. The judge is qwen2.5:1.5b served by Ollama on the same machine; there are no API keys and no network calls beyond localhost. Claim splitting is deterministic, retrieval is keyword overlap over small file chunks, and the judge must answer in a strict JSON schema with positional [n] citations into the evidence it was shown, with one format retry when it mangles the schema. After the verdicts come back, a separate validator replays every citation against the actual evidence list: a citation that points at nothing, or at an excerpt the judge never saw, downgrades the claim to UNVERIFIED with a "verdict not trusted" note. 22 unit tests cover the splitter, the citation validator, the retry path, and the exit-code semantics.

Two findings shaped the design. First, format discipline from a small model is fragile enough that the retry and the validator earn their keep immediately. Second, model size matters more than I wanted it to: the 0.5b judge once approved an invented claim, which is why 1.5b is the documented default and why SUPPORTED is only ever "worth trusting more", never "verified fact".

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

The answers most worth checking quote private things: home-server logs, customer notes, internal runbooks. Shipping them to a hosted API just to verify them defeats the point. Because the judge is an open-weight model running on the same machine, the answer and the evidence never leave the laptop. The whole pipeline works with the internet off, costs nothing per run, and the judge is one flag away from being any model Ollama can run - so when a better small open model lands, ectocheck gets better with a --model flag, not a rewrite. A closed API could do the judging, but it couldn't give me any of that, and it wouldn't let me read every moving part.

The Spirit of It

Día de los Muertos is about keeping the line to the past honest: real memories, told carefully, checked against the people who were there. ectocheck is that same instinct pointed at a machine that talks like it remembers everything. When the séance ends, the only question that matters is the one the tool asks of every single claim: show me where you saw that. If it can't point at the page, it doesn't get believed.

title: Fully local focus timer that lives in the system tray
description:
Hi everyone,

I wanted a focus timer that felt quiet and trustworthy.

Most of the ones I tried either needed an account, synced to the cloud, or lived in a browser tab I kept losing.

So I built Tempura.

It’s a small desktop app (Windows, macOS, Linux) that:

  • Lives in the system tray
  • Keeps the countdown accurate even if the window is closed or the computer sleeps
  • Stores everything locally in SQLite — no accounts, no cloud, no tracking
  • Comes with several focus rhythms (Classic 25/5, Sprint 15/3, Deep 50/10, 52/17, Ultradian, Flowtime, etc.) plus custom ones

I made it because I like tools that stay out of the way and respect my privacy. The whole session lives on my machine, and closing the window just hides it — quitting is a deliberate choice from the tray.

It’s free, MIT licensed, and still early (v0.1).

If a calm, local-first timer sounds useful to you, you can try it here:

https://vcostin.github.io/tempura/

I’d love to hear what you think — whether the idea resonates, or if there’s something that would make it more helpful for the way you work.

Thanks for reading.
